Not enough games center around killing Nazi Space scientists anymore, most games nowadays are unfortunately about demonising the Russians, which is just no fun.
And then comes The New Order, a fast paced, Nazi-murdering first person shoot-em-up, with a surprising amount of character in it.
The story, while not much to really write home about, does add some character to the protagonist BJ, making the relationships he forges with the other characters much more believable.
Anyway, the gameplay is the best thing about the game. As mentioned before, the game dumps you into a level with nothing but you and a ♥♥♥♥ton of Nazis between you and your objective. The levels have multiple routes, allowing you to stealth your way around if that's your thing. But sometimes, you just wanna kick the door down and wreak havoc, and the game gladly allows you to indulge in that playstyle. Each level grows in ludicracy to the point where the game takes you to the mother♥♥♥♥ing moon and back (literally), gradually building up to the final boss which will kick your♥♥♥♥♥many a time if you haven't played a game with an intense boss at the end for a while.
Now, no game is perfect, and The New Order certainly has it's flaws. For instance, the interludes between some missions in the Resistance HQ, while rich with lore and backstory concerning the world BJ lives in, notably slow the pace of the game and can be rather tedious after a particularly enjoyable mission. However, a semi-positive to this is, that these can be used as quitting points in the game if you don't want to lose track of what's happening in your mission.
Other than that, Wolfenstein: The New Order is one of the better FPS games of recent years and a breath of fresh air in the sea of modern warfare game that flood the market nowadays and earns a solid 9/10 from me. I sincerely hope anyone buying the game has as much fun as I did with it.

Max Payne 3 is without doubt one of the best games with cinematic aspects in it. From the Bullet Time jumps to the 360 degrees shooting, this game does it all right. Sure, there are many cut scenes in it, but in return you get 0 loading screens while still hearing a lot of cynical talk from Max in the cut scenes. The only time you need to load into the game is when you are going to the menu or when you are going into the story. Even in 2015, this is still a very unique feature as there are very little games that manage to get rid of loading screens.
Another thing that Rockstar did right with this game is Quick Time Events. Usually QtE's consist of a combination of buttons you need to push in order to complete it, but in Max Payne 3 you get shoot-outs in Bullet Time. If you fail these, you die.. simple as that. Thanks to the addition of Bullet Time in these shoot-outs, it feels really satisfying to do them.
In fact, Bullet Time itself deserves a spot in this short review as well. When I saw gameplay footage of this game before release, I was pretty sceptical about the new Bullet Time they implemented into the game. This was mostly because you were no longer able to move at normal speed while the rest moved a lot slower. However, as I started to play the game myself, I noticed that this was actually a good thing and added to the satisfaction of dodging bullets Matrix-style while making 5 headshots in 1 jump. Bullet Time is what gave Max Payne such an iconic gameplay in the first place and with the new Bullet Time they added in Max Payne 3, the gameplay feels even more satisfying than in the first two games.
This game element is one of the downsides of Max Payne 3. When you dive into the multiplayer aspect of this game, you will immediately notice that the game feels different: The HUD has a different design, there is not as much optimization and Bullet Time seems far less effective than in the Singleplayer game. Of course the gameplay should feel different, but in this case it feels like the group that made the multiplayer developed it completely on its own without any input from the singleplayer devs, resulting in a gameplay that users like a lot less than the Singleplayer gameplay. That's too bad, because this caused the Multiplayer to die within a few weeks after release.
The fact that I mentioned the port in the intro means something: This port is done extremely well! Seriously, if there was a price for best PC ports, this game would definitely win it. I run this game on a pretty low end laptop and I still manage to have a decent framerate while not being annoyed by very ugly graphics because of the low quality I play on.
Ah yes, the graphics.. I think that it is fair that the devs didn't call their low quality 'low' but 'normal'. Graphics are pretty darn good for a game released in 2012. The amount of detail put into this is amazing and definitely makes it more satisfying to explore Sao Paulo for clues, pain killers and weapons.
Max Payne is in my opinion one of the best games that came out in 2012, if not the best. The Singleplayer is done really well and things like the new Bullet Time make the experience even better than ever before. Multiplayer feels like it's a different game and I get the idea that Rockstar did not put much effort into it. Luckily, the great singleplayer, the perfect optimization for a PC port and very beautiful graphics make that multiplayer aspect seem like a very minor issue.
After almost three years, this game is still an example of proper porting, storytelling and gameplay and there are very few games that manage to set a standard for that long these days.
Since multiplayer is a bit of a bummer, I simply give this game a 10/10, but what it does deserve is a big fat

She was spared, tried to capture her and the story would've continued If i did. I tend to think she might attack again, wonder what her mother did to annoy her so much... and how were they seperated! A solid B-list action movie in video game form. I say this to its credit. The game is pretty entertaining throughout. It expertly manages to be serious enough to be engaging, but without taking itself TOO seriously. The gameplay is fast-paced and unrealistic, but the game is more engaging for it, because it never feels like it's wasting the player's time. The gameplay facilitates multiple playstyles, which is to say it allows the player to run-and-gun or take a more stealthy approach (to an extent, at least. Deus Ex this is not). The game has a decidedly simple premise (it's an alternate history where the Nazis won, so you have to take down the Nazis) so there's little dissonance between the game's narrative and its mechanics, which is refreshing. Wolfenstein doesn't really break any new ground, but it doesn't need to. It's not flawless, but it's a solid game and worth checking out if you find the game to be affordable.

It may look like Prison Architect and draw inspiration from Dwarf Fortress but Rimworld provides a unique 'colony simulator' experience all its own.

It's doesn't have Dwarf Fortress levels of detail (not necessarily a bad thing) but I think it will appeal to a broader range of players than DF thanks to the clean and clear visuals and more streamlined (but not simplistic) control you have over the world.
If you enjoy colony / base building games, I can almost guarantee you will get some satisfaction out of this game.  Like any game it's not perfect, but even as an 'alpha' game (it's better than most beta games) it is worth your time.
If you haven't played many/any games in this genre it might be a good place to start thanks to the clean visuals and clear feedback on your actions.  Just be aware that as with so many compex games these days, the tutorial is pretty crap (or does not exist).  You will need learn the game yourself by watching youtube plays, reading the wiki and the Rimworld/Steam forums.

"Alrighty, I'll play just for a little bit," I thought to myself. Actually, this is usually what I tell myself every time I start Planetside 2.. but it's never for just "a little bit." The battles can feel so real, they can become so epic that really capture your attention. You can be sitting in a base taking out an enemy or two who's trying to take it over and then realize that just over the horizon legions of tanks and enemy soldiers are rushing towards you. (Like a nerd this is the moment I turn on my battle music playlist on Spotify.) There are no NPC's. Just other players. What happens in this game is up to you. Guides are available for you on YouTube should you need the extra help. There are also great outfits (guilds) in the game that are willing to teach. On a personal note, one of the aspects of this game that draws me in so much are the environments/continents. Granted most of my time is spent fighting, but there are moments when I love to go exploring with a flash! I play VS on Emerald.

My squad was pushing up to take the farm compound. The squad leader orders me to stay back and support them with my scoped sniper rifle. While I am watching the roofs I hear a shot behind me. I immediately drop to prone and check the map. Nothing is showing up where I am, and that can only mean enemies. Thankfully I had positioned myself in a waist high poppy field so there is no way they can see me. The thing is though I can see them through the stalks of the flowers running by me. They also must have shot at someone else because they have no clue I am there. What the enemy squad thought was a great flanking route to take on my squad has now turned into their worst nightmare. As they approached me  I radio in my position to the squad leader and let him know of the situation. He cannot spare anyone to come back and aid me, so now it is up to me to keep them occupied. They run past and with their backs to me I get in the kneeled position and shoot two of them dead. I get prone and slink off to their right while they toss grenades into the field. I take no damage. They knew the shots were close but they do not know where I went. Their medic tries to go and revive one of the soldiers and I shoot him dead. They were a smaller squad of seven so I had just killed their only medic. Now I have effectively stalled their attack because there are only four of them left with no way to revive. They toss another grenade and miss again. I'm wishing now that I could hear their radio chatter because I am sure they freaking out trying to locate me. I slowly snaked up to the wall of the field and looked on the other side. I see two more and I take them out, but I get hit in the process and I go down. Moments later the last two are killed as my squad had taken the compound and had returned to aid me. Our medic revives me and I recieve verbal praise from my squad as we go back to occupy the control point.

It is a mix between a normal fps shooter, Battlefield for example, and Arma. It is probably the best fps on Steam right now and is only in Alpha. It is still a work in progress, but if they released it now it would still be better than 80% of other games on the market. Most players have microphones(recommend getting one for this game), and squads cooperate together to capture objectives. This game is a blast, and I get more immersed in it than I ever did in Arma. There is something about hearing your squad leader radio in "spread out" as an RPG explodes on the wall infront of you, sending shrapnel everywhere. Then a second of quietness and then the yells for a medic come over the radio. This game is a must have for anyone who enjoys fps games, working in teams, and military style gameplay.
P.S. Get a mic if you buy this game.

Max Payne 3 is without doubt one of the best games with cinematic aspects in it. From the Bullet Time jumps to the 360 degrees shooting, this game does it all right. Sure, there are many cut scenes in it, but in return you get 0 loading screens while still hearing a lot of cynical talk from Max in the cut scenes. The only time you need to load into the game is when you are going to the menu or when you are going into the story. Even in 2015, this is still a very unique feature as there are very little games that manage to get rid of loading screens.
Another thing that Rockstar did right with this game is Quick Time Events. Usually QtE's consist of a combination of buttons you need to push in order to complete it, but in Max Payne 3 you get shoot-outs in Bullet Time. If you fail these, you die.. simple as that. Thanks to the addition of Bullet Time in these shoot-outs, it feels really satisfying to do them.
In fact, Bullet Time itself deserves a spot in this short review as well. When I saw gameplay footage of this game before release, I was pretty sceptical about the new Bullet Time they implemented into the game. This was mostly because you were no longer able to move at normal speed while the rest moved a lot slower. However, as I started to play the game myself, I noticed that this was actually a good thing and added to the satisfaction of dodging bullets Matrix-style while making 5 headshots in 1 jump. Bullet Time is what gave Max Payne such an iconic gameplay in the first place and with the new Bullet Time they added in Max Payne 3, the gameplay feels even more satisfying than in the first two games.
This game element is one of the downsides of Max Payne 3. When you dive into the multiplayer aspect of this game, you will immediately notice that the game feels different: The HUD has a different design, there is not as much optimization and Bullet Time seems far less effective than in the Singleplayer game. Of course the gameplay should feel different, but in this case it feels like the group that made the multiplayer developed it completely on its own without any input from the singleplayer devs, resulting in a gameplay that users like a lot less than the Singleplayer gameplay. That's too bad, because this caused the Multiplayer to die within a few weeks after release.
The fact that I mentioned the port in the intro means something: This port is done extremely well! Seriously, if there was a price for best PC ports, this game would definitely win it. I run this game on a pretty low end laptop and I still manage to have a decent framerate while not being annoyed by very ugly graphics because of the low quality I play on.
Ah yes, the graphics.. I think that it is fair that the devs didn't call their low quality 'low' but 'normal'. Graphics are pretty darn good for a game released in 2012. The amount of detail put into this is amazing and definitely makes it more satisfying to explore Sao Paulo for clues, pain killers and weapons.
Max Payne is in my opinion one of the best games that came out in 2012, if not the best. The Singleplayer is done really well and things like the new Bullet Time make the experience even better than ever before. Multiplayer feels like it's a different game and I get the idea that Rockstar did not put much effort into it. Luckily, the great singleplayer, the perfect optimization for a PC port and very beautiful graphics make that multiplayer aspect seem like a very minor issue.
After almost three years, this game is still an example of proper porting, storytelling and gameplay and there are very few games that manage to set a standard for that long these days.
Since multiplayer is a bit of a bummer, I simply give this game a 10/10, but what it does deserve is a big fat

Bought it for US$2.
Ab-so-lute-ly fantastic.
But let's address the reason you're here first, and bust the bubble. There's no cake. Nor anything that resembles cake. There aren't even any drawings of it (unless there's an Easter Egg?) All sugary consumables are gone, except maybe you yourself. But that doesn't mean that the game is bitter or tasteless.
I mean, you get everything you have in Portal, and more. There's even a certain theme in the story that I never imagined there to be, because I didn't even know there would be a new character. But
it's simply fantastic. Speaking of friends, you get to reunite with a certain someone, and I'm sure they're delighted to be with you again despite once being burned out by your antics.
Sometimes hilarious, sometimes scary, you get to feel a lot of emotions when you play the game. You also get to see a lot more of Aperture Science and learn about its history, at least two new game mechanics, and GLaDOS herself.
As always, you never need to completely restart the level to complete the puzzle, which is something I loved about the original Portal. The visual, music and sound effects are great, as expected.
Unfortunately, I never played the co-op of the game, so I cannot comment on that. Though from the speedrunning at SGDQ it also looks fantastic, and GLaDOS trash-talks as usual. Hope to play it myself though, someday, maybe with Companion Cube.

Wolfenstein: The New Order represents a triumph in single-player FPSs, and has all the necessary elements I desire in a videogame: intense combat, large, loud and powerful weapons, likable characters, engaging plot and above all, a sense of being the one unforseen variable in the bad guy's plan, however powerful, however intelligent. This incarnation sees you as that monkey wrench in the strict order of the most terrifying government imaginable: a world where the Nazis won World War 2, leaving them free to impose their irredeemably twisted ideology on everybody. But they and their sinster General "Deathshead" made the most fatal error of all: Believing one B.J. Blaskowicz down and out. As the genre's original badass, you will wreak holy havoc with an arsenal of dual-wieldable weaponry, with the strength of numerical health and armor pickups at your side. The way you fight will earn you perks from Stealth, Tactical, Assault and Demolitions trees, and all throughout the levels are collectables, some for collecting's sake, and others that upgrade your maximum health or armor or give insights into the world and its characters. Any level can be replayed to scrounge for items you may have missed, and any unlocked upgrades are retained unless you start a fresh playthrough. The game's setpieces and musical accompaniment are also excellent, and the implemenation of modern shooter features is very subdued: You can use ironsights, use cover and lean around corners if you want, but it is completely optional, as is attempting to sneak through levels and use throwing knives and backstabs. Several of the weapons have useful alternate fire modes and one weapon in particular, the Laserkraftwerk, recieves several upgrades over the course of the game and goes from a novelty to a powerful heavy weapon. You also regenerate only a trace amount of health, forcing you to conserve it and search out healthpacks as you would in the typical 90s FPS. The explosive action is accompanied by a suprisingly lucid inner monologue from our hero, coupled with brief but powerful moments of quiet interaction with his friends, raising this Wolfenstein from a simple fragfest into a category occupied more often by films then games. The campaign is riddled from beginning to end with surprising twists and a number of moments that made me smile, tear up or throw my arm in front of my face in disgust. The New Order is a true cinematic experience and embodies what I love best in the genre. I intend to revisit at a later date.

The higher you level up, the more skill you will learn as you travel the lands. The most prominent thing in this game is lacked horribly; lore. Now if you want to learn more about the factions, and the lore just go to the wiki for it. There is no ingame lore currently. Now there are specifics to each faction.
-3 different factions enter through a wormhole, and it closes after the terraforming Auraxis. One is a company who is helping humanity rebuild after a costly war; This is the New conglomerate. They essentially fight due to being oppressed by the Terran Republic. They want freedom, but at the same time are the equivalent to terrorists. They want freedom, but are fueled by corporations as a private military force. The other is humanity's military; the Terran republic. Some say they closed the wormhole to prevent the knowledge of rebirth technology from ever making it back to earth which would be an end to their authoritarian regime. They are essentially the equivalent to communists, and as such is a bad thing if you have ever read a history book. The third faction is the Vanu. They are the scientists who came to auraxis to study the technology there. They essentially are technophiles who believe in evolving humanity even by force. They are the equivalent of a crazy religion.

Review from a guy who played the first game through maybe 10 times(the demo another 10 times) and the second "only" 4 times.
This is what games for adults should be. This is not a game for kids or teenagers. I'm not referring to the visual violence in this game, it's pretty similar to other games that have shooting as their main way of forwarding the story. The themes of this game and the plot around it is a lot darker than most games have and although it's not very complicated to understand.  It is necessary that who ever plays this game understands that this is not far away from reality, if at all. I'm not implicating that the city mentioned in the game is as bad as it shows here but world has places like this and games should be less afraid to use them as a way of telling stories without using overdone stereotypes.
Brazil as a setting is beautifully implemented and the fact that they used Portugese without translation in many places made the setting feel more immersive. Although the game itself stays pretty much MaxPaynish, this time it doesn't feel so unreal(e.g. loads of MIB's). Sure there is a lot to shoot at, but it's most of the time paced so well that it stays immersive. Almost all of the levels in this game feel necessary and fits into the story. This makes the game feel like a whole instead of sum of its parts. It feels that the story existed before the levels did, unlike so many other games these days.
Sounds are nice and the gameplay works even better than I expected. This is not an easy game either, and I decided to play it with the easiest setting to keep it moving forward. Even so I had to try some parts multiple times. Top of all that, the game works amazingly well on my old rig(E8500, HD4890, 4gb), and loading times were so good that I kept it on HDD instead of SSD.
Whoever wants to feel what games could really be if they would take themselves seriously, this is one of those cases. There's little forced humour and wacky situations in this game and the atmosphere stays the same from start to finish. Also I feel that 3rd iteration of Max Payne could be one of the best characters that I've played in ages. His choices and actions seem reasonable and sensible(not to me of course but to the character living them).
Wholeheartedly recommended.

Review from a guy who played the first game through maybe 10 times(the demo another 10 times) and the second "only" 4 times.
This is what games for adults should be. This is not a game for kids or teenagers. I'm not referring to the visual violence in this game, it's pretty similar to other games that have shooting as their main way of forwarding the story. The themes of this game and the plot around it is a lot darker than most games have and although it's not very complicated to understand.  It is necessary that who ever plays this game understands that this is not far away from reality, if at all. I'm not implicating that the city mentioned in the game is as bad as it shows here but world has places like this and games should be less afraid to use them as a way of telling stories without using overdone stereotypes.
Brazil as a setting is beautifully implemented and the fact that they used Portugese without translation in many places made the setting feel more immersive. Although the game itself stays pretty much MaxPaynish, this time it doesn't feel so unreal(e.g. loads of MIB's). Sure there is a lot to shoot at, but it's most of the time paced so well that it stays immersive. Almost all of the levels in this game feel necessary and fits into the story. This makes the game feel like a whole instead of sum of its parts. It feels that the story existed before the levels did, unlike so many other games these days.
Sounds are nice and the gameplay works even better than I expected. This is not an easy game either, and I decided to play it with the easiest setting to keep it moving forward. Even so I had to try some parts multiple times. Top of all that, the game works amazingly well on my old rig(E8500, HD4890, 4gb), and loading times were so good that I kept it on HDD instead of SSD.
Whoever wants to feel what games could really be if they would take themselves seriously, this is one of those cases. There's little forced humour and wacky situations in this game and the atmosphere stays the same from start to finish. Also I feel that 3rd iteration of Max Payne could be one of the best characters that I've played in ages. His choices and actions seem reasonable and sensible(not to me of course but to the character living them).
Wholeheartedly recommended.

Wolfenstein: The New Order represents a triumph in single-player FPSs, and has all the necessary elements I desire in a videogame: intense combat, large, loud and powerful weapons, likable characters, engaging plot and above all, a sense of being the one unforseen variable in the bad guy's plan, however powerful, however intelligent. This incarnation sees you as that monkey wrench in the strict order of the most terrifying government imaginable: a world where the Nazis won World War 2, leaving them free to impose their irredeemably twisted ideology on everybody. But they and their sinster General "Deathshead" made the most fatal error of all: Believing one B.J. Blaskowicz down and out. As the genre's original badass, you will wreak holy havoc with an arsenal of dual-wieldable weaponry, with the strength of numerical health and armor pickups at your side. The way you fight will earn you perks from Stealth, Tactical, Assault and Demolitions trees, and all throughout the levels are collectables, some for collecting's sake, and others that upgrade your maximum health or armor or give insights into the world and its characters. Any level can be replayed to scrounge for items you may have missed, and any unlocked upgrades are retained unless you start a fresh playthrough. The game's setpieces and musical accompaniment are also excellent, and the implemenation of modern shooter features is very subdued: You can use ironsights, use cover and lean around corners if you want, but it is completely optional, as is attempting to sneak through levels and use throwing knives and backstabs. Several of the weapons have useful alternate fire modes and one weapon in particular, the Laserkraftwerk, recieves several upgrades over the course of the game and goes from a novelty to a powerful heavy weapon. You also regenerate only a trace amount of health, forcing you to conserve it and search out healthpacks as you would in the typical 90s FPS. The explosive action is accompanied by a suprisingly lucid inner monologue from our hero, coupled with brief but powerful moments of quiet interaction with his friends, raising this Wolfenstein from a simple fragfest into a category occupied more often by films then games. The campaign is riddled from beginning to end with surprising twists and a number of moments that made me smile, tear up or throw my arm in front of my face in disgust. The New Order is a true cinematic experience and embodies what I love best in the genre. I intend to revisit at a later date.

And the leap into the 60's served the Wolfenstein's series supernatural theme well, by making it more scientific, albeit outside the norms of reality.
However, the id Tech 5 is not the best engine I've come across, and while bugs aren't many the overall stability and compatibility of the engine is a problem. I'm running a SLI configuration and sadly id Tech 5, which is supposed to be a modern engine, does not support SLI. Whether it supports Crossfire or not I do not know, but this has nonetheless left me rather annoyed. I was still able to achieve a solid framerate and good experience however.
Overall a great experience, both gameplay and storywise! However if you are running a dual GPU setup, I'd advise you to do some research before you buy the game.

Max Payne 3 is an excellent experience that blends together great third person shooter gameplay with a compelling narrative all backed up by Rockstars detailed world design. It is an absolute must buy on sale if you haven't played it already.
Max Payne is a retired NYPD Detective. It's been almost 10 years since the traumatic events of the first two games and Max is just about done with life. That is until all of a sudden Max is offered a job as a bodyguard for one of Sao Paulo's most prestigious families. An easy gig...
This review is written from the perspective of a fan of the previous Max Payne games as well as third-person shooters and story driven games in general.
On a purely functional level, Max Payne 3 is a very well designed third-person shooter. The robust animation system is extremely versatile and allows Max to aim towards all 360 degrees around him regardless of if he is stood up, down on the dirt or anything in between. This may not sound impressive, but you really have to appreciate that you can do this and the animation system and gunplay respond to your stance and direction accordingly. You can opt to play it as a Matrix-style action game, a cover based shooter or a bit of both. The game has amazing player feedback and ballistics tracking making every shot you fire and bullet you dodge feel really satisfying, especially when you pull of something like
. Accuracy is still a very important aspect of the gameplay and the player is certainly encouraged to go for those headshots. Max Payne's signature abilities to slow down time and "shootdodge", as Rockstar call it, also make an extremely welcome return from the previous games. However, something that doesn't return in Max Payne 3 from previous games is the weapon carrying system. Instead of being able to carry every weapon in the game in one leather jacket, the player is now limited to whatever is physically possible for Max to actually carry and fight with. It seems that Rockstar has done this to create more consistency between gameplay and cinematics for a smoother experience as Max will actually be carrying the weapons you're playing with during cutscenes. The guns themselves are all unique with varying stats that will suit different enemy types and situations. The health system is based on painkiller pickups like in previous games with no regenerating health mechanic. There are a lot of difficulty options available to suit both casual gamers and those after a punishing challenge.
The game is designed as a largely linear corridor third person shooter. As mentioned before, this iteration introduces a cover mechanic not present in previous titles, which can be nice for the more conservative player that likes to pick their shots. The game also likes to throw some scripted bullet-time sequences at you which encourage you to pick off as many enemies as possible for the duration of the event. It's sort of like a QTE, but with more control, see this
. The levels are designed carefully and fairly and if you die, it rarely feels "cheap". In addition, the AI enemies are smart and will take cover whilst also trying to destroy yours and flank you. You will fight against varying factions as the game progresses and their AI tactics and weapons reflect their backgrounds. You should also keep your eye out for hidden side paths, crevices and alcoves that may reward you with weapons, painkillers, clues (story based collectibles that give you little bits of info) and golden gun parts (which do pretty much as the name suggests).
The multiplayer community of this game is completely non-existent so if you want to have some slow mo action antics with your friends then you will need to organise it.
Where there is Max Payne, there is usually cynicism, misery, regret and self-pity all usually illustrated to you with nice gruff voice over by the amazing James McCaffrey. This title has done away with the graphic novel style of the previous two games and has gone for all out fully voiced and mo-capped cutscenes that make you question if you’re playing a game or watching a movie. However, whether or not this is good thing will depend on the kind of person you are. Some people have had some qualms with the way the story is presented in Max Payne 3. The first issue, is the fact that the game has this sort of blurry, colourful and sickness and/or epilepsy inducing filter that likes to pop up more than few times. The argument can be made that this filter on the cinematics and gameplay is an intentional storytelling device designed to reflect Max's condition in the context. However, despite the loss of the graphic novels, we have not lost Max's outlook on the world and just life in general. All the smarmy one liners and wise cracks, depressing thoughts, mind-wandering monologues and the general all round tone remains the same.
Another issue that people have had with the game is a quite big one for some people. So big, that I've had to start another paragraph. A lot of the time, in the middle of gameplay the game just relieves you of control to deliver you a cutscene. This may not seem like a big deal, but it does admittedly happen A LOT. The cutscenes themselves flow seamlessly with the game itself, with no loading, but they occur just a little bit too frequently for the liking of some people. Now if you’re going through the game for the first time and you want all that glorious story, chances are it won't bother you much. If you are a player that isn't really interested in the story and just wants to shoot guys then this will be a point of contention for you and your enjoyment of the game will depend on how tolerant you are of the cutscene interruptions.
Historically, Rockstar haven't really put much focus towards the quality of their PC versions, but Max Payne 3 certainly bucks the trend. For me (and many others from what I hear) the game ran a constant 60fps with most settings maxed and probably would have gone higher if my monitor allowed it to. This is on a 2GB GTX 770 with an i5 4670k with both at stock speed. The keys are all fully rebindable and I felt very comfortable playing this game with both a controller and M+KB. If this is what is in store for us PC gamers when GTAV finally comes around, then we will be in for a treat. Unfortunately the Rockstar Social Club DRM makes another return here, but I personally didn't have much trouble activating my game through it.
The game looks beautiful too. The environments are varied and the attention to detail here is just mind boggling. The physics on objects are also very immersive. The way that glass starts out getting riddled with individual bullet holes that develop into larger cracks which then develops into all out shattering and raining down (can be seen
) . The stressful feeling you get as your wooden cover slowly splinters and turns to shreds under heavy enemy fire are all results of Rockstars fantastic physics engine. Although fire and explosions are mostly part of scripted events in this game, they are still look excellent despite the lack of being able to influence them dynamically during gameplay. An example can be seen
. These are little things that you may not even notice, but that subliminal part of brain will notice these things and they all come together to make a thrilling experience.

I was, at first, a little apprehensive about a $30 early access title, but I recommend this game to anyone who might have any interest in a town/colony management game. It is pretty much finished and bug free, so this review stands even if they don't touch another thing in the game.
It gets compared to Dwarf Fortress often, and I think that's fairly accurate in a lot of ways. It's more like DF was back in the early days before the Z axis was added, minus much of the tunneling.
What makes this game worth your time and money is the strange situations and detail given to character's health and relationships leading to some neat stories and exciting moments. For example, my first colony was going fairly well, everyone got along for the most part except when the town's pet cat was butchered and cooked by (my) accident. Fistfights broke out, farming didn't get done, and there was a food shortage. I sent someone to hunt a doe but it was in a herd, and apparently alien deer are fiercely defensive; the entire herd pummeled the hunter to death and then ran through the main street in my settlement and beat everyone unconscious. Raiders then showed up and hauled off one of the women while the last two survivors wasted away in a coma outdoors. You can get all of this in DF for free of course, but not with this setting, presentation, or nice UI.
Losing is fun in DF, and it's also thankfully fun in RimWorld.

Don't believe the play hours; I've played this game since Alpha 9. This is an amazing colony-builder game where you control and try to survive with randomized colonists as various scenarios happen around you; this means that every playthrough is inherently different and you will evolve as a player as your colonies/tribes evolve. Despite the Early Access status of this game, it is by far and large a fully functioning game with relatively zero bugs. More content is being added by a very supportive development team, and now with this game being on Steam you have much more easy access to new updates and mod support if you wish.
The new scenario system added in this update (Alpha 14) is very interesting, and if you don't like the three vanilla scenarios, you can randomize them and/or find mods for them to make each playthrough even more unique. While the complexity of this game is far short of Dwarf Fortress, this game is still a gem for all players who enjoy the colony-building genre.

TL;DR Bottom
Rimworld... What can I tell you about Rimworld? This game has been under development for years and as such it's seen more than a few significant changes to the overall game. For those who have had bad experiences with early access games, I understand the hesitation. I've been there, I've got a handful of games that I wish I didn't get, Rimworld isn't one of those games. Tynan has worked so hard on this game, and listens to those who are supporting him.  I can say with out a doubt that this is hands down the BEST alpha game that I've spent money on.
Pros:
-- Replay Value; Not every playthrough has to be different, create your own scenario and watch how things unfold.
-- Permadeath mode option; For those who don't want to save scum. Bad♥♥♥♥♥♥happens. It sucks. Something so simple as a cougar could single handedly wipe out your entire tribe (sad experience that was.)
-- Art; it's beautiful for the style that it is!
-- Well optimized; This is a stab in the dark because I've got a high end gaming pc... But the game doesn't lag unless I'm playing on the huge map options, and even then it takes be hollowing out a few mountains and building a big base for it to start lagging.
--Active modding community; Constantly re-re-re-releasing their mods to keep up with the stage of the game. They have a wide selection that can really change how you will play the game!
Cons:
-- Randomness; You could literally be stuck in a 2 year toxic fallout and slowly lose all of the worth in your colony as they slowly start to become worthless and then food grows short until you all die... Not to a raid, not to explosions or illness. But a single map effect that lasted seemingly forever. (Personally I think it's a bit of a pro!)
-- Colony/tribe size;  If you play well you can end up with a tribe or colony too large, with no means to just tell them to leave. Killing them or selling them causes a colony wide mood debuff.
-- Addictive; Yes.. yes I know this seems like a pro as well. But when you spend 3 hours playing and expect it to have been only 30 minutes, that's a con!
I've been with this game for a long time, way before it was released on steam. I've seen the progression and I feel pretty confident in saying that I'll see it to completion.
Long story short; Do I recommend this game? Yes I'd give it a 8.5/10.

A really great game. Been with it since its early alpha stages. I remember staying up all night playing this game when I first heard about it, it's incredibly in depth. You will get attached to your colonists and they will die. Its constantly being updated and the modding community is incredible. You could easily stretch the vanila game to 1000 hours plus. Its easy to get the hang of, but difficult to master. If you're a fan of games like FTL, Duskers, any rpg or rts, this game brings the best of strategy and economy together in an incredibly personal tale of survival and the effect it has on people. All your colonists are by no means trained killers or carpenters, (though some might be) so there will be struggle and effects on their psyche, the mood and relationship system is really good, it gives personality to each pawn (colonist) in ways of permanent traits, and with how they react and talk to each other. conflict can come from your own people as if you slaughter a prisoner, they may become stressed and leave, fight with each other or break down. and I did say prisoners. Your colony doesn't have to be cold blooded murderers. There are many times where you can capture fallen enemies. Talk to them, convince them to join you, or harvest all of there organs and limbs. you can play it however you want. the combat system is pretty RNG, but is based off your colonists skill, with either shooting or melee combat. Individual limbs and organs are all modeled in the system so its very possible to lose an arm, have your leg blown off, get your fingers crushed. This of course doesnt always mean death. prosthetics and medicine can keep them alive, though dont expect "one arm Jim" to be a good crafter. Same goes for little Tessa's running career. damn tortoises. Theres a very in depth growing and hunting system too. food is your number one priority and is not always easy to get. in winter crops will not grow, and theres many biomes to choose from. Ice sheets are difficult, you need heat and greenhouses to survive. Rainforests provide lots of wood and cool temperature, but lots of man hunting animals and infections are there. deserts are blistering hot, but you'll never need to build greenhouses. Over all its a very varied and complex game, I havent even begun to scratch the surface. I Highly recommend this game for anyone who likes resource managment and rts games. seriously get this game.

A great run-and-gun FPS which nowadays are more rare than you'd like. With a surprisingly solid storyline and great soundtrack it delivers on more levels than I first expected it too. It's an overall refreshing take on the World War II/Nazi-Germany genre that has been done so many times, this time it actually felt fresh and new. And the leap into the 60's served the Wolfenstein's series supernatural theme well, by making it more scientific, albeit outside the norms of reality.
However, the id Tech 5 is not the best engine I've come across, and while bugs aren't many the overall stability and compatibility of the engine is a problem. I'm running a SLI configuration and sadly id Tech 5, which is supposed to be a modern engine, does not support SLI. Whether it supports Crossfire or not I do not know, but this has nonetheless left me rather annoyed. I was still able to achieve a solid framerate and good experience however.
Overall a great experience, both gameplay and storywise! However if you are running a dual GPU setup, I'd advise you to do some research before you buy the game.

The puzzles feel simplistic yet have the exact right amount of challenge that means you get a decent number of hours out of it, it's quite hard to say "that puzzle is done, quitting time" without running straight for the next one, and it's hard to get truly, truly stuck.  There's a lot of outside-the-box thinking to be done if you want those stars!
The levels look vast but feel small due to being herded back if you stray towards the distant pretty things, but soon you can learn where those boundaries can be pushed.  There are a lot of satisfying hidden puzzles and easter eggs to be found.
It's verbose, crazily so.  but manages to stay just within the bounds of pretentiousness, the story is light on detail but pieced together well over time to paint a good enough picture that it feels right.
In short, it's pretty good.

I usually don't write reviews, but RimWorld? ...this game deserves one.
RimWorld is a colony simulation game that has just the right balance of depth, complexity, and easy-to-use features.
Characters have random gen character traits which is one of the big highlights of this game to me. It has just enough depth to create really hilarious situations and memorable stories from playthroughs. Theres also an A.I. director which keeps each playthrough interesting and fun. Think of the A.I. director from Left 4 Dead except it controls weather conditions, raids, alien invasions, people going crazy, animals going crazy, things blowing up, or even hordes of squirrels ripping apart your colonists and everything inbetween. Oh, and theres also another A.I. that watches you play and displays hints if it sees your getting stuck on something. If that doesn't help you, theres many tutorial videos and playthoughs on youtube you can watch to get used to the game.
I've been playing RimWorld for a while before it got released on Steam and I cannot recommend this game enough; even though I've only scratched the surface with this review. It's worth the price.

I was, at first, a little apprehensive about a $30 early access title, but I recommend this game to anyone who might have any interest in a town/colony management game. It is pretty much finished and bug free, so this review stands even if they don't touch another thing in the game.
It gets compared to Dwarf Fortress often, and I think that's fairly accurate in a lot of ways. It's more like DF was back in the early days before the Z axis was added, minus much of the tunneling.
What makes this game worth your time and money is the strange situations and detail given to character's health and relationships leading to some neat stories and exciting moments. For example, my first colony was going fairly well, everyone got along for the most part except when the town's pet cat was butchered and cooked by (my) accident. Fistfights broke out, farming didn't get done, and there was a food shortage. I sent someone to hunt a doe but it was in a herd, and apparently alien deer are fiercely defensive; the entire herd pummeled the hunter to death and then ran through the main street in my settlement and beat everyone unconscious. Raiders then showed up and hauled off one of the women while the last two survivors wasted away in a coma outdoors. You can get all of this in DF for free of course, but not with this setting, presentation, or nice UI.
Losing is fun in DF, and it's also thankfully fun in RimWorld.

Simply put, this game is beautiful.
It had puzzles which were intellectually challenging without being frustrating, many of which actually made me feel clever for completing them, rather than simply acknowleging that I understood what the designer intended me to do, which was a major pitfall of many other puzzle games I've played.
On top of the base puzzles, there are hidden objectives within many puzzles, outside the puzzle areas, or even in the various overworlds. Collecting these was a huge challenge, but well worth the effort and massively rewarding, both individually and upon collection of the appropriate number of stars. The solutions for these required some serious outside-the-box thinking (often quite literally) and some of them were the most well-designed puzzles I've ever encountered.
This game is beautiful. I would have played it without any of the puzzles or narration just for the experience of exploring the worlds of Elohim's garden and finding the many hidden secrets within. I probably spend just as much time looking at the scenery as actually solving the puzzles and I don't regret it for a moment.
The writing is brilliant, subtly nudging you not towards a particular conclusion like many other games with a similar philosophical bent, but rather encouraging you to look deeper at your own convictions, whatever they may be, and not to simply accept what you believe without being able to back it up.
The narritive was of the "slowly uncovering documents that piece together the backstory" kind of thing, which normally I detest, since it feels like a cheap way of breaking up tiresome exposition. However the division of the backstory between text files hidden in computer terminals, recordings left behind by some mysterious woman, and the commentary by Elohim and Milton, each with their own adjenda and beliefs makes it much more interesting than a simple gradual linear reveal of more of the events leading up to the beginning of the story. I found myself actively searching levels for more tidbits of information about the world as I pieced together exactly what happened and where I was.
The inevitable comparison is to Portal, as is true of any puzzle game of this type these days, and sure portal's one mechanic was better than the puzzle mechanics in the Talos Principle, but Portal had many fewer mechanics to deal with. Plus, the story of Talos was more original, and the level and asset design blew it out of the water. During the game, I actually found the game difficult to compare with Portal, because the Talos Principle takes its ideas to the logical conclusion, and fells like a lot more love and care went into it.
Also, the soundtrack is pretty great, drawing you into the game, rather than distracting from it.
Though it may seem trivial, the options are very well designed, including many features that are amazingly convenient that are not included in many other games, such as motion-sickness options, color adjustment options, and the ability to load from any previous checkpoint in the game. These little touches give the impression that Croteam really thought about their players in the design of every element of the game.
On a personal level, I've found myself drifting away from gaming recently, abandoning singleplayer games for more social, multiplayer games that I can play with friends and family. This game was a massive exception to that. I found myself more immersed in this game than I have in any game I've played in years.
If you're on the fence about buying this game, I urge you to pick it up. I bought it on sale, and regret it, because I want to give Croteam more money for this. I'm glad they have a DLC coming out soon that I can pay full price for.

I LOVED this game! The puzzles are interesting, the scenery is beautiful, the music is fitting to the atmosphere, there are many secrets and easter eggs, and most importantly, the story and gameplay are equally amazing. You get a large array of choices in what to do; a minimalistic approach will not get you as good of an ending as trying for every secret and going the extra mile. You feel rewarded for putting in extra effort. The amount of gameplay is largely dependent on how long the player takes through each puzzle, but for the most part it's long enough for a thrilling adventure without outstaying its welcome. The game picks up intensity as you go along, ultimately leading up to an end-game that leave the player with a feeling similar to that of Portal or Bioshock. Contrary to what many people feel after the demo, the religious undertones are arguably minimal, and the puzzle difficulty scales very well with game progress. Even though it is a puzzle game, it does have a high intensity at times.

I wasn't that impressed by the trailers and neither am I impressed after finishing this game. Rockstar tries bringing a new take from the game's predecessors while sticking true in respects to the gameplay but falls under a destitute of good execution.
The game follows years after the events of the Fall of Max Payne. Protoganist Max is now a drunk alcholic Hugh Jackman wannabe and looks to start a new life in the city of Sao Paulo working as bodyguard for a rich family, the Broncos.  Of course, things go to♥♥♥♥♥♥very quickly, with the first two acts involving a hostage snatch at the Bronco family. One or two more sieges happens later on, but it gets pretty senseless by then, it just makes me wonder how these folks can be so calm about relying on only two freaking bodyguards.
The story, meant to be a focal point, feels just lackluster and cliche in many areas. Some of it is told through random flashbacks and all of it is narrated by the cynical Max Payne. Every now and then, there will be big bold words popping up on the screen with flashy flashy colors as the narration goes or during conversation. A stylishtic choice of perhaps, spicing things up, but ends up being more of an annoyance, serving no real purpose and meaning. A failed attempt at replacing the comic black-and-white panels the Remedy Max Payne games are known for.
There are plenty of cutscenes in the game ...which is fine, if not for the fact that they're used far too excessively and at times feels plain
.
Even the simplest stuff like opening a window or just pressing a button, you have to watch a cutscene of Max Payne doing these very simple actions. Ridiculous. Voiceovers aren't quality either, especially for the locals where the lip-synch is all over the place.
The gameplay on the other hand, is where Max Payne 3 shines at the most...somewhat. Despite being old and drunk, Max Payne is still able to utilize his secret Bullet Time superpower, which enables him to manipulate time and gravity to a crawl while headshotting all enemies in the vicinity. Bullet trails whizzing by and close-up kill cams coupled with the new Last Stand feature, makes for an interesting and delightful spectacle.
Max Payne now also has the common sense to take behind cover to avoid enemy fire. A simple cover system. A function some fans have called as game-breaking, though it's unarguably just as essential in any 3rd person shooter today. There's nothing really wrong with this, except for one problem the game has: Enemies don't throw grenades. This makes camping behind cover almost too preferential and advantageous to the player, forcing the enemy the only option of flanking and then getting blasted to shreds by blindfire. It's a gameplay decision that seems poorly implemented.
Thankfully the rest of the game don't suffer as much of issues. On the bright side, the enemy AI that comes are smart and act tactically well (while also being stupid enough to keep on thronging at you in masses). I LOVED this game! The puzzles are interesting, the scenery is beautiful, the music is fitting to the atmosphere, there are many secrets and easter eggs, and most importantly, the story and gameplay are equally amazing. You get a large array of choices in what to do; a minimalistic approach will not get you as good of an ending as trying for every secret and going the extra mile. You feel rewarded for putting in extra effort. The amount of gameplay is largely dependent on how long the player takes through each puzzle, but for the most part it's long enough for a thrilling adventure without outstaying its welcome. The game picks up intensity as you go along, ultimately leading up to an end-game that leave the player with a feeling similar to that of Portal or Bioshock. Contrary to what many people feel after the demo, the religious undertones are arguably minimal, and the puzzle difficulty scales very well with game progress. Even though it is a puzzle game, it does have a high intensity at times.

A level-based first-person puzzler that rewards exploration with an overarching storyline. For some players it's great to figure out a new mechanic for themselves, while others might feel a bit cheated when they weren't aware of certain possibilities. The game also have 30 optionally collectable stars that are for the most part VERY challenging to get expanding the playtime significantly. I'd say the main game has atleast 20 hours of gametime and with Steam Workshop, hopefully some dedicated fans will bring us more. The price tag is a bit high, but luckily there's a free demo you can try out first to see if it interests you. All in all one of the best games I've played in years and definitely worth a recommendation.

The first time I started up squad I was in a state of excited apprehension. The concept of the game sounds absolutely fantastic; and as someone who had never played project reality, I had no idea what to expect.
I spawned in on the USA side and quickly learned the buttons to speak to squad. The UI is fairly easy to work out: how to join a team, how to join a squad, where to spawn, what your role is etc. So anyway, I'm in the map now and start running toward my squad. Little do I know that I've spawned into the middle of a battle and bang I'm dead from an unknown enemy in an unknown position. "Ok" I think, this isn't as fast paced as I expected... Spawn in again, run over to my squad and die again. "This game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm getting a refund" I now think.
Thank God I did not refund.
After a bit of a learning curve, primarily because I'm totally new to games like this, I started to learn the tactics necessary behind the game. There are many! Once you become familiar with the game modes and the style of the game, its cracking fun. Playing the medic is satisfying getting your team mates up. Firing an RPG from a hilltop on an enemy base is exhilirating fun! The sounds in the game are amazing. The authenticity is really commendable. The more I play it, the more I enjoy it and I definitely recommend picking it up, even if the price point is a bit steep.
Cons wise I can't fault it too much. Optics for the russian/non-USA guns would be very welcomed. More maps and game modes would equally be good, as well as perhaps more customisation allowed for the loadouts. For example, it would be great to have the option to take an extra nade instead of my pistol. I also have encountered a few bugs, but for an alpha its suprisingly stable. If your team or SL is♥♥♥♥♥♥ then you're in for a rough time of aimless wandering in a huge map.
Overall I would recommend this game. It takes a while to get used to it, and it can be really frustrating sometimes when under fire from positions unknown or your SL is♥♥♥♥♥♥ But then when you have a good round, or an epic firefight it provides a satisfaction that not many other games can do. I look forward to the full release.

This game is pretty old, maybe writing the review now would prove to be redundant but meh I'll do it anyway.
I finished the game in approximately 9 hours. Which is quite longer than most players probably since I'm not exactly smart at these kinds of puzzle games. But that doesn't mean the game made me bored af. The game entertains you in lots of ways. Both from the actual game mechanics and from the snappy retort that Wheatley and GLaDOS spew out without reserve. I don't know if this game is actually comedic but it has some points for giggles, yeah, you'll laugh at yourself for not realizing to put that portal there sooner, or you should place that cube on the button first and then jump, you idiot.
The game's physics and mechanics are awesome, the way it made you fly and stuff, I love it. This game is pretty simple if you ask me, but there are so much combination of stuff going on in one test chamber you need to exploit all these simple things.The puzzle could get tiring somewhat if you have sat for hours without knowing what to do, but in the end you will ALWAYS figure it out.
There are some test chambers that, when you took your first step in, you'd think to yourself 'what the hell there are so many things going on, what am I supposed to do', and thats why I think the best way of solvng all the puzzle inside this game is through the process of elimination. Try out everything that seems viable and you'll get the answer, eventually.
If you are into puzzle games, I'd definitely recommend this game.
Oh yeah did I mention you can make your own test chamber and screw yourself up? yeah you can do that.

By yourself, it may have limited appeal. I was lucky enough to run into a game with another player and it was enjoyable until we both died and parted ways.
If this was a high priced game, I would warn you away. It is what I would put in the mediocre category. However, if you know this is a style of game you enjoy, I'd say it is worth $2 USD. The price they have set shows that they have a very realistic perspective of exactly what their game really is.

TL:DR = build a colony, watch your colonists die, repeat.
I bought this game way back in Alpha 4 I believe. It's been years in development but with every update comes a deeper, more refined game.
Like many people are saying Rimworld is an unholy union of Dwarf Fortress and Prison Architect, set in a Fireflyesc universe.
In the game you build and manage a group of stranded settlers. Watch as you settlement grows; your colonists develop, interact and eventually die. That last part is something you'll have to get used to as this game can be brutal.
Due to this undeniable fact of Rimworld the health system for a game like this is pretty complex with various body parts and effects being simulated. If your colonist gets a toe or two shot off his movement speed will be affective, if he catches a cold his conciousness is affected..  over time your veteran colonists will more than likely loose most of their appendages and require prosthetics.. one of my colonists has none of her original organs as well as having cybernetic limbs and eyes..."she's more machine now than man".
That is just one small aspect of the game however. There are others to worry about too, such as; seasons, temperature, colonist schedules, research, trading, diplomacy, to name a few.
This is to say Rimworld hasn't got it flaws, but with all honesty they are usually addressed pretty quickly. At the moment the AI pathfinding can be a bit iffy but chances are this will be fixed in the next update, a sign of a good developer is that they address the underlying flaws in their game before adding new features. An example ot this was the trade caravans and raiders attacking in extreme temperature regions in the previous alpha version. with Alpha 14 they no long do this... so you won't have a trail of corpses leading to your colony after an especially cold winter or hot summer.
Overall If your a fan of base builders or managment games then I would wholly recommend this game, even at the current pricetag. It is a game I always play at some point, and it's replayablity is probably one of it's strongest assets, due to it's procedual nature.
So please have a go, build a colony and watch it eventually been thrown into chaos either by famine, fire or intergalactic robots.

My review is something I originally wrote as a forum post in response to a comment claiming that Croteam's history of level design has gone a very long way toward making their puzzles excellent. And I agree with that, but I believe so much more than that.
But let me first begin by saying that the game has only crashed once, and it was during Steam-streaming, that its narrative and aesthetics, its design, engineering, personality, etc. are all excellent in my eyes, and that ALL of the puzzles absolutely can be beaten... you just have to think outside the box... very far outside the box... but that's part of the beauty, isn't it?
---
I'll be honest, I've never played Serious Sam... but then I've never played Wolfenstein, Quake classic, etc. - I was a sheltered child... so Croteam's history of level design is rather alien to me.
However I will say it hasn't gone totally unnoticed by me in this case. The puzzles feel rather satisfying either way, and come to think of it I kind of like the fact that even some of the late game puzzles feel - at that point - simple and easy. I could never figure out how much of it was me and how much of it was the puzzles themselves... I'm certain some of the reds and greys were just easy, but I'm also certain that a fair bit of it was because I'd learned new perspectives and habits, such as recognizing absolutely EVERY interactive item as a possible paperweight. Every fan, every panel, every jammer and connector is something to put on that button, and that's a concept that kind of escaped me early on.
There were also a few points that made me feel rather silly for not realizing the solution sooner, but then I began to realize from the narrative that it wasn't about intelligence, but perspective. So many of the solutions are very simple and maybe even obvious, but some are obscured by decoys and most importantly by one's own way of thinking, and that's nothing to be embarrassed about, but a thing to overcome.
The whole assembly of gameplay and the narrative all seem so very focused on pushing the player to reevaluate their way of thinking. It feels like a game about opening doors and broadening horizons, and I feel like it's infinitely valuable because of it.
Most intriguing to me is the neurological connections. The game consists of three separate aspects that are independent of one another and superficially only flavor each other, but outside the game they actually
interact. My experience has indicated the following.
Gameplay - Serves the purposes of exercising cognition and unlocking modes of thought conducive to philosophical debate. Also triggers endorphins, providing a clear neurological hook to coax the player deeper into the rabbit hole and condition them to be inquisitive by rewarding them for scrutinizing every detail, tinkering with what they're given and experimenting with different perspectives and modes of thought. On top of that, the endorphins might provide relaxation from any anxiety that might be experienced when asking the tougher questions.
- And then it serves its own purpose of being an enjoyable game and an intrinsic mental exercise.
Conversation - The player's debate partner through the game actually seems to complement this growth and fire it right back into the player's gameplay by asking them questions and then questioning their answers... it reinforces the scrutiny you're trained to exhibit and thus it streamlines the development of adaptation and flexibility required to beat the game.
- And then it serves its own purpose of being a philosophical exercise that constantly spurs the player to reevaluate their own position.
Archives - The archives occasionally provide some sample of philosophies that allow the inquisitive player to find new ideas and new perspectives, giving them more tools to face the intermittent debates.
- And then they serve their own purpose of building lore for the game.
It's a beautiful and intricate psychological and neurological medley, and I think that above all is what makes this game so popular... it doesn't just demand and demand and blindly challenge players and it doesn't hold hands... instead it pushes the player and equips them with the tools they need.

The developers of this game are making it out of pure love. They want to play this game literally as much as their biggest fans. Here is why...
The concept for Squad and a good chunk of its development team comes directly from the best Battlefield 2 mod of all time, Project Reality.
You want epic new age conflict? Got it. You want to chase Charlie from your favourite surfing spot in Nam? Got it.
You want some WW2 action? Sh%# they got that too.

And in case you were wondering, "has this guy just been too stoned to notice other titles?" I have BF4. Played it, liked it, then came crawling back back a month later to old faithful. Good old "PR."
Thankfully I'm not the only one, because Project Reality, just like Squad is by NO means a single player game.
(Even if you play the game you might want to check out these awesome trailers)
(with a standalone PR download link)
I would gladly pay $300 with a smile on my face for a remake of PR. Probably more. Nope, definitely more.
For less than $50 I feel like I still owe Squads team something. It's criminal.

I know what the Devs dream is. Its not money (though they need and deserve to earn a decent living).
I know because its the same dream I've had myself for almost a decade now, a fully encompassing, meaningful wargame,  built from the ground up. Where that sense of respect and consideration for the "soldier next to you" is very real. Because without their help, you may as well just find yourself a hole to crawl into.
Players, Its going to take a little while, but we'll get there....
Devs, I'll be your medic should you ever need one.
Whatever I can do to keep you in the fight.

Rimworld is a complex story driven colony survival simulator with (pausable) real time tactical combat, for which you need more than 2 brain cells to play. It's also a proof of concept that a good game doesn't need good graphics. Don't get me wrong it's not ugly, but it's not a beauty either.
Instead it draws its immersion and credibility from simulating a lot of things that most games would ignore. It gives you freedom of choice, with lots of (moral) decisions. It has a huge replayability by telling a unique story with different events each time you play.
Every colonist is unique, based on childhood and adulthood stories they will have or lack skills, traits and enthusiasm in certain skills. Each colonist can have his/her own customised priorities for tasks, daily schedules and outfits. Making it possible to specialize people for specific tasks.
Every colonist has a simulated psyche. Certain events will improve or worsen their mood. Having a good meal and all basic needs fulfilled will boost their mood. Seeing a person die or many corpses lying around will worsen their mood. This however is also based on their traits. A psychopath will not mind the death of others, while someone with bloodlust will even like it. Masochists will enjoy pain. A "Green thumb" will get a bit of happiness for every crop they sew. And it's not always the enemy attacks that will kill you. Often the most critical times are after fights when your colonists are wounded and about to break from the mental stress. Mentally breaking can lead people to going crazily wandering around, leaving the colony or even going berserk. There are so many things to take into consideration, like the beauty and space size of an area, or the quality of beds and furniture which will all affect the mood of colonists.
Every colonist has a body with simulated limbs and organs. Each part can be damaged or destroyed. Each part is responsible for either manipulation, movement, consciousness, eyesight, hearing, blood filtration, blood pumping etc. Those abilities are bound to the colonist's performance. A cook with only one arm and one eye would be terribly slow at cooking. An old person with only one kidney will most likely not survive an infection, or a sickness. Luckily there are (expensive) implants and bionics to compensate in the mid-late game. You can also take the morally low road and harvest needed organs from prisoners, which will negatively influence the psyche of every non-psycho in the colony. It is also technically possible to build a bionic superhuman that has most abilities improved, for a very high price of resources.
Had a nudist woman once who felt constrained by her cloths so I let her run naked. She got an instant mood boost for that. Got into a fight and took a bullet to the right lung. Survived the fight and got stitched up by a doc, but left with only one lung she was permanently slowed down afterwards. I took one lung from a pirate prisoner and implanted it into her. Had the whole colony mentally on the edge for days for having harvested organs from people ...
This and many other stories derive from the game's wonderful complexity. It produces more immersion than most other games which just look great, but are simply dead inside.
Im playing this game since 2 years now but it never gets boring. The storyteller will trigger events every now and then, which will force you to adapt to new situations. Be it a sudden solar flare, a sun eclipse, a pack of manhunting animals, a toxic fallout which will kill everything outside not under a roof, a pirate / natives / mechanoids attack, or a fallen chunk of ancient spaceship sending out psychic waves, driving every colonist crazy the longer you wait. The game gets constantly updated with new events which will keep it exciting for a long time.
Had an ancient spaceship fallen into the map, started to screw my colonists mentally. Shortly afterwards a group of natives entered the map and prepared for an attack. I sent my fastest colonist with a gun to the crashed ship and shot it. From the damage it spawned it's mechanoids, which angered some of the natives nearby. I retreaded my colonist and just watched the show. Part of the natives were fighting the mechs, the other part was on their way to my base. At that point a pack of manhunting boomrats also entered the map and started to attack the natives. Also one hare turned crazy and ran to my base (monty python anyone?) It was an epic fight, seeing all my enemies neutralizing themselves. In the end I just had to shoot the hare, while the remaining natives were fighting exploding boomrats and retreating in the end. Got a lot of loot for free. It was a good day.
The difficulty is customisable both by choosing a different story teller & hardness but also by choosing a biome. Each biome plays like a different game. In a tropical area you have a lot of wood, food and animals, while possibly getting malaria and sleeping sickness. In a tundra or desert environment you have to worry about the temperature.
Too cold and you can not plant anything and people might freeze to death, while most things won't spoil quickly. Grow your food in hydroponics (which are expensive and have to be researched first)  inside a warm room. This overall consumes a lot of energy.
Too hot and people might get heat strokes and foot will spoil quickly when not cooled. A freezer room is required to keep food cooled here. This also defines the outfit to wear.
Parkas and toques in cold biomes to keep warm,
while cowboy hats and leather coats in hot biomes to keep cool.
Gears and weapons are degrading, especially when stored outside. They are also craftable and the quality will depend on the crafters skill. Different gear will protect different body parts and are based by their quality values. However, research is needed for most technologies before they can be build. Trading with other factions or space traders will get you the other stuff you need.
It is also possible to tame animals with a high enough skill. Those can be bred and herded for meat, egg, milk, fur, wool or leather production.
The building mechanics are fairly simple, closing off an area with walls/and a door will generate a roof. (house)
Mining rooms into a mountain with no support in between will let the roof collapse. For those comparing it with prison architect, it is a lot easier to build rooms or add to an existing room. I would even say it delivers a way stronger game experience with just 10 colonists than prison architect with its 100-300+ inmates & staff.
It is possible to micro every colonist whenever needed on daily tasks (unlike in Banished). During attacks colonists are able to be drafted and controlled directly. Fights have a cover based system where positioning your pawns behind walls, sandbags, trees, or even stone chunks will give them more or less cover. The only thing that is bothering is the amount of friendly fire. So make sure nobody is standing in the line of fire.
In every fight there is a possibility that enemies are not killed, but incapacitated. Those can be captured and taken as prisoners. What you do with them is up to your moral compass. You can either treat them right, heal their wounds and try to convince them to join your colony, or you can simply sell them to a slave trader, or harvest their organs.
However bare in mind that it can be a slow game at times (fast forward is possible) and may not be easy to understand at first. But if you give it some time to learn it you will be rewarded with a great experience.
Rimworld is by far my favorite game since 2 years. It gives the player a lot of possibilities, with a love for details. It is kept interesting for a long time thanks to the event storyteller system. If you like games like Dungeon Keeper, Startopia, Dwelvers, Evil Genius, Dwarven Fortress, Prison Architect, War for the Overworld or Space Colony, you will probably love Rimworld.

Fantastic game. Wolfenstein:The New Order combines over-the-top sillyness and serious story telling to create an awesome singleplayer experience. Overall, the plot is very good and the game has great character development that you very rarely see nowadays in shooters. The game also allows you to make choices: You can go the stealthy approach and sneak about, using your knives and silenced pistols to take out enemies without alerting reinforcements, OR you can dual-wield shotguns/assault rifles/sniper rifles and mow through hundreds of enemies, both human and robot. I combined both of these routes and had a lot of fun. The post-war Nazi ridden world is terrible but beautiful. The gore system was a surprise, allowing me to gib enemies in different ways (World at War style). As far as performance goes, my relatively high-end rig (GTX 960 4 GB, 8 GB of RAM, FX-8320) handled the game very well, allowing me to max out the graphics with very few frame drops (and might I add that the graphics look gorgeous). Strangely, the only hiccups occurred during certain cutscenes.
If you want a game about killing Nazis and a mix of CoD:World at War, Metro, and a few others, Wolfenstein: The New Order is for you.

Wow. I've never had this much fun with a shooter than when I first played Serious Sam The Second Encounter. Seriously, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.
The story doesn't have much to talk about, but it's a shooter. Who the hell cares about story? To give you the basics without spoiling anything, this takes place in an alternate universe where the Nazis won WW2. But now for the real meat of this game, the gameplay. You have your basic fast paced, classic shooter gameplay. A.) regenerate health up to the next whole ten points(e.g. 138->140), or B.) regen your health to 20 when you really ♥♥♥♥ing low. Even better, you actually get to hold ALL the weapons(except for spin guns, which sucks). Plus, you can find upgrades for your guns, such as rocket launcher for your assault rifle, or bouncing shrapnel bullets for your shotgun.
As a bonus to all these good points, the game looks beautiful and runs smoothly.
Should you buy this? YES.
In the words of Shia LeBouf,
