I have mixed feelings about The Talos Principle. Ultimately, I recommend it, but not at its full price. If you are interested, buy it on sale.
Visually, this game is very appealing. I expected nothing less from a game built on the excellent Serious Engine 4. Every environment and item is gorgeously rendered. The audio was also exceptional, the music, sound effects and voice quality are all top-notch. The music especially puts you in the mood for each section you are in. My particular favorite is the music that plays in the messenger levels; a piano solo that sounds simulatenously melancholy and hopeful.
The story is like a mystery that the player must piece together as they move through the various worlds. I found myself reading every computer file and QR code to try and shed more light on what is happening, but by the time I got most of the way through World B, I had figured out the overall plot and the direction the game was prodding me towards. After that, the files mostly contained details that didn't really matter. Many of the files just contained fluff that isn't necessary to fully understand what is going on. But whether you figure out the story or not doesn't affect how the game will end. You can skip every computer terminal (except the ones in the tower) and all but one QR code and still get all three endings.
The puzzles were, for the most part, quite enjoyable. There were only a very few puzzles that I got stuck on and had to look up a solution for. Most of the time, the puzzles build on what you already figured out in previous puzzles, so you build your knowledge of how the mechanics work and use that to complete the harder puzzles. But sometimes, the game throws you a curveball that seems either lazy or uses a previously unexplained mechanic that the player would never have guessed would work. Thankfully, this doesn't happen too often.
Easter eggs. Man, does this game have a lot of them. While they aren't required for completion, they do provide a break from the overall serious tone of the game and are fun to figure out (Gnaar statue was epic). A definite plus.
This game is philosophy heavy, but is much less cliche than Anti-Chamber, which used a fortune cookie style that I quickly found annoying. The philosophy element in The Talos Principle is almost exclusively tied to the computer terminals, which are completely optional. Your responses to the "Serpent" are limited to pre-determined answers that a lot of people won't agree with, but to all those people out there who think that this game is belligerently challenging their beliefs, I say, the existential and metaphysical questions posed by this game are nothing new, and neither are the answers that are given. Also, the questions and answers about these topics are not limited to what is presented in the game. The game presents a certain viewpoint on humanity, the human soul, the value of human life, and humanity's relationship to God, but it does not represent EVERY viewpoint on those topics. So don't get too worked up about it. Remember that the philosophical element is mostly optional. Skip it if you want too.
That said, if you do choose to participate, the game can get a little preachy with its message and by the time I reached World C, I had gotten a bit tired of hearing the same thing over and over. From a storytelling standpoint, I can see what Croteam was going for here (child independence), but it started to bore me toward the end. I think more effort could have been made to improve the story by filling in the future plans for Humanity 2.0, because the ending leaves a lot of unanswered questions in that regard.
I think that Croteam put forth a good effort here, and showed that they aren't just about blowing up alien hordes. However, I feel The Talos Principle is overpriced, especially when compared to Portal 2, which is another excellent puzzle game with about the same playtime and overall level of quality.

Rimworld is an attempt to replicate a semblance of Dwarf Fortress's complexity with actual GRAPHICS. I've always felt DF was one of those games that was much more fun to read about rather than play, somewhat like Eve online. From what I understand Rimworld doesn't come close to emulating DF level complexity, but it is extremely intricately detailed in its own right.
Injuries are simulated all over the body(To the level that a guy can have his right ring finger bitten off by a beaver), colonists have their own personalities and wants/ skills, as well as unique traits. These make all the colonists feel more like real people as they have a semblance of personality, for example some of them won't really mind living in squalor, while others want an extravagant bedroom or nice chairs or something. You can assign tasks but not all of them can do everything so optimizing job priorities is a large part of the game's challenge. Colonists will develop relationships with one another, ranging from falling in love alll the way hating one another and starting fights. You really get the sense that yes, you can tell them what to do but they are their own self contained entities with wants and needs that require management or else on day they'll decide, "♥♥♥♥ it, I'm out" and start stabbing and eating everyone else or something.
Combat is more interesting too, with cover based shooting, melee combat, automated turrets, traps, etc. It is much more complex than the standard "Right click on someone and go hit him" of other similar games.
Rimworld's graphics are the simplistic, charming Prison Architect style, with similar mechanics in "zoning" and construction mechanics. This game has been in development for years and it shows, there are plenty of features and mechanics in this game, as well as a distinct lack of bugs (so far).
My one complaint is that there isn't much of an in game tutorial, but there is a helpful advice message system which helped me out a lot. Still, I would've preferred a small mini campaign like in Prison Architect so I can at least get a general idea what I should prioritize and what I should work towards, but I'm sure this information will come with time as I mess around in the game more.

Try again the next day... join an outfit... a squad... using the jetpack is cool... get shot out of the sky...  about 20 times... call it a night.
Try again the next day... outfit and squad not very helpful yet... spend these nanite thingies to get a 4-wheeler... epic first crash while running away from a fight... try again with a basic airship... crash almost instantly... in front of my whole team... call it a night.

I'm not a big fan of filler; That's why I couldn't finish skyrim, so I'll just cut to the chase.
◦ It starts out pretty strong and has some great features for a new game.
◦ It has a simple and intuitive interface. Gaining an understanding of most, if not all of the game mechanics takes less than 5 minutes.
◦ The first few games are intense and fun.
◦ Multiplayer is a nice feature and works(relatively) smoothly. The community seems nice enough.
◦ Decent sound track, albeit royalty free.
◦ A unique "sale" feature where different items are discounted every day.
◦ The game is simple, but so much so that enjoyablitily and replayability are nonexistant. None of the features themselves are bad... it's the lack thereof.
◦ The game gets old fast. There's no variation between save for what you do differently.
◦ No 'special variants' of zombies. The enemies are monotonous.
◦ No difficulty scaling based on the amount of players in game. It's virtually impossible to reach level 10 solo, but it's nearly impossible not to with three other people at your back.
◦ No upgrades. At first glance, this may not seem like a big deal, but eventually the horde can break your steel palisades in a matter of seconds, and your laser can do nothing to stop it.
◦ No progression. Once you die, that's it you start at square one again with nothing to show for it. There's a ranking system, but it doesn't mean a thing in the end.
◦ Overall, the visuals are adequate. It's not disappointing but it's certainly not impressive in any sense of the word.
◦ The setting is... Nonexistant... There's one 'map' and it's a lamp post surrounded by an expanse of concrete.
◦ There are only three character types and no customization whatsoever.
The game isn't bad by any means. I got it for 67 cents and don't regret the purchase. You get what you pay for; A couple hours of entertainment. While it's lacking in some ways, the features that are in place are, at the very least, executed well. If you're not impressed easily, there's little enjoyment to be had here, but if you're looking for some quick and inexpensive entertainment on the fly, it's definitely got you covered.

Max Payne 3 was Rockstar’s attempt at making a Max Payne game, as before it was Remedy who had done the previous two.  Now right off the bat let me mention that fans of the previous 2 may or may not like the new Max Payne character as Rockstar seems to have changed him or at least the game’s tone from at times a 4th wall breaking humor to an ultra depressed middle aged man with a serious substance abuse problem.  Max is still voiced by the same VO which is good because honestly I can only picture him doing Max’s voice.  I can see where some of the criticism is coming from as far as the seemingly negative way Rockstar has changed Max’s character and tone towards life.  However I can also appreciate the changes; Max is older, he has been dealing with the loss of so many of his loved ones that you can not deny what that could do to a person mentally.  The still framed pictures or comic book type loading and cut-scenes have been replaced with fairly well done but good looking in-game cut-scenes, which some people hate because well if you die a lot then you have to rewatch every single one multiple times and sometimes it just seems to take the game forever to load that section of the level.  Much of the cut-scenes have an odd video interference effect which some people complain causes headaches because it can cause the screen to flash different colors and tones rapidly.  It was honestly an odd choice because it happens throughout the entire game, not just when Max is under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
The combat however, at least to my memory, I still have my old Max Payne 1 and 2 disks here, has not changed in fact to me it has been improved dramatically, some ways it is a step back but I’ll get to that.  The animations, Max’s movements are very fluid and stunned me when I first saw them, Max no longer rigidly flys through the air and clips through walls and other objects, his body reacts differently to what he hits or slides along.  The gunplay and shooting in very pleasing however it seems to be more geared towards being somewhat realistic as far as weapon damage.  No longer can Max take hit after hit and a headshot from the enemy is an instant death, which is something very new to the series, at least as far as I can remember.  The slow motion gunplay as well as gunplay outside of bullet time is quite enjoyable and a vast improvement over what it was in the past, movement and aiming is much more fluid and responsive.  That being said one addition to the slow motion bullet time system that Max Payne has been known for is what amounts to a last stand, or rather if you are mortally wounded but still have painkillers in your inventory, the game will automatically pop the pills and you will fall in place while in slow motion in an attempt to kill the person who brought you own.  Doing so will allow you to recover from what would have been a death, failing to find any target let alone return the fatal shot to the enemy who shot you will result in death.  This plays into both this game’s improvement and a potential and constant problem; sometimes when you are put into last stand you quite literally can not see the person who shot you OR what normally happens is that Max falls in such a position that he can not actually get a shot at the target thus ending in a very frustrating death.  This unfortunately happens rather consistently throughout the game so that is one major negative that I can readily ID and say “I am honestly not sure that they REALLY play tested that idea”.
The story and setting are fairly different from what most Max Payne vets are used to playing, rather then New Jersey or New York apartments, side streets and allyways, fighting mobsters.  You are now fighting in Brazil against gangs, paramilitary organizations and state forces.  The settings are quite well done as is the atmopher, gone are you abilities to readily understand the NPCs within the game unless they speak English or unless you speak I believe Portuguese (I could be very wrong sorry) which makes you feel very isolated and even more alone many times.  The story can be either good or bad depending on how you look at it or what kind of story that you enjoy, some will like it, others will hate it, I happened to like it.
The music is another major factor to me if how I feel while playing, if a game has bad music while I’m trying to do action rolls and dodging the experience may not feel as good as a game that has a good sound track.  This title however does have quite a good sound track and the music fits many of the situations that you run into especially the last level song, it really gets you pumped to finally see the end to this story, to me anyway, others have said it was too house or techno and not fitting of Max Payne.  It will come to personal opinion honestly.  The sound effects are really well done, from the weapons fire, the explosions and the ambient environments everything feels like a lot of effort was put into making it feel right.  The past 2 Max Payne titles never really had any problems with this however I was happy that despite Remedy not making this game that Rockstar was able to keep that feeling.
The game also hits that little part of the brain for completionists, collectables for golden guns that actually have an in game benefit (mostly ammo capacity).  So depending on what kind of person you are, you may end up playing through this game several times trying to get all of the little bits and pieces which can further extent your play time.  It is however optional.
The multiplayer aspect is a different story as far as my enjoyment; while it is well fleshed out and not just some tacked on addition to meet the new generation requirement that every game needs multiplayer it is however not very fun.  I did try to enjoy it, I even played with a friend but after maybe 4 or 6 hours of total time in the multiplayer I had had enough and to me the combat did not transition well from singleplayer to multiplayer.  There are no dedicated servers so again PC gets a not so stable port for the multiplayer side of this game, it is Peer to Peer and in a game which revolves around slow motion and good aiming that is not a winning combination.  Some people may enjoy it others do not, and on top all of this from what I understand there is a serious problem with cheaters and hackers.
Over all at least for the main story, not the multiplayer aspect of this game, I quite enjoyed the third iteration of Max Payne even if it was done by Rockstar.  I enjoyed it and I felt that it was a worthy number to add to the franchise.

Positives:

This game has been on my radar for a long time, but it had the feel that it wasn't worth the full 60/50$ price tag. And when it hit the '15 Summer sale for roughly half-price, I jumped and I can say that my instincts were right. It's a fun game, but it's got some issues that don't kill it, but are there all the same.
The New Order surprisingly does a very good job of recreating a lot of the elements of the original games, scattering secrets across the maps and rewarding exploration. The item collection (especially the gold items) really brought back old memories of playing the very first Wolfenstein 3D while still being part of this game. It's also a refreshing sight to see a map screen come back into the FPS, giving me freedom to pick new directions or backtrack to find other things I might have missed. I feel even more encouraged to explore as the visuals are so well-done, character models and environments are very well-done all throughout the game and the only issues I had were most likely due to putting my settings above what my graphics card could handle.
The gameplay itself has good and bad elements, but more good than bad. The gunplay is solid, I only had to slightly adjust my aiming (normal for a different game, really) and I really loved the weapons and was happy to find that the developers had commendably dropped the two-gun limit so common these days. The guns also have very distinct uses and many gain new elements as you advance through the story, really opening up options in your tactics. Furthermore, the weapons have 'weight' when you're getting into firefights, especially when larger and more powerful weapons are capable of ripping away chunks of concrete. However, the dual-gun weilding really felt useless whenever I tried to use it (especially when it came to reloading) and while I'd try to experiment, it always seemed to use up more ammo than do damage. Sliding seems innovative, but it really didn't come into play for me save for some parts of the story where you had to slide to pass an obstacle, I never used it in combat. The stealth portions of the game were difficult to implement, as getting a good look at the environment and where you could go was difficult for me to do, ultimately, it devolved into 'lemmie get as many of these guys as quietly as I can, but once I hear a shout in german, I'm going Rambo on these Krauts.' Also, the 'cover' system was in serious need of help, for the very simple reason that the leaning around corners was so limited that it was just better to pop out and back. However, I still had fun, and it was definitely refreshing to play an FPS that didn't devolve into the standard Modern Military mindset of sticking to cover, regenerating health, and a freedom to become a wrecking ball of destruction on the battlefield.
The story is interesting, but it seems like the developers didn't quite do very well to develop the main villians in the game to really bring a point home. I think there coulda been more done to make characters more dynamic, hidden recordings or videos of the villians and their past 'experiments', maybe coming across some nazi soldiers being arrested for questioning authority or journal entries showing a struggle with the Nazi ideal? Again, not a dealbreaker, but too many elements of the story felt cliched or taken for granted when things could have been much more poigant.
As stated, the game is good, I really enjoyed a lot of it, and I also would recommend it to someone looking for a fun FPS shooter. However, there are still elements of the game that lack a little polish and could use a bit of tweaking to bring it to that level of being a must-play shooter... something we really need from an FPS that isn't your standard Modern Military approach.

Nevertheless, the steam's early access program will allow a better exposure of the game to gamers and will allow the developer, Tynan Sylvester, to make a great progress towards a final stage, which will, almost certainly, correspond to the players expectations/desires.
I can affirm that Rimworld will NOT be one of those games that enter Steam Early Access with no intents of future upgrades, on the contrary it will be similar to Prison Architect (which in my opinion, was a model of what every game should be in Steam Early Access).
When discussing what is great I would say:

The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzle game where you play as a robot awaken in a mysterious world by a voice named ELOHIM. You are tasked to solve puzzles, learn about the world that you're in, and figure out what purpose you serve. This game dives into Roman, Egyptian, and Greek mythology and philosophy along with files in computer terminals that are scattered throughout the world. Each puzzle has an obtainable sigil (And sometimes a Star). Once you have all of the sigils in a set, you use those to fill a perfect rectangle or square to unlock more areas (They look like Tetris pieces, but I like the name "Sigil"). The puzzles are actually very challenging. There are also 30 stars that are scattered around the world. Obtaining these stars are a little trickier than just regular sigils, but these stars serve a specific purpose and are used to unlock special areas. There are three different ending, those I will not spoil because that would ruin the whole point of me recommending you this game.
I love this goddamn game to no end. Everything about this game is so well executed. The visuals are beautiful and surprisingly optimized. The gameplay is smooth sleek. The audio is calming and ambient. The soundtrack is one HELL of a masterpiece. I love all of the well hidden easter eggs in this game, these include Portal, Serious Sam, A certain rock band, and other games. I love the extensive lore in this game. I recommend reading EVERY file in every terminal, it might seem like a hassle, but they are very good reads. Get this game if you're a fan of fantastically made puzzle games or looking for a game with amazing gameplay value.
UPDATE: The Road to Gehenna
The Road to Gehenna is an amazing addition to The Talos Principle. Gehenna is where forsaken people get sent away to by ELOHIM himself. Gehenna is also a chatboard where the forsaken people who are trapped in Gehenna can communicate with one another. Your mission, free those people and lead them to ascension. This addition brings 4 new areas (Not including the Special Area) that bring more difficulty to the table. All the puzzles' difficulty has been increased 5x and each star is mind-♥♥♥♥ingly hard to get.
Once again, I love this game and this DLC made me love it 10x  more. This addition brought me more than 25+ hours of gameplay (Because everything is so damn hard). Definitely pick up this DLC if you're an avid Talos Principle player like myself. One more thing... If you do get this DLC, I have two warnings: Beware the Crater and beware the Special Area.

Well this is a game right up my alley! A philosophical puzzle game about AI and philosophy of mind? Sign me up!
In The Talos Principle, you play as a robot about which is not much known. Guided by some apparent higher being called Elohim you solve puzzles, while collecting notes, audio logs and while talking to an intelligent terminal. The writing is fantastic and leaves it up to you to figure out what is really going on. It tackles topics such as Artificial Intelligence, consciousness, philosophy of mind, religion and of course the meaning of life.
I happen to know a thing or two about AI because I study it on University, and the game does a fantastic job in its smaller details to stay true to what is known about the field so far, which was very enjoyable to see.
The gameplay, mostly solving logic puzzles, often requires quite some out of the box thinking. While there are not a big amount of mechanics, the game manages through usually clever level design to feel very varied. Furthermore, the controls feel very "snappy" and never get in your way of solving a puzzle. There's barely any time restrictions either, so it can mostly  be done with guts alone.
This is certainly a game that makes you feel like you are smart. It nearly never compliments you with your achievements, and the levels don't feel designed to take you by the hand. This can lead to you probably feeling stupid at times for not seeing something "very obvious", but also that all the motivation to move on is intrinsic and not extrinsic, which is generally much better, thank you very much.
The game has one major problem though. It is pretty long. While Croteam clearly tried to make the puzzles as diverse as possible, with the limited amount of mechanics a lot of stuff can feel very repetitive despite those efforts. Sometimes the gameplay also feels somewhat incongruent with the themes of the story, though it can certainly be justified. For some reason this is also the first game I ever got motion sickness in, which hampered my experience somewhat. I can't quite place why this is though. Lastly, there are some tetromino puzzles that are really out of place, in my opinion, and very frustrating to solve. I just looked some of these up.
All in all certainly one of the "smartest" games I have ever played, touching some of my favourite topics combined with clever puzzles. This is by far the standout of the somewhat mediocre 2014, and definitely my favourite game of that year!

My Experience with Planetside 2:
I have played Planetside 2 a year after the Beta when it was still under Sony Online Entertainment (SOE). I have BR47+ characters in Briggs, Australia. Ever since there was little to no updates after the new continent "Hossin" was released, I quitted like how some Veterans quit a game if it didn't meet their expectation. Now that the new Construction Update and Performance Tweaks have been placed into the game after the switch of management to Daybreak Games, I am thoroughly enjoying Planetside 2 again. Some of my old clan mates are gone but that is to be expected
Update and Game Status:
- Lots of new content
- Healthy number of players all day long (Briggs, Australia)
Why Planetside 2 is fun:
- Dynamic Gameplay elements make it such that experiences are very varied (Can be a negative. Will explain later)
- Its Free
- Great Community (When played in platoons/outfits)
Why Planetside 2 is NOT fun:
- Zerging and Spawn Camping. When dynamic elements are captured and seized by the enemy, most solo players will either ignore or contest the area (usually without help). This results in mindless zombies walking around
- No friends? This will probably result in you not having fun
- Friends with no experience? You're probably both going to get wrecked and do a deservice to the game
What to do when jumping into Planetside 2:
- Find a INTERACTIVE platoon or a outfit (Outfits=Clans). The game is not all that fun playing solo
- DO NOT GET TILTED. Having a low k/d is fine in PS2 so long you help out others. Playing support in Planetside 2 can play a key role in victories
- READ UP AND WATCH VIDEOS. I can't stress this enough. Without prior knowledge of EVERY game mechanic, you'd be jumping in to a hell fire zone
- Expect Zerging. PS2 still has a "More people=victory" meta. Make sure you don't get demotivated from it and just spawn to another zone to fight in

You know that time when you don't really know a game, but when you watch few trailers or screenshots you just want to buy it? That is exactly what happened to me. Sure, I had seen the overwhelmingly positive reception on steam or the high score on metacritic, but that wasn't the reason. I just felt that this game was great. I would have never expected from the creators of serious sam to make a philosophical puzzle game with plenty of references to the old European culture. You'll visit places reminiscent of Greece, Rome, Egypt and the Middle Age, whilst solving increasingly difficult puzzles and accessing terminals which will raise your doubts about what's true and what is not and about the essence of the human nature. And in the end, you'll be free to choose which path you want to take and you'll be up for some surprises.
This game challenges you constantly with its puzzles and its questions and IT DOES NOT GUIDE YOU, you'll have to solve all by yourself.  This game is a true masterpiece and another proof that indie games can be just as good, if not better, than AAA games.
If you do not want your brain to be challenged, though, stay away from this game: you'll just find emptiness and all that the game wants to tell it's going to be lost.

This game was fantastic, but they didn't need to slap the Max Payne name onto it. I think I payed $10 on a sale for this and that was worth the price of admission.
From start to finish this game plays out like an epic action movie. There's a ton of cut scenes and a lot of times where you will have no control of action. If you can get past that you will enjoy this thrill ride. The day of this post there were no issues logging into Rockstar Social Club. I had no problems linking to my account that was already created. That said, you still won't be able to play multiplayer as the servers are shut down.
What gets me is that this is not a Max Payne game. There is no "Noire"  elements to the game unless you want to include an almost horror like twist towards the end. The only thing that makes this "Max Payne" is the incredible, sarcastic narration from the main character which is top notch the whole way through. One other thing that took me out of the game is how you will grab a gun and get the ammo for it only to have it disappear after the next cut scene is over. Also the difficulty (played on normal mode) ramps up a ton in the last few chapters and will leave you wondering what you did wrong. Other then that, WHOA!
First off, the soundtrack is absolutely incredible. Beyond that the sound design is brilliant. On a not so great 2.1 setup I was able to determine locations based on sound. Not something I'm used to and don't really think about. The club scene is a brilliant example of this. As you move through the club the music that is playing is filtered so well for the environment you are in at the time it really feels like you are there.  Also the graphics even on my modest setup made me go WOW more than a few times.
The gunplay..... OH the gunplay. So rewarding. But not once was I tempted to use dual wielding, a Max Payne staple. The bullet time effects are top notch, exactly what you would expect from the game the coined the term. The story is actually pretty good. Right up there with a big budget Hollywood action flick. Also Max will bring a smile to your face in the gravest of situations with his special brand of narrative, and that will keep you coming back for more.
Pros:
- Overall GREAT game
-AMAZING soundtrack that keeps you immersed
- Tight gun play
- Rewarding story
Cons:
- Multiplayer servers are offline (NO MULTIPLAYER)
- No "Noire" aspect to the game
- Disappearing guns
- Difficulty curve is VERY HIGH at the end
- Lots of cut scenes, some you can't skip
Sound: 6/5 (No Joke)
Graphics: 5/5
Gameplay: 4.5/5
Overall 4.5/5 and about 11 hours to complete.
If you're looking for an old school throwback to MP 1 and 2 you may be disappointed but there are moments that will take you back. If you're looking for a top tier, balls to the  wall, action thrill ride grab this on a sale and sit back with some drinks and painkillers, because you're in for a wild ride.

The game has gotten great reviews and, IMHO, they are well deserved. The Talos Principle a bit of a cross between Portal and the System/BioShock games. You're running around, solving puzzles while picking up bits and pieces of a story explaining what the frak is going on.
The puzzles are definitely the main attraction. You'll be using various tools (five by the end of the game) to solve puzzles that will give you access to a sigil, which is just a little tetris-like puzzle piece. You use these puzzle pieces to gain access to more tools and areas. I only found one puzzle that was timed (and failing it a couple of times brought on a little more dialog so I think I was meant to fail at least once). None of them require hair trigger timing, either. Your raw capability is going to be tested here, not your reflexes or your ability to think under pressure.
There are also stars spread around that act as extra hard puzzles. You'll often need to do some exploration just to find out where they are, never mind how to get them. There are a few easter eggs scattered around, too, to encourage more exploration.
The philosophy aspect of the game didn't work out as well for me. You get asked some good questions but your forced to pick from a few, short answers. Philosophy and short answers just don't go together. I found myself really wishing I could just type my answers and have the game pick that apart but I guess the technology just isn't up to it.
Save games left me a little cold, too. All the game seems to be saving is what puzzles you've solved, what you've read, and where you're standing. If you have a puzzle half finished then quit the game, you'll have to start over again. Luckily, once you know what you're supposed to do a puzzle only takes a couple of minutes to re-do so it's no big loss as long as you don't put the game down for weeks.
The graphics are quite pretty and the music is very well done.  They could have used more textures and more music but what game couldn't?
The game is very subject to spoilers. You're obviously going to be tempted to just look up answers to the puzzles. Don't! Just sleep on it. It's amazing how much easier a puzzle can be the next day. (Maybe because the game is making you so much smarter? Yeah, I think that's the best choice to believe in. ;) The story can be easily spoiled, too. Honestly, even the game's own trailers seem to give away too much IMHO.
So big thumbs up for this game to anyone who enjoys spatial puzzles.

is a small, unpretentious game that manages to do what it wants to do quite well. The objective is very clear: defend yourself against ever increasing hordes of attacting zombies (hey - that's in the title!). So I went into it, as in quite some of these small and cheap games, I do admit, for the trading cards, and since I love games with Steam achievements. During the first encounters things got on in a rather predictable way. I managed to survive several waves of attack circling around a single lamp-post with nothing but darkness surrounding me. There was the ability to buy new weapons and ammo in between the rounds, but no upgrade possibilities for the weapons, to name but one thing.
Also, I could place some fences, but that produced a rather weird result, since the fences can't be turned around so stand as soldiers in a row awaiting the onslaught. And slaughtered I got, out there on my own in the darkness.
This morning, I decided to give the multiplayer co-op a go, and made my game open to anyone who wanted to drop in or out. And that made quite a difference: people came and went, staying for some seconds or longer, and suddenly it proved to be quite some fun to blast away at those pesky zombies. I do have to admit I find it difficult to watch other players jumping around like grasshoppers on speed - be a man, stand your ground and shoot!!
All in all, a small diversion for the dead moments in between the more serious games, but hey, this game didn't pretend pretend to be anything more than just that.
UPDATE - August 2015
After coming back to this game after a year, I have to say the developers polished it nicely since then, adding some more interesting weapons and most importanly: zombies can drop extra powers for the player, such as invisibility or invulnerability. These help a lot and make the game more enjoyable. I was pretty impressed that multiplayer still seems alive, and I enjoyed hunting for some more achievements.

I am honestly completely flabbergasted as to how this could be reviewed so positively.  The storage requirements are ENORMOUS (a whopping 40+ GB), yet the optimization is garbage and the advanced customization options are junk; you can't even turn off the absurdly-overactive depth of field crap via in-menus, only turn it DOWN.  The story is a thoroughly-bland waste of effort and time, and the game frequently has you doing inane, boring garbage like looking around a safehouse to find a stupid folder so you can get to the rest of the game.
As for the gameplay itself, well, it's HORRIBLY antiquated and plain.  Enemy variety is poor, consisting of a very small handful of units you see repeatedly with different skins.  The weapons selection is very meager (pistol, automatic rifle, shotgun, sniper rifle, and a cutting tool), and the weapons themselves very unsatisfying; enjoy unloading entire magazines into the heads of some "armored" (even though they're wearing the same helmet as anyone else) enemies while they simply stand there and shoot you to pieces, never mind the 30-40 bullets slamming into their faces.  Enemies are consistently damage sinks, so you spend most of the game firing far too much to kill many of the enemies; I actually thought I was playing a couple of "boss" fights the wrong way, when it turns out there was no strategy at all involved other than "shoot a lot more than is at all fun".  The "overcharge" mechanic is worthless; extra health fades so rapidly as to last literally SECONDS, so the mechanic is completely pointless unless you spend most of your time standing on health packs.  And you know when games make the INCREDIBLY crappy decision to take away all of your weapons and ammo?  Happens.  All.  The.  Freaking.  Time.  So you spend the majority of the game trying to get back all of the weaponry you've already acquired several times, often with absolutely no explanation as to why you are now mostly unarmed.  The environmental destruction is also very minimal, with the most "impressive" examples being a few short concrete hallways.  The stealth gameplay is quite decent for an FPS, but the biggest motivation for using it is so you don't have to chew your way through more toe-to-toe combat; trying to avoid crappy gameplay by using mediocre gameplay isn't very fun, especially when you WANT to be shooting up a bunch of Nazis.  The story is so bland and uninteresting that I've basically been just avoiding it completely for the last several hours.  War is bad, Nazis are bad, killing is bad, yada yada yada.  Boring.  I honestly can't name a single character, and couldn't care less who lives or dies; I cannot fathom who thought it would be a good idea to shackle a Wolfenstein game to some "deep" story about loss and war, but they were wrong and failed at the execution.  Even the "climactic" final boss fight is AMAZINGLY uncreative and tedious; it ends up being nothing more than a race to dump damage into the boss before it kills you, because you get stuck in a room with hellishly-bad cover.  You end up spending the whole fighting running from health pack to health pack, with zero complexity or style to the fight other than "shoot a thousand more bullets".
Basically, the game is a massive grind.  They even managed to make killing Nazis on the Moon incredibly tedious!  You get shackled to battery-powered weapons, so if you aren't picking up batteries from EVERY enemy you kill (which is rather problematic since you want enemies to be dead far away from you, BEFORE they get close enough for you to grab batteries off them), you end up constantly having to charge off of wall outlets.  Yes.  Wall outlets.  To charge guns.  In the middle of combat.  So you can shoot Nazis on the Moon.
Honestly, I forced myself to complete this game just so I could delete this bloated waste of time from my hard drive.  Even at the $15 I got it for, this is one seriously tedious and uninteresting game.  The music is probably the best part, but I would've been much better off just buying the music than playing this game.  I would rather just play the original Wolfenstein than this game, because at least that one has the excuse of being more than 20 years old as a reason for being overly simplistic and repetitive.

The game has gotten great reviews and, IMHO, they are well deserved. The Talos Principle a bit of a cross between Portal and the System/BioShock games. You're running around, solving puzzles while picking up bits and pieces of a story explaining what the frak is going on.
The puzzles are definitely the main attraction. You'll be using various tools (five by the end of the game) to solve puzzles that will give you access to a sigil, which is just a little tetris-like puzzle piece. You use these puzzle pieces to gain access to more tools and areas. I only found one puzzle that was timed (and failing it a couple of times brought on a little more dialog so I think I was meant to fail at least once). None of them require hair trigger timing, either. Your raw capability is going to be tested here, not your reflexes or your ability to think under pressure.
There are also stars spread around that act as extra hard puzzles. You'll often need to do some exploration just to find out where they are, never mind how to get them. There are a few easter eggs scattered around, too, to encourage more exploration.
The philosophy aspect of the game didn't work out as well for me. You get asked some good questions but your forced to pick from a few, short answers. Philosophy and short answers just don't go together. I found myself really wishing I could just type my answers and have the game pick that apart but I guess the technology just isn't up to it.
Save games left me a little cold, too. All the game seems to be saving is what puzzles you've solved, what you've read, and where you're standing. If you have a puzzle half finished then quit the game, you'll have to start over again. Luckily, once you know what you're supposed to do a puzzle only takes a couple of minutes to re-do so it's no big loss as long as you don't put the game down for weeks.
The graphics are quite pretty and the music is very well done.  They could have used more textures and more music but what game couldn't?
The game is very subject to spoilers. You're obviously going to be tempted to just look up answers to the puzzles. Don't! Just sleep on it. It's amazing how much easier a puzzle can be the next day. (Maybe because the game is making you so much smarter? Yeah, I think that's the best choice to believe in. ;) The story can be easily spoiled, too. Honestly, even the game's own trailers seem to give away too much IMHO.
So big thumbs up for this game to anyone who enjoys spatial puzzles.

Age of Empires 2. Where to start?
I have been playing this game for YEARS. Don't let my measly few hours on this game make you think I don't play it much but I have clocked over 200 hours when I was younger. I would not put this and the original AoE down. This game is fantasic. You start off with a few villagers, a town hall and a scout. Not much. And then you have to start building, picking berries, killing sheep and other animals. And that's just for food. You have to chop wood, mine stone, mine gold and then you can start building bigger and better. And then advance through the ages until you build your wonder and keep it for the required time or until you vanquish every enemy team.
There are many different civilisations to choose from. Ranging from Brits to Japanese. And each civ has it's own look for the buildings and different troops. Every civ has the basic swordsman, scout, archer, ETC. However, each one has their own unique troops. Japanese have Samurai and so on...
This game has wasted many hours of my life - and that's a good thing.
If I am totally honest, the price is asking a bit too much £15 for this gem. Yes it may be much but usually on sale it's 75%-80% off which brings it to around £3 (about $5 I think) so pick it up when it is on sale. It is an ancient gem that is still amazing even today. And not to mention the vast amount of mods for this game: Texture replacers, new maps, resource mods and so on. I would actually rate this game 10/10 which is very rare from me. Thank you for reading the review.

Try this game if you are tired of limitations of session-based instanced game environments.
This game does not force you to do anything. It is persistent, it does not depend on you. It's not created just for you and a small number of players. Its a living large organism.
There is no "match" going on, no particular battle with clear start and clear end that you must attend. This is war, Edge of Tomorrow style. Battles sparkle and die out across vast landmasses. In this war you can be whoever you want to be, without comitting to any particular fight or role.
You can be a relentless heavy or light assault throwing your body at the enemy.
You can be an army engineer providing support for the troops and observing the battlefield from entrenchments.
You can be a frantic medic rushing from body to body, trying to keep the fight going.
You can be an introvert sniper lurking in the hills.
You can be a tanker.
You can be a pilot.
The list goes on.

The game is horribly balanced. Anyone who tells you differently is an elitest who just has so much time invested in the game they can't give you an un-biased opinion. Let me tell you why the game is bad.
Don't get me wrong, things are fun. Vehicles, Hundreds of players playing at a time, Tons of customization options you can buy with real $$$, 3 factions to choose from.
The problem though is, it's horribly unbalanced. As a new player, playing the Terran Republic faction, we lost to the NC = Blue guys, every single time. For about 3 days I played a little bit every day and every single continent I was on, was lost to the NC. Frustrated with the Terran Republic faction, I tried to play The Vanu. The Vanu gets slaughtered by both TR and NC, a few hours later. The NC faction wins the continent. Later I saw, the NC largely outnumbered both the Terrans and the Vanu. Unbalanced = not a fun experience.
The game has fun elements, and it feels great landing a kill, winning a dog fight, capturing bases. The fun elements are very far and few between, and you can only be good when your faction isn't being slaughtered, which is very rare thanks to everyone choosing to be NC. Just not fun unless you don't care about losing to the same faction every day.
Maybe if they added bonuses to lowest population factions, things would be better. Until I stop seeing the same faction win every single time, I will not support this game, or give them money.

The Talos Principle is, I imagine one would say, a first person puzzler. Beyond that, though, it is beautiful and thought-provoking on more than one level. There are puzzles to solve, and puzzles within puzzles, but also narrative puzzles and a lot of tiny little secrets peppering the different worlds. My favortie part, however, was the deep context everything was given. Fragments of text from Greek myths and William Blake are placed side-by-side; it is an historical smorgasboard of automaton theory and poetic engagement with what it means to be human. And, I suppose, what it means to play, to learn, and to progress (or not). I love it. Play it.

Wallpaper Engine is a really neat piece of software that lets you use animated backgrounds, minimalist games & apps as your desktop wallpaper. The trailer on the store page doesn't do it justice, there's a HUGE selection of backgrounds to choose from once you start using the Steam Workshop. Though it seems to be mostly anime, there is something for everybody. Even a sci-fi nerd like me found a bunch of space & sci-fi wallpapers to use.
Some of the Steam Workshop wallpapers are ripped straight from videos & games and include audio which you can disable. You can tweak the frame rates, playback rates/speed, color and aspect ratio. You can create playlists that basically work the same as a wallpaper slideshow would in Windows. If you're the creative type you can even create your own and upload it to the workshop. For achievement hunters, I would not recommend getting this if you're looking for something easy to complete because you need to create and upload multiple projects to the workshop.
Once you install it you can have it set to autostart with your computer and you can run it independently of steam. You can have it pause when out of focus, which is what I recommend you do if you're gaming or if you feel that still takes up too much resources you can quit out of it completely
10/10 as far as custom wallpaper software goes.

Rimworld is a complex story driven colony survival simulator with (pausable) real time tactical combat, for which you need more than 2 brain cells to play. It's also a proof of concept that a good game doesn't need good graphics. Don't get me wrong it's not ugly, but it's not a beauty either.
Instead it draws its immersion and credibility from simulating a lot of things that most games would ignore. It gives you freedom of choice, with lots of (moral) decisions. It has a huge replayability by telling a unique story with different events each time you play.
Every colonist is unique, based on childhood and adulthood stories they will have or lack skills, traits and enthusiasm in certain skills. Each colonist can have his/her own customised priorities for tasks, daily schedules and outfits. Making it possible to specialize people for specific tasks.
Every colonist has a simulated psyche. Certain events will improve or worsen their mood. Having a good meal and all basic needs fulfilled will boost their mood. Seeing a person die or many corpses lying around will worsen their mood. This however is also based on their traits. A psychopath will not mind the death of others, while someone with bloodlust will even like it. Masochists will enjoy pain. A "Green thumb" will get a bit of happiness for every crop they sew. And it's not always the enemy attacks that will kill you. Often the most critical times are after fights when your colonists are wounded and about to break from the mental stress. Mentally breaking can lead people to going crazily wandering around, leaving the colony or even going berserk. There are so many things to take into consideration, like the beauty and space size of an area, or the quality of beds and furniture which will all affect the mood of colonists.
Every colonist has a body with simulated limbs and organs. Each part can be damaged or destroyed. Each part is responsible for either manipulation, movement, consciousness, eyesight, hearing, blood filtration, blood pumping etc. Those abilities are bound to the colonist's performance. A cook with only one arm and one eye would be terribly slow at cooking. An old person with only one kidney will most likely not survive an infection, or a sickness. Luckily there are (expensive) implants and bionics to compensate in the mid-late game. You can also take the morally low road and harvest needed organs from prisoners, which will negatively influence the psyche of every non-psycho in the colony. It is also technically possible to build a bionic superhuman that has most abilities improved, for a very high price of resources.
Had a nudist woman once who felt constrained by her cloths so I let her run naked. She got an instant mood boost for that. Got into a fight and took a bullet to the right lung. Survived the fight and got stitched up by a doc, but left with only one lung she was permanently slowed down afterwards. I took one lung from a pirate prisoner and implanted it into her. Had the whole colony mentally on the edge for days for having harvested organs from people ...
This and many other stories derive from the game's wonderful complexity. It produces more immersion than most other games which just look great, but are simply dead inside.
Im playing this game since 2 years now but it never gets boring. The storyteller will trigger events every now and then, which will force you to adapt to new situations. Be it a sudden solar flare, a sun eclipse, a pack of manhunting animals, a toxic fallout which will kill everything outside not under a roof, a pirate / natives / mechanoids attack, or a fallen chunk of ancient spaceship sending out psychic waves, driving every colonist crazy the longer you wait. The game gets constantly updated with new events which will keep it exciting for a long time.
Had an ancient spaceship fallen into the map, started to screw my colonists mentally. Shortly afterwards a group of natives entered the map and prepared for an attack. I sent my fastest colonist with a gun to the crashed ship and shot it. From the damage it spawned it's mechanoids, which angered some of the natives nearby. I retreaded my colonist and just watched the show. Part of the natives were fighting the mechs, the other part was on their way to my base. At that point a pack of manhunting boomrats also entered the map and started to attack the natives. Also one hare turned crazy and ran to my base (monty python anyone?) It was an epic fight, seeing all my enemies neutralizing themselves. In the end I just had to shoot the hare, while the remaining natives were fighting exploding boomrats and retreating in the end. Got a lot of loot for free. It was a good day.
The difficulty is customisable both by choosing a different story teller & hardness but also by choosing a biome. Each biome plays like a different game. In a tropical area you have a lot of wood, food and animals, while possibly getting malaria and sleeping sickness. In a tundra or desert environment you have to worry about the temperature.
Too cold and you can not plant anything and people might freeze to death, while most things won't spoil quickly. Grow your food in hydroponics (which are expensive and have to be researched first)  inside a warm room. This overall consumes a lot of energy.
Too hot and people might get heat strokes and foot will spoil quickly when not cooled. A freezer room is required to keep food cooled here. This also defines the outfit to wear.
Parkas and toques in cold biomes to keep warm,
while cowboy hats and leather coats in hot biomes to keep cool.
Gears and weapons are degrading, especially when stored outside. They are also craftable and the quality will depend on the crafters skill. Different gear will protect different body parts and are based by their quality values. However, research is needed for most technologies before they can be build. Trading with other factions or space traders will get you the other stuff you need.
It is also possible to tame animals with a high enough skill. Those can be bred and herded for meat, egg, milk, fur, wool or leather production.
The building mechanics are fairly simple, closing off an area with walls/and a door will generate a roof. (house)
Mining rooms into a mountain with no support in between will let the roof collapse. For those comparing it with prison architect, it is a lot easier to build rooms or add to an existing room. I would even say it delivers a way stronger game experience with just 10 colonists than prison architect with its 100-300+ inmates & staff.
It is possible to micro every colonist whenever needed on daily tasks (unlike in Banished). During attacks colonists are able to be drafted and controlled directly. Fights have a cover based system where positioning your pawns behind walls, sandbags, trees, or even stone chunks will give them more or less cover. The only thing that is bothering is the amount of friendly fire. So make sure nobody is standing in the line of fire.
In every fight there is a possibility that enemies are not killed, but incapacitated. Those can be captured and taken as prisoners. What you do with them is up to your moral compass. You can either treat them right, heal their wounds and try to convince them to join your colony, or you can simply sell them to a slave trader, or harvest their organs.
However bare in mind that it can be a slow game at times (fast forward is possible) and may not be easy to understand at first. But if you give it some time to learn it you will be rewarded with a great experience.
Rimworld is by far my favorite game since 2 years. It gives the player a lot of possibilities, with a love for details. It is kept interesting for a long time thanks to the event storyteller system. If you like games like Dungeon Keeper, Startopia, Dwelvers, Evil Genius, Dwarven Fortress, Prison Architect, War for the Overworld or Space Colony, you will probably love Rimworld.

Been playing this game for about a year now and am glad it's finally on Steam. It's been a joy to see the game develop with each update.
If you're a fan of Prison Architect or Dwarf Fortress then you'll love this. It's part strategy, part experiment and the animals are a nice touch. The depth of challenges available is great as you can tailor the game to your mood, which is good for people (like me) who are terrible at rough difficulties. I'd like to see more faction relationships and security based options, as I think the current range could be more complex.
My main gripe about Rimworld is the name, as I tend to get funny looks when I try to talk about it.

The Talos Principle is, I imagine one would say, a first person puzzler. Beyond that, though, it is beautiful and thought-provoking on more than one level. There are puzzles to solve, and puzzles within puzzles, but also narrative puzzles and a lot of tiny little secrets peppering the different worlds. My favortie part, however, was the deep context everything was given. Fragments of text from Greek myths and William Blake are placed side-by-side; it is an historical smorgasboard of automaton theory and poetic engagement with what it means to be human. And, I suppose, what it means to play, to learn, and to progress (or not). I love it. Play it.

An excellent puzzle game from start to finish.
From the beginning, it allows you to teach yourself the concepts of the game's mechanics and slowly has you explore those core concepts while introducing new ones later on. Each level is not only a test of your puzzle solving ability; but also your ability to learn and try new things with concepts you think you know everything about.
There is an underlying subplot about philosophy, humanity, morality, consciousness, etc.. Following or understanding it isn't required to finish the game, but it's interesting how the game picks at your brain if you have the time.
Solving every puzzle stage in the game grants you an ending, but there are bonus puzzles to solve scattered in, around, and throughout the levels and stages that really test your ability to think outside the box.
All in all, one of my favorite puzzle games to date. A game that doesn't hold your hand, allows you to figure out the mechanics and concepts on your own, and challenges you to use these concepts in a way you previously thought impossible.

Do you want to explore the question of what it means to be human?
This is a walking simulator game of deep philosophical and ethical discussions wrapped in a Portal-reminiscent puzzler shell. If that sentence made your heart race faster, this is a game you will love.
That's the best way I can think of to summarize it. I like heavy games, where you catch yourself almost walking into walls after playing from the fugue that sinks over you as you work to process everything you just experienced.
For an example of such a state, my original review follows, unedited, from right after completing my first playthrough:
# # # # #
I'm not even sure what to say here.
Look, I love cerebral games, puzzlers and walking simulators especially.  Antichamber, Dear Esther, Gone Home, Mind: Path to Thalamus, NaissanceE, The Stanley Parable, Thomas Was Alone... for me the appeal is in how they make you think, using the medium to confront aspects of ourselves and our assumptions.  I LOVE that.  Sure, sometimes I'm in the mood to turn my brain off and shoot zombies or whatever, I'm not saying those aren't good too, but I want to make perfectly clear that I am a definite fan of this genre and have played my way through many other philosophical games.  Okay?  Okay.
This is without a doubt the best of them that I have yet had the privilege to play.
Is it exactly the same?  Of course not.  Every game I've listed touches on different aspects of the human condition.  And despite its sheer breadth The Talos Principle can't hope to cover everything they cover.  However, it is so... *polished*, so well-designed, well-put together, so -beautiful-, that I can't help but claim this is a better overall game.
It may not be what you're looking for.  If you just want to challenge your preconceptions of how puzzles and reality work, play Antichamber.  Just the walking without the puzzles, play NaissanceE.  A more personal introspection, go with Path to Thalamus.  Each of these games is different, after all, and one of those might appeal to you wherein the rest do not.  But if you're looking for a game chock-full of well-designed puzzles with a challenging yet fair difficulty curve AND hard-hitting questions of philosophy and ethics about what it means to be human and one's purpose in the world - questions that are posed throughout the entire game, not merely at the very end - then this is definitely the one to get.

Game crashed right after I played for about 5 hours a couple days ago to beat the game... game clock once again isnt workin... Apart from that, I really enjoyed this game. I haven't touched the multiplayer component as of now, but the single player campaign is stellar. There's something weirdly satisfying when you shoot down your enemies, especially when in bullet-time (slo-mo, almost like red dead redemption). Weapons have a clear impact on your foe's bodies, as they jerk appropriately according to where they've been hit. It's the little things like this, or like how when you fire at an enemy behind cover and your bullets hit the concrete chips of concrete fly off like they would in real life, leaving just some rebar and rubble. Game mechanics wise this game takes the base of grand theft auto 4's shooting and vamps it up a ton. As for the story.. well lets just say its a really long, superbly written tale. This is perhaps why the game feels like it wears on too long. Narration heavy and unrelenting, the woe's of Max Payne are seemingly neverending. This is understandable and has been done on purpose by the writers, given the past history of max payne from the previous games, and i must applaud them for showing the tole all of this violence can have on a man. Heed this warning though, you buy this game, don't expect a light & humerous experience. Be ready for social issues such as caste systems, corruption, and lots of realistic gore (not the type you'd find in borderlands which is overblown and made to entertain, but the type where someone's flesh burns off them in vivid detail right in front of you). Again, I really liked this approach, but its not for the feighnt of heart.

Been playing this game before it was on Steam and enjoyed it.
A mix of Prison Architect in the looks and feeling but with more Dwarf Fortress-like gameplay.
You basically own control on a few survivors on a very random biome and try to survive by settling in.
construct bit of wall by bit of wall, make a comfortable place for your colonists to survive the wild beasts and the heat or cold and start crafting and researching better technologies to finaly send your colonists back to space.
Pretty simple !
Though, you will learn to love your colonists. They are very precious, they will fall ill, they will get shot, some will die but you really don't want to be alone in there nor do you want to take care of a crippled colonist in those hard conditions.
There are a lot of features in the game:
- Mood, detailed health, drugs, psychology
- Temperature control with AC and heaters. You can even do a fridge room to keep your food from rotting
- crafting of gears, weapons, art, furniture ...
- research
- Capture / emprisonning / recruitement
- Animals getting crazy or retaliating
- mining, chopping, gathering
- Electricity : generators, batteries, solar panels, light bulbs, AC
- Defend, siege or attack
- Random events : People to rescue from a bad landing, travelers to greet and trade with, raiders
If I had to find a few CON, I would mention
- the kinda annoying interface where you can construct almost anything with whatever resource you have (wood, different stones, steel...) but not really obvious to do
- The strange kind of skill tree where some colonists are even completely unable of doing some tasks... so a bit of a luck there... but just annoying and forced me to cheat to get an extra colonist.
- The lack of clarity on the task orders, sometimes, like for research, you don't really know when the dedicated colonist will want to do that task and you can't force him.
- very limited resources on the map, no digging into lower grounds either.
- The very unforgiving battles. Your colonists are weak and you will need top notch gears to protect them a bit
But aboslutely great game !

- The soundtrack is perfection. Often in games I turn the music off after a while due to irritation, especially if I need to concentrate, but for the first time ever I have actually bought a game soundtrack off Steam.
- The puzzles, which come in 2 flavours. The tetronimo puzzles of which there is an entire free download to have fun with (Sigils of Elohim), and the logic type puzzles which remind me a little of Portal. There are no actual portals of course, but there are blocks and activators and fans and jammers, etc. There are only a few puzzles that require quick reflexes. Most of them can be pondered and contemplated and then pondered and contemplated some more. A few of the puzzles are a bit obscure, particularly involving locating and liberating all the optional stars (these are only required to unlock a few extra puzzles and an extra ending). Fortunately, there is always help to be found online for these things if you need a hint or a walk-through.
- The backstory. This can be largely bypassed if desired as it is given through archive type files, both text and voice, that are found during the game. There are snippets of mythology, science, literature, history and personal information such as letters and audio diaries. Some really hit me in the feels, which was a bit wrenching at times. It's not a happy backstory at all, but I think the whole thing ties together masterfully.
- The world(s). The environment is very pretty. It's peaceful. It's varied. It is also sterile. It feels desolate at times. Wandering around old ruins on a beautiful day with no birdsong or animal life beyond the crickets. Alone. For hours. It again ties in neatly with the story, though, and I confess I had to take a few screenshots.
- The religious allegories. Full disclosure here. I am knee-jerk hypersensitive to religious over- and under-tones. I really don't like them, but here it is all fitting. It's strictly allegorical, metaphorical and plot-driven. Also, it is a cheerful and shameless pick-and-mix of religions from Ancient Greek and Ancient Egypt mythology to Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism. Perhaps someone with a strong affiliation to one religion would find it offensive, I have no idea.
If you have a decent knowledge of different religions you may even find a few of the clever insertions amusing. I know I did. Samsara, I am looking at you, you unhelpful bit of gear.
- Revert to Back-up feature. The game makes autosaves regularly, this can be used to easily reset puzzles by holding down (default button) X. Even better, the game also stores the autosaves as a library of restore points. I love this a lot.
- The endings. I played through each of the main endings. There are three of them although there are some minor variations that depend on choices made throughout. Including a variation based on the finding of one significant easter egg =^.^= I found each to be satisfying and interesting in their own way. Also, the restore back-up feature means that you can even revert to a save just before the ending
and play through it again a different way.
- QR codes. I found maybe 2 that failed to show the message when hovering over with the cursor (irksome), but the fact that these are being used as a form of communication between artificial intelligences within the game amused me deeply. If you find paint lying around in the world you can use it to write your own messages -
One thing that drove me a little crazy was trying to debate philosophy with the computer. It's interesting and frustrating in equal parts, intentionally afaik. I was able to assert at one point that frogs are people too and after that the option to write that on a wall was available to me. This also amused me a great deal, considering I often refer to myself as one because of my username ;)
It took me about 40 hours to play the game through the first time at a gruellingly, leisurely pace. As in, I wandered around leisurely, exploring at great length, but I also played straight through, twice in a row, over the space of 4-5 days at the gruelling rate of 10+ hours a day, almost uninterrupted. I was freezing (Winter here), thirsty, hungry and in pain from being parked at my desk for such long sessions, but I wanted to finish one more puzzle, one more puzzle.
As for price, maybe it's on the hefty side. Who ever wants to pay full-price for anything? I was watching this game closely during the Steam sale and managed to grab it at an excellent discount, but when the upcoming DLC is released I doubt that I will wait for a sale. I want more!

One flaw for some would be buggy achievements at times but nothing that will interfere with the gameplay itself should be expected.

This game has rekindled my love for the first-person shooter. After a few years of mediocre beige porridge dominating the FPS market, Wolfenstein: The New Order gave me a well-built, tight FPS practically oozing character and detail.
Why you should buy this game
+Difficult without ever feeling frustrating. The learning curve is competently paced, and new weapons are added at a medium pace.
+Large open levels that reward exploration and skulking around.
+Hard-hitting, weighty weapons and a suite of stealth tools that makes killing Nazis fresh.
+Well-crafted story with detailed characters and character development. The protagonist, B. J. Blazkowicz, is not just a hunk of beef that can aim, but has an arc and a distinguishable character.
+Tons and tons of collectibles, from Nazified OTL records to pieces of concept art, all building a coherent and detailed world under the jackbooted heel of the Nazis.
+A sardonic and dark sense of humor that will have you reliably chuckling to yourself.
+This is one of the only WWII games I've seen that tackles subjects like concentration camps and Nazi race politics in a mature way.
+A kickass soundtrack full of metal and classic rock.
+In the space of a single cutscene, you go from calming down an enraged man yelling about his bad treatment by the Nazis to taking acid and having a guitar jam session with him.
Things that, despite their presence, still give this game the reccomendation by me
-A fair bit of texture pop-in, but that might be my Frankensteinian 2006 computer which runs on children's tears and hope dust.
-A bit vignette-y, if that's a word.
Buy this game!

Game crashed right after I played for about 5 hours a couple days ago to beat the game... game clock once again isnt workin... Apart from that, I really enjoyed this game. I haven't touched the multiplayer component as of now, but the single player campaign is stellar. There's something weirdly satisfying when you shoot down your enemies, especially when in bullet-time (slo-mo, almost like red dead redemption). Weapons have a clear impact on your foe's bodies, as they jerk appropriately according to where they've been hit. It's the little things like this, or like how when you fire at an enemy behind cover and your bullets hit the concrete chips of concrete fly off like they would in real life, leaving just some rebar and rubble. Game mechanics wise this game takes the base of grand theft auto 4's shooting and vamps it up a ton. As for the story.. well lets just say its a really long, superbly written tale. This is perhaps why the game feels like it wears on too long. Narration heavy and unrelenting, the woe's of Max Payne are seemingly neverending. This is understandable and has been done on purpose by the writers, given the past history of max payne from the previous games, and i must applaud them for showing the tole all of this violence can have on a man. Heed this warning though, you buy this game, don't expect a light & humerous experience. Be ready for social issues such as caste systems, corruption, and lots of realistic gore (not the type you'd find in borderlands which is overblown and made to entertain, but the type where someone's flesh burns off them in vivid detail right in front of you). Again, I really liked this approach, but its not for the feighnt of heart.

I know I might get flak for this, but if I could give this game a middle-of-the-road 'Eh' rating instead of a recommendation, I'd do that. I think the part that people will most find a problem with is that Wolfenstein: The New Order is exactly what it advertises itself to be. It's a shooter... where you kill Nazis... in pretty environments... like an action hero. It does that part fantastically. I just don't want to recommend a game because it did what it set out to do well. I rate it by how much fun I found it. The answer to that? A resounding... Eh.
To the game's credit, it takes the elements it sets out to perfect and does them to a tee. Combat flows seemlessly between a variety of creative environments, each new area feels rich and original, and the story has such an interesting vibrancy to it that there were times where I felt like the plot was the element keeping me going, rather than gameplay. The characters are interesting enough, and there are a handful of moments that tug at your heartstrings, which completely threw me off guard when I expected the main character to be another short-haired meat head white male who grunts out action lines. I mean, he -is- that, but it's still done well.
Unfortunately, that's where my praise ends. The stealth segments in this game are pretty laughable, with AI that makes Skyrim NPC behavior look revolutionary. The weapons feel like mild to major rehashes of traditional weapons (shotgun, rifle, pistol, AK47), and the few spins they do take on the weapon design feel unnecessary or slow. Even the enemy design gets a bit lazy. Big guy with gun shoot gun at you. Other big thing with gun also shoot. You shoot rocket at big thing. Big thing go boom. Repeat. The game is incredibly good at scratching the itch for a shooter, but once that itch is scratched, it almost starts to get irritating. Okay, I scratched the itch. Okay, starting to hurt now. OKAY YOU CAN STOP NOW.
Look, if you're a fan of a good shooter with a decent story, Wolfenstein: The New Order is good. Hell, it's flat out great. I, however, am starting to get bored sick of the same rehashed formula of the modern shooter, and there just isn't enough here for me to give a glowing review. Buy it on sale, if you're in the mood for a well done shooter --otherwise, a quick watch of a Let's Play will pretty much give you all you need to know.

Honestly, a really fun and adrenaline pumping shooter. The merc cards aren't as imbalanced as everyone says. I was doing just fine with base and low level cards before I got better ones. Probably one of the more addicting and mechanically sound FPS's out there right now and IT'S FREE. Can't beat free. As far as being "pay to win" goes... People come on. It's a free game. It is still enjoyable if you have paid zero dollars on this game like me. The majority of paid items and mercs just look cooler. They don't actually give a performance edge to the user. The only real complaint I have about this game is the player count is quite low. But that's not really the game makers' fault. More people just need to play this game. I recommend this game to anyone who has the capacity to blame theirselves for their performance instead of instantly saying the game is "pay to win". Like I said, I haven't paid a dime and I'm playing just fine and having fun.
EDIT: I did a little more research, it turns out this game is EVEN LESS pay to win than I thought. Finally for Steam!
After months of waiting the game finally launched on Steam and i received my key for it, as I bought this game directly from the game's website.
Now the game itself: Rimworld is definetly one of the best games I played in my entire life. It takes you into year 5500 and you and your people are building up a colony out of nothing. You can choose between the classic ship crash scenario where you land in escape pods, play as an wealthy engineer with high tech to begin with, a tribe which doesn't even know electricity or your own custom scenario which you can upload to the workshop for others to play as well.
Every playthrough is different: Once I had tp fight the cold of an artic biom, in another game I barely got my people save from heatstrokes in the desert. At the start of the game you will generate a random planet from where you can choose your place for the colony. You can use the same planet multiple times as there are hundreds of different locations to choose from (locations of the same biome are obvioulsy very similar).
Once into the game the real complexity of the game begins to show up: You need to build a base, give each colonist induvidual work to do, fight bad guys and react to different events like malaria, prison breaks, thunderstorms and toxic fallouts. Each character in this game has various traits and backstories. There is even a psychologic part in this game: Seeing someone dying, sharing bedrooms or attending a party will affect someone's mood. If the mood drops to low, a character might have a mental break down, binge on alcohol or even outrage and attack everyone else.
I could go even further but this is a review and not a wiki for the game.
Overall a great game with very deep mechanics and an interesting art style (runs on the prison architect engine).

I haven't gotten too far in, but from what I've played, this is hands down one the best third-person shooters out there.
The gameplay is so far from repetetive, all the bullet-time and diving around all over the place never gets old. Showing "killcams" with slow-motion bullets combined with the realistic physics and enemy reactions are just way too satisfying. Diving head first out of a window while picking off bad guys in slow motion never felt so good.
The story is average, but definitely engaging. Max's monologue throughout the game adds to the immersion, and the character development is spot-on.
Only negative I can really think of is the amount of cutscenes, they do a great job of telling a story in a movie-like fashion, but sometimes they can feel a bit unnecessary.

The Talos Principle is definitely one of my most memorable first person puzzle games sine Portal 2. The artwork, textures, and atmosphere are beautiful--Egyptian themes, Roman themes, Medieval themes, tropical paradises. The puzzles are so well thought out and engaging, yet they are not linear in nature. You can choose when and what puzzles you want to work on. Or if you are struggling on one, you can move on to a different puzzle and come back later. It provides a fantastic puzzle journey, with so many unanswered questions along the way. Where am I, who am I, what am I, and why do I need to collect sigils to obtain enlightenment? Someone else or something else is trying to communicate with me through a computer terminal. Who is it? What does he want? Should I trust him?
The story is mind blowing--an epic masterpiece.
