Just a notice, if you are thinking of buying Portal 2 instead of/before buying Portal 1: Don't. You won't miss out on a tonne of elements of gameplay, but you will miss some intresting story. Anyways, let me begin now.
Portal 2 is an intresting and intriguing video game. The story of the game is remarkably good for a video game, and will drive you to keep playing towards the end. The end, isn't far, sadly. You can get there in under 10 hours, just like the original Portal. There is, unlike Portal 1, a "community test chamber" option which allows you to play through user-created maps. But, honestly, there isn't much incentive to go play community maps and many people will just stop playing after they finish the story.
But, that doesn't mean it's a bad game. If anything, it's one of the best games you can get on Steam, and a good introduction to gaming, if you're new. The story, whilst short, isn't something you'll be forgetting really quickly after you finish the game. Of course, the ending to the series might dissapoint some as it leaves many questions unanswered. It'd be great if Steam could give us maybe some DLC or, heck, even a comic or a book which would answer these questions.
The ending being bad, should still not drive you away from the game. There is much more to this game than story. The mechanics and puzzles are enjoyable and the way the puzzles integrate with the story is admirable. I'd recommend this game to most, if not all, people in a heart beat.

I was about 6 years old when this game came out (not the HD version of course). I remember that i used to watch my uncle play this at the office when there weren't any clients around and ask myself why he found this game so amusing. At that time i was playing a demo version of "Lego Racers" when cereal boxes used to give you CD-ROMs. I asked him to get me the full version of that game, at that time and i couldn't understand what a "download" was, he simply was that computer wizard who could get me anything i wanted. There wasn't "unlimited internet" at that time, we used to turn off the phone when we wanted to get online so i never got the chance of playing "Lego Racers" and i got a zip file with "Age of Empires II" instead.
For many months i watched that folder on my computer and then i decided to play it. I remember playing with "El Cid", i didn't understood English at that time so i never got the first level completed. I tried to run from "King Alonso" and i never understood why i couldn't complete my mission. Years have passed, i played single player games with bots and learned the basic mechanics of the game. I've got "Age of Empires III" and my uncle was still playing "Age of Empires II" and i couldn't understand why once more. Why should he prefer it when there was a game wich was "the next" and with so better graphics?
I am 22 years old now, i learned a little of English and i have my internet access to do whatever i want. "Lego Racers" used to be my favourite and i never played it anymore, i played lots of "Age of Empires III" and got the collection on Steam to remember me what great games are. On "Age of Empires II", i went back to the "El Cid" campaign, fled from "King Alonso", got some villagers, built my empire and tried to destroy him without the game asking me to. I have failed miserably but this time i did just because i wanted.
"Age of Empires II" is a really well made game, i am not experienced in the "HD version" but i found many bugs that should be corrected. I am currently playing the game hoping that i could beat every campaign but sometimes it's just impossible.
Besides that, i don't know why i can play this game for 6 hours straight, i can't understand why this game is better than "Age of Empires III" but in all of this years i can tell you this: my uncle was right all the time for playing it and if you are reading this you are making the right choice.

And here I was again, sitting well and alone in my semi-comfortable chair, playing this game intensively, so that I forgot how much hours has passed, or perhaps, wasted. As I blast through the bloody corridor, full of virtual paramilitary dogs in the virtual world which is based upon a real life battlefield, rebuild and recreated so gorgeously that I mistook it as the real life counterpart.
More and more hours has passed, and then I realized an ironic fact that the screen shine brighter than my own future, but I don't care, I've been drugged by this game. I can't stop, and I won't stop until I've make a hole to every unfortunate man that I came across, in order to gain a piece of puzzle like those puzzle game  that I watch on those uninspired trivia shows where you get a piece of clue when you give the right answer.
I've been stuck between a rock and a hard place so many times, but not like this one. I've underestimated this game's difficulty, I've judged a book by its cover, I've been wrong. So wrong. The challenges presented is beyond my expectation, I come in with confident, and come out with slight frustration. By the sunny look of it, I thought it'd be an easy action game, given the fact that most action game nowadays has dumbed down difficulty. I've come unprepared. "I need to pick up my pace" I say, but it seems that I can't  really keep up somehow, but I managed to bear with it till' the end. I've tortured so many souls through a cycle of repeated death, because every time I press "retry" those unfortunate ones got killed over and over again, but amongst all, I am the one who has to get through this punishment so many times.
The rule of this game is pretty simple, walk down the linear war zone, kill those dozens of unfortunate hostile personnel that come in your way, do some magnificent dive shot and bullet time, take some painkiller if the pain is too much to bear any longer, if you're too slow to take some painkiller, kill the one who kills you. Eye for an eye. Repeat.
It seems so boring and repetitive, but the way the world is built and the masterfully written story is the driving force of this game.
You're Max Payne, a fat bald dude with a bad temper, the great American savior of the poor, a modern day-gun wielding, alcoholic, painkiller-addict, William Shakespeare. A bodyguard of a rich family with a never ending series of catastrophe follows them, an ex-cops, haunted by his tragic past. He chants poetry as the rain vertically pouring down his head, and the bullet run horizontally just above his head. He has an amazing story to tell, from the bloody dance floor, to the graveyard  where the dead bodies in the surface counts more than the one lies beneath the ground, and to the final showdown at the airport where signs the arrival of many men's death and the departure of their own petty lives, screaming bloody murder.
My words doesn't make sense, so does Max's but worry not, because just like math, a negative when multiplied with another negative, it end result is a positive, thus my words makes perfect sense. it might take time to digest my words, maybe because my improper wording, maybe its because of my grammatically deeply flawed English, but either way don't push your little pink, squishy matter inside your skull too much for giving this wannabe-poetic, review of mine some sort of thought and understanding that I firmly believe it doesn't deserve.

The Talos Principle is an amazing game with fantastic visuals and a very interesting storyline to accompany them. The gameplay is composed of puzzles involving redirection of lazers, placing cubes called hexahedrons on buttons, etc... These puzzle mechanics are very similar to those in Valve's Portal games, but The Talos Principle should not be compared to that franchise at all. It is its own concept. The story is driven by computer terminals, which are accessed as the player progresses, and Elohim, a disembodied voice that draws parallels to God. The game gives the choice between obeying or disobeying Elohim's commandments. Depending on what the player does, three different endings can be achieved. In conclusion, if you enjoy a game that makes you think not only about how to solve the puzzles within it, but also about such deep concepts as the reason for existence and what it means to be a person, this is the game for you. It is worth every penny paid for it and has my full recommendation.

The game also offers four in-game seasons. Spring, Summer, Fall and Winter. Biomes may vary on them.
-Biomes:
A variety of biomes are offer to play on. Each one of them provides with differents kind of wild life as well temperature and natural resource to use at your advantage.
-Colonist:
Each colonist have their own traits, likes, dislikes, relationships, friendships, opinions, gay, straigh, lessbian, cold blooded, nudist, night owls etc... you name it. Each, trait will have an impact against others as in real life of course. Is it good? Yeah, definitely. There's a lot of great puzzles and very few duds, at least with regards to the main puzzle rooms. Maaaybe a bit too many but I didn't really feel like the puzzles were repeating themselves, though the game might've been a little eager to add new concepts because you run out of new stuff and then end up with a lot of puzzles not using the new mechanics at all. There's a few basic jammer-only puzzles in the final world which just seems a bit off. But eehh puzzle order doesn't matter in the end, only the quality/difficulty and the difficulty curve is pretty smooth. A few cases of "how was I supposed to know that you didn't teach me that" that occur, something like three puzzles in the game I thought were pretty bad about that. But ehh.
The story's alright too, though it's mostly told in text documents and audio logs, or at least the backstory. The biggest reveltations are hidden away in the secret areas, too, which makes sense. The MLA segments can be a tad annoying since you're not really free to respond how you'd best want to respond and he asks a lot of leading questions but in the long run it barely matters anyways. I'm not a philosophy major or anything so I doubt it'll stick with me either but it's fair enough.
There are problems though. The game's physics are... not great. Quite a few times I feel like a puzzle messed up not because I did the wrong thing but because the game decided I wanted to put something in a completely different place. There are instances of needing to jump precisely but the game has a tendency to let you overshoot jumps. It can get frustrating, especially on the longer puzzles or when it causes softlocks/deaths. On that note. Dying resetting the entire puzzle? Well SCREW YOU TOO, game devs, that's just... not cool. Especially on the longer puzzles. It gets tedious, fast. Especially problematic is the final sequence in the tower, where one misstep can lead to a death or a softlock on a sequence of 5 or so smaller puzzles, and it's especially annoying happening towards the end... but really, I see no reason to not have checkpoints between the different sections of the puzzle, really now. Oh well. Mostly nitpicks but the game isn't smooth sailing the whole way through. Some of the stars involve basically looking for a needle in a haystack, up to a point where you have to find a connector hidden away up in a tree for one of them which is just... really dumb. A lot of the stars are good, fair puzzles, but there's a good chunk that aren't, at all.
I do like the game a lot overall, it's a fairly meaty experience and enjoyable most all the way through. I don't quite know if it's worth the $40 asking price considering that it doesn't exactly have high replayability as a puzzle game, nor are the graphics really that spectacular in any way, but. Definitely worth getting on sale.

Also the game has a stealth element but enemies keep knowing exactly where I am and start shooting before I even turn the corner (and you can't drag away dead bodies!?).
I know it's a ridiculous video game but a lot of things just don't make sense, like why would you have heavily armoured units walking around an enclosed area like a submarine or train? Also why are the guard dogs so easy to kill? Even on Uber difficulty you automatically stab them to death when they leap at you.
Enemies just don't feel like real people either. You just pump the alocated amount of rounds into them and then they die. I feel like it doesn't matter if I bother aiming at the head or the knee caps. And it only gets worse on Uber difficulty, where 'realism' (yes it's a game, I know) goes out the window, and I'm shooting a soldier point-blank with the autoshotgun in the head over and over and over and he ends up killing me first, but not before I've drained all the rounds in the magazine into his eye sockets. To me FarCry 4 had the same impact when I first played Crysis 1, and back in the day when I played Wolfenstein 3D.

I was about 6 years old when this game came out (not the HD version of course). I remember that i used to watch my uncle play this at the office when there weren't any clients around and ask myself why he found this game so amusing. At that time i was playing a demo version of "Lego Racers" when cereal boxes used to give you CD-ROMs. I asked him to get me the full version of that game, at that time and i couldn't understand what a "download" was, he simply was that computer wizard who could get me anything i wanted. There wasn't "unlimited internet" at that time, we used to turn off the phone when we wanted to get online so i never got the chance of playing "Lego Racers" and i got a zip file with "Age of Empires II" instead.
For many months i watched that folder on my computer and then i decided to play it. I remember playing with "El Cid", i didn't understood English at that time so i never got the first level completed. I tried to run from "King Alonso" and i never understood why i couldn't complete my mission. Years have passed, i played single player games with bots and learned the basic mechanics of the game. I've got "Age of Empires III" and my uncle was still playing "Age of Empires II" and i couldn't understand why once more. Why should he prefer it when there was a game wich was "the next" and with so better graphics?
I am 22 years old now, i learned a little of English and i have my internet access to do whatever i want. "Lego Racers" used to be my favourite and i never played it anymore, i played lots of "Age of Empires III" and got the collection on Steam to remember me what great games are. On "Age of Empires II", i went back to the "El Cid" campaign, fled from "King Alonso", got some villagers, built my empire and tried to destroy him without the game asking me to. I have failed miserably but this time i did just because i wanted.
"Age of Empires II" is a really well made game, i am not experienced in the "HD version" but i found many bugs that should be corrected. I am currently playing the game hoping that i could beat every campaign but sometimes it's just impossible.
Besides that, i don't know why i can play this game for 6 hours straight, i can't understand why this game is better than "Age of Empires III" but in all of this years i can tell you this: my uncle was right all the time for playing it and if you are reading this you are making the right choice.

Best game I've played in years. Tynan Sylvester is an inspired game designer who makes good decision after good decision. I've watched him improve a great-from-the-beginning RimWorld consistently with every Alpha Release and I've been on since Alpha 2.
The best way to summarize what makes RimWorld great is this: emergent gameplay. You will be telling stories about what happened to your colonists to your friends. Crazy stories emerge from this game. After playing for 200 hours you'll find new, clever ways to use the game mechanics because the interactions are so intricate.
It's well-designed. Immersive. Not flashy but rich. And frankly, this game is basically done. (Except I hope it's not because I can't wait to see what Tynan has in store for us next!)
Finally, Tynan is super communicative with the community. He discusses ideas and takes feedback seriously. He has an army of modders and community organizers helping him. And from what I can tell from his protege Piotr, we're in for some great changes in the future.
And then there's the modding. Oh the modding is done so well here. Mod support has basically been available from very early on and the community has produced a myriad of great ones. You won't run out of material, trust me.

Talos is one of the better 3D puzzle games I've played. The puzzles are relatively challenging, and although new concepts aren't introduced as frequently as they could be (I hope you love lasers), the overall aesthetic and gorgeous visuals engage the player to continue forward.
The backstory, and there's a lot of it, can be ignored, but it is recommended to read most of it, I'd say even more so than other 3D games with optional storylines like Metroid Prime. Some of the questions the game asks can be even more challenging to think about than the puzzles themselves. It's very philosophical and broad. What it means to be human is the overall theme, I think. Or maybe what it means to be conscious? The purpose of our lives? Most of it went over my head because I just wanted to solve more puzzles, but it all ties in to the actual sequence of past events you discover along your journey to either eternity or 'the truth' about what happened to a team of scientists tasked with preserving all the world's information before some cataclysmic event.
The puzzles, the story, the excessive amount of well hidden easter eggs, and the overall calm ambient aesthetic are all meticulously detailed and very engaging, well worth the asking price.

Bought this game from the Rimworld website, and I look forward to giving it many hours on Steam.
As a game, its a perfect example of how a dev should develop an 'early access'-type game. Do not be fooled by that label, it absolutely has enough to keep you entertained as is and a lazier developer would have probably finished up a little bit and kicked it out of the door already rather than humbly labelling what's available 'alpha'.
Instead this developer has given constant meaty updates with full explanations and patch videos, and so every time i stop playing for a month or two i get an email describing what fun new things to do and get dragged back in.
I have played a colony of animal breeders, training hordes of cobras to attack the enemy on my command.
I have played a colony of cannibals, luring in traders from the barren frozen wasteland and butchering them from food.
I have played a colony of mercurial cyborg-types. Replacing every limb they could with robotic improvements and harvesting the organs of visitors to keep my own colonists in top condition.
Occasionally i even play a perfectly normal colony of well-adjusted individuals who don't murder-hobo everyone they meet. Imagine!
Buy this game if you want a Scifi Dwarf Fortress which trades some complexity for a friendly and understandable UI, an enjoyable (and surprisingly fleshed out) combat system, and the ability to harvest organs for profit.

The third part of the trilogy drops the praised Noir flair and replaces it with a stupified storyline, a bitter and permanently angry mainprotagonist, characters you dont really care about, and broad daylight battles in the slums and swamps of Brazil with a ludicrous number of human enemies to kill. You basically run from one flashy, overstylized cutscene to the next one. Oh, and in between you shoot stuff.
Dont get me wrong. The action is fantastic! I would even say magnificent. Rockstar definitely know what they are doing, by showing us how to create a playable action movie and throwing the player in a constant adrenaline rush with an alarmingly intense addiction rate. The staging of the levels is over the top. Gameplay is all about style and being the personified one man army. But besides this aspect and the pretty awesome graphics, the game has not much else too offer. That said, I only played the singleplayer. And even finishing the game a month ago, I cant remember sh*t about the story. Maybe the multiplayer makes up for that.
Le conclusio:
You like fast and pure action games on hollywood blockbuster rating with lots of bullets and targets to shoot? Get this game for, I dont know, 5-10 bugs maximum. You will be entertained, guaranteed.
You loved the first two Max Payne's because of the Noir flair, the plot, the characters, and you are now looking forward to experience something similiar? Dont get this game.
Same same but different, I guess...

is very different from the first two installments in the series. And by very different I mean a world apart. First let me define what makes a Max Payne game a  Max Payne game.
The great idea about Max Payne is the noir setting - the game is story rich, the journey is simultaneously internal and external, with retrospection that gives us the background of Max Payne's pain and explains his daemons. The protagonist is a narrator in the sense of Philip Marlowe's novels, cracking jokes, sometimes sarcastic. Between levels there is more narration in graphic novel style, making the atmosphere denser and darker, but every sentence is a gem, a beautiful quote worth remembering. Still it can be skipped. Cutscenes are not obtrusive and not very frequent. And most importantly, although you would think this is somehow obvious, after a cutscene you don't switch to a default weapon.
Now Max Payne 3 has nothing in common with all this. I probably sound harsh, but it is honest to say that there is no game called Max Payne 3, there is a movie with occasional user input. If there is something overdone here this is the cutscene thing. You can not skip them, they are not interesting and on top of that are very long. They do not build the story that much and have I already told  you that they are long and boring? But that's not all. Because you have a cutscene every freaking 2 minutes. From every room to the other there is a cutscene with a incredible voice-over intoning "I have to go to the next room" or something of the sort.
About that dark atmosphere. The original was set in New York in the winter and the gameplay was during the night only. The third part is set in Brazil. Tropical, colorful, sunny and with a ridiculous language you don't understand. Retrospection does not add to the story. Why is Max drinking and chased by personal daemons is not explained in any convincing way.
The great innovation in the original was the bullet time. In critical moments you can slow-down the time and make shot(s) that are otherwise impossible. Bullet time was controlled by the user and because of that and its use in critical moments it was very easy to start - just press the right mouse button. And if you want to jump in slow-mo in some direction and make a shot in mid-air just jump in some direction while starting bullet time. Easy. But in Max Payne 3 you can take cover behind objects, so you peak behind your cover with the right mouse button. You start bullet time with a keyboard button and can dodge-jump-fire only in one direction. The good thing is that you can fire behind your cover without exposing, which of course is less accurate, but somehow I always forget about this option. And this spends much more ammo. But the stupid thing is that in order to make the game more cinematographic there is game-initiated bullet time, always after a cutscene, which makes is really annoying. So that is why although there is still bullet time in the new Max Payne, it is not like in the original and IMHO it is not an improvement.
The soundtrack of the original two Max Payne games was great. It helped the dark setting, but it was also beautiful. This is one thing where the  third game is no different than the original. Actually I write this review while listening to Tears.
The graphics of the original were really something for its time. In Max Payne 3 the graphics are really good but there is nothing spectacular. Still the details and the levels are well done.
In Max Payne 1 & 2 the gameplay is a standard 3rd person shooter. Bullet time and dodging mad it a real cinematographic experience, but in an unobtrusive way, so the gameplay is fluid. You can explore and stay in one place as long as you want. In Max Payne 3 the cutscenes and special action sequences are so numerous, it is more like a rail shooter. All this zipping, chain hanging and firing from a boat/SUV/car/whatever is actually just that. Rail shooting. Dropping you in a place you would not go in your right mind is just that. So you have much less control. This change again is not a positive one, IMHO.
The really annoying things (yes, it is not one thing)  about cutsenes are though:

So to visualize all this: Going through a firefight you go near the door of the next room. You lose control and a cutscene starts that just shows how you enter the next room. Behind a cover you see a bunch of bad guys. You go behind the corner, are seen by the bad guys, take cover behind something small and stupid in the middle of the room. Maybe bullet time switches on. Well armed goons are running toward you. You have a tiny amount of time to react before they come behind your cover, but you are not sure when the cutscene ends and if you are already in control. You start shooting only to realize that you return the fire with a 9 mm pistol, although you have a big freaking gun in your OTHER hand and you of course were equipped with it just before the beginning of the cutscene. Result - you are dead in a second, shot from an unknown direction. You are returned before the cutscene to reiterate the here described procedure.
worth the 4€. But do not buy the extras, because there are so many better background applications for free in the workshop.

If you don't like Rimworld, I don't think you can be classed as human any more.
Rimworld is one of the best possible games, and still it's not finished.
It offers much of the depth of Dwarf Fortress, the artistic style of Prison Architect, and the moddability of both.
Wraps it all up in a not-horrible User Interface, and then lets you fail spectacuarly.
You will lose your colonists, often. It may be to a hoard of bloodthirsty elephants who leave your entire colony splattered with a mix of their blood and the blood of your colonists.
It may be to a group of mechanoids falling out of the sky, and slaughtering your population.
It may be to a tribal raid, many of whom you manage to slaughter before finally succumbing to their sheer numbers.
It might even be to a toxic fallout that leaves your people trapped inside until the food and power run out.
It could be to internal politics, or a prision break, or a host of other possibilities.
But each time leaves a story, each story teaches you something new, and each new thing helps you eek towards finally building a starship, and fleeing the rimworld.
Your wallet might not like it, nor will your girlfriend (unless you get her a copy too).
But Rimworld really is a game well worth the price of admission.

Anyway, if you liked Portal, and would enjoy a game that has very similar mechanics/dynamics, but a MUCH more serious/dark tone (outside of the prolific and often hard-to-find easter eggs), then seriously pick this up. I am in my late twenties. I was around during the "golden era" of FPS -- Goldeneye, Perfect Dark, Halo, etc. In short, Wolfenstein: The New Order, is one of the best FPS I have ever played.
I don't really know how else to say it. The graphics are superb (though I wish there were more graphical customization options), the sound effects are great (the weapons have some serious PUNCH), the animations are fluid, and perhaps most importantly -- it's fun.
Also, the pacing is brilliant. New Order balances run-and-gun and stealth sections perfectly. In fact, it's not really the game that does it -- it's you. You can almost always choose how you would like to approach any given encounter (with few exceptions), and that's a great feeling. I personally prefer to sneak around and see how many guys I can silently take out.
Last but not least, New Order is actually a challenging game. I played on the hardest difficulty and felt challenged enough after the game was over, only to discover ANOTHER difficulty level had been unlocked (nightmare). Maybe I will try to tackle that at some point, but for now, I think I'll leave it be. I love the fact that it's available, though.
To me, New Order feels like it was made by some of the same people who worked on the great FPS of our past. It just does everything right, and it's an absolute blast. Whether or not this game is on sale, it's worth it. Get it.

This was phenomenal. The attention to detail, the puzzle difficulty, the cleverness, the writing. The settings and scenery were all great, too -- the graphics feel a bit dated, but they kind of feel like they *should*, if that makes any sense?
I generally solve these sorts of environmental puzzles rather quickly, but I'll admit, I was utterly stumped more than a couple times (and then realized the solution was in front of me the whole time, but I just hadn't noticed something).
The star puzzles, though -- I mean, in the star levels -- some of those are INSANE. I still haven't mucked through most of them.
Anyway, if you liked Portal, and would enjoy a game that has very similar mechanics/dynamics, but a MUCH more serious/dark tone (outside of the prolific and often hard-to-find easter eggs), then seriously pick this up. It made me feel feelings -- really deep ones -- with little more than scattered audio clips, lonely settings, and some odd blurbs of text.
Definitely didn't help wean me off my tendency towards personifying inanimate objects, though. Whew ... Not at all.

The perfect combination of historical allusions/content which further the depth of the story, challanging mind games, and philosophy.  It combines to create a game that leaves me thinking whenever I have to exit out of it.  Every document on the computers and every QR code connects so perfectly together in story and thematic ideas; I'm sure my high school Literature teacher would be impressed.
The gameplay is flawless, with the exception of the "final puzzle" which has no checkpoints, leading to be a frustrating time.  In many of the puzzles, there is more than just one way to do everything.
The easter-eggs and outside references are cleverly hidden, finding them increases the enjoyment even more.  It makes every player feel special.
The sound track is GREAT!  It provides the perfect background music to reading the archive files outloud, and sooths when frustrated at being blown up by that mine right as you were going to beat the level.
I found myself spending more time thinking about how I should answer Milton in order not to contradict myself and receive criticism than I would on the puzzles themselves.  The combonation of Milton, the puzzles, and the documents in the Archive crafted a story in a way I have yet to have seen in another games.  Multiple times I would do some cursory research on the topics of the documents in the Archive, learning how much each historical reference/allusion related to the increasingly dark story of the IAN staff.
This game blows all other games out of the water when it comes to story telling.  It might not be fast paced, but the entertainment value of the story and the philophic ideas it instills is tremendous.  When I finished, I was sad it was over, but I believe the developers timed the game perfectly resulting in the puzzle areas to be long enough to be satisfying, but not too long to be daunting.
CONCLUSION:
If there are a few things you should know coming into playing this game, that is: read all of the files on all of the computers you can find (there are more than just the ones in each world hub), and play it all in order to get the best experience (i.e. do the 'star' levels from A to C after completing all of the other puzzles on the main worlds).
Play this game in complete silence if you can; the feeling of being alone when playing this game really adds to the experience.  Do not be afraid to split up this game into shorter play times either.  One of the beauties of this game, is how continuous it can feel even if you only play in half-hour blocks.

This game starts off as a brilliant combination of old-school and new-(ish) school shooters, with a fun premise and a reminder of how much fun it is to blow away Nazis. I recommend the game for that initial rush of excitement, and because it's a mostly well-executed shooter with satisfying, if simplistic, shooting action.
But there are a ton of flaws. It does that thing where you stop just shooting Nazis, and spend more of your time fighting mecha-Nazi whatevers. The boss fights are uninspired and more frustrating than challenging. It has checkpoints. The bad guys best you in cut scenes in ways that would never work if they didn't take away your control. There are a bunch of doors that don't do anything. There are some supremely boring HQ fetch quests where you can't even fire your weapon at imaginary Nazis, and there are puzzles that aren't puzzling during the game.
This game commits a lot of design sins, but it still leaves you feeling good about your purpose. While my list of cons is longer than the list of pros, I don't regret playing through this game at all.

If you don't like Rimworld, I don't think you can be classed as human any more.
Rimworld is one of the best possible games, and still it's not finished.
It offers much of the depth of Dwarf Fortress, the artistic style of Prison Architect, and the moddability of both.
Wraps it all up in a not-horrible User Interface, and then lets you fail spectacuarly.
You will lose your colonists, often. It may be to a hoard of bloodthirsty elephants who leave your entire colony splattered with a mix of their blood and the blood of your colonists.
It may be to a group of mechanoids falling out of the sky, and slaughtering your population.
It may be to a tribal raid, many of whom you manage to slaughter before finally succumbing to their sheer numbers.
It might even be to a toxic fallout that leaves your people trapped inside until the food and power run out.
It could be to internal politics, or a prision break, or a host of other possibilities.
But each time leaves a story, each story teaches you something new, and each new thing helps you eek towards finally building a starship, and fleeing the rimworld.
Your wallet might not like it, nor will your girlfriend (unless you get her a copy too).
But Rimworld really is a game well worth the price of admission.

What do I even say about such a classic? It's fun.
Okay, allow me to elaborate.
I first played this game around when it came out on Xbox, when I was 11 years old. I beat it 7 times before I tossed my old 360 for a PS4. Later, when Portal 2 went on sale for $1.50 on Steam, of course I had to pick it up again. Goddamn, does this game age like a fine wine.
First thing's first, the core gameplay is simple: you have a gun that shoots portals. Easy peasy. The tricky part is when this basic concept is stretched to its limits. You have boxes, buttons, turrets, gels, springs, lasers, and so much other♥♥♥♥♥♥just flying around the screen at any given time. It's so much that the usage of portals just falls into the background. And that is the magic of this game: its ability to suspend your disbelief. Of course you can just shoot a gateway through space out of a handheld gun, it's just second nature. The gun is incredibly easy to pick up, and the mechanics are hard to master, and it makes learning how to use them that much more fun. It lends towards a tight, consistent 3D puzzle platformer that isn't muddied down by overcomplication.
And that's the other thing: the levels aren't too complicated. There isn't much room for experimentation: there's typically only one way you can solve a puzzle, and this makes the game an extremely consistent experience. The puzzles are still challenging, however, and this only makes them that much more satisfying.
The amazing gameplay is supplemented with a story that is fairly amazing. Of course, the original Portal had some story, but it was kind of in the background most of the time. In this game, however, story and gameplay are intertwined. You progress through the story with the gameplay, which is surprisingly not a feature most games offer. Each level completed rewards you with a bit of dialogue from whatever mechanical overlord of the week is overseeing your testing. Sometimes it is story-based, and sometimes it is just a bit of witty banter that helps establish the characters. Either way, this makes the puzzles satisfying, and ties them in to the story beautifully.
The varied level design is incredible, seriously. From the dilapidated levels at the start of the game, to the throwback levels in the middle, to the more.... strange backdrops near the end, every set feels unique, and it lends heavily to the plot of whatever area you're in.
Aside from all of that, the game is incredibly memorable. There are too many moments that have stuck in my mind permanently (moments that I will not list because this is supposed to be a spoiler-free review, for any poor soul who has still not played this game.) And there's a ton of easter eggs. A TON of them. Seriously, more than the average video game. I don't even think I've caught them all, and I've played the game 8 times.
And all of this is just the content in the single-player campaign. Most of what I've said can be applied to the co-op mode as well, with the added bonus of being able to ♥♥♥♥ around with, or just plain ♥♥♥♥ with, your friends. Combine these two campaigns with the levels available on Steam Workshop, and you've got hundreds of hours of content to work with, and unlimited possibilities.
So, while I'm just a youngster, and I may not have played all of the tried and true "classics" of gaming history, I will say without hesitation that Portal 2 is, in my mind, a classic, in every sense of the word. Please play it. You won't be sorry.

This game pretty much stands alone in its genre. I am almost positive that there isn't a single game in the world that could be properly compared to Planetside 2, and the massive scale of warfare that it gives you. Overall, this is a fun game, but in order to have fun you really need to power through the new player experience, which is honestly one of the worst in the world. The game dumps you into a hugs battle without any explanation, or even a rundown of the controls and mechanics (though the controls are fairly standard for a shooter). You'll basically be surrounded by fire and bullets, and you will be staring at strange icons and notifications that mean literally nothing to you... yet. And you need to be prepared to die. A lot. Because having a game like this, where it is just consistent combat, also means you are throwing in the least experienced players with the most experienced players with almost no barriers separating them. There is a huge learning curve that, with enough tenacity, you will eventually overcome. And if you are a new player, DON'T YOU DARE try flying, because you will not win. Period. Generally the most veteran players end up taking the air roles, so if someone green takes to the skies, all they see is free experience. Don't feed them, they are already very well fed without you. This isn't me being snobbish, as I am one of the people who fed them quite a bit. It simply isn't worth it. As you play more of the game and get a better feel for everything, you will be able to fly with more confidence. It's just something that comes with experience. So despite some minor bugs, and a few balancing issues, this is a very good game that has done something completely new and different. Planetside 2 stops being a game at a certian point, and becomes an experience. I would recommed it to people who like shooters, or want to get into the shooter genre, as long as you can bear with the horrible new player experience. And if you're on the fence about whether or not you want to get this game, just remember that it's free, and there is no harm done by downloading it and trying it out. Just go for it.

Mr. Cluck was the sole rooster of the small chicken coop, we established a few months after crash landing on the surface of the planet. Luckily some of the natives traded us some fertilized, hatchable eggs, and of the 10 or so birds, he was the only male.
So, Mr. Cluck lived the sweet life - as sweet a life you can live in this hostile environment. And sure, we lost a few chickens to the wildlife, but he was never one to stand down from a fight, no matter the danger.
We were pretty used to Mr. Cluck handling everything himself. He was an independent rooster and always stayed close to the coop. However, one day I noticed that he'd been awfully quiet lately. I only barely noticed him lying in the makeshift bed, because of the tiny, almost inaudible, whistling noise he made every time he took a breath.
Mr. Cluck was not in the best shape. Apparently he'd lost a leg to a stray bullet when raiders attacked earlier this week. Being unable to move he'd suffered severe frostbite from being outside and lost his beak, a foot and his tail. He wasn't ready to give up the sweet life, and luckily our trained dog Machete had taken pity of him and pulled him into the warmth of a building where one of the other colonists had fed him mashed potatoes and nurtured him back to life.
Also, he was delicious.
Here's to Mr. Cluck. One bad♥♥♥♥♥motherclucker.

One of the best FPS games I've ever played. The story keeps you enthralled. It's action packed and silly as hell.

The base game has been completely broken since November.  My list of critical bugs:
* If a farm is "targeted" by an enemy it cannot be worked, no matter if it is actually attacked or not.  This can be exploited as a denial of service type attack.
* Gates don't actually stop any units, even enemies.  Any unit can walk straight through a locked and closed gate, into your base.  Trade carts end up on the outside of a wall, and the enemy army end up inside.  Highly irritating.
* Multiplayer saves cannot be restored.  I understand they are aware of this, it wouldn't be such a problem if the game didn't crash in the middle of a match so easily (for no reason).
* The map generation scripts for several maps are still "missing" so only a small set of scenarios are actually playable.
* AI units just stand in front of walls and do nothing while they are slaughtered.  While amusing, this does take the fight out of the game somewhat.
* Pathfinding in general is horrendous.  Any group of units larger than 10, especially slow moving units for some reason always take the longest possible path and then get nearly to the goal and turn round and go back again.  I don't know if there is some sort of timeout and slow units hit this and they are forced to "recalculate" their path, but its very annoying.
Apparently the developers are "aware" of most of these issues, howver because they are hell-bent on releasing oodles of DLC these have been forgotten for months with no indication at all of when they will be addressed.  I would't mind if there was any signs of life from the developers themselves.
Suggestions for the developers:
* Unpin the countless "patch threads" in the forum that are several years old and completely irrelevant.  Keep the most recent patch thread in place so people can easily find it.  Pin a thread which indicates which bugs you are aware of and some indication of priority or timeline.  I'm sure (or I hope) you have an internal bug tracker, it wouldn't be too much to ask that we can get some indication of whether these issues are being fixed at all.
I really want this to be a positive review, but until these blatant issues are fixed I couldn't possibly recommend this game.

This is my first review, but this game holds a special place in my heart. My hour count does not take into account the hundreds or even thousands of hours I spent with the original edition during my childhood. As such I'm sure I may come across with bias, so take my review with a grain of salt.
Age of Empires 2 is a real tim... you know what it is. Its freaking Age of Empires 2. If you haven't heard of the franchise you've been living under a rock. Or too young to have played in its hayday.
Anyway, AOE 2 is a real time strategy game released in 1998, but don't quote me on the date. You control a small group of peasants and a horseman, from realworld factions circa 500AD onward, such as Britain, France, the Teutonic Empire, Persia, the Mongolian horde and many more. Your main goal is use that starting group to create a massive civilization to crush the other guy. It can be any combination of team upto and including 8 players, so games can become quite frantic. The remastered version has much improved graphics over the original, not that that is a challenge for such an old game. Mods exist that improve textures and such, but it is more than adequate
Single player:
You have the option to either play solo matches with or against the AI, which with the HD remastered edition has improved the AI quite a bit since the original release, in a variety of matches such as King of the Hill, deathmatch, the high resource endgame mode, Capture the relic, essentially capture the flag, the standard random map conquest and more.
Or play through the mostly, but occasionally very not historically accurate, single player campaigns. In which you play as a prominent historical faction or person as you complete their life's work, such as Genghis Khan, Joan of Arc, Attila the Hun, El Cid, etc. Or single matches taking inspiration from real world battles such as Agincourt, or the Viking attempt to secure a foothold in America. The at cost DLC, The forgotten empires and African kingdoms add more variety to the single player campaign as well with their new factions and stories. I personally really enjoyed the campaigns from the base game, but the new ones fell a little flat for me.
Multiplayer
Very similar to my first paragraph regarding single player. Up to 8 people, or AI bots if you want to coop the ai, do battle just as before. However this is where my negatives come in. The game can be super laggy, especially in large team games. Not always, but enough that I try to avoid them. (I have pretty good internet).
As an old game, it does have more than its share of bugs, and the pathing of your people occasionally is a little wonky. Nothing too bad if you can manage your base well, and you may not notice it much at first.
However there are people of all skill levels around and quite active, you can almost always find a game for YOUR skill level, or multiple to choose from. Not bad for a 12 year old game! And generally speaking I've not run into any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, though a couple trolls here and there. But I try to avoid rooms that are marked as way out of my skill zone so maybe I don't see the whole picture.
Bonus Round: Map Editor
This basically amounts to a modding kit for levels and maps. Everything you could want to make your own custom level, make it as ridiculous as you please, or keep it simple. Triggers for advanced events take practice and maybe an online guide but allows you to make yourown campaign level for friends or anyone else, as all map editor work can be put up on the Steam Workshop for others to try out. All in all a very cool feature present from the original release.
TL;DR
SIngle player
-campaign is fun, challenging, and you might learn something, though they took some creative freedom in some parts
-playing the bots with the new ai can be a good match, though the original ai is basically only good for beginners
-bugs here and there
Multiplayer
-buggy on occasion
-balanced user base
-surprisingly active community
-can be laggy, even with good internet
Map editor
-modding tool for custom levels, maps
-intuitive for the most part, triggers are challenging at first however
Final Score
4.5/5
If you're into RTS style games, this is a classic, and for good reasons. If this strikes your fancy, its more than worth picking up the base game full price, though I recommend waiting for a sale for the DLC addons.
If you're interested in youtubers to checkout, there aren't any big subscriber base names, though I recommend either/or Resonance22 or ZeroEmpires. Both give good commentary and especially Resonance is very good at teaching the hows and whys of competitive strategy to new players.

While I'm in no real position to comment on the philosophy explored in this game and if it's haughty or not, the basics of the questions explored in the Talos Principle serve as a strange yet engaging backdrop to what is a relatively straightforward puzzle engine.
Puzzles are sorted into major puzzle areas (lettered hubs) and then further into numbered sections (A3, for example). All of the puzzles in a section are part of the map, which is important for some of the side objectives (as you often need to connect parts of multiple puzzles together to complete them). This format means that you'll be solving approximately 140 different individual puzzles throughout your game time. Thankfully, this number isn't AS daunting, since you'll only ever use a core system of 7-10 game mechanics in combination to solve them.  Unfortunately, this also leads to a tendency to see similar puzzles with only minor variations to escalate the difficulty. The rules of the system are always very clear (at least in the 129 or so main puzzles), though in the side objectives, there are some unexplained or very obscured solutions. One example that sticks out to me is in A3 or A4, where one of the side objectives involves randomly finding an object hidden out of sight; many of these side objectives very much fall into Guide Damn It territory.
The puzzles serve to break up the pacing of the story, which involves a running struggle against a library assistant program, a collection of over 150 documents, a smattering of QR codes which contain messages from other puzzlers (your friends can also leave some for you), voice recordings, and the God Himself, Elohim. The story is roughly that of what it truly means to be alive, and is named after a fictional historical philosophical tenant, "even the most faithful philosopher cannot live without his blood." The implications of what makes an intelligence or physical form a person are important, given the circumstances. The actual underlying story is never plainly pointed out, only talked around, so I hope you like reading. A lot.
Controls are very standard and mostly helpful; jumping up ledges often requires only a press of the space bar, since your landing point is clearly shown for you (and you kind of magnetize to it in the case of moving targets), the placement of objects tends to snap into context-sensitive positions (ie placing a box on top of another box) (which mostly works except when you don't want the context-sensitive action), and there's not much more here than wasd, space, and the mouse. The tendency to want to snap to some things makes some things awkward; moving away from a fan, for instance, often takes an excruciatingly long time.
The graphics aren't really top notch, but they certainly do the trick and have some very beautiful landscapes at times.
Overall, after 100%ing the base game, I would very much recommend the game to anyone who is interested in philosophy. puzzle games, or mystery-lite storytelling. It seems like a good intro to the world of first-person puzzlers.

Been one of my favorite games for a long time. I would say its good for anyone who likes RTS (Real-Time Strategies) or TBS (Turn-Based Strategies). Take a person, crashed ship crew or small tribe through survival as you build a base, defend your base, expand your base and hopefully never die.
Thing about this game though, is that it isn't about making it to the end (I think right now the only end-game is building a spaceship and getting off the planet). The game is more about the adventure of your colony, the story that is told through your and the AI's actions. You may lose your whole colony and not be angry that "you lost", but instead you'll find yourself sad, watching the final bits of what was once your base burn to ash.
The LOOK of the game as of now isn't the greatest, but it does its job. The gameplay keep getting new additions and hurdles to get over. Pretty much every aspect of the game keeps getting better. Once you get used to one build and successfully get a colony off the planet, you'll find a new build of the game waiting for you packed with even more than you thought they could add. I shudder to think what the final game will be as the current Alpha build has SO many variables and things to manage. First it was defending the colony, then you had to defend against other colonies (AI) attacking,  then keeping the colony cool/warm depending the temperature, then you had to be sure colonists got along, then you had to deal with more threats to "turtling", forcing your colony to leave the base to deal with threats, then you had to..... I'm telling you, its been a journey, and with every build I find myself thinking "How in the hell am I going to do this?".
Want a classic game where you start out nice and easy and slowly build up difficulty? You got that. Want to just build a base and colony and keep it casual? Go ahead. Maybe you want to spin the chamber and gamble with Rando, the AI that doesn't have a pattern, just random chaos. You have options. Now you can even choose how your colony begins (starting colonists, money, material, food, etc), the characteristics of beginning colonists, where you start in the world, etc.
Story time! Remember how the game is about the journey and the story? You don't need to read further, but it gives insight to some of the game.
This was quite a few alpha's ago. I had a great colony built into a mountain. I had indoor farms, electricity for days, guns, turrets, the works. I figured the game was stacked in my favor, I was going to survive for as long as I needed. The AI had been unusually nice with large gaps of nothingness happening, allowing me to build up more and more and more... Then I was attacked, no big deal I fought them off and went on with my... other attack? I was attacked right after the first attack had failed. I fought these people off and took my wounded to the medical bay. Unfortunately out of the 3 starting colonists, only ONE had survived, Charlie. Unfortunately Charlie lost a leg, and at the time there was nothing I could do (now you can amputate, find bionic limbs, even put a peg leg on).
Charlie was fed often and had a dedicated doctor as the other colonists made food, cleaned up the mess of the attacks, buried bodies, etc. After two attacks I felt safe and confident enough so I made a backdoor into my base, why would I be attacked three times? Well I was. The backdoor wasn't quite finished and I was rushed with a huge wave of enemies. One by one my colonists all perished trying to defend the colony, the base in flames all around the battlefield... But Charlie still survived. Charlie lay there in the medical bay (now without power) and waited for his inevitable death. I kept the game going at a fast speed and watched and waited until the last of my colonists, the one colonist to make it from the beginnig, to die. I wasn't angry that I had "lost" the game, but I was sad for this one character, the hopeful journey that ended in flames.
I had another base that was more built outside in the open, but at this Alpha build there were new threats that would mortar your base, and mechanical units that were tough as nails. The base was another success and was doing AMAZING until I was hit off guard. Moods dropped, people died... Then a mortar squad deployed... Now with them you have to leave your base and go kill them, or they will mortar and mortar until you dont exist. Then the mechanical units came... Needless to say the giant complex of a base that I had was now burning as a beacon for the rest of the world.

Stories. I'll never forget some of the bases I built or the things that happened. The drinkers, The loners, The horrible deaths and more... If you like strategy, building up a base, managing a colony; Then don't let this game get past you by, you will LOVE it.

is an in interesting take on the Military Sim. It heavily focuses on squad based (obviously) infantry engagements, with the main goal to capture and hold more positions than the enemy. The HUD is very simple adding to the sense of realism. This game feels like a more realistic Battlefield, but not as complicated as Arma 3. So far it's an incredibly immersive experience that leaves you forgetting you're even playing a video game. It's very unique. Squad requires you have a great deal of patience, and are able to take orders from competent squad leaders. Without a good squad leader you can often end up in a state of chaos where the enemy can easily overrun you. So you need to be good at learning and adapting quickly to intense situations to get any enjoyment out of the game. A good mic helps too.
+ Incredibly Realistic Sounds & Gameplay
+ Requires heavy teamwork and voice communication
+ Gun ballistics feel very close to real life
+ Has a large playerbase
- Takes time and patience to learn
- Having a microphone is essential
- Price is rediculous for an alpha
- Some servers take the game way too seriously
- US servers are incredibly toxic compared to EU/AU

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a fresh take on classic shooters while improving on every single aspect of them
In this universe, the Nazis have overthrown the allies in WW2 and took possesion of the earth.(and the moon). High quality Nazi style architecture  and weapon design sets the ambiance accordingly.
Game is visually wonderful, rough on older computer though. Ran this on medium quality settings with a GTX 760 and an i5-3300 @ 3.00 GHZ.
Gameplay is very fast paced and arcade focused. The New Order features Dual wielding mechanics wich is very useful and easy to get used to. Every gun has an alternative mode that serves a completely new purpose. In the later levels, i had to use absolutely every weapon at my disposition to proceed. The enemies are relentless and very tough, they corner you, closes in on you when you reload etc. Smart gunplay, smart decisions taken by Machinegun.
Armor, Health, Collectibles and Ammunition placement reminds me alot the way Return to Castle Wolfenstein did it.Felt right at home.
Soundtrack is very poignant and fits extremely well with whatever happens on screen. Great score.
Lore is very profound for anyone who is interested by it, loads of collectibles and gun upgrades to find everywhere. Exploring the environments you find yourself in (albeit slightly linear) is rewarding for both it's eye candy and gameplay elements. Breath taking visuals everywhere you will look.
Finished the game in 14 hours, went out of my way very often to explore and enjoy the scenery. Played the game on I AM DEATH INCARNATE (Hardest one is Uber, right after  IADI) difficulty to add a little challenge, difficulty is very fair and rewards skillful play. I definitely recommend playing on the harder difficulties.
A definitive must play for anyone looking for a fresh and innovative Wolfenstein game while still keeping fidelity to the older entries.Would recommend a thousand time, an absolute ground breaking, memorable title.
Wolfenstein: The New Order sets the bar extremely high for all the upcoming shooters this generation.

This is my first review, but this game holds a special place in my heart. My hour count does not take into account the hundreds or even thousands of hours I spent with the original edition during my childhood. As such I'm sure I may come across with bias, so take my review with a grain of salt.
Age of Empires 2 is a real tim... you know what it is. Its freaking Age of Empires 2. If you haven't heard of the franchise you've been living under a rock. Or too young to have played in its hayday.
Anyway, AOE 2 is a real time strategy game released in 1998, but don't quote me on the date. You control a small group of peasants and a horseman, from realworld factions circa 500AD onward, such as Britain, France, the Teutonic Empire, Persia, the Mongolian horde and many more. Your main goal is use that starting group to create a massive civilization to crush the other guy. It can be any combination of team upto and including 8 players, so games can become quite frantic. The remastered version has much improved graphics over the original, not that that is a challenge for such an old game. Mods exist that improve textures and such, but it is more than adequate
Single player:
You have the option to either play solo matches with or against the AI, which with the HD remastered edition has improved the AI quite a bit since the original release, in a variety of matches such as King of the Hill, deathmatch, the high resource endgame mode, Capture the relic, essentially capture the flag, the standard random map conquest and more.
Or play through the mostly, but occasionally very not historically accurate, single player campaigns. In which you play as a prominent historical faction or person as you complete their life's work, such as Genghis Khan, Joan of Arc, Attila the Hun, El Cid, etc. Or single matches taking inspiration from real world battles such as Agincourt, or the Viking attempt to secure a foothold in America. The at cost DLC, The forgotten empires and African kingdoms add more variety to the single player campaign as well with their new factions and stories. I personally really enjoyed the campaigns from the base game, but the new ones fell a little flat for me.
Multiplayer
Very similar to my first paragraph regarding single player. Up to 8 people, or AI bots if you want to coop the ai, do battle just as before. However this is where my negatives come in. The game can be super laggy, especially in large team games. Not always, but enough that I try to avoid them. (I have pretty good internet).
As an old game, it does have more than its share of bugs, and the pathing of your people occasionally is a little wonky. Nothing too bad if you can manage your base well, and you may not notice it much at first.
However there are people of all skill levels around and quite active, you can almost always find a game for YOUR skill level, or multiple to choose from. Not bad for a 12 year old game! And generally speaking I've not run into any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, though a couple trolls here and there. But I try to avoid rooms that are marked as way out of my skill zone so maybe I don't see the whole picture.
Bonus Round: Map Editor
This basically amounts to a modding kit for levels and maps. Everything you could want to make your own custom level, make it as ridiculous as you please, or keep it simple. Triggers for advanced events take practice and maybe an online guide but allows you to make yourown campaign level for friends or anyone else, as all map editor work can be put up on the Steam Workshop for others to try out. All in all a very cool feature present from the original release.
TL;DR
SIngle player
-campaign is fun, challenging, and you might learn something, though they took some creative freedom in some parts
-playing the bots with the new ai can be a good match, though the original ai is basically only good for beginners
-bugs here and there
Multiplayer
-buggy on occasion
-balanced user base
-surprisingly active community
-can be laggy, even with good internet
Map editor
-modding tool for custom levels, maps
-intuitive for the most part, triggers are challenging at first however
Final Score
4.5/5
If you're into RTS style games, this is a classic, and for good reasons. If this strikes your fancy, its more than worth picking up the base game full price, though I recommend waiting for a sale for the DLC addons.
If you're interested in youtubers to checkout, there aren't any big subscriber base names, though I recommend either/or Resonance22 or ZeroEmpires. Both give good commentary and especially Resonance is very good at teaching the hows and whys of competitive strategy to new players.

It's hard to describe my feelings, having beat this game less than ten minutes ago. I did not expect to be moved as much as I was by a "Portal 2 style puzzle game", but then again, The Talos Principle is full of surprises. As a philosophy buff, the questions the game subtly asks of the player are both enjoyable and truly thought-provoking. This angle may not be for everybody, though, so if you want a game purely for entertainment, this may not be the game for you.
But a game's worth isn't measured by how deeply it makes you contemplate what it means to be human. It's measured in the more quantifiable aspects like graphics, gameplay, performance, voice acting, storyline, music, etc etc. I'll break all that down too:
Graphics: 9/10.
The Talos Principle is beautiful. The three main "settings" don't overstay their welcome, and each "stage" usually has a unique flavor- whether it's a small Greek island, a snowy Medieval castle, or an ancient Egyptian tomb. One thing I really enjoyed about the game is the semi-frequent graphical "glitches" which occur- purposely- and help immerse you in the setting. I'd give the graphics 10/10, but the shadows are very poorly detailed and I experienced some very minor issues.
Gameplay: 10/10
This is the meat of the game. It plays a lot like the original Portal, in that you basically solve puzzle after puzzle to appease a disembodied voice. Things are not what they seem, however, and the occasional scrap of information you glean from various computer terminals really help keep you creating theories and ideas about the "world" you're in. I don't want to spoil anything, but there are a lot of parallels you could make to Portal here, beyond just the puzzle-based gameplay. And speaking of puzzles, on the whole they are a lot of fun! Puzzles utilize different mechanics that you slowly unlock by progressing through the game, and no mechanic ever gets boring or frustrating (there are 7 total mechanics, 5 of which unlock as the game progresses). Puzzles utilize different combinations of these mechanics, and some puzzles are legitimately astounding- in particular, I recall a relatively simple puzzle later in the game, titled "Nexus", which blew my mind upon completion of the puzzle. Each puzzle rewards a "sigil". There are also "stars" you can find, which are generally much more difficult to locate and retrieve, and often involve utilizing multiple puzzles in a stage to unlock them. Out of 30 stars, I was able to find about 10 entirely independently, another dozen through use of a "hint" guide, and the final 8 I just had to look up the solutions to. Some are seemingly impossible to get, but for the most part the difficulty of them is just high enough that getting them is a challenge but not tiring. Ultimately, I can't believe how much this game hooked me with its gameplay- the only other puzzle game I enjoyed was Portal (and Portal 2), and I did not believe another game in its style would trump it.
Performance: 8/10
The game auto-assessed my hardware to "ultra" settings on everything, but occasionally I encountered screen tearing, minor lockups, and on one occasion, a complete freeze which left me to restart the game in "safe mode" (which is awesome that the game has it!). Nothing groundbreaking, as the game autosaves very frequently, and load times are almost nonexistant. Overall, I'm really pleased with how the game ran on my PC.
Voice Acting: 10/10
While the main character is mute, there are a few characters who regularly speak to you. The voices are appropriate, and you really get a sense of who each voice belongs to. It's hard to describe, but ultimately I felt the voices were perfect. Somewhat related, the sub-titles are also very well synced to the voices, and often I found myself pausing simply to listen to what was being said to me.
Storyline: 10/10
I'm sure some people would rate the story of this game as a 5/10, but as an ex-philosophy major, I found the story to be engaging and thought-provoking. You start out knowing nothing, but slowly cobble together bits and pieces of what the world you're in is, who the voices are who speak to you, why you are doing these puzzles, and ultimately, your purpose in all of this. While the actual "story", per se, is rather slow, the worldbuilding, character development, immersion, and ultimately enjoyment I got out of the game is out of the scope of a ten-point scale, and really beyond words.
tl;dr Overall score: 10/10
This is the kind of game I want to talk about with my friends, the kind of game I want my parents to play, the kind of game I get excited about when people tell me they've played it. The kind of game I'm happy got created, and even happier that I got to experience it. It's not everybody's cup of tea, sure, but games like this, well, remind me what is so amazing about being human.

Mr. Cluck was the sole rooster of the small chicken coop, we established a few months after crash landing on the surface of the planet. Luckily some of the natives traded us some fertilized, hatchable eggs, and of the 10 or so birds, he was the only male.
So, Mr. Cluck lived the sweet life - as sweet a life you can live in this hostile environment. And sure, we lost a few chickens to the wildlife, but he was never one to stand down from a fight, no matter the danger.
We were pretty used to Mr. Cluck handling everything himself. He was an independent rooster and always stayed close to the coop. However, one day I noticed that he'd been awfully quiet lately. I only barely noticed him lying in the makeshift bed, because of the tiny, almost inaudible, whistling noise he made every time he took a breath.
Mr. Cluck was not in the best shape. Apparently he'd lost a leg to a stray bullet when raiders attacked earlier this week. Being unable to move he'd suffered severe frostbite from being outside and lost his beak, a foot and his tail. He wasn't ready to give up the sweet life, and luckily our trained dog Machete had taken pity of him and pulled him into the warmth of a building where one of the other colonists had fed him mashed potatoes and nurtured him back to life.
Also, he was delicious.
Here's to Mr. Cluck. One bad♥♥♥♥♥motherclucker.

However, PC users have experienced a number of technical issues from day one on even the most suited gaming rigs. You shouldn't just crank everything up to max. If you are willing to do some research and learn how your different GPU settings will affect the game it is well worth it. First review so will keep it short.
I really liked W:TNO, I haven't played most of the more modern FPS games because they simply don't appeal to me. Parts of W:TNO carries over some of the better things about older shooters such as no weapon limits, exploration and challenging enemies in a variety of locations. The shooting is extremely responsive and feels very enjoyable, i found myself thinking "that felt really good to pull off" more than a few times.
The game looks good when maxed out, it's not anything super out of this world but the game looks good and there is a good amount of detail in some of the areas in the game, but otherwise the graphics do the job they need to and not much else needs to be said really.
In terms of the narrative, you can relate to most of the NPCs, and the humanity (or inhumanity) of the present characters makes it really easy to feel something in relation to the game world portrayed here. I found myself liking the characters a lot, but the lengths at which you get to discover or learn about the other characters is pretty limited, which is unfortunate because i really liked what back story or lore there was to the characters in this world a lot and felt like it could have been much further explored.
The weapons sound great, the voice acting is very well performed, and the original score to the game does a good job at accompanying the other games elements emphasizing the great work put into the other aspects of the game.
The game does a good job in terms of pacing, it starts off slow and teaches you the limits to the things that make this shooter different from other shooters, such as the sprint jumping mechanic, the exploration and the narrative driven action.
The only issues with the game in my opinion is that there are a few frustrating areas of the game where I had to turn the difficulty down from the second hardest setting in order to progress where i tried at least 10 times to get past, this is mostly due to poor level design in some areas. The bridge was a notoriously frustrating level and i found myself not having fun. The weapon and item pickups might get on some peoples nerves, having to press a button to pick up each instance of ammo or health but due to the overcharge mechanic i kind of like for health pickups specifically i can choose to get them now or save them for later, but the ammo pickups not being automatic is pretty tedious considering how you can't often afford to skip the ammo pickups at all on harder difficulties.
Overall the game does a great job at filling my desire for a good shooter with a decent narrative. The action is as good as  I can recall in recent years and for that alone it earns high marks. That said, the other areas of the game are good or great but not particularly revolutionary or showing quite the same level of detail or mastery as other games with bigger budgets or more resources. I would have really liked to know more about the Nazi controlled alternate history and am disappointed that I did not. There was also lots more room to expand on character lore or other story areas but at least what is here was well executed and sufficient on its own, if feeling a bit minimal.
The game is a solid 8 out of 10 for shooter fans, and should appeal to anyone looking to explore cool alternate history stories, or for anyone who wants to just see what its like to walk around the moon with Nazis.

This is my first review, but this game holds a special place in my heart. My hour count does not take into account the hundreds or even thousands of hours I spent with the original edition during my childhood. As such I'm sure I may come across with bias, so take my review with a grain of salt.
Age of Empires 2 is a real tim... you know what it is. Its freaking Age of Empires 2. If you haven't heard of the franchise you've been living under a rock. Or too young to have played in its hayday.
Anyway, AOE 2 is a real time strategy game released in 1998, but don't quote me on the date. You control a small group of peasants and a horseman, from realworld factions circa 500AD onward, such as Britain, France, the Teutonic Empire, Persia, the Mongolian horde and many more. Your main goal is use that starting group to create a massive civilization to crush the other guy. It can be any combination of team upto and including 8 players, so games can become quite frantic. The remastered version has much improved graphics over the original, not that that is a challenge for such an old game. Mods exist that improve textures and such, but it is more than adequate
Single player:
You have the option to either play solo matches with or against the AI, which with the HD remastered edition has improved the AI quite a bit since the original release, in a variety of matches such as King of the Hill, deathmatch, the high resource endgame mode, Capture the relic, essentially capture the flag, the standard random map conquest and more.
Or play through the mostly, but occasionally very not historically accurate, single player campaigns. In which you play as a prominent historical faction or person as you complete their life's work, such as Genghis Khan, Joan of Arc, Attila the Hun, El Cid, etc. Or single matches taking inspiration from real world battles such as Agincourt, or the Viking attempt to secure a foothold in America. The at cost DLC, The forgotten empires and African kingdoms add more variety to the single player campaign as well with their new factions and stories. I personally really enjoyed the campaigns from the base game, but the new ones fell a little flat for me.
Multiplayer
Very similar to my first paragraph regarding single player. Up to 8 people, or AI bots if you want to coop the ai, do battle just as before. However this is where my negatives come in. The game can be super laggy, especially in large team games. Not always, but enough that I try to avoid them. (I have pretty good internet).
As an old game, it does have more than its share of bugs, and the pathing of your people occasionally is a little wonky. Nothing too bad if you can manage your base well, and you may not notice it much at first.
However there are people of all skill levels around and quite active, you can almost always find a game for YOUR skill level, or multiple to choose from. Not bad for a 12 year old game! And generally speaking I've not run into any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, though a couple trolls here and there. But I try to avoid rooms that are marked as way out of my skill zone so maybe I don't see the whole picture.
Bonus Round: Map Editor
This basically amounts to a modding kit for levels and maps. Everything you could want to make your own custom level, make it as ridiculous as you please, or keep it simple. Triggers for advanced events take practice and maybe an online guide but allows you to make yourown campaign level for friends or anyone else, as all map editor work can be put up on the Steam Workshop for others to try out. All in all a very cool feature present from the original release.
TL;DR
SIngle player
-campaign is fun, challenging, and you might learn something, though they took some creative freedom in some parts
-playing the bots with the new ai can be a good match, though the original ai is basically only good for beginners
-bugs here and there
Multiplayer
-buggy on occasion
-balanced user base
-surprisingly active community
-can be laggy, even with good internet
Map editor
-modding tool for custom levels, maps
-intuitive for the most part, triggers are challenging at first however
Final Score
4.5/5
