I'll start by saying this game is good and it deserves recommendation, but only for those who are into this kind of game.
Disclaimer: I attribute my thoughts in this review to being spoiled by lots of games.
It's a beautiful atmosphere with 'ok' textures and acceptable presentation. The narrative is pretty good and the mystery behind the story is just the right amount. Even though the particle effects and objects to interact with feel a bit gaudy (arcade-like) or out-of-place, the music is great and the handling of certain aspects (the rewind concept and the vocals as you try to surpass a map boundary) is both unique and refreshing.
However, it's a puzzle game. Let me just say, I loved Portal and Portal 2.
But the puzzles in Talos Principle feel more like a barrier than part of the game.
So I fetch a bunch of tetris pieces (holding down shift through almost all the puzzles so I run faster because they're really simple) and I complete all the pieces and I walk through a portal...... and I'm in a hallway of locked doors.
Every time you progress, you end up with one more barrier ahead of you. There are islands in the distance, beautiful sunsets and icy vistas... but I always have to turn around and walk toward the corroded maze of brick walls and grates to do another chore. And another chore and another. The pieces feel like work and not fun, to me. I want so badly to immerse myself in story and dive deep into the digital library terminals scattered throughout the map... but the gameplay part is dirt simple enough where I'm not enjoying it.
The philosophical part of the game of "what makes you human" is not original but I liked that it was taken from a different perspective. It made me think for a bit, but I'm wondering if it's going to be drawn out and be the theme for the whole game. I forsee it getting tired and old halfway through.
I'll probably give it another go after a break, and I'm giving it a thumbs up because I think it's well-done, but it's something you really need to be in the mood for.

Is it worth checking out due it's uniqueness? I'd say yes. Is it worth investing a ♥♥♥♥ load of time and (possibly) money in? I'd say no.

Dirty Bomb is a fast-paced, role based FPS fragfest that is also highly objective based and uses a card system. Each character is unique in their roles, speed, arsenal, and gadget. Movement in this game is essential, and you really need to stay alert at all times while playing to avoid getting mauled. There's also a wall jump feature that allows you to traverse maps with ease.
For a game in its beta stage, it is very polished and has very few performance issues. It also has a unique art style that is very reminiscent of games like Crackdown and Brink.

If you have lots of time and patience to spare, I would give this game a try. Though I feel most reviews don't address a huge problem that the game suffers with, and that is how it treats new players. Orignally there was a tutorial for the game that new players had the option of playing. Sadly, consoles couldn't run it for some reason so it has since been removed. Granted you can look it up on youtube though it just isn't the same.
The first problem that people will likely run into is this. Where do I go, how do I get there, and why? The game often sucks at showing players where to go or how to get there. Once you get past that, you come across another problem. This being the guns. Guns have recoil, and sometimes certain sights won't actually work, and even hit boxes might not work depending on the distance.
Speaking of guns, you get a currency called certs just by killing players, capturing bases, defending them, etc. You use these to upgrade your armor or abilites along with purchasing guns. This is where the game seems to be the most hostile towards newer players. Since you likely wouldn't know which gun is better than others. Granted there is a VR training system, though recently the game doesn't put me there anymore it just forces me to choose a continent to battle in. Often times you will come across classes that have much weaker armor than you (I play as a heavy assualt, and I got killed by an infilitrator that used a smg. My shotgun did nothing to his health despite the fact it hit him in the head.) will overpower you. Though this is more of a thing with the players rather than the game itself.
Now the last problem is also connected to other players. This being teamwork. I have done this myself purely because no one was talking about a plan. Though most players seem to wing it and just try to go in and murder the enemy. This will sometimes work if the enemy doesn't have many numbers. If they do though, then often times you will just get murdered. Even if people issue orders (usually by using a mic) they are really vauge, as they are counting on people to understand what to do. We once took over an outpost and the self proclaimed leader stated that we should go somewhere. Though he didn't bother explaining where this somewhere was. Not to mention that when he went into a sundy (Sundies are basically driveable spawn points that can hold around 10 people) he didn't stop for anyone.
These are problems that just stood out to me though, there might be more or you might disagree with some of my points, and that is fine. If you do have patience and time, along with being willing to accept that you will likely die repeatedly, then I would recommend this game. It's generally good, I think the main problems are with players that are on the same team, not really communicating.

So Wolfenstein was a fun game, not a great game, but a fun one. The combat is a little boring and the main characters need to internally monologue everything to give you insight into the story bugged me.
There is a unique leveling system to Wolfenstein where by performing certain actions (by actions I mean murder) upgrade your characters abilities. This I found to be a nice change of pace compared to gear driven or level driven gaming.
The story itself feels like a nice "what if" story that almost makes you think ALIENS! at first but diverges into something a bit more unique. Most of the characters themselves are unique and well voice acted, giving you a nice insight into the world you are living. Though on a side note some of the character's behavior in the story is so odd I was left thinking the world had gone full stupid(no, not the enemies) . I wish there was a more open world aspect to this game because I was always left wanting to explore the world the NAZI's had created.
I did enjoy the hat tip to the original game that you discover in your hideout, having played the original I tried to use the hidden door to skip to the end boss to be slightly disappointed that you cannot.
The worst thing about this game are the controls, this games controls feel like a console port that didn't really think about the typical range of motion in a hand. I remember almost uninstalling this game in the very beginning because of how awkward it was.
Final verdict, try it when it goes on sale, it’s not such a great game to warrant the current 60 dollar price tag and I did complete the entire story and start a second game in the play time I have clocked on the game (it's really short).

It's definitely a good game, and a majority of players would like it. If you're converting to here from COD, Battlefield, or CS, have fun trying to get used to it, because it will be a bumpy ride. It's not unlike all of these games, in the sense that it's a first person shooter. There is ADS, but it's highly discouraged. The use of it will probably just get you killed, unless you're using a specific card or something. That brings me on to the next point, cards. Loadouts aren't used in the sense that it is your choice, or you have to buy it. It's an actual card that comes with the loadout. There are a few types of cards: Bronze, Gold, Cobalt, Logitech (I think is also cobalt) Silver, and i think just plain gray. All of these come with a loadout, Gold and Cobalt being the best two. Cobalt is a very low drop chance, and if you get it, consider yourself lucky. There's also the fact that you can't trade cards, but you can combine them, or reroll them if you will, for the price of some other cards of the same tier. Rerolling might be useful depending on your card strengths and weaknesses, it also might not be. The game is wonderful, nice and fast paced, and enduces lots of rage in those few chromosomes that you'll have left after playing.

There is not much destruction mechanics, BUT, there are deployables, that can be placed down (to be built) and demolished. Where you can Fortify Locations (Razorwires, Sandbags, Hescos, etc) and defend points.
If you get shot, you'd have to bandage yourself up to stop the bleeding, and get to a medic to let him patch you up.
There are several gamemodes now, to name a couple (I do not remember the exact names of the gamemodes):
-Goes along the lines of, 1 side defending weapon caches, while the other team goes for a Search and Destroy.
-Control Points! Both sides capturing points to reduce the tickets of the other team. (Imagine battlefield, but with
It can get slow at certain points of time, where you have to move your way from 1 objective to another.
You know you're getting shot, but not know where from.
Spotting an enemy can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ if they're too far away.

Currently, the game is in Early Access (Alpha), vehicles are not out yet,
If you prefer fast paced, COD style gameplay, this game is probably not for you. This game is slower placed, and tactical.
But overall, it's a good game. At this current state, I personally feel that it is worth buying, if you do not mind just infantry combat for now. But, you can hold it off a while until more updates whereby more features appear.

Dirty Bomb is a fast-paced, role based FPS fragfest that is also highly objective based and uses a card system. Each character is unique in their roles, speed, arsenal, and gadget. Movement in this game is essential, and you really need to stay alert at all times while playing to avoid getting mauled. There's also a wall jump feature that allows you to traverse maps with ease.
For a game in its beta stage, it is very polished and has very few performance issues. It also has a unique art style that is very reminiscent of games like Crackdown and Brink.
The balance in this game, while not perfect, is overall well done and very few, if any characters, feel underwhelming whatsoever.
My main (and only) gripe with this game is the characters, specifically revolving around how you have to grind to get them without paying cash. However, this is alleviated by a merc rotation system, which allows others to play as mercs they don't have purchased. Also, it seems that people don't realize that the cases beyond Bronze are purely cosmetic.
Despite the grinding that you'll sometimes have to do, this is a wonderful game to keep you on your toes and play the objective.

This game really surprised me.
The core puzzles are well done and challenge without becoming too esoteric.  Pretty much every item has more than one use, which can make some puzzles more difficult if you haven't worked out what the other uses are.  There are also strange ways in which you can seemingly break out of the intended solution; not all of these necessarily seem legit, but it means that there are puzzles with more than one solution.  Obtaining the optional hidden stars on the other hand is very challenging and you often have to take full advantage of these weird quirks to succeed.
Overall, the core puzzles represent a good mix of applying what you know with out-of-the-box thinking without drifting too far into either extreme (which would be boring or too gimmicky respectively).
But where the game really shines is the story.  It won't do any good to spoil it here, but suffice to say that I found the interactions with the computer terminals scattered around the world to be even more interesting than the puzzles.  Not only do they slowly reveal what is going on, but they will directly challenge your assumptions about consciousness, morality, and what it means to be sentient (or if that is even a meaningful term).
This is accomplished cleverly through a computer program that you interact with which asks you questions and responds to your choices.  This creates the feeling of actually having a conversation with someone rather than just being passively told things.  In the end, I found my own viewpoints legitimately challenged, and I can't even remember the last time I experienced that in any entertainment medium.
Some minor negative points: I found the tessellation puzzles to be a bit tedious, and some of the stars are hidden in exceptionally hard-to-find locations which makes roaming around the world looking for them tedious as well.
But overall, The Talos Principle is an amazing game that challenged my brain not just through puzzles, but philosophically as well.  Highly recommended.

This game was exactly what the FPS genre needed. Fast paced, great weapons, fantastic level design, memorable villains (well, they are Nazis).
Wolfenstein games were never bad, let's start with that. The last one from 2009 had pacing problems with its pseudo open world but, Return to Castle Wolfenstein was fantastic and this follows in that vein.
The alternative 1960's setting has a great atmosphere to it with it's hulking concrete buildings. You really feel oppressed, especially in the Berlin and London levels.
All engagements are fun. The guns have a great kick to them and there is enough variation to not get bored. Dual-wielding can be a bit... unwieldy. It creates a great sense of theatre but, is not effective. Due to the amount of kick that the guns have you end up missing a lot of shots. A couple of accurate bursts from a single rifle are much more effective.
There is a stealth mechanic present and it is surprisingly effective. You will end up using it at least a couple of times.
The game looks great. It uses Id Tech 5 and you can tell. You do get the feeling that some of the styling resembles Rage a bit. It even uses some of the same sound bites!
This Nazi killing extravaganza will take you about 10-12h on normal difficulty and it was the perfect length. It never felt like it outstayed it's welcome. There is no tacked on multi-player modes, frankly it does not need it.
To sum up, this game is definitely worth picking up. It does a lot of things right and brings the fun back to first person shooters, it has satisfying gunplay and does not outstay it's welcome. For the prices that I've seen this going lately it is definitely worth picking up.
Oh yeah, the Old Blood add-on is not half bad either :)

One of the very, very few games to draw me in for marathon sessions for YEARS on end. I got into RimWorld the day after the Kickstarter ended and have loved every single iteration of RimWorld. While a lot has been added to the game over the years, it has somehow retained the core of what made alpha 1 an absolute blast. It's a rare game where you grow attached to your pawns, to the home they've carved out of the wilderness, proud of the work you have accomplished and the threats you have survived.
And you will get attached, you will holler in rage when one of them dies, or loses an eye, or gets kidnapped. You will rage quit when raiders blow their way through your walls to get to the undefended innards of your base, torching and destroying whatever they see. You may even shed a tear when a beloved pet gets mauled by a cougar. But you know what else you will do?
You will start a new colony. You will fight tooth and nail to establish a safe haven for your burgeoning colony. You will learn from your mistakes and become better, stronger, smarter. You will learn how to survive on the Rim, to thrive, and maybe, maybe you will make it off the planet. Whatever you do, you will have fun. This is easily one of the best games I've ever had the joy to play. If you like base building, simulations, 'ant farms', you can only hope to fall in love with RimWorld.
I'm glad Tynan waited so long to put this on Steam, I'm not sure I want to know how much of my life this game has devoured. And to think, I still have to load up a mod or two someday, should I ever get bored with the vanilla game. So far, that has not been the case. A very loud and hearty recommendation from me.

The only thing that's worth to pay for would be premium[/b], to exp faster and have double exp weekends (or cosmetics such as helmets/armors/camos if you want to put some money into the game).

The Talos Principle is an artistic puzzle with existentialistic debates and a lot of puzzles. Most of the puzzles are similar to those in Portal, with a few Antichamber-like secrets. One of the many puzzles is its storyline which comes together from fragments of ancient mythos, scientific research, quotes from books and audio recordings. Everything takes place in scenic environments with glitches that betray the true nature of it all.
Although I found the in-game existentialistic discussions constricted, it seemed to have been intentional. It provided a variety of perspectives on the same subjects, which I've found to be very rare in video games and movies.
All in all, The Talos Principle is epic. Hopefully it will inspire a lot of existentialism-related video games in the near future.

This is an excellent game. Since (if you're looking to purchase this) you've probably played Portal 2, for ease of description I'll make a brief comparison of how this matches up to that:
+:
TTP has stronger story and mood development. It's got an elegiac, mournful quality to it that runs through everything: the music, the settings, even the terminal files. It's overall a more immersive experience as compared to P2, but it's also sadder, slower and more thoughtful.
-:
The individual puzzle design and overall game structure isn't as polished as P2's, though. This is partially because it has many many more puzzles than P2, so whereas with P2 every new puzzle had something new to show/teach you, concepts/tricks are frequently repeated in Talos, and levels can begin to feel routine/uninspired. Furthermore, the sigil jigsaw puzzles are...honestly a lazy bit of puzzle-writing and the worst part of the game; they really needed something more to save them from the unoriginality of using such an old puzzle trope.
This is not to say that the puzzles in TTP are bad; on the contrary, they are generally well-crafted, with many surprising twists and lovely a-ha movements. But don't go into it expecting the sheer, lean refinement of P2. Still, though, if you love doing puzzles just for the heck of it, then you won't mind the huge number of puzzles at all: even if the 100th isn't the most original after you've played 99 of them, it's still crafted properly and enjoyable, and after solving it you'll still be looking forward to the next 30.
Overall (and if you didn't play P2, to summarize): TTP is a game well worth buying if you A) enjoy puzzles, B) enjoy thinking about philosophy or C) enjoy mood pieces. If you enjoy two or (better still!) all three of these things, then you will likely find this game a personal "insant classic", as I did.

This is partially because it has many many more puzzles than P2, so whereas with P2 every new puzzle had something new to show/teach you, concepts/tricks are frequently repeated in Talos, and levels can begin to feel routine/uninspired. Furthermore, the sigil jigsaw puzzles are...honestly a lazy bit of puzzle-writing and the worst part of the game; they really needed something more to save them from the unoriginality of using such an old puzzle trope.
This is not to say that the puzzles in TTP are bad; on the contrary, they are generally well-crafted, with many surprising twists and lovely a-ha movements. But don't go into it expecting the sheer, lean refinement of P2. Still, though, if you love doing puzzles just for the heck of it, then you won't mind the huge number of puzzles at all: even if the 100th isn't the most original after you've played 99 of them, it's still crafted properly and enjoyable, and after solving it you'll still be looking forward to the next 30.
Overall (and if you didn't play P2, to summarize): TTP is a game well worth buying if you A) enjoy puzzles, B) enjoy thinking about philosophy or C) enjoy mood pieces. If you enjoy two or (better still!) all three of these things, then you will likely find this game a personal "insant classic", as I did.

This game was exactly what the FPS genre needed. Fast paced, great weapons, fantastic level design, memorable villains (well, they are Nazis).
Wolfenstein games were never bad, let's start with that. The last one from 2009 had pacing problems with its pseudo open world but, Return to Castle Wolfenstein was fantastic and this follows in that vein.
The alternative 1960's setting has a great atmosphere to it with it's hulking concrete buildings. You really feel oppressed, especially in the Berlin and London levels.
All engagements are fun. The guns have a great kick to them and there is enough variation to not get bored. Dual-wielding can be a bit... unwieldy. It creates a great sense of theatre but, is not effective. Due to the amount of kick that the guns have you end up missing a lot of shots. A couple of accurate bursts from a single rifle are much more effective.
There is a stealth mechanic present and it is surprisingly effective. You will end up using it at least a couple of times.
The game looks great. It uses Id Tech 5 and you can tell. You do get the feeling that some of the styling resembles Rage a bit. It even uses some of the same sound bites!
This Nazi killing extravaganza will take you about 10-12h on normal difficulty and it was the perfect length. It never felt like it outstayed it's welcome. There is no tacked on multi-player modes, frankly it does not need it.
To sum up, this game is definitely worth picking up. It does a lot of things right and brings the fun back to first person shooters, it has satisfying gunplay and does not outstay it's welcome. For the prices that I've seen this going lately it is definitely worth picking up.
Oh yeah, the Old Blood add-on is not half bad either :)

Wallpaper Engine is a really neat piece of software that lets you use animated backgrounds, minimalist games & apps as your desktop wallpaper.  The trailer on the store page doesn't do it justice, there's a HUGE selection of backgrounds to choose from once you start using the Steam Workshop. Though it seems to be mostly anime, there is something for everybody. Even a sci-fi nerd like me found a bunch of space & sci-fi wallpapers to use.
Some of the Steam Workshop wallpapers are ripped straight from videos & games and include audio which you can disable. You can tweak the frame rates, playback rates/speed, color and aspect ratio. You can create playlists that basically work the same as a wallpaper slideshow would in Windows. If you're the creative type you can even create your own and upload it to the workshop. For achievement hunters, I would not recommend getting this if you're looking for something easy to complete because you need to create and upload multiple projects to the workshop.
Once you install it you can have it set to autostart with your computer and you can run it independently of steam. You can have it pause when out of focus, which is what I recommend you do if you're gaming or if you feel that still takes up too much resources you can quit out of it completely
10/10 as far as custom wallpaper software goes.

Hmm, where to start. I've been playing Rimworld since one of the early alphas. I think it was Alpha 2 (currently we're on 14). Back then stockpiles was this 3x3 space that could hold infinite items, there was no cooking. Tynan hadn't introduced woodcutting, stonecutting, hunting, crafting, or anything really. I remember how bit a game changer it was when temperture was introduced and seasons were a thing in the game. Or how excited we were when animal taming was introduced in I think alpha 12 or how amazing it was when we got the alpha that added relationships and family structures to the game.
The point is I've been playing Rimworld for years now.
This has been one hell of journey and Tynan doesn't appear to be done yet.
As Tynan states, Rimworld is basically about the unfolding "story" of your colony. Do you build a self-sustaining colony? Do you build the ship and get off world? Or do you just die horroribly?
I think the sinister thing is that you are responsible for the survival for your colonists. Do you choose to butcher your dead to get through the winter or hold out and pray a tray ship stops by and has food for sale? Do you sell prisoners as slaves to make just enough money to buy that food? Or do you sacrifice possibly vital resources for cash? And isn't it your fault for not having enough food or researching how to grow food indoors?
What do you with your colonist who lost a leg in the last raid? Do you give them a terrible peg leg? Do you go through the trouble to research and gather resources to make a bionic leg? Pay massive amounts of silver to buy one (assuming anyone has it for sale)? Do you put the poor guy out of his misery? Do perhaps take a leg from the raider who shot him in the first place (you know, the one who took captive)?
Rimworld won't make you choose your morals. If you're lucky you won't have to. If not... well good luck.

Age of Empires 2 is one of the best strategy games I have ever played. It is simple to pick up, but difficult to master. Even though my steam says I only have about 15 hours on record at the time of this review, I have played this game well over 100 hours on different computers.
The graphics hold up even to today. The vanilla textures are pleasing to look at, and everything is nice and charming. Because this game has so few hardware requirements, you can have huge maps, tons of soldiers, and lots of different mods all running at once with little strain on your system.
The campaigns range in difficulty from super easy to rather difficult. Each campaign has you follow the history of some of the world's greatest military commanders, and you control the battles they fight in. The missions can last from 30 minutes to well over an hour, and are all fun with lots of hidden secrets. There are also many stand-alone battles, which usually focus much more on military tactics rather than exploration and resource management. You can also play a quick match with the setting, opponents, and goal of your choosing.
This game also has a thriving multiplayer scene. I've heard that many people have trouble with getting online to work, though, so you may run into trouble if you decide to play multiplayer. And for players who have played lots of strategy games before, you may find that the game is too easy, especially for some campaigns. Sometimes, the AI bugs out as well. For example, I had a group of knights run off and attack a mining camp when I explicitly told them to attack a barracks. These instances are usually rare, and they do not impact play that much.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game both at the sale price of roughly 4 dollars, and the full price. I also recommend buying all the available DLC, as they give you more civilizations and extra campaigns. This is an engrossing, fun strategy game that has stood the test of time, and will continue to be one of the top computer strategy games for years to come.

Absolutely recommending the game but there are some prerequisites for you to like the game in the first place:
1 - you like puzzles (literally puzzles, there are even some tetris-like sections and no puzzle is as fast paced as portal in any way)
2 - you like to think, elaborate, and you enjoy philosophy
Why? The point 1 (puzzles) because the game is really all about puzzles. You have many rooms (like the test rooms in Portal) where you have to reach a certain point. You are able to reach those points by interacting with some objects, going further in the game unlocks some 'gadgets'. The puzzles WILL get repetitive after a while bacause you unlock most things almost right at the beginning.
The point 2: there is A LOT to read and to listen to in the game. Basically everything is absolutely interesting and reading is not enough. You have to know what you are reading. The more you know about philosphy and culture in general, the more you will appreciate and understand the texts.
If you think you miss one of the 2 prerequisites, you will find the game either boring or meaningless (or both).

"I liked Portal 2, but can a puzzle game really claim to be worth forty dollars?"  Yes.  Without reservation, yes.
For one thing, I'm twenty hours in and about halfway through with the puzzles.  Mostly nonlinear, some of them really challenging and boy there sure are a lot of them.  The world is GORGEOUS.  Writing is pretty good conceptually and there's some good fresh concepts in here.  Talking about them much would be minor spoilers, but it's been a long time since I've had a good existential crisis.  Maybe best not to know exactly what's coming.
Portal aimed for dark and funny and hit the mark.  The Talos Principle aims for introspective, deeply philosophical and kind of scary, and also hits the mark just as hard.  There's some plot interactivity, and it feels meaningful.
I'd say this game is a huge underdog, but that would be unfair because almost everyone I know is recommending it.  Maybe even worth a buy when not on sale.

I've played a few early access games and Riwworld is one of my favourite games.   I've backed this back in 2013 and I tend to play couple of hours a week with it.   No two games are the same when playing and it can be super frustrating or super awesome.   I've still yet to actually escape from this Rimworld but I've loved every second.      The game can seem super complicated at first but it's easy to pick up the basics and you will soon be growing, mining, researching and maybe eating human flesh.
The basic premise of the game is you crash land on a planet and have to survive.   Will you dig deep into the mountains and make a fortress, build a massive log castle outside that might just get set fire to by raiders or wait and build up super strong stone walls.
Now about the game the standard vanilla rimworld is lots of fun and will give you hours of gameplay.  But then if you add in the fact this game loves mods and some of the mods people produce are insanely good.   Do you like zombies then there is a mod, do you like raiders on atv's there is a mod for that, how about mods that manage your resource levels yep again there is a mod.
With the inbuilt modding in alpha 14 it makes it super easy to apply mods and you can do it all from in game from the steam workshop which is AMAZING.   If you struggle installing mods as it seems complicated you will love this.
Oh and alpha 14 now has a scenario editor so you can create custom scenarios to play.   Imagine starting out a new colony with 100 pet elephants yes you can become hannibal and have a horde of elephants its mucho fun.
I think the price is fine considering this came out three years and I'm still playing it, it's still got an active developer and super passionate fans.  So don't think you are getting a buggy early game with placeholder game as you are buying an awesome game.

Here are a list of Pros and Cons:
Pros:
The game has a nice, clean feel.
The concept of building robots out of different cubes and then fighting with other players using their own bots is amazing.
There is a wide veriety of fun weapons and movement types.
The game never gets old, replayability is very high.
New updates containing new movement, weapons, maps, game-modes or other stuff are frequent.
The game's dedicated servers are very good.
The game is very fun to play with others.
The decelopers of the game always seem to be coming out with something new, and patches to keep bugs from slowly consuming the game are always being added.
The game is fun and not gory or violent.
Cons:
The graphics quality of the game is not 1st rate, even on Fantastic, the game is a little chunky.
Some of the recent updates have been unfair for certain bot types.
Recent upadates have made way for very annoying bots, such as Ion Distorter, (Shotguns,) combined with a Ghost Module, (Invisibilty Booster.) a few hovers and a couple thrusters. These 'Noob' Bots are generally easy to make, get, play, and ruin the lives of other players.
A lot of people including myself miss Tiers.

One of the very, very few games to draw me in for marathon sessions for YEARS on end. I got into RimWorld the day after the Kickstarter ended and have loved every single iteration of RimWorld. While a lot has been added to the game over the years, it has somehow retained the core of what made alpha 1 an absolute blast. It's a rare game where you grow attached to your pawns, to the home they've carved out of the wilderness, proud of the work you have accomplished and the threats you have survived.
And you will get attached, you will holler in rage when one of them dies, or loses an eye, or gets kidnapped. You will rage quit when raiders blow their way through your walls to get to the undefended innards of your base, torching and destroying whatever they see. You may even shed a tear when a beloved pet gets mauled by a cougar. But you know what else you will do?
You will start a new colony. You will fight tooth and nail to establish a safe haven for your burgeoning colony. You will learn from your mistakes and become better, stronger, smarter. You will learn how to survive on the Rim, to thrive, and maybe, maybe you will make it off the planet. Whatever you do, you will have fun. This is easily one of the best games I've ever had the joy to play. If you like base building, simulations, 'ant farms', you can only hope to fall in love with RimWorld.
I'm glad Tynan waited so long to put this on Steam, I'm not sure I want to know how much of my life this game has devoured. This is how a puzzle game is supposed to be structured. Guiding your hand at the beginning of new concepts, then gradually making it more and more difficult as you solve more and more, while not forcing your hand down a narrow path and showing you point blank what to do. This game can be extremely challenging, which makes it all the worth while when you solve a difficult puzzle without the aid of a guide (Full admission: I've used a couple, which only has made me appreciate the devs and more creative players that much more).
It also exposes the player to deep philosophical conversation points (What makes us human? What exactly is conscious? etc.), if they choose to. This game is also an open world. You don't have to solve all the puzzles to beat the game, and you don't have to read all of the text from the terminals, but I highly recommend you do so.
I've beaten this game a while ago (with all of the endings), but I've decided to re-play it with Serious Sam in place of Elohim (I got it for free as a promo, but it's now DLC). All in all, I would say it took me about 20 hours for my first playthrough, that's with not solving all puzzles and using a couple of guides when I got really stuck.
This game is an experience that is hard to match. If your a puzzle junky or an aspiring one, this is a must.
Also, thank you Croteam for your hard work at putting this on Linux, as well as your others!!

I don't normally take the time to go and write reccomendations, but wow. This game is amazing. It's definitely a puzzle game, with a really interesting story as long as you actually listen to the dialog and want to figure out what's going on. It's extremely immersive, just don't jump into the game thinking it's some pretentious indie game BS art piece whatever, the cynicism will totally kill any enjoyment you'll get out of it.
Each area has puzzles to do that you need to do to progress, each in it's own contained area, but getting the rest of the story and seeing more of the world relies on you getting gold stars, which for the most part, rely on you metagaming the puzzles, finding ways to break them and have them interact with each other and the outside world to unlock the stars. There are quite a few times where you really just need to stop and figure out everything out of the ordinary you can do with each puzzle to solve something in another area.
It's compared alot to portal, but it's nowhere near as lighthearted as portal. It's philosophical (Which I guess is where people thinking it's pretentious comes from, but come on, sometimes things are actually deep and you need to think and contemplate ideas. It's not bad to use your head people, not everything is handed to you on a platter!) and has some genuinely uncanny, sometimes even scary moments.
The best comparison to portal 2 I can think of is that the whole game feels like those moments (Mostly in the condemned underground testing area) where part of the puzzle is cut off or broken or something and you're suddenly taken out of the contained puzzle area to find some solution outside using the environment and unorthodox means to progress.
The whole game is like that, and because of that, you end up seeing a lot of extra things, secrets and easter eggs, of which this game has LOTS. Some are throwbacks to movies and other games (There were quite a few I didn't get, but plenty I did), and each one is a joy to stumble into. Some even give some more backstory. All in, they're all interesting, well hidden, and complement the mindset you have to put yourself in to get through everything.
If you're one of those people who just can't stop and take in the scenery, or you have absolutely no interest in story, pacing, puzzles, or thinking, and just need some quick action, this definitely isn't going to be interesting. If not, this is fantastic. It's challenging, engaging, immersive, and leaves you on edge, wanting to learn more and more.

Wolfenstein: The New Order follows vaguely along from Wolfenstein: 3D, and also led to the release of the DLC The Old Blood. The Fourth Reich have won WW2, but the Resistance are fighting back. In my opinion, this dystopian environment is an interesting one for a game, as there are many fictiocious people and objects that the game can create, such as Panzerhunds. The game's graphics are really good, and run well on PC. Having not completely finished the game at the time of review, the story is so far quite engaging, taking you from Berlin, then to London, Gibraltar, and so on. The game also captures well an idea of what the Nazis were capable of in WW2, and what the world would have looked like under their reign. There is never a shortage of ammo in a mission area which is nice. The only negative I feel about this game is that ammo/armour/health pickups have to be picked up individually, rather than just walking over them for pickup. Otherwise, the item system is OK.
Overall, the mindless carnage of killing Nazis is great, but  can becoming repetitive, and there are some small elements needing a fix that could make an even better game.

You will learn how to survive on the Rim, to thrive, and maybe, maybe you will make it off the planet. Whatever you do, you will have fun. This is easily one of the best games I've ever had the joy to play. If you like base building, simulations, 'ant farms', you can only hope to fall in love with RimWorld.
I'm glad Tynan waited so long to put this on Steam, I'm not sure I want to know how much of my life this game has devoured. And to think, I still have to load up a mod or two someday, should I ever get bored with the vanilla game. So far, that has not been the case. A very loud and hearty recommendation from me.

Age of Empires 2 is one of the best strategy games I have ever played. It is simple to pick up, but difficult to master. Even though my steam says I only have about 15 hours on record at the time of this review, I have played this game well over 100 hours on different computers.
The graphics hold up even to today. The vanilla textures are pleasing to look at, and everything is nice and charming. Because this game has so few hardware requirements, you can have huge maps, tons of soldiers, and lots of different mods all running at once with little strain on your system.
The campaigns range in difficulty from super easy to rather difficult. Each campaign has you follow the history of some of the world's greatest military commanders, and you control the battles they fight in. The missions can last from 30 minutes to well over an hour, and are all fun with lots of hidden secrets. There are also many stand-alone battles, which usually focus much more on military tactics rather than exploration and resource management. You can also play a quick match with the setting, opponents, and goal of your choosing.
This game also has a thriving multiplayer scene. I've heard that many people have trouble with getting online to work, though, so you may run into trouble if you decide to play multiplayer. And for players who have played lots of strategy games before, you may find that the game is too easy, especially for some campaigns. Sometimes, the AI bugs out as well. For example, I had a group of knights run off and attack a mining camp when I explicitly told them to attack a barracks. These instances are usually rare, and they do not impact play that much.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game both at the sale price of roughly 4 dollars, and the full price. I also recommend buying all the available DLC, as they give you more civilizations and extra campaigns. This is an engrossing, fun strategy game that has stood the test of time, and will continue to be one of the top computer strategy games for years to come.

Robocraft is a very good game. Here are some good (and bad, as not to be bais) points on why.
First and foremost, it's a very original game. While the aspects of building a robot to destroy other robots isn't exactly new, no other game has been to this scale, or has been to this quality. The building aspect is very, very good as there is so many different blocks to choose from, different weapons to attach, and all sorts of utilities.
And all of these amazing things are balanced by your power. If you have too many blocks, the game won't let you place any more. This makes the start of the game, where most of the blocks are locked off for a progressive feature, more fair. Being that the vehicles are generally smaller, with a little less firepower. This is a perfect levelling system, as your power increases with every level, also widening the amount of blocks you hava available. Some blocks, that are more powerful than others, require more power to place, so planning your vehicle is essential. Do you want to be a fortress? That can overcome any enemy with sheer heath and firepower? Or do you want to be a singular lazer, singlular block and a singular hover fan so you can zip around with a ridiculously small hitbox, creating havok like a bee at a picnic? It's your choice!
However, it would not be fair if I didn't mention a few downsides.
First thing people will notice is the difference in levels between players you are put against. As I mentioned before, the progression system allows for a good style of play, favoring those who actually spend time to play the game. However in most matches you will be placed with at least 1 or 2 players, both on your team and the enemy, that will be completely superior in every way, shape and form. Quite literally.
And also, there are some aspects that do favor a more pay-to-win style of gameplay. Again as stated before, with the progression system F2P players will have a blast, but it also leaves the gap for P2P players to stomp people down with their superior firepower, even at the same level. While most P2P features are merely cosmetic, there are quite a few that include both more of normal weapons and exclusive weapons and utilities.
But either way, the game is fun and very enjoyable. A recommendation to people who don't like to spend money to get a good game!

This is how a puzzle game is supposed to be structured. Guiding your hand at the beginning of new concepts, then gradually making it more and more difficult as you solve more and more, while not forcing your hand down a narrow path and showing you point blank what to do. This game can be extremely challenging, which makes it all the worth while when you solve a difficult puzzle without the aid of a guide (Full admission: I've used a couple, which only has made me appreciate the devs and more creative players that much more).
It also exposes the player to deep philosophical conversation points (What makes us human? What exactly is conscious? etc.), if they choose to. This game is also an open world. You don't have to solve all the puzzles to beat the game, and you don't have to read all of the text from the terminals, but I highly recommend you do so.

I don't normally take the time to go and write reccomendations, but wow. This game is amazing. It's definitely a puzzle game, with a really interesting story as long as you actually listen to the dialog and want to figure out what's going on. It's extremely immersive, just don't jump into the game thinking it's some pretentious indie game BS art piece whatever, the cynicism will totally kill any enjoyment you'll get out of it.
Each area has puzzles to do that you need to do to progress, each in it's own contained area, but getting the rest of the story and seeing more of the world relies on you getting gold stars, which for the most part, rely on you metagaming the puzzles, finding ways to break them and have them interact with each other and the outside world to unlock the stars. There are quite a few times where you really just need to stop and figure out everything out of the ordinary you can do with each puzzle to solve something in another area.
It's compared alot to portal, but it's nowhere near as lighthearted as portal. It's philosophical (Which I guess is where people thinking it's pretentious comes from, but come on, sometimes things are actually deep and you need to think and contemplate ideas. It's not bad to use your head people, not everything is handed to you on a platter!) and has some genuinely uncanny, sometimes even scary moments.
The best comparison to portal 2 I can think of is that the whole game feels like those moments (Mostly in the condemned underground testing area) where part of the puzzle is cut off or broken or something and you're suddenly taken out of the contained puzzle area to find some solution outside using the environment and unorthodox means to progress.
The whole game is like that, and because of that, you end up seeing a lot of extra things, secrets and easter eggs, of which this game has LOTS. Some are throwbacks to movies and other games (There were quite a few I didn't get, but plenty I did), and each one is a joy to stumble into. Some even give some more backstory. All in, they're all interesting, well hidden, and complement the mindset you have to put yourself in to get through everything.
If you're one of those people who just can't stop and take in the scenery, or you have absolutely no interest in story, pacing, puzzles, or thinking, and just need some quick action, this definitely isn't going to be interesting. If not, this is fantastic. It's challenging, engaging, immersive, and leaves you on edge, wanting to learn more and more.

Admittedly, this game is not that easy to "get into."  The game drops you in a newbie zone with little guidance on what to do or how to do it.   However, *when* you get the hang of it--and you will, it's controls are intuitive once you learn them--the game becomes much less about how to do things and more about what to do.  And there's plenty to do.
Join the infantry and assault a base on foot?  Check.  Pilot a ship to provide air support?  Check.  Command a tank and assault a base from afar?  Check.  This game has it all.
The game is extremely well balanced, and is definitely not "pay to win", despite the optional micro-transactions.  All weapons are fully balanced, trading firing speed for accuracy or faster projectiles.  Classes all are balanced, making each unique with their own strengths, weaknesses, and purposes.
Do you always get killed when encountering another player on foot?  No problem!  There are several "support" classes that will keep you involved in base assaults but out of the line-of-fire.  The game even offers support roles for ground (Sunderer) and air (Galaxy) transportation.
Overall, this game does not get the attention it deserves. While people fawn over TF2, Overwatch, The Division, etc.., this game sits in the background, but with enough players to support both heavy (100s vs 100s) and light (dozens vs dozens) battles.  A distinct downside of this game is the graphics requirements--I had to upgrade my card (to Radeon R9 380) to participate in the 100s vs 100s battles.  If your GPU is older, you can still play, but the smaller battles will not be as "intense."
My recommendation: Try this game, give it a shot.  Its free to play!

This game somehow strikes a balance across all forms of FPS gameplay; one minute you’re blasting away enemies with your gigantic guns in the middle of a Nazi base and the next you’re sneaking around corners and backstabbing enemy commanders before they can radio for help. You even infiltrate a Nazi base on the moon, because why not? Very rarely do I play a game that is such a refreshing and enjoyable experience from beginning to end. The gunplay is intense, the graphics are gorgeous, and the voice acting is absolutely top notch. The story is crazy and over-the-top while still managing to be emotionally compelling and poignant. And it's weird to say this but it probably has the most tasteful sex scene ever seen in a video game. In a genre that has become both overplayed and cliché Wolfenstein: The New Order manages to be the best first-person shooter I’ve played in years.

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

One of the very, very few games to draw me in for marathon sessions for YEARS on end. I got into RimWorld the day after the Kickstarter ended and have loved every single iteration of RimWorld. While a lot has been added to the game over the years, it has somehow retained the core of what made alpha 1 an absolute blast. It's a rare game where you grow attached to your pawns, to the home they've carved out of the wilderness, proud of the work you have accomplished and the threats you have survived.
And you will get attached, you will holler in rage when one of them dies, or loses an eye, or gets kidnapped. You will rage quit when raiders blow their way through your walls to get to the undefended innards of your base, torching and destroying whatever they see. You may even shed a tear when a beloved pet gets mauled by a cougar. But you know what else you will do?
You will start a new colony. You will fight tooth and nail to establish a safe haven for your burgeoning colony. You will learn from your mistakes and become better, stronger, smarter. You will learn how to survive on the Rim, to thrive, and maybe, maybe you will make it off the planet. Whatever you do, you will have fun. This is easily one of the best games I've ever had the joy to play. If you like base building, simulations, 'ant farms', you can only hope to fall in love with RimWorld.
I'm glad Tynan waited so long to put this on Steam, I'm not sure I want to know how much of my life this game has devoured. And to think, I still have to load up a mod or two someday, should I ever get bored with the vanilla game. So far, that has not been the case. A very loud and hearty recommendation from me.

I have been playing Rimworld since Alpha 9. This game is fantastic. If you like Dwarf Fortress, you'll immediately see the similarities.
No forgotten beasts or vampires, but there are psychic events, solar flares, solar eclipses, raiders, raider that kidnap your colonists, wild animal attacks, disease, infection, infestations, starvation, mental breaks, cave-ins, colonist fights, arsonists, lightning strikes. I am sure I am leaving other stuff out.
Colonists can also have wounds and diseases and health problems. Some of these are solvable. Diseases and wounds can be treated and healed. You can also perform organ extractions on raiders or colonists or by them from passing trade ships. Then use those organs to transplant a pair of lungs into someone who has lung cancer or maybe replace a lame leg with a bionic one.
With Rimworld you pick a "storyteller". Depending on what you choose determines how your game will go. Go easy mode and you'll get maybe a solar eclipse and then many months from that you'll get one guy trying to raid your colony. Go hardcore and you can have huge raids, power outages, fires, solar eclipses, wild animal attacks all happening at once or close in time. I think in this version raiders will also kidnap your colonists and hold them for ransom.
With this release, you also get scenarios where you can choose how you want to go. Want to play as the lone wolf in hellcious desert, you can. Want to start to 100 dogs, go on. Want to start a Mountainhome with 7 colonists in a mountainous area, go on. Like Shia says, "JUST DO IT!"
I cannot recommend this game enough and the developer is stellar. If you remember how good the Prison Architect guys were this guy is just as good. He is always available to the players via the Rimworld page or through the subreddit. He listens and makes time for the people who play his game.
Waste no time, buy it, play it, enjoy your Rimworld addiction!

I've been playing and creating mods for RimWorld for 6 months now, with countless hours spent. Here's my honest review.
Verdict;
Well worth the money - it's a game like no other, and it produces some lovely (and sometimes gruesome) stories. It's obviously inspired by Dwarf Fortress, and shares an art style with Prison Architect, but it doesn't feel like a ripoff/re-hash.
The good;
- It has a unique feel to it. From the opening guitar riff upon landing to the unique stories that will be told, the game will grip you.
- The game is relatively easy to mod, and
can be modded. There's an active and helpful modding community on the official forums
- The developer is active, and engages with the players. He's got more posts on the official forums than anyone else, and responds to questions both directly asked and posted on the forums and on the subreddit in a timely fashion. He's also open to discussion and feedback (to an extent, ofcourse).
The bad;
- Actual content in the game is fairly limited. Even though the game's systems allow for an enormous variety of interesting interactions, the game needs mods to really shine.
- The development team consists of two people. That's two people to do all the programming, but also community management, marketing, and so forth. Things aren't always done as fast as one might hope. Nonetheless, the game has seen regular updates - with the exception of a single planned 6 month hiatus.
- It's a small scale colony simulator. Development is focused on the narrative. That means that the focus is often more on creating an interesting story than on optimizing the game for larger 'management game' like colonies. While it's entirely possible to get massive (25+ colonist) colonies, at some point your colony will die an FPS death. Fancy hardware won't help much, since the CPU is the bottleneck, and the game is for all intents and purposes single threaded.
- While the UI is better than, say, Dwar Fortress (this game actually has a UI, so that wasn't difficult), it's not exactly pretty. Worse, it's often quite cumbersome to work with. (This is where many of my mods come in).
Nice

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

The Talos Principle demo caught me off guard, and after completing it, I decided I wanted to see an entire game of those mechanics. Unfortunately, the mechanics of the demo are essentially all the mechanics in the game. This leads into the negatives, which I'll state right away. The Talos Principle doesn't expand much on its mechanics in ways it could have, and if you are completing every puzzle in sequence like I was, by the 3rd area the mechanics feel stretched a bit too thin. Many puzzles feel similar to one another. Additionally, those hoping for a more upfront, easy to understand story may be disappointed.
All of these elements aside, I really enjoyed the Talos Principle, and using hint guides for some of the stars, managed to (mostly) 100% it. First off, the story of Talos is very intriguing and fun to unravel as you listen to the main human character recount the events that led to your creation and the current state of Earth.  If you enjoy being thrown philosophical and existential questions, the game has those in abundance. The payoff at the end feels very rewarding, and multiple endings allow you to witness the different paths possible for your character, although in my opinion one ending is clearly the best and most rewarding.
As far as puzzles go, if you enjoy other first-person puzzle games, you should feel right at home here (think Portal, Antichamber, etc.) Each level is nice aesthetically and has neat easter eggs and hidden treats for those willing to look. The atmosphere is very grand, ominous, and deserted. Talos really made me feel the weight of the human race, as I ran through the monuments and ruins of ancient civilizations.
Overall, Talos doesn't surprise you with how novel its mechanics are, although of them all, the Recorder is definitely the most interesting. However, it delivers with solid brain-teaser puzzles, and finding each secret star is a true challenge. The game nails presentation and structure. Despite these strengths, it stumbles by being a bit predictable, both in plot and puzzle sequence, and honestly, the game would have benefitted from being shorter.
Any fan of puzzle games should give this game a try; absolutely download the demo at the very least.

I was on the fence about this one because of the art style, and it looked like a kids game. I ended up picking it up on a Steam sale for my son, who wanted it. To my surprise this game is a blast. You pick one of four knights each with a special ability. Fire, Poison, Electricity, Ice, you get the idea. The powers give you a special attack that does significant damage, as well as decides the color of your knight. The game supports full controller, local co-op, online co-op, and local plus online co-op. This is the way it should be. Local co-op, and split screen belong on PC! The game features three modes, campaign, versus, and a jumping mini game (not my cup of tea, but some may like jumping). The campaign mode is where it's at. You, and up to three friends button mash your way to victory against the evil horde to save the princesses. The combat gives you some options aside from hack n slash, like your special power, bow, bomb, and a few simple combos. The music is great, they did a nice job on the tracks for this game. The monster design is comical, and slicing the heads off little minions is fun.  The game will run on almost any PC (Not your Commodore 64, but anything from 2010 and up should be fine). If you've been passing on this one, give it a try at the next sale.

I have been playing Rimworld since Alpha 9. This game is fantastic. If you like Dwarf Fortress, you'll immediately see the similarities.
No forgotten beasts or vampires, but there are psychic events, solar flares, solar eclipses, raiders, raider that kidnap your colonists, wild animal attacks, disease, infection, infestations, starvation, mental breaks, cave-ins, colonist fights, arsonists, lightning strikes. I am sure I am leaving other stuff out.
Colonists can also have wounds and diseases and health problems. Some of these are solvable. Diseases and wounds can be treated and healed. You can also perform organ extractions on raiders or colonists or by them from passing trade ships. Then use those organs to transplant a pair of lungs into someone who has lung cancer or maybe replace a lame leg with a bionic one.
With Rimworld you pick a "storyteller". Depending on what you choose determines how your game will go. Go easy mode and you'll get maybe a solar eclipse and then many months from that you'll get one guy trying to raid your colony. Go hardcore and you can have huge raids, power outages, fires, solar eclipses, wild animal attacks all happening at once or close in time. I think in this version raiders will also kidnap your colonists and hold them for ransom.
With this release, you also get scenarios where you can choose how you want to go. Want to play as the lone wolf in hellcious desert, you can. Want to start to 100 dogs, go on. Want to start a Mountainhome with 7 colonists in a mountainous area, go on. Like Shia says, "JUST DO IT!"
I cannot recommend this game enough and the developer is stellar. If you remember how good the Prison Architect guys were this guy is just as good. He is always available to the players via the Rimworld page or through the subreddit. He listens and makes time for the people who play his game.
Waste no time, buy it, play it, enjoy your Rimworld addiction!

I've been playing and creating mods for RimWorld for 6 months now, with countless hours spent. Here's my honest review.
Verdict;
Well worth the money - it's a game like no other, and it produces some lovely (and sometimes gruesome) stories. It's obviously inspired by Dwarf Fortress, and shares an art style with Prison Architect, but it doesn't feel like a ripoff/re-hash.
The good;
- It has a unique feel to it. From the opening guitar riff upon landing to the unique stories that will be told, the game will grip you.
- The game is relatively easy to mod, and
can be modded. There's an active and helpful modding community on the official forums
- The developer is active, and engages with the players. He's got more posts on the official forums than anyone else, and responds to questions both directly asked and posted on the forums and on the subreddit in a timely fashion. He's also open to discussion and feedback (to an extent, ofcourse).
The bad;
- Actual content in the game is fairly limited. Even though the game's systems allow for an enormous variety of interesting interactions, the game needs mods to really shine.
- The development team consists of two people. That's two people to do all the programming, but also community management, marketing, and so forth. Things aren't always done as fast as one might hope. Nonetheless, the game has seen regular updates - with the exception of a single planned 6 month hiatus.
- It's a small scale colony simulator. Development is focused on the narrative. That means that the focus is often more on creating an interesting story than on optimizing the game for larger 'management game' like colonies. While it's entirely possible to get massive (25+ colonist) colonies, at some point your colony will die an FPS death. Fancy hardware won't help much, since the CPU is the bottleneck, and the game is for all intents and purposes single threaded.
- While the UI is better than, say, Dwar Fortress (this game actually has a UI, so that wasn't difficult), it's not exactly pretty. Worse, it's often quite cumbersome to work with. (This is where many of my mods come in).

If you think its gonna be a super cool squad-oriented slog-fest with clunky movement and bad UI. Go for it.
I haven't gotten that feeling of being hunted lke i did in Arma. I haven't gotten that feeling of a dynamic back-and-forth struggle like i did in Battlefield, and i haven't gotten that feeling of exhilaration after winning a firefight in Insurgency.
My point being, even if its an early access, it would be nice to see some original and interesting gameplay that makes it a different game from its spiritual predecessors, rather than a crappy Arma-Insurgency-Battlefield thing with all the bugs, glitches, and other problems of an early access.

Dirty Bomb is one of the best free-to-play games out there, and in my opinion, definitely the best fps free-to-play.
As a first person shooter with set "characters" dirty bomb never fails to produce innovative game mechanics, with some favourite, more imaginative characters being sparks or fletcher. The weekly rotation allows you to have new experiences with the game on a regular basis. The gameplay itself is a solid, if somewhat relaxed experience, in which you are rewarded for both trying new mercs and gaining mastery with certain ones, investing in loadout cards for them. The fact that different mercs simply work better in different situation allows new players to try lots of different characters while not being rolled over by people that invest time into one character. Team play is a key aspect here, and some of the most fun I have had in an fps comes from two coordinated, evenly matched teams in Dirty Bomb.
I entered the game with a lot of suspiscion, as I do with most free-to-plays, as pay to win elements are very easy to include within the game. I was surprised to find that I was satisfied with what I had even 40 or so hours into the game, having not spent any money. It's neither a "grind for hours or pay some money" nor do the purchases make no impact at all, but the devs give you enough so that you WANT to go a little further and pay some money, but without needing to. I personally have only bought one bundle, and the game would have been well worth the price that I paid for it.
I strongly recommend playing it, however be aware of the dramatically reduced player base at this stage in the game's development. There are also a few balancing issues that the devs need to adress, but they are not significant. The devs are very committed to the game and the addition of mercs over time is a promising sign for the longevity of the games development.

Sequels are usually expected to live up to their originals. This is for all forms of entertainment; books, movies, and of course, video games. A lot of the time, sequels fall into two spectrums:
The first is being weaker than its predecessor, which can happen when elements are degraded to a simplier level, or the overall experience doesn't feel so much like something new; it feels like you're playing the same game again. Many sequels can fall into this category for being too much like its original, or downgrading from that point.
The second is the one that is to strive for: expanding upon story and mechanics and making the game feel the same but also different. New mechanics and properties that make you think differently than the one before it, that also gives the feeling of nostalgia and excitement from the original. This is what makes sequels great.
Portal 2 falls under the second category, which can be hard to pull off in such a fantastic way that VALVe did.
To really get a feel for this game, play the original. The story's initial concepts are applied and expanded upon further to such heights unexpected. Not only that, but there are various new mechanics besides "place your portal here, then here, then you're done." Such concepts are illustrated farther into the game with some of the most creative puzzles that really make you think.
The voice acting in this game is also spectacular, which is hard to say for a lot of games. For example, one character often messes up what he says, and stutters often saying words like "um"; though this may not sound particularly exciting, it fleshes out a character more and makes them more like the people around us (and ourselves), as we as people trip over words sometimes. Such things are hardly portrayed in video games, and even such small details as that are to be appreciated about Portal 2.
With the voice acting comes iconic lines that many players know, and sarcastic responses and comebacks around every corner. It made me chuckle at least a few times, because each character is enjoyable through the script.
Also, I would highly recommend co-op, but only after you play a bit of single player so you get a hold of the mechanics. The co-op courses are really fun to play and satisfying to solve with your friend. But we all know that one person is doing all the work while the other follows directions. There's even a joke about this in-game. Quite lovely.
In conclusion...Portal 2 was and continues to be an amazing experience. The story is more in-depth than that of the first game, so it takes a little longer to complete. This is not a problem, however, due to the fantastic puzzles, realistic characters, and entertaining writing.
This is truly one of the most wonderful games out on the market, and I would recommend this to anyone who played the first game.

The premise of RimWorld revolves around your colonists trying to survive on a planet

One example of a game I played recently was when my colonists were in a boreal forest

to comfort them--but not in the traditional sense. I used the AC system that was keeping my
food frozen (in hindsight I suppose I could have just left them outside, but oh well)
and using the exhaust from the AC system to keep the bedrooms warm.
Long story short, an event that caused my batteries to explode caused a fire in the bedrooms.
I tried having my colonists extinguish the fire but due to the combination of the heat from
both the AC and the fire, my colonists started to burst into flames, killing everyone but
one person.
Oh yeah, then their pet dog went rabid and killed the remaining surviver.
The versatility and replay value of this game is immense, creating hours and hours of

I hesitated to go back to Wolfenstein after the last outing that Raven Software put together, I do rate Raven software for many things, like COD map packs and their excellent single player games like Quake 4 and Singualrity.
The last Wolfenstein, aptly titled Wolfenstein was a run on rails shooter with almost zero storyline. All the hype and screenshots made it look great, only...it wasn't. Plus it had a tacked on multi player that made Wolf:ET fans shudder at its mention.
Now I say all that so that you know how cautious I was about going into this version of Wolfenstein, further more it's set in an alternative timeline where the Nazi regime has defeated the Allies and the whole world bows to the Reich.
It's years on into the occupation of the Americas and Europe and this is where we are greeted by a familar old face.
Enter BJ Blascowitz.
Now I won't say too much about the storyline and instead focus on what you get from this new title in the franchise.
Machine Games have developed Wolfenstein their own way, which meant NO Multiplayer, though I'm still hopeful that Paul Wedgewood and his team at Splash Damage will revisit the franchise and re-do Wolf:ET later in the future.
This single player adventure is fantastic. It's part movie and all FPS at the same time. The graphic details of the carefully crafted levels are a sight to behold, never has so much thought gone into the level design in a Wolfenstein title, it's gorgeous. The gameplay mechanics are easy to pick up and the gun play is filled with gibs galore.
This is a perfect continuation of the franchise, set apart by the timeline difference our Nazis are still Nazis and the tech is somewhat analog and plausible. I am loving the storyline and the characters that Machine Games have put together, the storytelling allows events to unfold as they're meant to without the rough crooked jump cuts from a Call of Duty single player.
In closing this is a must have single player for Wolfenstein fans, it's my top pick for 2014 single player titles next to Dying Light.

I played this game for hundreds of hours outside of Steam. Each update has made it better and better, it is one of the best Early Access games you can get and it's very playable at it's current state.

Some pros:
-Build a colony from nothing. There are many games recently that tried to do that, most failed however and the rest pale in comparison to Rimworld.
-Many things you can do with your colony, build a cow ranch, or vast fields of corn, produce weapons, armor, art pieces, produce drugs, or all of the above.
-Different biomes to choose from, all with their unique fauna and flora, there's even one purely made of ice floating on the sea.
-The AI in this game is one of the best you will find, something that is rare with modern games.
-The theme of Rimworld is very compelling. It has that sci-fi, wild-west feeling and with the new Scenario System you can even play as tribals.
-The combat is played in real time with the ability to pause whenever you wish, so it can be very tactical or very messy, depending on your playstyle.
-The artwork, although minimalistic is very well made and you can always tell what's going on cause of the smooth animations (not like Gnomoria for example).
-You will witness many crazy and hilarious things in the world of Rimworld.
-You can now travel to any location you want and start new colonies that you can simultaneously play with your original start location. This game just got 100% more fun.
Some cons:
-You can't dig down, or build upwards. The map has only one level. Which is not that big of a deal now that you can make caravans and travel to new locations.
There are many more good things to say about Rimworld, but I will leave that for people with better writing skills. All you need to know is, that Rimworld is easily in the top 5 of the best base/colony building games ever.
