First and formost... this game is fantastic... BUY NOW THEN READ MY THOUGHTS... I played the demo a while back after I saw it on sale several months ago and I said to myself "DAMM, should've bought it when i had the chance..." But now that this summer sale is close to end, buy it quick before its too late and goes back to regular price (even if you miss the sale, the game still merits a full price purchase) Ok now, lets cut to the chase...
I have to give to credit to the Graphics department for this. The is game is beatifully optimized for older running hardware and newer. I myself have a mid-high end and even at medium settings the environment feels rich and serene. The best part is you can tweek the video so much that eventually you'll find the perfect setting for whatever rig you're running.
The Aduio in the game is top notch. The ambiance of the world fit the game perfectly with a natural flow of the landscape. The music gives the player a tranquil pace of problem solving and relaxation without that feel of being rushed. The dialog is also another charm. The narration from the beginning gives you a feeling of importance and purpose to the world.
Gameplay Mechanics and Control is solid. Not much can be said here other than customization is up to player preference. It has controller support which can be customized to your likeings. Either way you choose the game handles exceptionally well.
Gamewise, the game can and will be overlooked easily. Mainly because a majority will take 1 glance at this and immediately think its another "portal" puzzle game. Yes and no, now here's why... Yes the game does impliment First person problem solving gameplay with levels incrementally getting harder. Though the meaty part of the game is the story and presentation of the world itself. I can ramble on for a while on how deep this game goes, but in short the game is Very Thought provoking and it grabs your attention immediately when entering the world. You're brought into this acient Rome like setting and then shortly discovering what you really are, making you want to dig furhter into the game as to why your there and your purpose... The game grasps on theological and philosophical concepts of many cultures of both acient and modern times. Thats just the heart of the game, and if your seeking for another puzzle "portal" like experience, this game will mental block you at times. making you rethink and approach a puzzle differently and/or experimenting and trying the :what if: method in order to proceed and you'll be surprised at how clever these puzzles are that your first instinct isnt always the correct 1. It's so rewarding when you can't figure out a puzzle only to come back to it later and realizing the answer in meer seconds. That's clever.
In conclusion the game is a great experience. It not only does what Portal did right but rejuvinates to the genre with a rich story and thought provoking plots that make you "think" And I do mean THINK. not just in problem solving but as a whole. Pick up the game while you still can on sale... You wont regret it!!!!

Defending consisted of camping for days. Stalemates where a spawn point is set up inside a cap and people forget the WSAD keys exist and become immobile.
Gameplay issues aside, the graphics while I didn't expect to be great, were kind of lackluster at longer distances. Either way, get insurgency - its cheaper and a lot more fun in my opinion.

AoE2 is a game I grew up with. At the age of 11 I came across the demo of this game, with no prior knowledge of RTS games as I started up the wallace campaign. My first reaction was that i became attached to the style of gameplay, which of course is building up the civilization and managing recources. Playing through the campaign I felt like I had a well enough understanding of how the game works that I launched a random scenario. And I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked...badly. For a late 90s game it stood out well and it stood proud as one of the great RTS games to date.
First off, lets talk about the graphics. It looks exactly the same as it did in 99'. Some may cry "but wait! This is an HD remaster! It should look better!" I say ♥♥♥♥ off to that. The games graphics arent what needed an update. It was the optimization that was needed the most. If i installed the game from the Ye' old disc, the game would run of course, but resolution would be ♥♥♥♥ed and the water would be all purple and pixilated.  But yeah I would understand the gripes with some saying it should be called HD edition, but in all honesty, the game works and is optimized well, so who cares?
The gameplay is next and it is still memorable and fun since the first day it was available. The goal is pretty much building up your civilization of your choice through the ages and fighting other players until an objective is completed, whether it being destroying opponents, collecting relics, killing the opposing king or other custom objectives. There are also campaign missions in the game. You get 5 campaigns  in the Age of Kings, as well as 4 campaigns in the Conquerors expansion, and even more in the next two expansions (purchased seperately) that were not even previously available when the game was available in retail! Unfortunately, the campaigns bore me after a while and thus we go into the the scenario portion. This is were the bulk of the game can be fun and challenging. First, you can select one of 5 difficulties that suit your play style, as well as selecting a civilization for you and the ai as well as the teams. I personally prefer 1 v 7 where i am the lone wolf trying to defend my land. There is multiplayer, which i have yet to play, and last but not least, there is a map editior so you can custom create your own maps and challenges. Overall, there are alot of modes to choose from and keep yourself occupied for a long while.
The music section is short. Its pretty much one track that is 40+ mins long. Nothing explosive or amazing, and is pretty forgettable, but does its job in being background noise.
Last but not least the civilization roster is stellar. With 18 to pick from (more with the purchase of the two new expansions) and each function in different ways, so you'll have fun discovering what is unlockable with each civilization. I think that fun in discovery might just be me.
Unfortunately, it doesnt go without saying that its not perfect. This game is not for everyone, and may grow tiresome to those that dont understand, or to those that think it is too slow of a game... or those that think its outdated and aged poorly (...). But yeah I understand their opinion on it.
Overall, it is still the same experience that i grew up with and love. If you are unsure if its worth a buy, wait till it goes on sale and check it out.

Well it's.. deffinately something, it's a very unique experience if you haven't played a game like this before.
The game is very intimidating at first but you just gotta throw yourself into it, make sure you have a mic, communicate, do your callouts and follow orders and you'll be fine.
My experience?
My first 30 minutes we wound up with a pretty silly team and a squad leader that didn't have a mic and we all formed a circle around this person and sacrificed him to Tony Abbott and Julia Gillard, but even though the squad was immature it went from stupid to very serious very fast and the game was a blast, I was confused at times but after you knock that first round out, hopefully it's a good one, the next one will be a better experience.
What is the game like?
In the games current state it's an advanced Insurgency that enforces teamwork and tactical thinking, however, the game has a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of content coming, Vehicles, Aircrafts, Logistics, Tanks, Maps, extra roles, map optimizations, ALOT, this game is meant to be the successor to Project Reality, it's going to be basically Project Reality 2, just at the moment it isn't quite that, hence why I said in its current state it is an advanced, mans version of Insurgency, not that Insurgency is bad, that's a ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant game. I can't wait for the rest of the content to come in, hell, once logistics come in, it'll be a huge game changer and make the game 100 times more challenging and a hell of alot more fun.
How good does it look?
Graphically the game is beautiful, it just needs some optimizations here and there, that's all, the Devs really did a good job here.
The Price tag?
Well $40 is way better than the $70US I spent when I pre-purchased the game, but at the moment $40 does seem like a bit of a rip off for it's current state BUT you're also paying for a roughly next gen miliary simulator that is going to be a ♥♥♥♥ing huge♥♥♥♥♥♥game with alot of content and mechanics and just look at the graphics provided, that's pretty good for what you pay for, the price tag is debatable but in the end, $40 is going to be a steal for what you'll be getting.
Should you invest this early?
I seriously doubt the devs will abandon the development, there's so many people hyped for it, so many people bought into it and alot of big youtubers have helped build the huuuge community for this game, so In my opinion, yes it is worth investing the money in, plus the game is a blast in its current state.
Is the community bad?
I can't say for foriegn communities but as for the Australian community, they do tend to be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s but it gets very serious very quick and everyone is patient, welcoming, helpful, basically the community is good, I was scared when I found out I was Squad leader and my random♥♥♥♥♥♥squad was very supportive and helpful for the time I was there before my internet died.
Is the Forum good?
hell yeah, if you haven't already, head over there and sign up, go looking around, there's alot of big names there and really helpful people, although you do get your trolls from time to time but they usually get snuffed out from what I've seen.
Want more Information?
Head over to
for the official forum and here's a good youtuber that has alot of information on the game + alot of Project Reality Content:
Final Thoughts?
Very good game, def worth keeping an eye on, I say yes to investing this early and it is an absolute blast, I can't wait for the extra content to be officially patched in. 10/10

What is so amazing about this game is that you can be whoever or whatever you want to be. Want to make a primitive tribe of people that relies on vegetables and spares everyone they meet? Sure. Want to be the bandit of the east who defends a vital chokepoint and tries to rob passer-bys? Be my guest. Want to augment your population into cyborgs and eventually replace them with a society sustained only with robotic AIs? Might need a mod or 3 for that, but sure. Want to lug  your defeated foes into a secret hidden cave compound, butcher them for parts, make beautiful furniture out of their skins and feed the remains to your colonists? uh.... no, why would you even think about that? I, er, never even consider that possibility nor have I done this for the majority of my playthroughs as a viable means of sustaining my colony, oh no sir.
Regardless of your reasons, as long as you have a little something called being a sick- IMAGINATION, you can make this game into anything you want, be it tribesmen, bandits, corporate branches, remnant of aperture lab or even as sickos that sells skin and skin accessories, you can find your place in rimworld, where your dreams will be your pawn's nightmares coming to life (see they wanted to get killed, which is why they don't attack enemies unless you draft them first; it's actually a feature, not a poor implementation). A brilliant franchise re-imagened.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is a game that I did not expect to be as good as it turned out to be. I went into it with minimum expectations and expected to just kill some time, what I got was an experience that I loved. The game has some great shooting mechanics, very nice graphics and superb level design. It was very satisfying to tear through hundreds of Nazis in the world of The New Order. The story is actually pretty good too, it has some interesting characters and the dialogues are very well done. The game also provides some quiet time moments for you to get your bearings before you are put up against yet even more Nazi soldiers, which I like. It makes you appreciate the combat a lot more.
There is room for stealth, a lot of sections in the game give you the option to go full stealth. I myself quite enjoy stealth games, so definitely a one up for that. Of course you can also always go loud, your hand is not held nor are you held back by rules. It's just you versus Nazi Germany.
Would I recommend it? Of course I would. The game offers such a good single-player mode that I can't not recommend it.
Oh yeah, also, dual wielding semi-automatic shotguns. Yes.

The Talos Principle is a first person puzzler game which has beautiful graphics and wonderfully memorable music. The atmosphere of the game grabs you from the start with its amazing puzzle design and great writing. Provoking narrative, philosophical and metaphysical questions, this game really makes you wonder. Even though it’s very demanding and intense, I couldn’t put the game away when I played it. You constantly have questions that you want answered and it makes you keep thinking, even when after you stop playing.
You play as a sentient artificial intelligence placed within a simulation. From the start you have this narrative voice who explains himself as your god, your creator. You question his logic and you read from other people who both obey and disobey him. As you follow the storyline you read a lot of texts which are written by various people iside the game.
As you are artificial intelligence yourself you also communicate with a help program who asks you tons of questions. You constantly wonder why you are in this simulation, how to get out, what’s outside of the simulation, who’s behind it, there’s always so many questions!
One thing I didn’t like about the game or what I would want to see more of, is that you should question Elohim (your god) and his logic straight to his face. I would like to see more chaos from Elohim and his reaction as you confront him. Much like Glados from portal who tries to kill you when you don't do as she says.
If you’re not the kind of guy who plays for the story, then maybe this game is not for you. I try my best to read everything and follow every single bit when I play. Either way this is one of my favorite and most memorable games I’ve ever played and I would suggest this game even though it’s quite challenging.

This is a very fun game for the low low price of free. The developers are very interactive with the community and put out weekly dev videos with their community manager every week. If you don't have money, but have a computer that can play this game and enjoy first person shooters, you'll have some fun here.
Pros:
- Free. All the people who complain about pay to win have no real argument. I've put zero dollars into the game, and unlocked all the mercs, and most of my desired loadout cards. Completing the missions, clearing undesired missions and repeating this will get you what you want/need.
- Variety of mercs. There are a wide variety of mercs to fill different rolls.
Cons:
- Unoptimized. While the game has been improved since I started playing it with the MOFO update, it still isn't as good as it can be. This is likely due to the limited staff at spash damage.
- Lack of meaningful updates. I've played the game for about a year, and there have been no new mercs, maps, or weapons introduced. The game seems to be on maintenance mode / life support for the time being. Peolpe are waiting for the merc Turtle, but again due to the limited staff, I don't see him coming out before the game's fan base / community moves on.
- Unbalanced teams. With a relatively small community with a handful of skilled players the game struggles with balance. When you see a player with the level / rank in the triple digits, 75-80% of the time they are in fact VERY good at first person shooters and dirty bomb. When one of these people graces your server, the team they join will 9 out of 10 times be the winning team, unless their team is so unskilled that they can't hold their own against the enemiy.
- Skilled players kill servers. Again in relation to the above, when a skilled, popular, regular player joins your team, players will quit the server rather then be ground into dust. This is the consequence of a small community IMO.
- Lack of custom/private servers. All servers are run by splash damage and there only likely ever to be 3 or 4 that are to be joinable and playeble at the same time.

AoE2 is a game I grew up with. At the age of 11 I came across the demo of this game, with no prior knowledge of RTS games as I started up the wallace campaign. My first reaction was that i became attached to the style of gameplay, which of course is building up the civilization and managing recources. Playing through the campaign I felt like I had a well enough understanding of how the game works that I launched a random scenario. And I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked...badly. For a late 90s game it stood out well and it stood proud as one of the great RTS games to date.
First off, lets talk about the graphics. It looks exactly the same as it did in 99'. Some may cry "but wait! This is an HD remaster! It should look better!" I say ♥♥♥♥ off to that. The games graphics arent what needed an update. It was the optimization that was needed the most. If i installed the game from the Ye' old disc, the game would run of course, but resolution would be ♥♥♥♥ed and the water would be all purple and pixilated.  But yeah I would understand the gripes with some saying it should be called HD edition, but in all honesty, the game works and is optimized well, so who cares?
The gameplay is next and it is still memorable and fun since the first day it was available. The goal is pretty much building up your civilization of your choice through the ages and fighting other players until an objective is completed, whether it being destroying opponents, collecting relics, killing the opposing king or other custom objectives. There are also campaign missions in the game. You get 5 campaigns  in the Age of Kings, as well as 4 campaigns in the Conquerors expansion, and even more in the next two expansions (purchased seperately) that were not even previously available when the game was available in retail! Unfortunately, the campaigns bore me after a while and thus we go into the the scenario portion. This is were the bulk of the game can be fun and challenging. First, you can select one of 5 difficulties that suit your play style, as well as selecting a civilization for you and the ai as well as the teams. I personally prefer 1 v 7 where i am the lone wolf trying to defend my land. There is multiplayer, which i have yet to play, and last but not least, there is a map editior so you can custom create your own maps and challenges. Overall, there are alot of modes to choose from and keep yourself occupied for a long while.
The music section is short. Its pretty much one track that is 40+ mins long. Nothing explosive or amazing, and is pretty forgettable, but does its job in being background noise.
Last but not least the civilization roster is stellar. With 18 to pick from (more with the purchase of the two new expansions) and each function in different ways, so you'll have fun discovering what is unlockable with each civilization. I think that fun in discovery might just be me.
Unfortunately, it doesnt go without saying that its not perfect. This game is not for everyone, and may grow tiresome to those that dont understand, or to those that think it is too slow of a game... or those that think its outdated and aged poorly (...). But yeah I understand their opinion on it.
Overall, it is still the same experience that i grew up with and love. If you are unsure if its worth a buy, wait till it goes on sale and check it out.

The Talos Principle is a first person puzzler game which has beautiful graphics and wonderfully memorable music. The atmosphere of the game grabs you from the start with its amazing puzzle design and great writing. Provoking narrative, philosophical and metaphysical questions, this game really makes you wonder. Even though it’s very demanding and intense, I couldn’t put the game away when I played it. You constantly have questions that you want answered and it makes you keep thinking, even when after you stop playing.
You play as a sentient artificial intelligence placed within a simulation. From the start you have this narrative voice who explains himself as your god, your creator. You question his logic and you read from other people who both obey and disobey him. As you follow the storyline you read a lot of texts which are written by various people iside the game.
As you are artificial intelligence yourself you also communicate with a help program who asks you tons of questions. You constantly wonder why you are in this simulation, how to get out, what’s outside of the simulation, who’s behind it, there’s always so many questions!
One thing I didn’t like about the game or what I would want to see more of, is that you should question Elohim (your god) and his logic straight to his face. I would like to see more chaos from Elohim and his reaction as you confront him. Much like Glados from portal who tries to kill you when you don't do as she says.
If you’re not the kind of guy who plays for the story, then maybe this game is not for you. I try my best to read everything and follow every single bit when I play. Either way this is one of my favorite and most memorable games I’ve ever played and I would suggest this game even though it’s quite challenging.

This is a quick review since I've only just finished the first 'world'.
The Talos Principle is an excellent puzzler, let me start with that. I've solved all but a couple of them in maybe 2-3 minutes, but the shorter were no less gratifying than the longer. The graphics and atmosphere are awesome. It's a great game to throw your headphones on to and get lost in the brain-teasing fun. The narration/voices are done very well and overall I would have to give the game a preliminary 5/5.
The game consists of going through 'portals' to different areas in each 'world'. So far as I can tell, there are three worlds
. The narration is not overwhelming; in fact, the 'elohim' tells you up front that he's not going to give you any assistance since 'you need to find your own path'.
If I could give you one piece of advice for this game, it's this:
This is where the game truly shines in my opinion. All aspects - voice, text, environment, puzzles, they all point to questions of existential nature. It's very much a game with philisophical implications. At one point you are asked to prove you are alive, that you exist. They give you four options. The whole time in the terminals you are interacting with a program (or is it? Seriously, I have no idea...) that always surprises with its responses.
All in all - and again, being only about 1/3rd of the way through the game - I wholeheartedly recommend it. Do yourself a favor and BUY THIS GAME. I got it on sale for about half price, and even if I'd paid full price, it's well worth it.

Sequels are usually expected to live up to their originals. This is for all forms of entertainment; books, movies, and of course, video games. A lot of the time, sequels fall into two spectrums:
The first is being weaker than its predecessor, which can happen when elements are degraded to a simplier level, or the overall experience doesn't feel so much like something new; it feels like you're playing the same game again. Many sequels can fall into this category for being too much like its original, or downgrading from that point.
The second is the one that is to strive for: expanding upon story and mechanics and making the game feel the same but also different. New mechanics and properties that make you think differently than the one before it, that also gives the feeling of nostalgia and excitement from the original. This is what makes sequels great.
Portal 2 falls under the second category, which can be hard to pull off in such a fantastic way that VALVe did.
To really get a feel for this game, play the original. The story's initial concepts are applied and expanded upon further to such heights unexpected. Not only that, but there are various new mechanics besides "place your portal here, then here, then you're done." Such concepts are illustrated farther into the game with some of the most creative puzzles that really make you think.
The voice acting in this game is also spectacular, which is hard to say for a lot of games. For example, one character often messes up what he says, and stutters often saying words like "um"; though this may not sound particularly exciting, it fleshes out a character more and makes them more like the people around us (and ourselves), as we as people trip over words sometimes. Such things are hardly portrayed in video games, and even such small details as that are to be appreciated about Portal 2.
With the voice acting comes iconic lines that many players know, and sarcastic responses and comebacks around every corner. It made me chuckle at least a few times, because each character is enjoyable through the script.
Also, I would highly recommend co-op, but only after you play a bit of single player so you get a hold of the mechanics. The co-op courses are really fun to play and satisfying to solve with your friend. But we all know that one person is doing all the work while the other follows directions. There's even a joke about this in-game. Quite lovely.
In conclusion...Portal 2 was and continues to be an amazing experience. The story is more in-depth than that of the first game, so it takes a little longer to complete. This is not a problem, however, due to the fantastic puzzles, realistic characters, and entertaining writing.
This is truly one of the most wonderful games out on the market, and I would recommend this to anyone who played the first game.

I have been playing this game since Alpha 5, July of 2014. It is hands down one of the best time wasters I own, and I easily have a thousand hours into it.
It isn't the most complex game on the market, but it is definitely meaty enough to take more than a few playthroughs to experience everything it can throw at you.
It's the type of game where you can alter the way you play depending on your mood. If you want a focused, in-depth experience, you can set a higher difficulty and play inside the box. If you're looking for something easy to occupy your second monitor while watching Twitch, a few simple mods will make things much, much easier.
The modding community is also top-notch. There are active modders on every single update who bring new ways to enjoy the game from the vanilla experience. Some mods proved so popular that Tynan actually incorporated them into the vanilla game.
This is an early release title, but this isn't the kind of early release title that you kick yourself for buying afterwards. (This is certainly no CubeWorld- a game which I bought at nearly the same time). This is a fully fleshed out rogue-like game which will allow you to enjoy dozens of scenarios start to finish. And because of the "storyteller" system, and the random attributes of the starting colonists, each playthrough will feel a bit different.
I believe that the only reason Tynan considers this as an "alpha" is simply because he wants to add so much more to it. There is currently only one "definitive" way to end a game (without dying completely). I imagine that he will add many more over the course of future development.
And now that my Steam download is nearly finished, I'm heading off to enjoy the brand new Alpha 14.

Does this game break any outstanding barriers when it comes to FPS? No.
Is this game's single player FPS just as good or even greater than Metro? Yes, and depends who you are.
When I was first recommended Wolfenstein, I really couldn't care for the series. I knew it was some old time Doom sort of game that probably hasn't seen a good upgrade. It was recommended again and I caved. I'm glad I did. The story starts off with you, an American soldier, in WW2 fighting off nazi's. Not just any nazi's though, these ones are quite technologically advanced and have some odd soldiers on their side. Eventually, the main character
The character then leaves rehab as patients start disappearing and the home care workers are forced out. The real story and fun starts around this point.
The story lead up is a bit slow, but the game has no problem giving the player different experiences as an FPS. You will fly a plane, you will drive a car, and other small gimmicks that make the game enjoyable. It adds depth and makes the game that much more profound to continue playing. I would put this shooter on par with metro as dismemberment and effects when shooting a soldier are quite spot on.
My absolute favorite feature about this game (which I hope every game may incorporate) is the ability to control your movement behind cover. Are you behind a wall? Are you crouching behind cover? In any scenario, the player (on a controller) can hold L1 and with the joystick position the player around a wall or over cover to minimize exposure to enemy bullets. There are no shortage of weapons to choose from, and they made it possible to dual wield almost any gun. A specialized laser weapon is also given to cut through certain obstacles to enable progression throughout the story. The laser weapon can also be changed into a high burst beam where it can be used against enemies. Other weapons feature some sort of modification when it comes to shooting (often right D pad changes the fire settings). What is quite remarkable is the scenery's reaction to bullets. Enemies that are hiding behind cover can have it be shot away by the player leaving them vulnerable. This also applies to the players scenario where taking cover for too long behind a breakable barrier will lead to damage due to absent cover. Unlike call of duty, the environment can be to an extent blown away and damaged by bullets or explosions. Although it's not to the extreme where things will start disappearing, the concept of being able to almost destroy any cover an enemy is hiding behind is quite appealing, visually and for the game play. The AI's do not seem linear and will seek to come to you from any side. Flanking is not as popular as Deus Ex in this case, but traces of enemy brilliance are there.
The
are quite neat and the graphics play well. The game can ask quite a bit from your machine at times. I have not noticed any frame rate issues (either than you may need to V-sync) and that the sounds are rich and plentiful.
The
is great, and even develops the main character. I was hoping as so because "killing nazi's" attitude gets real old, real fast.
I want to give this game an 8 for being a good FPS shooter giving the player quite a bit of control over what goes on, but I feel like that little bit more is missing. Could easily be an 8 with local co-op or multiplayer.
RATING : 7.65/10
For future Wolfenstein's, maybe add a multiplayer depth for a lot of re-playability (or local co-op) and adding more explosive/modifiable environment options would be fantastic. The ability to shoot away cover is huge, but imagine having more control of what the room looks like.

RimWorld is a wonderful indie title, best described as a management sci-fi basebuilding survival game. I've put hundreds of hours into it prior to the Steam release, (anyone who purchased the game prior to Steam gets a Steam key) and totally recommend it. I first found out about the game when Quill18 played it back in Alpha 8. The developer is quite active on the game's forums and subreddit, and frequently expands the game with large updates that include several new mechanics without overwhelming the player. RimWorld has a tutorial system that tries to help you with only the things that you don't already know, but sometimes is a little bit intrusive. The game features three "AI Storytellers" that further along the story of your colony with events, weather conditions, raids, trade caravans, etc. These storytellers take a role similar to the Dungeon Master in Dungeons & Dragons, letting the player enjoy their game, while they give you a story to play with yourself. The game also has an exceptional replay value, which is built even further upon in Alpha 14, which gives players the ability to create their own custom scenarios and upload them to the Steam Workshop. The game has given me hours of fun, and continues to do so whenever I boot it up. A spectacular game, great for anyone who has some time on their hands.

I have been playing Rimworld since early alpha and watched this game grow up with each new version. If you like simulation games, strategy games, survival games, management games, this is a must have.
The easiest way to describe this game is as a more user friendly version of Dwarf Fortress. The game starts with three survivors (which you can customize or randomize, also change the number fo starting survivors as of this version) crashing on an alien planet (also randomized, you can choose in what kind of biome they crash) and are in charge of their survival. You will have to set up their jobs to build a base, provide food and cook it, defend from enemies, craft clothes, weapons or even art, trade with spaceships or nearby colonies, and so on. Your colonists gather experience in different areas as they perform their jobs, they will also develop a relationship with each other, maybe even fall in love and marry.
More colonists will join your colony, sometimes wanderers that just show up, maybe a lost son or brother or mother of one of your colonists, sometimes one of your former imprisoned enemies can be convinced to become a friend, sometimes another crashlander joins.
As time goes by, more and more invaders set an eye on your little colony... will you be able to survive and eventually escape the planet, or will only bones and graves remain of your once prosper colony? Or will the strain of this harsh live be too much for your poor colonist and they end up killing each other?
The game is still in early access, but it has an amazing amount of content, definitely worth the price. Just try it out, you can always refund, but the two hours will fly by and you will be hooked. Have fun!

I spent the first 20 minutes in Squad not knowing what to do.
I spent the next 15 minutes trying to kill someone. I didn’t.
Then the game ended.
Undeterred I picked a new server and got ready to roll into the game with guns blazing.
Twenty minutes later, I still hadn’t managed to shoot a single insurgent.
It took me a full 45 minutes to get my first confirmed kill.
The first half an hour in Squad was awful, the HUD wasn’t intuitive, and I had no idea what the point of the game was.
The next hour was filled with short and intense firefights, slow and steady progress and some of the best teamplay that I’ve ever experienced.  Squad’s gameplay bursts to life once you start actively participating in your squad and communicating with your team members.  Each kill you achieve brings you one step closer to victory, and every death you experience cripples your squad.  Squad is an immersive and realistic experience, filled with tense moments, bitter defeat and sweet victory.
One of my most memorable moments in the game occurred about halfway into the match.  We had just managed to capture the Market and parts of squad 1 were with us(squad 2).  After an incredibly tense firefight, we had finally managed to take down the insurgents and were stationed in a defensive position, looking out towards no man's land, on the lookout for the opposing team.  One of the cool features of Squad is proximity communication, in other words you can push-to-talk and those that are near you will be able to hear what you have to say, with the voice getting quiter the further away you are from the speaker.  One of the members in squad 1 activated his proximity communication, and started talking to us about a firefight that he had experienced the other day.  What happened next was a couple minutes of players, sitting in a circle swapping war stories as if they were old soldiers.  It was an incredibly rewarding and organic experience....until we got way too distracted swapping war stories, and got overrun by the insurgents.
In CS:GO are punctuated by a bursts of activity, gunplay and death, Squad’s gameplay is much more of a slow and steady burn.  At its core, Squad is a game that revolves heavily around teamwork and being able to communicate effectively with the rest of your squad.  Communication with your squad and your team is especially important and the game allows you a multitude of ways for you to communicate with your squad, your team, and those in your direct proximity.  You’ll need to work together with your squad in order to capture and control each base.  This will require large amounts of teamwork and for you to have complete trust in your squad to watch your back.
The gameplay in Squad is deadly, with death occurring quickly and oftentimes unexpectedly.  You'll run and duck as a shower of bullet peppers the wall behind you, grip your gun tightly as tracer rounds fly above your heads and breathe a sigh of relief when your squad rounds a corner in order to back you up.

OK. I am gonna try to be calm with this one. So it's Castle Crashers! It's of course amazing! It's from Behemoth! But I will give it to you like a professional.
GAMEPLAY- It certainly has veriety when it comes to the gameplay. Controls are at a fast pace and the combat is all around great. You can move freely from the front to back of the stage. New combo's keep being unlocked with more intresting (slightly harder) buttons to press when in combat. I love how you can move free so you need the Gameplay at a 10
APPEAL- Well, Castle Crashers is long and has quite the challenging stages! It has...odd things sometimes but we all know how the Behemoth is. I would say that this goes to a more hardcore smackdown type game lover, because betting up baddies is what it is about! And then there is LASTING APPEAL, which is a full blown insanity meter from when you start a boss. I can play it quite continuiosly but when it's time for a boss fight, you wanna drown your tears in popcorn and a E rated game. So overall a 9 for both appeal areas.
Presentation- The game has really no amin flaws with presentation. Frame rate was made better in a recent update. The combat does not fall behind, but I kinda wish you got up from the ground quicker, because when someone got me with an arrow, by the time I get up he has got another loaded. The shield runs well and it is great how right smack dab in the middle of a swing, your shield comes right out so nothing hurts you. (Except for arrow's on the other side.) I would give it a 8 in presentation.
Fun- Overall, the main thing is fun. And this is where we see Castle Crashers at best! Who can get enough of the mindblowing hacks and slashes? Arena for the ones who could really step it up. This game redefines the shooter genre because of how it handles kills and deaths. In order to get a death you must first be down and choose to "Give Up" instead of waiting for a medic. When you give up it also gives a kill to the person that downed you. However, if you choose to wait for a medic you are penalized a death. So, if you run around with your squad you'll have a better chance to get revived and keep your K/D ratio. However, on the flip side, if you are surrounded and it is hard for your medics to get to you then you may have to "Give Up" and respawn.
Each time you respawn your entire team loses a ticket, so medics are an integral part of the game. On top of that, the game doesn't show you your kill/death count until after the game has ended. I really like how Squad is team based and how it gives you the opportunity to choose when you die. However, I feel a price of $25.00USD would be a more fair price.

I've been playing Rimworld for about a year, and it's easily one of my favorite games of all time, which is saying something because I've been playing video games for about forty years! The best part of this game is the stories that it generates. Here are three of them (some games heavily modded):
The first game of Rimworld that I ever played was going great until the raiders came. My colonists put up one hell of a fight, but after driving the raiders off all of them were incapacitated except for Sally, the neurotic brawler. As her compatriots were bleeding out on the ground, she decided that she wanted to go play horseshoes. Nope. I ordered her to rescue her companions. Then she wanted to play chess. Huh-uh. I ordered her to bandage their wounds. After that, she wanted to go grab a bite to eat, but I ordered her to feed her fellow colonists first.
Finally, when she was able to tend to her own needs, she found that she had fed all of the meals to the other colonists, leaving her with only a few raw potatoes. She ate them and went to bed.
Great, I thought. Crisis averted.
Then she woke up in the middle of the night. One by one, she killed all of the other colonists as they lay helpless in their beds. Then she went outside, stripped off her clothing, and wandered around in the snow until she died of exposure.
Mass murder in Rimworld often begins with eating a raw potato.
In another game I played, we managed to capture a raider who had a great set of skills, but a really high recruitment difficulty. We kept him around trying to recruit him for over a year, but when food became scarce I had to consider whether to cut him loose, or cut him up (y'know, for food). I hadn't come to a decision yet when the colony was raided again. We fended off the raid, but one of my colonists lost an arm in the process.
At that point, my choice was clear. I tried to recruit the raider one more time, and failing that, I sent in the doc.
As my colonist admired his shiny new arm, I realized that I now had a use for the stubborn raider: spare parts!
Years later, when the raider finally hobbled out of our compound on two peg legs, he had only one eye left, no limbs except the ones we'd made for him, and his nose was gone. Oh yeah, and he was naked, too... we took his clothes before we let him go.
Recycle!
In my most recent playthrough, the colonists walled in a large area soon after they landed, trapping a few animals in the process. I soon ordered one of the colonists to hunt these animals for meat. This was no problem until the colonist tried to hunt the tortoise. As soon as the bullet penetrated its shell, the tortoise flew into a rage. The tortoise was on him like lightning (that is, if lightning moved really, really slow) and bit his toe off.
As the tortoise chewed idly upon the aforementioned severed toe, I took a closer look at him and found that this wasn't his first rodeo. He'd been shot and stabbed before. This was a tortoise that I could respect.
I left him alone after that, adopting him as a kind of mascot, but not really bothering to tame him and make him a part of the colony. But Tess, the colony's warg, was not as impressed as I was. She considered the tortoise as a snack to be consumed at a later time.
So it wasn't long before they decided to rumble. Tess got the short end of that encounter, and for her trouble she got three shattered legs that had to be amputated and replaced with peg legs (remember, mods).
At that point I named the tortoise Lemmy. Because he was a bad♥♥♥♥♥
Lemmy spent the next few years wandering around the compound (Tess, meanwhile, got a fourth peg leg after an unfortunate incident with a cow).
But eventually as the compound developed, there were fewer and fewer dandelions for Lemmy to eat. Afraid that he would starve, I decided to tame him. It was easier than I thought it would be, and the first thing that Lemmy did was to head outside of the compound (as a member of the colony, he could open doors now).
Not long after, as Lemmy munched on dandelions, he was attacked by a group of tribals. At 191 years of age, Lemmy wasn't as spry as he was when he was in his seventies, and he was cut down before he could fight back. As he lay bleeding out in a patch of his much-loved dandelions, he would have given the tribals the finger.
But he didn't have one. Because he was a tortoise.
If you spend fifty years as an underappreciated musician, some nerd will eventually name a turtle after you. But not a real one, though. A fake one. On the computer.
tl;dr: Learn to read, lazy♥♥♥♥♥ And buy this game.

They put a lot of effort into this game and it shows, in terms of production values the game is nearly perfect. The graphics are very good even on low settings, but the game is optimized well enough to run smoothly on a year-old low/mid range laptop. Fans of the previous games made by Remedy may be disappointed, as 3 has some major stylistic differences. The graphic novel storytelling has been replaced by cinematic cutscenes which, while competently made, have a visual style that I personally found irritating, and the game is very cutscene-heavy. The film noir aesthetic is almost completely gone and the style is more reminiscent of something like Die Hard 4. The story is also heavier and more serious than the previous games and doesn't have any of the weird/quirky humor.
The gameplay is generally fine, though again, fans of the previous games might dislike the more modern design choices such as heavily cover-based shooting and limited amount of weapons you can carry. If you want to play this like the old Max Payne games, I recommend playing on Easy, as the game is quite challenging and the Medium difficulty already had some tough firefights that might become frustrating for the average player (they did for me, at least).
As you can probably tell, I came into this game as a fan of the series, and overall I was slightly disappointed with some of the stylistic choices Rockstar made, most notably the heavy reliance on cinematics. Still, Max Payne 3 is by no means a bad game, and it's easily worth the price, especially when it goes on sale (which it does frequently). I'd give it a 7/10, probably an 8/10 without fan bias.

My overall opinion on portal 2:
Portal 2 is a fun time, and the summer sale was a great time to buy it, as I only payed $2.23 for it (in a bundle containing portal as well) I have had tons of fun doing co-op play with my friends, and some of the community levels are really impressive.
Expands on the original portal
has plenty of puzzles to solve
has a level builder for those who are creative (unlike me)
has co-op
charming characters
To be honest, I'm actually having a hard time thinking about cons while writing this, most are nitpicks, or related to my computer's hardware.
The single player mechanics are basically the same as the original portal. you have the "aperature science handheld portal device" or what I just refer to as a portal gun, and you use it to traverse your way through test chambers. The voice acting is great, and the story is great. There is a wide variety of player-made test chambers, some of them are really impressive, and I honestly have no idea how people even come up with those types of puzzles.
The Co-op mode is where I spend most of my time playing Portal 2. You take control of one of two robots, Atlas or P-body. It doesn't really matter which one you play as, but the host is always Atlas, and the second player is always P-body. Both are charming characters. In co-op, both players have their own portal gun, which each work exactly like in single player. Both players need to work together. I found co-op most fun while playing with a friend I was talking to via discord/skype, as the in-game way of communicating, known as the "ping" tool isn't the best. The ping tool helps for marking locations to your partner, you can use this to indicate where to place a portal, or which button to step on. While In-game, you can press the tab key on your keyboard to see your partner's view in the bottom right corner of your screen. Oh yeah, there's also a split screen mode if you plug in a controller. I personally haven't tested this, but I assume it works same as it does on console versions. Overall, Co-op is fun, but mainly with friends. There are also plenty of co-op community levels to enjoy.
I really enjoyed portal 2, the story was engaging, the co-op is super fun, and you will never run out of levels to play. I would reccomend playing the original portal first though, it's pretty short and its cheap. It only took around 3 hours, I completed it before even touching portal 2.

Nov 2017 Update::
The developer continues to put out new and excellent content for this game. Original Review::
(Even though Steam does not show much time played, I have played this game since its first alpha release, all provided steam-free)
RimWorld is a fantastic game remenescent of Dwarf Fortress. Originally backed on Kickstarter, I have been following this project since its beginnings (years ago), and I have to say that I am impressed with how far it has come!
The game is constantly being updated, and though the updates do not come out every week, when they come out they usually add some great new content, fix bugs, and improve gameplay.  Not to mention, with every update thus far, Tynan provides a great Youtube video that details some of the biggest/best additions/updates in that release.
If you enjoy simulation games, similar to Dwarf Fortress, Towns, Craft The World, etc, then you should definitely give RimWorld a chance!  The graphics might not be the prettiest around, but if you played any of the previously mentioned games, then you probably don't mind that at all (I know I don't).
In RimWorld you control a group of survivors (and as of update 14 you can now play as a pre-existing colony as well!) that have crash-landed on the planet, RimWorld.  With a top-down view of the planet, you provide general instructions for your group to try and get them to start building shelter, collecting food (farming, hunting, cooking, etc), and preparing for any number of bad scenarios (tribal raids, weather, mad squirrels that will kill off half of your colony, tons of stuff).  Colonists have their own personalities, the map you play on is randomly generated, as is the contents of that map; this results in a unique experience every time you play.
With update 14, I am looking forward to playing with the new Scenario system, to see what sort of crazy randomly-generated scenarios/challenges I can get.

Although Steam tells you something different, I have bought this game soon after it's Kickstarter campaign and easily collected over 100 hours of playtime in the past three years. I can say that this was literally the game I waited for without knowing it when I first saw it. While it has an excellent presentation it gives you the complete freedom of choice how to develop your colony on the one hand, but also an ultimate goal, building a spaceship, on the other.
Before you keep on reading a word to the few negative reviews from new players: Yes, this is a complex game. As someone said on the discussions: "It's not a FPS where you start on heroic difficulty becasue you know shooters." It's a game with many mechanics you will have to learn before beeing good at it, I recommend enableing the adaptive tutorial to learn the basic systems. It's also a very slow paced game with eventual peaks in form of raids or such. The two hours you have to decide if you want to refund are not nearly enough to see all the facades of the game and get a complete picture of it. Now on to the positives.
Wether you want to build an underground complex or a large fortress, all stragtegies are viable and have their own advantages and disadvantages. If you need to hold a large base you will have lots of walls which you need to defend and the enemy may break through at different locations. But while you can keep your entry small and defendable if you go underground, you eventually will have to fight bug hives which can spread sub-surface and enemies which are equipped with granades and pickaxes in order to dig their way to you.
The incredible amount of replayability also thrives from the different biomes and the recently added scenario system. Each of the eight climatic environments has unique weather, animals, diseases and challenges. The scenarios give you the ability to never play twice with the same starting condition, may it be the number of colonists, items and conditions of the map or forced cannibalism.
There is also an active mod community which has specialised on vanilla- and lore friendly mods that truely expand the game to it's full potential. Every veteran will be able to give you a list of some length with mods that he/she considers necessary to play the game. Of course it's not unplayable without mods but they do add many quality-of-life improvements which make playing the game easier.
Many people ask why they should pay 30$ for an early access title. Bear in mind that the early access is there to indicate that the game is still beeing worked on. However it has met all his goals, is polished, optimized and generally bug-free. You are basically looking at a finished game which will get expanded in the future and thus is marked as an early access.
The developer, Tynan Sylvester, who made this game almost on his own, usually releases new mayor builds every three to four months, introducing new and basic game mechanics, like the scenario system, but we will have to see how steam dynamic will change this. If there are bugs which survived the extensive testing phase, you can count on a hotfix beeing published within days.
RimWorld is what it says: a story generator. Usually I'm very suspicious about games who claim that, but in this case it is totally correct. Stories on the forums range from prisoners getting torn apart in order to sell their organs to colonists which give their lives in a heroic last stand to save the colony. If you're not sure, head over to the
and read one or two to a glass of your favourite relaxing drink.
Anyone who has an interest in strategy, building and/or science fiction should buy this game and probably wont be disappointed.

Not often have I been more excited about a game, before it even came out. And I have to say, I haven't been disappointed and am absolutely hooked.
This game isn't for everyone. It's slower paced than most other shooters. Death happens without always being able to tell who shot you. Sometimes it's hard to tell the difference between friend and enemy. The game relies heavily on teamplay and voice communication - which can be difficult in a server filled with mostly new players. But when those few experienced Squad leaders step up to lead the squads, and voice communication within and between squads gets off the ground, and squads work together as a team, magic happens.
In no other game have I ever had as much fun as in this one. In no other game have I felt so ridiculously happy and PROUD about a game well played. This game has proven to be more social for me than many MMO's that I played, which are supposed to be built around the social aspect. Even if a match is lost; if your squad worked well, it was still rewarding.
Of course, being an early alpha game, it's far from finished. The performance isn't great on slower systems, because it's graphically not well optimized. There are no vehicles in the game yet (at the time of writing), so expect long stretches of running across terrain (which I personally don't mind about at all. It brings immersion, it gets voice chat with your squad off the ground, and it makes sticking together and staying alive that much more important). There are currently "only" two active game modes and six maps (with several control point layouts, however). But all of that still already manages to produce these experiences that have been better than any others that I have had in gaming.
Graphics are nice. 36-versus-36 battles are impressive to watch on the map. Large-scale strategy becomes an actual factor. Sound is AMAZING - let me stress this again - it is AMAZING. Guns sound like paintball rifles if you're used to games like Call of Duty, but watch any military footage or talk to war veterans and you'll realize that *this is what it sounds like*. You'll hear loud bullet impacts around you before you hear the soft pops in the distance, because of sound's travel speed. You'll hear gunfire and explosions in the distance. Vision gets blurred as bullets hit around you.
This game is intense. Even if this would be it, it'd still be my favourite game - but this is only the beginning. And I'm thrilled to think about all that's yet to come. With the devs from the Project Reality mod behind it, I have faith that they'll put their everything into making this game the best that they can. And in my opinion, with this game in its current state - on top of their well-functioning, still-alive Project Reality mod for Battlefield 2 - they've already proved their worth twice.
Hope to see you in my squad some time. :-)

This is a challenging first person puzzle game set in a captivating world. There are three "worlds," each with their own beautifully rendered historic / cultural themes, along with a futuristic tower that you ascend as you progress through the game.
The puzzles ramp up smoothly in difficulty, with easy tutorial-like levels in the beginning to sometimes maddeningly complex levels near the end. If you find the standard puzzles too easy, there are additional "star" puzzles that require more outside-the-box thinking, often involving elements from multiple puzzle levels or even the environment outside the puzzle levels.
After a while, you start to recognize common puzzle mechanics, and as a result some of the puzzle might start seeming redundant and tedious. However, the star puzzles are constantly fresh and challenging. It's almost as if the normal puzzles are merely appetizers, while the star puzzles are the main course in this game. I think you would be doing a disservice to yourself if you didn't at least attempt to solve all the star puzzles.
If you get stuck, you might be tempted to look up solutions from google-sensei, but believe me, it's a lot more satisfying if you solve it yourself. You can always leave a puzzle and come back to it later. There are also many Easter eggs in the game, some of which you might stumble across as you're banging your head against that one puzzle you can't solve. So I guess that helps ease the pain. Some puzzles have multiple solutions, so keep that in mind.
As for the story, it's not a straightforward storybook plot that's spoon fed to you. It requires a bit of inference and noticing of subtle details, like the timestamps of messages you come across. Even then, it's not a story that will appeal to everyone. It revolves around metaphysical themes that touch on predestination, purpose, creation, and humanity. If this sounds like a lot of BS to you, then you probably won't like the story. I personally found it interesting enough. But even if it's not your cup of tea, it's not necessary to enjoy the game, as the puzzles are the real meat of the game.
As someone who sometimes gets dizzy/headaches from playing first person games, I appreciate that the game includes a FoV slider. The music is atmospheric and enjoyable, but it's nothing that stands out or catches your attention. I eventually turned it off and put on a podcast in the background.
The one critique I have about the game is the "alternate" ending you get if you unlock the extra level in the tower is uninspiring and unsatisfying. I suppose there is the satisfaction of simply solving it, but even so, it would be nice to have a better reward for it. Also, while there are barcoded messages scattered across the world that your character automatically translates for you when you view them, there is one barcode message that won't translate and requires you to use a barcode app on your phone (or google) to translate. That, I feel, is an unnecessary tedium and only serves to break immersion. However, these are small gripes for an otherwise fantastic game.

I highly recommend this free-to-play MMO RTS FPS if you're into a massive clusterf*ck of 3 different factions fighting across infantry, air- and ground vehicle combat across 4 well designed massive continents.
This game offers up a unique variety of playstyles, catering to every type of player both casual and hardcore competitive in a massive arsenal of weapons and vehicles, some unique and some shared across all factions. With all the well balanced weapons, you will have a hard time deciding what you like the most, because there is so much to choose from. Vehicles are spawned by a currency called Nanites, where each and every player has the opportunity to spawn the vehicle of their liking (if enough nanites have built up over time) and managing accessibility to that vehicle via a user friendly panel to kick and restrict vehicle access.
Once you're indulged with all the various combat possibilities, you have the option to join or create a squad that consist of 12 players, thereafter you can branch a squad out into a platoon, with up to 4 squads! Creating a total of 48 possible players per platoon, this enables the leadership roles to coordinate everyone to broaden the strategic element that the game offers.
The game also enables you to create in-game outfits (clans) with a 1000+ members, helping establish communities from within which further cultivates the growth of the games development. Outfits come in all shapes and sizes from small casual outfits for friends enjoying their time together to massive communities of hardcore infantry units to shape the outcome of a battle.
Due to the scale of player population, servers are restricted to massive dedicated servers situated in the majority of populated regions such as NA, EU and AU. Although I play on a european server with 180-200 ping, I'm astonished at how well the hit registration copes with the high latency and even more amazed at how these servers host all these players at a stable rate.
For the most part the community is supportive and will look to assist and welcome new players among them, where the majority of squads are always open to anyone, regardless of their rank, to join in on the fun. With each faction exerting it's own vibe and way of doing things, you will encounter lots of different players aligning themselves with a different faction, each pledging loyalty to the cause. However do not fear, you can tell them apart easily by their distinct colors.
Vanu Sovereignty [VS] - Lasers, Drugs and Spandex, these guys don't mess around when it comes to looking fashionable as f*ck and kicking♥♥♥♥♥at the same time.
New Conglomerate [NC] - Cardboard box ninja rebels, loyalist band of brothers that persistently fail to give up, which I envy.

Not often have I been more excited about a game, before it even came out. And I have to say, I haven't been disappointed and am absolutely hooked.
This game isn't for everyone. It's slower paced than most other shooters. Death happens without always being able to tell who shot you. Sometimes it's hard to tell the difference between friend and enemy. The game relies heavily on teamplay and voice communication - which can be difficult in a server filled with mostly new players. But when those few experienced Squad leaders step up to lead the squads, and voice communication within and between squads gets off the ground, and squads work together as a team, magic happens.
In no other game have I ever had as much fun as in this one. In no other game have I felt so ridiculously happy and PROUD about a game well played. This game has proven to be more social for me than many MMO's that I played, which are supposed to be built around the social aspect. Even if a match is lost; if your squad worked well, it was still rewarding.
Of course, being an early alpha game, it's far from finished. The performance isn't great on slower systems, because it's graphically not well optimized. There are no vehicles in the game yet (at the time of writing), so expect long stretches of running across terrain (which I personally don't mind about at all. It brings immersion, it gets voice chat with your squad off the ground, and it makes sticking together and staying alive that much more important). There are currently "only" two active game modes and six maps (with several control point layouts, however). But all of that still already manages to produce these experiences that have been better than any others that I have had in gaming.
Graphics are nice. 36-versus-36 battles are impressive to watch on the map. Large-scale strategy becomes an actual factor. Sound is AMAZING - let me stress this again - it is AMAZING. Guns sound like paintball rifles if you're used to games like Call of Duty, but watch any military footage or talk to war veterans and you'll realize that *this is what it sounds like*. You'll hear loud bullet impacts around you before you hear the soft pops in the distance, because of sound's travel speed. You'll hear gunfire and explosions in the distance. Vision gets blurred as bullets hit around you.
This game is intense. Even if this would be it, it'd still be my favourite game - but this is only the beginning. And I'm thrilled to think about all that's yet to come. With the devs from the Project Reality mod behind it, I have faith that they'll put their everything into making this game the best that they can. And in my opinion, with this game in its current state - on top of their well-functioning, still-alive Project Reality mod for Battlefield 2 - they've already proved their worth twice.

This game would be better than Overwatch if the devs buckled down and tuned a few things properly, removing the need for that Beta tag.
Personally, I feel that it is anyway, but only slightly.
Cons:
-No Party system; players must find an empty enough server and hope they get their friend's team.
-Characters are very expensive. This is mitigated by there only being a need to own perhaps 5, two solid freebies, and a free rotation, but it's disheartening to see that nobody will EVER decrease in price.
-Explosives have a clear advantage over bullets in most cases. Characters can resist a great amount of bullet damage, which is fine, but will often die instantly to explosives, which also require less aim. Nader, the Demoman/Junkrat character, is the most able to abuse this.
-Seemingly no matchmaking system. Utter morons are frequently on the same team as level 100+ demigods.
-No Overtime, but matches don't instantly end once literally unwinnable.
-VERY slow levelling, which is made a problem by the janky rewards system in early levels giving items which can't be opened until later. Credit income is also terrible at base.
-Ugly "Beta Build" watermark.
Pros:
-3-hour Mission rotation, which is a great balance between dailies or just expecting grinding to progress.
-Solid character balance. While some characters are UP and never seen, there is no unanimously OP character, except perhaps the perpetually 3/5ths normal price Proxy.
-Destroying Iron loadout cards gives you the exact amount it costs to make another, so you can reroll for a loadout you want at that level. Loadout cards beyond Bronze offer no gameplay advantages, so it's not P2W.
-No Roadhog or Pharah
-Walljumps
-Generally a really solid team game, which would make it ideal with a party system. Pacing and shooting both feel good.

I was a backer of this game on Kickstarter, so I’ve been playing it for a long, long time.
It’s one of the more enjoyable “ant-farm” games I’ve played.  I enjoy it more than Dwarf Fortress (make no mistake, it’s a DF clone) as I prefer the sci-fi angle.  It’s also (at the current build) much less demanding than DF.
There is a lot to like about this game, but I’m going to focus on what I don’t like:
•	No Z-axis.  It would be nice to be able to dig up or down to extend the map.
•	Too many pawns just can’t do something useful.  This has been somewhat mitigated in the latest build.
•	Priorities not detailed enough.  Colonists will haul rocks to the trash before hauling food.
•	Trade ships are required, but incredibly (game-breakingly) rare.  Can be adjusted with Mods.
•	No way to effectively mitigate some events.   Really, I can create a solar panel, but I can’t make fuses?
Honestly, most of those are nit-picks, and they can be worked around (you can use the developer tools to force a trade ship, and fix many of the other issues).  This is an early access game, so all of that is subject to change.
All in all, this has been a very fun game to play.
And, unlike DF, you can win this game.  So, losing, while fun, isn’t your only option.

Robocraft is a driving shoot-em-up where you build cars, tanks, robots, planes, helicopters or whatever weird creation you can think of and drive them out to fight each other.
You are granted a light walker, a hovercraft and a tank to get you started which you can use or dismantle for the components.
There are a few different game mode:
The tutorial tells you how to place blocks in edit mode, how to move a walker and tells you to kill a stationary bot. You then recieve a reward crate.
2 teams fight to a specified number of kills. After death you respawn and are shielded for a few seconds
A variation on basic or previously removed pit or elimination with additional rules such as weapon limitations. Changes every few weeks.
2 teams fight to fill their base with crystals. There are 3 capture points on the map, if you hold all 3 you can shoot into the enemy base to steal their crystals. If you hold at least one tower your base is protected by a shield which blocks enemy fire and bots while regenerating allies. Every 5 minutes a crystal appears which the losing team can destroy to equalise the scores.
The same as basic but it's just you and AI bots. A good place to test new builds
A wireframe VR style map for testing robots.
Battles give crate drop rewards containing up to 4 random items for non-premium or 8 if you have premium, a better performance grants you a better quality crate. Items you don't want can be recycled for a small amount of robits which you can use to buy parts or even complete bots in the Community Robot Factory(CRF)
No, the game is not pay to win however paying for premium does double your reward from battle and triple what you get for recycling components. You can also buy premium crates which means you are paying for random items all of which can be obtained as free drops anyway.
You may notice several reviews say the game is pay to win but I can only assume they don't actually know what pay to win means. You pay to reduce the grind and get a few more colours to paint your bot not for any kind of advantage.
An ELO system has now been added which increases or decreases your rank based on whether your team wins or loses, this is an improvement on when there was no form of balancing but it doesn't take player performance into account so it only works if you play in a platoon.
Rather than filtering bots by relative strength Freejam opted instead to make smaller bots have a larger energy pool to fire longer before recharging weapons, at the same time big guns naturally have a high energy drain. This encourages people to make smaller bots with over sized guns or larger bots with smaller guns. As a new player if you try out your starting walker expect to be matched against all manner of weapon and module combinations likely including a dual chain shredder walker and a teleporting shotgun hover. To put simply 2 of your starter bots are completely impractical and obsolete under the current balancing system.
This in theory doesn't sound a bad idea especially since it now only uses the free ingame currency.
Put your bot designs up in the CRF and if anybody buys your bot you get 25% of the robits they spent.
In practice this has lead to a serious lack of creativity, expect to see duplicates of the same bot in some battles and a few core designs that have been widely bought in the CRF making up a frustratingly high percentage of bots.
When you finish a battle instead of getting robits towards buying the parts you want you get a crate containing a few random parts. For me I already have plenty of components to play with so this isn't an issue.
Its the new players who suffer under this system, most weapons require at least 5-8 of the same weapon equipped to be effective, likewise most movement parts require you to have multiple of the same item. You will likely find that after a few battles you have a selection of new guns and movement part, you will also likely find you only have 1 of each. Do you want to sell items that you likely want to try later anyway at a greatly reduced value until you can afford enough of the part you want to try out or do you want to slowly grind until you eventually have enough of something different you can equip.
At one time the game was completely different, you had a tech tree. To buy new parts you first had to research them with research points gained from battle. Your bot size was limited by your level and the size of your bot determined what battle tier you fought in. Researching parts gave you something to work towards, getting that extra CPU from a level so you could add to your bot likewise gave you something to aim for.
Now you can buy anything from the start and anything can drop in random chest, levels are simply free crates. The only form of progression is in the MMR teirs of normal mode but unless you play in a platoon you will just yoyo with no progress.
This is the primary battle mode replacing Battle arena and therefore needs to be able to hold its own. Unfortunately you spend more time waiting for timers than fighting. Once you are ahead the only thing left to do is spawn camp.
The maps are so small that if your team goes for the equaliser you can't be stopped, on 1 map you can even shoot it from within your base, good luck getting ahead on capture points though, you're likely just prolonging the battle.
Previously different bots could approach a fight in different ways to all offer a different advantage, for example you could have your tanky and dps bots take a straight kill the enemy on advance approach, while fast bots flank or split push. Now mobility is far less useful to a team since you need to destroy defending vehicles to capture a point and a single tanky vehicle can block a capture point for a good amount of time.
Progress was made in this area with all players now having to load in before the battle starts. Unfortunately if 1 player fails to load in everybody gets kicked back to the main menu. This isn't much of an issue with the 5v5 setup for normal and basic but Brawl can be rather difficult to get into a game under elimination rules.
Crash a hovercraft into a heavy tank and chances are the tank will be flipped into the air while you glide straight though feeling barely a bump.
Test map to me highlights the design decisions frequently made by Freejam. This is supposed to be a map to test your bots and has a shortcut from the edit screen to test your current creation during the build process. Sounds like a useful feature but as usual there is an issue.
The physics in test map don't match the physics in battle, this is most noticeable with hovers and flyers. A hovercraft which is perfectly balanced in test map and glides like a hawk could have a 45 degree lean in battle or spin wildly out of control due to a bad centre of thrust.
A plane which flies perfectly in test map could prove to be too heavy to leave the ground or completely uncontrollable due to poorly placed thrusters.
Mode names may seem a petty thing to have an issue with but its more the combination of the two. Changing Deathmatch and Battle arena to Basic and Normal just makes it sound more childish or overly casual. Combined with the big blocky mode selection screen gives almost the feeling of a mobile port.
While I enjoyed the core build, drive, fight concept of the game it lacks the pace, diversity and strategy it once had.

The Talos Principle is a game that many people will immediately compare to Portal. This game is better than Portal.
In the Talos Principle, you are a robot. Literally anything further than that is a unknown to you. Your goal is to solve puzzles using objects scattered around the world, use the "sigils" (tetronimos) you gain from beating these in block puzzles to unlock new things, and ultimately solve every last puzzle across the land.
But things are more complicated than that. There are glitches in the code, a terminal tells you. Things aren't as they seem. But how does the terminal know? Who is to say that the terminal is right and the omniescent voice telling you what to do is wrong? Are you even a robot? Could you be human all this time? What even defines a human?
The Talos Principle is a puzzle game that combines traditional 1st person puzzle solving with ridiculously in depth philosophy and stunning graphics. A careful balance between the gameplay though, as whenever you seem to grow tired of philosophy or solving endless puzzles you can always find something else to do, like find the hidden stars across the land (which I should mention are ballbustingly cryptic, this is CROTEAM we're talking about) or explore for more terminals and hidden lore. The Puzzles themselves are a mix between "I beat it in 10 seconds" and "♥♥♥♥ it, i'm looking up a walkthrough" and are extremely copious in amount as you explore the world further. I never felt like I was doing the same stuff over and over again in the puzzles, which was surprising due to the sheer amount of them in the game.
The story is revealed to you through terminals as you beat puzzles, and sometimes Elohim (a voice in the sky) will pipe in as well. The "story" is more philisophical debate than actual plot, and for that reason I wouldn't recommend the game to people who aren't interested in philosophy (but if you're not sure, go for it- this is a great way to get into it).
