This is a long review, so I'll start by jumping to the conclusion:
Rimworld is a graphically appealing colony management game, set on a distant world, with a strong 'wild west' vibe. If you enjoy colony management games with a good balance between strategic depth and fun, then this is a game worth checking out!
Now for the wordy bit of the review:
To be clear, this game was given to me over a year ago by the developer, and again, recently I was offered an opportunity to play the steam release a few days ahead of the official unveiling (Alpha 14) That being said, I'm an avid fan of the colony management genre and judge the game against the likes of Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria, Prison Archetect, and even the oldies like Startopia and Dungeon Keeper.
First, let's get the comparison to Dwarf Fortress out of the way; Rimworld is not as complicated as DF. But then, what game could ever claim that? But Rimworld does an amazing job of distilling the fun from the complexity. You will find yourself building traps to blunt raider attacks, large industrial areas, prioritising research and even delving into animal husbandry. Whatever you do, it'll focus more on being a game, than a complex world simulation.
That said, there's a lot of strategy involved, it just never feels like fun is taking a back seat to it!
The visual aesthetic closely resembles Prison Architect, so if you're familiar with that game, and enjoy the art style, then you'll find a lot to like about Rimworld's clean, sometimes cartoony graphics. Rimworld also boasts some amazing audio assets and impressively atmospheric music that really helps to set the mood in the game!
The difficulty is highly customisable, and combined with the detailed scenario editor, allows you to tailor each game to suite your particular skill level. Want steadily rising levels of tension and challenge as you play? Then pick an AI storyteller that will emphasise dramatic pacing and adjust in game events to match your situation, keeping you on your toes but never throwing truly impossible odds your way. Want a relaxed experience where you can focus on learning the game? Pick (or create) a scenario that affords you a generous set of starting conditions, and an AI story teller who will give you plenty of time to prepare or recover from each event... the game can be as brutal, or as gentle as you want it to be! :)
Finally, as for longevity, without even touching on the topic of modding (Rimworld has one of the most rich and active modding communities I've seen in these kinds of games!) the base Rimworld experience offers enough potential to adjust your game and starting conditions that I find it unlikely that anyone will grow bored. There's enough strategy involved in making a successful colony, and enough difference to be found in the various events that might occur, that you're virtually guaranteed a different experience each time you play.
In my opinion Rimworld is a solid example of a colony management/simulation game, where the raw fun of the game has not been hidden beneath the complexity of the simulation, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to any fan of the genre.

The Talos Principle is a game that many people will immediately compare to Portal. This game is better than Portal.
In the Talos Principle, you are a robot. Literally anything further than that is a unknown to you. Your goal is to solve puzzles using objects scattered around the world, use the "sigils" (tetronimos) you gain from beating these in block puzzles to unlock new things, and ultimately solve every last puzzle across the land.
But things are more complicated than that. There are glitches in the code, a terminal tells you. Things aren't as they seem. But how does the terminal know? Who is to say that the terminal is right and the omniescent voice telling you what to do is wrong? Are you even a robot? Could you be human all this time? What even defines a human?
The Talos Principle is a puzzle game that combines traditional 1st person puzzle solving with ridiculously in depth philosophy and stunning graphics. A careful balance between the gameplay though, as whenever you seem to grow tired of philosophy or solving endless puzzles you can always find something else to do, like find the hidden stars across the land (which I should mention are ballbustingly cryptic, this is CROTEAM we're talking about) or explore for more terminals and hidden lore. The Puzzles themselves are a mix between "I beat it in 10 seconds" and "♥♥♥♥ it, i'm looking up a walkthrough" and are extremely copious in amount as you explore the world further. I never felt like I was doing the same stuff over and over again in the puzzles, which was surprising due to the sheer amount of them in the game.
The story is revealed to you through terminals as you beat puzzles, and sometimes Elohim (a voice in the sky) will pipe in as well. The "story" is more philisophical debate than actual plot, and for that reason I wouldn't recommend the game to people who aren't interested in philosophy (but if you're not sure, go for it- this is a great way to get into it). It's also a lot of reading as the story comes through chat logs, emails, and an archive of old libraries.
Despite all this, there are some shortcomings, although few and far between. There are some puzzles that are more "action" oriented, and while most are fine there are some that add unnecessary frustration and pain due to their out of place nature (whoever designed "Egyptian Arcade" needs to be banned from making puzzle games). There are also multiple endings, and while I haven't gotten to them all yet I'm assuming based on how the story unfolded that I'm going to have to make multiple saves for it which is a huge pain.
Overall, I highly recommend The Talos Principle. At 15 dollars (current price, on sale) it's an absolute steal. Even higher than that it's worth it. At 40 dollars I'd still say it's abosolutely worth the money, but be weary if you're not into philosophy at that price because reading tons of text and debating with a computer is about half the game.

Build insane, fully customisable robot battle vehicles that drive, hover, walk and fly in the free-to-play action game Robocraft. Add weapons from the future and jump in the driving seat as you take your creation into battle against other players online!
is a creative game allowing you, the player to build tanks, planes and anything you wish.The game is a multiplayer online experience on the line of "World of Tanks". :Negative: The game is fairly entertaining, however there is not really a good matchmaking system thus you might get paired up against a very powerful team. The seperation of tiers helps this, but the game still is not very well balanced. The game is free to play so if are willing to put in some time, you will not lose any money. The biggest problem however is that it takes a long time to get anywhere. You can not build a plane until halfway through the game, and this put a damper on my spirits when I first booted up the game. When you get to the fourth tier, you will start noticing a big problem. The railgun( ie sniper rifle. The rail gun puts a very big handicap on people trying to get through the game as you will notice yourself getting repeatedly picked off multiple times. Now, for most fps players you're probably thinking "Well that doesn't seem like a bad problem as most shooters have very big sniper problems". Well the sniper problem tends to be a bit bigger in Robocraft due to the fact that the maps are very open, meaning there is less cover to hide behind. There is also a shortage of maps, as there are only 5 different maps to play on. The servers are also very buggy as you will most likely have to resolve crashes and restart your computer frequently.:Positive: The game allows much more freedom than most games as you are actually able to build your own tank rather than choose from a preexisting one. The game is great for creative people who also want some action out of their creations (for those of you that have played Minecraft and wanted to build a giant siege engine you know what I mean). The game is of course still free to play so if you are unsure you can easily download it,and create an online acount. For those of you that might not have internet I am afraid there is no way for you to experience this. Robocraft is a fun and enjoyable experience with a lot of big problems that may or may not be fixed.

This is a long review, so I'll start by jumping to the conclusion:
Rimworld is a graphically appealing colony management game, set on a distant world, with a strong 'wild west' vibe. If you enjoy colony management games with a good balance between strategic depth and fun, then this is a game worth checking out!
Now for the wordy bit of the review:
To be clear, this game was given to me over a year ago by the developer, and again, recently I was offered an opportunity to play the steam release a few days ahead of the official unveiling (Alpha 14) That being said, I'm an avid fan of the colony management genre and judge the game against the likes of Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria, Prison Archetect, and even the oldies like Startopia and Dungeon Keeper.
First, let's get the comparison to Dwarf Fortress out of the way; Rimworld is not as complicated as DF. But then, what game could ever claim that? But Rimworld does an amazing job of distilling the fun from the complexity. You will find yourself building traps to blunt raider attacks, large industrial areas, prioritising research and even delving into animal husbandry. Whatever you do, it'll focus more on being a game, than a complex world simulation.
That said, there's a lot of strategy involved, it just never feels like fun is taking a back seat to it!
The visual aesthetic closely resembles Prison Architect, so if you're familiar with that game, and enjoy the art style, then you'll find a lot to like about Rimworld's clean, sometimes cartoony graphics. Rimworld also boasts some amazing audio assets and impressively atmospheric music that really helps to set the mood in the game!
The difficulty is highly customisable, and combined with the detailed scenario editor, allows you to tailor each game to suite your particular skill level. Want steadily rising levels of tension and challenge as you play? Then pick an AI storyteller that will emphasise dramatic pacing and adjust in game events to match your situation, keeping you on your toes but never throwing truly impossible odds your way. Want a relaxed experience where you can focus on learning the game? Pick (or create) a scenario that affords you a generous set of starting conditions, and an AI story teller who will give you plenty of time to prepare or recover from each event... the game can be as brutal, or as gentle as you want it to be! :)
Finally, as for longevity, without even touching on the topic of modding (Rimworld has one of the most rich and active modding communities I've seen in these kinds of games!) the base Rimworld experience offers enough potential to adjust your game and starting conditions that I find it unlikely that anyone will grow bored. There's enough strategy involved in making a successful colony, and enough difference to be found in the various events that might occur, that you're virtually guaranteed a different experience each time you play.
In my opinion Rimworld is a solid example of a colony management/simulation game, where the raw fun of the game has not been hidden beneath the complexity of the simulation, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to any fan of the genre.

Best puzzle game. It's often compared with Portal, but I think it's even better.
The puzzles themselves mostly reduce to a towers of hanoi type of resource management and sequencing. I'm someone who's quite good at puzzle games, and I found the star puzzles / bonus levels to pleasantly difficult. In particular "Nerve Wrecker" in world A's bonus levels really lived up to it's name, but it was a good kind of hurt. But at the same time, the pacing is perfect. Difficulty ramps up gradually, and there are no time restrictons on any puzzle
. The game gives a fair amount of choice in the order that puzzles can be completed in, and all the most difficult puzzles
are optional.
The art is brilliant. The worlds themselves are gorgeous and engaging. The philosophy is poignant and deep without the gross Philosophy 101 feeling that lesser games evoke when they try this. It touches on topics near and dear to me like transhumanism, the nature of free will, and the idea of the good. Not just touches, but really covers in satisfactory depth. Here, too, the pacing is brilliant, with the nature of the story being revealed gradually, but optionally. Players who have no desire to engage with philosophical aspect of The Talos Principle are never forced to; The terminals that they're delivered through can be ignored entirely (Although I personally believe anyone who chose to would be missing out)
In conclusion, 12/10, game of the year (all years), A+++++++++

The thing with Max Payne 3 is, that it lacks that film noir style, dark, rainy, snowy, setting (with 1 flashback exception). I understand that rockstar felt they have to change things up. But they already did with this very tense story, the short bursts of all out action, split by cinematic sequences. This being said, I miss the nostalgic feel of Max Pane 2: The Fall of Max Payne. I mean MP 3 (haha what a stupid abbreviation) has some references  to the likes of Mona Sax and Baseballbat-Boy, but I think there was a lot more potential. I understand the formerly noted change of gameplay, but I think Rockstar should've taken more risks by furthermore add to the franchise. And I'm by no means demanding a new love affair or such thing, since that would dilute the storyline and nostalgia of the prequels, something successors should never do, but I would've appreciated more deviant characters, that are crazy and unusual. Maybe even a new brazilian style mascot with maybe a short passage of similar gameplay as the "escort mission" of BB-Boy in MP 2. Given that is a fairly absurd example, but that character is in the series since the first game and I think a llitte more than just one or 2 references would've sufficed.
Yet it is very enjoyable, but doesn't run very well on my newish mac. It's not the hardware but the engine an port to Mac. In a few instances in very specific parts of levels, there was a sudden avalanche of graphical glitches like particle effects appearing completeley black, and the shading messing up, resulting in triangles and circles showing as black outlines in the level. But again other level where running perfectly fine.
Anyway for people who grew up with the Max Payne series, it is going to lack some Fan Service, but again will astonish you with brutally, brutally realistic sequences of a crook getting bursted by Max, which in it self is shockingly good and rewarding. Especially after you tried the same section around 10 times (on hard) and finally get that last enemy and finally clear the section.
So yes its worth it. I personally would love a Max Payne 2 remake with this new engine though (and a better port for Mac but thats secondary), and believe it would be the better Max Payne 3.

Early access often times goes poorly; Rimworld is the one example that i can point to that not only does early access right by releasing regular game updates constantly expanding on its features; it is one of the best games i've ever played (don't be fooled by my play hours, been playing it for about 800h before steam release).
First of all, don't get fooled by Rimworld being "Alpha", it is a fully functioning game with many more features than most full release strategy games, it only is still alpha because the dev still wants to add ever new features.
Rimworld is an excellent colony building game where you control a small group of spaceship crash survivors (or any other background you wish to have) that have to survive under extreme odds, each of them having different skills, traits and behaviour patterns that you need to account for. You will cheer for your colonists, you will cry over their dead bodies, and believe me there will be dead bodies... the difficulty is very high, but adjustable. Different storytellers will give you different challenges at different rates and of adjustable severity.
Is this game worth the price? Definitely!

This is truly a wonderful puzzle game. Puzzle designs are inventive, and it has got a decent (though at many times, vague) philosophical narrative.
If you've played a game like Portal and liked the puzzle solving there, then I suppose you'd like The Talos Principle as well. Some puzzles will have you stumped for a while, but thankfully the game has an "open" system where you can play puzzles in any order you like, so long as you have unlocked an area. Many times, I'd skip a difficult puzzle after pulling my hair out for an hour or two, only to return after playing all other puzzles in a given area to solve it within seconds or minutes. Perspective matters.
It's nice how the game has multiple endings based on how many puzzles you solved (there are basic puzzles, advanced puzzles, and then collecting stars), as well as depending on how well you listened to or disobeyed Elohim. And say you get Ending A...the game has a unique save system that allows you to go back a little in time to experience another ending, instead of needing to start a wholly new game. Though in one case, if you do something, it wouldn't lead to one particular ending no matter what.
I solved every single puzzle, and it took me 20 odd hours to complete the game. I didn't go hunting for the stars though, cause that seemed quite challenging and I thought I got what I needed out of the game by then already.
There's also a text based choice mine-game with the computer program, that is kinda interesting.
My singular complaint would be that the game kinda drags along around the 2/3rds point. It definitely could have been condensed a bit more, something which the devs have admitted in their post-mortem. Also, it was kinda disappointing that the 3rd area looked a lot like the first area...would have been nice if there was a whole new setting/landscape. The visuals as such while impressive, did get boring after a while.
Overall, I would say this is a great game. It has got multiple tiers of puzzles, so you can choose to do the easy ones, or the challenging ones, or the hardcore ones (getting all stars), and get "rewarded" accordingly with different endings. The narrative at times also makes you to pause and think for a moment, ponder over what was just said. Oh, and the soundtrack...SIMPLY AMAZING! This is the first time I have purchased a soundtrack for a game on Steam!

Don't let my Steam time fool you. I've been playing this game since November of 2015. I have probably put around 200 hours or so of time into it since then. Skip to the conclusion if this is a bit too long for you, but I'll try to keep it short.
So what's there to like about this game?
-Great and Helpful community (check out the forums for the game sometime).
-More mods than you can shake a manhunter pack at.
-Fun and unique gameplay (at least to me). The closest comparison to another game I can make is perhaps Prison
Architect just because of the style of top-down control over your colony, but that's where comparisons really end.
-Fun and unique story building. You are building a home (or escape) on this distant RimWorld. Your colonist count will almost always stay below 20 and you will level and up and develop your colonists, learn their names and perhaps grieve for them if they die in a raid or a tragic accident.
-Near-infinite replayability. Want to be a neolithic tribe using only stone weapons and tools? Awesome. Want to be a medieval tribe? Industrial? How about spacer tech with power armor and energy rifles while you laugh as the enemies' bullets simply bounce harmlessly off your colonists' armor? You can do it all. And with different mod packs, you can modify the experience to suit you. Too hard or too easy? There are mods for that. Not enough diversity of equipment, clothes, weapons, etc.? There are mods for that.
What's not to like?
-Hm. I thought I had something for this section. Sometimes stupid A.I.? This is my biggerst and probably only complaint about the game. The colonist AI sometimes requires a little micromanagement on the part of the player, but Tynan has been making it better with every update. A fine example would be your colonist going and trying to pick up food from a raider siege camp and getting ripped apart by a hail of bullets. This was fixed with a new AI system in which the player can set each colonist to react differently to nearby threats (run away, ignore, fight back and so on).
Conclusion:
If you like strategy games or immersing yourself in a story you create, then this game is for you. Prison Architect players will probably like it. Sims players will probably like it too. Any rogue-like players should enjoy it as well due to the randomized starts and worlds, as well as the new and optional permadeath system.
I'm a huge fan of this game, and this is my first review for a game on steam, even though I have a library of over 150 games. And with Steam's refund policy, you may as well give it a shot, right? It doesn't take much to make a map, pick a spot and randomize a few colonists and give the game a go. It has a good, non-intrusive tutorial system in place to show you the ropes as well.
Some people might say "30 dollars? That's way too much!" And in most cases, I agree with you. The only games I think I paid full price for on Steam were Fallout 4 and Dark Souls 3. But this game is worth every penny.

Wolfenstein: The New Order best exemplifies the cyclical nature of the FPS market. A decade ago, the FPS market was littered with World War 2 shooters, including the Wolfenstein franchise's best entry, Return to Castle Wolfenstein, and since then the shooter market has migrated away from Nazi culling and has placed it's cross hairs on the insurgents, terrorists and Russians that populate the modern landscape. The ebb and flow of first person shooters has brought us full circle in 2014 with the latest entry to the franchise that gave birth to what has become, arguably, the most popular genre in all of gaming. The New Order mixes the classic, gib infused, lead slinging, Nazi mutilating gameplay that defined the series with modern design elements like stealth and multiple time lines for added replayability. This kind of retro game design is ambitious to say the least, so has MachineGames pulled off a Cirque de Soleil worthy performance or has it fallen and racked it's testes, rendering this classic, macho franchise an impotent eunuch?

Perhaps no other element best exemplifies this clash between modern design and retro sensibilities than The New Order's plot. It's a battleground unto itself where some startlingly realized character relationships find themselves at odds with the sheer absurdity of it's alternate take on history. Three years after the events of the original game, the Nazi's have developed advanced technology that have allowed them to turn the tide of the war. In a massive Allied assault on a weapons laboratory run by General Deathshead, B.J. Blazkowicz suffers a near fatal encounter with the sadistic general, enduring a critical head injury that leaves him in a vegetative state. Like the second coming of Christ, Blazkowicz comes to fourteen years later to find that the  Nazis won the war by being the first to utilize nuclear weapons, and it's up to him to become the messiah of the resistance movement that rages against the Third Reich in a fight that stretches across the globe and even to the moon. It's a narrative that is gloriously kitschy and slightly reminiscent of Iron Sky, though without the clever satire. Counter balancing the B-movie sci-fi narrative are some character interaction s and relationships that are extremely well realized and engaging. Some of the antagonists in The New Order are extremely memorable in ways that so few antagonists have been in recent games. Frau Engel in particular stands out, with her Raiden-esque androgynous male companion and devious, psychotic games. The game's levels are littered with newspaper clippings and audio logs that flesh out this vision of a Nazi ruled world.

Without a single Tommy Gun or Garand in sight, the gunplay in Wolfenstein's latest entry sets itself apart from the seemingly ceaseless wave of World War 2 based first person shooters that inundated the market pre 2007. Weapons have a very heavy feel to them with high recoil and their propensity to cause Nazi skulls to erupt like melons dropped from a fourth story window. Adding to the carnage are goodies like an underslung rocket launcher for your assault rifle, shotgun rounds that bounce around corners and the ability to dual wield most weapons. The lack of recharging health and collectable armor give the impression that The New Order is an old school run and gun affair but strangely it's not... Stealth is a viable option and generally recommended. Sneaking up on a Nazi and carving him up like a Christmas ham can be just as satisfying as perforating him with an entire magazine. Unfortunately, the stealth also exposes what proves to be The New Order's greatest fault, the enemy AI seems to have suffered from the inbreeding of the master race. Enemies are not terribly perceptive and have little interest in preserving themselves or employing cunning strategies to put an end to your rebellion. Despite the fact that you will find yourself tackling waves of enemies, don't expect to be flanked or flushed out of cover. Wolfenstein does provide some challenge despite the dim witted opposition, unfortunately it's the result of foes that are massive bullet sponges. In the later portion of the game a large number of armored enemies can make progress slow going, and the possibility of running out of ammo is very real.

While most of the weapons in The New Order fall into conventional categories for FPS weaponry, there is one unique and welcome addition to the arsenal: the LaserKraftWerk. It's part tool and part Nazi exterminator, allowing B.J. to cut through metal grates exposing, collectables, items and hidden passages. Through the course of the game's 15 hour campaign, the LaserKraftWerk is upgraded allowing it's beams to be reflected, target several enemies, and fire in full auto.

Levels in The New Order are often sprawling and offer multiple paths to an objective. This creates the illusion of occupying a real place instead of a methodically scripted, linear level and also provides numerous opportunities for collectables and easter eggs to be tucked away for those keen on exploring to dig them up. Among these collectables are bits of the Enigma code which gives players a puzzle that, when solved, unlock four additional game modes. Unfortunately silly scripted sequences do interrupt the flow of these levels, it's touch of modern design that The New Order could certainly do without. Variety is commendable and over the course of the lengthy campaign, you will help B.J. fight off Xenomorph inspired robot dogs,  break into prison, hijack a U-Boat and tour Nazi occupied London. In addition, there are two separate timelines that alter some of the game's events providing a small incentive for players to play through the game again.

MachineGame's brings to life a fanciful interpretation of Hitler's neoclassic and art deco laden vision of a world constructed by the Aryan people, though it's largely rendered in an oppressive gray that the fuhrer would surely disapprove of for his ideologically driven utopia. Strands of 1950's futurist design also round out the art direction, bringing to life the most absurd and fantastic elements of the game. Some of the environments can get a bit repetitive since there is little reprieve from the cold muted color pallet and unwelcoming locals but some unique and arresting locations prevent players from becoming too disenchanted with the visuals. Characters look great in stills but their googly doll-like eyes make them look lifeless and disturbing in action but their animations make up for some of this as characters emote in a convincing manner. Thankfully, the voice acting is top notch and more importantly there are German voice overs sparring players from suffering through silly faux German accented English performances or worse, the 1950's American cinema trend of having English actors play Germans.

Out with the old Wolfenstein, and in with The New Order. MachineGames has delivered a strong game that pays homage to the legacy of Wolfenstein while providing some modernizing gameplay elements and, for the most part, they make it work. The abhorrent AI is the strongest detractor that this gloriously absurd first person shooter has but strong level design, visceral weapons and an irreverence for history and realism are a breath of fresh air. While the lack of multiplayer will be a hard blow for fans of Enemy Territory, the robust single player experience complete with unlockables makes The New Order worth the price of admission.  If you can put up with this wild alternate version of history and the bullet sponge Nazis that populate it, The New Order is worth playing. It wobbles and slips on the high wire bridging old and new, threatening to fall, but it makes it across; bravado and manhood in tact.

A long time ago I used to watch the RC youtuber, Lathrix, almost everyday. He made many creative, original, and effective bots. My favorite bots were his flying walkers, which I dont see used anymore in RC. One night my friend showed me how to get the game through Steam, and I was instantly hooked. I built robots with all of the different weapons and movements, which were gain with their amazing "tech tree feature." I enjoyed the tier system and worked to move to different tiers, and built new bots for each one. I even spent some money on Galaxy Cash, which was the cash you could buy for money back then, and then I bought cosmetics with it. The best part about GC was that it want pay2win cash since it wasnt too hard to get parts with the other free in-came currency. My goal was to reach tier 10 and make a megabot. In all I was having a blast with the game, but then, the game starting to change dramatically. My robots gained more cpu and brought me up into higher tiers, which made them obselete. Then the worst part happened, the tier system and tech tree was destroyed. Everything I wanted to do in RC was gone, and my interest slowly faded away.
A year later I came back to the game, around the time of Thanksgiving. I was shocked at what I saw; the game and meta completely changed. Everyone was using the new mech legs, and my bots were very weak. They added a new loot system which made it very hard to get good gear, and overall, lessened the essence of creativity. Every game I get crap I dont need, and its not very rewarding even if you win. New weapons and modules were added that made the game a bit better, but also made it worse. The only non anti-air gun left is the plasma, and the role of aircraft has faded. FreeJam says the new loot system helps newer players, but it just ruins their gameplay experience. They cant built good and creative bots. Veterens of the game also suffer. Remember when I told you I bought cosmetics for real life money? Well now you can get them from loot crates and we dont get a compensation for the money we spent.
Premium is almost a must have if you want to succeed. The game has become pay2win, and it is no longer fun. The new meta favors unoriginal bots that usually consists of flying teslas or one legged mechs with a chain shredder. The player base has dramatically decreased since the early stages of the game.
FreeJam, if you are listening, please listen to your players and go back to the original game. As of now, I do not recomment Robocraft. (Press F to pay your respects to the old robocraft and GARY, we miss you)

Quick Tip: Force Triple Buffering & Vertical Sync in Nvidia Control Panel (Can be found usually in your windows tab panel bottom right of toolbar). In options find your Wolfenstein game under "Manage 3d Settings". I have a faily powerful rig and had huge tearing issues especially in cut scenes until I forced on the above. I also turned on higher quality textures which made the game seem a little prettier. This really improved the game later on for me and may have improved my impressions earlier in the game.
1-5 hours:
Well I have to admit I came into this game after playing Dying Light and was pretty underwhelmed with Wolfenstein at the start. The game was playing a fine line between sarcasm and seriousness and the ID engine just felt so old, boring and predicatable. The poor optimisation and tearing did not help the early stages and the levels were overly linear and the cutscenes didnt really impress early on. Going back to the game a second time I have to admit once I fixed the tearing I actually enjoyed these sections more. I think going back and forth into menu settings early on trying to get a stable frame rate broke up the gun and fun play.
I still think that the game early on still underwhelms, the levels are very old style and not in a good way, later on the old style is done much better and with some clever design and variation.
The story and flow at times feels very forced, and its not until a third of the way into the game that you really feel and see the sarcasm and then the story becomes a lot more tongue in cheek and a lot more enjoyable.
One of the biggest shame early on especially in plot, enviornments and cinematics is the lack of building on the impressive imagary and developing the details of this new Nazi world. I'm not asking for Deus Ex depth, but there was so much potential here to flesh it out and give it some character. This could have been Wolfensteins real selling point but the whole setting is under developed, and the little depth in nazi newspaper clippings and the general atmosphere especially early on is lacking.
Early on I definately enjoyed the perk system it was quite nice to have little goals to achieve to level up my skills, was quite rewarding and made me experiment with different strategies and weapons. I do think the perk system could have been better utilized and given more breadth. But in general it was a cleverly done perk system that could be used or ignored.
5-10 hours
By now I had really got into the game, its sarcasm, the plot was improving, the weapons and gunplay were excellent, the enemies all had something about them. The game breaks up into traditional missions which is quite old style and at first I didnt like it, but you get used to it and it gives the devs a chance to better break up and flow the game. Can be annoying when you are like me and are a weapon and ammo hoarder and then start a new mission and you lose everything or start with totally different weapons then you finished the last level. But the plus is the devs can force you to try new weapons, balance the sections and push you in directions that make the game flow better.
The variations in landscapes is not to bad, little repetivive but I've seen and played far worse in many shooters. The level design I think picks up in the middle, still linear but many levels have multiple routes, the enemies are no pushovers and there are a couple of difficult fight sections and boss battles.
I really started to enjoy the game at this point, I tackled many sections in many different ways, I dont think the game or the ID engine is built very well to do these different strategies but the option is there to go in gun-ho or be more stealth. Just dont expect to do things perfectly as its really not possible, just go with the flow, which the game does quite well in the mid section of the game.
11-Finale
Few more frustrating moments with difficult sections that seem harder than they should be, could be down to me but the spike in difficulty already is obviously trying to extend the game as you are coming to the end. It does feel like an overly short shooter, probably by 3-4 hours but its nothing awfully short.
In general I enjoyed many of the gun fights, and some sections I had to replay a fair few times as I went in with the wrong tools/weapons.
The final boss fight is at best ok and not too 1 dimensional, I won't spoil anything but it has some frustrating moments and do be prepared to move fast and work out the ways to disable the last boss, just shooting will waste ammo and time. As most bosses once you work out his weaknesses he can be quite easy, but if you dont work out the strategies and best weapons you may get frustrated.
An interesting ending that left things open especially if you wait until the very end credits.
Pro's:
+ Good gunplay and solid AI
+ Nice perk system can be used or ignored
+Variety of environments (Neo Nazi architecture is great)
+ Middle section of game
+ Sound is not bad some good use of music composition
Cons:
- Poor frame-rate at first though I was able to vastly improve this
- Linear maps
- ID Engine is so dated and random (some amazing textures so god awful)
- Very forced story especially at start
- Nothing revolutionary or innovative here
- Little short for a stand alone single player game
- Wolfenstein is famous for its mutliplayer. Miss this but understand developing costs.
- Size of file makes little sense (30+ gb)

Nine years after the events of Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne (2003), Max finds himself living a degenerative lifestyle,  painkillers and scotch is the treatment for the past that haunts him. (Max Payne 2001)
You find yourself in the city of Sao Paulo, Brazil. Employed by real estate mogul Rodrigo Branco, as a personal bodyguard, protecting the wealthy Branco family. Even though he is far from home, trouble has no problem finding Max (as usual). As things starts to go down the drain; Max is forced into action-packed scenarios while relying on the abilities he attained from the experiences of the past.
Pros
+ Great work by Rockstar Toronto bringing a fantastic PC port.
+ The atmosphere is great, where the game wants you to feel like you're in Max' shoes as you end up in the less kind parts of Sao Paulo. Lost, and not finding yourself exactly welcome...
+ James McCaffrey does a top-notch job in voice acting Max Payne (for the third time in the series).
+ A great written script, where you'll hear Max's thoughts semi-narrating the story.
+ Rockstar should have won a price for just the animation work, making change of weapons, to diving, bullet-time, sneaking, walking, running or simply seeking cover.
+ Amazing visual / graphic accomplishment.
+ Great nVidia 3D Vision - 3D Ready
+ Great replay value.
+ Top notch multiplayer (at least it was, cannot comment on current amount of population that resides online today.)
Cons
- Even though a lot of the lose ends do get tied up when you least expect it beautifully; there are still things that comes short.
- Requires you to install Rockstar Social Club.
-
(As the story is divided with cutscenes; there is not possible to skip them; as the game is loading. However, you do not want to skip any scene while playing through it anyway; but a game like this with high replay value, it can become tiresome.)
If you love pulling the trigger, Max Payne 3 is for you.

I wrote an unfair review for this game about a year ago. I had returned to it after its full release and it had gone through many changes since early access. The review I had written was out of anger to change and I didn't give any of the changes a real look over or chance. So here is an updated review after playing again.
Robocraft is a fun and unique game that allows full control over the building and planning of your own battle robot. There are different types, such as a tank, cruiser, plane, helicopter, and more. There are many options and infinite designs that are rewarded or punished based on how well they are built. The building is my personal favorite part, but taking it out to battle adds life to your build.
In early access, there was a progression system and you unlocked movement and weapons overtime. You used a currency in game to then purchase parts you had unlocked. I will say now that is was way more grindy than the new system. Which is an advantage I had overlooked. There was and still is a premium option that can be purchased with real money. I had previously refered to this as a pay2win system. However, it only really speeds things up a bit. There are NO weapons or movement parts unobtainable without premium. The only unobtainable things without the use of premium are cosemtic; Robocraft is not at all pay2win.
I think anyone considering getting this game should definetely give it a go. It's free after all. If leftofnever sees this, I would like to apologize for my unfair review I had made a year ago. I am enjoying your game again just as much as I did when it was in early access.

Fairly new to PS2 here is the jist. It's a MMO FPS. Exactly what it says it is. It's slightly slower paced out of combat than most FPS because of the scale (though not by much). It does what it is suppose to. Provide you with a much larger scale battle than other FPS games.
But it does have the drawback of any real goals. It's good for a log on and fight, but thats it. It can be massive fun for a awhile (I cant seem to play more than a couple hours before I get bored). The objectives simply go "You take a base, they take a base". Back and forth with no real impact on anything. More resources, for more fights. Thats it. So if you want to jump into a massive battle, take a few bases, and have some fun, that is what PS2 is here for. If you're looking for immersive goals and a game with a deep sense of reward you wont find it here.
Weapons/classes/vehicles are fairly well balanced. Just keep in mind the learning curve. Figuring out what works best in what situations. If you're new, stick to Koltyr (the newbie zone) until BR15 to get into the swing of things. Even then you will have vets make a new character to come in and frag the new guys to death. Aiming isnt "put the dot on him, shoot, and hit him perfect". Weapons have a cone of fire, some like launchers, have an arc that you need to compensate for distance.
All in all, its alot of burst fun. But sustainability will be based best on a more casual playstyle for most. Dont burn yourself out.

Nine years after the events of Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne (2003), Max finds himself living a degenerative lifestyle,  painkillers and scotch is the treatment for the past that haunts him. (Max Payne 2001)
You find yourself in the city of Sao Paulo, Brazil. Employed by real estate mogul Rodrigo Branco, as a personal bodyguard, protecting the wealthy Branco family. Even though he is far from home, trouble has no problem finding Max (as usual). As things starts to go down the drain; Max is forced into action-packed scenarios while relying on the abilities he attained from the experiences of the past.
Pros
+ Great work by Rockstar Toronto bringing a fantastic PC port.
+ The atmosphere is great, where the game wants you to feel like you're in Max' shoes as you end up in the less kind parts of Sao Paulo. Lost, and not finding yourself exactly welcome...
+ James McCaffrey does a top-notch job in voice acting Max Payne (for the third time in the series).
+ A great written script, where you'll hear Max's thoughts semi-narrating the story.
+ Rockstar should have won a price for just the animation work, making change of weapons, to diving, bullet-time, sneaking, walking, running or simply seeking cover.
+ Amazing visual / graphic accomplishment.
+ Great nVidia 3D Vision - 3D Ready
+ Great replay value.
+ Top notch multiplayer (at least it was, cannot comment on current amount of population that resides online today.)
Cons
- Even though a lot of the lose ends do get tied up when you least expect it beautifully; there are still things that comes short.
- Requires you to install Rockstar Social Club.
-
(As the story is divided with cutscenes; there is not possible to skip them; as the game is loading. However, you do not want to skip any scene while playing through it anyway; but a game like this with high replay value, it can become tiresome.)
If you love pulling the trigger, Max Payne 3 is for you.

Being a hard core wolf3d player I had to play this game. The graphics are amazing as usual and though at the start I felt a bit uncomfortable it soon grew on me like an unlikely beard.
The guns are nice and you do enjoy employing various methods to extract death on your enemies. I wasn't so enthusiastic about having dual weapons slow down your walking speed, but then again when I'm holding 2 machine guns I'm more interesting in making a lot of moving things very dead.
I thought that idea of having to press the Use key in order to pickup ammo and health kits was a little bit not thought out. There is some advantages such as picking up exactly what you want (not wasting a good health kit when your health is 99% for example), but there is the opposite disadvantage of accidentally using a health kit right next to some ammo thus boosting your health up to 120% when you didn't really need it. Most FPS gamers are used to just collecting ammo and guns by walking over it and (i don't know if this is just me) pressing the Use button on almost anything just incase it activate something or opens a secret.
Over all I loved the game and it incorporated the essence of what it is to be Wolf3D, so I loved that. I did feel though that the game was a rather short. Return to Castle Wolfenstein seemed a lot longer to finish than this one.
I realy didn't care much for reading the letters nor the articles found randomly, I felt they were extra filler that didn't do much to game play unless I was missing something. The enigma puzzels seemed cool at first because I had no idea how I Was supposed to use them, then when I figured it out I felt not really bothered to. I was more interested in killing things than figuring out how to solve a puzzle. If I wanted to solve puzzels I would have played a different game.

I will go on record to say I fully expected Wolfy TNO to suck. From all of the previews and trailers, it came off like a wacky but derivative Call of Duty game with Nazis in it. I'm very glad to say I was completely dead wrong.
Wolfenstein the New Order is surprisingly enough a sequel to Wolfy 09 and Return to Castle Wolfenstein. It has a vastly different approach then either of those two games. TNO takes place in an alternate reality 1960 where Germany won the war after discovering the Atom bomb. This allowed the game to have extremely good imagery like sci-fi war mechs and power armor alongside classic Wolfenstein tropes like over the top guns. You have a really cool arsenal of weapons ranging from dual wielding assault rifles to hand held lasers that let you melt holes in walls.
However what TNO does best is it expands upon previous games. The protagonist Bj Blazkowicz isn't a static brick in this game like he was in Wolfy 09 or RtCW. He has a surprisingly good internal monologue that portrays him as a very shell shocked and emotional individual, completely unlike the stock American action film portrayal previous games had. This actually makes the storyline far more relatable then it was in previous games.
With the gameplay and story locked down, the last most defining feature of TNO is it's art direction. From it's enemies like I mentioned earlier to it's really top notch aesthetics. The maps remain fairly linear and enclosed but it makes up for it with the impressive attention to detail in many of the levels.
Wolfenstein the New Order is how you do a sequel to a retro game series well. You do your research and pay respect to earlier games while also expanding upon the mechanics. It's a very charismatic yet humble game, and it comes very highly recommended from me.

In short...

Age of Empires II was one of my favorite games not just in the RTS genre, but of all time. I'm a huge history buff so being able to play through some of the most important events of the medieval era was great (even if some things aren't historically accurate, such as repelling a Mongol horde with a sports car outfitted with machine guns.)
The best way to approach this is to break it up into parts based on expansions. Let's start with the base game and The Conquerors.
The game itself was rather faithfully ported. Calling it an HD remake is a slight bit of a stretch since the only real changes were some improved textures and widescreen support but I don't remember it looking this clean when I first played it all those years ago. As time went on patches improved performance and mechanics, such as increasing the number of units you can move at one time and increasing the framerate, both of which were very welcome changes to the game. Everything is intact from the initial release, and I still love playing as the Mesoamerican civs that were added in The Conquerors. Add in Steam Workshop support and you can find all sorts of textures, sound packs, and replacements for buildings and units to further customize your experience.
And then we move onto The Forgotten and this is where the game slips. The Forgotten was a fan made expansion that added five new Civs to play as and a few new campaigns to complete, but you can easily tell this was not official. For example, the Indians use the soundpack for the Indians from Age of Empires III. The same is true with the Slavs using the soundpack for the Russians from III. I also deplore some of the writing in the Campaigns; In one mission I had to infiltrate a camp with two really powerful Man At Arms and as I approached the camp, one of my men mentioned how crawling through sewage would give them the Black Plague to which his partner quipped back he would show him his Black Plague if he didn't stop complaining. On top of that most of the Campaigns are short with some as short as only three scenarios, and some of the missions are grindfests or fetchquests.
The Forgotten did add some new architecture and units that are cool, on top of adding the ability to research another Unique Tech for all Civs, but overall you can tell it was done by amateurs.
This brings me to the latest expansion, The African Kingdoms. Aside from becoming a rather amusing image macro utilizing the cover art, AK added four new Civilizations each with a five scenario campaign focusing upon medieval Africa to varying degrees from the Berber Invasion of Spain to Portuguese exploration. Once again new units and techs were brought to the table but while some techs seem useless depending on your strategy, each Civilization seems failry evenly matched against the others but they're all very similar to begin with.
If you want a simple review of this game, get it if you are looking for a relaxing RTS that has some historical value that spans the rise and fall of many medieval empires. While it may feel archaic compared to more recent RTS games, Age of Empires II HD has stood the test of time that seems to have claimed many of the Civilizations featured in this game and it's expansions.

Wolfenstein The New Order has renewed my faith in the FPS genre. For the last few years now we've been getting very mediocre FPS games with a few good ones, like Borderlands and Deus Ex, slipping through the cracks. The FPS genre has become more about multiplayer focus with a tacked on single player, rather than a quality SP. Wolfenstein: TNO was able to break the mold and give us something truly amazing FPS. A quality single player experience that has character development and an amazing storyline. Most importantly, they didn't feel the need to tack on a multiplayer in order to make it sell more. They simply made a single player FPS that was able to sell on its own merits.
The story follows BJ Blaskowitz who has been the protagonist in every Wolenstein game to date. The game takes place in the 60s with the Nazi's winning WW2 and now controlling the world. So of course, Captain Blaskowitz has to go in once again and take down the Nazi's.
The gunplay is the shining jewel of this game. Instead of just giving you the standard two guns, with generic weapons, the game goes back to when FPS's gave you an arsenal at your disposal. You can have up to 10 weapons on you, ranging from an assault rifle to a laser railgun. All the guns feel heavy and realistic, adding to the quality of the game. The best part imo is the ability to dual wield any gun. Say you're fighting an armored enemy and one shotgun isn't doing it, well, press the magic key and you start dual wielding dual shotgun that just level any enemy. It is restricted to just shotguns. You can dual wield any of the weapons in your armory.
The game also has an amazing perk systems. Instead of the standard upgrade system where you gain experience and use points, The New Order has you upgrade your skills through doing specific things, such as kill x amount of enemies with dual wielding or with stealth kills. Once you get this perk, it makes whatever it was stronger or easier to use. Its pretty fun to go through and level up everything just to see how strong you can get.
Visual are top notch. Quality kill animations and textures, as well as high quality cutscenes. You can tell they spent a good amount of time with visuals.
Pro: Too many lol
Great story
Amazing Gunplay
Fun Perk System
Good character development
Quality visuals
Good replay value
No pointless multiplayer
Cons:
Poor optimization for AMD: I run with Nvidia, but apparently if you run with certain AMD cards, the game will have extreme FPS drop. My friend runs with a 290X and he gets only 15 FPS on low.
If you like the FPS genre but are like me and are just tired of the same old mediocre shooters, then do yourself a favor and get this game. I got it for $60 when it launched and I never regretted it. Now you can get it for $20 and it is literally a steal. One of the top 5 games on 2014.  9.5/10.

The Talos Principle is a fantastic puzzle game.  If you are coming to this strictly for the puzzles, then you certainly wont be disapointed.  As all good puzzle games should, the early game is quite basic and easy, offering little challenge as it introduces the different mechanics.  But as you progress to the later stages, the complexity builds and so does the satisfaction received from each riddle solved.  That said, approximately 10% of the puzzles felt broken in a weird way that made me feel like I either solved it in a way they didn't intend, or had to employ a maneuver that I wasn't aware I was capalbe of.  However, when assessing the game as a whole, the puzzle design is quite superb.  Beyond the main game puzzles where each solution grants you a piece of a key to unlock the next area, there are these meta-puzzles in the hub world.  These particular puzzles are an order of magnitude more difficult than your critical path puzzles.  I only solved a handful of these and they proved non-essential to completing the game.  I'm sure there is some additional mythology explained when you complete these, but that vague offer was not enough to make me muscle through them.
I came to this game after seeing some gameplay footage and watching a couple of the beginning puzzles solved.  I had little interest in the lore, but it proved to make provide a unique and interesting setting.  You play as the creation of Elohim, a Yahweh-esque god who provides bits of narration along the path through the game.  There are also audio logs and termials that allude to a deeper history than the "you are my child, this is the creation I made for you, when you are done come be with me in heaven" narrative that Elohim is telling you.  I didn't spend much time digging through terminals and reading text logs because I have never found that story telling technique effective at enriching the narrative.
Overall,  The Talos Princible is a rock-solid puzzle game with plenty of head scratchers that make you feel incredibly smart when you reach the solution.

Fantastic little game, haven't found any bugs recently.
If you like Prison Architech/Stonehearth/Banished/Dwarf Fortress etc type games, you'll probably like this one too.
I've been playing this for years, thrilled to see it finally on Steam and hats off to the game makers for giving pre-Steam owners a free key, top notch.
The developers are also very in-tune with their playerbase and actively take feedback into the game updates, many mods have been incorporated into the game as well as tweaks and other features recommended by the community - a rare commodiy, they actually listen.
*Do not expect to 'win' in this game*
It is a storytelling game, there are challanges you can win, challanges you will lose.
You basically start off with 3 'pawns' (little characters to do work for you) and make a base to survive, whilst trying to feed your little pawns, give them big enough bedrooms and provide for all their needs (food, tempreture, armor, health), you will be making defences to survive the waves of mobs and random disasters that may befall your bunker, eventually making a space ship to get off the planet only to fall onto another planet on the outer rim. You can use local tribes and colony's for trade to offer much needed goods and silver currency.
Disasters could be anything from random beserking man-eating squirrels to toxic fallout which slowly poisons outside pawns... or simply the pressure of cramped living taking a toll on your pawns, eventually leading to one of them slapping the other to death in fits of anger, or maybe they'll get on and shack up together in a single bedroom. ;)
If your pawn loses a leg during a firefight/melee fight etc and you manage to capture a prisoner, np! Saw off the prisoners leg and attach it to your damaged pawn, sawing off their legs is a good method of keeping them in one place, albiet a little cruel... but funny none the less, especially if they start to rage... Oooo I feel like such an evil troll sometimes.
The game comes with a built in 'adaptive tutor' to give you basic tips when you first start out, it can be disabled and re-enabled at whim via the game settings, but for more detailed gameplay information, your best seeking out the wikipedia.
And if you get bored of playing the raw Rimworld experience, install some mods! There's a ton of mods on the workshop; some to expand content, others to fix 'niggles' which will probably just be fixed in future updates. Just remember to install the mods appropriate to the version (A17 mods for
A17 version etc) to avoid most errors.
Defintely one of those games you'll keep coming back too, well worth a position in the Steam library and worth the price.
Get it otherwise you'll regret it.

As you can tell from my playtime, I'm a huge fan of Robocraft and seriously looked to Freejam as prophets of the next big wave of Robot based gaming. But alas, the dream of a perfect robot game was slowly but surely whittled down one feature at a time in order to cater to the impatient.

I have played Rimworld since Alpha 10 (before it was on Steam) and have since then spent several hundred hours with this great game - and I expect to spend several hundred hours more.
Rimworld's gameplay is a mixture of the great feeling of building an efficient, good-looking and armed-to-the-teeth colony out of nothing, survival against all odds and, for a game, pretty deep emotional connection to your colonists.
------------------------------------------
With this game, I have built the following (as a caveat, I mostly play with mods):
A farming colony started by a bunch of teenagers, who spent several years rearing cattle, goats and chickens, having beautiful gardens and every leisure mankind can think of, building a blooming colony with golden floors and beds, not allowing any person to join the colony over the age of 20.
An ice colony, where the few colonists had to survive in a small, dark cave in the mountains, feeding off the few animals that ventured into the area - not being too squeamish about eating the rare visitor that froze on the way to the colony either - all while frantically trying to get to a tech level high enough to build a hydroponic farm.
All colonists were obliterated when an alien ship crashed and they had to fight with bows against laser beams.
A dwarf-like colony, deeply rooted in the mountains.
One day a horde of about 50 manhunting wargs appeared and killed a group of colonists that were sent to get some supplies that fell from the sky, one of which was the wife of my best soldier.
While he was still grieving, the colony had an attack by a centipede, which first destroyed the food supplies and proceeded to lay fire to the colony, while my grief-stricken and starving colonists fought a desperate battle, firing out of doorways, tending to the wounded and extinguishing fire.
At last they managed to kill the centipede, but the stress was too much for the grieving widower, who went on a rampage and killed or maimed the rest of the colony.
------------------------------------------
Apart from being a great game in itself, Rimworld has other favorable points:
- A very active modding community who produce lots of content, making the replay value of the game very high and changing the gameplay considerably in many cases, catering to the many different tastes we players have.
- A great lead developer, Tynan Sylvester, who takes his community seriously, listens to their wishes and is very active on the forums, all while obviously being a really nice guy.
- A great forum community, who can talk about the most horrible or tragic things they have done/experienced in their colonies in such an amiable, friendly and funny way that quite often, after being fed up with reading the newspaper, I ended up reading forum threads at Ludeon about the heroic stories of other colonies and the crazy ideas people came up with there (making a colony where everyone wears a cowboy hat made out of human skin is just the start).
Last but not least, the lead developer has freely given a Steam key to everyone who bought the game before the Steam release - which he did not have to do and which most companies would not have done because of the sales they would miss out on.
If you like base-building and/or survival, buying this game is an excellent choice - the price is higher than many Early Access titles, but with the current - already very polished - state and the content of Vanilla & player-made mods, very well worth it.
This game is so much better than I expected and I expected big things, be prepared to work in a team, no John Rambo's in this game. Highly recommended

I can't think of enough good things to say about this game. From start to finish I loved every bit of this game. When it first popped on steam I didn't want to pay full prize for what I thought was simple a puzzle game. When Steam had this on sale for twenty-something dollars, I pounced on it. Knowing what I know now, I would've definitely paid full price. This is a full game; not some dinky puzzle game with the same puzzles over and over.
The game mechanics are easy enough to pick up, but it's crazy how many ways they can up the ante. I won't go into details about them because i'm sure there's a hundred other reviews that already have and probably better than I would.
There's a level of philosophy dished out with every new level through old looking computers. Each ".txt" file gives you a glimpse of story, philosophy, or character development which adds to the overall emotion of the game. There is also Audio files from a main character (if you'll call her that) which get more intense as the story moves along.
One of my favorite parts of this game is the little nerdy secrets you run across in the game that provide no real significance to the game other than proof that this game was a work of passion. At one point I found myself in a cave looking at a giant prism akin to the pink floyd album cover complete with music similar to it (I didn't recognize it if it was actually their music). Another time I noticed the level design accommodated an extra area so I thought I'd take a look. Being mostly through the game I was paying alot of attention for these things. I ended up in a walled off courtyard with a ladder leading up to a small balcony with pictures of the making of the game and the gamemakers themselves :)
Another secret area involved skirting the boundaries of the level. Finding myself next to a church I heard *presumably* a priest yelling "money! money! money!" and some other similar things from within the church.
Anyways, I really enjoyed this game. I thought it was going to be a good puzzle game but it turned out so much more. It really makes you question humanity on some levels. I loved it.
9/10
P.S- If you do get the game, you can skip getting all the stars, unless you really want to. The ending isn't as good :)

Do you like trying to get a handful of people to survive the harshest of situations?
Do you like having FUN of the dorfiest sense?
Do you like seeing an entire colony of well-mannered individuals devolve into cannibals due to an untimely blight accompanied by a volcanic winter?
This is your game.
All jokes aside, allow me to elaborate, and preface with the fact that I've got at least two-hundred more hours logged into the game before its release on steam.
This game is difficult, but much like Dwarf Fortress or various roguelikes it is a 'difficult' that is fun and rewarding. Can it be unfair at times? Sure. But for the most part this game challenges you and gives you that 'A-ha!' moment that comes with understanding how best to deal with a situation.
Its graphics resemble Prison Architect, but that's no detractor - It's simple and illustrates everything you need to know on screen without having to pick through ASCII. The spritework has a crispness to it that's really smooth, and for the setting it works amazingly well.
Now, you might be asking yourself if this game is solidly worth the $30 pricetag, especially having the stigmatized 'Early Access' descriptor pinned to it. Without a doubt I would recommend it, sale or no, as it has the feel and polish of a full-release game that delivers a lot of play despite being made mostly by one person. As mentioned before, I have another two-hundred hours on top of my play-time in Steam, and I fully expect hundreds more as time goes on and this title sees more and more added to it.
TL;DR
This game has solid graphics for the style of game that it is, it's fairly fluid and is relatively bug-free, has hundreds of hours worth of content by its own despite being 'Early Access', and can only get better with time. 10/10, imo.

I went into this thinking that it was just a game, but within moments that viewpoint forever changed.
All 3 main squads ran up atop a hill and crouched down, the 3 squadleaders all came together and quickly discussed how we should proceed to attack the enemy, it was decided that Squad 1 would capture the first objective and then Squad 2 would charge the 2nd and Squad 3 (my one) would assault Objective 2 by going for a flank. After a few minutes of wandering the forest in a line formation of 9 men, many gun shots and explosions could be heard coming from the 2nd Objective, we even saw a few terrorists running past but we were given strict orders to not fire due to the risk of our cover being blown. Damaged by the shrapnel of the blast I crawl back to the cover of a large rock and apply bandages to my wounds, the medic beside me attempts to run over and revive the squad leader but gets popped in the side of the head from a well placed shot by an enemy sniper. What a surprise. I was searching for a good old FPS and, well, every reviews got me to play Wolfenstein The New Order.
The reviews were already impressive, but when I finally played the game, it stroked me: every aspect is nailed down.
FPS campaigns since the last decade have been generally poor, devolving, except from a few games like Bioshock 1 and 2 and Bulletstorm.
Here, to begin, the set and background of the game stands out from any other, while giving you that nostalgic WW2 feeling that we all got sick of a while ago with all the Call of Duty and Medal of Honor. The introduction is so fast, no "noob tutorial", it throws you into this mess with big action sequences and then introduce you to the stealth mechanics in like 15 minutes after launching the game.
I gotta say, the writing is mind-blowing. I wasn't expecting that from an FPS, even less from a "Wolfenstein" title. The pace is excellent, the characters have identity, cut scenes are energetic. It borrows a lot from cinema, particularly from war movies. I respect the writers so much managing to create this serious and depraving world while constantly making fun of the genre and being so self aware.
That, in my opinion, is already enough of an argument to make you play the game. Now, if I tell you that the gameplay is the best from a FPS I've seen in ages ? It goes back to old mechanics of FPS with health and armor bars, and of course health kits and pieces of armor to pick up. Welcome back also to the almighty weapon wheel, with knifes, grenades, pistols, rifle, sniper rifle, a multi-tool laser thingy, a shotgun. And, hold on to your breaches: mounted guns, dual wielding for all weapons, tones of upgrades (like a rocket-launcher on your rifle or shrapnel ammos for your shotgun), and perks you unlock with achievements that makes you progressively the ultimate bad♥♥♥♥♥Nazi-killer.
Beside the crazy action, the stealth sequences are actually the main mechanic. You have Nazis dispatched all over a map, making rotations, you have to kill the generals to avoid backup in case you failed at being a ninja. If you failed, you know things happen like throwing a knife at an armored guard (*bling*, it bounces)... Well, I guess you gotta take a rifle in each hand and slay all those fascists in a glorious bloodbath. I guess failing isn't so bad for once !
Beside fights being more and more chaotic and goddamn hard (I played the game in hard difficulty, it's very fun... until the last painful third of the game), an abrupt end, and a FOVated rendering a bit too noticeable, there is nothing to say against Wolfenstein The New Order.
While finishing the game (after 12 intense hours) all I was thinking was "man, I hope I will have time to re-play it". And you have reasons to do so: collectibles, unlocking all the perks, and make the other choice you made at the beginning which changes an important aspect of the scenario.
And kill more nazis. Yes, this is the main reason.

when you're playing it --not just 'how do I solve this puzzle', but broader questions about conscience, existence, and what it means to be alive.
The Talos Principle begins with you, a robotic being, waking up from slumber to the welcome of a god-like voice. It belongs to 'the creator', a being named Elohim, who claims to have created the world around you as a garden. Your purpose, he explains, is to solve puzzles and collect his sigils, which will allow you to become immortal. His only covenant is that you do not climb the Tower, which he says will lead to disaster and your inevitable death.
Yes, this is a very puzzle-centric game, but despite how difficult some of the puzzles can be, they're all genuinely fun. This game is just brimming with secrets, and some hilarious easter eggs, which kept me searching the game for hours longer than I'd expected. I'd say it's probably got 15 to 20 hours of solid content, maybe longer if you're determined not to use a guide when you're stuck.
I can't emphasize this enough: if you want a game that makes you think, and has a chilling yet beautiful story, buy this game. We all need more games like this.

The cons -

All in all, the pros greatly outweigh the cons. 9/10

2/3 Arma, 1/3 battlefield = a really nice team based shooter experience. In the current alpha it is a little rough around the edges, but generally nails the experience so far (1/2/16).
Pro's : Best communication and teamwork experiences I have had in a game so far. Running around with a pro squad and flanking an enemy FOB, tearing them up with nades and mopping up with a brutal execution session is highly satisfying. Gun mechanics feel solid, shooting sounds are awesome. Everything in the game mechanics (even spawning) is geared towards promoting teamwork.
Con's: When I finally see an enemy under iron sights, I get so excited sometimes I can't click my mouse. Cheaters/hackers are no fun and hopefully less prevalent as development goes on. I hope that textures (especially tree foliage) and draw distance are fine tuned a bit more as development goes on (hard to criticize EA game for that). Oh and the server browser is pretty terrible right now. WTF guys let me sort by ping ;)
Note: Vehicles are not yet implemented. The game is quite fun without them, but I am interested to see how they change the game dynamic.
Bottom line: 'Squad is like Arma, only you don't have to pretend it isn't boring the $hit out of you'.
If you expect to play Call of Duty (or even Battlefield), know this is a different experience. You can call it more 'mature' if you like, but it definitely requires some more patience and a whole lot more intelligence over voice chat.
Voice chat is not optional, as sharing intel on enemy locations is a vital part of actually being able to shoot the things with your bang stick. The player community seems to be 98% awesome so far and 2% 'typical', so generally things are great right now for new Squad mates joining up.
When the dust clears and your team is clicking, this is one of the most fun multiplayer experiences out there.

I have been playing this game now for some time, and backed it on Kickstarter in 2013.  Since this time the game has continued to grow and develop at a great pace.  This review is based on Alpha 14, the last version before Steam release.  I estimate that I have approximately 200 hours of play.
The setting for this game is a group of people in a sci-fi frontier backdrop (Firefly) trying to survive.  Rimworld is described as a "Sci-fi Colony Sim" by the creators, whilst accurate it is a rather dull description of what is a very fun and exciting game.  This game has the depth of Dwarf Fortress with the aesthetics and visual style of Prison Architect.  Throw in a great 'western' (as in cowboy) soundtrack and you have something pretty special.  This is a niche game, it is not for people who prefer form over function, but after watching the trailer you will know if that is you or not.
This game is hard on its default / average settings.  Your colonists will get sick and die, you will run out of food, wildlife and raiders will attack, colonists will freeze to death or go mad, and natural phenomenon will thwart best laid plans.  Luckily, the amount of customisation available is huge.  You really can tweak most options in the game, by changing your starting climates, picking your storyteller type and difficulty and selecting custom rules.  You can select a random group of survivors or re-roll them as many times as you like.  Options that are not changeable in game are often mod-able.  The Ludeon Studios forum has hundreds of mods available, although many will likely require updating to be compatible with the Steam release.  I would like to thank the creator of “EdB Prepare Carefully” for making a mod that I find it hard to play the game without.
The sandbox in this game is rather large.  If you wish to build a small cannibalistic tribe (yes, you really can) that live in wooden huts in a jungle, you can.  If you want to build into a mountainside for the true Dwarf Fortress feel, you can.  Want to tame animals to attack hostile entities or help with hauling, guess what, you can.
The story progresses nicely at a pace determined by the storyteller options you selected at the start.  A typical playthrough will have you rushing at the start to get shelter, and food.  As you expand and more colonists join you will look towards researching new technology, and upgrading security measures.  After a source of electricity is constructed, you can really start to grow.  All the while you will have a number of challenges, some brutal, some comical.  I recall one raid that followed after a solar flare
My only criticism of the game is that at the time of writing this, you cannot visit other colonies on the world map to raid or trade with them.  I would not be surprised however if this changes in the future.
EDIT: Regarding the only criticism above, it has now been added!

The Max Payne series is one of my all-time favorite games. I still have fond memories of playing 1 and 2 back in the early 2000s. Playing Max Payne 3 now feels like reconnecting with an old friend you haven't seen in more than a decade. He's little older and gained a little weight, but he's the same guy you loved hanging out with back then.
For me, this is what exactly playing an action movie feels like. I didn't mind the lack of open world freedom at all. The developers were responsible for the story, the pacing, the voice acting, the dialogue, the cutscenes, the music, etc. (all of which were fantastic by the way), while I was responsible for the operatic, gun-blazing action. Perfectly fine with me.
Truly a first-class experience that I still think about now a couple of weeks after I ended it, and that I'm sure I'll remember for a long time. Great job, developers!
So what's next for Max? I read a review online where the reviewer said that it should stop at 3. I kind of agree. While I love the games and would want another chapter, I wouldn't want my memory of the quality of the trilogy to be sullied by a poorly made sequel. But more importantly, I just want Max to be happy and find peace, and it looks like he got it by the end of 3. Such is the magic of the storytelling here; I find myself really caring for the character and wouldn't want him to go through hell again. Let's give him a break!

Extremely fun, mostly balanced game. Skills in other shooters easily translate over. The game does not give you a particular advantage with new guns, rather they are 'side-grades' that fit some playstyles better than others. Also, map knowledge and the flow of combat usually determine your survival rather than your skill, so you may die often until you start to memorize Auraxis like the back of your hand. All that being said, you will die in this game. A LOT.
Vehicle combat is both challenging and fun in that engagement strategy usually begets victory rather than sheer skill or outfitting. There is an extremely high skill cap to Air to Air dog fighting that may seem daunting to new players. This game always rewards coordination and team play, but these are required to truely excel in vehicle combat.
This game has one of the best communities in all of online gaming. Planetside veterans have a level of humility that is almost endemic to this game; really refreshing from other game communities like League or Battlefield.
I highly recommend this game, I also recommend going premium as it supports a group of highly dedicated developers.
