I finished the game tonight 2 hours ago. It is now 1 AM and I have spent two hours online researching things I may have missed. This is by far the best-written game I have ever played, and its philosophy could really use a proper analysis from someone like TheGameTheorists so I can be sure I didn't miss anything. Never has a game left me with so many questions! The world building is tremendously well-done as well, and the subplots (like that of Alexandra's) are often emotional and compelling. This game must be played.
As for the puzzles, they are quite fun and challenging, but they can get frustrating and repetitive, as there are a lot of them. One review I read (I think it was the AV Club) said the reason they don't hold up to Portal's puzzles is that while this game only allows one approach to each puzzle, Portal gives you more freedom in puzzle-solving mechanics. Fortunately, you can actually pick the order that you do the puzzles in, as opposed to a Portal-esque one at a time approach, making the game feeling not quite open-world, but not quite linear. The story and countless Easter eggs remedy the imperfection of the puzzles. If you like the choice elements of games like The Walking Dead, this is meant for you. The ending I got (you heard me right, multiple endings are always a treat) was very satisfying. I was relieved the ending did not let me down after all of the build up. This game can be enjoyed even if you don't know a thing about philosophy, as I myself know very little.

Having played all Wolfenstein games going back to the original id bombshell of the early 1990's, this particular version takes the game to new heights. The graphics and visual effects are very good and the audio is also excellent. Stealth is a major factor in survival and can be used to eliminate with great success on most of the enemy including the nasty 'Armoured Dogs' that proliferate the game. Don't try this though on any mechanised robotic device as failure will be certain and will set you back somewhat causing you to start again from the last checkpoint. (Albeit not a major problem).
Weapon options although at times limited do not seem to hinder the main character to any great degree as he is able to despatch most opposition with a minimum of fuss. Planning how you go about this is the important thing to consider as opposed to what you have to do to complete the task at hand. Bear in mind also that you need to replenished ammunition and health/armour regularly so take time to look around for possible and usually neccessary pickups, (approach and gather anything that glows for they will most likey be usable items).
You can collect 'Trophies' as well so investigate unusual looking objects and read notices on walls and desks for information (although this can be a little tedious at times when you are trying to get things done).
If you see a bed, have a sleep and you may be surprised at what happens when you do and my opening line will give you a hint as to what to expect!
The game is not open world in as much as you cannot simply move around free to do things as you wish and unlimited exploring is not an option, you go where your mission directs you and that's it!
This leads me to my main dislike, too many cutscenes that slow down gameplay. At times the player (me at least) is left saying "Not another one, I just want to get on with the game!"
I guess the creators were trying to incorporate the feeling of abject misery (the prison scenes alone will assert to that), but may have allowed that idea to stem the flow effect as in pulling on the reigns which brings you to a grinding halt. This then gives the game a 'Build it up as you go' arrangement where you are completing missions which only help to build a small part of the next objective. For me that scenario can get a little tiresome, I am sure for others it is more than acceptable so it is all about what an individual wants and expects from a game, but these are my views and I accept that.
In conlusion (and now that I have completed the game), I recommend it as on the whole it is very good but for me at times a bit depressing. If that was the aim of the developers then they succeeded, I just felt a bit hobbled! The real action takes place about a third of the way through and from there it takes off and is excellent and should not dissapoint.
Took approx. 15 hrs to go through first time (not bad), but missed many items that I will collect next time through. I would rate this game 7.5/10 and my screenshots will give you an indication of gameplay.
Certainly worth a go, but maybe best to wait for a sale.
Also, a strong suggestion is to play Wolfenstein 'The Old Blood' first....It is a prequal and it does flow on to 'New Order'. Had I done this I would have started New Order with a different mindset and understanding.

Extremely fun, mostly balanced game. Skills in other shooters easily translate over. The game does not give you a particular advantage with new guns, rather they are 'side-grades' that fit some playstyles better than others. Also, map knowledge and the flow of combat usually determine your survival rather than your skill, so you may die often until you start to memorize Auraxis like the back of your hand. All that being said, you will die in this game. A LOT.
Vehicle combat is both challenging and fun in that engagement strategy usually begets victory rather than sheer skill or outfitting. There is an extremely high skill cap to Air to Air dog fighting that may seem daunting to new players. This game always rewards coordination and team play, but these are required to truely excel in vehicle combat.
This game has one of the best communities in all of online gaming. Planetside veterans have a level of humility that is almost endemic to this game; really refreshing from other game communities like League or Battlefield.
I highly recommend this game, I also recommend going premium as it supports a group of highly dedicated developers.

I have played Rimworld since Alpha 10 (before it was on Steam) and have since then spent several hundred hours with this great game - and I expect to spend several hundred hours more.
Rimworld's gameplay is a mixture of the great feeling of building an efficient, good-looking and armed-to-the-teeth colony out of nothing, survival against all odds and, for a game, pretty deep emotional connection to your colonists.
------------------------------------------
With this game, I have built the following (as a caveat, I mostly play with mods):
A farming colony started by a bunch of teenagers, who spent several years rearing cattle, goats and chickens, having beautiful gardens and every leisure mankind can think of, building a blooming colony with golden floors and beds, not allowing any person to join the colony over the age of 20.
An ice colony, where the few colonists had to survive in a small, dark cave in the mountains, feeding off the few animals that ventured into the area - not being too squeamish about eating the rare visitor that froze on the way to the colony either - all while frantically trying to get to a tech level high enough to build a hydroponic farm.
All colonists were obliterated when an alien ship crashed and they had to fight with bows against laser beams.
A dwarf-like colony, deeply rooted in the mountains.
One day a horde of about 50 manhunting wargs appeared and killed a group of colonists that were sent to get some supplies that fell from the sky, one of which was the wife of my best soldier.
While he was still grieving, the colony had an attack by a centipede, which first destroyed the food supplies and proceeded to lay fire to the colony, while my grief-stricken and starving colonists fought a desperate battle, firing out of doorways, tending to the wounded and extinguishing fire.
At last they managed to kill the centipede, but the stress was too much for the grieving widower, who went on a rampage and killed or maimed the rest of the colony.
------------------------------------------
Apart from being a great game in itself, Rimworld has other favorable points:
- A very active modding community who produce lots of content, making the replay value of the game very high and changing the gameplay considerably in many cases, catering to the many different tastes we players have.
- A great lead developer, Tynan Sylvester, who takes his community seriously, listens to their wishes and is very active on the forums, all while obviously being a really nice guy.
- A great forum community, who can talk about the most horrible or tragic things they have done/experienced in their colonies in such an amiable, friendly and funny way that quite often, after being fed up with reading the newspaper, I ended up reading forum threads at Ludeon about the heroic stories of other colonies and the crazy ideas people came up with there (making a colony where everyone wears a cowboy hat made out of human skin is just the start).
Last but not least, the lead developer has freely given a Steam key to everyone who bought the game before the Steam release - which he did not have to do and which most companies would not have done because of the sales they would miss out on.
If you like base-building and/or survival, buying this game is an excellent choice - the price is higher than many Early Access titles, but with the current - already very polished - state and the content of Vanilla & player-made mods, very well worth it.

Do you like trying to get a handful of people to survive the harshest of situations?
Do you like having FUN of the dorfiest sense?
Do you like seeing an entire colony of well-mannered individuals devolve into cannibals due to an untimely blight accompanied by a volcanic winter?
This is your game.
All jokes aside, allow me to elaborate, and preface with the fact that I've got at least two-hundred more hours logged into the game before its release on steam.
This game is difficult, but much like Dwarf Fortress or various roguelikes it is a 'difficult' that is fun and rewarding. Can it be unfair at times? Sure. But for the most part this game challenges you and gives you that 'A-ha!' moment that comes with understanding how best to deal with a situation.
Its graphics resemble Prison Architect, but that's no detractor - It's simple and illustrates everything you need to know on screen without having to pick through ASCII. The spritework has a crispness to it that's really smooth, and for the setting it works amazingly well.
Now, you might be asking yourself if this game is solidly worth the $30 pricetag, especially having the stigmatized 'Early Access' descriptor pinned to it. Without a doubt I would recommend it, sale or no, as it has the feel and polish of a full-release game that delivers a lot of play despite being made mostly by one person. As mentioned before, I have another two-hundred hours on top of my play-time in Steam, and I fully expect hundreds more as time goes on and this title sees more and more added to it.
TL;DR
This game has solid graphics for the style of game that it is, it's fairly fluid and is relatively bug-free, has hundreds of hours worth of content by its own despite being 'Early Access', and can only get better with time. 10/10, imo.

[Edit - 3/24/16 - lots of the issues are being sorted now...server browser has been updated. UI has been updated. I very rarely run into cheaters on good servers. Rendering engine has been updated & draw distance / anti aliasing has been improved. I'm still definitely playing squad and can't wait for further updates. ]
2/3 Arma, 1/3 battlefield = a really nice team based shooter experience. In the current alpha it is a little rough around the edges, but generally nails the experience so far (1/2/16).
Pro's : Best communication and teamwork experiences I have had in a game so far. Running around with a pro squad and flanking an enemy FOB, tearing them up with nades and mopping up with a brutal execution session is highly satisfying. Gun mechanics feel solid, shooting sounds are awesome. Everything in the game mechanics (even spawning) is geared towards promoting teamwork.
Con's: When I finally see an enemy under iron sights, I get so excited sometimes I can't click my mouse. Cheaters/hackers are no fun and hopefully less prevalent as development goes on. I hope that textures (especially tree foliage) and draw distance are fine tuned a bit more as development goes on (hard to criticize EA game for that). Oh and the server browser is pretty terrible right now. WTF guys let me sort by ping ;)
Note: Vehicles are not yet implemented. The game is quite fun without them, but I am interested to see how they change the game dynamic.
Bottom line: 'Squad is like Arma, only you don't have to pretend it isn't boring the $hit out of you'.
If you expect to play Call of Duty (or even Battlefield), know this is a different experience. You can call it more 'mature' if you like, but it definitely requires some more patience and a whole lot more intelligence over voice chat.
Voice chat is not optional, as sharing intel on enemy locations is a vital part of actually being able to shoot the things with your bang stick. The player community seems to be 98% awesome so far and 2% 'typical', so generally things are great right now for new Squad mates joining up.
When the dust clears and your team is clicking, this is one of the most fun multiplayer experiences out there.

Croteam is best known for making games about a buff guy in a t-shirt dual wielding miniguns to shoot headless kamikazes with bombs instead of hands who run at you screaming AAAAAAAAAA while the protagonist makes fourth wall jokes and rock music plays in the background.
Then the Talos Principle shows up completely out of nowhere, and surprises everyone as a pseudo-philosophical-puzzle-platformer with a striking level of depth. It must've been at least decade since the last time I couldn't find any plotholes in a game, and the last circumstances I would expect to break the streak would be in a Croteam title. The puzzles are what you'd expect, but the story is airtight, and the game is riddled with such a gargantuan amount of secrets that you can go grey without finding them all. There is literally a 2 hour playlist on youtube showcasing nothing but easter eggs. Note: Be warned that the steam achievements contain spoilers. Do not read them lest you find your experience ruined.
This game is undoubtedly a dark horse which had never been thought of, and in the last place you'd expect. I cannot recommend it enough to any fan of the genre, the studio, or to anyone who is easily amused by pseudo-philosophy. You have no excuse for not buying it, should a less pricey version show up.

I have been playing this game now for some time, and backed it on Kickstarter in 2013.  Since this time the game has continued to grow and develop at a great pace.  This review is based on Alpha 14, the last version before Steam release.  I estimate that I have approximately 200 hours of play.
The setting for this game is a group of people in a sci-fi frontier backdrop (Firefly) trying to survive.  Rimworld is described as a "Sci-fi Colony Sim" by the creators, whilst accurate it is a rather dull description of what is a very fun and exciting game.  This game has the depth of Dwarf Fortress with the aesthetics and visual style of Prison Architect.  Throw in a great 'western' (as in cowboy) soundtrack and you have something pretty special.  This is a niche game, it is not for people who prefer form over function, but after watching the trailer you will know if that is you or not.
This game is hard on its default / average settings.  Your colonists will get sick and die, you will run out of food, wildlife and raiders will attack, colonists will freeze to death or go mad, and natural phenomenon will thwart best laid plans.  Luckily, the amount of customisation available is huge.  You really can tweak most options in the game, by changing your starting climates, picking your storyteller type and difficulty and selecting custom rules.  You can select a random group of survivors or re-roll them as many times as you like.  Options that are not changeable in game are often mod-able.  The Ludeon Studios forum has hundreds of mods available, although many will likely require updating to be compatible with the Steam release.  I would like to thank the creator of “EdB Prepare Carefully” for making a mod that I find it hard to play the game without.
The sandbox in this game is rather large.  If you wish to build a small cannibalistic tribe (yes, you really can) that live in wooden huts in a jungle, you can.  If you want to build into a mountainside for the true Dwarf Fortress feel, you can.  Want to tame animals to attack hostile entities or help with hauling, guess what, you can.
The story progresses nicely at a pace determined by the storyteller options you selected at the start.  A typical playthrough will have you rushing at the start to get shelter, and food.  As you expand and more colonists join you will look towards researching new technology, and upgrading security measures.  After a source of electricity is constructed, you can really start to grow.  All the while you will have a number of challenges, some brutal, some comical.  I recall one raid that followed after a solar flare
My only criticism of the game is that at the time of writing this, you cannot visit other colonies on the world map to raid or trade with them.  I would not be surprised however if this changes in the future.
EDIT: Regarding the only criticism above, it has now been added!

Talos Principle is a puzzle game, but like no other. Some might say "Wow it's just like Portal, but without the Portal Gun". It's not. I find it much more challenging than Portal, and after playing this, Portal seemed way easy, even the Advanced Chambers. Enough with talking about Portal, let's get on with Talos Principle. The puzzles in the game can be very fun, and sometimes brain-racking. You collect Sigils, which are basically 3-D Tetrominos, and use them in their own unique puzzles, which can sometimes pose a challenge themselves. You can unlock tools to use in more puzzles using some of the Sigils. The Sigils themselves have different colors, Yellow ones unlock tools, Green ones unlock more Worlds, and Red Sigils are for a place you musn't go, for it means certain death. The Worlds in Talos Principle have a couple themes, World A has an ancient Roman theme, World B is a Land of Death, ancient Egypt theme, and World C is based of the Middle Ages, with big castles, gargoyles and snow. You have one "person" that talks to you throughout the game, his name is Elohim. "My child, this is my garden, and you may walk through it freely". "But there is one place you must not go, do not ascend the Tower, for it means death to your kind".
The graphics are great in Talos Principle, even though I have to run it at lowest settings, you can stick your face right next to a wall and see great detail, not just a blurry texture.

Likely the best shooter to come out of 2014,
is a fantastic return to form for the genre that many of its fans (like myself) have come to know and love.
What I mean to say is that this is a game inspired by more retro sensibilities, but not to the point that newcomers will be turned off. Many shooters have a low barrier of entry, and this is no exception. It has regenerating health, but it only rounds up to the nearest 20 (for example, if you have 30 HP, you'll recover to 40 after regen kicks in). Medkits and scavenging scrap metal from enemies for armor are your primary means of surviving a gunfight. Stealth takedowns are present, but there's not really any point in the game where you instantly fail.
This, admittedly, gets particularly laughable in a level where you infiltrate a prison to free resistance fighters, but all the guards have batons and you have a knife, and you'll almost always win in a melee stand-off if you keep mashing the right mouse button. It's pretty indicative of how present-day shooter mechanics don't always mesh well with the old guard, but alas, the result is not much less palatable.
Weapon upgrades are plentiful, and you're rewarded for exploring levels with medkits, ammo, and the occasional upgrade. But this isn't merely something tacked on; you can unlock new fire modes and weapon capabilities like a laser BFG that bounces off of walls and can blind enemies. As for exploration, while it's been said that there are multiple routes in this game, it's a bit lacking. They certain exist, but the game is not nearly as non-linear as you might think upon hearing the term. There's still a story, after all.
Speaking of which,
has received a lot of praise for its writing, which I can certainly say is worth playing the game for. It's not exactly genius, but the narrative, the characters, and the world are all interesting enough to keep you wanting to play from start to finish to see what happens next. I think what I liked most about the narrative is that the game is basically self-aware: it knows the player character, BJ Blaskowitz, is a giant Nazi-killing war machine, and characters frequently give you a slap on the butt to go take care of it. A more inept shooter would, say, have you play an American soldier, running around like Miss Daisy's driver while killing the entire Russian military single-handedly. Fortunately, this game's story never gets intrusive to the point that you're not having fun, something I think a lot of recent video games are guilty of.
Ultimately, though, the writing is but icing on a very delicious cake. It's the gameplay that counts most, and while it's definitely a fun shooter with plenty of enemy, level, and weapon variety, you'll almost certainly find little things to complain about. The personal upgrade system feels tacked on, requiring you to do certain things to unlock new upgrades like carrying more knives. Sure, they're nice to have, but I don't think I ever
to unlock them. It was just another upgrade system that felt stapled onto a game that never needed it. Stealth is forgiving and you can kill an enemy quickly if they've detected you, and they won't alert others, including commanders who can actually call for reinforcements. The problem is, your only silenced weapon is the pistol with a silencer. It's not inaccurate, but if you miss an enemy's head from any distance you could modestly call "lengthy," they won't die. Meanwhile, if you throw a knife at any part of their body, they'll ragdollize in an instant. It's not the best implementation of stealth I've seen, but it does its job without infuriating me, and frankly, I'll take it if it means we can see games actually do stealth properly.
The biggest problem I have with this game is probably in terms of performance. Texture pop-in is present, and the game is capped at 60 FPS, even with v-sync off. There doesn't appear to be a way to configure your anti-aliasing, either, which is baffling; even the worst PC ports tend to have at least
option. Turning shadow resolution to the maximum is inadvisable unless you have a very top-tier system. Keep it at 4096 or lower if you're not satisfied with your performance. It's not immediately obvious, but you can change texture filtering and lighting quality with the "Additional Quality Settings" option. Why they aren't separate, I don't know. I blame these performance issues on the choice of engine: id Tech 5. If you played Rage at launch, you're well-aware of how awful a port that game was, with a lot of the same issues I'm mentioning: lack of options, texture pop-in, and AMD users were horribly shafted. This game doesn't have nearly the plethora of problems Rage did, particularly this long after launch, but for those looking to break in their new PC, be advised.
I recommend
to pretty much anyone who got into gaming in more recent years, and to those who feel they've been burned on shooters as of recent years. If you're looking for innovation, look elsewhere. But if you're willing to play a game doing things that have been done before, but does them well, it's an easy recommendation. I'm happy that this game got as much praise as it did, because in an era where overhyped garbage takes precedence with the gaming community, it's nice to see a lesser-known albeit talented developer receive their dues.

Rimworld is taking the development approach that slowly building on a solid foundation is the way to go with frequent updates and mod support.
Full Review:
Text Summary:
I used to love dwarf fortress, but never could get used to the control scheme. This game has the foundations for the same scope and scale, but it's not there yet.
But what is here is a solid foundation, the core loop for the building, expanding, relationships and the foundation for the various aspects of progression, i like the entire scale and way trading works and the way crafting expands the abilities and scope of the game.
Sadly the assets and abilities are not there yet, and it needs massive expansion - but the base assets are great and core gameplay is VERY well put together.
currently a very solid gameplay experience, but gaps in both story and world are readily apparent, and are logical instead of abrupt. Clear places where content is waiting for the developers to add and the modding community to expand.
I personally am not a fan of the sound design and assets, as i feel they are very sub-par in conveying information. The UI and general Graphics also need a ton of work, between displaying alerts and positions (especially on higher resolutions) and character animations.
Where i am a fan of is the enticing pull of one more try when your colony dies of starvation and when you get eaten by a mystic horse or when you get killed by raiders or when....
but... I still restarted my next colony after starvation killed my previous and i already cannibalized half my people and had them eat their loved ones.... and that is pretty damn good for a little indie game just hitting Early access.
tl;dr : the foundations are solid
Its a fun game to play with some friends, but it takes to long to level up and get almost no cash when you win or lose to buy new characters or cases.

Oh boy, PlanetSide 2 eh?
I've had a fairly rocky relationship with this game, had (mostly) good times, some (pretty) bad times, and some times inbetween.
This game is not forgiving to new players. I think there's never been a better time to start playing, but let me assure you; You run in guns blazing, you're just going to get mowed down. There are  some scary good people out there who will wreck you from above, on foot, or within a ten ton steel death machine known as a "Tank" before you can scream "Loyalty Until Death!". These are people who know tens of ways to get the upper hand, and have no qualms about using them against you. For the longest time, these people will be gods, and you'll feel like the cannon fodder you are.
However.
The first time you're charging accross a field with 50 other players, rockets screaming around you, planes swooping overhead, tanks mercilessly shelling your position, comrades falling left, right and center, it hits you. You feel like this is your moment, this is what gaming should feel like.
Big.
Panic inducing.
Exciting.
Every bullet fired, every rocket launched, every plane flying sorties, they're all because somewhere in the world, someone is doing those things. Every grunt you kill, every tank you destroy, every plane you ground, you have just ruined someone's day.
And it's AMAZING.
From piloting a suit that has cannons for arms capable of mowing down entire squads, to jetpacking (Yes, it's a verb now) onto a roof to rain hell on those unfortunate enough to stay grounded, to the intricate ballet that is dogfighting, to jumping in a tank with a friend to bring mechanized death onto anyone who DARES get between you and where you want to go,
PlanetSide 2 has you covered.
Until a sniper gets you, the git.

>Extremely team play focused.
>Engagements are often long and exciting.
>Firefights however are fast and bloody.
>Locating and identifying contact is just the right level of difficult.
>Maps are vast and offer many different approaches to objectives and multisquad coordination.
>No kill indicator - this can sound like a pain but it adds a nice level of immersion, realism, and suspense - not being sure if you actually downed your contact.
>Medics are done well. They can revive the team but will eventually run out of supplies to patch people up. Keeps from having those Arma revive contests.
>Very clear VOIP chat - also squad based so you don't get the full team chatter you find in other games.
Some negatives:
>Server browser is a little sub par - not detremental but makes it a little more difficult to hook up with friends.
>No in game friends list - little hard to drop in on a friend already playing as you need to actually locate the server in the browser.
tldr: Great game, especially for Early Access. I have been having a great time. I hope the devs continue doing what they are doing and get a lot of support.

The Talos Principle is a game unlike any other game I've ever played. At first it seemed to be quite similar to games like Portal, but that notion was quickly wiped away as I discovered and explored the open world of The Talos Principle. The Talos Principle is a progressively challenging puzzle game at heart, but it is unlike other games in the way it delivers it's story and puzzles. As you make your way through the beautiful sounds and scenes of the game a story unfolds inside and outside the places you explore, rewarding you for testing the boundaries of this well designed game and sparking interest in the story at every turn. The major difference about the story of The Talos Principle is that not only will it make you wonder about the plot within the game, but it will also make you question your own personal beliefs outside of the game, and in a unique way incorporates you personally into the story.
The Talos Principle has been the first
to ever make me really think deeply about life, theology, philosophy, and the possibilities of artificial intelligence. I think The Talos Principle will be remembered as a game that not only provided players with enjoyment, but also left them with deep thoughts to ponder as they proceeded with the rest of their lives.
I highly recommend this game, I will definitely replay it, and I will most likely gift it to several friends.

As a long time fan of the Wolfenstein franchise I have to say I really like this game. They nailed the feel of running around gunning down Nazis and their collection of techno-monstrosities. Looking for Nazi gold is always a classic and the perk and health and armour upgrade systems are quite nice.
The story however is where this game really shines. It is anti-Nazi but the game threw ball bearings under my feet several times and made me question if I was really playing with the good guys. The Nazis are obviously terrible with their political policies of executing babies with deformities and enslaving political prisoners and criminals. But on the flip side they have built a society that is quite a marvel. They are planning on terraforming planets, they have a permanent base on the moon. The resistance on the other hand are portrayed as oppressed freedom fighters but some of the actions done by the resistance question if we're really better than the Nazis. It has a great philosophical depth that I didn't expect.
Of course if you don't care it doesn't detract from the Nazi killing at all. I wouldn't call it a direct sequel but it has some minor ties to the Wolfenstein game that came out in 2009. Some characters and stuff you might recognize if you played both games.
The combat system is nice. You can dual-wield most weapons and each weapon have two firing modes. The Bot AI isn't stupid and varies from character to character which is not something that I often see in FPS games. (To be fair I don't often play FPS games)
I recommend this to anyone who likes the Wolfenstein franchise or if you want some good story with their one man army killing machine simulator.

Wolfenstein: the new order could have been both the best singleplayer game under the wolfenstein name and a bit of fresh air to the FPS market.

-very nice writing, very atmospheric, many memorable characters. cheesy plot is cheesy.
-nice ideas, foremost the dual-wielding.
-map design is in many places very good, with multiple optional routes.
-perks are mostly handled nicely and add to the experience.
-there is a recurring villain that you dont get to kill, which is a nice touch.
-brutality. the developers wanted brutality, so they implemented it very nicely.
with only these, i'd rate this game 11/10.
HOWEVER....
-it is 2015, so checkpoints instead of free saving is not allowed. that alone drops the ball so badly.
-enemies which are essentially quicktime events are just bad design, looking at you panzerhunds.
-map design at the endgame drops the ball very badly. this combined to the checkpoint system is a sin that is clear for everyone to see, yet was for some very obscure reason implemented. staring at loading screens is not game experience, so putting checkpoint-four gajillion nazis-bossfight-some more nazis-next checkpoint isnt fun or good design.
-enemy design of the endgame isnt really intuitive nor fun. "well, lets make an enemy that has billion hit points and spamsrockets/lasers/automatic shotgun" did not work in far cry 1, hasnt worked in any game between this and far cry one including Bioshock infinite, and DOES NOT WORK HERE, EITHER.
some claim the game is "short", but IMHO it is just as long as it should be.  fixing just a few mistakes would have made this a masterpiece. unfortunately, they werent fixed.

TL;DR: Great puzzle game with captivating story presented through clever philosophical dialogue. It just drags on a bit.
Portal comparisons are inevitable, so let's get this out of the way: The Talos Principle is like Portal in that it is a first-person puzzle game and shares many of the same puzzle elements, like cubes, lasers, and emancipation fields. However, the game plays much differently. It's much more open compared to Portal's linearity. The story is much more somber and is presented almost in the background. If you chose to, you could ignore it completely, which would be a shame.
That's because Talos's story is presented brilliantly through audio & text logs (like hundred of other games) and through philosophical conversations with the game's AI character. It's very well done (it could have easily been boring or too abstract) and is what makes this game stand out to me.
Now for the rest of the good stuff:
What I didn't like:
I feel like this game may have been better if they cut out the worst 1/4 or 1/5 puzzles from the game, as I felt the game just dragged on toward the end (assuming you're completing all puzzles). I probably would have stopped if the story wasn't so captivating; I really wanted to keep playing to figure out what was going on. I probably won't replay this game, at least not for a long while.

I will start off by saying that I cannot recommend this game enough to fans of puzzle games. While not as fast paced as Portal, the level of thought needed to solve these complex puzzles is just crazy. So many of the puzzles, once I solved them, I thought to myself, "there's no possible way that what I just did was intended by the developer as the way to actually solve it. Surely I found a loop hole." Even now, I'm still certain of that. Some of the ways I solved many of the puzzles just seems like I broke the game in order to pull them off.
I haven't even gotten to one of the best parts of The Talos Principle, which is the story. To make a Portal Reference again, I never went into portal expecting much in the way of it's plot. The same applies to The Talos Principle. I figured it would just be a fun puzzle game from the people who made the over the top shooter series Serious Sam, which it was. but holy crap... the story. Not since Planescape: Torment has a game made me think so much about philosophy so much. Bioshock and Bioshock Infinite are definitely up there, but The Talos Principle is on a whole other level of philosophical questioning. As with any of my reviews when it comes to story, I do not want to say too much, but I will say this, explore and interact with everything that you can. Push yourself to be engaged. The terminals.... oh the terminals.
I never talked about the graphics and such, but the game is very, very pretty. Better yet, it runs great and has a ton of graphical setting options (perhaps too many as many of them I have not clue what they do). The sound design is fantastic and I almost thought that I lost my sanity at one point due to the mind games that the game played on me.
Overall, if you love puzzles and a little bit of reading doesn't scare you, then you simply have to play The Talos Principle. It is now my most favorite puzzle game ever beating Portals 1 & 2, Braid, Limbo, and all others.

Played the first two Max Payne games and loved them? Give Max Payne 3 a miss. It has virtually nothing in common with the first two games.
1) "Stop The Pirates By♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Off Your Legit Customers"
The stupid Rockstar Social Club is absolute rubbish. You need to install this and be connected to the net to play this game. But that's not the bad part. The Social Club is buggy as hell.
After the initial sign-up and install, things were fine. The game starts up, goes to the load screen. Press Enter to continue. Okay! Oh wait, nothing happens, because the Social Club is ticking away in the background, logging you in. Wait for the login confirmation at the top of your screen. Ah. NOW press Enter to continue.
A few gaming sessions later, Rockstar Social Club ceases to log in. The "Press Enter to continue" button taunts me. I hit the home button to open up the Social Club overlay. I try to log in manually. It says it can't connect my Rockstar Social Club account to my Steam account. Handy! Now what? Ctrl + Alt + Del to close off the game.
There are listed fixes to this issue. You know what? I don't think I could be bothered. Why not? Read on.
2) "Trade In A Noir-Inspired Wise♥♥♥♥♥For A Self-Pitying Bum With No Redeeming Qualities"
Okay, so Max has lost his family, been forced out of his home country, and he's addicted to painkillers and booze. They tried to play the "Man With Nothing To Lose" card, and failed miserably. Not only is Max not the lovable anti-hero from the first games, but he isn't even the protagonist of a tragedy-tale, because he has NO redeeming qualities. There's a reason why Scarface was a successful flick. The writers of this game have some learning to do. I should NOT want to reach my hand through the screen and throttle the main character for all his self-pitying whining.
3) "Fans Loved The Comic Cutscenes- Let's Trade That For Shaky Cam!"
Loved the comic cutscenes from the first two games? They're gone, now. They've been replaced with in-game graphic cutscenes with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ filter overlay and abundant shakey cam. Standing still in a slowly moving elevator? SHAKEY CAM! Having a calm conversation? SHAKEY CAM! Don't forget all that tacky filter work, and random pull quotes from dialogue up in the air. It's like they tried to make Max Payne 3 gritty and edgy, while simultaneously forgetting all about what made 1 & 2 gritty and edgy.
4) "Epic Slow-Motion Bullet Battles? PFFT. Here, Hide Constantly Instead!"
Seriously, one of the biggest pulls on the Max Payne franchise was the use of bullet-time to make battles epic. In Max Payne 3, you'll end up quickly dead if you use bullet-time to the extent you used it in the first two games. Nope, you have to spend almost all your time hiding behind things instead. Use a bullet-time dive ANYWHERE, and you'll probably be leaving yourself open to get punched full of holes the second you hit the ground (even if you killed everyone during your dive, because new mobs burst out of nowhere as soon as you clear the room). On that note...
5) "Let's Take A Well-Written Franchise And Turn It Into A Mindless Shoot-Em-Up  (While Hiding Behind♥♥♥♥♥♥"
Tedium! This game is incredibly repetitive, which isn't helped by the "have to hide constantly" gaming mechanic. Enter a room, hide behind something (this is usually done for you via shaky-cam cutscene), then clear the room from the safety of your cover. As soon as the last mob is shot, more mobs will run into the room for round two. Kill all of them, enter the next room. Rinse and repeat. Even the "mini-games" (i.e. shoot mobs while riding a speedboat) feature the exact same action. If the mobs are unarmed, fill them full of holes from your cover. If the mobs are wearing flak jackets, head shot them from your cover. If the mobs are wearing helmets and body armour, head shot them a few times... from your cover.
The story is nearly non-existent. Yeah, they try to lay down a big conspiracy, but it's absolutely uninteresting. Max is never properly motivated to do the things he does. The characters are paper thin. Therefore, we never care about what goes on. Again, it's all about being gritty and edgy through superficial means (blood, gore, swearing, drugs) without the help of a proper damn story.
Overall, these issues probably wouldn't have bothered me so much if Remedy hadn't already set such a high bar for the franchise. Maybe you should stick to writing Grand Theft Auto, Dan Houser.
Edited to add: Oh, I forgot to mention the numerous times the game would crash to the desktop (no warning or error message) while gaming, loading, or quitting. This was before the epic "I will cease to work" from Social Club.

The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzle game that's been widely compared to Portal, although the more I played, the more differences I found. You're cast as a newly activated humanoid robot, tasked by the disembodied voice of Elohim with collecting sigils on your path to enlightenment. It starts out quite serene but also quite exciting - you're a new creation with an entire world made just for it - but cracks quickly begin to form.
Painted messages speak of doubt and mistrust, your surroundings occasionally buzz and flicker like a hologram glitch, and the library system is filled with eerie existentialist messages. And, most importantly, there's an ominous tower, which you've been strictly instructed not to climb.
The game allows you to pick the order of puzzles, with three hubs containing numbered doorways. Through the doors are smallish maps with a few puzzles. Complete them and you'll get a tetromino 'sigil' which gives you access to later levels and equipment.
I more or less played in order, but I found the difficulty level was all over the place. I'd go from completing 3 or 4 puzzles easily, first time, to spending half an hour on one, just pulling my hair out! Only to follow it up with a few more easy ones.
Still, something kept pulling me back in. I'd just get so irritated with a puzzle and walk away only to come back in an hour, desperate to finish it. I mean, I'd almost argue that the lack of hand holding kind of mimics the idea of being a new creation, exploring a new world, and then trying to find meaning in that.
I think it adds context, and I liked the character of the game, and the fact that it's always reminding you that nothing you see around you is real. You're a robot, but you feel like a human - but what makes us human? Just that human vs AI concept, I find that really interesting.
Overall, I think they've been quite ambitious and unique with their approach - especially with regards to the story, which I definitely appreciated.

Before, in the older game, the T10 would absolutely decimate the little tiny vehicle, but now it feels like they could almost go toe to toe. All vehicles use the same tier of block, same base defense, and MOSTLY same firepower. It's very bland and does not feel good. At this point there's not a reason to bother to get to end game gear because you can already destroy end game robots with a near-beginner robot.
Instead of tiers we get this♥♥♥♥♥♥show of a number that doesn't mean anything to the player, it just means you have more blocks and more guns and you'll be matched with people who have, you guessed it, more blocks and more guns.
Variety in robots:
Variety doesn't exist, it's not viable in this game anymore. This game used to have a problem in the past with huge tanks with tons of blocks being the meta. It's even worse at this point. Just slap on mech legs and 1000 blocks, combined with auto-healing and essentially no down-side, and there you go. You have a dominating robot that will completely wipe the field. With no questions asked.
Leagues:
Nothing really needed to say here. This is just a desperate attempt to grab attention of MOBA players.
Pilot Seat:
Do not, I mean do not ♥♥♥♥ing get me started on the removal of the pilot seat. Why the ♥♥♥♥ would you do that FreeJam?
The pilot seat was a FANTASTIC mechanic. So many different techniques and designs came out of that. Techniques such as triforcing, which essentially is just redirecting damage (I'm not even too familiar with it myself) to less useful blocks. But FreeJam decided that using your brain and creating a good design was too overpowered so they wanted to simplify the game. Now just slap blocks everywhere and dominate your foe.
Medics/Auto-heal:
Auto-healing is probably the worst mechanic to come out of this, no longer do you have to worry about actually trying to create a good design that will continue to work even with large amounts of damage done. No longer will you have to actually THINK to either focus on defense, mobiltiy, or offense. If you take any damage, simply run behind cover for 10 seconds and heal up. No medics requried. Medics are pretty much obsolete at this point. A crappy design could, and does destroy actual good designs because they can just go behind cover, and heal up. It really stagnates the game and slows it down a TON. Medics were high praise back then. I remember people thanking medics (They still do) but medics are obsolete, they are, I hate to say this, but they are worthless. Players no longer need to work together. They can solo and tank then go back to cover and don't need their team to back them up. Which leads me to my next segment.
Teamwork:
This was tough. Even back then, many players did not work together. Medics were the great equalizer in teamwork though. If there was a medic, people would group up, they would help each other. Retreat into cover-but not to get healed by themselves, it's because they depended on their TEAM/THEIR MEDIC. Teamwork wasn't perfect back then, but it sure as hell isn't any better now.
Megabots:
Megabots, not exactly a mechanic, but more of an ENTIRELY DIFFERENT WAY TO PLAY THE GAME. Megabots battles were ♥♥♥♥ing epic. You had these robots that had LITERAL THOUSANDS of blocks battling it out like Godzilla vs. King Kong.
FreeJam is willing to remove players' thousands of hours of work on these megabots but not willing to revert back to the better, more complex, more in-depth mechanics.
Gunplay:
Ah, the good ol' memories of choosing what gun and what playstyle you want to try in a match. Now you don't have to choose! You can slap them all on, especially now that 1 single gun could be just as good as 6. Gunplay was simple back then, Pick your weapon type. Then blast the enemy and play to the advantages or disadvantages of your weapon. Now you can put em all on and you can be everything! You can be a bomber, a sniper, a infantry unit, and even a medic. A ♥♥♥♥ING MEDIC. You are your own army, go take on the entire world with your arsenal of guns. Yeah, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
False Promises:
Remember the HUB? EVERYONE was talking about that when it was planned. It was a hub, where a robot could just hang out and mess around with the other robots, a place to show your build, a place to chat, a place to make friends. This would've been the perfect alternative to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ CRF that we have now. Remember the MOBA mechancis that were talked about but never implemented? Remember the different pilots that had special traits and abilites but were never added?
In conclusion:
This game could've been so much more. They decided to appeal to the broader audience and simplified the game. At it's core, it's just slap cubes in a shape that looks pretty, and shoot other pretty looking creations. I have more to say butsteamhasalimitonreviews

Now thats great. I'm more then willing to pony up the cash to make sure a game gets what it needs and doesnt find itself at the bottom of the barrel with all the other F2P titles. Infested with micro transactions and hackers... Charge a few bucks to get more quality into the game. Understood...
But ah! Then came the "Early access" formula soon after and dollar signs gleamed in developers eyes.
Ten bucks? Sure! Twenty bucks? Sure!.. $40.00???? Laughable... Especially for the state that the "game" is in at the moment. You're not getting much. And if my gut is right, there won't be much coming in the future. It'll be yet another early access title that the devs spend all their time beating back bugs to keep the community happy, at the expense of content. All the while collecting their fat checks at the end of the week and still crying poverty.
This has become the new formula for game development and capital success in the game industry.
The game doesn't work on AMD cards. So don't even bother if you have any card from AMD.
Now if I'm wrong and If these devs don't follow suit and screw everyone over like every other Early Access title out there, if they pull out all the stops with the small fortune theyve made thus far and manage to deliver an amazing game. Then maybe I'd say the asking price is worth it. However,  I'd say wait for that day to come before spending the ridiculous price of forty dollars for this.
For the time being I recommend "Insurgency". The devs were'nt greedy and released the game back in January of 2014 with a price tag of $15.00 and continue to polish and update it on a weekly basis. Not to mention it goes on sale constantly, so its not rare to grab a copy for $4.00 on a holiday. Realism at a realistic price.
So in closing, Keep an eye on Squad, it has potential. But, I am still one of those that feel that "Early access" has been abused and has now become the death of gaming as we know it. And with the game of averages showing that the majority of Early access titles are polished turds on a shingle.. No diamond in the rough will change my mind, and the minds of many. Let's hope that "Squad" is a diamond though.

A decent epilogue to Max Payne 2 and in its own right a rather interesting reconstruction of the American myth of redemptive violence.  Not a bad shooter either; emphasis is more on movement and efficient use of limited resources (ammo, health, bullet time, painkillers) rather than cherry-tapping while leveraging unlimited ones (cover) to win a fight.
The writing is where it shows serious weaknesses.  The first two games were written by Sam Lake.  His approach to Americana is similar to Shigesato Itoi's Mother trilogy.  Even when serious a charming mixture of affection and wry humor throughout provides a tongue-in-cheek quality ensuring the game doesn't take itself too seriously.  Max Payne 3 is written too earnestly, and is too blatantly a copy of Man on Fire, to ever have that detachment.  Dan Houser (perhaps best known for his work on the Grand Theft Auto series) does not bring the kind of pen from which the earlier games benefitted.
Worth a purchase and playthrough at least once.

What makes this game shine is how the cross channel communication works between the many numbers of squads on each team. There are constantly new objectives based on how each squad leader reacts to different situations. This sets a foundation for a truly dynamic gameplay experience.
There are three channels of communication.
-Squad leader to all squad leaders.
-Squad radio.
-And local voice that has a 20 metre range where volume decreases the further you are away from each other.
The visuals are very impressive for the sheer scale of the maps and the modelling/texturing of characters and objects are of a very high standard. I have managed to find a happy medium where I achieve a fairly steady 60 fps at the cost of over 3500mb of vram.
The explosions and smoke effects are very well done but can impact framerate in some situations. But that's really not worth moaning about, for me at least.
The sound in this game is unbelievably breathtaking and really forces you to fully immerse yourself deep into fight.
The guns are to be mastered, but once mastered become an extension of you as you lean around corners checking your sectors and controlling your recoil.
The community is absolutely brilliant. You will find really cool people from all around the world. I've lost count how many new friends I have made and I only got this game 4 days ago.
Sometimes you may find someone teamkilling but very very rarely and sometimes you will join a squad where the squad leader has no clue whatsoever.
If you do find a squad leader like this then you can either help this poor soul out with some encouragement or quickly join a better squad with just a couple of clicks of the mouse and hopefully with a bit of luck you will end up with a squad leader who can be considered a veteran of the game who knows their onion's. And I guarantee you that you will have a blast.
Its early access so things can only get better and I am really looking forward to the future of SQUAD.
And finally I want to thank my good friend atrOx who bought me this game as gift because he's cool like that. Thank you atrOx your a star mate  :)

I'd like to compare The Talos Principle to games like Myst URU or The Vanishing of Ethan Carter for its heartbreakingly lovely visuals, puzzles and RPG sandbox. But I can't, because The Talos Principle is /far better/. There is an astoundingly deep and fascinating story you discover as you wander from area to area, each with jaw dropping graphics, the type that make you ache to really /go there/. And puzzles? Oh my lawdy chile are there puzzles! Hard man sized puzzles that will make your brain bulge like an alien species from Star Trek when your done. You know those commercials for Brain Games? Fuggetaboutit, /these/ are brain games! And you /want/ to work them, hard. Why? The mystery built into the game, the story, is so good you have to know more, and you /need/ to see whats behind that door, because it'll be more mind exploding than what was behind the last door you unlocked.
I think theres a lesson here for how schools should function.
The soundtrack is also achingly, hauntingly beautiful, perfectly setting the atmosphere for what your seeing. I think they pace the game extremely well, you're going to find puzzles that need to be hammered at for awhile, but not until deeper in and farther up (pun intended). Unlike Vanishing of Ethan Carter its not a short game, theres a lot of play time in this, and unlike Myst URU its extensible so more puzzles await after you finish the game proper. Get it now, your heart, your brain, and maybe your soul will thank you.

I have a lot to say about this game. Mostly good, very few of it bad.
The game starts off during world war 2, the player taking the role of William "B.J." Blazkowicz. After
him and his other comrades blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and a shrapnel is lodged into the back on Blazkowicz's brain. He is then put into a coma.
He is found unconscious, and put into a hospital/home for the mentally/physically disabled. Over the years, nazi officers take pateints to experiment upon. Fast forward to 1960, World War 2 is over. HOWEVER, the US surrendered, and Nazi Germany has won. On the very day he regains control of his body. officers visit said home and shut the place down. He stabs the officer who is about to kill him, makes an escape with the woman who had been taking care of him for the past 14 years, and set out to take down Nazi Germany with the resistance group.
Even though it was released just last year, it gives off the feeling of an old style shooter. And no, I do not mean that in a DNF bad kind of way, it feels properly modernized and doesn't reek of old formulas mixed with new. It feels very solid and satisfying to play. No DLC, no day 1 season pass, no shoe horned in multiplayer, no microtransactions, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, just a single player campaign first person shooter. as it should be.
Story felt very solid, makes you feel for the main characters, especially with what happens to some of them. And no, you do NOT need to play the older Wolfenstein games in order to enjoy it (but you should since Wolfenstein 3D is pretty good even if it is 20 ish years old at this point.)
However, only real complaint I have is it is not very well optimized. Everything is set to low at 1080p, framerate is all over the place, sometimes as low as 18 FPS, and sometimes as high as 60. And on top of that, with that uneven framerate, dialogue/lip movement did unsync and become out of place. If you have a lower end rig, be aware that you might not be able to run it at full capacity unless you do some overclocking or lower the resolution.
All in all, performance issues aside, it is a very solid single player first person shooter. One of the most satisfying FPS games I've played in years
And I CANNOT wait for The Old Blood to come out.

I'd like to compare The Talos Principle to games like Myst URU or The Vanishing of Ethan Carter for its heartbreakingly lovely visuals, puzzles and RPG sandbox. But I can't, because The Talos Principle is /far better/. There is an astoundingly deep and fascinating story you discover as you wander from area to area, each with jaw dropping graphics, the type that make you ache to really /go there/. And puzzles? Oh my lawdy chile are there puzzles! Hard man sized puzzles that will make your brain bulge like an alien species from Star Trek when your done. You know those commercials for Brain Games? Fuggetaboutit, /these/ are brain games! And you /want/ to work them, hard. Why? The mystery built into the game, the story, is so good you have to know more, and you /need/ to see whats behind that door, because it'll be more mind exploding than what was behind the last door you unlocked.
I think theres a lesson here for how schools should function.
The soundtrack is also achingly, hauntingly beautiful, perfectly setting the atmosphere for what your seeing. I think they pace the game extremely well, you're going to find puzzles that need to be hammered at for awhile, but not until deeper in and farther up (pun intended). Unlike Vanishing of Ethan Carter its not a short game, theres a lot of play time in this, and unlike Myst URU its extensible so more puzzles await after you finish the game proper. Get it now, your heart, your brain, and maybe your soul will thank you.

I enjoyed the philosophy, and found the plot emotionally and intellectually engaging.  I could write several paragraphs about that, but not without spoilers.  Suffice to say, they handled their core conceit expertly, and built a very solid philosophical underpinning for the game, to the point where at some places, it's hard to tell without Wiki what is a quote from an actual philosopher and what is fabricated for the game.
The gameplay is easily comparable to Portal.  Very clever puzzles, and a well designed mixture of difficult challenges and training wheels levels that are never quite easy enough to feel like a chore.  I was also very impressed with the hidden star puzzles (although the one that requires you use an ASCII lookup table was a bit silly).
The graphics are pretty, although the scenery is not terribly diverse.  The voice acting is quite good - I really liked Alexandra's voice actress.  She does an excellent job of conveying emotion and personality in a few well-written lines.
In summary: highly recommended.  Thanks, Croteam!  I'm always excited to see great new entries into the adventure/puzzle genre, and this is the best I've played in a long time.

Max Payne 3 is the latest installment in the popular and award winning Max Payne franchise. Unlike the first two titles however, Max Payne 3 is fully developed and published by Rockstar Games whose notable works include the popular Grand Theft Auto (GTA) franchise.
Once again the player steps into the shoes of Max Payne, a former New York City Detective who, after the events of the first two games, went on a downward spiral both in career and personal life. Now, 9 years since the last game, Max retired from his job as a detective and now works as private security contractor in Brazil. Things were going well (aside from the Pain Killer addiction and Alcoholism), until he's caught in another conspiracy, this time, involving gang violence, a corrupt police department and the kidnapping of the members of a famous and wealthy family.
+ Gorgeous Graphics and Visuals (Except for the Filters, See Cons)
+ Great new Setting (Brazil)
+ Scenic locations and flashbacks (Brazil and New Jersey)
+ Great sounds, voice acting and soundtrack
+ Good story writing (albeit a bit more generic compared to the last two games, it's still very well written)
+ Improved gameplay (added a new cover system and 'last man standing' among other things)
+ Large weapon variety
+ Collectibles that reward the player with either additional story or improved weapon upgrades
+ Intense and action packed combat
- Excessive cutscenes
- Extremely long loading times that make some cutscenes technically unskippable (“Still Loading” after 3 minutes of cutscene I want to skip is unacceptable, specially on an SSD)
- Excessive use of Filters that can cause headaches
- Unnecessary Multiplayer
- Rockstar Games Social Club
- MASSIVE 35 Gigabyte Storage requirement (probably because of Con #1 see above)
-
GREAT GAME and I liked it. As a Max Payne fan, I was pleased with how Max Payne 3 wraps up the sad and emotionally crushing life that Max has lived. The Graphics were gorgeous with a scenic new location in São Paulo, Brazil. The story was a bit more generic than the deep emotional roller-coaster of the first 2 games but nonetheless, it's still very well written. Gameplay was improved by adding new weapons, last-man-standing, and a cover system to boot. The game does suffer from a very long loading time, excessive use of special effects filters and long cutscenes which made the game size a whooping 35 gigabyte.
All in all, Max Payne 3 is a GREAT GAME and a GOOD SEQUEL / Franchise Finale. I can recommend this game as it is in full price but if you are, get the regular Max Payne 3 and not the complete version. The DLCs are all for multiplayer and skins with no additional story or missions. With that said, the game does go on Sale very often.

Personally I can't recommend this game. To be honest I expect a lot more from the trailer and screenshot, and even though I know the game will involve shooting most of the time, the gameplay makes it really hard to enjoy.
Pro:
- Great graphics.
- Interesting, profound and funny dialouges.
- Very interesting plot.
Cons:
- The gameplay is very dull, you have to follow the storyline so strictly, which makes the game very hard to enjoy. The idea is to hide, dodge some bullet, save your painkillers for the rainy days and shoot anyone on sight. The world of Max Payne 3 is strictly restricted to the plot, and makes the exploration very dull. You can hardly interact with anything, except for weapons and objects that help progress the story.
- Weapons are few and somehow uncreative. Most of the time time you either find pistols, Uzi and shotguns. Even when you almost finish the game there aren't many new weapons to try. Worst of all, the weapons don't give you the feeling that they are different: a lot of time using diferrent guns feels so similar, which is, again, dull and boring. And, dude, you can't even melee unless you get too close to the enemies.
- This is minor, but the cutscenes are sometimes painfully long, and you cannot skip because it is "still loading".
- The game is too intense, even for easy mode. The player is required to use bullet time extremely wisely, because if it runs out then you are either screwed or will have to waste a lot of bullet for one guy. That alone makes it hard to enjoy the game to its full extent, whatever that extent is.
- For a game with massive shooting gameplay and number of enemies, sometimes you will expect to go stealthy and take out the enemies wisely, but in this game, "stealthy" doesn't exist. You always have to shoot your way out, wich makes the gameplay, again, predictable and dull.
- Why the heck is this thing so heavy???? I understand the graphics are guilty of this, but 35 - 40Gi??
For those reasons I above I didn't really enjoy the game, but this is only my opinion, those who loves shooting entirely can try, but I can't recommend this.

When i first bought squad my expectations was more about the hype of playing a shooter that basically relies on voice chatting for playing. When I started playing the alpha almost 1,5 year ago it was game in early stages with lots of bugs, but still in a rarely complete state for being a game in early alpha. Now it has vehicles, mortars, supply trucks, more infantry models etc, and still there is more yet to come with tanks, helicopters as well as fixed wing aircraft.
This is probably the first online game I`ve played, in which basically the wast majority of players cooperates within the squad. Sure there is incentive to do it, but you could also just run around by yourself. That is an option. But what strikes me is that all the matches I`ve played so far is how everyone gets along cooperates on free will. And people do tend to look to the squad leader for advice on how to procede and the most of the time, the chatter is friendly and in an advisory manner. I have not faced internet trolls so far in this game. Similar VOIP are featured in Insurgency for example, and in that game most VoiP is complete nonsense and trolling is common.
The genious construction of squad is that the squad leader pretty much decides what the squad is supposed to do, and even kick people out who is not following instructions. The squad leader decides were to build fortifications as well as rally points and outposts to respawn. And people tend to listen, even advice someone who is new to the role. It`s in everyones interest to succeed and therefore aid the squad leader and follow commands, even ask of orders.
A good squad leader can really make all the difference. One of the more memorable experiences was I can share is before vehicles was implemented and the squads had to move on foot across the map. We were moving towards a capture point with a really strict squad leader, that kept track on everyone, and everyone followed. We reached a hill next to the town were the capture point was and stayed and reconed the area, seeing another squad who has yet to see us. Our squad leader insisted to us all to hold fire until the other squad was close enough, then screamed out "open up on them!" All hell broke lose and the other squad took lots of casualties while retreating. I have not experienced anything liked it in any other multiplayer shooter. Ever!
Already in an early alpha state this game was quite beatiful and that has only improved! It`s reminiscent of the Arma games, but with a more limited area on which you are fighting. The sound effects are really great and when everyone opens up you really feel like you are in a war zone ith all the radio chatter going around! Last time I played I ended up in a furious firefight over a capture point, with bullets flying all around us and the enemy dropping mortars like crazy. With high volume on in my headset. the experience was almost terrifying. It really gives you a small taste of what real combat might sound like.
Graphically, the one thing I do miss is the way aiming with the weapons work. If you do not have magnifying scope, and aim by crosshairs or red-dot sight you will not get any zoom at all. This can be a bit annoying for a game that places lots of emphasis on long range combat. Also, a small detail is to improve the way scopes work. Would love to see scopes working as they do in Insurgency were you zoom in the scope but not on area around the scope.
I would never see me go back to Battlefield series after playing this game. It is realistic and exciting at the same time, without a doubt one of the best gaming communities around today. It`s highly recommended if you enjoy battlefield, insurgency and those kind of games that depicts modern conflicts, but feel that they can be a bit arcade.

I sit here writing a review on software that allows me to watch the Game of Thrones intro sequence on my computer. Now you may ask, why am I doing such a thing? I mean, media players are boring, and there’s really not much choice in terms of good ones apart from VLC. Well, I’m not reviewing a media player today. Instead, it’s an early access program found on Steam called Wallpaper Engine. What’s so interesting about Wallpaper Engine? Let’s find out.

I think we can all agree that desktop backgrounds in Windows, indeed most computers, are pretty boring. You’re allowed a static image and not much else. Even less if you’re in a corporate environment with strict IT policies. Sure, you can clutter up your icons into any configuration you desire, but that background is just there. There are some programs out there that attempt to jazz up the desktop. Rainmeter is a fan favourite, which can add widgets to a Windows desktop. Deskscapes is another, which allows for animated wallpapers. While Rainmeter is free and the assets are pretty handy, there’s nothing quite like a properly animated wallpaper for that intimate feeling. Wallpaper Engine tries to fill that gap, and while it’s still in Steam Early Access, it seems to do a very good job.
The program comes with some inbuilt wallpapers, which are all animated and of very high quality. You can even play a movie as your desktop wallpaper, as long as it was encoded in something Wallpaper Engine can read. You can also download ready made themes from the program’s Steam Workshop. There’s some really good work there, yet there’s some really questionable “work” there too. But then, when you have a literal open mod system like Steam Workshop, it’s inevitable you have to take the good and the bad. Be warned though, some of the wallpapers are pretty big. We’re talking over 500MB, which is supposed to ensure fantastic quality, but doesn’t mean that’s what you’ll get. If you have a widescreen monitor, Wallpaper Engine will default to fill your entire screen, which can hide details or large bits of the scene itself.

If you haven’t guessed, I really like Wallpaper Engine. It’s cheap, simple and gives users something to do with their desktop backgrounds other than stick a static image up, however nice it might be. You can purchase Wallpaper Engine from Steam for US $3.99. It’s in early access and therefore still subject to the usual warnings about paying to participate in beta programs. But, for this kind of functionality and plain simple ease of use, why the hell not?
The Good -
Cheap
Great functionality
Flexible
Doesn’t impact on performance much
The Bad (This is NSFW Bad) -

I have a lot to say about this game. Mostly good, very few of it bad.
The game starts off during world war 2, the player taking the role of William "B.J." Blazkowicz. After
him and his other comrades blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and a shrapnel is lodged into the back on Blazkowicz's brain. He is then put into a coma.
He is found unconscious, and put into a hospital/home for the mentally/physically disabled. Over the years, nazi officers take pateints to experiment upon. Fast forward to 1960, World War 2 is over. HOWEVER, the US surrendered, and Nazi Germany has won. On the very day he regains control of his body. officers visit said home and shut the place down. He stabs the officer who is about to kill him, makes an escape with the woman who had been taking care of him for the past 14 years, and set out to take down Nazi Germany with the resistance group.
Even though it was released just last year, it gives off the feeling of an old style shooter. And no, I do not mean that in a DNF bad kind of way, it feels properly modernized and doesn't reek of old formulas mixed with new. It feels very solid and satisfying to play. No DLC, no day 1 season pass, no shoe horned in multiplayer, no microtransactions, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, just a single player campaign first person shooter. as it should be.
Story felt very solid, makes you feel for the main characters, especially with what happens to some of them. And no, you do NOT need to play the older Wolfenstein games in order to enjoy it (but you should since Wolfenstein 3D is pretty good even if it is 20 ish years old at this point.)
However, only real complaint I have is it is not very well optimized. Everything is set to low at 1080p, framerate is all over the place, sometimes as low as 18 FPS, and sometimes as high as 60. And on top of that, with that uneven framerate, dialogue/lip movement did unsync and become out of place. If you have a lower end rig, be aware that you might not be able to run it at full capacity unless you do some overclocking or lower the resolution.
All in all, performance issues aside, it is a very solid single player first person shooter. One of the most satisfying FPS games I've played in years
And I CANNOT wait for The Old Blood to come out.

I was on the fence about this one for months after it released despite all the praise it received. This was mainly because of how average I found the 2009 effort from Raven Software. Rest assured, that Wolfenstein: The New Order shares only the genre and franchise with that release. The New Order is an almost perfect blend of old and new FPS design and mechanics.
You'll have control taken away for flashy scripted events but you can also duel wield sniper rifles because, why not? You'll get button prompts and move through linear environments but you'll still be shooting an awful lot of Nazis with a variety of weapons. There is a progression system but no regenerating health. There is a significant story element but you also won't have limits on the weapons you carry. All of these seemingly contradictory design choices come together in a highly polished and well crafted game. Wolfenstein: The New Order is probably the best FPS I've played since Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare.
If you're on the fence then you need to get off.

My con's list might be a bit large, but that's only because its alpha and there are obviously going to be problems, people should know what they are buying. Its an awesome game and you will enjoy it, just be prepared for a few minor flaws.
Pro's -
The game run's smooth and looks great with UE4
The communication layout is great, easy to talk with squad, other SL's and even a vicinity chat to say goodbye to the enemy before you shoot them in the♥♥♥♥♥

Con's -
Hackers, I know its only been out for a little while, but there is a hacker or two in every single lobby I've joined. Sounds like fire works, and will drop your frame rate to about 5fps and make it unplayable until they are kicked. Then the server gets closed and you have to find another one to play on. Game developers have become pretty lazy when it comes to hacking prevention. Squad is a fun game, but 40$ and they don't even have protection against little scripters??
