He's been through a lot, has Max Payne. Not only has he been lumbered with a ridiculous name, straight out of a cheesy comic book, but he's developed an addiction to painkillers, washed down with gallons of cheap whisky. It seems he's trying to dull the pain of losing his family in mob conflict. One might suppose that he'd want to move somewhere quiet and live out his life peacefully, but this dog thinks he's too old for new tricks, and perhaps the same is true of this series.
MP3 is a violent third person shooter, with a gimmicky (but admittedly cool) "bullet time" mechanic that lets you slow down time to pop enemies before they can react. This has been in the series since the very first game, and it still feels pretty badass to burst into a room, hit slo-mo, and neatly execute five startled enemies before they can even grab their guns. Weapons feel weighty and sound good, and bullets can blow huge chunks out of people this time around, which is sure to delight players and ratings board officials alike. You'll be grateful of bullet time, as this game doesn't pull any punches. I played on normal but still found myself dying in every other fire fight. Checkpointing is generous so you won't get frustrated, and I actually appreciated being able to redo a section in a cleaner, more stylish fashion.
So far, so Max Payne. One big change is the loss of the oddly charming comic book panel cutscenes, replaced with more traditional in-engine videos, which are certainly well directed and more than capable of progressing the story, but which are far too frequent for my liking. You can scarcely open a door without control being snatched away from you, sometimes with no more purpose than to introduce the next few baddies which you'll murder in less time than it took to watch that cutscene. It feels like the only reason for these to be here is to disguise loading and allow for another internal monologue from Max about how crappy the situation is, which is surely one of the only joys left in his life. My girlfriend remarked that he loves the sound of his own voice, which isn't stricly true as he doesn't speak very much, but you'll grow very familiar with his thoughts. It's a good thing, then, that the actor who plays him does an excellent job and that the writing is good, even if it just shamelessly apes hard-boiled noir fiction without adding anything new.
The story chugs along at a fair old clip, and there's a bit more variety in locations than with previous games in the series. As a bodyguard for a rich family in Sao Paulo, Max will get to shoot up his fair share of swanky hotel rooms and VIP clubs, as well as eventually taking the fight into the slums - or favelas - although nobody will notice a bit more destruction there. It rarely seems like you've time to take a breather as everywhere you go, more and more people seem to want to kill you, but poor old punching-bag Max doesn't seem to know when to quit. As with the new Batman games, the trials that Max goes through actually show on his bullet scarred skin and increasingly dirty and torn clothes, but the less said about his hawaiian shirt the better.
The whole game is overlaid with graphical filters. The graphics seem to glitch and blur, and colours pulsate in vibrant shades. I actually really like this effect, but I'm sure there will be plenty of people that hate it and I don't think it's possible to simply disable it.
I'm not completely finished with the game, so can't speak for its running time, but I think it'll clock in at around ten hours, which is respectable. Although the biggest criticism I can level at this game is the intrusive cutscenes, there are a few other niggles which I'd like to get off my chest. Whenever a cutscene ends, Max is left holding his pistol, even though I had been using an AK before it started, so there's a hasty swap as the lead starts flying. Annoying. Another thing is the lack of grenades. In the options there's a button dedicated to throwing a 'nade, but I've yet to find a single one in all my hours of play. The enemies have plenty to throw at you, but they don't drop them on death. Why not?
I don't think anybody would accuse this game, pretty and polished as it is, of being a classic. It's got satisfying combat, hampered by an incessant need to shove movies in your face, and a lot of interesting settings which you won't really get to explore as you're thrust from one combat scenario to another. If you switch your brain off and just get on with things there's a lot to enjoy, and honestly, Max himself is a pleasure to be around. Just, keep your medicine cabinet locked.

The Talos Principle is a puzzle game developed by Croteam (the same developers behind the Serious Sam videogame series). You control an android that finds itself awake in a world filled with human ruins. It's then reached by the voice of a being calling himself Elohim and revealing to the protagonist to be its creator and god: Elohim devised a series of challenges to test the android's faith, which it must now complete in order to better understand the world around it and fulfill its supposed destiny as a chosen one.
The game itself is your typical puzzle title fare with open world elements: you can move around a huge map that contains three minor hubs (included a special location, the Tower, accessible only via special means). Each hub contains roughly seven areas you can access that contains from three to five puzzles. Every puzzle awards you a distinct sigil: green sigils are used to advance in the game, yellow ones to unlock new gadgets necessary to solve later puzzles, red ones to witness a specific ending and starts as bonus collectables able to unlock yet another ending. While the green and yellow sigils are considered the easiest to obtain, the red ones and the starts are far more difficult to find. During your adventure you'll unlock special gadgets required to overcome certain puzzles: learning to use them, especially in tandem with one another and the other elements of the challenges, is vital to proceed through the Talos Principle. The game has a total of three different endings: each of them have a distinct requirement, which basically boils down to how many sigils you have collected and of what kind.
The visuals of the game are rather simplistic, but not ugly in the slightest: the three main areas have each an hystorical motive (ancient Rome, ancient Egypt, the Medieval Age), with the environments being rendered in high detail. Each section of the three hubs have also its own weather to further make them unique. The soundtrack is also rather fitting as well, further enhancing the quiet mood of your discovery journey.
Aside from the main beef the puzzles are, the Talos Principle offers you other things to do or to check out, should you desire: there are computer terminals scattered through the various areas that contain messages and bits of texts to better understand the setting and the theme of the game; you can use these terminals to have a rather long philosophical debate with an artificial intelligence named Milton; you can check for the messages some mysterious NPCs left for you and, should you find some paint, write some yourself; you can find audio logs from lost time capsules or ghosts from the other androids that came before you. All this features help enhance the philosophical nature of the game itself, with many elements making you question if your character really is a thinking begin, what is the purpose and the substance of the world you find yourself in and the true nature and purpose of Elohim himself.
The only issue I had with the Talos Principle is about how little information you are given about what you can and can't do in the game's world: once you recive a certain gadget, for instance, you are basically thrown at the wolves and had to master it quickly in order to advance, so expect to do some experimenting with everything at your disposal in order to learn how to use some gadgets effectively. Another lack of information from the game's part is abour the endings themselves: it's extremely difficult at a later point to know precisely what you have to do to make the game just end, let alone taking all the steps to reach a specific ending. You are pretty much aimless for a large portion of the game. While this somehow forces you to explore the game's world hunting for stuff, finding yourself wandering aimlessly at some point is nor funny nor engaging.
The Talos Principle is both a great puzzle game and a good philosophical introspection journey that will entertaing bot the fans of the genre and other players just looking to try out something new

“The Talos Principle” is a first-person puzzle game that revolves around using the tools in your environment to collect Tetris pieces referred to as sigils. Using these sigils, you’ll unlock more areas and tools to use and to solve progressively more complex puzzles. This simple backbone forms the basis for what is the single best puzzle game I’ve played to date, and likely will be for years to come, as it nails every core aspect of what makes a game great with near-perfection.
The first thing that struck me about the game from the moment I started it was the music and atmosphere. That may seem obvious since it’s the first thing you’re subjected to, but being a 3D puzzle game where you have a character that moves around the environment, it’s a massive plus to have a good atmosphere. During my playthrough of the game, which took about 21 hours, I never once got bored or tired of the environment or music. The game in general has a very calming vibe, and since it lacks any sense of humor outside of Easter eggs, it tends to put you in a different state of mind while engaged with it. The static environment goes well with the music, and both work towards keeping you calm and focused on the task at hand, which you’ll need to be if you want any hope of completing this game.
That takes us to the gameplay, where “The Talos Principle” does exactly what every puzzle game strives to do. While it starts off fairly simple - halfway through the first area in the game I still wasn’t being challenged - it has a difficulty curve that makes sense. The puzzles get progressively harder as you go on, naturally, but take a step back every time a new mechanic is introduced, it gives you time to learn about the new tool you just unlocked before it goes back to showing off brilliantly designed puzzles. It paces itself well, and it deserves a lot of respect for managing to keep the curve so consistent, with very few hiccups along the way. It also includes a side puzzle in some cases, in the form of collectible stars. The game has multiple endings, and it appears that one of them requires finding 30 stars throughout the game, but if you’re like me, good luck figuring out how to get anything other than the obvious two.
The game’s story is where this game stands truly head and shoulders above any competition. From the very start of the game, it establishes a god constantly watching over you and occasionally speaking to you, who identifies himself as Elohim -- no coincidence that this is the hebrew word for God. The game is heavily philosophical, although you probably guessed that from reading the title, and it puts you in the same kind of mental dilemma as Eve; this is also where the endings come into play. I won’t spoil the endings beyond what Elohim himself tells the player, which is the game gives you two obvious choices. Collecting all of the sigils unlocks the “Gate to Eternity” where Elohim promises eternal life, or you can choose to defy him. The fourth area of the game is the tower, where he tells us not to go. The player is enticed there by a computer program, called Milton, who engages in philosophical debates at certain points in the game. While ultimately the final choice rests in the players hands, the game gives some heavy hints towards one of those endings being the one and true ending.
The game makes you think, not just logically but also in terms of philosophy as well. The debates I had with Milton stuck with me throughout the whole experience, and the fact that sometimes I still wonder about my responses to his questions just goes to show how well made this game is as a whole. The writing serves the story very well, and never undermines it, the environment and atmosphere as a whole is a masterpiece, and the gameplay itself shows incredible skill in terms of creating a puzzle game. “The Talos Principle” is one of the few experiences that I can say, every person who loves games should give it a chance. It even has a demo which is becoming increasingly rare in modern gaming. There’s almost no excuse to not check it out.

The Talos Principle is a puzzle game developed by Croteam (the same developers behind the Serious Sam videogame series). You control an android that finds itself awake in a world filled with human ruins. It's then reached by the voice of a being calling himself Elohim and revealing to the protagonist to be its creator and god: Elohim devised a series of challenges to test the android's faith, which it must now complete in order to better understand the world around it and fulfill its supposed destiny as a chosen one.
The game itself is your typical puzzle title fare with open world elements: you can move around a huge map that contains three minor hubs (included a special location, the Tower, accessible only via special means). Each hub contains roughly seven areas you can access that contains from three to five puzzles. Every puzzle awards you a distinct sigil: green sigils are used to advance in the game, yellow ones to unlock new gadgets necessary to solve later puzzles, red ones to witness a specific ending and starts as bonus collectables able to unlock yet another ending. While the green and yellow sigils are considered the easiest to obtain, the red ones and the starts are far more difficult to find. During your adventure you'll unlock special gadgets required to overcome certain puzzles: learning to use them, especially in tandem with one another and the other elements of the challenges, is vital to proceed through the Talos Principle. The game has a total of three different endings: each of them have a distinct requirement, which basically boils down to how many sigils you have collected and of what kind.
The visuals of the game are rather simplistic, but not ugly in the slightest: the three main areas have each an hystorical motive (ancient Rome, ancient Egypt, the Medieval Age), with the environments being rendered in high detail. Each section of the three hubs have also its own weather to further make them unique. The soundtrack is also rather fitting as well, further enhancing the quiet mood of your discovery journey.
Aside from the main beef the puzzles are, the Talos Principle offers you other things to do or to check out, should you desire: there are computer terminals scattered through the various areas that contain messages and bits of texts to better understand the setting and the theme of the game; you can use these terminals to have a rather long philosophical debate with an artificial intelligence named Milton; you can check for the messages some mysterious NPCs left for you and, should you find some paint, write some yourself; you can find audio logs from lost time capsules or ghosts from the other androids that came before you. All this features help enhance the philosophical nature of the game itself, with many elements making you question if your character really is a thinking begin, what is the purpose and the substance of the world you find yourself in and the true nature and purpose of Elohim himself.
The only issue I had with the Talos Principle is about how little information you are given about what you can and can't do in the game's world: once you recive a certain gadget, for instance, you are basically thrown at the wolves and had to master it quickly in order to advance, so expect to do some experimenting with everything at your disposal in order to learn how to use some gadgets effectively. Another lack of information from the game's part is abour the endings themselves: it's extremely difficult at a later point to know precisely what you have to do to make the game just end, let alone taking all the steps to reach a specific ending. You are pretty much aimless for a large portion of the game. While this somehow forces you to explore the game's world hunting for stuff, finding yourself wandering aimlessly at some point is nor funny nor engaging.
The Talos Principle is both a great puzzle game and a good philosophical introspection journey that will entertaing bot the fans of the genre and other players just looking to try out something new

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a pleasantly surprising mix of well designed, amazingly fun FPS mechanics with complexly written, emotionally invested storytelling. Don't judge this book by its cover as what appears to be another Nazi slaying shooter is in fact one of the most memorable and powerful gaming experiences I've ever had. This is definitely worth a look on sale, even if you're not ordinarily a shooter guy/gal.
Following a near-fatal head wound during a crucial mission that would determine the outcome of World War II, Captain William BJ Blazkowicz has been in a comatose state for 14 years. He wakes up. The year is 1960. The war is over. The Nazis won. The New Order rules all over the world.
This review is written from the perspective of a fan of action shooters and story driven games, but no experience with previous Wolfenstein games.
First and foremost, the New Order does a great job with its shooting mechanics. At first, a lot of the guns may feel a bit typical (pistol, assault rifle, SMG) but they game really gets its progression right and you unlock more and more weapons and upgrades all with their own quirks and gimmicks. The game doesn't bury itself in the details of how it's possible that you can dual wield shotguns and assault rifles or how your able to carry pretty much every weapon at once. The gunplay is pretty satisfying, especially when you land that awesome brain-spraying headshot or you fire enough shrapnel shards into a dude to turn him into Swiss cheese. That's not an exaggeration either, this game spares no detail when it comes to gore and violence. One moment that struck me early was throwing a grenade into a bunker and then wading through all the chunks of Nazi afterwards. Exposed ribs and everything, nasty stuff. You can also do an action slide and the lean and cover mechanics work really well too.
The gameplay and level design is much more open ended than your average shooter. You are fairly often, given the option to sneak around with a suppressed pistol and a few knives (which can be thrown or used for some gnarly and well animated stealth takedowns). The key thing to remember here is the fact that it is an option. Regardless of whether you sneak through the hidden vent with a knife or kick down the front door with a shotgun in each hand, there is no real right answer. This game isn't like Dishonored or Deus Ex however, and you cannot play the entire game like this, but the option is there frequently enough to satisfy a first person stealth action fan such as myself. The game also rewards your chosen playstyle with a well-designed perk system similar to Elder Scrolls, but far more substantial. You won't find any generic "movement speed increased by 3%" or "headshot damage increased by 5%" here. Every perk is something meaningful, noticeable and based on the playstyle it’s tied to. The 4 key areas you can get perks for are:
This involves avoiding detection, getting stealth kills, silently scooping up pickups like health etc. The rewards make it easier to do these things like moving quieter, carry more knives, noise travels less far.
This involves getting headshots, using cover and accurate small arms weapons. The rewards include faster reload, magazine size and increased health regen.
This involves dual wielding and using heavy/laser weapons. The rewards include more movement speed and armour gain.
: This involves the use of grenades and other explosive weapons. The rewards include more explosive capacity and increased effectiveness of explosives.
The good thing about these perk paths is that they all remain open for the entire game, allowing you switch your playstyle on the fly to whatever you feel like. Another advantage of the open levels is the ability to explore for collectibles and side paths/objectives. Whilst this game does go a quite a bit overboard with the collectibles (132 total) they can be worth getting depending on how you feel about the narrative and cosmetic rewards. However, the key overarching theme that this game has giving the player the choice of how they want to experience it. If you’re playing it as a linear corridor shooting gallery you can do that and be done in 8 hours or you can take your time to sneak around and explore the world and be done in 12+ hours.
It is also worth noting that the AI is no pushover, at least on normal and up difficulties. They will take cover and try to flush you out of yours with explosives or flanking as much as they can. Your health regenerates, but only to a certain point. If you want to stay alive you need to be very aware of the health, armor and ammo pickups laying around.
For someone going in expecting a mindless Nazi slaying simulator I was supremely surprised by this games narrative. The story is excellent and the voice acting performances are top notch. All the characters are very well fleshed out and varied and it all feels very original and unique compared to other shooters out there today. It's a new twist on the classic World War II shooter. I went into this game having never played a Wolfenstein title before and I came away incredibly impressed. There are some really harrowing and tense moments in this game that made heart sink into my stomach or try to beat out of my chest. Even the villains are given more background beyond the fact that they are Nazis and that's why we should hate them. The soundtrack is great and always fits whatever happens to be going on perfectly whether it's pumping me up or freaking me out. There are even two branching storylines that make a few changes to the game both story and gameplay wise if you’re after some replay value. There are however a few moments in the game that are bit confusing in the sense of the tone and emotion the writers are going for in certain contexts, however this is a minor blip in an otherwise amazing narrative.
One thing that this game did really well, not just for a shooter, but for videogames in general is the romance plot. It felt very believable and tasteful and to be honest it's probably the best romance plot I've ever seen done in a video game. Story wise, The New Order blew my expectations out the water and then some.
The New Order definitely relies more on its art style over actual visual fidelity. It's not as "cartoony" as something like Dishonored but isn't exactly photorealistic either. It holds a middle ground that looks pretty good, but it isn't exactly anything to marvel at. A lot of the basic wall and ground textures aren't too hot. The gore and lasers are probably best looking aspects of the game.
The developers managed to get this game working at 1080p 60fps on the current gen consoles so pretty much all modern PCs shouldn't have any issue running this game with similar results. Do be aware that it doesn't run any higher than 60fps. It ran perfectly for me (i5 4670k, GTX 970, 8GB RAM) and for many people I know with a range of different systems.

“The Talos Principle” is a first-person puzzle game that revolves around using the tools in your environment to collect Tetris pieces referred to as sigils. Using these sigils, you’ll unlock more areas and tools to use and to solve progressively more complex puzzles. This simple backbone forms the basis for what is the single best puzzle game I’ve played to date, and likely will be for years to come, as it nails every core aspect of what makes a game great with near-perfection.
The first thing that struck me about the game from the moment I started it was the music and atmosphere. That may seem obvious since it’s the first thing you’re subjected to, but being a 3D puzzle game where you have a character that moves around the environment, it’s a massive plus to have a good atmosphere. During my playthrough of the game, which took about 21 hours, I never once got bored or tired of the environment or music. The game in general has a very calming vibe, and since it lacks any sense of humor outside of Easter eggs, it tends to put you in a different state of mind while engaged with it. The static environment goes well with the music, and both work towards keeping you calm and focused on the task at hand, which you’ll need to be if you want any hope of completing this game.
That takes us to the gameplay, where “The Talos Principle” does exactly what every puzzle game strives to do. While it starts off fairly simple - halfway through the first area in the game I still wasn’t being challenged - it has a difficulty curve that makes sense. The puzzles get progressively harder as you go on, naturally, but take a step back every time a new mechanic is introduced, it gives you time to learn about the new tool you just unlocked before it goes back to showing off brilliantly designed puzzles. It paces itself well, and it deserves a lot of respect for managing to keep the curve so consistent, with very few hiccups along the way. It also includes a side puzzle in some cases, in the form of collectible stars. The game has multiple endings, and it appears that one of them requires finding 30 stars throughout the game, but if you’re like me, good luck figuring out how to get anything other than the obvious two.
The game’s story is where this game stands truly head and shoulders above any competition. From the very start of the game, it establishes a god constantly watching over you and occasionally speaking to you, who identifies himself as Elohim -- no coincidence that this is the hebrew word for God. The game is heavily philosophical, although you probably guessed that from reading the title, and it puts you in the same kind of mental dilemma as Eve; this is also where the endings come into play. I won’t spoil the endings beyond what Elohim himself tells the player, which is the game gives you two obvious choices. Collecting all of the sigils unlocks the “Gate to Eternity” where Elohim promises eternal life, or you can choose to defy him. The fourth area of the game is the tower, where he tells us not to go. The player is enticed there by a computer program, called Milton, who engages in philosophical debates at certain points in the game. While ultimately the final choice rests in the players hands, the game gives some heavy hints towards one of those endings being the one and true ending.
The game makes you think, not just logically but also in terms of philosophy as well. The debates I had with Milton stuck with me throughout the whole experience, and the fact that sometimes I still wonder about my responses to his questions just goes to show how well made this game is as a whole. The writing serves the story very well, and never undermines it, the environment and atmosphere as a whole is a masterpiece, and the gameplay itself shows incredible skill in terms of creating a puzzle game. “The Talos Principle” is one of the few experiences that I can say, every person who loves games should give it a chance. It even has a demo which is becoming increasingly rare in modern gaming. There’s almost no excuse to not check it out.
5/5

I recommend this game 10/10 for its uniqueness, beautiful graphics, at times ethereal music and captivating story-line. It's way more than a portal clone-- people naturally think that once they see the turrets, boxes, and switches, but this game is much more ...
The Tetris-block (aka sigil) puzzles and progressive rewards kept me going and craving more, through all 3 worlds and oh yes I did venture to that forbidden tower!
There are about 5 different endings, depending on what you do (or don't do...), just do the 3 worlds, or climb the tower, or go after the bonus star worlds. Easter eggs also change the content of the endings, so replay or reload to get the different ones -- good replay value there -- I ended up doing the most basic ending (which I laughed at) and then did the maximum everything hardest ending, very nice visual sequence and totally worth it.
That said, great easter eggs and bonus stars throughout that pay homage to other games, variety of complexity to keep you challenged and make you think before you leap... You have unlimited rewinds (like extra lives) so don't worry about doing something stupid, you'll respawn from predictable save points automatically.
Excellent story-line with a few plot twists, The Talos Principle poses several philosophical questions from various ancient cultures along the way, what is it to be sentient, to be conscious, to exist? Without giving away spoilers, the intro video and pics don't do this game justice, you eventually get the feeling something is wrong and the world around you may not be what it seems... did it just flicker? Was that a ghost I saw run past? Hmm...
Conversely, if you don't care for the philosophy you can skip through 90% of the CRT sequences and just play through doing the levels, though you'll miss out on the premise of the environment and why your cybernetic-looking self is there.
For Serious Sam fans (or if you want that sort of dialog instead of the voice-in-the-sky Elohim guiding you), get the DLC, it's a hilarious twist that changes the overall vibe of the game.
Steam workshop folks, I'm hoping other people develop more content for this, I can envision a few diversions but will leave that to your own imagination...

With some background and research into beginner's guides, Planetside 2 does not have the learning curve you'd expect. It's not a broad character-based game like DoTA where you have to sink several hours to get a feel of some concepts. Planetside 2's gameplay is simple and similar to many other shooters:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
You create a character out of three factions and play around in six classes (some general ones like Assault, Engineer, Medic, etc. included). You spawn yourself wherever a conflict is occurring and support your faction in said conflict. Whether it be defending a base or capturing one, you're there spawning tanks, healing heavies, and shooting faces. A hexagon-styled map shows you the control of your faction in the continent (with two possibly being locked because of a faction's takeover). All you have to do is advance/defend with the rest of your teammates until the continent is yours. Additionally, you may join squads/platoons to organize armies via chat.
The menu is stock-full of buttons but in general it's nothing new. You can upgrade your class/vehicle abilities and unlock new gear using Certs (a currency earned by, well, playing). You can view the map and strategize with your teammates. You can check up on Directives that provide goals to reach for Certs and other bonuses. You can even view your statistics and laugh at your K/D ratio! But trust me, with the multitude of ways to possibly die, this game is all about it. You can't start the game, nor even exit it, unless you sign in to it (you have to ctrl-alt-del to exit). It is a poorly programmed piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ The sign up process is broken. After finally getting it to accept my password (by Googling for people who had the same problem) it then makes you link it to your Steam account. This process is broken, and fails every time for me. Whether this is due to programming error or server problems or what, I don't know. The forums suggest restarting the game multiple times or trying again later.
Edit: After finally getting it working and playing the first few levels, I'm sorry to say that in spite of what others have said, I found it to be one of most unenjoyable "games" I've played in a very long time. It's basically an interactive movie, with overly long cutscenes, interspersed with bad third-person shooter gameplay. It's almost a shooter on rails. When you restart the enemies are always in exactly the same places. Also the crosshair seems to be bugged a lot of the time (it either disappears or jumps erratically). I think it's designed for consoles with autoaim enabled, so that it turns into "click fire to contine the story".
Gameplay consists of spending 5-10 mins watching cutscenes, then 1-2 mins of point and click killing (so long as the crosshair allows you). If you fail, just repeat again. The enemies will always be in the same places and move in the same way. The slow motion adds nothing. It's there because it was in previous games, but it doesn't form an integral part of the gameplay. It's completely linear and you get the sense that the gameplay segments are just there to open up the next cutscene, which are the main focus. It's scattered with set pieces which function as "do what Max does in the story next or fail".
Considering that the gameplay is not fun at all, this might as well be a movie, except that what little I got of the plot was mind-numbingly boring and it seems to want you to not care at all about any of the characters. It's amazing that such a big budget can be blown on creating such a mediocre game. It's as if nobody involved knows why games are fun. All the design decisions revolve around the aesthetics and trying too hard to be cool, right down to the pointless words interspersed in the custscenes. Rockstar should stick to sandbox games, as they clearly don't understand linear or story-driven games.

Once the initial appeal of the game wears off, it deepens. The game is set up in a fairly straight-forward way -- you have worlds you can go to and in each, there's puzzle chambers. The story to the game is unobtrusive. If you want to explore it, you find it yourself rather than it coming to you. For the most part, anyways. The game gives you a sort of deep and hollow feeling to indulge when you're playing it as well. Something about all of the old and beautiful ruins you're submerged in combined with you being alone, save for someone who seems to be testing your worthiness is odd. Especially because his voice is fairly sparse. The Talos Principle presents a world that is desperately trying to insist that it isn't dead, and the scenery encourages you to shoulder on even when you get to a set of puzzles you don't particularly like.
The only thing that I have to say about some of the puzzle design in this game is that it -is- sometimes frustratingly precise. That is to say, I found that occasionally, when solving a puzzle I had the solution, but I had to tweak it -just so- in order to get it to stick. I didn't like this, and it especially bothered me in The Iron Curtain in particular. (Involving grabbing a diverter...thing. Saying anymore'll ruin it for you.)
I don't think this is an experience that anyone should pass up on, in my opinion. It's excellent work, and it deserves more attention than it gets.

So yeah, play it, its one of best game sequels i have honhestly played (and those arent few)

A game that somehow manages to be completely ridiculous and have an incredibly powerful and interesting story at the same time. The story really is the best part of the game, the way it focuses much more on human nature and the relations between the characters than anything else. There are some serious tearjerking moments in this game, and some moments that leave you pretty damn shocked. It's like nothing I've seen in a videogame before, and it could rival the most well written of movies. This is how you do "cinematic" games right, without compromising any of the gameplay for it.
The gameplay's good, too, with really solid shooter mechanics and a pretty decent selection of weapons (really helps that you can dual wield almost any weapon, including shotguns and, yes, sniper rifles). My only gripe is that the later levels stop being conducive to stealth (which is viable in most of the game otherwise) and it starts to introduce a lot of frustrating bulletspongy enemies right before the end. I've seen much worse, though. I'd without hesitation call this game my favorite single player shooter ever.

Here's what made me quit the game just now: There's a hostage situation, a number of people are held in a room with half a dozen guards. Max Payne 1 or 2 might have had a quick camera swoop to show you the situation, and then let you handle it however you want, probably by jumping through the door and killing everyone in the room in slow motion. Max Payne 3 shows you the situation, lets you walk up to the door and ... takes control away from you. Now you watch as Max opens the door, strolls into the room and has his weapons taken from him. He just stands there as a hostage gets executed and every enemy escapes right in front of him. What the hell?!

Absolutely phenomenal game.  Worth every penny.  The puzzles in each instance range from ridiculously easy, to extremely challenging (some people find all of them very easy and I hate those people, cause they are far smarter than I :P).  The farther you go, the more they range from complex, back to puzzles that make you scratch your head because you overthought far too much and added too much complexity, all the way back again to puzzles that require extraordinary outside the box thinking to solve.  You can come up with solutions too that the designers didnt see.  I managed several that later were not considered by anyone else i could find.  That is part of the genius of this game.  The graphics and soundtrack are flawless if your PC can handle them at their best.  The gameplay is simple and 100% reliable.
Many of the star puzzles will drive you bananas and often require all the thinking and experimenting you can come up with, and even then I still needed help at times lol (often smacking myself after I finally saw or accomplished the solutions)!  Read everything you can find too, and install a QR reader on your phone.  The endings are all worth trying out.  This is a game for people with an intellectual bent, and the philosophical reading (from all the greats) and challenges will have you thinking.  Better yet they are real philosophical challenges that people still grapple with today.
Secrets everywhere too :D Explore everything!

A superb sci-fi tale, brilliantly written, with engaging gameplay and ingenious puzzles of ever-increasing difficulty.  Throughout the beautiful world of The Talos Principle, you will come across terminals with quotes by major writers and philosophers, simple yet in no way simplistic thoughts by everyday people, even seemingly meaningless discussions in chat rooms that suddenly reveal unexpected depth: the sum of all human knowledge and experience, that we must not allow to perish. The Talos Principle is not only a sophisticated puzzle game, but also a deeply humane and elegant work of art, that dares to tackle complex subjects, without ever forgetting the primary objective of any game : to be, first and foremost, fun. A masterpiece!

With HD though, i can come back to the game i used to play a great deal once again, with the steam service allowing multiplayer to once again flourish. I recently bought the game through a sale with expansions, i have done one Deathmatch against the AI that lasted 10 hours of play and a few hours on the campaigns. the only really notable things stand out, the fire effects on buildings, the smoothness in the animations and finally how much stuttering a 8 player random match with 7 AI's takes out of a powerful computer system.
However it all seems good so far, but being the original game has probably just been optimized and touched up in the code and such, it is the same game i have always played in the past.

The Talos Principle feels like a Portal game that grew up a little.
Pros:
- The puzzles! They range greatly in difficulty, with some that left me baffled for nearly an hour. Additionally, you'll find yourself learning about the game world via deduction and guesswork, which is an extremely enjoyable way to play. You are never explicitly told how things interact with eachother. It is up to you to experiment and come up with your own ideas.
- The secrets. There are 40 easter eggs in this game. There are 30 hidden stars that, more often than not, require you to break assumptions you've made about the game. There are hidden texts, speeches, and so much that adds flavor to what could have been a less fleshed out world.
- The philosophy. This might not be for everybody, but I found the discussions held within the game to be engaging on an intellectual level. Some of it came off as a little too much for me, but overall I enjoyed the questions it brought up.
(Possible) Cons:
- The game dropped frames occasionally in one particular area of the game. Not severe, but enough to make me dislike going to the location.
- Some of the puzzles relied more on reflex and dodging, with the penalty of the puzzle resetting from the start if said actions were failed. I still enjoyed them, but I know others might not.
- I found the puzzles exploitable from time to time. I'm pretty sure I never found the actual solution to three or four of them. It's not neccessarily a problem that spreads throughout the entire game (or even an actual problem), but it might bug some.

Hands-down one of the brainiest games I've ever played.  I can't help but admire how much thought went into Talos Principle, the way it uses its premise as a puzzle game to springboard into a meditation on sentience.  It can get a little frustrating in the later stages of the game when you're having complex philosophical arguments while being limited to multiple-choice responses, but that's a small limitation in a game that overall makes its point very well.
The puzzles themselves are generally well-designed, and the difficulty scales well--early puzzles teach you simple principles that get applied in increasingly complicated ways in later puzzles.  You might get hung up on one or two puzzles, but ultimately they all have logical solutions, even if a few of them require you to think outside the box.
If you're interested in philosophy--particularly epistemology--and/or you like puzzle games, pick this up.  You won't regret it.

A gem in terms of game design. The Talos Principle offers diverse, clever puzzles that properly challenge the player, without ever being either too punishing or too obvious. The game has beautiful graphics and an atmosphere that really sets the overall tone, and delivers a minimalistic story that seamlessly meshes biblical mythology with eschatological science fiction (mostly in a non-intrusive, player-driven way). I actually (and not just rhetorically) found myself wondering at some of the philosophical questions the writers threw at me, pausing at times to read over a text or listen to an audio for the second time, alternately challenging *POSSIBLE SPOILERS* the voice in the sky and the uncanny word-processor in the terminals *END OF POSSIBLE SPOILERS*. As I advanced through the game, it really felt like progress – learning new mechanics, new questions, new theories as to what the answers might be; not to mention the knowledge of past (fictional) players who came before, and how to build upon their insights. In a nutshell, this is a very mature game, bold and confident, and deservingly so. The only negative comment I can make is that it instigated my curiosity a little too much a bit too early, and I found myself rushing through the last two chambers in a state of frenzy – just so that I could fully understand the story and how everything fit together. Overall, it was a great experience.

A very high quality game for early access - it's almost like a finished product already. Very few bugs to speak of other than the occasional floating weapon, but this isn't exactly game breaking.

The lighting is awesome and I love the microphone effects when someone talks near you that isn't on your squad's radio - if they are in a building their voice actually echoes and the voice comes from the player model making it seem like it's really that person talking. As they run past you there is a change in volume and it's harder to hear them the further away they are.
Another great thing about this game is the community - as I'm writing this the game costs £29.99 and I think it's really put the "trolls" off of purchasing it. Everyone in the game seems committed to playing it properly, not running into a battle area, constantly team killing or spamming the mic.
One major problem is that you connect to games through a server browser and cannot use the Steam "Join Game" feature on friends making it very hard to get a group into a game. Even just getting into a game on your own is a challenge. I'd really like to see a system like CS:GO added so that you can create a lobby with friends then search for a nearby server as a party and automatically join when one is available with enough spaces, it would make the whole process so much easier and wouldn't discourage people from playing.

Today, I'll be reviewing Robocraft, or what is left from it after the amount of updates to make devs more money.
So to start this off, Robocraft was a great game -- I played it a long time ago when there were Tiers. The system worked like this: You buy an item, the item has "robot ranking", if your robot ranking is high enough, you advance to next "tier", where only bots from the same tier are (or from higher if you had a party). The way the money worked was pretty straight forward -- you can buy with real money special points which can get you anything from tech points to the weapons you cant afford, but as much as I can say it was pretty balanced and not pay2win.
The system is currently really terrible because of multiple reasons: Pretty much you can share your robot. Don't take this the wrong way -- it's a nice touch that you can try other player's, but this pretty much killed the must for building your own.
So much stuff was changed -- tech tree was completelly removed so now everyone can buy anything. This means you can get against yourself 5 lock-on missile launchers that are pretty much undodgable, unless you have an obstacle between you and the robot that shoots them. The thing I loved in old robocraft was the amount of free premium codes -- there were so many premium codes for free to help you climb. I feel like it's rare to have any currently. The most terrible thing however is, that you no longer drop raw money from battles -- depending on your position in ladder you get a box that varies on rarity, obviouslly the better you play the better you get. To get most money devs made it that you get 4-8 items, but half of them are ONLY for premium users -- what has actually happened to me was getting multiple legendaries, why is that bad? They were all in the premium-only section and I didn't have premium.
tl:dr - The devs ruined this game from its original version, which was playable without tons of pay2win content.

Max Payne 3 is the third installment in the series. You play as a drunken, drug addicted ex-cop turned private contractor.
Visually Max Payne 3 is stunning. Easily one of the most beautiful and high quality games of 2012. There were no problems with broken textures or inconsistancies between textures. Max Payne 3's visuals are simply lovely. 5/5
The audio in Max Payne 3 is clear and crisp, with no audio firing at the wrong time. The soundtrack and voice acting is eventful and emotional, and you don't feel as though the dialog is repeating. 5/5
Max Payne 3's story is, again, one of the best of 2012. While there are some issues with the plot designed to keep the story moving along, they are hardly an experience altering issue. Max Payne 3 has all the required elements in a story, and keeps you interested the whole way through. 4/5
Mechanically Max Payne 3 suffers a bit on the PC. At more than one point during the game events failed to fire, leaving Max stuck in areas after having killed all of the enemies. This was quite frusterating due to having to restart the area. This can have a rather large negative impact on the gameplay experience. I also encountered a bug in which Max would not actually pick up ammunition, despite input. 3/5
Overall Max Payne 3 is a great game. There are some issues with it mechanically, but this is made up for in the looks and sounds the game has to offer.

A beautiful first-person puzzle game that deserves to be listed with Antichamber and Portal among the best puzzle games ever made.
The puzzles are clever are difficult enough to be challenging, but not so difficult that I ever needed to use a hint guide. You'll feel challenged but will rarely be stuck on a puzzle for long. Most puzzles involve the movement of objects and none require precise timing or twitch skills.
Then there is the excellent backstory, which you learn mainly through partially-corrupted text files on various computer terminals. I won't spoil anything about it, but the world of Talos is deep and cleverly constructed. Even on the surface the story works well, but it also works on deeper levels. The game is dripping with metaphor, self-reference, and philosophy. It questions the nature of consciousness and belief without really imposing any answers.
There's about 25 hours of content here and all of it is worthwhile. Highly recommended.

Comparisons to Portal 2 are aplenty, and in terms of gameplay they're definitely spot-on, but The Talos Principle takes itself a lot more seriously than Portal does. This is a game that makes you think much like Portal does (with the spatial/physics puzzles) but then also lets you ponder what it even means to be able to think (the underlying plot).
The way this works is there are tons of metaphors in the game, the most obvious ones being the garden of Eden, the tree of knowledge, and God and Lucifer. Next to that you will also find bits and pieces of old philosophical treaties and historical written sources. Whereas Portal is bring you a light-hearted Saturday morning cartoon, TTP tries to take you on a philosophical ride. The downside to that is that sometimes you'll be faced with a choice and none of the answers to the posed question will suit you. Either because you'll have a different opinion, or because somehow the question seems flawed, but this is something that is probably unavoidable given the nature of philosophy.

Let's not sugar coat it since nearly everyone knows what the Wolfenstein series is about. In this game you will shoot, stab, burn, explode and quite possibly kill Nazis.
That being said, Wolfenstein: The New Order is nothing short of a labour of love. Developers MachineGames have taken the very sensitive subject of WWII, the Nazi regime and the Third Reich and rather than trivialize the antagonists you face into overly-cartoony 'bad guys' or present a hyper-realistic and overtly controversial take - They have skated that fine line in between, with the grace and subtlety of an Olympic figure skater.
In terms of gameplay, New Order works on three pillars: Shooting (surprise surprise), Stealth and 'Tactics'. Each pillar is represented via both in-game actions and a perk tree that is influenced by these actions. Perks are persistent but must be unlocked through gameplay feats which range in difficulty - If you find that you've spent a good portion of the game using Stealth you may have already unlocked perks that allow you to sneak faster or carry more knives for stealth kills; Using cover often? You may have gained tactical perks that allow you to throw back grenades.
The game never bottlenecks or shoehorns you into a specific way of playing, you are completely flexible in how you approach each fight, which I personally loved since there are times when you really do just want to go guns akimbo with two assault rifles and charge, slide and shoot through the thick of it.
New Order's story is about a man out of time, the (legendary) B.J. Blazcowicz, and the struggle you face (through him) in setting things 'right'. Blazcowicz, throughout the game quietly utters out afterthoughts and well-wishes, offering you insight into how he is experiencing the events the player leads him through.
This not only enhances the gameplay but gives the player an impression of actually sharing the events of the game with its protagonist: You sneak through an enemy bunker and he gives you HIS thoughts (and no I don't mean some 8 year old catchphrase like a certain other FPS protagonist).
The character never physically or emotionally detaches from the player, and you want what he wants - Blazcowicz is not a psychotic and irredeemable murderer, he's a soldier who is fighting so that he has a home to return to, he wants to go back to the peace and freedom he loves, with the people he cares for. And really, what more reason is there to fight?
In closing, if you love story-driven action games then Wolfenstein: The New Order's got it in droves, and it's a damn solid single-player FPS. Don't let prejudgements and prejudices keep you from playing this game, it is truly an instant classic and a worthy evolution of its lofty forefather, Wolfenstein 3D.

Max Payne 3 is the third installment in the series. You play as a drunken, drug addicted ex-cop turned private contractor.
Visually Max Payne 3 is stunning. Easily one of the most beautiful and high quality games of 2012. There were no problems with broken textures or inconsistancies between textures. Max Payne 3's visuals are simply lovely. 5/5
The audio in Max Payne 3 is clear and crisp, with no audio firing at the wrong time. The soundtrack and voice acting is eventful and emotional, and you don't feel as though the dialog is repeating. 5/5
Max Payne 3's story is, again, one of the best of 2012. While there are some issues with the plot designed to keep the story moving along, they are hardly an experience altering issue. Max Payne 3 has all the required elements in a story, and keeps you interested the whole way through. 4/5
Mechanically Max Payne 3 suffers a bit on the PC. At more than one point during the game events failed to fire, leaving Max stuck in areas after having killed all of the enemies. This was quite frusterating due to having to restart the area. This can have a rather large negative impact on the gameplay experience. I also encountered a bug in which Max would not actually pick up ammunition, despite input. 3/5
Overall Max Payne 3 is a great game. There are some issues with it mechanically, but this is made up for in the looks and sounds the game has to offer.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a surprisingly good game in terms of both gameplay, story and overall design.
I had a great time playing through the game, where one playthrough on hard mode took around 16 hours to complete with some searching for collectibles during my first playthrough, which is a great deal more than most shooters nowadays. The games story is interesting and the level of detail in the fictional 1960's under nazi regime is very well made - especially if you go deeper into the world and read letters, newspaper articles scattered around the gameworld ot is clearly that they have taken it to a great length to create a believable gameworld. The various characters in the game have personality and are quite interesting, both friendly and evil characters and the dialogue is for the most part very well written and goes a bit above and beyond most shooters, while balancing between the satiric and the serious.
The gameplay itself is ok - it has the feel of retro shoot-em-up while offering in most cases to be played either stalthy or guns blazing. The game is not especially hard and with the perk-upgrade system and some overpowered weapons it was not very challenging even on hard mode. Some sections though can be quite hard or annoying due to a sparse checkpoint system.
The game offers two different storylines and while I have not played both yet it does not look like they differ much apart from some other characters, shortcuts and collectibles. The story and the game however is interesting enough to afford a second playthrough.
All in all this is a game that I enjoyed greatly and would reccoment to everyone who likes an well made shooter with an interesting story and a wery well made and detailed gameworld.

It's been a long time, Max.
Max Payne 1 and 2 were high water marks for third person shooters, the first for its gunplay and style and the second for pairing those elements with a tight story focus.  The second game wrapped things up conclusively, such that fans could be justified in scoffing at the idea of a sequel.  I certainly did when Max Payne 3 was announced, and it took a while before I could give it a fair shake.  In the end it's not without problems, and any recommendation should come with a few warnings attached, both for series fans and people just looking for a shooter fix.  Still, credit where it's due, Max Payne 3 earns the right to the title, even if (or perhaps because) it brings a different aesthetic to the table.
On the gameplay front, MP3 mostly succeeds at combining cover-based shooting with the more frenetic, two-fisted gunplay of the first two games. The mechanics and effects of shooting - how bullets hit the environment, how enemies react to being shot, how the guns sound and feel - are quite solid, though I do miss the old unlimited inventory for weapons. Cover works fine, bullet time is largely intact, and (on hard at least) your BT gauge recharges while you're under fire, as opposed to solely through kills. The "Last Stand" mechanism gives you a chance to take down your would-be killer after an otherwise fatal injury, provided you're carrying painkillers.  Other gameplay modes remove the feature, but I found it a welcome backstop that didn't cheapen the danger of each encounter.
There's a good variety of environments for each chapter, and even the dingier locations usually don't settle for brown and gray.  A couple flashback chapters touch on Max's life after the second game, and how he got to Brazil in the first place. An exploration element encourages you to look around, as each chapter has various clues that either explain the immediate situation or give broader context: a newspaper with financial reports, invoices, conspicuous bloodstains, etc. These don't affect the narrative in any way, but it did well to invest me in what was going on. Favelas in video games always seem to overstay their welcome, but I rarely got tired of one place before being carted off to somewhere else.
There are significant problems, of course. Level design is sometimes conducive to good gunfights, but too often you'll shootdodge, kill an enemy or three, and land right in the open where you are killed on the spot. I wound up using blindfire a lot simply because sticking my head up for more than a second was profoundly unwise, often getting me shot by enemies I didn't even know were there. Last Stand can sometimes trigger with an obstacle blocking your line of sight, preventing you from killing your target and forcing you to die.  You can't even reload the last checkpoint during this, and must instead wait to die before doing so.
The game's cutscene-heavy approach has an awful habit of yanking control and dumping you in a dangerous starting position. Worse, it often inexplicably switches Max to a handgun regardless of what you're carrying, meaning you will start several fights under fire and waste precious seconds switching back to your main gun. Exploration is undermined at times by NPC friendlies urging you to hurry up, and you wind up in contrived shooter situations with annoying regularity: turret sections, forced slow-mo dives/breaches, escort missions, etc. To their credit, the escortees usually have the sense to get somewhere safe, but a few will die over and over until you figure out what you're doing wrong.
Storywise, I went in with low expectations but was pleasantly surprised at the overall quality. New York Noir has been swapped for a somewhat surreal stranger-in-a-strange-land motif. There's no Norse mythology, but Max remains the fallen hero to end all fallen heroes.  He has since spent his life in a haze of booze and pills, and he's only just waking up to the larger goings-on. The highlighting of key words in a conversation works well with the use of unsubtitled Portuguese, giving the impression that Max, who doesn't speak the language, is gradually learning to pick things up from context.  I'm curious if a native speaker can attest to the authenticity, but careful cutscene direction helped to establish characters' intentions, and the game did an excellent job selling the atmosphere to me.
The plot was intriguing and smartly grounded, a contrast of South American politics and high society with crushing poverty and pervasive corruption; less shadowy conspiracy and more the kind of evil that might actually happen when no one's looking. The writing does stumble at times, and Max's voice is wasted describing basic actions, like turning a valve wheel or picking up another bottle of painkillers. The game also lacks for a strong, memorable villain, but many of the main characters did make lasting impressions and offered glimpses of deeper personalities. A quiet conversation between Max and his employer was one of the game's high points, where the latter dissects his own flaws with brutal honesty.
Max himself starts off as the alcoholic, anti-heroic killing machine advertised in the trailers, which is a bit of a backslide after MP2, but it's handled plausibly. It quickly becomes obvious that for all his claims of being burned out and washed up, there remains a decent person on the inside: torn between being unable to forgive himself and wanting to be something other than a walking, talking action movie stereotype, and still thinking like a cop besides. He's not too jaded to be horrified, and not too busy feeling sorry for himself to fight a grave injustice; a failing, flailing mess of a man that still knows right from wrong.
Few things can top the artistry and efficiency of "I had a dream of my wife. She was dead, but it was all right," and nothing in Max Payne 3 quite gets to that level. Instead it shoots for something else, confidently building its own atmosphere and narrative, and taking its own chances with the character. Doing my best to discard nostalgia, I don't think it's as well written as the first two games and it was sometimes frustrating to play.  Nonetheless, it's a respectable and respectful followup, a late welcome back for a series I didn't think I wanted to see again.
Like its namesake, Max Payne 3 can be a hazy mess of issues that are more than skin deep.  But also like its namesake, the game succeeds where it counts: killing an army of bad guys in style, all of whom can't seem to grasp that the crazy, wordy substance abuser with the guns stubbornly refuses to die.  Get a good sale price and there's no reason not to pick it up.
Trust us now.  It's time to let me go.

This game is very much
new player-friendly. Attempts to balance out some of the learning curve with a low-level, smaller-scale tutorial continent sort of fall flat because said continent is almost always completely empty. It's hard to learn the game when your only option is to go straight into the fray with other players who are both much more experienced and well-equipped than you. (Higher levels can purchase straight damage reduction with certs, thankfully not station cash.)
This is one of those twitch shooters where millisecond reactions mean the difference between life and death. You can't take much damage before dying, and many times, you will be killed without really knowing how, why, or what you did wrong. Though the game tries to show you a player's view cone after they kill you, this means little if they are, say, a sniper and you don't know the map or where they may have shot you from.
It's a shame because the idea of huge pitched battles could be incredibly fun, but often times they quickly devolve into one-sided, spawn-camping curbstomps. If you know what you're doing, you'll likely have fun and much of the dreadful grind has indeed been polished out. Unfortunately, if you're a new player that's just getting their feet wet, you'll feel much like a scrawny nerdy kid in dodgeball with a bullseye on his shirt.

If you are looking for something that is a decent single player story driven game with no MP functions this is the go to game.  You have about 20 hours or so of game time, which is considerably long compared to todays humdrum offerings.  Enemy AI is decent and in many ways exploitable which is good and bad.  Boss battles are somewhat cool, but cliched, like the London Monitor that beat whole armies in the story is beaten by you by exploiting weakspots that im surprised noone else figured out, you shoot the central eye to temporarily disable it, then shoot it in the rockets to destroy them and then shoot the underside a couple times and its dead.  The game ending is cliche, but not bad.  The really negative things are certain events that occur can kill you without you realizing it like opening certain hatches can leak dangerous gas, in the moon base mission, there was a train event on a destroyed bridge that you had to traverse and I fell for no reason out of the level, and other issues.  Certain enemies become bullet sponges when they really shouldnt, like heavy soldiers that can take as much damage as the hulking cyborgs and such.  Other than a couple gripes with those issues its a decent game.  The first portions of the game are more tactical with more openness to explore, the moon base and final missions corridor crawlers that are more restricted but still decent fun.  Your character can upgrade perks that add abilites to the game, like throwing knives and carrying extra munitions and such.  All told its a visually amazing looking game with great cinamatics and detailed explosions, though every character has eyes that look like they have jaundice or something since they all look yellowish but not bad.

The Talos Principle is a fantastic and truly unique experience, and I strongly recommend it to anyone who likes puzzle games.
Gameplay involves using objects in your environment, such as boxes, fans, and "connectors", to reach a puzzle piece ("sigil") at the end of each level. In addition many of the levels have optional star pieces, which are more difficult to obtain and require a lot of creativity and/or careful observation. The overall difficulty is similar to Portal.
The game is set in beautifully rendered outdoor environments, and I found myself taking breaks from puzzle solving just to explore. (I had some problems with motion sickness at first, but the sensitivity settings fixed that.) Most of the levels have easter eggs and other features to discover.
Overlaying the puzzle gameplay is a story with strong philosophical themes, exploring topics we rarely see in games, like what is the nature of reality, and do I have a free will. You have some genuine choices to make and at least three entirely different endings.

Max Payne 3 has to be one of the games I have had the most mixed feelings about in a good while.  The game does a lot right, delivering quality graphics and sound to match with a notably good soundtrack with decent voice acting. You really do feel like Max Payne himself, thrust into an alien and hostile environment as a naive gringo.
In my opinion the game fails mainly in terms of its... feel. It can feel tense and overwhelming at times as Max faces wave-upon-wave of enemies, with sometimes only as little as a baggage trolley for cover (not ideal when the enemy AI likes to flank Max). Yet you have the Max Payne series gimmicks of diving forward with bullet time, which can more often than not end up spending one of Max's pill bottles and gaining little compared to if he had just stayed behind cover. Is the game supposed to be fun? I'm not so sure and I'm not so sure games even have to be. But there is a real contradiction between the absurdity of a single American Rambo tearing down actual armies, the diving forward with bullet time; and Max's frailty. It's very easy to find yourself on the wrong side of a Retry screen if you play recklessly, yet intuitively this feels like the sort of game in which you should. Instead, often it is better to retreat and find good cover than it is to dive forward clutching not one, but two Uzis and letting rip.
This is not Max Payne 3's only failing. The story, to me, was completely unengaging. Which is especially problematic when Rockstar insisted upon making most cutscenes virtually unskippable. This would be fine if they were few and far between but I have never encountered so many cutscenes in a third-person shooter; so many situations where the player loses control, loses agency for Max to simply walk through a door, or for Max to simply crouch behind cover. The player can do this! These do not need to be cutscenes! This was definitely a deliberate choice by Rockstar and in my opinion, a terrible one.
Collectibles like Clues and Golden Guns were particularly annoying in my playthrough of Max Payne 3. Golden Guns are sometimes hidden in levels in various nooks and crannies for the player to find, but Max Payne talks to himself saying things like "I had to move fast" - encouraging, perhaps unwittingly, the player to move on and leave the collectibles behind! The collectibles felt more like a hindrance than anything else.
Overall this game frustrated me as the potential was truly there. Varied locations; good graphics; good sound; strong animations. But the feel of the game turned into an arduous slog, weighed down by its self-important, overbearing story with its serious tone in an absurd situation.
Not recommended.

The story is straightforward and the game is easy to pick up and play.
GRAPHICS:

The campaign is short, but there are multiple characters to unlock, lots of weapons and animals to unlock and 99 levels to max out, making it a game you can spend some serious time with.
Two other negatives:
The game is not worth the high price. Buy it on sale instead.

The Talos Principle is a fantastic and truly unique experience, and I strongly recommend it to anyone who likes puzzle games.
Gameplay involves using objects in your environment, such as boxes, fans, and "connectors", to reach a puzzle piece ("sigil") at the end of each level. In addition many of the levels have optional star pieces, which are more difficult to obtain and require a lot of creativity and/or careful observation. The overall difficulty is similar to Portal.
The game is set in beautifully rendered outdoor environments, and I found myself taking breaks from puzzle solving just to explore. (I had some problems with motion sickness at first, but the sensitivity settings fixed that.) Most of the levels have easter eggs and other features to discover.
Overlaying the puzzle gameplay is a story with strong philosophical themes, exploring topics we rarely see in games, like what is the nature of reality, and do I have a free will. You have some genuine choices to make and at least three entirely different endings.

Compared to all of the other creative voxel combat games out there, Robocraft feels alot more polished for multiplayer combat.  It isn't extremely complicated where you'd have to spend hours working on a design to do well, but it also does take a bit of thought and knowledge of the mechanics to design something good.
I've given this game a recommendation, but I would not have always done so.  This game has changed drastically since I started playing it and will likely continue to change drastically, so take that into account.  A lot of the other reviews mention the epic loot update / crates.  While I think these were a bad idea for them to add in their first implementation, the devs have made them more bearable and awarded much more frequently.
They've made plenty of other big changes and questionable decisions, and they don't look like they'll stop any time soon.  There WILL be massive changes to core mechanics that make a bunch of your bots barely if at all usable, if that's something you can't tolerate then stay away from this game.  I for one like that the game changes this rapidly and drastically as it forces redesigns and shakes up the meta every now and then.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is one of the most satisfying single-player FPS's I've played in a while. "Single player" is a big keyword for this one because there is no muliplayer to speak of, which is almost unheard of for the genre. Yet, the decision seems to have ensured a game that grips from beginning to end of its campaign and feels thoroughly worked and impeccably designed. That's not to say it doesn't have issues, just that those issues are the result of a little too much care rather than too little.
Some have said this is a game where the story and presentation have taken precedence over the gameplay, and while I disagree with them it's obvious this game has almost Kojima-lite focus on narrative that's uncommon. For the most part, it's an incredibly solid narrative, especially for a shooter. Your protagonist Blazkowitz may be a cartoonishly square jawed military stereotype by design (big shades of Brad Pitt's Aldo Ray in Inglourious Basterds) but as the game goes on these cartoonish elements intermingle with a sincerely compelling and at times emotional story of human beings turned to military machines through an endless decades long war. Reconciling both of these elements can be a little problematic, but if the game tries to throw a little more meaning into the fact that you've blown away hundreds upon hundreds of soldiers than is quite earned, this is made up for by the fact that the game still can make you feel for its supporting cast. You've got an incredibly diverse group of folks that are all quirky and cool in their own ways, and some truly grotesque, awesome villains, and this makes the story elements work incredibly well.
This extends beyond the game's cinematics into gameplay, and this is where you see Wolfenstein's presentation really shine. Firstly, the production design's absolutely marvelous. On a technical level you've got some strong iconic designs with masterful shape language, which helps immensely when you have to see what mechanical monstrocities you're about to take on. Level designs are distinct and the layout has plenty of thought for different ways to approach combat situations. At times, especially early on, the game can seem excessively linear and CoD-esque with its cinematic moments, but when combat starts, and it goes on for a while, it's surprising how much thought can be put into shooting Nazis. Generally, I started stealthy, knifing and sniping all I could until the inevitable discovery, and then the game got gloriously chaotic, with lasers, rockets, dual-wielded lasers and assault rifles, and grenades flying all around. The return to health kits over recharged health is very welcome, as now you have to charge forward to actually win combat situations when you're in the red as cover affords no take backs from poor choices. The game also lets you overcharge health if you pick up extra med kits, which offers the level of thinking whether you want the boost or to save it for an emergency.
I also have to really praise the sound design in this game, as it's just awesome. Yes, every gun is satisfying and bass-y, the kickback really works in this game, but in addition you'll have some really effective story driven choices. Take moments of death where a split decision has to be made, and the foreboding music that kicks in, seeming to rise as the danger gets closer. Or take some really interesting underwater and outer space segments where sound is drowned out almost entirely from within your suit. Take the moments where a subdued acoustic track plays, then builds to a fully orchestrated version of that track as the really impressive stuff starts happening. It's all super smart and kicks the game's storytelling up a lot.
If I have one complaint that kind of puts a damper on all this wonderfulness, it's that the game spreads itself a bit thin. Engaging as the narrative often is, it can just as often be episodic and jarringly paced, as you find yourself jumping rather suddenly into levels without any clue how you got there because you blinked for a second during a cut-scene. There are also a big number of loose ends that I imagine are being saved for some theoretical sequel. I also loved things like the incredibly brief shootout on the surface on the moon, but these scenarios are so brief that I found myself wanting the gameplay idea to be pushed into further, more complex territory. Imagine the tactics of regular combat without sound and reduced gravity.
But that's nitpicking, if you've been starved for good first-person shooting this is your fix. There are no mediocre RPG elements dragging it down like Far Cry 3, and there's a shocking amount of soul to go with it. Plus its incredible visual and audio elements and it's a complete experience and the rare AAA title that gets it right.

Let's get this out of the way immediately; I wouldn't buy this game at full price. But then, it's regularly on sale, and it has come a long way in the last two years.
Now, I grew up playing the original Age of Empires: Rise of Rome, and Age of Empires II: The Conquerors games, so I knew exactly what to expect with AoE II: HD. The graphics are only slightly updated, but honestly that was barely an issue for me. The massively improved AI (one that doesn't just resign at random) is a major factor; they actually pose a threat now. Another big factor is the increased map size and population count combination; the original game always felt like you needed a lot more units, even with a 200 pop limit. The Forgotten Empires expansion adds quite a nice selection of new civilisations, some of which offer slightly different strategies. Also, AoE II has graphical issues on modern GPUs, so this is the best way of playing the classic game.
Now, for the negatives. For the greatest time, this game performed abysmally on the biggest map size and with high populations, which is absurd. They've largely fixed this... but it's still not great, and still relies way too much on a single core. And I have issues with ridiculously high pings when playing online with a friend (who lives in a foreign country, but we have no ping issues in games like Left 4 Dead 2), which have never really improved. The AI, on water maps, has a tendency to build so many boats that the game becomes nigh-on unwinnable (unless you can build a mass of castles near by and not get wiped out in the process). It has also proven to be tempermental when run in windowed mode, and units occasionally bug out and get totally stuck, meaning you have to kill them.
In conclusion; if you liked AoE II, you'll love this. Get it on sale, as it's a very fair price when 75%/80% off. But wait for a sale. If you didn't like AoE II for any reason other than you felt it was too easy... this probably won't change things for you.
