The Talos Principle is one of the most thought provoking first person puzzle games I've ever played... In fact, it just might be the ONLY one in it's genre. The puzzles are clever and a bit difficult at points, causing you to play a level for like half an hour until you realize that you've been at the level for half an hour. Also, the music... oh my... In each world there are terminals that contain text and HTML files. While I don't mind reading, it gets a bit tedious having to read quite a bit of long passages. Overall, I rate 9.5/10. The best of it's very unique kind!

What kind of game is this?
It is a puzzle game. If you imagined Portal, without its portals, but still utilizing block, beam, and platforming puzzles, that is the core gameplay. Not necessarily the core facet of enjoyment though.
It is a mysterious game. You get dropped into the world, and told to solve puzzles for God. But simply looking at yourself in 3rd person reveals your shape to be a robot, and there are other clues delivered that all is not what seems to be.
It is a compelling game. The main narrative is that you solve puzzles to attain eternal life. However what compelled me to play were the fragments of text and audio that filled the background of the world you are in, a conversation with a PC-based intelligence, and the desire to see the forbidden knowledge.
It is, at times, a frustrating game. There are many puzzles where careful thought is all that is required. And there are puzzles with bombs and turrets that require exact execution. I was initially playing on my laptop with the touchpad, but you'll need either a mouse or a gamepad for later puzzles.
It is a beautiful game. You will observe beautiful landscapes from Greek, Egyptian, and Medieval architecture. And in the bits of data, you will see some beautiful and sad bits of story. If I seem vague, it's because I do not want to spoil it. If you are still undecided, there are lets play videos that can help you see the core gameplay.
It's a game by Jonas Kyratzes. Whether you look at his text based games such as The Matterof the Great Red Dragon, the object hunting game You Shall Know Truth, or a similar puzzle game, The Infinite Ocean, they are not just games, but also ideas.
In short, I recommend this game.

My first response when I hear of supposed philosophical games is a weary caution. In my experience, games have a tendency to either over simplify deep topics, or to present an obvious bias, both of which has a tendency create a very pretentious atmosphere.
Talos Principle doesn't commit any of those mistakes, or really any major mistakes at all. It's an elegant, well-written game with interesting and difficult puzzles. The difficulty curve and pacing of the puzzles is nearly perfect, although, to be honest, the puzzle-solving aspect did feel just a little bit stale towards the end. New mechanics keep getting introduced throughout the game, but the later mechanics are just not as interesting or satisfying as the earlier ones. This is very subjective of course, and you may have a different opinion of the late game mechanics. However, not all mechanics are used in all puzzles, so even towards the end each new puzzle will feel very different from the last.
The puzzles are broken up nicely by optional, but highly recommended interactions with a computer archive and its snarky AI archivist. The story, which has heavy religious and philosophical overtones, is told through these computer terminals, but also through Elohim, the omnipresent voice in the sky, and sound bytes scattered throughout the world. The world itself is also littered with religious symbols and similarities, mostly inspired by Christianity, but other religious inspirations are also prominent.
Accompanied by a fantastic soundtrack that always matches the scenery, the result is a very relaxing, sometimes even serene game with a genuine and interesting philosophical story and well-paced, difficult puzzles. It is one of my favorite games I've played in 2015 so far and I highly recommend it.

Like most games these days, this one has two elements: plot and gameplay.
As far as gameplay is concerned, the puzzles are well put together and have that same sort of elegant simplicity that Portal had.  Expect to solve them with sudden flashes of insight, rather than slow grinds.  However, I feel the developers' choice of nonlinearity here was a double-edged sword, for while it makes it easier to step away from an overly-difficult puzzle, it also makes it harder for the game to "train" you effectively in some of the more complex concepts.  In turn, this results in the puzzles having uneven difficulty levels at times.  This may be more fun with two people at one computer; alternatively, take a break when you get frustrated and the ideas will eventually come to you.  It's probably a bad idea to try to complete the whole game alone in one sitting.
On to the plot.  Above all else,
.  The plot is much more interesting when you don't know how the game ends.  With that out of the way, I should note that the philosophy presented in this game is well researched.  Either that, or Croteam reinvented half of modern philosophy from first principles, which would be even more impressive.  They also manage to avoid the jargon that so commonly infests philosophical discourse these days, making the game accessible to a wide audience (though it does lead to occasional loss of precision).  I find it difficult to discuss the plot in any further detail without spoiling anything, so I should close by noting that it was, in my opinion, well-written.  It requires the player to think critically about all available information, which sets it well apart from most games.  While I feel they could have done certain things differently, I'm not convinced those alternatives would have produced a substantially better game.

I'm a remarkably discerning gamer. I have played hundreds upon hundreds of games, and few have actually managed to change my life.
The Talos Principle is one of those games.
I started playing this at a very difficult time of my life, when I felt like I didn't have control over the circumstances surrounding me. I was crushed by a sense of powerlessness, and naturally, games provided a small sanctuary from that. However, I couldn't convince myself that the empowerment I felt was real; after all, it's just pixels on a screen.
This is the only game I have ever played that legitimately made me feel like I was living in another reality. From the pitch-perfect visuals, to the soul-infiltrating soundtrack, to the remarkable performances on display, to, most importantly, the goddamn writing, I was sucked in from the start. Whenever I accessed one of the story-driving terminals in the game, I felt a sense of discovery and wonder that I've never felt before in a game; the superb quality of the writing, and obvious classical literacy of the developers, helped with that considerably.
And then, the puzzles. Oh my dear lord, the puzzles. I was challenged, driven to madness, validated, and forced to think in ways I didn't know a game could push me to think. This was true accomplishment. When I got that final star (yeah, I played a lot), I felt like the king of this wonderful, apocalyptic, serene, beautiful little world Croteam managed to create.
After all of those trials and tribulations, heartbreak and awe, experiencing the ending was a form of real-world nirvana. I have never felt so awed, fulfilled, and humbled by a piece of entertainment. The Talos Principle goes beyond the genre, elevating itself to a place alongside some of the greatest philosophical works of all time. It's personal, epic, powerful, and nuanced all at the same time. In short, it's perfect.
Even if you don't enjoy puzzle games, I invite you to step inside the world of ELOHIM. The Prophet is waiting.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is one of the most satisfying single-player FPS's I've played in a while. "Single player" is a big keyword for this one because there is no muliplayer to speak of, which is almost unheard of for the genre. Yet, the decision seems to have ensured a game that grips from beginning to end of its campaign and feels thoroughly worked and impeccably designed. That's not to say it doesn't have issues, just that those issues are the result of a little too much care rather than too little.
Some have said this is a game where the story and presentation have taken precedence over the gameplay, and while I disagree with them it's obvious this game has almost Kojima-lite focus on narrative that's uncommon. For the most part, it's an incredibly solid narrative, especially for a shooter. Your protagonist Blazkowitz may be a cartoonishly square jawed military stereotype by design (big shades of Brad Pitt's Aldo Ray in Inglourious Basterds) but as the game goes on these cartoonish elements intermingle with a sincerely compelling and at times emotional story of human beings turned to military machines through an endless decades long war. Reconciling both of these elements can be a little problematic, but if the game tries to throw a little more meaning into the fact that you've blown away hundreds upon hundreds of soldiers than is quite earned, this is made up for by the fact that the game still can make you feel for its supporting cast. You've got an incredibly diverse group of folks that are all quirky and cool in their own ways, and some truly grotesque, awesome villains, and this makes the story elements work incredibly well.
This extends beyond the game's cinematics into gameplay, and this is where you see Wolfenstein's presentation really shine. Firstly, the production design's absolutely marvelous. On a technical level you've got some strong iconic designs with masterful shape language, which helps immensely when you have to see what mechanical monstrocities you're about to take on. Level designs are distinct and the layout has plenty of thought for different ways to approach combat situations. At times, especially early on, the game can seem excessively linear and CoD-esque with its cinematic moments, but when combat starts, and it goes on for a while, it's surprising how much thought can be put into shooting Nazis. Generally, I started stealthy, knifing and sniping all I could until the inevitable discovery, and then the game got gloriously chaotic, with lasers, rockets, dual-wielded lasers and assault rifles, and grenades flying all around. The return to health kits over recharged health is very welcome, as now you have to charge forward to actually win combat situations when you're in the red as cover affords no take backs from poor choices. The game also lets you overcharge health if you pick up extra med kits, which offers the level of thinking whether you want the boost or to save it for an emergency.
I also have to really praise the sound design in this game, as it's just awesome. Yes, every gun is satisfying and bass-y, the kickback really works in this game, but in addition you'll have some really effective story driven choices. Take moments of death where a split decision has to be made, and the foreboding music that kicks in, seeming to rise as the danger gets closer. Or take some really interesting underwater and outer space segments where sound is drowned out almost entirely from within your suit. Take the moments where a subdued acoustic track plays, then builds to a fully orchestrated version of that track as the really impressive stuff starts happening. It's all super smart and kicks the game's storytelling up a lot.
If I have one complaint that kind of puts a damper on all this wonderfulness, it's that the game spreads itself a bit thin. Engaging as the narrative often is, it can just as often be episodic and jarringly paced, as you find yourself jumping rather suddenly into levels without any clue how you got there because you blinked for a second during a cut-scene. There are also a big number of loose ends that I imagine are being saved for some theoretical sequel. I also loved things like the incredibly brief shootout on the surface on the moon, but these scenarios are so brief that I found myself wanting the gameplay idea to be pushed into further, more complex territory. Imagine the tactics of regular combat without sound and reduced gravity.
But that's nitpicking, if you've been starved for good first-person shooting this is your fix. There are no mediocre RPG elements dragging it down like Far Cry 3, and there's a shocking amount of soul to go with it. Plus its incredible visual and audio elements and it's a complete experience and the rare AAA title that gets it right.

Although the game is a good looking one, I still despise this game and i'm really surprised by the positive feedback by the community. A couple of reasons why I wouldn't recommend this game:
Too long and too many cut-scenes. MP3 is too much like Call of duty and the newer "shoot-and-kill endless number of enemies"-type of games. This includes too long cut scenes. I swear, at some moments, I felt like I was watching a movie instead of actually playing a game. A huge disadvantage comparing to the previous titles. My theory is that the developers just had to save time and money and to do that, they take as much control from you as possible.
The second reason can be connected to the above. Just like new shooters like CoD and Battlefield, there are just too many enemies that run up to you one at a time. For crying out loud, whats wrong with fewer, more challenging bad guys?
Plot-protected enemies. Yes, it's all over the place. There are just too many occasions where you end up thinking "Yes, I won! Give me the reward and lets move on to the next challange" just to see the bad guys making a dramatic escape, rendering the played sequence redundant. Fine, a couple of these getaways are fine, it adds to the suspense. But when these moments come stacked, you end up losing motivation, cause you know you'll never solve this problem until the very end. I prefer smaller challenges in greater number so you get that feeling of accomplishment when proceeding through a game.
Positives:
The game looks good and has a nice 3-weapon system.
To summarize:
This title is not a worthy sequel to the brilliant classics that is Max Payne and MP2. MP3 is just too "modern" and leaves a bad taste in your mouth.

On the surface, The Talos Principle is Portal-like puzzle game, and perhaps many people are satisfied enjoying the it this way. Alongside these "test chamber"-like areas with lasers, gates, hexahedrons (cubes), and enemies, though, is deep philosophy. It is expressed through direct debate on computer terminals throughout the game (that I found sincerely challenging) and in the entire nature of the experience.
Why am I, an android, running around what looks to be ancient Greece or Rome using high-end technology to collect Tetris pieces? Wait, did that tree just glitch? Who is this Elohim who speaks in a booming, godlike voice about my purpose? Audio diaries and fragments of text documents fill in what I found to be a very compelling world: one in which I honestly didn't know how to proceed when given choices.
This game is worth your attention. It has challenges and goals for different skill levels that can cater to a wide audience. Single puzzles or the more difficult stars feel fantastic when finally completed. Sneaky Easter eggs lie in wait, as well, for the observant and those willing to break the rules of these puzzles. I felt my suspicions and trail and error were often (but not always!) rewarded with the game saying, "We were expecting you," which is a nice feeling.
The challenge and fun of the puzzles with the sci-fi/philosophical questions The Talos Principle raises make this experience one I will remember. It's beautiful, well-designed, and very smart. Highly recommend.

Let's get this out of the way immediately; I wouldn't buy this game at full price. But then, it's regularly on sale, and it has come a long way in the last two years.
Now, I grew up playing the original Age of Empires: Rise of Rome, and Age of Empires II: The Conquerors games, so I knew exactly what to expect with AoE II: HD. The graphics are only slightly updated, but honestly that was barely an issue for me. The massively improved AI (one that doesn't just resign at random) is a major factor; they actually pose a threat now. Another big factor is the increased map size and population count combination; the original game always felt like you needed a lot more units, even with a 200 pop limit. The Forgotten Empires expansion adds quite a nice selection of new civilisations, some of which offer slightly different strategies. Also, AoE II has graphical issues on modern GPUs, so this is the best way of playing the classic game.
Now, for the negatives. For the greatest time, this game performed abysmally on the biggest map size and with high populations, which is absurd. They've largely fixed this... but it's still not great, and still relies way too much on a single core. And I have issues with ridiculously high pings when playing online with a friend (who lives in a foreign country, but we have no ping issues in games like Left 4 Dead 2), which have never really improved. The AI, on water maps, has a tendency to build so many boats that the game becomes nigh-on unwinnable (unless you can build a mass of castles near by and not get wiped out in the process). It has also proven to be tempermental when run in windowed mode, and units occasionally bug out and get totally stuck, meaning you have to kill them.
In conclusion; if you liked AoE II, you'll love this. Get it on sale, as it's a very fair price when 75%/80% off. But wait for a sale. If you didn't like AoE II for any reason other than you felt it was too easy... this probably won't change things for you.

Challenging puzzles that force you to think out of the box. Almost never frustrating, you learn very fast how to use the game mechanics. A ton of easter eggs.
Furthermore, the art and the music are stunning.
I had to look sometimes to solutions in the most advanced levels (for collecting hidden stars), but most of the puzzles are possible and do not require any technical skills.
Only real criticism: if you want to play a "philosophical" game, this one doesn't do the trick. If you have studied philosophy a bit (particularly ethics and analytical philosophy) you will certainly be disappointed.
It ressembles Braid in a certain way: the creators had an ambitious message but it is only given to us through texts. The technical limitations of video games make it impossible to build ones own mind, let alone discussing an idea or a concept. If your are looking for a game with a strong intellectual message, I suggest you look at today's independent table-top RPGs rather, naturally less limited in terms of interactions.

"First day off the sauce and somehow I'd still ended up in the gutter."
"I needed to find a way upstairs.  Surely no one would notice another hole in the wall."
"I started to wonder if my luck had finally run out when I realized it had, a long time ago.  It's why I was here."
-Max Payne
Good old self-deprecating Max is more quotable than ever before in
, the latest installment by
into one of my favorite series.  The above are just a tiny sample of the nonstop narration he delivers to flavor the single-player campaign experience.  In my opinion this alone would justify playing through the game, even if it didn't have solid mechanics, excellent visuals and fun features like Bullet Time.
My time played (almost 10 hours as of this writing) reflects campaign completion on the Hard setting, some dabbling in the arcade mode and a few rounds of the extensively fleshed out multiplayer modes.  Even a brief foray into multiplayer reveals that there's plenty of progression to be had for those willing to pour hours into it.  Like any brilliant solo campaign, this one is an absolute thrill ride but feels tragically brief once finished.
The story is not what I'd call ambitious but for the most part holds up well: Max is a classic and highly satisfying tale of tragedy with dark comedy mixed in.  He's simply one of the most likeable antiheroes I've come across in gaming.  The choice of setting provides an interesting, colorful departure from the grit and grime of the noir style that characterized the previous games (but don't worry, there's some of that here, too).  Fans of the IP will recognize a few throwbacks to those predecessors.
Gameplay is functional and engaging.  Level design is mostly good, but here and there feels uninspired/recycled, which makes me wonder about the quality of all those DLC map packs I didn't buy.  Bullet time is tons of fun, rewarding twitch aim & fast reflexes.  On Hard difficulty there were only a few encounters I had to replay, and the frustration was minor so I'd recommend that setting.  Multiplayer--despite the variety of play modes, maps, weapons and avatar customizations--did not capture my interest, nor did I find the progression or social systems appealing.  I'm sure it comes down to personal preference, so I recommend you at least try it out, but for me personally there are better options when it comes to online shooters.  The arcade modes and time trials were also only of marginal interest to me so I won't discuss them here.  The strength of Max Payne 3 for players like me lies in the campaign.
The game appears bug free and has only minor issues.  During my hours played it only crashed once.  It ran smoothly with settings maxed--granted, the game is two and a half years old at the time of this review, but the visuals hold up well enough to triple A standards unless you're talking about top of the line resolutions.  I found it odd that weapons with a laser sight attachment were less accurate/useful than the standard ones due to the loss of crosshairs on screen in aim mode.  Also a bother was how the triggered Bullet Time would force me into my 1-handed weapon; threw me off a bit if I was using 2-handed and suddenly encountered an event.  On rare occasion activating Bullet Time will send you jumping over the edge of something like a building or dock, which is instant-death bad news, so be careful to avoid that very annoying problem.  The last and worst offender I have to mention is Rockstar's Social Club which in my opinion is an unwelcome and failed DRM-like hoop to jump through.  If when you first launch the game you can't sign into your account, go to their website and change your password then restart the game and it should log you in and let you register/activate the game just fine.
I had a great time with this one and honestly would recommend it to any gamer who enjoys the action shooter, which Rockstar does extremely well.
TIP: Use your Bullet Time wisely, as it will make fights much more manageable and sometimes save your bacon.  Timing and position are important.
TIP: Keep your gun reloaded to avoid having an emptied clip while downed.  Downed w/no bullets = dead.

So I guess I'd become what they wanted me to be, a killer. Some rent-a-clown with a gun who puts holes in other bad guys. Well that's what they had paid for, so in the end that's what they got. Say what you want about Americans but we understand capitalism. You buy yourself a product and you get what you pay for.
Nine years after Max Payne 2, Max finds himself drinking away his sorrow after he got fired from the NYPD, for consorting with the criminal Mona Sax. He has developed a drinking problem and his addiction to painkillers has gotten worse. He has moved back to where he lived with his wife and daughter: Hoboken, New Jersey. Max gets into a confrontation with the son of the local mob boss Anthony Demarco. And an old friend who claims to have been on the police academy with Max, Raul Passos,  finds him at the bar, hoping to recruit him for a private security job in South-America. Max resists, but after he kills the son of Anthony Demarco, he has no choice but to flee from his home.
Of all the three Max Payne games, Max Payne 3 has arguably the best gameplay of them all. The controls are very solid, and the gameplay can be very addictive. The good old bullet-time is back, and works mostly the same as it always has. Instead of being able to carry your whole arsenal with you, like in Max Payne 1 and 2, You can carry up to three weapons. Two small ones, and one big one. If you want to duel-wield your small weapons, you have to drop your big weapon. This is actually very fun in my opinion, this way you have to use every gun at least once. Max Payne 3 has fourteen chapters instead of three parts with each seven to nine chapters. Max Payne 3 is also way more linear than its predecessors. This seems like it has less content, but Max Payne 3 is the longest of the bunch, which will take the average gamer around thirteen hours to complete.
Next to the story mode, Max Payne 3 has a surprisingly fun multiplayer mode. You can create your own character to use in various different modes. Or if you bought the DLC, you can play fan favorites in the free for all deathmatch mode, like Vladimir Lem, Valerie Winterson, Vinnie Gognitti, Mona Sax and more. The game also has a multiplayer survival mode, called Dead Men Walking. In this co-op mode, you play as Max or Raul Passos, and must fend of waves of enemies, which can be very addictive and fun.
Max Payne 3 is a different kind of game than its predecessors. The gameplay is way more solid, and the change of setting may anger a lot of fans. But this change is very welcome in my opinion and works really well. The story has as in every Max Payne game a few twists and turns, which are still very well done. Many fans say that Max Payne 3 has gone away from its roots too much, but it's still a game about Max Payne, and it's still a very good game with a very interesting and dark story.

Short version: Epic af and grindy af
Long version:
Pros:
1. You wanna be a fighter pilot? Be one and buy better upgrades in-game the better you get.
2. You wanna be a tanker? Be one and buy better upgrades in-game the better you get.
3. You wanna push the frontline along with other grunts? Be one and buy better upgrades in-game the better you get.
4. You wanna pilot a gunship and shoot everything? Be one and buy better upgrades in-game the better you get.
5. You wanna build a base with your buddies and make it your own personal outpost? Make one and buy better upgrades in-game the better you get.
6. You wanna feel extatic and epic? Solo capture facilities not at all-out war while taking care of reinforcements.
7. You wanna feel more extatic and epic? Go to the frontline where the main fight is. join the tens or hundreds of infantrymen and try making a difference.
Cons:
1. You wanna command a submarine or a huge warship? Yeah well you can't.
2. You wanna get high-end gear in a day? Yeah well you can't.
3. You wanna run it on an old laptop at 60fps? Yeah well you can't.
Summary:
The game is epic and there are moments where you will ragequit because everyone has a better framerate and performance than you, but there are also moments when you stand on a hill and look at the 100 infantrymen running and gunning across a desert or some other flatland while fighters fly above and often get shot down taking a few infantrymen with them when they hit the ground. The game is also very grindy. You need to get good in order to get more certification points so that you can get even better. It's a never-ending cycle. On the other hand the game is also extremely rewarding. Your first NS-44 Commissioner bought for 1000 certification points (without involving real money) makes you wanna brag considering the fact you wasted about 2-3k cert points earlier for upgrades you thought were needed. Lastly, Planetside 2 WILL crash and it WILL have poor performance unless you have a top-notch rig or settings down low.

If this game was skynet's new approach to taking over the world by convincing you that the machines are human and that you are a machine then it would work and I would gladly surrender to my new human overlords. This game is possibly the best example of games as an art medium. It is exceptionally philosophical. It doesn't merely ask you what it means to be a person; it forces you to think about it. And it does so beautifully. The graphics and over all presentation of the game is stunning, the graphics are not only well optimized (so it will run perfectly on a 290x or a 7850) but are gorgeous (not just on a 290x does it look good, it still looks exceptionally good on a 7850) the amount of detail put into the environment is astounding. And the philosophical arguments made by the game are not merely made towards you, but by you. You have to take a position, you are not thrown into having to make a choice immediately but you have to decide what you believe at some point. The puzzles while obviously comparable to portal are unique, while some of the ideas are shared; the challenge is less in understanding how gameplay mechanics work but in how to apply them. While the puzzles in portal are admittedly more exciting on average the puzzles in The Talos Principle require more thought and also come in greater quantity. Fortunately the puzzles can be left if they become tiresome so you can go and work on another, but there puzzles of different types that are abundant as well, block puzzles, computer hacking, and the biggest known to man: the meaning of life and what it means to be alive. If you know this company from Serious Sam games and are wondering how a game like that (while fun is no philosophical master piece of puzzles) then I would see why it is surprising (Serious Sam is fun but only has the developer and a few game assets in common with this, and almost nothing else.)  They didn’t merely try their hand at making puzzles, they demonstrated expertise at it. Only a few company’s come to mind that have made games so different but so good. Croteam, I think it is safe to say that you have succeeded in making something completely unique and incredible. Thank you…
In other words it’s a pretty good game you should try.

Right now, Robocraft is very addictive, dispite the few flaws it has. The Devs seem to have ironed out alot of the issues that the older robocraft once had, however if you are a fan of the older version, you may not enjoy this game. Robocraft, as of today is a completely different animal than the older versions. The learning curve is far less now than before thanks to the tutorial mode. Building bots is still fun, and the community robot factory has many robots to choose from if you have enough in game cash called Robits. There are newer maps, several modes to play, and a loot crate system that provides you with random items. The clans mode is now functional including a bonus season exp system that offers more robits if you join or make a clan. Recently, our cpu caps have been increased beyond 1750cpu, and new modules help with the battle.  Choose from these modules : EMP burst to stun your enemy, DSM to shield from enemy fire, BLM to blink (warp) away from danger, GHM to Go invisible for a short time, and WEM newly renamed Weapon Energy Module to Pull more power from your parts for emergency weapon power.
As with many games, there are some cons and bugs that still need to be ironed out, but the game is still being developed, and you should know better to not complain too much, as nothing is set into stone.
Things to remember, have a gigabit connection,fast computer, updated graphics card, and a nice antivirus suite that you can control,on your end. This will ensure most of the problems you have are on thier end,not yours. Even then this is not going to be 100% possible that problems will leave you alone. Robocraft servers are constanly updating, going down, maintence, and the occasional ddos attacks and other technical problems may happen.

There's one rule you need to learn before playing PlanetSide 2 - you are absolutely expendable. Your KD does not matter. You are just fodder in a grand conflict of hundreds of people being thrown at each other to die in a glorious(or less than glorious) fashion.
And that is why this game is so freaking refreshing in FPS market covered with K/D ratio focused shooters that are so obsessed with telling you how great and important you are. Its specifically BECAUSE you do not matter that everything you do can matter - you do not need  to "score kills" to be useful and help your side. Teamwork is rewarded. Objective play is priority. You might not shoot someone in the head but you might heal, you might repair, you might build or you might serve as something as simple as a body-shield for your friend who is doing something far more important.
So if you are tired of shooters like Call of Duty or Battlefield and want to  take part in a glorious giant battles that last for hours, then grab some friends and join in.
You might not score "the kills" in your first time playing, but sure as hell  you will have a chance to find yourself in the middle of something mind-blowingly grand.
Planetside 2 does what CODont.

The Talos Principle is an interesting and intelligently designed puzzle game that also seeks to explore themes of philosophy, Humanity and religion. You awaken in a garden, and a disembodied voice gives you the task of solving a series of puzzles.
I don't want to say too much more about the story, because it would spoil the sense of mystery. As the game begins, you don't really know who or what your character is, where you are, or what has happened to the world. The answers have to be pieced together from clues found in computer terminals or by exploring the environment, but there is a feeling that things may not be what they appear on the surface.
The goal of each puzzle is to collect a "sigil" (like a Tetris block) which is hidden within an obstacle course. There are various hazards blocking your path, such as forcefields, explosives and motion activated machine gun turrets, and you need to use other objects to deactivate or bypass them. Use cubes to weigh down pressure plates, or connectors to redirect laser beams to activate switches. Powerful fans can send objects (or yourself) flying through the air, and some mind bending puzzles even allow you to co-operate with your own clone.
I personally found the difficulty to be spot on. It challenged me, but I always felt like I was making progress. It helps that the world is designed in such a way that several puzzles are available at a time, so if you do get stuck somewhere, you can move on to attempt a different puzzle, and come back later. The sigils are colour coded based on difficulty. Greens and yellows are relatively straight forward and are used to teach the player new concepts, while the reds are much more advanced, so they had me scratching my beard for a while until I finally got that "oh, of course!" moment.
There are also a number of "stars" to collect, and this is where the game went beyond my puzzle solving ability. These are what you might consider to be the "secrets". Many of them are easy to find, but add an extra layer of complexity to an already completed sigil puzzle. Other stars are hidden in places that are difficult to even see, and have really crazy solutions. These are the hardest puzzles, so solving each one feels amazing, but I've only managed to collect about half of them so far. I've got a strong suspicion that the story has multiple endings, one for collecting all the sigils, and another that is unlocked by collecting all the stars, as a reward for completionists.
The graphics are fantastic, with detailed ancient architecture and lots of colour, from the sandy pyramids of Egyptian themed levels to western styled cathedrals surrounded by trees. The graphics menu is the most detailed that I've ever seen, with dozens of settings to tweak. I'm getting a constant 60 FPS having turned off motion blur and shadows AA with everything else enabled/high. I haven't encountered any bugs or crashes.
I definitely enjoyed playing The Talos Principle. The closest reference point I can think of is the Portal series. I think there are similarities with the first person perspective, and some of the puzzle concepts, which test the same logical part of the brain, so I think anyone who likes Portal should consider picking up The Talos Principle.

Played for 4.5 hours the previous days, and I can easily say that this is the most tactic game. It's like Arma, but not as huge maps or large teams, but until now there's no vehicles in the game, but it's confirmed that it's coming soon.
For the first time ever, unlike Battlefield 4, the squads of 9 keeps together through the whole round. When the round starts, the group leader sets a alley point we have to move up to, and settle down and build a base. The base building is really amazing. You can also build ammo crates and spawnpoints.
The map variatation is good, with a lot of different terrains.
It doesn't requires a lot of skill to play, but rather teamplay and tactic (taking cover, supressing fire, etc.)
Here's my story of my first 30 minutes:
My squad leader sets an alley point, and tells us to regroup a couple of meters outside of the main base.
The whole Alpha team of 9 follow that order, and we move in position ~400 meters. We can see a small village, and we decides to settle down there, and waits for ~5 minutes to see if the Russians follows the south road, which is being held my Bravo team, or the North road, where we waits. Two of us decides to leave our settlement, and walks of top of a hill to scout for them. We can see the russians holding their ground between their main base, and the Bravo team. We reports that to the rest of the Alpha team, and we follow the north road to flank them. When we spotted the first russian, we waited for everyone to get in position, so everyone  could get a clear shot. After 10 to 15 seconds, everyone is in line and we engages the enemy. We took a couple of them, and they backed of. Then the Bravo team comes to ambush them. They went stright into crossifire, and we took their base.
The game needs a bit of polishing, and bug fixes, but not really a big deal. If you're into tactic shooter, then don't hesitate buying this.

First off, you better have a good internet connection, or get this on disc.  Because this game is huge.  Apparently the devs do not know what compression is.
That is my only gripe about
.
The rest of it, dare I say, is fun.  Really fun.  It is a solid FPS and is very welcome in the age of bland FPS games that are poorly written and rip off other artists' graphical styles.  The weapons handle well, kills are satisfying, and you have a
, which hearkens back to the old retro FPS games like, well, Wolfenstein.  While some of the things like the slide mechanic and the cover system took some getting used to, they work.  Even though I mainly used the cover system to farm kills for the weapon upgrades you get from killing enemies from cover.
The stealth mechanic works too, nowhere near as good as something like
, but I like to think that the Nazi AI is intentionally stupid to show how complacent they have become after their victory.  Which leads me to another point.
The Worldbuilding.
It's great.  You can tell that there has been some serious effort put into the worldbuilding of this game.  From the diary entries of one of the main character's cousins after the victory, to just looking around and seeing how different this world looks, it is all very well done.  In the fascist-industrialist way, the Nazis have built and rebuilt massive cities over oceans of concrete.  Propaganda speakers spout information about the greatness of National Socalism along with the weather report.  The military has a retro futuristic look along the lines of
.  Giant robots with lasers, troops in power armor, laser weapons.  It's all ♥♥♥♥in' great.  Hell, even
songs are in German.
This is a solid game with solid worldbuilding and fantastic gameplay.  Definitely get it if it's on sale.

A couple of weeks have passed since I finished the Talos principle, so now I can make a sober estimate of it :-) And I must say I still love this game! It’s great, intriguing and intelligent. It gives you hours of excellent puzzles, pleasing views and two characters to talk to.
Speaking about puzzles… they are interesting, not “carbon-copied”. Sometimes confusing but not pushing you to look for walk-through (except for the stars, they do :-D). Some of them require a kind of twist of mind (yes, I’m talking about the cloning-machine) but there are no puzzles you can stuck forever in. If you did, just go and sleep on the problem, you will easily solve it next morning :-).
However the game doesn't make you only solve puzzles, it also raises some philosophical issues. Talking to the Serpent “ex machina” is always confusing. He is a sophister and even a troll from a certain point of view. What makes you human? Will you live forever if all of your thoughts are put in a machine? How can you say that some people are better than the other? And remember there are no correct answers, the smart-аss computer will always find a defect in your reasoning.
What I meant to say I didn’t enjoy a puzzle game so much since Portal (the mother of all first-person-puzzles, in my opinion). And however Talos resembles Portal sometimes, I can’t even say it makes Talos worse. Sure it is more like casual games, where if you stuck somewhere, you may simply step back to solve other rooms and come back later. The game’s plot is not narrative, you don’t have even talk to the “Serpent” to pass the game, just listen to Elohim and do what he says (stay away from the Tower especially ;-)). From this point of view Portal looks better, its plot is more integral and Portal has inimitable humor as well. But Talos offers a few different endings, a bit of nonlinearity and a possibility to interact with other characters.
Don’t want to choose, love them both!

I know that the $39.99 price seems high for an early access shooter, but if you're looking for an excellent realistic shooter that doesn't run like garbage (on at least most systems it seems) look no further.  This game has the perfect balance of battlefield and ArmA that I've ever seen.
*Communication - The VoIP is excellent and you can really tell where your teammates (or enemies) are and their direction/distance.  It's easy to distinguish between squad and area chat, and they are both crucial to success.
*Gameplay - Excellent.  Being in a squad that communicates both within themselves and making sure that the squad leader is working with the other squads creates a sort of dance to the battle that you can literally watch from the map as a grunt. The guns feel incredibly realistic, forcing you to carefully take shots, and make sure you watch for movement.  There are very few icons or ways to help you spot enemies or differentiate from allies.  You will often find yourself waiting for your squad leader to let a nearby squad know which direction you are coming from to avoid friendly fire.  Incredibly immersive.
*Audio -  I love the variation of sound in this game.  One minute you'll hear birds chirping and the constant chatter of your squadmates about who knows what, and then suddenly an RPG goes lands near your squad/force.  The cries for medics fill the air, bullets whiz and snap past you, and all of your teammates return fire and it is absolutely deafening.  It becomes difficult to hear individual voices as everyone yells out where they see contacts and the cries from hit soldiers.
*Visuals - Definitely need some work, but Unreal Engine 4 definitely holds up with the early alpha animations.  The main issues I have with the game in this regard are the character models during the prone phase and overall character animation.  Static models that don't have very fluid motions.  Textures look great, performance is excellent considering optimization tweaks are still needed, and most 1st person animations are very well done.
*Overall - I love this game.  It is exactly what I've envisioned for a squad based reality shooter since I first loaded up the battlefield 2 demo when I was just a kid.  I love being able to hear the voice chat of enemies nearby after we just started assaulting them.  I love knowing that my squad leaders have to be working together to accomplish anything.  I love that I cant just unload in an area and expect to kill anything unless i'm very close. Give this one a shot.  If you still don't like it within two hours you can always ask for a refund.

This is a very fun game with some unfortunate drawbacks.
The plot here is surprisingly good
This is not The Last of Us or Grim Fandango. Your purpose is to shoot things, lots of them, with your guns. Lots of guns. The rest of the plot is just emotional filler: There's a point where you have to choose
There are also some cliché love interests and personal relationships, like the George/Lenny relationship from Steinbeck's Of Mice and Men mirorred in Karl and Max. That is a good way to describe the entire plot, really: it's not original, but it's deeper than you expected and draws you in a little. Still, there are major flaws: Blaskovich is,
, a completely emotionless robot-soldier. He has monologues about seeing things and feeling things but none of them are believable.
It's one of those games where other characters are constantly saying "You go take care of this thing! You're such a hero soldier!" as if that explains how Blasko is able to survive so much punishment and emotional abuse without so much as blinking. There's absolutely no character development, and at the emotional climax of the game, when
There are no 'questionable' choices. Blasko is basically a fleshy gun holster, and there's enough character provided to prove that he's a
fleshy gun holster, and nothing beyond that.
There are also some other problems I had with more minor specifics of the plot:
There's also a point where a character is holed up in a room shooting nazis. She opens the door, shoot more nazis, and then takes cover behind the wall, when the last nazi finally decides he's had it and just shoots her through the wall. He could have done it earlier, of course, but then where would we get our heroic sacrifice and dramatic tension?
In the end, the story is generally done very well, and much better than you would expect from a first-person-shooter title like this. However, it falls prey to a lot of the same clichés and inconsistencies that you see in B-action movies, and it ends up being harder to take as seriously as you feel like the developers wanted you to.
This is a place where the game really pulls out all the stops. First, I really hope you like film grain. You better love film grain or this game is most definitely not for you. Otherwise everything is perfect. The design of the mechanical monsters seems strangely period-appropriate and the environments look really pretty. Takedowns and stealth kills are flawless and seamlessly integrated into the combat. The menus are beautiful, the weapon-select wheel could be a little streamlined but otherwise looks really good as well. I really enjoyed the art direction for this game, and even if I hadn't, I'd still admit that it is as appropriate for the setting as it could be.
What behooves me most to mention is the cinematography. You're going to see some really amazingly cool cut scenes with beautiful graphics, amazing direction, and breathtaking cinematography. If this were a movie, I'd pay for the 3d version. It's so. Good. You can check out my screenshots for some highlights, although I haven't tagged them all for spoilers yet. (be warned!) I have to take off a point for the suffocating amount of film grain (turn off post-processing? But people WORKED on that!) but otherwise it's a perfect score.
This is a great game with great gameplay that is marred in a couple ugly places. The guns are responsive and fun to use, stealthing is fun and not too hard to do, and exploring can be fun. Everyone will talk about dual-wielding in this game and that's because it's worth mentioning - other than being the only part of the game that really breaks new ground in the shooter arena, it's also a hell of a lot of fun and as streamlined to control as could be. Which leads me into my two major complaints:
-the game is pretty generic. Dual-wielding will be the only thing you haven't seen before. With these guns, anyway.
-some enemies are too hard. It doesn't matter how much you can dual-wield if you get shot to pieces within seconds anyway.
Finally, an honorable mention for the final boss:
Also there are perks. I forgot about them, which should tell you how important they are to the gameplay. The answer is not very, and they're not implemented very well.
There are a lot of things I like about this game but after 10 hours I had to force myself to enjoy them. The combat gets repetetive quickly, the story is just an amalgam of tropes, and the graphics are good but not top-tier for the time period. I was engrossed for 10 hours and then couldn't be bothered to touch it again until I forced myself to finish the story in the remaining five. It's objectively a good game, but some parts of it could definitely just be more fun. I'd recommend this, but not for full price (depending, obviously, on how much cash you have to spend) - $20 or $30 is an ideal price for this game.

Its not often that i call a game a masterpeice, but Max Payne 3 is deserving of the title. Many have claimed the new Max to be a whiny and unfaithful to the orgininal series, but the pure striking visuals mixed with an intense soundtrack and gritty atmosphere asorbs you into the game as you play. The dialougue is some of the best, and the cutscenes have a special vibe to them, a stylized approach that soaks into gameplay and sticks with you long after you finish the game. Even though the plot has some holes, the game is still well worth the money. The final few shootouts, including the one in the Airport lobby tied a game up as best as you possible could, and Max's character progresses in a subtle yet substantial fashion. The ending might be cliched to some, but to me it was the perfect ending to an brilliant series. Part of me wants a Max Payne 4 even though they would have to pull something out of their♥♥♥♥♥to make it, but most of me wants the series to die in peace with this final hurrah of a game. I would go as far to say one of the best games i've played in the last 10 years.

While not the best, it's still pretty damn good, even the low settings looked pretty nice. I had to lower the graphical settings a little due to minor frame rate issues (dropped to about 20-ish) but possibly that was due to it being on High. After that, game worked like a charm.
Sometimes you're going to be frustrated at Blasko because he just won't vault over a ledge or a knee-high fence. Stealth and combat mechanics are pretty solid, although it's pretty hilarious when you throw a knife into someone's knee and you see them keel over dead. You can choose to approach a room using stealth or guns blazing. However, there will be times where it is pretty much compulsory to go guns blazing.
This game utilises a perk system, whereby you have to complete optional "objectives" such as kill 20 Nazis with a silenced handgun, or have 30 headshot kills, etc. You have to option to Dual-wield pretty much everything, which is exceptionally fun if you run around just gunning people down. However, it does not fully support the act of Sniping. So if you get this game fully intending to sit in a corner and snipe everything, don't expect much from the sniper rifle as it only comes with 2x zoom and unsilenced.
Boss battles are absolutely epic,
although the final boss battle seems to be pretty anti-climatic.
To be honest, I don't really remember much of the story. All I remember was:
1. Kill all the Nazis.
2. Rescue Anya (in this case, the damsel in distress).
3. There's a main villian called "Deathshead", but I can guarantee you that you will forget about him throughout the game and remember a crazy female German with her equally psycho lover.
The plot definitely succeeded in making me get goosebumps a few times, and the main characters are pretty well-built in terms of personality.
While it is not good, it is not bad either. The ending seemed a bit rushed and just didn't live up to the magnificence of the rest of the game (especially after the mini-boss fight before that which made me horribly sad and depressed, I would not spoil too much).
The soundtrack and music for this game is one of the best I have ever heard. There will be a few moments in the game whereby the music will induce a feeling of sadness or rage depending on the situation. Personally, the soundtracks in here are one of my favourites.
While this game isn't the best I have played, it is definitely in the top few. Definitely recommended to get it.

Planetside 2 is a free game, and a good one at that. Set in a sci-fi era on the planet of Auraxis, air, land and infantry battles rage on in the same battlefield! All of those different elements in combat affect each other, fighters supplying air support while tanks with transport vehicles roll out to divide and conquer. Three factions fight for control of Auraxis, who are the Terran Republic, New Conglomerate, and Vanu Soverignty.
The Terran Republic (a.k.a. TR) is the conservative republic that seeks unity with fast firing ballistic weapons coupled with high capacity magazines. They were the founding faction before the Vanu and New Conglomerate broke off.
The New Conglomerate (a.k.a. NC) is a faction of freedom fighters who believe that a miserable man is better off than a contented slave. Their arsenal includes coilgun and rail weaponry, which are slower firing and sport higher recoil but pack a large punch.
The Vanu Soveriegnty (a.k.a. VS) is a group of alien worshippers that utilize ancient Vanu alien technology in their armor and weapons. Their main maxims center around technology equals might. While their weapons may not hit as hard as the NC or fire as fast as the TR, their reload speed is pretty quick.
Team-work and joining a squad or platoon is important! Only with those elements can this game be actually enjoyable.

Dirty Bomb is a game that is the result of a rampant orgy between Call of Duty, Overwatch, Counter-Strike, and Team Fortress 2. That said, Dirty Bomb takes the best elements of each game and molds it all into a skill based, fast, frantic, frenetic shooter where aim regularly decides engagements, all characters are useful in both competitive and casual, and you will never feel like you died because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ balance. Medics can actually survive 1 on 1 encounters rather reliably, Engineers are relevant to both DPS and Objectives, the Assault Mercs never feel too slow where they might feel irrelevant (compare Rhino to Heavy or any of the tanks in Overwatch), Recon Mercs are creatively designed and just as deadly up close as they are at range, and the Fire Support Mercs make for great support and DPS without sacrificing viability in other areas. Dirty Bomb succeeds where other shooters fall short. It's got a more active and responsive developers than TF2, it's faster paced and more rewarding than Overwatch, the gameplay is fast paced and frenetic like Call of Duty, and its competitive scene is flexible and more intuitive than Counter Strikes. If you have a shooter itch that the above mentioned games have failed to scratch, Dirty Bomb is just what the doctor ordered.

Planetside 2 is a free game, and a good one at that. Set in a sci-fi era on the planet of Auraxis, air, land and infantry battles rage on in the same battlefield! All of those different elements in combat affect each other, fighters supplying air support while tanks with transport vehicles roll out to divide and conquer. Three factions fight for control of Auraxis, who are the Terran Republic, New Conglomerate, and Vanu Soverignty.
The Terran Republic (a.k.a. TR) is the conservative republic that seeks unity with fast firing ballistic weapons coupled with high capacity magazines. They were the founding faction before the Vanu and New Conglomerate broke off.
The New Conglomerate (a.k.a. NC) is a faction of freedom fighters who believe that a miserable man is better off than a contented slave. Their arsenal includes coilgun and rail weaponry, which are slower firing and sport higher recoil but pack a large punch.
The Vanu Soveriegnty (a.k.a. VS) is a group of alien worshippers that utilize ancient Vanu alien technology in their armor and weapons. Their main maxims center around technology equals might. While their weapons may not hit as hard as the NC or fire as fast as the TR, their reload speed is pretty quick.
Team-work and joining a squad or platoon is important! Only with those elements can this game be actually enjoyable.
Imagine yourself following a squad of fellow soldiers, checking corners and eventually reaching the Control Terminal of a hostile facility. The engineer quickly places down his anti-infantry turret while the Heavy Assault takes out his light machinegun and sets up behind a crate as the terminal's control turns over to your side. A few minutes later and the base will be yours! The infiltrator cloaks and disappears behind the corner, scouting for potential threats. An allied Galaxy dropship supplies more men to help your point defense and a Sunderer is hastily deployed to provide your force with a spawn point for reinforcements.
With organization, Planetside 2 can be a really good game. Although the new player learning curve may be steep, player-made guides on Steam and videos on Youtube can assist with knowledge of what to do.
See you on the Planetside!

"The Talos Principle" is a first-person puzzle game. If puzzle games do not remotely interest you, then this would be the point of time where you would stop reading the review. If you've read this far, I'm honestly rather impressed. As long as you are still reading, allow me to delve a little deeper into this game.
The Talos Principle heavily deviates from the formula which Croteam had initially established with their Serious Sam franchise (High-Action First Person Shooters). This game is said to have been founded in the midst of the development of Serious Sam 4, and I consider it a huge blessing that this game saw full development and a final release.
There are no firearms, rocket launchers, or portable cannons for you to collect. Instead, you solve complex puzzles, and are rewarded with sigils (little tetris-shaped pieces used to progress further with the game). There is no absolute linearity. Instead, you have access to many different puzzles and worlds at a time (Although, you will require certain objects for later puzzles by collecting sigils). There are no one-liners spoken by a war-torn Serious Sam. You, the player, aren't even human! It is your task to delve into the world presented before you by a Benevolent God named "ELOHIM", and question the meanings of the Serpent haunting Computer Terminals planted all over the land.
These puzzles can test your patience. If you have a low-tolerance for periods of problem-solving, seriously, stop here. Some of them had a tendency to stump me for a fair amount of time. I must admit, however, that it felt exhilarating to finally uncover those solutions via trial and error. There's something rather satisfying about collecting spinning, Tetris pieces. To me, at least.
The game's plot itself focuses on deep, philosophical points. What does it mean to exist? What defines a person? Can frogs be people, too? What is the point of my existence in this world of puzzles? That said, if the story and philosophy does not remotely interest you in the slightest, it's completely optional. You are free to roam the lands of ancient ruins/architecture, solving two different kinds puzzles (sigil collecting, and fitting these sigils onto square/rectangular shaped boards), locating secret collectables and easter eggs (Croteam has included many of these, so be as curious as humanly possible), all with the option of a story. But a little reading/listening really wouldn't harm you, so I recommend you pay attention and learn more about the wolrd around you. This is the kind of game that requires plenty of attention.
The music is once again taken by the reigns of Damjan Mravunac. Deviating from the percussion beats from Serious Sam, The Talos Principle's soundtrack removes all forms of percussion, and immerses you with the game, courtesy of its relaxing, sometimes heavenly tunes. One of the most beautiful, soothing soundtracks I've heard in a long time.
If there are problems which I must address, it would only consist of the elusiveness of certain secret collectables or secrets. If you do own a device which can scan QR codes, don't be surprised if you find yourself doing some research on the one code which the game won't bother translating for you. Fret not, almost all of them are automatically translated once you scroll your mouse over their imprints. Hexadecimal numbers have also invaded some of the scriptures which you find in the computer terminals mentioned earlier. It's not entirely necessary to translate them, but if you enjoy deciphering those, it should be a whole new treasure hunt for you (if you've garnered an interest in the story to begin with).
In conclusion, this game is an absolute masterpiece. In order to understand how beautiful it can be (both visually and philosophically), you must play it. It is certainly worth the investment. As bold a statement as this may be, this game is a prime example of how video-games can transcend to their own form of art. There was a lot of love put into developing this game, and Croteam delivers it perfectly.
Oh yes, and there's DLC that you can purchase which replaces ELOHIM's voice with Serious Sam, sporting brand new dialogue from John J. D himself. 10/10.

Dirty Bomb is a game that is the result of a rampant orgy between Call of Duty, Overwatch, Counter-Strike, and Team Fortress 2. That said, Dirty Bomb takes the best elements of each game and molds it all into a skill based, fast, frantic, frenetic shooter where aim regularly decides engagements, all characters are useful in both competitive and casual, and you will never feel like you died because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ balance. Medics can actually survive 1 on 1 encounters rather reliably, Engineers are relevant to both DPS and Objectives, the Assault Mercs never feel too slow where they might feel irrelevant (compare Rhino to Heavy or any of the tanks in Overwatch), Recon Mercs are creatively designed and just as deadly up close as they are at range, and the Fire Support Mercs make for great support and DPS without sacrificing viability in other areas. Dirty Bomb succeeds where other shooters fall short. It's got a more active and responsive developers than TF2, it's faster paced and more rewarding than Overwatch, the gameplay is fast paced and frenetic like Call of Duty, and its competitive scene is flexible and more intuitive than Counter Strikes. If you have a shooter itch that the above mentioned games have failed to scratch, Dirty Bomb is just what the doctor ordered.

Bad,

To conclude, I recommend this, but also recommend extreme moderation with regard the story. It's self-paced, but if you blow through at the pace you want to, you'll find yourself facing a 5-6 hour wall of average-quality puzzler with no story in sight, just to get that ending unlocked.
Still.

I went back and forth on this game a few times.
Pros: It's a refreshing puzzler, with some very good mechanics, some puzzles that are too easy, and some that are trickier, but in a good way. Only once was I stuck in a puzzle so hard that I ended up looking to hints, and honestly, it was more a matter of not thinking of certain mechanics than it was a failing for the game. For that matter, though, I definitely had to do plenty of thinking. In addition, I considered trying to 'action' my way through a couple puzzles and learned really fast that this is a puzzler above all else, and if you try to skip a section by doing it by acting instead of thinking, you will fail.
Conversations. The conversations are actually quite enjoyable, to the point where they were more fun to me than the puzzles at times. It does suffer a bit of Mass Effect style assumptions with your dialog choices, but in the end it comes together in a way that I appreciated, and I didn't feel terribly shoehorned the way I do with a lot of other games.
Con: The stars. The bloody stars. Yes, they're only needed for the third ending, the secret one, but... ugh. Some of the mechanics and manipulations you need to do in order to discover them are asinine. There are at least three times where you need to discover literally invisible devices in order to get one, another one or two where you need to defy gameplay convention, and at LEAST five times where you need to actually remove elements from a puzzle to accomplish it, which makes the puzzle unsolvable if you haven't done it already.
In addition, one mechanic in particular is never demonstrated, and is required for stars, and later for puzzles. I'm speaking particularly of your ability to place crates on top of the floating enemies and ride on them. There is NEVER an indication that you can do this until you manage to get to an elevated position with a crate in your hands, and wait for an enemy to get close enough, a situation that pretty much would never appear unless you were deliberately trying for it. This could've been avoided by simply having one crate on one enemy's head sometime in the game, teaching you the mechanic through simple observation.
All in all, I don't regret my purchase of the game. Had lots of fun with it, got all the endings with a bit of guide help, and enjoyed it. Voice acting is excellent, the gameplay is good, the puzzles are mostly good [grr stars], the music is top-notch, and the storyline is both thought-provoking and loaded with plenty of 'feels' moments. There is a plot thread or two I felt was unresolved, but the ending [#2 being the real one] was still satisfying.

I’ve been pleasantly surprised by games before, but never have I been so biased against a game prior to its release then subsequently impressed by every aspect of it upon playing. “From the developers of Serious Sam, one of my least favorite franchises. I bet I will really enjoy this,” I sarcastically said to myself when the pre-order page went up. I did enjoy it. It is wonderful. It is easily one of the best games I’ve played.
The Talos Principle is one giant existential question that can be answered through solving over one hundred smaller, physics-based puzzles under the guidance of your maker, Elohim, whose intimidating voice attempts to influence you from above at every turn. This might seem a strange way to label the game’s genre, but it’s accurate and the story manages to never feel at all pretentious despite addressing philosophical subject matter. While the majority of your time is spent solving the smaller puzzles, it always feels as if you’re doing it for a higher purpose or to unravel the larger mystery looming overhead, so the game successfully maintains a careful balance where both the story and puzzles are one and equally important.
This journey takes you through several temple-like environments, each containing a number of doorways leading to distinct worlds. In each of these worlds, you’ll find several self-contained puzzle areas that can also occasionally interact with each other in an advanced way to reveal secrets, and you'll access computer terminals to gradually uncover lore, important context and bits of the story. Completing puzzles rewards you with pieces used to solve tetromino puzzles that unlock doors to new environments, even more puzzles, and new tools used to steadily increase puzzle difficulty and prevent them from becoming stale.
Solving puzzles requires manipulating and avoiding mobile mines, turrets, laser beam connectors, fans and cubes, as well as cooperating with recordings of yourself replaying your actions, but it never gets frantic and you’ll never feel hurried. There’s no real dexterity or speed requirement here, so you can relax and figure things out at your own pace.
Initially, puzzles aren’t very challenging but you’ll come to appreciate how increasingly clever they are. At some point, I thought I’d outsmarted the game only to discover later this isn’t possible and it was always meant to be so open and unrestrictive. The most difficult puzzles are only required if you want to find all of the secrets within the game and discover as many answers as possible, which is highly recommended and completely worth the effort.
The Talos Principle takes itself seriously and explores concepts like faith, free will, humanity, loyalty and purpose, with your journey unfolding much like that of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden: In the beginning, you don't know or question much and simply follow instructions but, by the time you wander around and have your first taste of knowledge, you may develop a thirst for it and begin to question everything around you. It's easy to become completely engrossed in the setting.
If you don't enjoy reading in games and skip through text, you'll miss out on a lot of what makes The Talos Principle more than just another good game, but it's still worth playing even for the puzzles alone. On a technical level, the game is impeccable: graphics, sound, voice acting, controls and optimization are all top-notch, and there are even settings for proper AA and field of view. The environments are beautiful, as is the soundtrack.
On a final note, QR codes that reveal text are left behind on walls by NPCs and friends who have played the game before you and you can also leave these pre-written messages for your Steam friends. One of these messages claims you’ve discovered the most beautiful spot in the game and, as there is a number of beautiful landscapes, I had been trying to decide where to leave that message for quite a while. I had been playing in first-person the entire time and ultimately left the message somewhere I never expected to: next to a mirror I encountered late in the game. It’s something that will only make sense if you end up loving the game as much as I do, but it was completely appropriate.

Dirty Bomb is a fast paced, OBJECTIVE game. The game has a diverse ammount of classes. The game also runs on a unique card system. The cards rarities goes as follow... Lead, Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Cobalt, and Special edition. (There are also default cards as well when you unlock a character.) These cards can be unlocked from "crates" which can be bought with  in-game credits.(Special edition cards are recived through special crates.) Default cards are the weakest with no perks, while bronze is the "strongest" with three perks. Lead has one perk and iron has two perks. Bronze, silver, gold, cobalt, and special editon cards all have three perks but different skins for your weapons and you character. There are three game modes. Execution mode, Stopwatch, and Objective mode. In Execution mode you have one life, no respawn until next round. There are two objectives, kill all of the enemy team, whom is defending, or destroy one of the objectives. In Objective mode you have three individual objectives through out the map. Destroy one, you go on to another. There are also defenders like in the other two modes. You also have optional side objectives you can do. Stopwatch mode is like objective mode but teams switch to see who can be the fastest at destroying the objectives. Who ever destroys the objectives faster wins. These are some of the basics. Indeed a fun game.

You like the pew-pew? Assault a base on foot with your faction.

For example in Indar there are sprawling caynon networks where from squads can deploy ambushes or using the dense trees of Hossin for cover against enemy air.

A great puzzle and philosophy game that definetley has potential to become a classic (think
).
A little overpriced, in my opinion. Almost 40€ for this game is a bit much, 50% off would be much more reasonable. But I understand why the game is priced in such manner...
Singleplayer (
version is available) in this game is great. Although some puzzles are surprisingly hard to solve, this game never lacks from motivation. What is the Tower? Who is Elohim (
Elohim means God in Hebrew. At least that's what the game tells you)? Why are you here, and what is your purpose? Easy and hard puzzles are woven together in a perfect mix.
At first glance, the puzzles may seem very repetitive, they have a small variations that help you figure out ways to solve harder ones. Stars (
) are hidden here and there and encourage players to explore the vast empty worlds of, well, you'll find out soon enough! But also computers with emails and other interesting info surrounding the "Eternal life" project (including time capsules and cryptic QR codes in some quite interesting places). And if you can't think of an anwser to a puzzle, takea break and suddenly,
you get a aha - impression!
The most interesting and downright different part about this game is that you can
or just stick to what Elohim wants you to do, that is, complete all the puzzles. The story has similarities with
(so has the gameplay) but its far from a rip off.  You are a

First off, this game requires some things to enjoy: liking puzzles, a love of words and interest in philosophy. Do you have these things? Good. You're in for a treat.
The Talos Principle makes no pretense to appeal to those who prefer a story outright told to them, or to those who swear by traditional plot narratives. In this game, the world has populated itself with challenges to overcome - both in puzzles and in piecing together what came before and your purpose in it all. The philosophical bulk comes in questions posed along a transhumanist route; heady ideas on an individual's role in the propogation of its species, what makes a human "human" and what is our consciousness anyway and more are given to the player to contemplate, both in the context of our civilization/lives and within the context of this game's narrative. It takes a certain amount of cerebral involvement to take in and fully consider, so be prepared for that (and if you're interested in this game in the first place, you should have no trouble wanting to dive in). The game's delivery of these questions almost borders on pretentious, but considering that it's all in the context of the game's world and plot (which is to challenge the character in order to spurn on growth) I'm willing to say it isn't pretentious in most respects.
The puzzles themselves are actually quite satisfying - eventually they involve a number of elements which interact with each other in meaningful ways, and while I only had to look up the solution to one of the required puzzles, the difficulty of the puzzles is definitely nothing to sneeze at. Further challenge is available in the star puzzles. There are also Tetris-like puzzles where you're given a set of shapes to fill a squared grid out - this is entirely my preference but I hated those. Thankfully, they're only like 1/8 of the puzzles, and there's a handy Steam guide for solutions.
The puzzles and narrative feel quite divorced from each other, but I found both to be worthwhile experiences, in their own ways. Mileage may vary depending on what you like. I wholeheartedly recommend this game - its challenging ideas have opened up new avenues of thought to me, and deepened my appreciation for humanity's progress so far, and where we will inevitably go. But again, your mileage may vary.

I've been a fan of puzzle games for some time. They're not ones I normally go after regularly, but whenever there are ones with distinctive properties, I will consider. The Talos Principle without a doubt was one that caught my eye.
If you've played the Portal series, you'll feel some similarities between the two in that they both tackle the first-person action puzzle genre. (Though The Talos Principle does allow third-person as well) The way they do it is different in some cases. In the case of The Talos Principle, there are many puzzles to be had with a less linear approach and are player paced. There is a rather interesting and detailed plot to follow that is told through finding various text resources, audio logs, and even events that occur within the game. There is a deep philisophical approach to the game that has you thinking and even questioning things. I adore it for that reason. I think you'll be intrigued and even surprised at times by what the game presents to you and even challenges you on.
The graphics in the game are beautiful, being built on the Serious Engine 4, part of a series of engines Croteam has used and developed over the years. There is good use of texture detail throughout and even being sure to use detail textures when looking at things close up. Environments feel well done and all have their own theme and feel as you go along.
Music and sounds are nice. The music in particular was great and helped provide a nice mood for the game as you solved puzzles or contemplated what you've learned or have faced. I found some of the sound effects were oddly low quality or just lacked fidelity to them. This was mostly noticeable for the footsteps your character made. A lot of the other sounds seemed fine and did not have this issue.
The gameplay was quite satisfying. As mentioned earlier, players set a bit of a pace as to how they tackle puzzles. For the most part, you can do these in any order. Though, the beginning of the game has more of a guided pace to it, and appropriately so, in order to grasp and learn new concepts and items to play with as you get into more advanced puzzles. I felt the way this was done was very nice. I remember when I first started playing, I dreaded some of the red sigil puzzles as they seemed so intimidating and difficult. But, there was a charm to this in that, as you did more of the simpler puzzles, it gave you a better sense of how to do the harder ones. The only negative I have on this was there were quite a few puzzle-piece puzzles you had to solve in the game. But, these were spread out decently enough.
Since this game uses the Serious Engine, there are plenty of things to customize for controls, graphics, sound, game play, etc. There are even options to help with people who get motion sickness from playing games of this nature.
I have really enjoyed this game from start to finish. Not only did I feel accomplished and enjoyed the ending, it made me think and learn quite a bit about ourselves. By that, I mean us as a people and life in general. I've considered myself a fairly philisophical person, but this game has surprisingly broadened that a bit and has offered me a rather distinctive experience that I did not quite expect. This is especially true from a developer that we've known to do more of the action first-person shooter fare. I appreciate they took what was just something to fool around with at the time and made something great with it.
I can recommend this game to just about anyone that likes puzzles, but most importantly, if you are into the more deeper of thought and exploring the more philisophical elements of things. Certainly, one doesn't even need to fully appreciate the latter elements to enjoy the game, but if you do, it makes it all the better. This has been an experience for sure and I look forward to more content in the future.
