Let me begin by stating that I have never played the original 'Wolfenstein 3D' but I have played the fabulous 'Return to Castle Wolfenstein' and the not so fabulous 'Wolfenstein'. Before its release I watched a trailer for the game which featured sci-fi robots and I thought to myself ''Oh no, they've messed it up again, gone too far''. But then I bought the game (on discount) and played it. So, what did I think?
I freaking LOVE this game! It's easily the equal to 'Return to Castle Wolfenstein' in respect of the story and theme. BJ Blazkowicz is back and as mean as ever, more so even. His character is really fleshed out and in part is helped by the stunningly voiced cut scenes.
Your array of weapons are varied and actually look like they could have been manufacted in 'The New Order's' time in history. The ability to dual wield left me with a big grin on my face while I laughed myself stupid as Nazis were shredded before my eyes. If going in loud isn't your thing then the game offers you the chance for stealth. I'm not much for sneaking but I have to say I was impressed and found I regulary used it in certain situations.
To enjoy this game to its max you must play it on über difficulty! The perk system is nice, once you use a certain weapon for some time or perform certain attacks you gain a perk increasing your proficiency in that item or that attack. Going around the games' world you pick up records which you can play at your leisure. These are great to listen to and the devs really went that extra mile with these.
I've yet to complete the game, only three more missions to go but I don't want it to end. Once it does I know I'll be left with wanting more. I want to explore ALL the planet and kill Nazis, not just a few pre-selected areas of the world. Hopefully an expansion pack will come out to let those who hunger for more gameplay continue to rampage through squads of Nazis with glee.
If you're a fan of the series or just FPS then this Nazi killing, gore filled, violent shooter is for you! It holds nothing back, is unapologetic and I love it for that.

This game is honestly one of my favorite gaming experiences from the last decade.  I grew up playing 2D side-scrolling beat 'em ups in arcades (yes, those still existed in my day), but it has been quite a long time since I've played anything new in that genre.  Enter Castle Crashers.  This game had a ton of hype after its success on consoles, and luckily it lived up to that hype.  Castle Crashers is a beat 'em up with a couple of twists.  It adds combos to the combat system, which mixes things up and adds variety.  In addition the characters level up and have stats that you can put experience points into, as well as you're able to equip different weapons with different stats.  These RPG-like additions mean that you can play the game in different ways (rely on speed, heavy damage, magic, etc.).  This really adds to the game, and ensures that you have a unique experience.  While the story is a bit weak, the overall length of the game and the variation in game levels is phenomenal.  The game even offers a new game+ mode after you beat it.  This game screams multiplayer, but I played it predominantly as a single player due to a lack of friends interested in playing.  While I ran into no problems playing the regular mode as a single player, about halfway through the new game+ mode I found it too difficult to progress.  I suppose I could have grinded my character's level at that point, but instead I chose to start a brand new character and play the game in a different manner this time (I would rely on magic).  Overall this game is a joy, and builds upon and improves on the formula set out by such classics as Double Dragon and Final Fight.  This game is so good that it makes me wonder why it took so long for someone to rejuvenate the beat 'em up genre.  This game is fantastic and I would rate it a 9.5/10.

Dirty Bomb is a fast paced, OBJECTIVE game. The game has a diverse ammount of classes. The game also runs on a unique card system. The cards rarities goes as follow... Lead, Iron, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Cobalt, and Special edition. (There are also default cards as well when you unlock a character.) These cards can be unlocked from "crates" which can be bought with  in-game credits.(Special edition cards are recived through special crates.) Default cards are the weakest with no perks, while bronze is the "strongest" with three perks. Lead has one perk and iron has two perks. Bronze, silver, gold, cobalt, and special editon cards all have three perks but different skins for your weapons and you character. There are three game modes. Execution mode, Stopwatch, and Objective mode. In Execution mode you have one life, no respawn until next round. There are two objectives, kill all of the enemy team, whom is defending, or destroy one of the objectives. In Objective mode you have three individual objectives through out the map. Destroy one, you go on to another. There are also defenders like in the other two modes. You also have optional side objectives you can do. Stopwatch mode is like objective mode but teams switch to see who can be the fastest at destroying the objectives. Who ever destroys the objectives faster wins. These are some of the basics. Indeed a fun game.

A superb, philosophcial title that is worthy of all the praise it has received.
As nearly everyone else has been saying, this game is like Portal. The similarities lie mostly in the puzzles where you have to toy with certain objects in order to gain access to an area. Not too easy, not too hard, the puzzles are accesible and enjoyable to all.
But I think what separates this game from most others is how it interacts and conveys messages to the gamer. It doesn't bluntly try to beat a lesson or "truth" into your head; nor is it extremely vague where you can't discern anything. And it doesn't merely present philosphical themes or ideas and leave you to make something out of them.
It presents ideas and then directly challenges you on topics including personhood status. This happens when you interact with an advanced AI at terminals between puzzles. The AI is not afraid to poke holes in your theories and ask deeper questions about the topics at hand as you struggle to coherently conceputlize said topics.
There are texts and an occasional audio log dispersed around the world and puzzle chambers. Most often they display diverse perspectives from all of the other AI's that roamed the world before you. They could be discussing the "God" (Elohim, your Father figure in the game), the "reality", or the darned puzzle. I think these texts provide a nice historical (and sometimes even purposeful) feel to the world that prevent it from seeming too ordinary or mundane.
To reap the most out of The Talos Principle (besides solving the puzzles), you need to invest the energy into reading the texts,contemplating the "reality" around you and thinking about the questions presented to you by the AI. If you do that, you might come away thinking that this was not just a fun game, but a life changing experience.

This is a game where you can dual-wield shotguns and kill Moon Nazis.
This is probably the highest profile single-player FPS in quite some time. It was advertised as an old-school run-and-gun game much like Painkiller or Doom, but it's actually closer to playing like Half-Life 1 and 2. You progress through linear levels that you can either take stealthily or Rambo-style. The graphics look nice, although the colors seem a bit muted and there is no option for anti-aliasing. The game is fairly well optimized and runs at a pretty smooth frame rate even on low end machines.
The storyline plays out like a mix between Inglourious Basterds and Iron Sky. In this universe, the Nazis won World War II and have taken over the world. You play as BJ Blaskowicz as he wakes up from a coma in 1960 and joins the resistance. There are newspaper clippings all over the game detailing the history of this alternate world, and you get a few Easter eggs like a record by "Die Kaefer," titled "Das Blue U-Boot."
This isn't an easy game by any means. I died a fair amount on medium difficulty. The game uses a hybrid of old-school health packs and modern regenerating health. Armor does not regenerate but health will regenerate to the nearest multiple of 10 (if you get shot so your health is 75, it will regenerate to 80 but not more) and you can overcharge health for those reckless guns-blazing sections where you know you are going to take more damage than normal, but the overcharge will eventually level out to your maximum health. This means there are equal amounts of balls-to-the wall corridor shooting sections and large open stop-and-pop arenas. It feels like a merger of both 90's and 2010's FPS design philosophy. You are encouraged to search the whole level to find secrets, like gold, enigma codes, and health upgrades.
This is a story-based single-player game, so there is no multiplayer. There are currently no expansions or DLC's. What you pay for is the full, complete finished game. It feels like a breather from a market saturated with $60 games that only feel about 60% complete without DLC.
I would recommend this if you want to shoot Moon Nazis in the face with a laser cannon.

Castle Crashers, developed by indie game developer team Behemoth, is an action-packed beat em up game with co-op in which the player(s) initially play as one of the four brave magical knights who were in the middle of partying until the evil dark wizard crashes the party by invading their home castle, absconding with their beloved king's power crystal thingy and pilfering the four charming princesses. The knights then set off on a quest to retrieve the crystal and princesses; all the while they beat up brutish barbarians, hell demons, relentless undead, and more dastardly beings and bloodthirsty horrors. You can bring up to three more friends to journey with you through the perils of that is mutant corn and team killing. Yes, as you save a princess (you save one at a time throughout the game) she will offer you a kiss of gratitude. However, she only has enough room on her luscious lips for one lucky warrior. If you're by yourself, cool. If you're with others, well in that case what better way to decide this dispute other than the gladitorial slaughter of comrades? Anyways, as you progress in the game and beat it a couple times with certain characters, you unlock more characters to play as. When you beat the story as one character, you'll be able to play Insane mode on that character. Insane mode being basically what its name entitles: Insane difficulty.
Now you may be thinking that I'm a complete numbskull for saying "No" for my recommendation on Castle Crashers.
Just try to hear me out a bit on this one, because
As you can see I've been playing it for quite a while. Not for an obscene amount of time but long enough to at least know my way around. I've even played it before the whole Remastered update with some friends. I've completed normal mode on both singeplayer and multiplayer; I've had fun playing, especially on multiplayer with my friends.
Now coming back to play it in its "Remastered" state, I would say it has definitely been improved. I'll be honest, I wasn't very excited, nor pessimistic at all, about the anouncement of the update but I thought it was rather nifty.
But of course, despite the polish (which was absolutely needed since it was released on Steam, mind you) I remembered why I had quit playing the game for a while in the first place.
Whatever was the reason you may ask? Well... It's simple.
No no, it is fun. It's fun to play with friends, screw around, and behead them for the love of a princess. "With friends."
By yourself, it could be fun the first few runs, but the action can get stale pretty quickly once you've beaten the story many times on multiple characters. But even with others, whether it be friends or strangers, the game still gets boring once you know the tricks behind this game.
Oh sure, different characters can possibly make for different movesets, right? Yeah, not really. The melee moveset on all the characters is the exact same (except Green Knight which has a visually different hard melee attack, but is otherwise functionally the same). The magic attacks on each character are somewhat different, but quite a bit of the characters are functionally clones of each other.
The Remastered update is indeed nifty, but I haven't found the changes as exciting. As far as I've experienced it's mostly reworked weapon stats, better performance, visual changes, and the addition of a new minigame. Otherwise, I may just be an elitist scumbag but I was a bit disappointed with this update. Who knows, perhaps there'll be more updates? I don't know.
These reasons, maybe even some more, are the main contributers as to why much of my interest in Castle Crashers has deteriorated.
+ Satisfying to hit enemies
+ Fun co-op
+ Different weapons and animal orbs (basically pets) which provide different stats and effects
+ A variety of playable characters
+ Different enemy types
- AI can have unfair advantage over player at times as well as be straight up annoying (there's a fine difference with me between challeging and annoying)
- Can get pretty monotonous, especially on singleplayer
- Some glitches that can really break the game depending on situation (most that were already there before Remastered)
- Quite a bit of the characters are clones of each other functionality-wise
- Singleplayer story can very much be outright harder than multiplayer story
+/- Connecting to a multiplayer session now just puts you in a random session. You are unable to pick a session.
These are basically all of the things I can come up for now.
Look, Castle Crashers is a cool game to play every now and then, especially alongside others. But I have just come to be disinterested in it for the most part. The campaign can just become straight up tedious and boring, and there is still room for improvement (i.e. fixing at least some more glitches, as in the ones that were already there before). For me, the Remastered update has failed to reach the hype it had set forth and had therefore soured my taste for this game into not recommending it very strongly.

Let me begin by stating that I have never played the original 'Wolfenstein 3D' but I have played the fabulous 'Return to Castle Wolfenstein' and the not so fabulous 'Wolfenstein'. Before its release I watched a trailer for the game which featured sci-fi robots and I thought to myself ''Oh no, they've messed it up again, gone too far''. But then I bought the game (on discount) and played it. So, what did I think?
I freaking LOVE this game! It's easily the equal to 'Return to Castle Wolfenstein' in respect of the story and theme. BJ Blazkowicz is back and as mean as ever, more so even. His character is really fleshed out and in part is helped by the stunningly voiced cut scenes.
Your array of weapons are varied and actually look like they could have been manufacted in 'The New Order's' time in history. The ability to dual wield left me with a big grin on my face while I laughed myself stupid as Nazis were shredded before my eyes. If going in loud isn't your thing then the game offers you the chance for stealth. I'm not much for sneaking but I have to say I was impressed and found I regulary used it in certain situations.
To enjoy this game to its max you must play it on über difficulty! The perk system is nice, once you use a certain weapon for some time or perform certain attacks you gain a perk increasing your proficiency in that item or that attack. Going around the games' world you pick up records which you can play at your leisure. These are great to listen to and the devs really went that extra mile with these.
I've yet to complete the game, only three more missions to go but I don't want it to end. Once it does I know I'll be left with wanting more. I want to explore ALL the planet and kill Nazis, not just a few pre-selected areas of the world. Hopefully an expansion pack will come out to let those who hunger for more gameplay continue to rampage through squads of Nazis with glee.
If you're a fan of the series or just FPS then this Nazi killing, gore filled, violent shooter is for you! It holds nothing back, is unapologetic and I love it for that.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a great addition to the Wolfenstein series. After a long sprint of mediocre games, Wolfenstein triumphantly returns with an excellent story-driven arcade FPS. It tends to feel a lot like playing a Bioshock game, which isn't a bad thing. With its' divergent storyline, Wolfenstein has managed to capture my attention. Fans of would-be history games will love this.
It is the 1960s and the Nazis have controlled the world for quite some time now. B.J. Blazkowicz, the protagonist of the series, awakes after a head injury to find that the United States no longer exists and is determined to find a resistance. Once he does, the Resistance, led by a charasmatic woman named Caroline Becker, embarks on a quest to take down the Nazi empire from the inside.
- An incredible storyline set in a 1960s Nazi ruled world.
- Aestheticaly pleasing :]
- Mixed loud and stealth play
- Great divergent-style weapons; Weapons that could have been.
- Great mix of enemy personel.
- A break from the traditonal Wolfenstein games (Which isn't such a bad thing)
- Protagonist's voice acting can be a bit annoying (constantly whipsering soliloquies in a Christian Bale Batman way)

- Wolfenstein: The New Order is a very fun game. When it comes down to the wire though, it is still simply another arcade FPS along the lines of Bioshock, Serious Sams, etc. The saving grace of this game is the great story. The action is also quite fun. The weaponary you will use in The New Order are divergent designs of real weaponry from the WW2 period. Overall, I enjoy playing this game and the replay value is on the higher side of the scale. If you love killing Nazis, WWII history, or even just Wolfenstein in general, I recommend!

CONS:
Pay 2 Win period. Don't waste your time. (Boosters not sustainable by regular play). However you can after an extreme amount of time get most of what "paying" will get, except the formentioned boosters.
Some weapons/upgrades are however Pay Only, however they seem to be niche more so than OP, from my limited time experiencing them.

Of course weapons made for this will vary with results, however this can be experienced with the same gun with varying results, with no explaination. (However that is semi-realistic at least right?)

PROS:
You can obtain *most* things freely. But there are options you can not (excluding skins, they are somewhat usefull, but being lit up like a christmas tree they rarely matter). The biggest here is maintaining charge for the boosters.
The battles can scale from 1 on 1 to 200 v 200 in moments.
A pro and a con at the same time; squads make a huge difference and can make a battle on their own. WIthout good squads your team is likely guaranteed to fail. And with a squad,  one can expect performance to scale from a 25 to 200% boost if teamwork is used. This can be a bad point too as the team without co-ordination is easily crushed and makes it heavily unbalanced. (So get some leadership fast or sink with the ship).
Conclusion:
(Opinion) The game is unique, and is worth trying, if Pay 2 Win isn't a huge sticking point for you. If it is as for many, it is painful.

Expect massive cert walls to the bases as usual, and necessary items are again cert blocked like proper anti-air or repair. (Same with anti-air for soldiers). Again, long time playing can buy you those however.
The game needs a massive performance overhaul as comparable and even far more taxing games run on a scale of 3-5x faster, so there is no excuse other than the work it would take to bring the game up to pace.

This is a game deserving of its hype.  I'm a huge fan of Portal and Portal 2 and this definitely scratches that itch in a wonderful way.  The story isn't as elaborate as Portal 2, most of the narrative is in text and audio logs strewn about the environment (not hugely hidden but some are a bit out of the way).  I'm usually not a fan of stories told this way because its often difficult to get all of the important bits and too many details are offered implicitly which sometimes goes over my head, but that isn't the case here at all things are spelled out nicely.  There's also several choices of ending depending on choices made.  Its a very philosophical story that will challenge you, quite literally, to defend your definition of life and consciousness.
Gameplaywise the game plays in the first person, like Portal.  Each world is divided into small hubs with individual puzzle levels inside, with some hubs and levels containing hidden stars needed to unlock one of the endings.  These stars can be quite tricky as sometimes you'll have to think outside the puzzle room in order to get them, which was a very exciting prospect.  The puzzles themselves amount to getting from point A to point B (which has a sigil piece you use in special puzzles to unlock new areas, see the free Sigils of Elohim game to get a feel for these, which also unlocks 3 extra stars if you finish it).  The tools to get from point A to B involve blocks, redirecting two colors of lasers, and disabling force fields and turrets, and finally actually being able to record yourself and have that recording exist in the world to help you accomplish things, like standing on a button to open a door or carrying you across the level on a platform.
The big thing that really struck me with the gameplay of this game is how tightly everything was put together.  This game has been tested so extensively you pretty much can't break it.  Every level is put together just perfectly to work the way the developers intended.  On rare occasion I did find myself getting stuck somewhere I couldn't get out, mainly because I tried soemthing crazy, on those occasions you can easily hold down the X button to reset the level.  Additionally, the most innovative feature to first person puzzlers is what I call "snappy" items.  When you're carring a box an outline of that box shows up on places where you can put it, and on buttons and platforms the box snaps perfectly into place.  Want to place a laser guiding mirror on top of a box?  It will just snap right in place if you're pointing near it.  Want to try making a big jump?  Feet will likely show up at the destination and you just press space and boom you jump over.  Too many times watching my girlfriend play Portal she would try the correct solution, but slip up on a jump and decide that wasn't the answer and look for other solutions.  This mechanic stresses finding the solution to the problem, and not worrying about the skill or dexterity to make tricky platforming happen.  I found it extremely refreshing and original and it made figuring out what I could and couldn't do much much easier.
Graphically the game is gorgeous.  Lots of outdoor environments, from deserts to snow, almost every level was beautiful and had something new to take in.  In spite of all the graphical splendor the game kept an extremely steady frame rate, and with more graphical options than I've ever seen in a PC game you're sure to be able to set the performance to your liking.  You can even adjust how fast your character moves!
I played the game in Linux using the proprietary Nvidia drivers and had no issues whatsoever and what seemed like excellent performance throughout.  The amount of work put into the Linux version was incredible and I very much appreciate.  Mouse and keyboard options were plentiful and the mouse felt especially sharp and precise.  I spent about 25 hours pretty much 100%ing the game, though one secondary choice has 3 mutually exclusive options, so I'll probably play the game again down the line to see what those give, although I don't believe they change anything but a couple of conversations.
If you like Portal, you will like this.  If you thought Portal was too easy, you'll like this.  If you like puzzle games, you'll like this.  Its one of the best entries in the genre.

I play video games for fun. A few months ago, if you asked me how I feel about puzzle games, I'd say that even the thought of them makes me anxious. But then again I kept hearing some great recommendations for a first person puzzle game that came out a long time ago and people were crazy about. When I finally tried it out I almost played through it in one go. My mind was blown and I thought "Surely this is a unique thing and no other puzzle game will ever come close to being this amazing." And then The Talos Principle came along. Again it surprised me. I hadn't heard about it until well after the release and I saw the positive reviews piling up.
This game starts in a gorgeous setting which resembles ancient greek or roman ruins. You are presented with a series of puzzles and your goal is to collect the item at the end of each level in order to advance to the next area. There seems to be an interesting story that unfolds gradually as you progress and unlock new mechanics. The narrative, the ambient sounds and soundtrack are amazing and contribute to the overall aesthetic of the game.
The puzzles themselves start off pretty simple, but eventually become quite challenging. They become even more difficult if you want to get the stars (secrets) in some of the levels.
As the story unfolds you are presented with some philosophical questions that can keep your mind occupied for hours after you've closed the game. I feel like it's the video game version of Interstellar or Inception.
The game does have some similarities with the Portal series, so it's a must own for any Portal fans, but it's a completely different experience. Steam workshop support enables the community to create cool mods and you get the option to start the vanilla version or the moddable version when you press the Play button. This means you can heavily mod the game while still keeping an unaltered version you can go back to at any time. I look forward to the dozens of hours I'm going to put into beating this game.

This is a game deserving of its hype.  I'm a huge fan of Portal and Portal 2 and this definitely scratches that itch in a wonderful way.  The story isn't as elaborate as Portal 2, most of the narrative is in text and audio logs strewn about the environment (not hugely hidden but some are a bit out of the way).  I'm usually not a fan of stories told this way because its often difficult to get all of the important bits and too many details are offered implicitly which sometimes goes over my head, but that isn't the case here at all things are spelled out nicely.  There's also several choices of ending depending on choices made.  Its a very philosophical story that will challenge you, quite literally, to defend your definition of life and consciousness.
Gameplaywise the game plays in the first person, like Portal.  Each world is divided into small hubs with individual puzzle levels inside, with some hubs and levels containing hidden stars needed to unlock one of the endings.  These stars can be quite tricky as sometimes you'll have to think outside the puzzle room in order to get them, which was a very exciting prospect.  The puzzles themselves amount to getting from point A to point B (which has a sigil piece you use in special puzzles to unlock new areas, see the free Sigils of Elohim game to get a feel for these, which also unlocks 3 extra stars if you finish it).  The tools to get from point A to B involve blocks, redirecting two colors of lasers, and disabling force fields and turrets, and finally actually being able to record yourself and have that recording exist in the world to help you accomplish things, like standing on a button to open a door or carrying you across the level on a platform.
The big thing that really struck me with the gameplay of this game is how tightly everything was put together.  This game has been tested so extensively you pretty much can't break it.  Every level is put together just perfectly to work the way the developers intended.  On rare occasion I did find myself getting stuck somewhere I couldn't get out, mainly because I tried soemthing crazy, on those occasions you can easily hold down the X button to reset the level.  Additionally, the most innovative feature to first person puzzlers is what I call "snappy" items.  When you're carring a box an outline of that box shows up on places where you can put it, and on buttons and platforms the box snaps perfectly into place.  Want to place a laser guiding mirror on top of a box?  It will just snap right in place if you're pointing near it.  Want to try making a big jump?  Feet will likely show up at the destination and you just press space and boom you jump over.  Too many times watching my girlfriend play Portal she would try the correct solution, but slip up on a jump and decide that wasn't the answer and look for other solutions.  This mechanic stresses finding the solution to the problem, and not worrying about the skill or dexterity to make tricky platforming happen.  I found it extremely refreshing and original and it made figuring out what I could and couldn't do much much easier.
Graphically the game is gorgeous.  Lots of outdoor environments, from deserts to snow, almost every level was beautiful and had something new to take in.  In spite of all the graphical splendor the game kept an extremely steady frame rate, and with more graphical options than I've ever seen in a PC game you're sure to be able to set the performance to your liking.  You can even adjust how fast your character moves!
I played the game in Linux using the proprietary Nvidia drivers and had no issues whatsoever and what seemed like excellent performance throughout.  The amount of work put into the Linux version was incredible and I very much appreciate.  Mouse and keyboard options were plentiful and the mouse felt especially sharp and precise.  I spent about 25 hours pretty much 100%ing the game, though one secondary choice has 3 mutually exclusive options, so I'll probably play the game again down the line to see what those give, although I don't believe they change anything but a couple of conversations.
If you like Portal, you will like this.  If you thought Portal was too easy, you'll like this.  If you like puzzle games, you'll like this.  Its one of the best entries in the genre.

I play video games for fun. A few months ago, if you asked me how I feel about puzzle games, I'd say that even the thought of them makes me anxious. But then again I kept hearing some great recommendations for a first person puzzle game that came out a long time ago and people were crazy about. When I finally tried it out I almost played through it in one go. My mind was blown and I thought "Surely this is a unique thing and no other puzzle game will ever come close to being this amazing." And then The Talos Principle came along. Again it surprised me. I hadn't heard about it until well after the release and I saw the positive reviews piling up.
This game starts in a gorgeous setting which resembles ancient greek or roman ruins. You are presented with a series of puzzles and your goal is to collect the item at the end of each level in order to advance to the next area. There seems to be an interesting story that unfolds gradually as you progress and unlock new mechanics. The narrative, the ambient sounds and soundtrack are amazing and contribute to the overall aesthetic of the game.
The puzzles themselves start off pretty simple, but eventually become quite challenging. They become even more difficult if you want to get the stars (secrets) in some of the levels.
As the story unfolds you are presented with some philosophical questions that can keep your mind occupied for hours after you've closed the game. I feel like it's the video game version of Interstellar or Inception.
The game does have some similarities with the Portal series, so it's a must own for any Portal fans, but it's a completely different experience. Steam workshop support enables the community to create cool mods and you get the option to start the vanilla version or the moddable version when you press the Play button. This means you can heavily mod the game while still keeping an unaltered version you can go back to at any time. I look forward to the dozens of hours I'm going to put into beating this game.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a great addition to the Wolfenstein series. After a long sprint of mediocre games, Wolfenstein triumphantly returns with an excellent story-driven arcade FPS. It tends to feel a lot like playing a Bioshock game, which isn't a bad thing. With its' divergent storyline, Wolfenstein has managed to capture my attention. Fans of would-be history games will love this.
It is the 1960s and the Nazis have controlled the world for quite some time now. B.J. Blazkowicz, the protagonist of the series, awakes after a head injury to find that the United States no longer exists and is determined to find a resistance. Once he does, the Resistance, led by a charasmatic woman named Caroline Becker, embarks on a quest to take down the Nazi empire from the inside.
- An incredible storyline set in a 1960s Nazi ruled world.
- Aestheticaly pleasing :]
- Mixed loud and stealth play
- Great divergent-style weapons; Weapons that could have been.
- Great mix of enemy personel.
- A break from the traditonal Wolfenstein games (Which isn't such a bad thing)
- Protagonist's voice acting can be a bit annoying (constantly whipsering soliloquies in a Christian Bale Batman way)

- Wolfenstein: The New Order is a very fun game. When it comes down to the wire though, it is still simply another arcade FPS along the lines of Bioshock, Serious Sams, etc. The saving grace of this game is the great story. The action is also quite fun. The weaponary you will use in The New Order are divergent designs of real weaponry from the WW2 period. Overall, I enjoy playing this game and the replay value is on the higher side of the scale. If you love killing Nazis, WWII history, or even just Wolfenstein in general, I recommend!

The main game doesn't take all that long to 100%, but the community content available for the game adds a truckload of extra lifespan to the experience. Given that, it may be worth the $40 price tag, but personally I'd probably wait for it to be on special again. I am stingy when it comes to entertainment, though.

This is hands down one of the best puzzle games I've ever played.  The difficulty is paced well and you usually have enough options open to leave a puzzle behind and tackle it later if you get stuck.  It's reminisant of portal 2's design, where you have set piece rooms requiring you to combine multiple elements to solve the puzzle.
Aside from the gameplay, the graphics are pretty amazing for the genre of game this is.  The atmosphere this game generates is phenomenal when the sound design, art, and story telling all come together.
The plot is a carrot that will keep drawing you forward, forcing you to solve more and more puzzles so that you can understand anything about the world you find yourself in.  The story is revealed slowly through snippets of text, requiring the player to piece together the narrative through the course of the game.
Overall this is one of the best games I've played in a long time, and look forward to playing it again after a few months to see how my perspective on it has changed.  Would highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys tricky puzzles, lovely atmosphere, or clever writing.

A very interesting game concept, that is otherwise ruined by its developers' bad decisions. The best part about it is lack of "pay to win" - in the actual match, premium players are not favored in any way over free players. This however, together with unique gameplay concept, is the last of good things that can be said about Robocraft.
Flawed match-making mechanics are possibly the worst thing. You are frequently paired against bots significantly stronger/weaker than you. My bot armed with 4 disintegrator lasers and only a few electroplates is very often thrown into matches where I can see a similarly-sized bot, covered generously in electroplates, armed with 6 such lasers, and equiped with highly advanced gear, like EMP emitter and blink drive.
Aside from that, the game suffers from poor balance. Some items are ridiculously overpowered (to the point that a newbie player randomly aquiring such gear can easily derail low level matches), some on the other hand, are underpowered.
As the game rewards you very poorly between the matches, it quickly becomes tedious, as time-consuming grind is the only way to aquire more components to upgrade and expand your bots.
Last but not the least, some of the mechanics are outright hostile to the player. For example, there is a punishment for leaving the game during a match! Possibly to keep raging players from quitting the match when losing, it does nothing of the sort, as people are quitting the matches just as often as in other games. This only punishes players who exit the match without any ill intentions, and actually introduces toxicity.
Overall, the game looks like it has potential, but it needs more reasonable management to actually be enjoyable. As it is now, you should stay away, unless you want to get frustrated by a very unfinished game.

Max Payne 3 is interesting because it both stays true to certain aspects of the series while deviating from others entirely. Combat is great, and the "realism" added to combat (limited weapon inventory, for example) doesn't hurt the fun of game like many other modern shooters. Cutscenes, although frequent, were balanced pretty well for me, but some might find them too intrusive. Unfortunately the game seems to ignore some of Max's character development from the second game, but Max goes through other interesting changes in 3 as well.
Stylistically, it pays more tribute to neo-noir than the classic film noir that inspired the first two games. This is not a flaw. In fact, it's a refreshing change of pace and an interesting approach. The video feedback effects and transitions in cutscenes are an interesting evolution of the graphic novel cutscenes of the originals. The vistas and dirty streets of Sao Paulo provide interesting evironments and exciting combat encounters, and the more realistic/serious tone of the game makes it a bit more thoughtful than the rest of the series. That being said, the writing lacks the creativity of the previous games. There's an occasional metaphor but for the most part it lacks the poetry of the (admittedly sometimes silly) dialogue and narration of the first two games.

This game is what I would call a classic of the modern gaming era. It's not exactly new, but it still manages to keep a certain freshness to it, which is actually quite impressive.
When I say "classic", I mean a game that is a sort of important pillar to gaming in general. Now, I wouldn't say that it changed the whole industry per say, but I still consider this one to be a game that is part of my childhood to an extend. Many can possibly relate to that thought, I'd wager.
Now, what exactly is Castle Crashers? Well, to resume the whole experience in a single sentence, it's basically a "smash right through the enemies, save the princesses and defeat the evil king". Sounds simple, doesn't it? That's no surprise; because this game is simple.
The true experience truly comes to life when you bring a friend or two along the ride. As most multiplayer games, having someone to play with you really is a must to enjoy the full adventure. Honestly, playing through this game alone is kind of boring, and considering that the designs of the levels highly support multiplayer, trying to go through the game alone can prove to be a chore. Then again, I did play and finish it alone the first time, but when I replayed it with a few folks, my overall opinion changed drastically.
This game is huge. Don't let the tiny sixteen bucks tell you otherwise; it's probably one of the biggest adventures I've seen for a Smash 'em up. The adventure itself isn't much to speak about, my friends and I started from the beginning and finished after around four sessions of one hour each. What makes this thing so huge is the unlockable content. There are a ton of them, such as characters, pets, weapons, levels, and even a secret difficulty. You'll be grinding and repeating the same levels many times to find rare items and weapons if completion matters to you.
I'd like to speak about the difficulty, since I feel like difficulty is something that matters for many players and buyers. The game in itself isn't harshly hard. Most bosses have simple patterns, the level designs can be either fair or sometimes overwhelming, and the overall product will not make you frustrated to the point of screaming. Of course, I won't say that it is an easy game either; sometimes it feels like the game throws so much at you, I find it almost unfair. Without spoiling too much, the final boss in particular has a lot of annoying patterns that can drag for a while, especially if alone.
Upon finishing the game, you will have the option of changing to an even harder difficulty. I will warn you : It is cheap. Enemies are insanely powerful, and quite frankly, it's not fun. If that sounds appealing to you, then go ahead and try it. I, for one, will stay away and advices you to do so as well.
The game has two primary mechanics : Physical attacks and Magical moves. Physical attacks are, as the name says, attacks with weapons. The damage that you will do to enemies is generated by how much points to give to your Physical stats. Magical moves are attacks composed of magic. Giving points to this stat will not only grow your magical abilities and make them more powerful, it will also make the range and overall usefulness much more adaptable.
The best idea would be to try to make a balanced knight, since enemies later on will either be extremely resistant to Physical attacks or highly resistant to Magic. You always need to have an alternative, or else it becomes truly bothersome.
I believe that I mentioned every aspects worth mentioning. This game is great, and while not a masterpiece by any means, it should prove itself quite worthy of your purchase. Do not forget to try and ask a few friends if they wish to play along!

Max Payne 3 is interesting because it both stays true to certain aspects of the series while deviating from others entirely. Combat is great, and the "realism" added to combat (limited weapon inventory, for example) doesn't hurt the fun of game like many other modern shooters. Cutscenes, although frequent, were balanced pretty well for me, but some might find them too intrusive. Unfortunately the game seems to ignore some of Max's character development from the second game, but Max goes through other interesting changes in 3 as well.
Stylistically, it pays more tribute to neo-noir than the classic film noir that inspired the first two games. This is not a flaw. In fact, it's a refreshing change of pace and an interesting approach. The video feedback effects and transitions in cutscenes are an interesting evolution of the graphic novel cutscenes of the originals. The vistas and dirty streets of Sao Paulo provide interesting evironments and exciting combat encounters, and the more realistic/serious tone of the game makes it a bit more thoughtful than the rest of the series. That being said, the writing lacks the creativity of the previous games. There's an occasional metaphor but for the most part it lacks the poetry of the (admittedly sometimes silly) dialogue and narration of the first two games.
Overall it is one of the best shooters I've played on a technical level, and it has an above average / good story to boot. Its visuals and style elevate it beyond a generic action game and definitely make it (for fans of shooters and cinematic games) worth playing.

I thought it was excellent.  Some puzzles games I have to set down for awhile and come back to, but this one is entertaining enough to have a long sit down with.  I think I liked it more than Portal 2 (I mention this because I often found myself comparing it while playing this game).
The puzzles are very well made, and can take a good deal of time trying figure out.  There was a lot of content, and it would probably take the average player about 20-25 hours.  Unlike Portal 2 there's a lot less humor and the story is a serious one.    There are I think 5  elements you might be using for any given puzzle, and the mechanics are a lot of fun to play with.
The game has a lot of philosophy in it and actually made me stop a few times to think about my own existence.  Not many games do that!
Although I have finished the story line there are still secrets to find which likely will unlock another area of the game.  I don't usually see games to 100% full completion but I think I may this time.  This only happens if a game has lasting appeal.  Thoroughly enoyable and a great brain-twister, highly recommended.

On a whim, I picked up a game that Steam had under the “recommended for you” section named “The Talos Principle”. At a glance, it looked like a handful of games in the puzzle genre (most notably “Portal/Portal 2″) so I thought I’d give it a go.
Right from the outset, it’s pretty clear this is going to be not just a logic and reasoning puzzler, but a philosophical examination of what it is to be human. To be a person. You’re aware from the start that you’re being tested, but I’m not really going to say a lot more here about this, beyond that I was impressed at the layers of depths that went into the philosophical side of the game. That way, if others want to play and have it unfold out for them, they can remain unspoiled.
Beautifully rendered, there’s something haunting about wandering through the ruins of human civilization while reading blog posts, irc chats, new reports, etc, about what happened to mankind, what they thought about great things (and some not so great), and how they faced their own extinction.
In fact, my only real complaint about this game was the fact I kept getting motion sick from the first person point of view, but that is a limitation of MY design, not theirs.
Also worth a mention here is how elaborate and frequent the easter eggs in this game are. I stumbled across one entirely by accident that was easily the creepiest moment in the game for me.
Check it out. The structure of it is done in such a way that you can do a section at a time, over a long period of time, if you wish. It doesn’t require you to sit and play for 12+ hours in a row. Which I find ideal given how busy I am lately.

After years of being bed-ridden I still have the physical prowess of a soldier.  I'm surprised as you.  You'd think after 20 years of not moving a muscle that I would become weak, but maybe the "Dickshead" did something to me while I was held down.
I enjoyed killing Nazis then, and I enjoy killing Nazis now.  It helps that I can easily move around in the world and control my weapons as I would my hand.  No one ever thinks about how natural some weapons should feel and I'm glad the makers of these death machines knew what they were doing.
While I still feel the same rush of killing, one thing that has changed is how beautiful the world is.  I don't remember how vibrant Nazi crimson blood was.  I guess I just enjoy the sight of it more.  And the look of pleasure or fear on Anya's face draws me closer to her every time I look at her.  She is so real, just like the others in this god-forsaken world.
I would change nothing about my story, my path, my life.  I will embrace what I am, a killing machine with no remorse and no mercy.  I am the tip of the spear for the resistance and every death by my hands will echo through eternity...

Best FPS I've played recently, fantastic storyline (really,
good). Honestly I think there are only a couple of things I can really fault with this game: Texture pop-in, the size and (maybe?) the price. First, texture pop-in appears to be engine-based, for some reason id-Tech stuff doesn't like AMD GPUs, RAGE had the same problem with texture pop-in (still does). The second problem - the size - is also engine related, as it uses 'super-textures' so instead of using the same texture multiple times (thus creating tiling) it uses larger textures which cover sections of the level, each one custom made. So with these large textures the game size goes up, but unfortunately I feel the fidelity hasn't, some areas look rather blurry when they shouldn't. I mean Crysis 3 is only 10.5GB installed and it looks fantastic even on lower settings. Lastly the price, I got this at -66%, I'm happy with paying that, but I'm not sure I'd have been comfortable at full price.

Dirty Bomb is a good game.
Dirty Bomb got off to a very rocky start, with poor gameplay balance and disappointingly repetitive gameplay. It got so bad that I dropped the game after a few months. Around a year later, I've started playing the game again, and goddamn, the contrast in the game's quality is staggering, but somehow I can't pin down what changes made it this way.
This game would solid enough to justify a $15 - $20 price tag if it had no microtransactions. This may be a red flag for some, because a lot of free games are unbalanced in favour of paying customers. In Dirty Bomb, every character and all their loadouts are available for free, with only a couple hours of grinding to get a non-default merc, and cases containing loadouts are regularly distributed to you and don't need keys. Paying doesn't give you a unilateral advantage, it just lets you get more options and some cosmetics faster. I think part of the reason you never feel like it's pay-to-win is because despite looking like a discount Overwatch, Dirt Bomb is focused on movement and gunplay, not character based abilities or specific guns. And the gunplay in this game is great, landing shots is satisfying but never challenging. Kills feel earned and deaths rarely feel unfair after you learn the how the game works.
The game's biggest issue is balance. Not of the playable classes, those are mostly fine, but matchmaking is the biggest flaw this game has. Teams are often poorly balanced, even in ranked, and there is no party system outside of ranked so playing with friends is a challenge. Queue times can often exceed 10 minutes in ranked, even then someone might get salty and leave.
This game isn't necessarily for everyone. I hate to sound like an elitist, but if you're only used to Call of Duty and Battlefield you might not like this game. If this were a game that cost a lot of money or had more intrusive micro transactions, I'd probably be a lot harsher. But given that you can have a lot of fun for free, it's easy to forgive its flaws. If you like fast paced shooters and mobility, give try Dirty Bomb, it's worth it. Also the progression doesn't ruin the game unlike many games.

Max Payne 3 is a technical masterpiece. The game is beautiful, runs smoothly, plays like a dream, and was clearly a labor of love.
But inside, it is a bag of misshapen ideas that don't fully come together. Max Payne, a noir crime series focused around organized crime in New York City and one violent, uncontrollable cop who seeks revenge for his wife's murder, is unrecognizeable amidst the ghettos of Sao Paolo, Brazil. In a massive change of direction for the series, Max works as security for a wealthy family living there, and uncovers a very unclear, difficult to navigate plot with corrupt cops and militias or something, with malicious intents that somehow remain nebulous even when they are revealed towards the end. Our villains are forgotten the moment the credits roll, their motives are in question the entire time, and the plotline only becomes more and more confusing. The writing, dialogue-wise, is excellent, but the plot structure is flawed and unsatisfying.
I do wish to address the gameplay. Overall, the gameplay is fantastic, it is one of the smoothest third-person shooters I have ever played. There are criticisms I have, for example the "last man standing" mechanic where you get shot and must shoot the person who shot you quickly (time slows down) or you die and must restart. Not to mention the fact that sometimes the shooter will be behind an obstacle and you can't shoot him, it is incredibly disruptive to gameplay. I have often cleared a room efficiently and effectively, only to be forced into this situation and have it result in my death. However, if you enjoy shooters, it is a very fun and satisfying one to play.
There is another element to the gameplay, however, that I wish to address, and that is the sheer brutality. Through Max, you will slay hundreds, perhaps thousands of men. Max Payne 3 does a better job than most games of getting it's enemies to look and behave more like real people. For this reason, I began to have a mental backlash to killing so many people. I found myself pushing to make it through the end of the game so I wouldn't have to play anymore, and after completing it, I felt disgusted by the idea of shooting another person in a game for a long time. I choose to leave this note without criticizing it or praising it. It lowered my enjoyment of the game, but I also believe it could have been a strongly successful desired effect, since the main theme of the story is brutality.
Do I recommend Max Payne 3 or not? I have chosen to say no, because I did not enjoy it. It took my favorite parts of the Max Payne series out and gave me a story I didn't feel compelled to see the end of. If you enjoy this game, I do not criticize you, I fully understand why some people would believe that. But if you are on the fence about playing it, please at the very least make sure you have played Max Payne 1 and 2, and prepare yourself for "unrelated Sao Paolo-set shooter guest starring Max Payne" if you decide to play this as well.

There's a good mix of people liking and disliking this game. Both sides are plausible. It's an action packed realistic first person shooter, but has a huge learning curve. There's also the arguement of whether or not the game is P2W or not. I'm not really going to go into that. I played this game when it first came out, when I had a computer that was hardly capable of anything. A few years later when I had an actual good PC, I got addicted. It's not a game that you would play forever. For me, I play it for a bit, then leave it, then later on go back on and play it for a few more hours. I've personally had a lot of fun playing this. If you're looking for massive open worlds and dozens of player controlled battles to delve into and thats free to play then I would recommend this. If you're not a fan of huge learning curves, then this game might annoy you a bit.
NOTE:
All of my reviews are laid out in a particular format that fits the game.
Planetside 2 is one of my favourite MMOs, mainly for how immersive it is. The game is split into 3 factions: Terran Republic, New Conglomerate and the Vanu Sovereignty. People who've played the first game might recognise some of the lore in Planetside. The war is set on a planet called Auraxis. These 3 factions are fighting for control of 4 different continents; Indar, Esamir, Amerish and Hossin. These continents are filled with different bases to conquer and defend. Bases are crucial to conquer the continent, and are hard to conquer without a good number of people. The factions have their own stories behind them. The Terran Republic are from Earth, and believe in law and order. The New Conglomerate are freedom fighters, seen as terrorists, that are against the Terran Republic's control. And finally the Vanu Sovereignty, which see technology as the way for humanity to achieve greatness. At the beginning of the game, you get to choose which faction you want to fight for. You are given 3 character slots, so you can have a character for each faction, (Unless you get membership which gives you an extra slot). As I mentioned before, all the battles in this game are player controlled, meaning there are no NPCs. Continents can have up to thousands fighting, making it a very realistic experience. The game has 5 different classes, each with their own unique role. These are: Infiltrator, Light Assualt, Combat Medic, Engineer, Heavy Assualt and a special class, MAX. As well as battling on foot, there are vehicles that can be brought into the fight. These can range from tanks, to mobile spawnpoints and even to aircraft. The game allows you to set up squads which bring players together to conquer bases or sneak behind enemy lines making this a very realistic yet futuristic experience.
As mentioned earlier, it's an FPS with a huge learning curve. The game tries it's best to give players the help they need to survive in battle by giving tutorials, and recently, a smaller continent before people of battle rank 15. Some people find these helpful, others don't. I covered quite a bit in the About section. The game is split into 5 classes, the world map is split into 4 contintents plus the added smaller continent, vehicles range from tanks to aircraft and much more. There's just one tip I must give, never go alone. Unless you are really stealthy, you won't survive by yourself. The game prompts you to be with a group of people, or at least be there when a fight starts. The game allows the creation of squads that people can create and invite friends or other random people to join them. For people not wanting to make squads, there is an auto join option which will automatically put you into a squad. There are also groups called Outfits, Planetside 2's version of a clan. Some of these have guidelines to follow before joining, which should be displayed by the owner of the outfit. The game has a vast amount of different weapons for different classes. To buy these weapons, you are given 2 different payment options. Certs, which you passively gain from kills, capturing bases, completing missions etc., and finally Daybreak Cash, which you pay real money for. This is where the arguement for the game being P2W comes from. Some weapons require you to pay Daybreak cash, and not certs. Some people think these are the better weapons, and the ones that you pay certs with are terrible. You can either pay for a certain amount of Daybreak Cash, or get the monthly membership that gives you 500 daybreak cash per month, along with other things.
Another note worthy thing, this game requires a good internet connection. A bad one can result in many problems.
If you have a good PC, you can see the amount of effort that the developers put into the game. In all 4 continents there is an amazing amount of detail, with the environments, the bases and even things like vehicles.
Graphics however is a different matter. I can run the game fine on ultra, but I've seen many problems for other people. Running this game on high can give serious lag and Framerate drops. Also having a bad internet connection can affect the game badly.
I found the in-game hud quite easy to follow. When taking damage, your health and shields appear at the bottom middle of the screen, right above your ability, and ammo. On your left you have a minimap, showing the local area. The top left part of the screen shows the chat, and the top right shows the kill chat. There's quite a few settings when scrolling through the options, nothing that was too hard for me to find. I didn't have any problems here.
- Highly Realistic
- Huge Worlds
- Dozens of player controlled battles
- Plenty of content
- Beautiful design
- Still gets updates
- Huge learning curve
- Highly graphic dependent
- Possible P2W elements
- Requires good internet connection
After getting the gist of it, this has become on of my F2P games. Sure, it ain't perfect, but hell is it fun. Diving into a huge battle, explosions all around me with guns blazing never felt more fun. If you can handle the learning curve, this can be one of the best MMO/FPS game ever made!
Final Verdict - 9/10.

By no small measure, Wolfenstein: A New Order is a cut and dry FPS actioner. From the dual weilding impossibly hefty assault rifles to impaling Nazi craniums with short-end daggers, the player finds his/herself leadened by swollen rage directed squarely at the Third Reich, in all its pixelated glory. Nonetheless, burrowed within such gory tomfoolery, there is a significant command of craft to be found.
[SPOILERS ABOUND] We, As B.J Blazkowicz, following an unsuccessful invasion of a Nazi fortress, finds ourselves wheelchair bound inside a Polish sanitorium, where we remain for...TAHN-TAHN-DUMMM...fifteen or so years. Awakening to find the world overtaken by Mein Kampf rhetoric, our protagonist takes it upon himself to reinvigorate a floundering resistance, in the hopes of ultimately thwarting the now globally reigning regime, one eviscerated Aryan at a time.
Firstly, let it be said that any fan of the series will find themselves wholly satisfied. This is a mechanically sound product, fast paced and uncompromising in its quest for unadulterated adrenalin. The action is pervasive and unwavering, relenting ever so slightly during forgettable lulls of clunky stealth. Nonetheless, when chaos ensues, the game's AI is sufficiently formidable (on harder difficulties anyway), while enemy variants are appropriately diverse, ranging from light-to-heavy shock troops to armored robotic monstrosities.
Below Average PC Optimization: while running 2 Nvidia 680Ms with an Intel i7 3940XM (theoretically sufficient to run the game at recommended spec), significant screen tearing was experienced, with multiple V-SYNC buffers proving fruitless.
It goes without saying that A New Order's plotline is 'by the numbers' at best. That said, I found myself floored by the  immensely intimate level of heart and depth carried by both starring and supporting characters throughout the narrative. Blazkowicz, for example, is on the surface a Type-A 'Murican sadist. However, nestled beneath his borderline sociopathic veneer is a forlorn, battle weary warrior, yearning for days of peace and sun.
All told, Wolfenstein: A New Order is a mindless, well executed blast, at once bombastic and (suprisingly) tender.

The game makes teamwork easier for the players with Squads, (small 8-12 man teams) Platoons (Multiple Squads) and Outfits (mass group of players under 1 banner, Much like a clan). It also has Squad VC, Platoon VC, and Outfit VC. Did I mention it was teamwork based?
TL;DR
Planetside 2 is fun and challenges your individual and teamwork skill.

Review Aimed to New Players: Yes, it is an old game. Yes, even with the HD enchance the graphics aren't that great. Does it plays as it looks? Nope. While it is indeed an old game, AoEII was known for being so modern in its mechanics that it revolutionized the whole RTS scene to the point that newer games tried to be like AoEII and not the inverse. Considering this, you can see features such like pathfinding, balanced civilizations, mass stack of units, group controls, up to date hotkeys and a myriad of other things common in the RTS of our days. So yes, it is an old game, but it does not play like an old game.
What makes AoEII so good compared to RTS of its time or present time?
- The game is forgiving in small errors because confrontations are focused in tactical endurance and slow advance rather a clash of sweeping offensives. This is one of the few games where when you can truly say "I may have lost this battle, but not the war!". So things are more aimed toward who makes more errors (and the importance of those errors) rather about who makes the first error and dies. This add a lot of depth, playability and strategy to the game, both for newbies and veterans.
- You have a myriad of civilizations who specialize in different things and each one posses an unique unit (or some, two). Yet, the bonuses and differences between civilizations aren't sharp, so aside a few particular cases you won't find yourself in the situtation that a civ. pick (or random) can determine the whole match or even influence too badly on it. The civilizations are properly balanced, so you can pick favorite ones and be sure you will rock on it as long you use their advantages wisely (and patches their weaknesses).
- The game is extremely friendly to new people since it includes one of the most memorable tutorial campaigns (featuring William Wallace!) ever made, making sure in a fun and quick way that players can manage the game. While it can take a time to learn about all the units and specific details, since the game only possess four ages and the units upgrades are straightforward, a player can plan an (effective) tactic without much knowledge. The matches can be played on Slow Mode so the reaction and reflect factors of the RTS doesn't hit them hard. There are maps like Black Forest that are easy to wall, thus winning you time to compensate differences in skill levels.
- The Single-Player posses a heck a lot of content with a myriad of different campaigns and random maps. The campaigns (excepts those from the expansion The Forgotten) features an amazing voice acting that will enchance your experience greatly. Wanna learn about medieval history (specially for school/college LOL)? This game and its campaigns will teach you and motivate you like nothing else you can find in your way!
With that said, the game possess a flaw for new players in multiplayer and it is the resource gathering. Actually your capacity to quickly collect resources possess a snowball effect that can put you ahead several minutes (even half an hour!) of your opponent in development, giving an easy win to those who can make a lot of resources in the Early and Middle game. This is easy to improve with some practice, tips or tutorials, and resource gathering is actual fun here with the ever useful villagers (that also rocks as offensive and defensive machines since they can repair key units and position holding building during battle, just like making new main bases or frontline bases to battle). Yet, this can be frustrasting at first when someone wins you only because they handle the resource gathering better.
Nonetheless, this game rulz and I totally recommend it, not only for old and veteran fans, but for new people as well!

GOOD POINTS -

Dirty Bomb is a good game.
Dirty Bomb got off to a very rocky start, with poor gameplay balance and disappointingly repetitive gameplay. It got so bad that I dropped the game after a few months. Around a year later, I've started playing the game again, and goddamn, the contrast in the game's quality is staggering, but somehow I can't pin down what changes made it this way.
This game would solid enough to justify a $15 - $20 price tag if it had no microtransactions. This may be a red flag for some, because a lot of free games are unbalanced in favour of paying customers. In Dirty Bomb, every character and all their loadouts are available for free, with only a couple hours of grinding to get a non-default merc, and cases containing loadouts are regularly distributed to you and don't need keys. Paying doesn't give you a unilateral advantage, it just lets you get more options and some cosmetics faster. I think part of the reason you never feel like it's pay-to-win is because despite looking like a discount Overwatch, Dirt Bomb is focused on movement and gunplay, not character based abilities or specific guns. And the gunplay in this game is great, landing shots is satisfying but never challenging. Kills feel earned and deaths rarely feel unfair after you learn the how the game works.
The game's biggest issue is balance. Not of the playable classes, those are mostly fine, but matchmaking is the biggest flaw this game has. Teams are often poorly balanced, even in ranked, and there is no party system outside of ranked so playing with friends is a challenge. Queue times can often exceed 10 minutes in ranked, even then someone might get salty and leave.
This game isn't necessarily for everyone. I hate to sound like an elitist, but if you're only used to Call of Duty and Battlefield you might not like this game. If this were a game that cost a lot of money or had more intrusive micro transactions, I'd probably be a lot harsher. But given that you can have a lot of fun for free, it's easy to forgive its flaws. If you like fast paced shooters and mobility, give try Dirty Bomb, it's worth it. Also the progression doesn't ruin the game unlike many games.

This checks all the boxes for a generic, boring shooter trying to edge in on the realism scene that inevitably devolves into a haven for tryhard elitists. It has:
-needlessly lengthy animations
-extremely low player health (which all realism shooters should have, however Squad has no ballistics system)
-exaggerated recoil
-very, very few weapons
-clunky animations
Red Orchestra 2 should be the metric against what all realism shooters should be measured in terms of features and gunplay. It has flawless weapon animations, ballistics, and keeps weapon handling tight and nonintrusive while staying realistic. Squad is basically Insurgency with fewer guns and a very obvious ArmA II vibe in the map design and game layout.
It simply isn't worth $40. Play ArmA II if you want a milsim shooter and Insurgency if you want tactical realism. Squad fits between these two but falls short of both.

The 340 hours on record should say it all, this is a fun game.  However, it does have a very sharp learning curve which is not helped by the game pointing you towards the relatively fragile Light Assault.  Like all FPS this game takes practice and the light assault is one of the less forgiving to new players.
My advice for new players is to start with Heavy Assault, its armour and shields will help you stay in the fight long enough to get you used to the game.  Medics and Engineers are the next resilient and are not hampered by their specialised roles.  The medic’s assault rifle is particularly  effective in mid-range fire fights.
Things to keep in mind; when you pull the trigger you show up on everyone’s mini-map and if you spray and prey you will miss.   Suppressors and scopes help with this but keep in mind that suppressers hurt the effectiveness of your weapon at mid to long range.  My own thoughts are the increase in stealth offsets this but that's opinions are divided.
Also flash suppressors are not suppressors, they have some use but actually increase the range at which you show-up on the mini map so make sure you equip the one you intend.
Finally find an outfit that is active, it's a unit based game and solo heroes don't tend to achieve much.

Really great game. It is a bit of a throwback to the old days of shooters. For instance, you can carry 10+ weapons at a time, and you have to pick up ammo and health. The one gripe I have with that system is you have to tap a button to pick everything up, rather than just walking over it, it's a minor annoyance though. Gun play is tons of fun, progression system is cool, challenging you to do things you wouldn't normally do. The story is honestly very good. It's captivating, in depth, and even emotional at times. They have made a world here that feels really alive. It sounds ridiculous at first, but this alternative history is very interesting. The devs have done a great job immersing you in the world, and creating a cast of antagonists that you just can't wait to kill. Back to the gun play, it's over the top and rightfully so. In fact, everything about this game is fairly over the top. The boss fights (which are lacking just a bit, but still fun), the story itself, the voice acting, and how your character manages to experience wounds that would kill any normal person, but he manages to brush it off. The story offers replayability as well. In the beginning you make a very tough choice that has repercussions on the story later on. Overall, this is a must-have. It's hard for me to recommend anything for 60 dollars but if you're looking for something new and you don't mind spending that much, don't hesitate.

The Talos Principle is philosophical puzzle game that can be played in first or third person view. To start this review, I would like to say, what is there not to like about this game? The Serious Engine allows this game to have some of the most beautiful environments in up to date graphics. Which truly makes an immersive atmosphere. The music for this game is also pleasant and fitting for the game and helps the environments in adding a serene and magical feeling to the game. Then the game itself performs well and have had very few issues with the game as well as being well balanced in difficulty as you travel across the game's many puzzles. Also, with there being a large number of puzzles to solve and a hefty sum of reading to do, the game does what it is suppose to do - make you ponder things that you may or may not have before. It gives you a perspective on many things and possibly new ones that seem genuine. The reading would probably make you think the game is boring but if you read well and really apply the words to the game or maybe even other things, it is important. The game sort of teaches you how to think and how not to or what not to think. The envoking mystery of the philosophy is what makes this game enjoyable. I absolutely enjoyed this game from start to finish and would recommend it to anyone that has a computer.

It's hard to imagine that Castle Crashers is a 7 year old game. It still looks amazing and plays like a dream, far better then a lot of recent beat-em-ups and action games. It features a fully co-op campaign and a lot of zany mini-games and absurdist jokes. It's quite a treat.
I originally played the game back in 2008 when it first launched on Xbox 360. I found it a joy and immediately got my friends into it. We spent many a night besting the levels and doing our best to max out our characters. It was a true joy to have a new age, HD beat-em-up with game mechanics that actually advanced the genre.
Blocking has long been something missing from beat-em-ups. The simple, cynical reason is that these old games were made for the arcade scene. Staking the odds in the players favor might make them feel more empowered, but it also would limit the amount of quarters you'd be getting from any individual. Blocking didn't make sense from a business standpoint.
While Castle Crashers isn't the first beat-em-up to feature such a simple maneuver, it adds a lot of complexity on top of an already deep brawler. There are combos, magic and a lite-RPG system to grade your progress through the game. Leveling up and getting new skills makes the minute to minute gameplay very compelling and prevents the gamer from ever reaching a brick wall, in terms of progress.
I can't say that every single level is 100% perfect, but the game rarely has a dull moment. Even when it does, the bright colors and brisk framerate help keep your mind engaged. The recently released update (which mirrors Castle Crashers Remastered for Xbox One) improves a lot of the stability and balance of the game. Certain joke characters are now actually viable as a means of besting the bosses.
One mini-game was removed in the new update, but it's abscence isn't missed. I'm not sure why they didn't leave it, but I don't really care that it's gone. The new mini-game, Backoff Barbarian, is a blast. It's strange to see arrows instead of controller inputs, but being as this is the PC version, I am willing to let that slide.
The graphics have also received a nice boost in size and clarity. Neglecting to use them still provides a solid image, but the larger sprites make the game feel alive in a way that wasn't possible before. It's also far easier to discern what is going on in chaotic scenes, which is definitely a welcome change.
About the only downside is that this update doesn't include the two DLC characters. Those are relatively cheap and the proceeds go to charity, but it would have been nice to give players access without asking for more money. Regardless, the price of the game is cheap and definitely worth it, so I can't complain.
That I'm still thinking about this game and playing it after nearly a decade is a testament to how good the quality is here. Castle Crashers is absolutely a classic of the genre and one that ever fan of old-school, 2D style brawlers should own. Now that is plays better on PC, you really don't have much of an excuse to skip this.

If you like Portal, this is a must (if you haven't played Portal, get it and this both). Not only it's full of entertaining puzzles, it also gives the player the chance to learn more about the world the game is set in. If you like a good story you'll enjoy looking for terminals and reading the documents you find, if not, you can just skip it all. A big plus is that almost all of the puzzles aren't timed so you can take your time thinking about it and, if you are stuck and unable to solve one of the puzzles, you can just leave and go solve another one. A negative side for this game is it's graphics: while the areas themselves are beautiful, there isn't much variation and after doing few puzzles in the same level, it starts looking boring and dull. Also, at least at the time I played it (few months ago), only few of the latest save files were preserved, so, if you wished to revert back to some time ago (to try different choices, check different endings), you had to backup them manually. Overall, I'd give it a score of 9/10.
