Squad... wow. There isn't much more to say about it.
You play a variety of roles, in a variety of teams. You're goal is to work together with your squad (hence the name of the game) and capture points and other tasks similar. Immediately upon joining your first game, you will come to realize the intensity of this game. This isn't for the weak-hearted; this is for those looking for a fun, challenging and realistic gameplay experience.
Game Play: 8.5/10 - Since it's in alpha, there are still some minor things that could be improved, but overall gameplay is rather fluid and seamless.
Graphics: 9/10 - Let me tell you, these graphics are perfect. They capture things perfectly and only help support the realism and intensity of the fire fights. Probably one of the key things that makes the game so incredible, and I only expect the graphics to get better as it exits Early Access.\
Sound/Audio: 8/10 - After playing for a while, you get used to the gunshots. Let me tell you, though, that when you first join and you here those gunshots go off and those explosions, there isn't anything quiet about it. As I said before, it only helps to capture the realism and in a way, makes it scarier, like an actual firefight.
The community of this game is incredible. You don't see 12 year olds screaming in to their microphone, or trolls hoping to ruin the game experience for you. The developers interact closely with the community, and everyone is supportive of eachother. When in combat (and out of combat) I feel like they are brothers to me, and I don't want any of them to get shot up. There is a sense of comradery, and that's what makes the game so excellent.
Final Notes: I personally was avoiding early access games, as I had been let down in the past. I decided to go on a limb after seein the glowing reviews of Squad, and let me tell you, I was not dissapointed. This is not your average early access game. If anything, this game is almost ready for launch; that's how well set up it is. So, even if you are one of those people who are against early access, I encourge you to take the chance like I did and get this game. You won't be dissapointed.
Final Score: 8.7/10
TL;DR: Get the game.

Because everyone loves B.J.'s... I mean B.J Blazkowicz...
Wolfenstein the New Order is the reboot of the long standing franchise as envisioned by Machine Games. Wolfenstein is credited as being the first ever stealth game with Castle Wolfenstein from 1981, and it's sequel, Beyond Castle Wolfenstein from 1984. The most famous game, and the one veteran FPS players remember the most is Wolfenstein 3D by ID Software, a title that was a revolution at the time, and ID's first venture into the FPS world, even before the almighty Doom. Wolfenstein was a pioneer in 3D gaming for PC's back in the day, and The New Order respects it's heritage by taking the franchise to a whole new direction.
This is the first Wolfenstein game that has a story, a well thought, engaging, thought provoking story. The plot allows for character development, and this is the first FPS that actually made me care about what happens not only to the protagonist B.J, but also with everyone he interacts with in the fight to cripple the Nazi oppression, and B.J's main antagonist, General Deathshead.
The story takes place in an alternate timeline where the nazis have won World War II. It starts in 1946, but the majority of the game takes place in 1960, 14 years after B.J goes through a traumatic experience.  This is all that I am going to say when it comes to the game's story, because it truly deserves to be experienced spoiler free.
Wolfenstein is a tribute to the FPS's of the 90's, but mixed up with some modern mechanics. The end result is very satisfying,  and feels both modern and retro, and in my opinion the way Machine Games pulled it off, deserves praise all on it's own.
Gameplay is over the top, violent and incredibly fun. You can dual wield every single weapon in the game, knives, shotguns, machine guns and even sniper rifles. Yes, you read that right, you can dual wield sniper rifles. I can't think of any other game that allows that. The shooting mechanics are easy to master, and the over the top violence suits the game theme well. This is a Mature rated game for a reason, there is an abundance of blood, guts and nazi brains.
The game mixes traditional shooting with stealth, rewarding both styles equally. It is up to you how you want to play the game, and you will discover that some levels are better done in a particular way. It has a perk system that allows you to unlock more abilities by performing in game actions, and these are separated into 4 different types, Stealth, Tactical, Assault and Demolition. It adds a layer of strategy that is welcome in this style of game, as far as I am concerned.
Wolfenstein The New Order uses the ID Tech5 engine, which is both a good and a bad thing, depending on who you ask. If you have a capable enough PC, you will be blown away by the detail and visual effects, particle system and the textures. This game looks amazing at 1080p with all the details on Ultra. If you have a mid range PC, you may experience texture popup, which breaks the immersion in my opinion, and poor frame rate, so be sure your machine can handle this game before you decide to buy it, it can be very resource intensive.

I was very excited to play Max Payne 3 after I installed it (huge download - 30 GB). I had not played a Max Payne game in the series, but the best part is that you don't need to in order to play and appreciate this game. This game has a lot going for it. Great graphics, good sound effects, and most importantly a grippy story. Let's see how it fares.
Story: 8 out of 10
As Max Payne, you are a hired mercenary to basically protect the Branco's family. Things go from bad to worse, I am not going to discuss the story due to the fact that I don not want to spoil anything, but I will say I really enjoyed it. It was not the best story I have ever played in a video game, nor was it intended to; but it is a mature tale that moves the player from firefight to firefight. Overall, I was interested from the beginning to the end, which not many games can do successfully.
Sound: 9 out of 10
All the weapons and sound effects are what they should be. I especially like the sound of the shotguns and Desert Eagle for they sounded extremely beefy. The voice overs, especially Max Payne are great and keep you interested in this washed up hero.
Gameplay: 8.5 out of 10
The firefights in this game are estatic, fun, and intense. I just wish there was a larger variety of things to do rather than just shooting and looking for clues/golden guns parts. What it does do thought, it does it in spades. The bullet time effect is awesome (especially when you are just beginning to use it), and when the game zooms in on your last victim in the combat space, the game is extremely gruesome. Weapons, ragdoll, and weapon handling were obviously a big focus of this game.  Max Payne (you as the player) also handle extremely well, from firing each weapon realistically and hunking down for cover.
Multiplayer: N/A (No interest in playing the multiplayer for this game. The game is not too populated so I would pass on the DLC and Season Pass for this game).
Graphics: 8.5 out of 10
This game is a beast to run, but looks extremely good when maxed out. I was able to maintain a constant 60 fps with a AMD R9 290, but in order to run this game at such high settings, you are going to need some serious hardware under the hood. I loved how you as a character change visually every mission. It really makes you feel the Max is an actual person. Over time, Max gets cut up and hurt pretty bad. Weapons models and environments look great as well. Overall, other than being a performance hog, the game is a pretty good port.
Overall, i highly enjoyed Max Payne 3 and would recommend it to anyone looking for a fun action game with a mature story. I will point out however that there are some major problems with the game's DRM system (Rockstar Social Club). The game would frequently crash on start up, and this lead to doing some major research. Even then I could not get the game to run on every startup. Other than these technical issues, the game is definately worth playing. Finally, I would just like to mention the game can get pretty hard at times. I originally was playng the game on Hard but dropped the difficulty down to Medium for the last two missions. Regardless, Max Payne 3 is an excellent game, is deserves your time.
Max Payne 3: 8.25 out of 10
*Would have been an 8.5 if it were not for the technical issues.*

Max Payne is a truly noire story with a very iconic dark and gritty narative of the classic hard-boiled city detective, who goes through trauma on a daily basis while half-drunk and shot up on pills. While there is absoloutely nothing funny about Max Payne's story, it's of couse a bit of a parody on the noire genre.
As a third-person shooter, the game employes bullet-time, basically matrix-like dodging maneuvers and is generally just very well made. The soundtrack and the story are both excellent also.

Never thought I'd say this but I've finally found a game better than Portal. There's humor, but subtle. The puzzles are first rate and not frustrating. Enough flexibility that you can leave one be and do another one and come back to it. The overall story is superb and emotionally charged (the emotions however, are those stemming from philospophical musing, not the raw and heady emotion of an FPS game or a standard adventure game). The music, artwork, ambience and really just the sheer quality and quantity of **thought** that went into this game is staggering. After 15 years of gaming, I finally get to play a game about which I have **no** complaint (believe me, I'm trying). I haven't sat through a game for more than an hour at a time over the past 4 years (growing old I guess) but I'm pulling all-nighters on freaking work-days just to play one more puzzle in this thing. Sleep eludes me :( ... all I see in my mind are boxes and tripods and fans and stars (those triple-damned stars!! Where are they all????). Recommended if your life has seemed strangely empty since Portal (1) and you don't care for cutscenes interrupting your gameplay and you **crave** an intelligent game with beautiful game mechanics, nice control and a world that I'm playing tourist in (taking screenshots by the dozen each session ^^). Highly recommended. First review on Steam as I just *had* to congratulate the game makers for a truly magnificent game. Bravo! Just ... bravo!

A massive bolt of destruction lands behind you, throwing you forward as a lightning tank approaches your flank. A friendly heavy jumps over you, lobbing missiles at it while yelling at you to take cover inside the capture point. You quickly run as a friendly medic falls in behind and begins to heal you. Ears still ringing from explosions, you throw down a land mine near the entrance. An engineer takes up by the window with a gattling turret, throwing shots at nearby enemies. You hear the landmine explode.
A ball of plasma scores your chest as you fall to your knees, weakened, but not dead yet. As you lay there, you notice the engineer is on the ground next to you, gasping for his last breath. The medic quickly begins to heal you, but is suddenly cut down. You quickly jump to your feet, running out of the building and to the nearest armored vehicle you can find. You see a slight distortion in front of you, almost as if the light itself is being bent around in awkward angles. As you lurch yourself forward, an apparition appears, and plunges his knife into your chest and vanishes. You slowly fall to the ground, blood spewing from your wound. You think to yourself.....goddamn this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing...

This game is pretty incredible. The story is a thrilling and brilliant continuation of the first two games, and Rockstar has done nothing but improve on what gameplay Max Payne 1 and 2 provided for us gamers. The cream of the crop I'd say is the story, and it keeps me coming back, but so is the gameplay. The graphics for Max Payne 3 are okay; they're not brilliant, and blurring for the distance can seem a bit odd at times, but otherwise it's excellent and it fits this chapter of Max Payne. The AI is excellent; they -will- try their hardest to make certain you die, and believe me, you'll be dying a good amount in this game. Enemies typically act differently depending on how -you- act, and it's no easy task to face off against five to fifteen goons in one go. Cover is useful but in many cases is destructible, so you as the player are forced to adapt.
Shootdodge is great, but it can be abused, sometimes ridiculously so. I wouldn't exactly call this a criticism; I'm certain it was meant to be used. In Hard and Hardcore? It's most certainly extremely helpful and sometimes necessary, but not all the time. They've done well with the Bullet Time™ mechanic that has been so engraved into the Max Payne series.
What really makes this game - and I want to stress this - is the physics engine. I know, it might sound ridiculous, but it's ONE of the main reasons I'm constantly coming back to play this game after a long day at work. Finishing off enemies at a time is so satisfying. They truly die as they would depending on where you shot them, when you shot them, etc. It makes killing people in Max Payne 3 so crazily satisfying, not to mention awesome. They've done so well with the Euphoria engine here, and they've continued it on into Grand Theft Auto V, which I'm looking forward to playing on Steam.

This is a fantastic example of deep, powerful storytelling in games. It feeds you information bit by bit (quite literally), and you slowly start to build a picture of what you can see around you, and what you -cant-. Overall, the story is a very spiritual one, delving into the ideas ranging from spirituality, religion, authority, and determination. It covers a wide range of topics such as the philosophy and psychology of AI, and the Human Condition.
On top, it's just as good and -hard- of a puzzle game as Portal was, sometimes even -more- difficult due to the fact that some techniques might not make sense right away, things that aren't explicitly explained. Puzzles can be abandoned and retried at a later date without consequence, but you have to complete -all- puzzles to properly advance to the next sections.
The puzzles themselves are deliciously satisfying, and infuriatingly difficult at times.
On top of that, the entire game is photo-shoot beautiful, I found myself taking numerous screenshots just to preserve some of the beautiful sights the game had to offer.
All in all, fantastic play, definitely worth every penny. And shockingly from the company that came up with Serious Sam, this level of depth was a -nice- refresher. Thank you for this.

This game is great!
Why?
Squad is a very realistic game that requires teamwork to get a win.
For teamwork you don't just need good aim or a ♥♥♥♥ing beastly weapon, you need communication!
How do you communicate in Squad?
In Squad you have 4 ways to communicate with teammates
1. Chat. It's useful when you want to tell your whole TEAM something, for example the coords of an enemy FOB.
2. Commander channel. This voice channel is used by Squad leaders. It is used to communicate with other allied Squad leaders.
3. Squad channel. Squad channel is used to talk with your squad. Everyone in the squad can hear you, and you can hear everyone from your squad, no matter where you are on the map.
4. Local channel. Local channel is used when you are talking to teammates that are close to you, the further you are away from them, the quieter you can hear them / they can hear you. This channel can be used by anyone in the team. It is also useful for when you are engaging with 3 squad members for example, if you're not engaging with your whole squad, use local channel so you don't confuse your other squad members that are not engaging with you.
You're probably asking yourself, how do squads work in this game?
A squad exists out of 9, it could also be less then 9.
For example,
In a 72 player server, you have 2 teams, these teams exist out of multiple big and small squads.
All of these squads have a squad leader, they will lead their squad to victory by giving them tasks (capturing flags, flanking,...), building rally points, fobs,...
and obviously good communication.
Every squad has roles that players can select to play as.
You have 7 roles in each squad.
Marksman, Medic, Squad Leader, Grenadier, Rifleman/Fighter, Rifler, Light Anti-Tank.

This is a fantastic example of deep, powerful storytelling in games. It feeds you information bit by bit (quite literally), and you slowly start to build a picture of what you can see around you, and what you -cant-. Overall, the story is a very spiritual one, delving into the ideas ranging from spirituality, religion, authority, and determination. It covers a wide range of topics such as the philosophy and psychology of AI, and the Human Condition.
On top, it's just as good and -hard- of a puzzle game as Portal was, sometimes even -more- difficult due to the fact that some techniques might not make sense right away, things that aren't explicitly explained. Puzzles can be abandoned and retried at a later date without consequence, but you have to complete -all- puzzles to properly advance to the next sections.
The puzzles themselves are deliciously satisfying, and infuriatingly difficult at times.
On top of that, the entire game is photo-shoot beautiful, I found myself taking numerous screenshots just to preserve some of the beautiful sights the game had to offer.
All in all, fantastic play, definitely worth every penny. And shockingly from the company that came up with Serious Sam, this level of depth was a -nice- refresher. Thank you for this.

More video than game.  Skip it.  The number and frequency of cut-scenes is absolutely obscene.  The most obnoxious of any game I've ever played.  It completely ruins pace and momentum in order to hide poor level design.
The gameplay that's there is decent.  When you don't need to take cover to survive and can use bullet-time (which has been rolled back from what it was in Max Payne 2) the combat feels fun and engaging.  However, every single thing you do is interrupted by in-game or recorded cut scenes.  Which are unskippable.
On top of this, the game is plagued by a VHS and after-image effect which makes no sense in the context of the story, its characters, or the presentation.  There is no rhyme or reason to this effect, just a frequency which bests Max's unending monologues.  What was completely endearing in the first two games has become, with Max Payne 3, a crutch which ruins the original charm and overstays its welcome.  What was once a treat now feels like a punishment.
I wouldn't even recommend this game on a steep discount.  Play Max Payne 2, instead.

Squad is the game I've been waiting for for a very long time.  Since before I knew it existed.
I like games like Hostile Intent, Insurgency, Arma, etc. I enjoy more casual games like the Battlefield series, but let's be honest, I prefer games that are more realistic and punishing.
Squad is like taking the best things of Insurgency, Arma, and the Battefield series, combining them, improving them, and then adding to them.
The maps are large, to say the least. The terrain is excellent, and still being improved.
Weapons are fantastic. Iron sights and limited scopes currently. Very well balanced, and they hit hard. No ammo counter or magically refilling magazines.
When you get critically hit you start bleeding out and need to bandage, or find a medic. Medics can pick you up from being downed, but it takes time, and after being downed twice, you won't be picked up again, you have to respawn. Just one of many game mechanics that I feel really balances things out. You can't be revived 37 times in a row by a medic sitting behind the wall reviving you over and over.
9 man squads are well balanced. You can't make a new squad to get the one sniper class or rpg. As more people join your squad, the rest of the classes are unlocked, to make sure every squad is balanced.
You can communicate to your own squad anywhere on the map, and in direct chat you can communicate with other friendlies from other squads. It's very well done. The in game voice quality is the best of any game I've ever played.
Squad leaders can communicate with other squad leaders via a 3rd voice chat option to coordinate attacks/defense/assistance.
Squad leaders, when near 1 friendly player, can drop a rally point, where their own squad members can spawn. It only has 9 spawn points, and you can only place 1 every 2 minutes. If an enemy gets near it it goes away.
Squad leaders can also build FOBs, where any player on your team can spawn, and there is no limit to spawns. You spawn faster at fobs than rally's. Your squad leader can design defensive structures to secure your fob, and the other players have to get out their shovels and build what the squad leader designed.
FOB building is very well done, in that it takes time, resources, and teamwork to build, and they can only be build a certain distance apart, so you don't end up with teams having 20 spawn points all over the map. On a good team you generally will see maybe 2 FOBs, possibly 3. Again every aspect of the game seems very well balanced, and it's still in its infancy.
This game is amazing as it is, and it doesn't even have land or air vehicles yet. It's constantly being updated and worked on. It's only getting better.
You haven't played a great large scale realistic FPS until you've tried Squad.

This game is basically the new PR (project reality - a mod for BF2), after the events that went down between the team. you can google for more of that info.
it has some very glaring problems currently that i would like to point out. one is the server browser. if you play in a group, it is very hard to coordinate which server to join. one person may see a server on the browser list, while another may not because it does not display all available servers - we aren't sure wether this is region based, ping based, or what. also, there is currently NO DIRECT CONNECT option via console commands, so external tools to view various browsers are essentially informational only at this point in time. if you play a single person, this might be a non-issue. if you play with friends in larger groups, it proves to be very annoying as people start shouting possible servers to join, only to find out that half of the people in the chat cannot see that server in their browser list. this usually requires a game reboot in order to hopefully see that server.
base building is partially overpowered, as the only way to destroy objects currently is to use the shovel. explosives do not destroy or damage buildables.
the graphics are very good, however i feel the field of view and the relative sizing of items is completely bonkers. I play on a semi-standard 27" screen at 1440p resolution. i have this monitor overclocked to between 96hz and 120hz. on Epic i can generally run at a decent 30-40 frames a second with a 4th gen i5 and a R9-280. i turn down some of the settings in order to increase my frames to match the frequency of my monitor. this is kind of a big deal, the reason being that, i've noticed there is some weird lag or latency issues with regards to frame rates. as frame rates drop, there seems to be an exponentially increased input lag, to the order of extremely noticeable. its very evident during the longer animations which i have another problem with - which is a carry over from the old Project Reality days. the longer animations its very easy to notice these and will get you killed as you transition from one weapon to another, even more so when your FPS drop. using squads in-game FPS command (stat fps) you can view the frames and time taken to render in ms. as frames drop the ms increases. at 30fps i've noticed that shooting there is a very odd delay between clicking the mouse and the time the weapon takes to go off.
there is a very odd correlation between distances and the way the game renders it. guys at 100 meters with my current settings are essentially 6-10 pixels big. thats probably a bit of an exageration, but I cant really put into words how off the relativity of distances and sizes things are rendered at. this makes engaging targets out beyond 50-100 yards basically pointless.
the recoil on some weapons is completely rediculous, a good example is the M249 SAW or the RPK. while i realize that maybe due to balance they put the recoil so high to discourage ramboing, there is no deployment system currently in the game, so even prone trying to suppress an enemy squad on a hill is basically pointless. as well the "suppression" - there is very minimal effect.
some of the sounds are very good(ie firing a rifle), which really helps with immersion, while audio positioning is pretty bad. i run audiophile headphones of different variaties (beyerdyanmic DT770 pro, AudioTechnica AD-700x, superlux 668b) through a Fiio DAC/AMP setup, and in most games I can tell distance and direction very very well. in this game it is very hard currently.
some minor things is that there is currently no back-up sight option for the weapons with scopes (ie M4 w/ ACOG). the PSO scope on the Draganov is completely incorrect as far as the distances relative to the impact points of the BDC, and the ranging reticle (the stadiometer) is off. while trying to use the M203 in order to range with it you have to basically point to the target and range manually. there is currently no way to range other than guess with the GP-25. there is no range adjustment at all for any sights other than hold-over. there's no breacher class yet, so no grappling hooks, no C4, no shotgun. the kits are too basic. there's no mounted weapons yet. the lighting in this game is god-awful. i basically turn off all the shadows otherwise the entire game would be pitch black.
overall, its a work in progress. a fairly decently good work in progress. it has many pros versus other tactical shooters. Insurgency was always a pretty crap game for me, I had so many problems with it. I like ArmA but the problem there was BI studios basically gave up on ArmA 3 and went with some kind of space-aged garbage instead of sticking to standard weaponry and vehicles. the other problem with ArmA is the fact that noone plays in actual squads/groups in most game modes as there is no benefit to playing in one unlike PR/Squad's gameplay. I shouldn't have to installed 80gb of mods to fix Bohemia's lack of focus.

I will not go deep into gameplay as plenty of reviews are available.  I will just say this is not an easy game to get into, but once you get your bearings it's an incredibly rewarding experience.  Read on for details.
To give you an idea of the community PS has, I served the Terran Republic for 8 proud years in PS1 over Johari, then Markov, and finally Gemini with Black Company as a combat medic, rising to the outfit rank of Captain.  We disrupted enemy supply lines by hot dropping in enemy territory, blowing up generators, and blocking enemy resupply runs. My first commander, 888, taught me everything I know.  Our elite Galaxy transport pilot was a housewife who had to leave to make dinner when hubby got home (boo!), and we actually had a couple retired vets as mechanized infantry and air support.  I realize some of that sounds absurdly epic for a video game, but it's exactly the lasting experience you get.  All veteran PS players have resumes like that, and happily swap war stories as the battle rages around them.
The game itself has some flaws and bugs, but those are almost irrelevant (as long as you can actually play) since the game's true strength is in its organizational framework that makes working with other players fun and rewarding.  Don't get me wrong, I really think the gameplay is strong and real money purchases are not overpowered, just look elsewhere for in-depth analysis.
I really think that if you are new and want the full experience, you MUST interact with people and join an outfit.  That way you can see how the game strategies work, what bases and base installations are important, etc.  Concerted operations in the game are fluid situations, you are not likely to get a strong understanding from a static online guide.  If you try to solo without knowing that stuff, you will suck and quit.  Once you get the hang of things you can, if you want, then leave your outfit to Lone Wolf; and you'll know enough to have fun doing it.  You will have a better understanding of what the coordinated groups are trying to do, too.  Or, if you're feeling lazy, you can hit Instant Action, and just go Zerging (PS jargon for joining a horde of other players and overpowering enemy positions with brute force numbers and minimal coordination).
Again, I have to stress how much being in an outfit is what makes this game great, definitely when you start - and still a great option later on.  All that said, it's a time drain.  I was pretty dedicated back then, nowadays I got too many other things to do to really get into an outfit, but I still jump into squads now and then and pitch into the never ending war.

This review analyzes the design of this game. If you just want to see whom I would recommend it to, skip to the last paragraph.
I think it is very appropriate to compare this game to Portal and Antichamber. It tries to be both but is definitely worse than either of of the formerly mentioned.
The game is bifurcated; it has a narrative and then it has puzzles. What made Portal's narrative great was the way it interacted with the gameplay, the Weighted Companion Cube being the most prominent example. In Portal you always carried your Portal gun. In The Talos Principle the tools you use inside puzzles are never even mentioned by Elohim(the GLaDOS of this game).
Similarly to Antichamber you can solve the puzzles in many different orders but, unlike in Antichamber, you eventually have to solve them all. In The Talos Principle puzzles reward you with "sigils" - tetrominoes that you need to collect to unlock areas. Compare this to Antichamber where solving a puzzle instantly lets you into a new area. It does not help either that The Talos Principle's puzzles are quite repetitive and can take up a lot of time even if you know the solution immediately.
Still, there are good things to say about this game. Unfortunately they all concern the part of it where the player spends the least amount of time: the Overworld connecting the puzzles. I really (rogue)liked the fact that you could not explore all the options in the dialog trees that asked you philosophical questions. It felt like your choice really mattered. I also think the story was a very solid interpretation of The Book of Genesis.
I actually remember one well designed puzzle. It tricked the player into imagining a complicated solution when the actual solution was simple. The problem is that the puzzle was not very enjoyable. It was actually rather frustrating, probably due to the fact that the game does little to encourage lateral thinking elsewhere.
The most interesting design failure in my opinion is needing to open a puzzle lock every single time you unlock something (and also to open semipheres that have no reason to exist in the first place). They are generally easy but potentially frustrating yet they serve as a very elegant "are you sure" when they are used to climb the forbidden tower.  Everywhere else they just push the reward one step further from the player.
Conclusion: Don't play this game unless you don't mind repeating the same solution patterns(get all the items, put block on fan and connector on block) tens of times to get mere minutes of quality multiple choice dialog. Also, if you are looking for a challenge you will be dissapointed, because most of the difficulty in this game will arise from not knowing something in advance or being too impatient and dying to enemies.

Robocraft, the bot design game that has made so many people mad, and happy. There is no place to start or end when placing a review on this game, simply letting everyone know that it is recommended to read up on what the game has to offer, before playing and having the chance of being dissapointed. The current 'loot' system that Robocraft has in place can at times be frustrating, but it can also be very rewarding for new players. The reason for this is that the 'item' gain is not done by earning currency each match, but by getting a 'loot crate' varying in quality the better you do. Whilst this might seem fair, know that there is a completely random chance of getting any item in the game, with only a slightly higher chance of better items in the better crates. Yes, this means that an 'expert' at Robocraft could get a few building blocks from coming top 3, or a beginner could get a lockon missile launcher right off the bat. While this might be unfair, all robot pieces have their own unique play styles and advantages. I personally have enjoyed every hour of time put into this game, and do not regret anything I have to do with it. I can only hope the developers at Freejam can make a more 'publicly acceptable' game in the future.

After sinking well over 250 hours into this game, I feel that I can write a proper review.
Planetside 2 is a wonderful game that is terrible for new players. The first 10 or so hours were the player must learn almsot everything about the game is very difficult to get used to, and there is very little help or direction as to what the player must do. The new player "inexperience" takes a lot of time, and either joining an outfit (group of players) or reading the wiki to understand the basics is almsot essential.
However, once the player gets past the learning curve, there is a lot to love. Huge 96v96 fights are not uncommon, with dozens of infantry running around tanks, all while aircraft duel above them. The variety of classes means that there is a playstyle available for everyone, and switching classes is as easy as pressing a button.
While weapons can be purchased for real money, everything can also be purchased with in game "certs." Certs are surpisingly easy to come by once the player learns the ins and outs of the game. While weapons can be brought, the default gear is probably amoung the best, as they are jack of all trades, and can be used in more or less any situation to reasonable effectiveness. Other weapons are sidegrades, tailored to work very well in a certain situation, but not so much in others. The only things that are not purchasable with certs are cosmetic items.
Daybreak Games has recently been stepping up their game (pun intended) and have been trying to get the game where is should be, as evidenced by the recent Construction Update, a week after which the test server already had the contents for the next update, ready to be tested and balanced.
I only have two complaints about the game: One is the community. Many players that have been playing for upwards of three years now have sown their salty tears across the battlefields, and are not the most graceful in helping newcomers. However, this is just a fraction of the community, albiet a rather vocal once.
The other complaint is the optimization. This game reqiures a decent rig to play on anything other than "slideshow mode." Running ultra is all but impossible in large fights, unless your machine is a serious thousand-dollar gaming rig. However, the game is still enjoyable on low settings.
All in all, the game is good, and I recommend that anyone tries it.
TL;DR: Get this game.

I was ready to believe the hype. I wanted to enjoy this game. And I did, for the first five hours or so. But after that, it became tedious. By the half-way mark the game ceased to be a rewarding experience and became a chore, a checklist to finish and finally reach what turned out to be an unsatisfying ending.
The philosophical aspect of the game followed the same arc as the puzzles: from interest to fatigue. The insights into the moral and philosophical complexities of AI begin well, and discussions with the Milton Library Assistant are a fun mental exercise. Unfortunately, as the game progresses, the existentialism of the computer program becomes more hackneyed and less insightful, and the game gives you fewer and fewer good choices as answers. The discussions devolve into the game writers leading you into poorly worded and poorly thought out ideas, and then force you to either acknowledge the fallacy in your argument or leave the discussion with a "well, screw you" response. The worst of it is, this begins to happen just as the puzzles start to become monotonous, which is precisely when you want the storyline to pick up the slack.
In defense of the game, the start was well-paced, and the learning curve was appropriate. The most enjoyable aspect of the game was exploration: there's plenty to see and read, and there was satisfaction and intrigue as your character progresses and learns more about the world he is in and what the backstory is. It could be worth playing, although I'd only buy it on sale, and I'd recommend taking plenty of breaks. Also, if it's starts to become tedious, don't bother finishing it. I wish I had the ten or so hours I spent completing the game back, and had just watched the endings on youtube instead.

In terms of gameplay style, this is very much like Battlefield. Several classes, all with unique perks (medkits, ammo resupply, turrets, anti-vehicle weapons, cloaking, jetpacks, and more), as well as ground vehicles and air vehicles made for either transportion and combat, and one of them even acts like a tanky spawn point for spawing in for battles so you don't have to walk all over or drive to where the fighting is.
The unique aspects of Planetside 2 come from the faction system and the continents present in the game. Every faction is unique in just about every aspect, from voices available, to armor, weapons and weapon functions, and even the sound they make when you coak as an infiltrator. Each faction fights for control of the continents on the planet, and after any faction reaches 15 VP (Victory Points)  on one continent, that continent is locked down and they gain a passive buff, such as health regeneration or reduced cost for air/ground vehicles. Only two continents can get locked down at a time, and they eventually unlock to be fought over once more. Battles in this game are huge, and can get VERY hectic, so expect your FPS to drop pretty fast once the fighting starts getting bigger and bigger (the game is pretty optimized though!)
Being a F2P shooter, one might expect that its pay to win but thankfully its far from it. The progression in this game doesn't change whether you pay or don't, it only becomes faster. All weapons in this game are considered side-grades, that are only bought to complement a specific playstyle rather than be a straight buff to damage or handling. While you can buy weapons with cash rather than certs, all of it is easily obtainble by just playing. You can get by in this game with just the default weapons with a few attachments of your choosing and do just fine. You buy weapons and attachments with certs, which are also used to upgrade a class of your choosing. The upgrades can be passive, like resistance to infantry arms to reduce damage, increased ammo storage, or quicker shield regen. Active upgrades, such as the jump jets for the Light Assault, allow the class to manuever in air with less downtime at higher ranks and quicker regeneration; or the Heavy Assault to get an extras shield ability that allows them to mitigate more damage.
The game lacks a proper tutorial, however, which is sort of the downfall of it. Even the Koltyr planet, meant for newbies, doesn't seem to do much as they encourage you to simply hop into battle. Still, the game is basic enough and there are plenty of guides out there to help familarize yourself with classes, their abilities, and much more. This review only glosses over some of the things in this game, there is still quite a bit of things here like base building/construction, vehicle progression (they also take certs and can be specialized!), customization, etc.

Let me start off by saying that Age of Empires II is one of my favorite games of all time.
I never played it as a kid. Matter of fact, a friend of mine bought me a copy of it about 2 or 3 years ago and we played one or two games. It was fun, but I never really picked it back up after that because I didn't think I'd like playing solo.
Fast forward to about 3 or 4 months ago, and I am playing this game nonstop. I don't know exactly what it is. Maybe it's just the sheer replayability, or if it's the pick up and play style, but this game keeps me entirely entertained for hours a day.
Pros:
- Incredibly easy to learn, and you will find yourself getting signifigantly better with each game.
- Different every time you play, considering Civ bonuses and random maps
- Flawless steam integration
- Decently active multiplayer, despite being a decade and a half old
- Steam Workshop support
- Low-end, so it will run on damn near any machine; no matter how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ your 8 year old compaq is
- Just plain fun
Cons:
- Graphics are a bit outdated, but there are high-res Texture packs in the workshop that aim to fix that.
- Most popular multiplayer games are against people who are going to be a lot better than you. You will lose. (Better to play with friends if you're new)
- Slightly unbalnced civs. Sometimes when you do random civs, you'll get one who's bonus is just trash, so I recommend picking a specific one. (The Huns get +20 production speed on mounted units /winkeyface)
All in all, a fantastic title, worth every penny, and I'd reccomend it as a great start into the RTS world if you've never played; and if you like RTS games, then you propbably already have this game.  9.5/10

A third-person shooter featuring Max Payne and his trademark "slow motion" action, set in a crime dominated Brazil (not very far from the truth, unfortunately).
Unlike other games in the series, Max Payne 3 attempts to address social issues instead of the main character’s personal issues, such as police violence, the gap between the rich and the poor and drug trafficking in Brazil.
Here, the rich try to live the American life style, while the poor are slaughtered. Payne witnesses a favela raid and a prison riot, in scenes reminiscent of some Brazilian movies like "City of God", "Carandiru" and "Elite Squad".
Even after facing a satanic cult, Max Payne is still surprised by the violence of the Brazilian police. In this game, the police are the real enemy, not the gangsters. The police are involved in the most heinous crimes, with the support of a corrupt politician.
The game features a São Paulo dominated by organized and disorganized crime. A Brazil that worships soccer, where poor people are killed by the police, while the rich are vying with each other through drug watered parties. Is this so far from reality?
There are two interesting characters: the American ex-cop who does volunteer work in Brazil, and the sex tourist. Both sides of the relationship between Brazilians and Americans. But in the end, Payne is the hero. Not unlike any american action movie, after all.

PREFACE: This game is NOT pay to win! Don't believe the lies! More on this below.
Planetside 2 is unlike any other gaming experience you've ever had.
There's a reason why so many people say that Planetside 2 ruined every other online FPS game for them. Nothing comes even close to the scale this game provides and to the many playstyles it has to offer.
Imagine your favourite Battlefield title, only with incomparably larger maps (we call them continents) and up to 1000 players wreaking havoc across them in more ways than you can count.
You can try and capture enemy bases in an organized attack with dozens of your friends while preventing the enemies from snatching your own territory in return. You can harvest resources and build outposts. You can even just have some casual fun blowing stuff up. But however you choose to play the game, you will be having the most epic fights of any FPS game out there.
Whether you want to focus on infantry or vehicular combat, the game has you covered.
You can be a dedicated sniper/recon, a medic, an engineer, a sturdy heavy assault or a jetpack-toting light assault that can ignore many obstacles and surprise enemies with their pants down. You can even climb into a MAX, an exo suit designed to absorb lots of damage and break a stalemate. The infantry play greatly rewards skill and accuracy, with a big emphasis on burst firing, headshots, positioning and awareness.
Are you a tank buff? Look no further: depending on your choice of faction you gain access to 3 unique two-man tanks, each with its own strengths and weaknesses, all featuring projectile drop and giving you much room to grow in skill. A good tank crew can have a massive impact on the battlefield.
Are you a fan of aircraft? Planetside provides several, from the light empire specific fighters, which work like a cross between a jet and a helicopter, allowing for every manoeuvre you can think of, to the powerful 3-man liberators and larger 6 and 12 man transport ships. Whether you're looking to provide air support to your faction, or simply scour the skies looking for enemy air to engage, you're sure to have fun, epic battles.
There are also lighter, one-man tanks, 3-man buggies and an ATV, which can be equipped with an invisibility cloak for surprise attacks and stealthy passage through enemy territory.
There is so much depth to this videogame that you can literally play it for thousands of hours without ever getting bored of it, since you can keep rotating through the many different playstyles available in order to keep it fresh. Really, Planetside 2 is like several solid games packaged into one, and all of it FOR FREE.
There are some who will argue that the game is P2W but if you pay attention you'll notice that most of them have barely played the game for any substantial length of time. What they are experiencing is simply the learning curve of the game, which is admittedly a bit tough at first, but rather than allowing time for their skill to mature they chalk it up to premium items/features. THIS IS FALSE. The only payed-for exclusives are purely cosmetic. Everything else, you can obtain at a reasonable pace through playing the game. I should know. I never spent any money on it.
Do yourself a favour and try this game out. Have patience, look for tutorials, ask for tips whenever you get the chance. Once you're through the baptism by fire that all of us have gone through you'll start having crazy amounts of fun!

Valve Software’s brain-loosening puzzle-platformer Portal 2 came out aaaaaall the way back in April of 2011, but the developer has continued to support it through add-ons like free downloadable content (DLC) and a level editor for the PC version. This month, PlayStation 3 owners who sprang (or fell, depending on how you feel about it) for a Move motion controller received their special Valve time with the release of the platform-exclusive DLC, Portal 2 In Motion.
----------
WHAT YOU’LL LIKE
Cool new mechanics…
After you pick up an item, you can hold out your Move to activate One-to-One, which you can use to rotate objects in real time (hence “one-to-one”) by turning your controller.  You can also get boxes across gaps, through holes in walls, and around obstacles. It has a bit of a learning curve, but it makes sense and feels natural once you’ve done it a few times.
Portal Surfing lets you grab a portal you’ve already placed and drag it along a wall or rotate it. I didn’t see its value at first, but then I learned that the game knows which side of the hole is “down,” which means that you can reorient portals to do things like launch Repulsion Gel across a room by turning the portal upside down or accessing a hard-to reach spot by turning the portal sideways and sliding it into a narrow space that you wouldn’t normally be able to fire at. On a more basic and functional level, though, Portal Surfing is a quick and easy way to fix those times when your placement is just a little bit off.
Scaling allows you to resize a crate to hit two buttons simultaneously or make a giant, heavy box to break through a glass floor. It’s also a really cruel way to destroy a turret. Scaling also presents some interesting new possibilities for puzzles; in one room, I had one box that I had to use to hit three switches. The solution involves stretching the square crate into a rectangle and extending it through different portals. It required the kind of weirdo lateral thinking that we’ve come to expect from Portal games, and the “A-ha” moment when I figured it out was as satisfying as any in the main game.
Of the three additions to your scientific arsenal, One-to-One is by far the most ingenious addition for its sheer simplicity and the options it opens up. Adding that third dimension to item handling could have created a depth-perception nightmare, but Sixense deftly avoids that by adding little lights to switches; the lights turn on when a box is over the button. And setting turrets on fire using a laser beam and a reflective cube is extremely satisfying and fun..

Let me start off by saying that Age of Empires II is one of my favorite games of all time.
I never played it as a kid. Matter of fact, a friend of mine bought me a copy of it about 2 or 3 years ago and we played one or two games. It was fun, but I never really picked it back up after that because I didn't think I'd like playing solo.
Fast forward to about 3 or 4 months ago, and I am playing this game nonstop. I don't know exactly what it is. Maybe it's just the sheer replayability, or if it's the pick up and play style, but this game keeps me entirely entertained for hours a day.
Pros:
- Incredibly easy to learn, and you will find yourself getting signifigantly better with each game.
- Different every time you play, considering Civ bonuses and random maps
- Flawless steam integration
- Decently active multiplayer, despite being a decade and a half old
- Steam Workshop support
- Low-end, so it will run on damn near any machine; no matter how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ your 8 year old compaq is
- Just plain fun
Cons:
- Graphics are a bit outdated, but there are high-res Texture packs in the workshop that aim to fix that.
- Most popular multiplayer games are against people who are going to be a lot better than you. You will lose. (Better to play with friends if you're new)
- Slightly unbalnced civs. Sometimes when you do random civs, you'll get one who's bonus is just trash, so I recommend picking a specific one. (The Huns get +20 production speed on mounted units /winkeyface)
All in all, a fantastic title, worth every penny, and I'd reccomend it as a great start into the RTS world if you've never played; and if you like RTS games, then you propbably already have this game.  9.5/10

Killing Nazis is still very, very fun.  But when the dust settles, you're left with a title that has little to no replay value.  Could you play it through again?  Sure, but your experience wouldn't be any different from the first time you played it.  Terribly disappointing in this regard and as such, it's not worth paying full price.  This is a game that you should be able to rent, not own.

I really can't praise this game enough.
I tried playing the earlier Max Payne games but I never got around to actually completing them. I bought the game on 360 the day it came out and had some fun with it. Beating the campaign on Medium and playing an hour of multiplayer. Then nothing else.
I built my PC two months later and that Christmas I bought the game again. Only just this week I managed to actually complete the thing.
And yeah, I did have loads of fun in it. I even had the game on Hard difficulty (It isn't really that hard anyway).
Max Payne 3 is an AMAZING port by Rockstar. I ran the game on High/Very high settings at 60-80 FPS. On a GTX 560.
The gunplay is solid, which makes the game fun. The bullettime is satisfying and mouse controls make the game much easier to use than console controllers(Obviously).
Did I mention that you can get fantastic screenshots from this game from the gameplay? I'm not kidding. Look at my screenshots on this game.
The Multiplayer portion is well, multiplayer. But, it is fully fleshed out. Character customization, custom classes, EVEN BULLETTIME IN MULTIPLAYER. That's pretty cool. Though, I'm not that much of a competitive multiplayer person but I can see why people like it.
The extra modes like New York Minute and Score Attack give the game more replayabillity, making you want to go back and get a platinum on a level.
The only real pain that I have with this game is that the unskippable cutscenes make the game a bit of a drag when you just want to have fun. And sometimes in the final stand mode (or whatever it's called. The one where you kill an enemy and take a painkiller) it can get VERY frustrating when you are blocked near a wall or a door causing you not to be able to see the enemy that you NEED to kill in order to stay alive. So you just slump to the ground and restart the latest checkpoint.
Overall, I think Max Payne 3 is a great game for the price (Usually on sale for $6) and is very fun if you like shooting dudes in style.
The last couple of levels are pretty boring and the ending is poor, but the majority of the story and the gameplay in general live up to the franchise! :) 10/10

This game hurt my sense of reality.
From the moment I first booted up, I sensed that I would have to think WAY too hard about everything.
I was right.
In brief, if you like first-person puzzle games and having to think *way* too hard about moral, philosophical, ethical, and existential choices, this is the game for you. It is an amazing arrangement of game and story elements that is definitely worth experiencing. Not for the weak of heart, Not Safe For Sanity. Took about 50 hours to beat, will take probably another 50 hours to 100% and hunt down all of the easer eggs, of which there are dozens. Well worth the price, if you ask me.
Since this is a first-person puzzle game, invariably the comparison must be drawn between this and the Portal franchise. I would have to say, in my experience, that this was significantly more difficult, not only because of the difficulty of the puzzles, but because of the length of the game in whole.
The gameplay elements introduced are not terribly difficult to understand. Each tool introduced is a fairly simple concept on its own, and the way they interact is fairly obvious and intuitive, yet they are combined into some of the most elaborate skinner boxes I have ever experienced. What is even worse, though, is that the levels that only make use of a single mechanic were somehow infinitely more difficult to wrap my head around, though I think the hardest of the lot still managed to incorporate a couple of tools.
The story elements to this game are a perfect example of the sort of non-interfering plot that I would like to see more of in modern gaming, and hearkens back to a metroidvania style of storytelling. There are no cutscenes (except perhaps in the end, but at that point it's well deserved) and no point during which control is taken away from the player in order to convey the story, but there is a clear story being told, and if you want to learn more, there are dozens of hidden gems, notes, stories, messages, and various other bits of story sprinkled around the environment for you to discover.
I do have a few complaints about this game, but they are very minor.
I found that the tetromino puzzles were incredibly tedious and added nothing to the overall experience except a bit of frustration; I basically brute-forced all of them except the last three (which made neat little symmetrical patterns and thus were easy to figure out) or made my S/O do them for me.
The constant back-and-forth lift riding I think was supposed to also contribute to that 'metroidvania' feel that the game has, but ended up being tedious as well. I guess it was like a glorified loading screen, in a way? I really liked how the environment was designed, but the amount of time it took to go from one area to the next was slightly annoying. Perhaps if I had just fully completed each area in turn it wouldn't have been quite as annoying? Maybe that's why there's an achievement for that...
There are also some elements that I really did like that had basically nothing to do with the gameplay. This will, however, be spoilerific, so if you care about that sort of thing, I will summarise to "I really like the characters.".
*** SPOILERS START HERE ***
I really appreciated the diversity of the cast of characters portrayed in the nuggets of information strewn about the various archival computers. The 'protagonist', Alex, is a female working in STEM, which is fantastic, and many of the other characters are from various ethnic and cultural backgrounds, including two (presumed) male characters who are in a relationship.
The backdrop of the whole story, that there's some kind of illness wiping out all humans, is both tragic and extremely heartwarming. The severity of the situation brings people together, and in humanity's last few moments, reflects an ideal society we all would like to see. It makes me afraid and contemplative and worried and all kinds of things, because it made me think about mortality, which is... I don't know... probably good. I like things that make me think.
Finally, the fact that, between every character making assertions about how the world works... I just... I couldn't even figure out what was going on. What do you do when your options are to side with a liar or side with someone lying by ommission? I'm glad I stuck to my guns, which ended up being "everyone is wrong", because it turned out that Milton was *just* cynical and not especially helpful, but EL-0 HIM was just infinitely full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Everyone was wrong except me, and maybe that's not the best lesson, but I sure as hell liked it... or at least my ego did.
Maybe I'll update this in a week or so once I've had some time to digest things a bit more.

I have a bit over 1000 hours in this game now. I have to say it really is a great game for the princely sum of free (and would easily be if they actually charged for it upfront imo).
I want to get this out of the way as a player with a lot of time in this game because this is the big question: It really is not pay 2 win, which most "freemium" games do turn out to be, but theyve struck a good balance with this one. All the stuff that affects gameplay can be earned with time/XP, absolutely nothing like that is locked behind a hard paywall, and even then disregarding general knowledge of the game, a skilled FPS player could come in cold and hold thier own using the default guns for the most part, MAYBE youd want to get a 2x scope for your default rifle ASAP to replace the iron sights but thats only 30 certs, about 45 mins of playing if you dont know what youre doing. This is the way ive been playing actually, the only money ive spent has been a nominal sum on a small number of cosmetics, just to show some love and keep the game running. The biggest "hump" you will encounter in this game is always regarding mere knowledge and skill, never financial. Its the same for all large scale games, its just wholly up to you to git gud. Now with that cleared up...
A big problem with this game was it was billed as combined armed continent sized warfare, and it is that, but more often than not it played like a nutso 100v100 deathmatch/KOTH FPS game. That has finally changed now with the release of the content update that lets you construct and defend your very own bases, seperate from the permanent bases scattered around. Now this game is feeling more like a warfare sim and not just a giant deathmatch bash. Its the closest thing to a relaunch this game is likely to get i think, and its a good one.
One last thing, i challenge you not to grin the first time you find yourself advancing as a bloody battalion of 150+ players and steamrolling a base all the way to a capture, then moving on and doing it again until you face a force that can stop you. No other shooter game can come close to what this game can do.

Has anyone here seen the movie John Wick? How about Dredd? The Raid? Because this game represents everything that is great about those movies. The plot is simple. Not bad, or stupid, just simple. It exists for one reason; to drive the action from set piece to set piece, and make you hate the villain. And it works. Wolfenstien: The New Order gives the player a wonderful variety of ways to work through each set piece, which are all sprinkled with a good variety of enemies. The levels avoid many of the standard FPS level settings, and each provide a new set of visuals and obstacles to work around. The weapons each have great sound and visual design, and all feel great to fire. The writing is surprisingly solid, as is the voice acting. I have trouble suggesting this game at the full sixty dollar price, but at forty dollars it is a very easy to suggest to any fan of single player FPS.

This game hurt my sense of reality.
From the moment I first booted up, I sensed that I would have to think WAY too hard about everything.
I was right.
In brief, if you like first-person puzzle games and having to think *way* too hard about moral, philosophical, ethical, and existential choices, this is the game for you. It is an amazing arrangement of game and story elements that is definitely worth experiencing. Not for the weak of heart, Not Safe For Sanity. Took about 50 hours to beat, will take probably another 50 hours to 100% and hunt down all of the easer eggs, of which there are dozens. Well worth the price, if you ask me.
Since this is a first-person puzzle game, invariably the comparison must be drawn between this and the Portal franchise. I would have to say, in my experience, that this was significantly more difficult, not only because of the difficulty of the puzzles, but because of the length of the game in whole.
The gameplay elements introduced are not terribly difficult to understand. Each tool introduced is a fairly simple concept on its own, and the way they interact is fairly obvious and intuitive, yet they are combined into some of the most elaborate skinner boxes I have ever experienced. What is even worse, though, is that the levels that only make use of a single mechanic were somehow infinitely more difficult to wrap my head around, though I think the hardest of the lot still managed to incorporate a couple of tools.
The story elements to this game are a perfect example of the sort of non-interfering plot that I would like to see more of in modern gaming, and hearkens back to a metroidvania style of storytelling. There are no cutscenes (except perhaps in the end, but at that point it's well deserved) and no point during which control is taken away from the player in order to convey the story, but there is a clear story being told, and if you want to learn more, there are dozens of hidden gems, notes, stories, messages, and various other bits of story sprinkled around the environment for you to discover.
I do have a few complaints about this game, but they are very minor.
I found that the tetromino puzzles were incredibly tedious and added nothing to the overall experience except a bit of frustration; I basically brute-forced all of them except the last three (which made neat little symmetrical patterns and thus were easy to figure out) or made my S/O do them for me.
The constant back-and-forth lift riding I think was supposed to also contribute to that 'metroidvania' feel that the game has, but ended up being tedious as well. I guess it was like a glorified loading screen, in a way? I really liked how the environment was designed, but the amount of time it took to go from one area to the next was slightly annoying. Perhaps if I had just fully completed each area in turn it wouldn't have been quite as annoying? Maybe that's why there's an achievement for that...
There are also some elements that I really did like that had basically nothing to do with the gameplay. This will, however, be spoilerific, so if you care about that sort of thing, I will summarise to "I really like the characters.".
*** SPOILERS START HERE ***
I really appreciated the diversity of the cast of characters portrayed in the nuggets of information strewn about the various archival computers. The 'protagonist', Alex, is a female working in STEM, which is fantastic, and many of the other characters are from various ethnic and cultural backgrounds, including two (presumed) male characters who are in a relationship.
The backdrop of the whole story, that there's some kind of illness wiping out all humans, is both tragic and extremely heartwarming. The severity of the situation brings people together, and in humanity's last few moments, reflects an ideal society we all would like to see. It makes me afraid and contemplative and worried and all kinds of things, because it made me think about mortality, which is... I don't know... probably good. I like things that make me think.
Finally, the fact that, between every character making assertions about how the world works... I just... I couldn't even figure out what was going on. What do you do when your options are to side with a liar or side with someone lying by ommission? I'm glad I stuck to my guns, which ended up being "everyone is wrong", because it turned out that Milton was *just* cynical and not especially helpful, but EL-0 HIM was just infinitely full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Everyone was wrong except me, and maybe that's not the best lesson, but I sure as hell liked it... or at least my ego did.
Maybe I'll update this in a week or so once I've had some time to digest things a bit more.

I have a bit over 1000 hours in this game now. I have to say it really is a great game for the princely sum of free (and would easily be if they actually charged for it upfront imo).
I want to get this out of the way as a player with a lot of time in this game because this is the big question: It really is not pay 2 win, which most "freemium" games do turn out to be, but theyve struck a good balance with this one. All the stuff that affects gameplay can be earned with time/XP, absolutely nothing like that is locked behind a hard paywall, and even then disregarding general knowledge of the game, a skilled FPS player could come in cold and hold thier own using the default guns for the most part, MAYBE youd want to get a 2x scope for your default rifle ASAP to replace the iron sights but thats only 30 certs, about 45 mins of playing if you dont know what youre doing. This is the way ive been playing actually, the only money ive spent has been a nominal sum on a small number of cosmetics, just to show some love and keep the game running. The biggest "hump" you will encounter in this game is always regarding mere knowledge and skill, never financial. Its the same for all large scale games, its just wholly up to you to git gud. Now with that cleared up...
A big problem with this game was it was billed as combined armed continent sized warfare, and it is that, but more often than not it played like a nutso 100v100 deathmatch/KOTH FPS game. That has finally changed now with the release of the content update that lets you construct and defend your very own bases, seperate from the permanent bases scattered around. Now this game is feeling more like a warfare sim and not just a giant deathmatch bash. Its the closest thing to a relaunch this game is likely to get i think, and its a good one.
One last thing, i challenge you not to grin the first time you find yourself advancing as a bloody battalion of 150+ players and steamrolling a base all the way to a capture, then moving on and doing it again until you face a force that can stop you. No other shooter game can come close to what this game can do.

So, here I am, writing another review.
Castle Crashers is a 4-player coop side-scrolling 2.5d brawler game, cooked up by The Behemoth, ex-newgrounders and creators of Battleblock Theater.
You play as a knight (or one of the many unlockable characters, ranging from skeletons and fire demons to aliens and ninja pirates), sent out by the somewhat cowardly king to rescue his 4 daughters, as well as a magical crystal, which were captured by the Evil Wizard. On your journey you will have to fight your way through hordes of barbarians, polar bears, fishmen and an assortment of other enemies (many of which you can later play as), as well as a number of powerful bosses. You can do this alone, or with up to 3 friends, online or through LAN. Then, if you complete the campaign, you can enter Insane Mode - essentially a repeat of the campaign, but with new weapons (also, all the enemies' stats are multiplied by 10).
Finally, there's several multiplayer modes, such as Arena (which is actually a number of different competitive gamemodes, most of which feature you beating up your friends), or All You can Quaff (in which you have to eat a number of different foods faster than your friends do).
In short, a really fun game to play with your friends.
I rate this 9/10 (one point deduction because the characters are somewhat unblanced)

After what seems like an eternity since “id” (id Software) created the first true First Person Shooter with Wolfenstein 3D back in 1992. Can the FPS Masters of ‘id’ pull off another cult classic? their resume is quiet extensive with other popular titles like Quake and Doom under their belt, they are no strangers to building a great First Person Shooter and the New Edition Wolfenstein: The New Order is sure to not disappoint.
Passing the development duties to MachineGames and published by Bethesda Softworks, Wolfenstein: The New Order is set in an alternative history in the 1960’s where Nazi Germany Won the Second World War. You play a War Veteran William “BJ” Blazkowicz who you may know is the same identity and character look from the original Wolfenstein 3D.
The Story line while segmented into chapters, shows the fight against the Nazi War Machine. Three years after the events in Wolfenstein (1992), the Nazis have developed advanced technologies which enabled them to turn the tide of war against the allies. You join the Resistance and within critical missions you undertake and bring down the Nazi war.
An immersive experience all round, From holding twin giant machine guns to scaling the side of a tower. The difficulty settings will test your skills, and keep you on your feet. While Wolfenstein: the New Order is a more modern take on the cult classic it does it justice and even builds on the already ever popular franchise.

Rockstar proves to be a worthy successor of Remedy and returns with Max Payne 3 for an exceptional experience in the saga which we all love. Leaving New York, Max moves to Sao Paolo to start a new life, but he quickly gets into a huge trouble and needs to do things in the Max way.
The story and the narration (specially the voiceover) are exceptional and really fun to listen. The script is clever and Max has some really good lines. It’s almost like reading a very good book, except the shooting of many-many bad guys. This might be a problem for some FPS lovers who do not like the frequent interruption of long narrations between action sequences, but for me it worked great.
Beside that the action itself is greatly polished and smooth. Bullet time works just as in Max Payne 1 and it is very fun to use, and necessary to use to remain alive. There are many type of weapons, guns which most of them you can dual-wield and there is also a neat cover system to enhance the action. Grenades can be only used in Multiplayer, and there are NO additional tools or gear you could use (like bulletproof vest or knifes for melee).
The game is beautiful and highly detailed with care which is Rockstar’s strength. The map design is amazing with the detailed interiors, makes the world really alive and immersive.
There is also multiplayer with deathmatch and some survivor co-op missions (which are fun) but we all know that this game is played for the single player experience. And in that part, this game did incredibly well.  More co-op missions with story elements could be good though.
This game is a true gem in the TPS library of games and an exceptional story which everyone needs to see and play. I have replayed it for the 2nd time just to be part of the story again. May Payne is the man.

You truely are a creature wandering through someone else's creation. Everything is new, everything is mysterious. Curiousity is overwhelming and you have freedom, yet feel like some omniscient being is continuously guiding your fate from within you.
The game starts. A deep, booming voice calls on me and begins giving me information about the ruins i see around me. I run around, find a puzzle. Perfect! A goal to work towards! computer script comes on the screen performing "logic checks".
Half hour in, I find a computer on a thin pedestal. After talking to a mysterious digital intelligence, I find a letter from my dad telling me that the world does not come with an instruction manual. Another is an excerpt from "Athena in the Garden of Hisperides."
Ten munites later, I'm wandering through an island of ruins and come upon what seems to be a holographic replica of my own robotic form. It runs, seeimingly aimlessly. I follow it out of sheer curiousity. It stops. It bursts into a cloud of binary digits.
I have played this game for an hour at this point. I have had goosebumps the entire time. This is a game like no other. There are puzzels to keep you focused on a goal, but plenty of time for free reign and exploration. It has already raised so many questions for me and is beyond stimulating.
WHEN you buy this game, allow yourself to be overcome by curiousity. The gothic singing in the background will help you with that mood. While many games may be great for action or graphics, this game is great because it makes you think. It takes your brain and throws questions at it, leaving you trembling. If that is not what you look for in a video game, you should seriously reconsider your criteria.
Comparing this game to Portal is very difficult. Portal is much more guided and explained, and the focus on the puzzles is much more prominent. The Talos Principle is centered around philosophic questions, and puzzles exist simply as decorations that fit seamlessly into the vast and awe-inspiring landscape of the rest of the game.

Wolfenstein: The New Order takes you to an intriguing, disturbing world where Nazis hold unquestioned authority. A small pocket of resistance fighters desperately clings on to hope in their midst, and you are instrumental to their struggle.
There is no multiplayer mode, and the game is all the better for it. Machine Games have focused all their effort on producing a stunning campaign of Nazi-fighting chaos. The gunplay feels fantastic, the perks and collectibles are fun to get, and the story is more compelling than it has any right to be. Who would have thought that a game with literal Nazi space robots could elicit such emotion from the player?
I can't think of anything I would change in this game. My issues with it are entirely technical in nature. The game has pretty intense system requirements, so make sure your computer can handle it, and that you have 45 gigabytes (really, now?) available on your drive.

If you played and enjoyed Project Reality you will love this game it has the exact same feel because it's the exact same dev team but in a modern engine. I am so pumped about the future of this game once they finish implementing the rest of the road map.
The immersion is fantastic you really feel on edge the entire time and almost phyiscally duck your head as bullets crack over the top of you. Being hit makes you cry out over VOIP for a medic so they can prevent your immediate death from bleeding out. Taking objectives requires teamwork and tactics and squads that can perform well together will really shine.
The biggest draw for me is how realistic tactics like flanking, supression fire, suprise attacks and cover really are completely effectively compared to any other class of shooter where rate of spawn and volume of fire are the only considerations. But yet it remains action packed and fast paced unlike the Arma series which has always felt clunky and almost boring in comparison.

My very first impression of The Talos Principle, like many others was that it has a huge Portal influence but as I played in it becomes clear that it may have Portal's beloved environmental first person puzzle mechanics but it's also so much more and unwise to harshly compare the two.
It's a game that outdoes itself, standing taller on it's own than Portal; containing many thrills for those who wish to delve deeper into the philosophy tidbits and escape the comic relief of the Portal games for something a bit more grown up. The comedy is still totally available though, because Croteam thought of
too with the Serious Sam DLC.
This game feels like a journey made just for you but that's just because The Talos Principle is insanely well crafted and I say crafted not made because it obviously takes some skill to create something so polished on every front. From the impeccable controls, to the beautiful puzzle scapes, to the smart voice acting and to the clever puzzles themselves. This is a title that virtually leads you down the garden path to mental satisfaction.
Length wise it's perfect; just enough that you're satisfied but also left with a small stinging disappointment that it's all over, enough to bring you back for perhaps a second installment.
In short I'm very impressed. The Talos Principle is a work that catapults environmental puzzle games back into the limelight and is genuinely a piece that anyone can enjoy.
