Valve Software’s brain-loosening puzzle-platformer Portal 2 came out aaaaaall the way back in April of 2011, but the developer has continued to support it through add-ons like free downloadable content (DLC) and a level editor for the PC version. This month, PlayStation 3 owners who sprang (or fell, depending on how you feel about it) for a Move motion controller received their special Valve time with the release of the platform-exclusive DLC, Portal 2 In Motion.
----------
WHAT YOU’LL LIKE
Cool new mechanics…
After you pick up an item, you can hold out your Move to activate One-to-One, which you can use to rotate objects in real time (hence “one-to-one”) by turning your controller.  You can also get boxes across gaps, through holes in walls, and around obstacles. It has a bit of a learning curve, but it makes sense and feels natural once you’ve done it a few times.
Portal Surfing lets you grab a portal you’ve already placed and drag it along a wall or rotate it. I didn’t see its value at first, but then I learned that the game knows which side of the hole is “down,” which means that you can reorient portals to do things like launch Repulsion Gel across a room by turning the portal upside down or accessing a hard-to reach spot by turning the portal sideways and sliding it into a narrow space that you wouldn’t normally be able to fire at. On a more basic and functional level, though, Portal Surfing is a quick and easy way to fix those times when your placement is just a little bit off.
Scaling allows you to resize a crate to hit two buttons simultaneously or make a giant, heavy box to break through a glass floor. It’s also a really cruel way to destroy a turret. Scaling also presents some interesting new possibilities for puzzles; in one room, I had one box that I had to use to hit three switches. The solution involves stretching the square crate into a rectangle and extending it through different portals. It required the kind of weirdo lateral thinking that we’ve come to expect from Portal games, and the “A-ha” moment when I figured it out was as satisfying as any in the main game.
Of the three additions to your scientific arsenal, One-to-One is by far the most ingenious addition for its sheer simplicity and the options it opens up. Adding that third dimension to item handling could have created a depth-perception nightmare, but Sixense deftly avoids that by adding little lights to switches; the lights turn on when a box is over the button. And setting turrets on fire using a laser beam and a reflective cube is extremely satisfying and fun..

At the bottom of this review contains a message to the developers regarding gameplay mechanics.
----
Squad is one of the next big military simulator based shooter games that's working through its Alpha stages. It's current build is still in test phases, yet already offers intense gameplay with an incredible amount of potential, especially since this game as a somewhat direct response to the limitations to project reality, a milsim modification.
Such a feat for a great game also lies within the community that plays it. For the most part, everyone seems to be fully immersed into the environment, a handful of maps with only a few specific locations for objectives, yet has miles and miles of details, distant houses and rolling hills, settlements and farms. This tells you immediately the ambitions of the developers and how much they want to expand this game into having enormous amounts of content in the future. The players, are able to tactfully (or not) navigate around these expansive terrains and establish forward operating bases so that other players may spawn in that location, or a rally point so your squad specifically can have a limited time to assist your squad leader.
All of these features are a direct result of player communication and teamwork. A good squad will always keep their head in the game and keep each other updated, and learn the game more. With a realistic environment and sense of danger, you are able to put yourself in a position where you play into the game’s world, making it all the more an energetic rush of adrenalin and fear.
Please don’t become Interstellar Marines, you have the potential to make this into such a great product that you guys will be sitting on mountains of cash, you probably feel that way already. The only downfall is that you guys have to stop those idiots using smoke grenade exploits and that “lost connection to host” anomaly that kicks you out of your game every so often, bordering on “occasional”.
Another qualm that I am sure will be figured out soon is a way to keep people working as a team and stop with the MLG pro counterstrike tier combat. Finally, a favorites system would be so helpful for singling out the best servers for players so they don’t have to go through server listings on the other side of the planet where ping is just nonexistent.
A serious rating from me personally? 8/10.
One point for connection problems and a few glitches, other point due to a small fraction of the community bending the direction of the approach this game is meant to have, either by not being a team player, or trolling, exploits, making fun of people that are immersed and taking it “seriously”.
Message to developers:
I've noticed something that you should consider looking into. For me, aiming isn't necessarily a problem, but when I am firing at a target at two hundred meters, moving the scope a single centimeter doesn't really have a smooth transition, it has this minor, blocky flick to the next pixel and that makes it extremely hard to get it lined up with my target. I understand that it should be difficult to aim, but this minor thing really throws me off when I am taking down targets.

It would make a huge difference for many that really do try to legitimately line up shots rather than relying on unfounded casual shooter skills.

Having not watched any gameplay nor even read any reviews, Wolfenstein was a game I had next to no information on before diving right in. I had one recommendation from a friend that coaxed me in to giving this a try. And of course knowing the original was already enough to have me interested.
The intro had me a little worried at first I was playing the next COD game and hadn't realised. This soon passed however, and wait, what? Robots? ROBOTS!? I missed that part in my history classes! Like I said, I hadn't watched or read much of anything before playing and well, it showed.
The game is larger than life as it takes on this alternative reality where Nazis rule the earth. The game stays somewhat faithful to the original with it's use of health packs. I had feared the game would go down the Halo route and give a two-gun cycle. It doesn't. You have a nice selection of guns at your disposal with a nice secondary fire function to boot. In fact it also lets you duel wield two massive shotguns. Hurrah!
It does bring in a shallow form of stealth which in a lot of cases is too easy. On occasion it felt like a bullet to a guy's wrist would kill him instantly. I would say some sections were baffingingly easy but other parts were definitely a challenge. The end boss anyone?
The story was unexpected too. The characters had a lot more depth to them than I'd anticipated. It also encourages a second play through for those who didn't save Fergus. WHO WOULDN'T SAVE FERGUS ANYWAY?
The gun cutter was brilliant. How I wish Alien: Isolation had a gun like that...

Sorry, I just cannot recommend this game for the full price. for 5 it's a bargain, for 10 it's okay. For 20 it makes me wish Steam had a better return policy.

After a few days playing, I will gladly give Wolfenstein: The New Order top marks for being a proper Wolfenstein game, a proper alternate history game, and a slightly jarring murderfest. Recommended.

The Good:
- Raises some interesting philosophical questions about society and evolution.
- Solid puzzler, nothing special, but it's there.
- Interesting storyline that makes you want to explore the world and seek out information that are not neccesarily required to forward the story. This is probably the games strongest point.
- Interesting personalities within the game.
Things that can be improved:
- I'm happy to see the developers incorporate some semi-deep philosophy into the game. But the implementation of it should have had some more thought put into it. For example: The player is often stuck in philosophical discussions with other personalities/intelligences in the game where the other part presents the player with a philosophical question and the player responds with one of four replies. This is very frustrating since the responses are extremely specific and allows for no interpretations leading to the player not feeling satisifed with his/her options. It would have been better if the responses were more general and allowed for more interpretation. Better yet would have been if the player did not respond in words at all, but in action instead. An action can have a billion reasons behind it, but a phrase is more limited.
- The puzzles are solid, no question about that, but they do not stand out above other puzzle-games. Once you get the hang of how the designer thinks, it's basicly just a treadmill to the endgame. Sure there are some "extra" hidden puzzles, but frankly, the same idea applies there. It feels like someone thought "Ok, we need something more difficult, so instead of doing A, we're going to do B to throw the player off". But once you figure out how the "extra" puzzles work, then again, it's just a treadmill, the only slightly hard part is to actually FIND the puzzle (or more specific, find out where you want to go).
In short:
- Decent puzzle gameplay, somewhat mediocre. Great storyline with a lot of interesting ideas and philosophies. Probably would have been a better book than a game.
Is it worth it?
- It is NOT worth the current pricetag of 39.99 if you only want the puzzle-element of the game.
- It MIGHT be worth 39.99 if you want a somewhat deep and interesting philosophical storyline (you'd have to be pretty damned starved for philosophy though).
I got it on sale for 19.99, and i think it was a good buy. I might even have bought it for 29.99.
That being said. I do hope to see more from these developers. And i definetly hope they stick to the philosophical stuff.

Overall the game is pretty solid, for a eailer release game. You can really play throught it and enjoy yourself. My main issue was the lag spikes but with the newest christmas eve patch they seem to have fixed that.
Pros: Sounds are A++ one of the best sound packages for any FPS on the market. The noise of the round cracking when it gets close to your head, or when other players are shooting around you sounds extremely authentic. Even when you shoot inside a room, the sound changes pitch.
Weapons calibration seems pretty dead on, US military trains to hit targets up to 300 meters away, most engagements in game are any where between 25 and 150 meters which brings into account accuracy.
Realism, Round count is key since you don't have a counter on your HUD, reloading is also a manual task when your magazine is empty as it is in real life.
Teamwork is everything, you can get massive kills and still maintain the same score if killing the enemy isnt nesscary to the mission.
Cons:
The most annoying part of the game wasn't the game itself, it was finding a server to play the game on. I wanted the full experience with the most number of players as possible, But, I also wanted the low FPS that I know I can handle, the problem was, not enough servers of my choosing,
It would be nice if there was a auto join feater on top of the manual choosing server to facilitate with finding the best server for you.
Maybe a dedicated section for Squads to train, I understand there is a training map but maybe a area where squads can work on military battle drills.
More specifc roles in the squd, The ability to have teamleaders would help out immensely at Base construction and would also take the place of squad leader when the SL falls.
better mapping system, using a military style MLGS grid system similar to ARMA 3 lay out would make it easier in identifying targets
All and all its a great game and in a year time this game will be more polished and will only get better.

A very polished and fun FPS experience but if you were expecting something innovative or new, you won't find it in Wolfenstein: The New Order. It nails down the core elements of what makes a good FPS: great visuals and audio, weighty guns that sound and feel great, enemies with a solid (but not spectacular) AI, somewhat linear but well executed level design, and an adequate challenge level.
It also adds something few FPS games feature and that's a captivating setting and story. Even if, like me, you're not the biggest fan of the FPS genre, the story and characters will keep your interest throughout the entire 8 hour campaign. There is little else to do after the story aside from replaying the campaign. No multiplayer or post-campaign gameplay here, and I'm perfectly fine with that but it does leave little value in terms of replayability, something to keep in mind if you plan the buy the game at full price.

Admittedly, I've only played the game for a pretty short time in comparison to some of the other players out there, but I think I've had enough of an experience to write a pretty accurate review.
This game was once a pretty decent F2P with a relatively unique concept of 'build your robot, use it to combat others' creations' that got me hooked early on. The maps were a little lacking, but offered a satisfying amount of strategy, such as where to set up if you were going to take a sentry-styled defence, what overhangs or mountains you could use to take cover from airborne units, and so on. It was a little tedious to grind for components to build bigger, better robots, but it was on a level where you wouldn't lose all enjoyment in the game to get that piece for your project. Premium was little more than a way of supporting the devs and getting some bonus colours for your robot, and helping your entire team to gain a little extra XP. There was little importance in designing any other kind of robot that wasn't a small glass cannon or a massive punching bag with tens of guns, but as it was early access I figured it may evolve further down the track.
At 10 hours, I completed a deal for a short period of premium and a unique robot. However, the game couldn't handle me having weapons above my level, and so I was pushed up to level 88, where I was now being matched with far more experienced players with better gear, and couldn't compete with my lack of currency that would have been accumulated in the grind. And so the game was pushed into the corner to gather dust.
Then today I saw a new update had come out, and decided to wipe away the cobwebs and give it another go, hoping that there may have been a change to skill-based matchings. What I found was shocking, to say the least.
Immediately I had my suspicions when I was greeted with a log-in crate bonus, where half the items awarded were locked behind a premium pay wall. I shrugged it off as just another incentive to get premium, and proceeded to look over my old ship. gave it a little bit of a re-design and messed around with the new equipment screens to get accustomed to them, and the new currency. Thought it was incredibly annoying that the sell value of pieces I already had was, what, about 10% of the buy price? Unless of course you had premium, then you would get 3x as much from selling. But again, I gave the game the benefit of the doubt and figured I was being encouraged to play for my pieces, rather than sell any junk from the crates. I hopped into a game, and finally realised that it was everything I was trying to deny.
The game before had been very encouraging of paying for benefits, but now it is nothing but a cash grab. The updates that have come out since my last playing upon closer inspection only seem to benefit premium players, and not ACTUALLY enhance the experience for all unless you had handed over a bunch of cash. Unique pieces with OP effects such as a 'blink' feaure, tracking missiles etc., were only available if you were willing to either grind for countless hours or hand over another wad of money. Premium players also gain XP twice as fast as their non-premium counterparts, rather than their commitment benefitting their team. There have been no updates to strategy, it's still either tank through everything or create a tiny OP plane to obliterate the opposition. As stated earlier, the loot in crates is half-blocked behind a pay wall, and selling prices for junk is tripled if you've given money to these uncaring devs that now only design new content for premium players who continue to throw money at them.
Normally I don't write reviews. As a matter of fact, this is my first, and was sparked from the disappointment I now have in this game that once had so much potential. By all means, try it out for yourself if you want to, but I cannot recommend it to anyone. I don't intend to change this review, even if the devs (by some miracle) realise what they've done and fix it, because my respect for them, and this game, is gone.

It looks like just a puzzle game, got your boxes, lights, gravity manipulation, etc, but there is so much more to it. Take the time to read everything, and pay attention to the story, and try to formulate your own opinions of what is going on. It is amazing.

Not only is there a rich backstory that you slowly uncover about how you got to where you are, the entire game is filled with mythology, philosophy, ruminations on consciousness, the meaning of life and what it is to be human, the uncanny valley, epistemology, exisistence, society, morality, and more, all existing on top of the Garden of Eden story. It's not for the weak of mind - the game really makes you think about things - but if you are like me and enjoy reading this sort of thing, it is the first game I have found that REALLY gets into it. Too many "philosophical" video games have basic moral choices, grade school level philosophy, storybook plots, etc, but this one simply exists - there are no choices, you just decide, there is little to no forward plot motion (normally a bad thing, but in this game it gives a sense of eternity, which fits nicely with the theme), the endings are just there, with nothing said about them, and your decisions don't have obvious outcomes, you just decide.
Nothing has ever created the experience of "what it is to be a human" since the first time each person realises that they actually ARE human.
tl;dr
+ great atmosphere
+ awesome philosophy
+ good puzzles (no speed or timing based things, it is all about planning and big-picture thought)
+ looks amazing
+ riveting "plot" (if you can call it that in this)
- you have to read, if that's not your thing, then don't play it
- it's the same thing over and over (perfect for this game's atmosphere, but I could see people with short attention spans getting bored)
- I didn't buy it sooner

I will start off by saying this is the best game I have ever played.
I have played other games for longer. I have had more fun and laughed more from other games. But I can say without a doubt this game is the best I've ever played.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is a brilliant game. It's a thrill ride of ups, downs, and killing Nazis. The story is one of the best I've ever seen a game, and it's blend of adrenaline-pumping action with genuine moments of sadness and regret from the characters is very rare in a modern-day FPS. It expresses the true machinelike evil of the Nazis, and people dogged resiatance to them. Even in the darkest moments of the game, someone will always bounce back. Although it' s fictional(duh) and contains some fantasy elemenst (Jewish superweapons, anyone?), the story hits home with every one of us. Although we are thrust into the story just like that, Aas we sneak our way through each level and then inevitbaly  screw up, get caught, and bring out the dual-wield laser guns and automatic shotguns, we begin to understand what we are fighting for: freedom, and what we are fighting against: oppresion, imprisonment, gruesome cruelty(this gmae lives up to it's ESRB rating, and not in a good way) and of course, Nazis. The end, although bland, still left me in shock and awe from just everything this game has to offer. There were times when I almost felt like crying(as much as a game can make you cry), and throughout it all it was evident everyone was suffering(including the protaganist). The story is beyond anything else you will likely see in another FPS for a while. It's great.
Gameplay wise, Wolfenstien offers some refreshing mechanincs will still keeping true to the classic FPS elements that make the genre so popular. It offers plenty of options to stealth around; when the enemies start rolling in it offers some serious firepower. Nearly every weapon has an unlockable alternate firing mode and can be duel welded. With the lasercraftwerk, this game's equivalent of the gravity gun, you can do all kinds of stuff as you find new attachemnts for it, although its feels a little limited due to specific surfaces you can use it on. It also can provide a helping hand when your low on ammo and need a boost in firepower. The manual leaning is much preferable to an automatic system, although the controls are a little strange. I especially liked the no nonsense health value; get shot and the number goes down, get one the various helath kits in the game and the number goes up, if its gets to 0 you die. The armor is the same. Although a little unrealistic(especially with the armor), its provides a refreshing idea instead of the overused "immersive" health. Stealth is also quite good. Sneaking behind walls and shooting commanders when no one is looking gives me a thrill like no other. An early game choice determines whether you use stealth/lockpicking(my choice) or explosives/grenades(I think). Overall, some refershing ideas give the game a different look and feel then most FPS's.

Now that my glowing review is over, we get to the not so great parts. Its just a couple so I made a list instead.
Overall this game is thrilling, adrenaline-pumping, and a little bit disheartening. Some things the Nazis do in the game are quite appaling, but they really show the cold killing machine they were. Plus you kill an absolute buttload of them. When you take away the story, the mechanics, the characters, all the AAA fluff, this game is about killing Nazis. And that's a game I'd like to play.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

If you play The Talos Principle, you will compare it to Portal. It's inevitable, the games just have too much in common - there's even an Aperture easter egg!, so it's not like the developers are trying to deny it. Having said that, you shouldn't make the mistake of dismissing TTP as cheap imitation, for not only does it bring enough novelty to the table in terms of gameplay, but the plot is surprisingly deep, which is unexpected in a game developed by the makers of the Serious Sam series. Good on you, Croteam!
The Talos Principle has layers: If you can't be bothered to read a lot of text, then it's a nice-looking first-person puzzle game. If you start hunting for secrets, looking into every nook and cranny (which can be frustrating, because Croteam's approach to secrets is quite old-school), the duration of the game will be extended dramatically. And If you put on your OCD hat, and start obssessing about everything, including hexadecimal chunks which can be converted to ASCII,, you're looking at 30+ hours of gameplay.
Beyond all the puzzles, there's a touching and thought-provoking story which I won't spoil here. I will only say that the game often invites you to examine fundamental aspects of humanity, and leave it at that.
My only - and not that serious - beef with TTP is that, mechanics-wise, movement can be quite "clunky", especially with regard to placing objects or jumping, and definitely when PRECISION is required. You will end up having to learn how the game expects you to move (as opposed to what feels intuitive, sometimes) and act accordingly in order to make progress. Anyway, it doesn't ruin the experience but, in the few moments when I cursed at the game, this was the reason.
Have I mentioned how pretty the game looks? With the possible exception of water effects (which are known to pose a technical challenge), the game is positively beautiful, especially when you're navigating an open area with far-reaching landscapes.
All in all, a surprising and tremendously enjoyable experience. Strongly recommended for fans of the Portal series and Philosophy undergrads.

Wolfenstein: The New Order, this is a game the surpassed my every expectation. What at first glance looked like a generic dull shooter at E3 and PAX turned out to be my Game of 2014. In order to explain why the New Order is so good Im going to take apart each bit of the game and talk about the amazing things within those catigories.
Preformace/Graphics: Wolfenstein is set in a dark dreary world that is filled with demonic set pieces and destroyed ruins littered around the game. The game's graphics have a very cinematic feel throughout the game and almost reminds of the look of Bioshock one and two. The graphics are, while not "Next-Gen" (Even though many games deeming to have "Next-Gen" graphics have been failing as of late) are graphics that are stylistic and go perfect with the atmosphere of the world. From a destroyed bridge to the damn moon the sets and graphics never fail.
Gameplay: The gameplay reminds me of an old school shooter feel, quite similar to game like Bioshock. The gunplay (At least on PC) is extremely smooth and rewarding but never fails to give you a challange at times. The selection of guns are huge from burst fire laser rifiles, old school revolvers or a mini gun. On top of all that all weapons can be dual weilded, and while I personally prefered to just use one weapon in one hand throughout the game the option is still a good design. There is also a fair bit of interesting puzzles and jumping to take a break from the constant fighting. And if shooting nazis is not your thing, the game had a very good stealth system which is just as viable as running in guns-a-blazing.
Story: Its not usual these days that we get a game that has actual in depth writing and voice acting as well as fun gameplay, however Wolfenstein pulls this off quite well. Wolfenstein's story is disturbing, their are many graphic scenes that can pull at your heart strings even. Without spoiling anything I'll run down some of the great story elements within the game. For one the relationship bettween the main character and his girl is sweet and non-forced making it quite believeable. The inner monoluge from the protagonist throughout the game adds a somber feel to almost any scene and also gives us a small backstory of our hero. Finally any scene with deathshead is disturbing, suspensfull and downright creepy. Something in which a game should have.
This is an amazing game, I defintly would say to pick this up on steam or what ever console you may desire since it is a instant classic and my game of the year.

Robocraft is a great example of a game that has many cool and interesting ideas, but is ultimately frustrating, unfair, and disappointing.
Robocraft is a multiplayer arena shooter that pits player-controlled robots against eachother. The gimmick is that you can build these robots up from scratch with parts that you find through opening boxes or crafting. I have to give credit where it's due, and compliment that there are a lot of different types of robots that you can construct, from tanks, to cars, to helicopters, to planes. Additionally, you can strap on a variety of different weapons onto your creations.
So where does it go wrong?
For starters, it's a free-to-play game with a fairly pay-to-win model. Players can purchase 'premium time', either temporarily (1-day subscriptions, 1 week subscriptions, 1 month subscriptions, etc.), or permanently (which will set you back 49.99 USD). The perks for premium players are too good. For instance, premium players get twice the amount of XP earned, they get additional item slots, and receive 3x the amount of robits from dismantling items. Additionally, they aren't hobbled when opening loot crates, as they may keep all the items inside, while non-premium players only get to keep what's in the front row (roughly 40-50% of the content. Have fun not getting that orange in the back row because you dared to play for free). There are a few more perks that escape my mind, and not being able to look up the premium features on the robocraft wiki due to it being terribly outdated doesn't help either.
This results in games where premium players are going to have better machines, reap better rewards for winning, and enjoy more facets of the game in the process. Speaking of the matches, many of them tend to boil down to either savage stomps, or your team getting reamed by players who build in-meta robots, such as almost un-hittable drones that deal insane DPS. The game favors players who strap as many parts on a robot as possible, rather than trying to prioritize certain features of the robot. "Do I want my robot to be more agile, or deal more damage, or have more durability?". None of these seem to matter. I've had much more success with building a bulky flat-bed of guns, than careful consideration of which parts to include and which parts to exclude. It seems as if this game lacks any depth to make most of these builds even remotely useful, let alone viable.
Many of the robots you'll encounter are tanky as ♥♥♥♥, which mean one-on-one fights usually drag on for an insufferable amount of time. As if all of this wasn't enough, the devs thought it'd be funny to bring in special modules that grant robots special abilities (think MOBA-style abilities, such as blink/flash from DotA/League of Legends.). These include EMP (Large AoE stun that leaves your robot defenseless and immobile for 5 seconds or so), a blink (that works pretty much like a short-range teleport), invisibility (self explanatory), and a large bubble shield (that lets allies shoot through, while enemy shots are blocked entirely).
This doesn't sound too bad, right? Except for the fact that these are all legendary items, and that players can stack several abilities on their robot. This is where the extra item-gain, salvage value, and XP gain really starts to show how imbalanced the game is. Players that weren't lucky to open crates containing these items (or that got cucked out of items because they were on the back row of the chest), are now objectively disadvantaged in matches. And these are only some of the game's problems.
In conclusion, I cannot recommend this game. It has far too many flaws, both technical and design-wise, to warrant spending any money on. If you'd still like to try it, by all means give it a shot, since it is F2P. Just be warned that it might turn out to be a complete waste of your time.

The words to describe this software are
Wallpaper Engine is the new hot thing and it is amazing and something that I dreamed of for a very long time. What Wallapaper Engine is, is genius. It allows you to bring life into your Desktop with fantasticly created live moving wallpapers. Yes. "Live" "moving" "wallpapers".
This is going to be a relitively short review which with my case usually isn't going to happen, but we'll see. This isn't something like me to do but there's not much to say about this software it's that
Upon purchasing and opening wallpaper you'll be greated by a simplistic tutorial screen which tells you the basics about WE (Wallpaper Engine). After you complete short introduction you will be left looking at the screen with multiple default live wallpapers you can select. All you have to do is double click to automatically select and apply the new wallpaper. Or you can single click and on the right you'll be greated by a menu which allows you to slightly customize some wallpapers like changing the colors that are displayed. Or some user created wallpapers may or may not have sound, personally I like to mute the sound from the wallpaper, some people like to have it playing. And leading on from "user created wallpapers"..
Yes. You can create your own personal wallpapers and share them on to the Steam Workshop, using their own wallpaper editor allowing you to create a live wallpaper in many different ways. Meaning you can also browse thousands of user created wallpapers and install them with ease of simply pressing the "Subscribe" button. You can either browse the workshop directly from WE or from Steam Workshop. I like to browse directly from WE just because I have my filters there already set. The most common created wallpapers are favored by most but not everyone like me, i'm speaking about wallpapers which are really Weabo-ish or anime (however you want to call it) I find those wallpapers weird however that's why they have introduced filters which eliminates the problem for me and many others!
Now i'll speak about something that a few things people may worry about. And that's if their hardware is capable to handle it. My answer to your question if your pc can handle it is "Yes. Your PC has very high chance of operating well with WE." I say this because at first I thought that WE will work bad on my ancient PC and that my CPU will explode, however that's not the issue. It does not lag my PC what so ever. And trust me when I say I have an ancient pc. All the specs I have are very old.
Now if you know for sure that your pc won't run it, there is still a chance that it will run it because there are a few options you can enable or disable. Those are: Optional to run in 32/64bit (Big difference) or if you want the live wallpaper to be running whilst you have a game fullscreen (this means the wallpaper pauses once something is in fullscreen so your games performance isn't affected. It also has a few other options but those 2 that I said make it more friendly for your PC.
For those interested. My PC specs are: CPU~ Intel Duo E6850 3GHz 2 cores | GPU~ Asus GTX 660 | RAM~ 8GB DDR2
I recommend for people with lower amounts of RAM to maybe stick with the 32bit version as WE uses up RAM rather than CPU. For me WE uses 3.5% of my CPU and 78MB of RAM. So as you can see, that's almost nothing.
Installing wallpapers from WE is even more great if you have a fast internet connection as most wallpaper size varies (highest download for a wallpaper I downloaded was 500MB, lowest 800KB)
Also an answer for those with multiple monitor setups. Yes, Wallpaper Engine does work with multiple monitor setups and from what I saw, oh my god it looks even more awesome.

I swore to myself to make a new review when I hit 100 hours on this game, and here it is.
So today, I have lots of things to say compared to my last review.
In this game you need to be loyal to your faction, maybe in the beginning you could play the 3 factions to test them out but after that you need to be loyal to it just like your country in real life (it's not like you could test other countries lol).
For me, I choose the TR best faction of them all for me, high fire rate and huge mags. Then there is the NC and they do alot of damage. And for last the VS, the gays for short, you will have a hard time seeing them at night and they have no bullet drop and high accuracy.
You can have a lot of different roles in this game : Pilot, the air game is really strong in this game, you could pick a galaxy it's like literrally a flying whale, it's really slow and carries infantry. Then there are the ESF, these are the terrors of the skies, each faction have a different one but in short they are all jet fighters. the others aircrafts are a bit boring so up to you to discover them. The next role you can have is with all the ground vehicles : there is the flash, it's a quick quad, you pick it when you need a cheap transport. Then the harrasser, it's a really fast buggie that really harrasses the enemy, very fun to use. Then the tanks, the lightning that is nice but it's the cheap alternative of the main battle tank that each faction has a different one. And the sunderer, it's literrally a spawn point and can be a transport too but mainly a spawner. I won't talk about the Ant because it's boring.
Now we are getting and the most fun part and the most boring one : Infantry. It's usually fun but sometimes when you are overrun it can be frustrating. As infantry you can go as light assault, it's a flank class that can fly with a jetpack, use it with c4 and you are OP. Then the medic, it goes by its name he heals and revives teammates. Then the infiltrator, i'ts a sniper that can cloak (become invisible). The heavy assault, he is your worst fear in close quarter and in air because he can have a rocket launcher that ♥♥♥♥ing locks!!! Engineer is basic, you repair vehicles and give ammo oh waw, and you can plant turrets that's nice. And for last you have the MAX, basically a beast, you need a team to bring him down, no chance against him when you're alone except if you have c4.
Now let's talk about the maps, they are a few goods and the rest is♥♥♥♥♥♥
Indar is the paradise for air game, vast desert and some lil tunnels it's sick :)
Hossin is very good for infantry and tank play (swamp) but for air is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Esamir is a frost desert, nice for tank play but air game is kinda ok but it could be better with some cover.
Amerish is a bit of the polyvalent map, good for everything (mountains/valley).
And Koltyr the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cousin, I don't think it can be considered a map because it's really really tiny but it's like the training map for noobs.
You will be considered a noob for a long time, when you will hit the level 20 you won't be that much of a noob but still.
One last tip, don't waste your certs on weapons, do it on vehicles, i know i say some maps are ♥♥♥♥♥♥ because the air game is wack but understand me I am a pilot. (banzai) :)

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I've played this game since launch ( I haven't used the steam client for it since 2013 ) and it is still one of the marvels of Massively Multiplayer gaming. This game presents combat on a scale unrivaled by any current title out on the market, and it's done this for 3 and a half years. There is no other game out right now that can simulate the strategic importance of manpower allocation, while simultaneously providing a great shooter experience. You can kiss your 5v5, 8v8, 12v12, 24v24, and 48v48 shooters goodbye because when it comes to sheer size the 450v450v450 over the 64 square kilometer maps of Planetside blow all these games out of the water, not to mention that the game also has a player base construction system as of a week ago, turning this game into the Massively Multiplayer version of a love child between CnC Renegade and the Battlefield franchise.
All praise aside the game still has issues, the new player experience is awful, the tutorial sucks, mostly because it no longer exists, and the game will not hold your hand beyond a short message each time you encounter a new aspect of the game. Due to the game's sheer size the game is riddled with bugs, thankfully the majority of the major ones have been fixed in the time since launch, but there are still a few stinkers here and there. The game game map's massive size also means that on off peak hours finding a fight can be difficult, but still possible on if you look hard enough.
So, do I recommend this game? Yes, if you are willing to endure the gauntlet of skill curve of Dark Souls and the level of tutorial of Dwarf Fortress. This game can easily be the best you've ever played, if you take the time to learn it.
Here's a few tips for new players:
Don't be discouraged by dying a lot, lots of people in a fight means you will get shot from everywhere. (Including your teammates if you aren't careful)
Start by playing a support class, (Medic and Engineer) this will allow you to contribute to the team without worrying about getting a ton of kills, and will help you learn how the battles flow so you can understand how to play the combat classes more effectively.
Join a squad! The game is an MMO, which means playing with other people is the mainstay of the game, good squad leaders will help you learn the game as well as find, or make good, fun, fights for the squad to participate in.
Commit at least 10 hours to the game before you decide to put it down. I know a lot of people think the game should sell itself in the first 30 min of gameplay, but this game almost never does, and if you put it down before you see the depth of the game you will have deprived yourself of one of the best Multiplayer experiences in the industry.

Squad, A game created by the development team of the highly sucessful project reality mod. So what is squad?
Squad is a game of which two sides are pitted against eachother in the battle to capture strategic locations, reinforce, and dominate the other team. Your team is divided into squads, with a maximum of 9 players in each squad. Each role serving a specific purpose, from healing the wounded to supressing enemies and providing covering fire for your squad members. This game relys soley on working together as a team. Discussing tactics, and applying them to the battle layed out ahead. The community in this game is outstanding. Even if you're new to the game you're always welcome to ask advice and everyone will give you honest answers. Its a relatively easy game to pick up and play if you enjoy hardcore FPS games. Squad gives you the opportunity to carve out your own story throughout the gameplay itself, due to the fact that you may not know how many enemies are head of you, and youre relying solely on your squadmates to help you through the battle.

Wolfenstein: The New Order, this is a game the surpassed my every expectation. What at first glance looked like a generic dull shooter at E3 and PAX turned out to be my Game of 2014. In order to explain why the New Order is so good Im going to take apart each bit of the game and talk about the amazing things within those catigories.
Preformace/Graphics: Wolfenstein is set in a dark dreary world that is filled with demonic set pieces and destroyed ruins littered around the game. The game's graphics have a very cinematic feel throughout the game and almost reminds of the look of Bioshock one and two. The graphics are, while not "Next-Gen" (Even though many games deeming to have "Next-Gen" graphics have been failing as of late) are graphics that are stylistic and go perfect with the atmosphere of the world. From a destroyed bridge to the damn moon the sets and graphics never fail.
Gameplay: The gameplay reminds me of an old school shooter feel, quite similar to game like Bioshock. The gunplay (At least on PC) is extremely smooth and rewarding but never fails to give you a challange at times. The selection of guns are huge from burst fire laser rifiles, old school revolvers or a mini gun. On top of all that all weapons can be dual weilded, and while I personally prefered to just use one weapon in one hand throughout the game the option is still a good design. There is also a fair bit of interesting puzzles and jumping to take a break from the constant fighting. And if shooting nazis is not your thing, the game had a very good stealth system which is just as viable as running in guns-a-blazing.
Story: Its not usual these days that we get a game that has actual in depth writing and voice acting as well as fun gameplay, however Wolfenstein pulls this off quite well. Wolfenstein's story is disturbing, their are many graphic scenes that can pull at your heart strings even. Without spoiling anything I'll run down some of the great story elements within the game. For one the relationship bettween the main character and his girl is sweet and non-forced making it quite believeable. The inner monoluge from the protagonist throughout the game adds a somber feel to almost any scene and also gives us a small backstory of our hero. Finally any scene with deathshead is disturbing, suspensfull and downright creepy. Something in which a game should have.
This is an amazing game, I defintly would say to pick this up on steam or what ever console you may desire since it is a instant classic and my game of the year.

It's a fairly bad console port. Out of all the things that impressed me positively or negatively, that's the biggest one. It reeks of console-specific "features", that, of course, are useless and annoying on PC, and every self-respecting PC gamer should be able to identify and condemn these specific "features". First of all, is the aiming. It's bad. It doesn't allow you to finely control the sensitivity, the sensitivity is controlled in big chunks, so it's either too fast or too slow. Even if you put both horizontal and vertical sensitivity on the SAME value, it's still different, and you can't get them to match perfectly, because, I said previously, the horizontal-vertical sensitivity difference is fairly small, and the values to which you can adjust the sensitivity are big. So it will never match. It's annoying. Then it's the movement and sprinting. Sprinting is done Gears of War style, when you press shift you basically become a tank. Super-slowly moving either left or right while you race ahead. Not the best way to do sprinting. Movement is very wonky. It's one of those cases where Rockstar tried to make the movement more reallistic than it's fun to play. And that's not fun to play. Max stutters a lot when he encounters an object, and switching quickly from moving left to right is a nightmare, it takes AGES! Not very good when you're in a tight situation. I crouch a lot behind cover, a habit from the old days, when you didn't stick like glue to walls to the press of a button. Crouching is also a nightmare, it takes 2 seconds for Max to switch stances, and that's only when the button decides to work. If you press it too quickly, the system goes crazy and Max freezes in place like a massive idiot, becoming a glorified bullet sponge. But what are you going to do, it's easier for console scrubs to press a button and become glued to the wall, than to actually manage moving while crouched... Between all of these control and aiming issues, the game became quite challenging even on Easy... I'm used to more responsive games, coming from a background of mainly Counter-Strike, where the aiming and movement is supposed to work perfectly, like clockwork. And more and more modern games suffer from this issues, because they don't spend enough time to polish the PC port, so that it becomes decent. Like I said, I was a little disappointed by this game, I didn't expect to have so many issues with a Rockstar game. The story is a good Max Payne-like story, I enjoyed it until the end, and it's really worth playing. The multiplayer on the other hand is very disappointing. Especially now, 3 years down the line. Again, this being a Rockstar game, and quite a good one as well, I expected more people to play it. But it's a wasteland down there. The only mode still being played, although you have to wait a few good minutes to get any players at all, is Team Deathmatch, the most popular gamemode in all of online gaming... The others are barren as a desert. No one playing them. I had to get a friend to buy the game, just to try the coop horde mode it had, since no one was connecting to my lobby. And when you finally do get matched with someone, it will mostly be with very high level players, which all of them have better guns, better perks, better everything, so you don't stand a chance. Again, probably because of the very low player count, it had to match me, a level TWO (2) against a team of level FIFTY (50) or close to that, otherwise none of us would be playing any multiplayer any time soon. All in all, I would recommend the game for singleplayer, it's a good story, about 8 hours long, the rest I spent in multiplayer, and if you're not a very picky gamer, like I am, you could get easily used to the control issues the game has, but don't have any expectations from the multiplayer aspect of the game. I bought it at a sale, I recommend you wait for one as well.

Max Payne 3 is a game that doesn't play like the previous games, doesn't look like the previous games, but ends up feeling a bit like the previous games.
It seems like the new development team really nailed the tone and writing, but had no idea how a Max Payne game plays. They have the individual gameplay elements down like dual wielded pistols or the bullet time jumps but they are executed in a way that makes them obsolete in the context of the game. Unlike the previous games Max Payne 3 is a cover based shooter, and jumping around the battlefield mid combat is as good an idea as it would be in a similar real life situation. You end up♥♥♥♥♥first on the floor and become an easy target. The dual wieldin is also completely useless because every enemy can be killed with a single headshot from every weapon, and the dual wielding only serves to waste bullets, and on top of it it also forces you to drop your two-handed weapon (usually assault rifle/shotgun). It's weird that these elements were implemented in the first place when the development team clearly wanted to go for a different pacing and vibe on the combat system. This makes the game seem somewhat confused about its own identity.
They tried to implement some "Max Paney" elements into the game by creating QTE and on-rails sections into the game. While they do look cool it still feels like a bit desperate attempt to make the game more like the previous ones in my opinion and I can't help but feel that they tried to take the easy route with this decision.
The game also has some extremely low quality textures on the environments. Some textures are flat out pixelated on the highest settings. The game is not even an open world game but rather it's extremely linear so they really don't have a reason to have such horrible low quality textures. The game demands a huge chunck of hard drive space and this combined with the low quality textures kind of makes you wonder why it's taking all that space.
Is the game any good though? Yes it is. All these glaring flaws are mended by the extremely good writing and most of the time good looking cutscenes which are heavy on camera movement and quick cuts. They are very movie-like and enjoyable. Bad texturework aside the game also nails the feel of every environment with great mapping. Even the combat system is enjoyable even if it's a bit derivative.

A quite neat wallpaper application.
I'm testing this software on my laptop 5200u, 16 GB RAM DDR3L, Intel HD+840m, SATA HDD, 1366*768 resolution, Windows 10 x64 with 15 mbps internet speed.
Wallpaper Engine's UI is simple... and rather bland - it doesn't need tutorial to understand and navigate around. You can select/search local files to activate (or workshop files that have been downloaded) and you can browse/search the workshop directly inside the app to subscribe and download it. Within main UI you can also make 'playlist' similar to when you queue MP3s on Winamp/Foobar/Spotify. Overall the UI is pretty basic but it gets the jobs done.
When pulling data from Steam workshop, the performance overall is impacted if the file being downloaded is big e.g: video wallpaper around 700 MB. It takes as much as 80% of my harddrive alone. Understandable though, but it does affect the app's own performance if it's playing video + music as it causes stutters. People with more powerful rig and notably SSD prolly won't see this performance hit.
The software is smart enough to detect if there's full screen app active - so it stops its operation, and there are options to adjust so your performance loss when using the software in the background is suppressed. The biggest performance hit comes when you play high resolution video (1080p/60fps). If I use it, it causes a big performance drop for my laptop. Switching to other app as full screen app instantly stutters everything for a second, and if the video background has music attached, it also freezes a bit. Thankfully for a normal live wallpaper, I can use it just fine with no noticeable performance drop.
As for the workshop itself - which I deem as the main strength of this app as crowd-sourcing app contents still surpasses developer's contents in terms of richness - , you can select from many styles of videos or live wallpapers. There are thousands materials to select from already, and growing, making the selection pool pretty large. You can use an in-app editor to make your own and upload it for free, or monetize it if the users give you approval (like Steam's Greenlight system).
Honestly I can do nothing but recommending the app. It's cheap, has crowd contents, allows you to upload your own creation and really I've had fun tinkering so even the experience alone is well worth the money. Just be wary if you use a toaster like me, don't have too high of an expectation.

You play as a newly awaked AI, standing in a lush grecian garden where a booming voice from above introduces itself as God and orders you to solve puzzles and collect Tetris pieces, which are used to make keys and object that opens up more puzzles. Said puzzles are nothing spectacular, the usual box/pressure plate/beam of light/ stuff, but engaging enough.
Immediately there's the sneaking feeling that you're simply a rat in some behaviorist's experiment, a feeling underlined by various messages left by other researchers, interspersed with philosophical texts, discussions about various levels of reality and historical notes about fallen empires.
If you think all this sounds a bit pretentious, then you're not entirely wrong. The game takes itself spectacularily seriously, and there is not a single tongue in a single cheek to be found. But it works. It works so damn well. Right off the bat, the game forces you to consider questions of conciousness and identity, the relationship between creator and the created, the conflicting values of freedom and security; all while the looming feeling of being nothing more than a datapoint in a graph creeps ever closer. It's a game where you solve box puzzles one minute, then ponder what it means to be a human the next minute. More impressively, it makes you feel like these two tasks are actually interrelated.
If you like science fiction, logical paradoxes, puzzles, and/or heavy religious metaphors, then this game is for you.

Squad (Version Alpha 8.9)
Graphics - 3.5/5 Stars
Sound - 5/5 Stars
Gameplay - 4.5/5 Stars
Closest thing i have found to fill the void of military combat experience.
No Icons telling you where the enemy is, no "X" pop up for when you hit an enemy. No battle annoying battle voice over explaining whats going on, its up to you and your team to work things out for yourselves.
Squad has a great feeling of supression, suspense and the combat situations are so broard you never know what you are in for. Every match i have played so far plays different and you don't find yourself getting frustrated with too many cheesy tactics like, bunny hopping, twitch sniping or totally un realistic player movement.
Squad simulates how vulnerable one might feel in a combat situation, it simulates the feeling of desperation, the need to make a well planned decision, which will benefit the whole team. For one instance  that may last a short time, or  perhaps what seems like forever, you find yourself under fire. You can hear the bullets flying past you, see some of them landing, perhaps near you or a squad mate, who you keep a close eye on because the bullets seem to be snapping in and close around and you want to know where they are coming from...  Now what do you do?  Ask the squad mate who your eye is on, wtf those bullets are coming from?  Do you quickly lean round that corner in the direction of the bullets for a peak and risk getting your brains blown out?  Do you blast off a few sprey and prey rounds, hoping to distract the enemy, or maybe this action will reveal your position? You must be careful because just firing blindly might give away your exact position.
Do you get on your microphone, talk with your squad mates  to ask for help and ask for a situation report for where the enemy are and where the best place for you to be is.  The questions are now gone and you had best make a decision and quick!  In that moment it feels like your decision will affect the outcome of the whole match. You must learn to communicate in a fast and clear directional manner in order to convey a strong working plan, who the other squad mates will adhere to.
The communication in this games works wonderfully. You chat with your Squad.  9 players in total which creates a full Squad of soldiers. Each squad has a leader, who co-ordinates attacks/defence and has coms to the other squad leaders. Each squad has a unique player roll to fulfil. Medic, Sniper, Fighter, Gunner, Scout, Squad Leader and more.  You MUST communicate with your squad and leader and squad mates. This game does NOT tell you where to go or what to do, it is all up to every player as an individual to make decisions and inform each other of plans. Squad leaders have the ability to mark the map with icons that will be visible for the whole team,  for suspect activity,  known enemy spots, base building and more. Squad leaders will communicate together to get all the squads on the team working as a whole.
Contrustion is a big part of Squad.  It allows the Squad leader, when enough points are available to place build orders which other squad members can build once placed. Things like sand bag walls, hesco walls, mounted weaponry, ladders, ammo crates, outposts etc. THis part of the game is what makes Squad unique and if your a battlefield fan, thi part of the game is what will put a smile on your face.  I don't want to say too much about it because i don't want to spoil the fun.
Communicating with the mic is vital, it is the only way to inform/be informed as to how the battle is playing out. It comes down to how well each team can say what they mean to say to their team in order to get a clear picture of whats going on.  The game forces you to use your brain in ways that alot of people will find hard to do. You have to be able to multitask and think clear, as i imagine real soldiers would have to. You need to be able to use your compass, the map, learn on the spot how to verbally explain to other players where those enemy you caught a glimpse of might be. Or explain how an entire squad is flanking towards your friends from a certain position.
Conclusion pending....

When you play this game, and when it is played right, players become brothers.
Here's an example from tonight. I was pinned down today on Chora outside an enemy compound, with only myself alive and a medic who is helplessly bleeding out next to me. He stayed on coms and described where he was shot from and continued to encourage me while I fought the attacking squad. He stayed conscious long enough and didn't respawn to have a full conversation with me, just because. We reminisced on the fun times we've had on the battlefield, and the future to look forward to. Before the future came, however, his unconscious self bled out, and never in my gaming life have I felt such a pang of sorrow [except Brothers in Arms: Hells Highway. That game made me cry tears of war.].
You don't find communities that go out of their way to help each other like you do here.
I'm not going to tell you every experience you will have here will be an enjoyable one. If you have a Squad Leader who doesn't know/care what he's doing, it won't be as fun. If you are in a squad of people who don't talk, you will quickly find yourself outsmarted by the enemy and hopelessly overrun. However, if you get into a good server, a good community, a smart squad even, who works together, talks, plays for the team and not the individual... you can work together. With real people. Throughout the world. Working together as one... and be victorious.
How cool is that?

As long as you have some tempered expectations this game is brilliant. I can't speak for the multiplayer as I've never touched it but the single player story is everything it should be. Series purists might be put off by how often there are cut scenes and dismayed by the fact that there are numerous fail conditions that can happen that don't involve Max soaking up bullets or explosions. The bottom line is that you get to watch a lengthy summer blockbuster action movie where you play through all the shootouts of which there are many.
Mechanically the game is damn near flawless (minus one arbitrary "boss" encounter) in that precision and quick thinking are rewarded properly. Making good use of the cover system, bullet time, and shoot dodging are essential to beating the game on harder difficulties where even on normal you WILL get flanked by aggressive enemy A.I. that won't let you "stop n' pop" like in other shooters. The guns all have a certain weight to them ( a .50 Desert Eagle just "feels" heavier than a .45 in a very noticeable way) and you'll be forced to mix up your arsenal often. Finishing the game was a satisfying experience and while I didn't feel compelled to return on higher difficulties right after my first pass I came back later with renewed appreciation.
Visually the game holds up really well 2 years after release. Some finer textures and such might not fare well to heavy scrutiny but the environments are varied with tons of background detail and props while the character models respond to gunfire in a sickeningly visceral way. It's pretty hard to take a screen shot that doesn't look good when you are in a shootout. Aurally the voice acting is solid, the soundtrack is top notch, and the various sounds of battle compliment the action well.
One of the more common gripes I've heard about the game is that the story is lame and it is excruciatingly linear, to the point where on a few occasions if you explore the same area for too long when no enemies are around you'll trigger a fail condition because you didn't follow your companion and he's killed in a short cut scene. I can understand that frusturation. What I don't understand is how some would interpret the story as simply dumb and completely senseless without thinking about it. Unfortunately explaining it would be a spoiler but since the story is about Max and is from his perspective that is PRECISELY how it is meant to appear. You are meant to be Max in this situation but you are not meant to influence him. You are meant only to see and feel how he does and not decide who he is. You're meant to get clarity at the same time he does and it does seem dumb as hell when it all falls together,  right? Max thinks so too. There's also a lot of nuanced visual flourishes meant to convey Max's mental issues and state that some might have mistaken for simple grittiness or what have you. Either way the game is considerably smarter than the trailers would have you believe.
In conclusion I get the impression that the game was a critical success but commercially floundered, considering how quickly it went to sale prices and how frequently the game is 80% off. Maybe I'm just being pretentious in thinking that I "get it" while others looked down on a decidedly less gamey Max Payne. All I know is that as a standalone product the single player game is worth the 20 dollars it goes for now. If you like good action games and can take the time to enjoy a decent narrative then you'd be a complete dunce for passing this up when it's on sale.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

A compelling storyline that doesn't take itself too seriously (how can you when 1000 foot tall robots roam the world seeking to destroy all against the reich?). It has fun while telling a interesting story of "What if the Nazis had tech similar to Metal Gear?" and the subsequent overthrow of the world because of it. The Relationship that develops between Blazkowicz and the female interest seems to launch a tad pre-maturely but again, it is just a game. You're very quickly launched into a cell of resistance fighters that attempt to overthrow the oppressive Nazi regime through various missions both covert and overt, all very fun!
The gameplay is fun and boasts weapons ranging from handguns to ludicrous double wielded assault rifles...Personally I don't see the point in dual-wielding anything unless you find yourself face to face with a tank of an enemy, but at that point if you're above any difficulty higher than easy you would be dead anyway at such close ranges. There is a skill tree that unlocks depending on your style of gameplay, a very nice idea that plays out fairly well giving you "perks" as the game progresses. Early on you are given a special gun that cuts through metal, this would be "The new order's" version of the Portal gun/Gravity Gun or unique equivalent weapon. It upgrades throughout the game however and becomes stronger against enemies but the basic principle that it will help you advance into different areas remains the same.
There are plenty of collectibles to find along the way that you should keep your eyes open for. Also, some of the easter eggs are a very cool addition akin to bioshock infinite using real songs that were done in a style of the 1920's era music, only in this game they are the forced creations of talented musicians that were faced with the choice to write for the reich in German or die (The beatles are among the musicians).
Overall I would say that this has been a very good purchase and this was a game that I did not see coming as one that I have enjoyed as much as I have! As far as cons go my only complaint would be the low texture maps throughout the game...unfortunately a staple of Bethesda games.

This game. This game is bloody great. How on Earth it is possible that a Wolfenstein game of all things manages to have one of the best stories from 2014, I have no idea. But somehow Machinegames pulled it off with The New Order.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is an old-school FPS, with an emphasis on large levels with cleverly-hidden secrets everywhere and where encounters can be approached in multiple ways. Do you sneakily stab the Nazis to death without triggering a single alarm? Do you charge in, guns blazing? Do you avoid them altogether? Much is possible in this game, and it's lovely. Also, there is no progression-treadmill-multiplayer-thingamajig in this game. It's just a big campaign, and to me, that's definitely a plus.
The game is really rather over-the-top in many ways. For instance, protagonist B.J Blazkowicz is capable of ludicrous feats such as dual-wielding shotguns or sniper rifles. The campaign will take you from setpiece to setpiece, including a ruined bridge, an actual concentration camp and a Nazi moonbase. Despite the relative seriousness of the game's story, you will come across delightfully cheesy lines like "I'm comin' for ya, you f**king Nazi space man!". Award-winning dialogue lines, if you ask me.
Overall, it is a very lovely game with fine FPS gameplay and a strong story. Nothing is perfect, however, and this game is no exception. If you ask me, there are three downsides to The New Order.
The first one, ridiculous bullet-sponginess. Yes, I get it, lots of the enemies are wearing magic super-armour that is generally amazingly protective. But I just cannot suspend my disbelief when an enemy manages to take three full shotgun clips to the face, at close range, whilst only being mildly inconvenienced by it. Many a time have I stared at the screen in disbelief as an enemy just kept trucking along after I emptied two shotguns at once into the general direction of his head. And of -course-, Blazkowicz does die rather easily when he gets shot like that. It's stupid, it isn't fun and I'm not ashamed to admit that I turned the game's difficulty down in order to keep the stupendous bullet-sponginess to an absolute minimum.
The second downside is the game's engine. id Tech 5 is an exceedingly wonky engine. It's what makes this game reach the staggering file size of 50GB (because 'megatextures', what a lovely buzzword), and it causes rampant texture pop-in. Like, really bad pop-in. Turn around and you'll see that everything is a blurry mess for a few seconds because the game doesn't load the textures unless you look at them. Normally I'd attribute that to an issue with my system, but the same problems plagued other id Tech 5 games (RAGE is a notable example), so... I'm pretty sure it's safe to say that id Tech 5 is just janky.
The third and final downside is the character of Max Hass. The New Order has lots of very interesting and well-written characters. I mean, how often do you see a wheelchair-bound old woman with a colostomy bag in video games? It's such a shame, then, that the writers felt the need to be contemporary and inserted Hodor from A Song of Fire and Ice/Game of Thrones into the cast. Max Hass is a gentle giant of a man with the mental faculties of a toddler, who is only capable of saying his own name. The only difference between Hodor and Max Hass is that one's vocabulary solely consists of "Hodor" and the other only says "Max Hass".. It's lazy, uninspired and I didn't like it.
Despite those issues, however, I would wholeheartedly recommend Wolfenstein: The New Order. It's a great time. The setting is remarkably well put-together, the story is memorable and the gunplay is wonderfully over-the-top. With two different timelines, depending on which choice you make after the prologue, there is also quite some replay value. So, yes. Grand stuff.
