One of the reasons I bought Wolfenstein: The New Order was the astonishing rate of positive reviews. But were they true?
HELL YES! I enjoyed the game from the first moment to the last, the plot is really well written, and even a person who haven't played its predecessors will quickly find himself in the world of Wolfenstein. Playability of this game is through the roof - you can almost feel the joy of killing every damn Nazi (maybe I'm just a sick person). Graphical side of the game is generally satisfying.
The controls are very responsive and after a few hours of play you already feel like an MLG pro. Perks are cool addition (they are kinda standard in most FPS games) and are not that hard to get. Same goes with achievements, most of which are progress related or simply obtainable by getting a certain perk. The characters are very well designed, e.g. Deatshead makes an impression of a real sick mind, striving for power, and through the cutscenes you can almost see why so many people fear him.
Minor flaw of the entire production is the level of difficulty. Personally I think that the hardest difficulty is relatively easy, and for an experienced player finishing Wolfenstein on UBER is not that big of a challenge. Also I can admit that lower difficulties are designed well to fit the casuals that don't want to challenge themselves, but to enjoy this amazing plot.
Last but not least, let's talk about collectibles. Some of them are quite hard to find, but that only makes finding them more satisfying. Moreover, the Enigma Code puzzles are cool addition to the game, and allow us to unlock bonus game modes.
To summarize - I really enjoyed every minute of the gameplay, and I think the game is worth every penny. I'd recommend it to everyone 10/10

I would like to start by syaing this is one of the best purchases I have ever made.
Despite it's older graphics and mechanics, this remains one of the greatest games, in my opinion, ever made.
This game has provided me with countless hours of entertainment and what's best is that each game is different. With the expansion packs the variety of civilization is extreme ranging from the French and British to the Aztecs and the Mayans to the Berbers and Malians. so without further ado, here is my official thoughts:
Pros:
-Variety of civilizations to play as and face in combat, each with their own pros and cons and abilities
-A multitude of maps to play on
-Several different game modes
-Countless hours of historical Campaigns
-Easily usable multiplayer
-Easily controlled with excellent combat mechanics
-You can also make your own campaigns and scenarios if you really want
Cons:
-Some bugs that need to be worked out but that will be worked out in time
-The AI is kind of stupid sometimes
-Very rock, paper, scissors (Spearsman beats knights, Knights beat siege equipment, etc.), but this is easy to overcome.
So in all, I give this game a 9.5/10, because there is always room for improvement. I will heavily advise you to consider this game.

Okay, so it's been a while since I've played a corridor shooter, and Wolfenstein: The New Order is pretty much as corridor as you get. That is, it creates the corridor from moldy concrete, slaps on some German writing and inserts some Nazis who have the audacity of being in your way in getting from A to B. The graphics aren't much to write home about, though, and I had to adjust some settings in a config file just to get antialiasing to work. It's pretty straight forward, and Blazcowicz's personal viewpoint and story is interesting. However, this is where the game loses it slightly. TAKE NOTE: SPOILERS AHEAD! There's a TL;DR summary at the bottom for slackers unwilling to read my in depth critique.
There are a few plotholes here and there, such as how a man confined to a wheelchair for more than a decade can walk - nay - sprint after only a few minutes. People usually need years of therapy to learn to walk again if they've wheelchair bound. Secondly, why is it that Blazcowicz (the protagonist) is able to do everything he does? He is repeatedly shot, stabbed, beaten yet is still able to fight Nazis on the moon, sneak into bases and dual wield everything from assault rifles to energy weapons. I get there's a factor of suspension of disbelief but in a few minutes you destroy the London Monitor. It's name sounds like a newspaper from the 60s but it's actually a giant, almost invincible robot which you destroy while hiding in some tunnels. I don't believe any of Blazcowicz's actions could not have been repeated by anyone else. If he could take down the monitor, surely The Resistance could have pooled together some resources to take it down.
What would have helped is if the game made the build up to facing the monitor a bit more epic. They did it with the Panzerhund, so the monitor could have received similar attention. It oppresses millions of people and is extremely powerful. Perhaps The Resistance could have sent Blazcowicz on a series of missions designed to equip him with gadgets to take the machine down, and perhaps he could have had a few close scrapes with it before needing to settle a score. What you get is a glimpse at the start then it suddenly pops up after you get back from the moon, and you kill it in a few minutes. Yes, I know big bosses tend to be taken down relatively easily in corridor shooters, but armoured Nazis gave me more of a challenge.
Anyway, while I enjoyed the gameplay and story, the ending seemed to sputter out a bit after some great build ups along the way. Frau Engel was a great character, but she lost credibility when, after getting her jaw crushed, instead of running away from the machine that hurt her, she crawls up to you and, with some clarity, swears vengeance. Someone with a broken jaw would struggle to speak and how in the heck did she know the machine disobeying her was your fault?
If you're willing to overlook its flaws and plotholes, it's a fun shooter and hopefully we could see a sequel after a disappointing ending. The game seems to thrive on delivering justice and revenge on the Nazis but the ending leaves you wondering what all the effort was for. Especially because you've been metering out punishment and there seems to be little satisfaction for players hoping to see Deathshead really get what he deserved. It's kinda like finally capturing a tyrant and just when you're about to dispense some suitably violent and painful justice, he commits suicide, making sure to laugh before he pulls the trigger. You're left wondering what all the effort was for.
TL;DR:
Why do I recommend it though? I like Blazcowicz's character and the gameplay was fun - dual wielding autoshotguns does make you feel like a badass. It's a pity about the plot holes, but there's enough story to keep you progressing. There are also perks you can unlock, which will aid your play style, such as whether you prefer stealth, going in guns blazing or even becoming a demolitions expert. Overall it isn't too bad and the gameplay alone is worth it. Oh and there are secret modes to unlock, so keep your eyes peeled for enigma codes.

The max payne series is one of the best damn story driven series I have ever played. Max payne 3 has an amazing story that ties in with max payne, and max payne 2. It still has a shoot em' up feel but with great narrating by the main character and great voice acting it's almost like your controlling a movie. You almost feel max's emotions through the computer, anger as your betrayed by the man you once called your best friend, and sorrow as you visit the grave of your murdered wife and one year old child. The game itself is very pretty, the graphics amaze me, from the ghettos of New York to the slums of mexico; every chapter is a new look, a new experience!
If your a gamer who loves a great story this game is for you. If your a gamer who looks to doge bullets and shoot thugs in slow motion, this game is for you. If your a gamer who likes to enjoy the sights and bathe in the awesomeness of the graphics, this game is for you. I love this game. The gunplay is tight, with a relatively high time to kill. The classes are varied and offer different experiences. The vehicles are fun, and you have a lot of customization options for weapons and slots such as stealth modules and extra directional armor. There is a large selection of guns that excel in different situations and ranges.
The best part about this game is that it is NOT PAY TO WIN. The weapons you can purchase are easily accessible for someone who never pays a dime, and there are no definitive best weapons. Each weapon has a niche, such as a slower firing long range weapon with low recoil at range, or a fast firing short range weapon with high recoil at range.
You will die a lot in this game, but what can you expect with some fights reaching 96+ vs 96+ players? The learning curve is a bit harsh, as FPS skills in other games don't really transfer to this game. However, once you get past the learning curve, you are left with an extremely fun game with a lot of different stuff to do. From large infantry fights under intense aerial dogfights, to tanks shelling an armor column, to a sneaky mobile spawn point under an enemy base, you can almost always find a role that fits your play style.
The game is free, so there isn't anything to lose trying it. Note that the Steam version downloads the game launcher, and  then the launcher needs to patch so expect a good deal of downloads.

Absolutely fantastic 3D first person puzzle game.
Did you love Portal 1 Challenges?
Did you love Portal 2 for its puzzles?
If the answer is yes, this game will blow you away. Cleverly split into more and more advanced "worlds", each with islands, each of those with several puzzle rooms, this game will truly test your brain.
There's also a story segment, which, so far, seems optional - you can ignore all the computer terminals if you just want to solve puzzles, or you can embark on a philosophical journey of "What makes you a person?".
The puzzles have differing difficulty, indicated by the color of the sigil (puzzle piece) you are trying to collect - with green ones being easiest, and red ones (so far) being hardest. There are also many secrets hidden around the world which provide additional challenge.
Perhaps the greatest thing as far as DESIGN of the game is concerned is that you can solve the puzzles in different order, so there is very little risk of getting stuck on a particularly difficult puzzle and not be able to progress - just leave the room, solve something else, and then return. Midway through World 1, you already unlock World 2, so gating is very soft in this game.
Graphics and sounds and music work perfectly - the worlds have well designed aesthetics, sound effects are useful, and the background music can occasionally chill you to the bone. Narrative voices fit their purpose flawlessly.

I can't recommend this game highly enough.
If you like first-person puzzle games, you'll love it.  If you think you'll like first person puzzle games, this game will suck you into the genre.  You'll get the itch.
IMO, it's harder than Portal 1 or 2, but easier than something like Antichamber.  The open world layout lets you solve at your own pace.  Stuck on a particular room?  Try some others, learn a new technique, and come back later.  As with all games of this nature, solving an especially grueling puzzle makes you feel f-ing GREAT.
The atmosphere, environment, soundtrack, visuals, and, especially, the story (vague but approachable, best discovered over time) are all TOP NOTCH.  Plus, it's actually quite educational if you take the time to read the texts about ancient mythology/literature.
I rarely buy games full price when they're first released, but I did so will glee when I heard about the Talos Principle.  I don't regret it for a second.
The only negative I would cite are the Tetris-like door puzzles- they seemed to me more guesswork than anything, and could really be frustrating.

This game is amazing.  There is a pretty steep learning curve (I hated it the first couple hours), but it is well worth sticking it out: there really is no comparable game out there.  You can play as infantry, ground vehicles, and aircraft all in the same theater.
The Good: Huge variety in play styles.  Great community.  Can always find at least a couple good fights any time of day.  Huge incentives to join a squad and work together.  The new construction system adds whole new dynamics to the game and has drawn quite a few idle players back into the fray.  There is a "VR" zone that you can use to test out any weapon/class/vehicle in the game without getting shot in the face the moment you step out of a spawn room.  The premium access system is a good way to build up "certs" quickly.  The core players of the game are merciless and very skilled.
The Bad: You spend a lot of time grinding out "certs" against core players who are merciless and very skilled.  Infantry upgrade weapons are generally side-grades that are more specialized than the very good basic weapons, but will generally beat out the basic weapons in their area of specialization.  Vehicles are expensive to get competitive (although the basic free vehicles in the game have enough functionality to give you a taste of what you would like to work towards).  Game is a system hog, requiring quite a bit of computer horsepower to run adequately.

Max Payne 3 isn't looking to reinvent the wheel and it's safe to say it hasn’t changed much from previous games in the series. It’s still a short, linear, straight action-packed third-person shooter. Each of the 14 chapters begin with a cool cinematic, after which you start at point A, clear rooms after rooms of enemies, essentially just shooting your way to point B, enjoy another cutscene, repeat. But with that said, was it fun? Well, that depends.
Story-wise, I can't say the plot is too elaborate. It has a very predictable twist and the ending is somewhat disappointing. However, the originality of the story lies in the presentation. The cutscenes are fun to watch, the voice acting is top notch, and the writing is clever. For fans of hard-boiled and noir detective fiction, the way the protagonist narrates the story is a real treat. It may come across as cheesy sometimes, but I just loved every line of it and felt it did a perfect job giving you a glimpse into the psyche of Max. Fans of the series will feel right at home with the narrative. It also helps that the amazing graphics and sound go a long way toward giving the game a realistic feel.
My first complete playthrough took me approximately 8-10 hours, and I enjoyed every minute of it, but whether or not it's fun enough to justify a buy will be based on your tolerance for linear and somewhat simple gameplay. The shooting and slow motion mechanics can be very fun once you get them down but don't expect the game to reward you with ability or weapon unlocks that can open up new strategies--combat stays the same from beginning to end. Seeing as the game is relatively short however, it shouldn't get repetitive enough to make the first playthrough feel like a grind. The story is engaging and does a good job adding more layers to Max's persona, whom despite his flaws, is truly a great protagonist and a hero that you love to cheer for.

But a bunch of new games coming out had to hop on the 'me-too' train and adopt mechanics I loath, so I didn't buy them. My FPS library shrunk and was nearing complete abandonment.
Just when I was about to give up on FPS's, I watched Ross's basic tutorial from Accursed Farms YouTube channel on Planetside 2, and finally understood the basics. Too many tutorials talk about the unlocks/random tid-bits, and not enough about how to generally move quickly about the map. Once I knew this, then I could worry about unlocks.
So then I could play, but now that I was seeing the core of the game, I began to think it would get repetitive and I would get bored of it quickly. But then the construction update came out. Those spawn-camps and boring captures disappeared, as armies could build at either side of a contested point and compete for it continuously.
Is this a cosmic coincidence? I dunno, but this one-two punch has made me go from a quick rage-quitter to someone who actually wants to devote time to the game.

I got it only because it was on a discount. Don't get me wrong it's a good game with an excellent story, but I felt as if the gameplay was fairly basic. It's an extremely linear game and the length is shorter than I expected. Usually, if a game relies on the story to propel and keep people interested, it should be pretty lengthy. I felt it was rushed a little, but it did keep my interest until the end.
The gameplay was medicore at best. You fight the same enemies in similar scenarios in almost every chapter. There are few weapons to use, but honestly I found myself using the same three all the time; the laser, assualt rifle and the knife. Honestly, you could kill all the enemies on a chapter with just a knife. The A.I reacts so slow to your actions. I found myself at some situations just rushing into mass gunfire with a knife and stabbing everyone to death and losing very little health.  The "boss" battles are a joke. They were too easy in my opinion and I was playing the difficulty under Uber. Half the time the boss would get stuck in a spot, making it even easier to defeat, especially the last boss.
The audio mix is noteworthy. At certain chapters it really enhanced the atmosphere and created almost unforgetable moments. I really liked it when a fist-pumping track started playing while I was mowing down nazi's.
It was a good game, but I don't really understand why some people beleive this game is perfect. It's a good experience, but you you can simply watch Youtube videos to figure out the story. I think people should get this if it's on a sale, but at full price, I don't think so. There's not enough content in my opinion to justify a $79.95 price tag.

Very good, challenging (but not TOO challenging) physics and logic puzzle gameplay, gorgeous visual rendering, many many hours of playable content and bonuses (hidden areas) - what's not to like? The best thing about this game however is the masterful fusion of non-finctional and fictional (very plausibly derived works of nonfiction) philosophical discourse and mind experiments into these game elements! Yes, that's right - usually, attempts to pull off this go horribly wrong, with the results being some combination of incoherent, irrelevant, simplified to the point of rendering it futile, etc - but not so here! One gets the impression the developers are well read themselves and/or they got some effective guidance from elsewhere.
The content itself is pleasingly in depth and well explored, but importantly, it is relevant to the events and basis of the game's plot, new ideas being introduced at appropriate moments to encourage introspection and exploration of the ideas. Similarly, developing an understanding and appreciation of the concepts introduced pays off in later gameplay and developing an attachment/interest in the characters.
Highly recommended!

TL;DR: Man, what a game from Croteam, the same team that made the leave-your-brains-outside Serious Sam FPS games. I mean, this game is a total 180 degrees from those. But it's a good thig, it's a very good thing. Totally recommended to everyone who likes, or thik might like a puzzle game. This one here is a winner, a true gem from the sidelines. Support Croteam, BUY IT!
The long version:
First of all, I'm going to mention Portal, but not because I feel this game rips off Portal, but because I think this game is on the same level. Simply put, Talos Principle is a magnificent puzzle-game. This is one of the games, that made me think the puzzles even when I was not playing the game. Something that Portal games and for example The Swapper did for me also, and that's a clear sign of a great game.
For people who are worried about the amount of content, worry not. There are a LOT of puzzles in the game, all ranging from good to unbelievable clever ones, from easy to clever tricky ones to absolute brain twisters, the range is huge, but NEVER unfair. The way you need to solve the puzzles also varies a lot - sometimes you have to be looking for right angles, sometimes thinking outside the box and so on. It has also enough mechanics to keep the challenges fresh and the progression going forward all the way thru the game. And don't forget the secret/special goals, some of them being really tricky ones.
If you like stories, there's parallel story lines/contributions in this game. The least effor needing one is told via "master's" voice, the second is also voice recordings you try to find from the levels while the third one, the most philosophical bit, is told thru text and conversation via computers you find in every level. It's really up to you how much you want to invest in the story. If you're into philosophy, this game tackles quite deep into the question of "what's the definition of being (a person)". I'd say the level of interest in philosophy plays a huge role whether the story works for you or not.
Some reviewers have critisized the art direction, or the contuinity of the worlds' aesthetics. I don't fully agree with the critisim. And here's why: the locations actually fit into the thematics of the game. The underlying theme is a very traditional philosophical question, and there's a clear tone towards philosophy in this game and the environments are part of that. The Greek looking theme: pretty clear, when you talk about philosophy. The Egypt theme: also very important location in philosophy (it is believed, taht the whole philosophical way of thinking things began from Egypt). The middle-age theme: also a huge part in philosophy. So those locations aren't just pulled out of hat, the developer clearly have had some point in those. But I agree, that it might be a bit uncoherent for people who aren't that into philosophy. Graphically this game is good looking. Animations could be a bit better, but not really a big thing in a game like this.
So, is there anything I would change in the game? There is something (nothing is perfect, right?). First of all, eventhough I said earlier, that all the puzzles are good, I still think the amount of puzzles could've been edited a bit or at least the grouping of those could've been done a bit better. There's a part in the game, where the difficulty of the puzzles are a bit of a rollercoaster - while some puzzles might be easier, then there can be a huge difficulty spike in the next puzzle. Small thing in a semi-open game like this, but it could've been done a bit better still. Second one (A SLIGHT SPOILER AHEAD): the last level has a time limit, which IMO is a questionable design choice in a game, that otherwise son't hurry the player at all. I understand, it's the last test, but still, I felt it was a bit out of the place, especially when you have to start the whole puzzle from the beginning if you mess up. Other than that? Not really anything else.
In my books Talos Principle is one of the best puzzle games out there, a total gem.

Brutal, gruesome, gory and at times almost poetic in its attempts, albeit weak, at emotional resonance with the player, Wolfenstein: The New Order is a fantastic First-Person Shooter. The shooting mechanics are slick and well-designed and the simple modifications available for weapons from dual-wielding shotguns that fire ricocheting shrapnel to silenced pistols expands the shooting experience in a very natural and fun way. It's refreshing to blast your way out of a crowded area with two massive shotguns only to crouch behind cover, pull out a pistol, screw on a silencer and quickly and quietly take down a sentry before moving forward into another area where you can then pull out a large laser weapon and take on heavily-armored super soldiers. The enemies themselves are relatively smart and will try to flush you out of cover and force you to engage them and this in addition to the variety of enemies makes most encounters somewhat different from the last 3 or 4. That being said, some enemy types are merely reskins with a different loadout and slightly adjusted health so the variety could be better but it's by no means an issue.
The graphics are very impressive and performed well at high-settings on my machine (ATI Radeon 7850 2GB, 4.4GHz Quad-Core, 16GB RAM) however there were a few areas where low-res textures were plainly obvious which detracted somewhat from the experience.
The game is quite linear in terms of story, although you are offered a choice early on in the game that determines whether you go through the rest of the story with one character or another. This character fills a specific role that doesn't change in either 'timeline' so it's a really big shame that this choice isn't more profound. While the story is quite linear, a lot of the levels are designed in an open-ended enough fashion so that aside from the set-pieces you can choose between going stealth or guns blazing and the laser cutter that allows you to open up certain areas is a very nice touch as it gives a feeling that you're able to adapt the conditions to suit your play style and not the other way around.
A few really awesome things:
-Most of the german accents were very well spoken - really helps with the immersion for a German-speaker like myself
-The nightmare section - awesome! - although it was a shame that when you got to the end of the level you woke up, I would have loved to play through some more areas
-The weapon/combat perks were a fun way to force me to intentionally mix up my combat style in order to get certain benefits
A few points of criticism:
-Deathshead's German accent sounded awful
-Very little time spent on the lunar surface... I was disappointed
-When the recordings by Anya of Ramona's diary entries get added, each time there's this loud notification sound that genuinely scares the s**t out of me when I'm in the middle of sneaking around Nazi installations. Stop that, seriously.
-Some boss (and mini-boss) sections are very poorly sign posted e.g. in the final battle I died around 20 times before finally killing the S.O.B. but I never knew how close to the end I was each time because there was no easy way to tell - the gradual degradation of the level was a helpful indicator but I found myself saying many, many times "how much worse can this get before it's over?"
Overall 7.5/10 - definitely worth a buy if you like FPS games

So you're deciding to pick up Max Payne 3, but you're unsure if it's the right match for you? Well, let me give you a break down as to why I think this is one of the best games to come out in the last 5 years.
Max Payne 3 is a narrative third person shooter that follows the life of a man who's living on his last thread. And I put heavy emphasis on narrative. Even though there's plenty of action to be had, this game wants you to care about Max Payne as well as give a purpose for all the killing you're about to do. So expect a half and half- not quite Metal Gear Solid, but some may definitely be put off by having the keys taken away every now and then for the sake of plot. So if you like your game jam packed with action with little interference, you may want to hold off for a sale to try this tale.
Hands off to Rockstar on this one, though. The world they've built is so fresh and believable, you really feel like you're in another world. Sao Paolo and the Brazilian locales are all wonderfully and meticulously realized, it feels more real than any other game that's come out. Civilians are everywhere, living their lives regardless of the incidents around them. Police roam the streets and favelas, issuing curfews and exacting brute force when insisted. The enemies don't speak in thick American accents. Hell, half the time the protagonists don't speak english (or  translated), leaving the player to feel alienated and alone. This ties in perfectly with the character of Max- with the loss of his family, his lover, and his career, Max is a drifter with no place in this world and its up to you to push him through and give him a reason to live and a peace in his heart.
MP3 still retains the action packed gameplay from before, however this time it's a bit slowed down. Max needs to take cover far more often, as the enemies can finish him off really quickly. Max feels a bit clunky, but I can understand this as representing the character himself- An out of shape, drunk pilled up wreck of a man. You still chuck pills to heal yourself, you still rack up bullet time from kills and headshots, and you can still shoot dodge, causing max to leap in the direction you choose while being able to fire your weapon , with or without bullet time (though the latter will just be real time).
The weapons range all over the place from pistols, to SMGS and LMGs. You can dual wield any 1h weapon, which causes Max to drop his 2h weapon automatically, a puzzling choice to be sure. Max also has a melee attack, and if you're low or empty on ammo the move can steal another enemies weapon.
Taking cover is pretty similar to other TPS of the time and it's a little stiff. You need to press the cover key to actually take cover, which can lead to some frustrating moments. Similarly, the roll action is rather poor and inconsistent. You'll get the timing down by the end, but it's still one of my least favorite moves. And last but not least, this game is challenging. Expect yourself to be on your last pill, bleeding out, and entering a room with 10 militia rolling in with full body armor. I've beaten the game on all difficulties, and I highly recommend starting on normal or easy, the latter will make you cry.
So all in all, if you're interested in the game and have read this far into the review, then I recommend getting this game. The story's fun, it time travels all over the last few years, it never stays still for too long, and it has wonderful (if sometimes corny) voice acting and motion capture. Do note that the multiplayer is all but dead except for cheaters, so it's probably not going to satisfy any MP itch. Average campaign is probably 9-12 hours first time through on normal, and there's plenty of reason to go back through with different game types and challenges.
One last thing to note, Rockstar's DRM is so awful that you may run into some problems. There'are plenty of walkthroughs and troubleshooting tips to get pass the Club sign in, but keep in mind it's pretty inconsistent.
The storyline is very dramatic and unique. Very recommended to try this game out if you are looking for somthing new and puzzle type game.

TL;DR: Man, what a game from Croteam, the same team that made the leave-your-brains-outside Serious Sam FPS games. I mean, this game is a total 180 degrees from those. But it's a good thig, it's a very good thing. Totally recommended to everyone who likes, or thik might like a puzzle game. This one here is a winner, a true gem from the sidelines. Support Croteam, BUY IT!
The long version:
First of all, I'm going to mention Portal, but not because I feel this game rips off Portal, but because I think this game is on the same level. Simply put, Talos Principle is a magnificent puzzle-game. This is one of the games, that made me think the puzzles even when I was not playing the game. Something that Portal games and for example The Swapper did for me also, and that's a clear sign of a great game.
For people who are worried about the amount of content, worry not. There are a LOT of puzzles in the game, all ranging from good to unbelievable clever ones, from easy to clever tricky ones to absolute brain twisters, the range is huge, but NEVER unfair. The way you need to solve the puzzles also varies a lot - sometimes you have to be looking for right angles, sometimes thinking outside the box and so on. It has also enough mechanics to keep the challenges fresh and the progression going forward all the way thru the game. And don't forget the secret/special goals, some of them being really tricky ones.
If you like stories, there's parallel story lines/contributions in this game. The least effor needing one is told via "master's" voice, the second is also voice recordings you try to find from the levels while the third one, the most philosophical bit, is told thru text and conversation via computers you find in every level. It's really up to you how much you want to invest in the story. If you're into philosophy, this game tackles quite deep into the question of "what's the definition of being (a person)". I'd say the level of interest in philosophy plays a huge role whether the story works for you or not.
Some reviewers have critisized the art direction, or the contuinity of the worlds' aesthetics. I don't fully agree with the critisim. And here's why: the locations actually fit into the thematics of the game. The underlying theme is a very traditional philosophical question, and there's a clear tone towards philosophy in this game and the environments are part of that. The Greek looking theme: pretty clear, when you talk about philosophy. The Egypt theme: also very important location in philosophy (it is believed, taht the whole philosophical way of thinking things began from Egypt). The middle-age theme: also a huge part in philosophy. So those locations aren't just pulled out of hat, the developer clearly have had some point in those. But I agree, that it might be a bit uncoherent for people who aren't that into philosophy. Graphically this game is good looking. Animations could be a bit better, but not really a big thing in a game like this.
So, is there anything I would change in the game? There is something (nothing is perfect, right?). First of all, eventhough I said earlier, that all the puzzles are good, I still think the amount of puzzles could've been edited a bit or at least the grouping of those could've been done a bit better. There's a part in the game, where the difficulty of the puzzles are a bit of a rollercoaster - while some puzzles might be easier, then there can be a huge difficulty spike in the next puzzle. Small thing in a semi-open game like this, but it could've been done a bit better still. Second one (A SLIGHT SPOILER AHEAD): the last level has a time limit, which IMO is a questionable design choice in a game, that otherwise son't hurry the player at all. I understand, it's the last test, but still, I felt it was a bit out of the place, especially when you have to start the whole puzzle from the beginning if you mess up. Other than that? Not really anything else.
In my books Talos Principle is one of the best puzzle games out there, a total gem.

Robocraft is a lovely multiplayer game, standing out from similar "build your 'robot'" games in that its voxel-like building system gives you superb amounts of control over building, compared to "head, body, legs" style of bot construction. And, after you build such a robot, you can then take it into battle and play in a variety of gamemodes against other players, such as deathmatch and a territory control "battle arena".
That out of the way, let's list off some pros/cons:
PROS:
F2P, only thing really throttled by paying is the obtaining of cosmetic parts, which you cannot buy with earned ingame currency. There is a grind, as most F2P games have. My advice - tanks are cheap, start out with building some until you get better weapons.
Custom Games - if you can find a friend, you can host your own matches, whether for mayhem or testing game mechanics on each other.
Great sound/music design - You'll be hard pressed to take issue with the rumble of large tank treads, the futuristic whine of VTOL wings, or the familiar thwa-thwap-thwap of a helicopter as you pilot your robot amongst others.
Premium membership- the bonuses of a premium membership are mainly cosmetic, but they also provide a 3x recylce value that's super useful if you're stuck in a grind. For the cost of about 1$, you can paint your robots, scrap what you don't need, and get double XP and crate loot for a day! Of course, there's also a 50-60$ lifetime option if you have deeper pockets.
CONS:
If you have satellite internet or internet that tends to give up frequently, I'd wait for the devs to implement a game reconnect feature. Currently, some players have issues with "desyncs" which can kick you out mid-game. I very rarely have this issue, but I can't speak for everyone.
Some movement parts are rather twitchy/buggy. I remain confident they'll fix them, as there used to be a lot more movement parts that were downright unusable in early access but got improved/fixed.

An epic rollercoaster of Nazis, razormouth robot dogs, Moon Nazis, blade happy Nazis, Nazis, bullets going through Nazis, sharp pieces of metal in the process of violently entering Nazis, and robot Nazis. But seriously, Wolfenstein: TNO is one of the best shooters I have ever played. It emobodies a classic action movie, and an unbelievably good one at that. The game revolutionizes senless bombastic violence, and makes slaughtering evil Nazis more of a blast than EVER! Although some sort of Co-op or Multiplayer mode would be awesome, this game more than stands for itsself as a singleplayer campaign.
Pros:
-GREAT Gunplay
-Excellent, Grade A+ story even through all of the senseless violence
-Very creative enemies, MOON NAZIS!
-A believable alternate-timeline
-Very well fleshed out characters
-Voice acting is high quality
-Weapons play very differently and options for upgrades are well varied
-Stealth is present and often well done
-Level design and environment is very creative
-Those robots tho...
-Difficult and challenging, but often not too much
-Creative and extremely intimidating bosses
-Provokes thought
-Right off the bat, a major choice is presented.
-Replayable due to alternate choices and collectibles, and also cuz it is a blast
-Music is awesome!
-Blazkowicz isn't just a muscled meat monster of an army ranger, he is a realistic character that isn't a gunweilding fearless god that is immortal.....
Cons: (mostly performance issues on AMD)
-MAJOR performance issues on AMD systems, I had DAYS of trouble and had to modify my installation. Still had texture issues (pop-in) and also had an issue after alt-tabbing/maximizing the game where it went into slow motion
-Boss difficulty curve toward the end is kinda ridiculous, end boss kills you endlessly if you aren't careful
-(Minor) Blazkowicz is a little bit of a Chuck Norris-y character and somehow survives several brutal injuries
-Difficulty can sometimes spike pretty dramatically
-(Minor) Some of the collectibles are almost impossible to reach
-(Minor) On AMD systems, texture pop-in seems inevitable
Altogether one of my favorites of all time. Worth any price IMO.
TL:DR- All around one of the best frickin games I have ever played.

Honestly, the game is pretty dated. I play it with a friend who played it a long while back.
It's a decently fun game. Nowadays it's simply not good enough to suck me in, make me play it alone as someone new to the series. However, I can see completely why people who liked the game when they were younger would want to play it again, because the game is about as good as these older games get, and is probably exactly what those who played AoEII in the past will expect from it.
-----
Gameplay: The gameplay is pretty satisfying. You build up a small kingdom by constructing various buildings to produce different bonuses for your "empire." However, the thrill of seeing the little settlers at work eventually turns into the disappointment of having to actually fight people with a cumbersome system that rewards spamming swarms of units instead of actually having any real tactics whatsoever. If I could give the pre-battle and post-battle parts of each game two separate scores, it'd be 7.5/10 and 4/10, but as it is I'll just give the whole thing a
.
Graphics/Visual Experience: It's an old game, but it's not hard to tell what's going on. When playing, I do feel "sucked in" to the game's environment. However, units have a tendency to clump up when there are enough of them (and more often than not, there is), which makes things difficult.
Sound: The game doesn't feel cluttered with unnecessary soundbytes or loud music. The music creates a good feeling but I personally found it grating after a while. The experience, however, is not ruined by Spotify running quietly in the background. It's a game that demands attention, so the game's natural ambiance caters to that requirement.
Replayability: Pretty good. Each game has the potential to play out differently from the one before.
How it Runs: It's an older game so unless you're trying to run it on a TI-83, it'll probably work.

I went into this "re-boot" with very low expectations. I still got disappointed.
The last Wolfenstein re-boot (Return to castle Wolfenstein) was a pretty good game. In fact the engine it ran on was so awesome that it even spawned it's own multiplayer spin off. Perhaps unsurprisingly the newest game appears to be  trying hard to emulate COD or BF. The controls feel clunky and the "open world" is riddled with invisible walls. The story is served trough a, forced, mixture of cutscenes and gameplay. You know the kind where the entire thing is really a cutscene except from the part where you walk from A to B and shot a monster and then the scene continues. Initially your character falls into a coma. Sporting some hilariously disconnected scenes where we are supposed to develop feelings for our nurse because she is spoon feeding us for what seems like an eternity. While a plot like this might work in a movie it's somewhat hard to care when your just a floating camera. After all the reason why this even works in a movie is because of the dynamic between two actors. Not being able to make any form of reaction makes the whole thing very emotionless in a game. So when the Nazis; taking away the nurse, made my character stand up and start killing them it felt more comical than anything else.
In this game it would seem that a fair amount of the action takes place outside, this makes the open world aspect a huge joke. Ironically a slightly more enclosed game with multiple paths from A to B would have been better. After all having actual walls blocking you is always an improvement compared to invisible ones.
The developers have also, probably purposefully, created sneak and all-out-attack sections of the maps. The only issue is that you can't really tell which one your in. Causing several scenarios where you run out of ammo only after realizing that this area was intended for a sneak approach. This is bloody annoying when your just interested in having a good time. That said the sneaking is decently implemented and very rewarding experience when it succeeds.
Overall this is a bad game. Your money will be well spent elsewhere. Even nostalgia can't outweigh all the annoying deaths you will encounter as a result of poor design.

The New Order is a great shooter with surprisingly strong storytelling chops. The characters are intriguing and flawed in their own ways, and B.J. Blazkowicz feels surprisingly human despite being a basically immortal♥♥♥♥♥kicking machine. The primary antagonists are nazis, so they are easy to hate and you don't have to feel bad about melting their faces off with a giant laser like you might if they were a different, not-nazi enemy. This is a game that revels in violence and mayhem, celebrating your own unique approaches to nazi murder. Some areas are tough as hell and might require a different approach to get through alive, but failing for the 1000th time doesn't feel frustrating because playing the game is so damn fun. Finally beating a difficult bit is extremely satisfying because you worked hard to achieve it. Weapons are a pleasure to use and killing nazis never gets boring. As a cherry on top, the game looks stunning in motion as well.
Thankfully, The New Order doesn't take itself terribly seriously. Nobody ages a day in the 14 years between story points, you can dual wield assault rifles and shotguns, the nazis have a base on the moon (at which you can murder them in waves), and you can sleep in a certain bed to have nightmares about playing the original Wolfenstein 3D.
Only disappointing part is that one of the boss fights about 3/4 through the game is pretty boring and not as challenging as the rest of the game. Most of the other bosses are pretty challenging and interesting to fight, though.

Great first person shooter with massive maps and massive battles with potentially hundreds of players on each side.
There are 3 factions: VanuSovereignity, NeoConglomerate and TerrainRepublic. VS are sci-fi style with hovertank and plasma weapons. Their weaponry is mixed. NC are mercenaries with gauss weapons. Their main battletank is closest to normal tank. They have heavy emphasis towards shotguns. TR are "the empire". They use regular weaponry and tend to have large clips on their weapons. Their main battletank has 2 barrels.
The best quality of PS2 is that its sandbox styled. You can do what ever you want. If you like to play with other people you can join someone's squad or start your own (quality of playing with squad depends on 75% leader and 25% members in my opinion). You can go solo and still be part of large battles, take potshots at the fringes or even infiltrate enemy bases and cause havoc there.
Planetside 2 is free to play, so you can use real money to buy stuff. However, everything that actually affects gameplay can be unlocked by playing within reasonable amount of time. You can trial any weapon for 1h per day. Most weapons are sidegrades and most stock weapons are actually quite good. Having large arsenal means that you can tackle wider variety of situations.
I'd say PS2 is pay for convenience and pay for bling.
This is a great incentive to actually buy their stuff and support the continued existence of Planetside 2.

I don't know how to feel about this game. I mean it is great. It handles like it should, there are enough guns, upgrades, and collectables to keep things from getting stale. The graphics are some of the best I have seen, and matching it with some great depth of field really makes it feel like you are there when you run it on full specs. There are a few things this game really got right like the super powerful chain guns, collectibles that do things, and game feel. There are enough enemies and boss fights to keep it from getting boring. The alternative history got my brain hard as a rock. You even get to go to the moon. Now the down side. The story. You only get to walk on the moon for like a minute and there are like three enemies. It is like they couldn't figure out what way to go with it. It is serious at some points, then it is goofy, then it gets self aware and makes fun of itself. The character building is almost good. All of the characters grow, but they never become really human. With the 6-8 hours you get to spend playing the story they have to rush though a lot of stuff, and they show you flash back to things you never get  to do in the game, know the medium show dont tell. The love story is forced, the friends are mostly two dimensional, and the enemies are great. I didn't know that you wanted to make the people you want to kill the most fleshed out characters. They like to make you use the lazer gun. It really isn't the best, and they force it on you a lot. It is a good story, but you can't tell it right in such a short time. In all I loved it, but it seems like there was a lot of game left out here. 8/10

This is without doubt one of the best games I've ever played. I like it more than Portal 2, and I like Portal 2 a lot.
9/10
= Long version (you can skip to the short one in the end) =
Though they're of the same genre there are some notable differences between the two games: Portal focus more than a bit on [not-that-much] fast paced actions and movement skills, Talos focus quite entirely on meditating to find the solution; in my opinion Portal is similar to Tetris and Talos is similar to chess.
You can play The Talos Principle focusing only on puzzle solving, there are no restraints to this, but you will lose one of the best videogame-story so far. It's a story about the meaning of life, humanity, history, past, future, everything. Be awared that this story is told in an uncommon way, you will have to "dig" a bit to find it: explore carefully the levels to find their slightly hidden secrets, scan QR codes (use a smartphone app), read text files and e-mails on computers and so on.
All these small "frames" make a complex story and sadly it's easy to miss something important, perhapse this is a cons of this game.
Level design is really good, surroundings are beautiful, poetic and amazing and you never have the feelings of a "small" and linear game. Some puzzles are hard but if you're fine with Portal and The Talos Principle Public Test (basically a free demo; you should play it to decide whether to buy the complete game or not) you shouldn't have problems with this.
There's little to no tutorial and some puzzle may seems hard/impossible to solve but when you understand the mechanic behind the objects involved you will see it's easy, this could be another cons though it has a meaning for the story (you impersonate someone/something which goal is to learn).
Music. Just astounding and perfectly filling, in my opinion one of the best videogame OST ever composed:
= Short version=
Pro:
+ interesting concept/subject
+ novel idea
+ good level design
+ good story
+ good music
+ good length, without ANY cinematic, scripting o QTE, which are a mean of cheating in regards of play time
+ few to none boring parts
+ mindblowing philosophy and questions
Cons:
- minimalistic tutorial, it has a meaning in the story but sometimes you can find yourself stuck because you don't fully know game mechanics
- the story, while beautiful, is not that easy to fully reveal
- there are multiple endings but if you're not careful you can lose your savegames after getting one, preventing you from getting all the others without replaying the WHOLE game
In my opinion this game hasn't got the success it deserves: if you find interesting please buy and spread it between your friends. And the beautiful soundtrack has only 18k views on YouTube after 3 months.

I have only finished the single player campaign so far, but wow. It is rare that a sequel can top an original, whether it be a movie, game, or anything for that matter. This game literally has 100 times more content than the original, has great graphics for a 2011 computer game, and unlike some games, has a complex and well set up storyline. I didn't get this for $20, but it is completely worth the $20. At first I thought it was gonna be just more levels but when the testing facility was falling apart (as evident by the preview images above), but it became so much more than that.
The gameplay mechanics perhaps quadrupled from the last game. If you played the original, you know you played with cubes, companion cubes, buttons, momentum, turrets, rocket launchers, and deadly goo, not to mention moving platforms and of course the iconic portal gun. Now take all these things and add laser grids, "discouragement redicrection cubes" that direct lasers, light walls, vortexes (excursion funnels), crushers, and cube-turret combos known as frakenturrets. But the most interesting mechanic is the goo. Four types of goo lead you to some interesting level solutions.
The levels are unique as well. Some mimic the environment of the original game, while others play more into the storyline and feel less like levels and more like "open world" environments though they certainly aren't open world.
The voice acting is on point. The characters can get you to hate them, laugh at them, pity them, etc. Minor spoiler: One of the funniest parts was when Wheatley asked the player to say apple. You respond by pressing space and jumping, which of course confuses Wheatley.
The storyline is a good combination of mystery, adventure and action. There are a few plot twists as well.
Not really into storylines? Then buy the game for the level creator so you can make challenging puzzles for the entire Steam community. Want to play with someone else. Use the Co-op mode and play unique levels designed just for two people.
So what are you waiting for? Buy it already!

I went into this "re-boot" with very low expectations. I still got disappointed.
The last Wolfenstein re-boot (Return to castle Wolfenstein) was a pretty good game. In fact the engine it ran on was so awesome that it even spawned it's own multiplayer spin off. Perhaps unsurprisingly the newest game appears to be  trying hard to emulate COD or BF. The controls feel clunky and the "open world" is riddled with invisible walls. The story is served trough a, forced, mixture of cutscenes and gameplay. You know the kind where the entire thing is really a cutscene except from the part where you walk from A to B and shot a monster and then the scene continues. Initially your character falls into a coma. Sporting some hilariously disconnected scenes where we are supposed to develop feelings for our nurse because she is spoon feeding us for what seems like an eternity. While a plot like this might work in a movie it's somewhat hard to care when your just a floating camera. After all the reason why this even works in a movie is because of the dynamic between two actors. Not being able to make any form of reaction makes the whole thing very emotionless in a game. So when the Nazis; taking away the nurse, made my character stand up and start killing them it felt more comical than anything else.
In this game it would seem that a fair amount of the action takes place outside, this makes the open world aspect a huge joke. Ironically a slightly more enclosed game with multiple paths from A to B would have been better. After all having actual walls blocking you is always an improvement compared to invisible ones.
The developers have also, probably purposefully, created sneak and all-out-attack sections of the maps. The only issue is that you can't really tell which one your in. Causing several scenarios where you run out of ammo only after realizing that this area was intended for a sneak approach. This is bloody annoying when your just interested in having a good time. That said the sneaking is decently implemented and very rewarding experience when it succeeds.
Overall this is a bad game. Your money will be well spent elsewhere. Even nostalgia can't outweigh all the annoying deaths you will encounter as a result of poor design.

The New Order is a great shooter with surprisingly strong storytelling chops. The characters are intriguing and flawed in their own ways, and B.J. Blazkowicz feels surprisingly human despite being a basically immortal♥♥♥♥♥kicking machine. The primary antagonists are nazis, so they are easy to hate and you don't have to feel bad about melting their faces off with a giant laser like you might if they were a different, not-nazi enemy. This is a game that revels in violence and mayhem, celebrating your own unique approaches to nazi murder. Some areas are tough as hell and might require a different approach to get through alive, but failing for the 1000th time doesn't feel frustrating because playing the game is so damn fun. Finally beating a difficult bit is extremely satisfying because you worked hard to achieve it. Weapons are a pleasure to use and killing nazis never gets boring. As a cherry on top, the game looks stunning in motion as well.
Thankfully, The New Order doesn't take itself terribly seriously. Nobody ages a day in the 14 years between story points, you can dual wield assault rifles and shotguns, the nazis have a base on the moon (at which you can murder them in waves), and you can sleep in a certain bed to have nightmares about playing the original Wolfenstein 3D.
Only disappointing part is that one of the boss fights about 3/4 through the game is pretty boring and not as challenging as the rest of the game. Most of the other bosses are pretty challenging and interesting to fight, though.
Highly recommended. As I'm sure many others have said, kind of a cross between Portal and Myst. Wonderful game, buy it now, it's worth whatever they're charging.

I, personally, am someone who has played Robocraft quite a bit. However, due to numerous patches that have been steadily lowering the quality of the game, I decided to take a break- in the 6-9 month length. Today, I decided to dust off the old game and try it again- and let me tell you, it's only gotten worse. Robocraft was a game that started off with a great concept and limitless potential; I tell you, I see none of that game left. To put it bluntly, in my playtime today I saw no real content updates or additions since I decided to quit; I'm sure there have been bugfixes and QOL adjustments, but there is no new content- this was an automatic turnoff to me, because I wasn't satisfied with the content there was when I WAS playing- and over a minimum of half a year, they should've managed to do something, but such was not the case.
In fact, I lucked out, and chose to play the day that a brand-new patch came out, a patch that the developers claimed was the "biggest" patch in well over a year. Do you want to know what it actually was? The developers spitting in the face of all their veteran players, and removing some of the last vestiges of replayability that the game had. Every advantage that veteran players had, aside from parts collected, was removed- and, to null even that last part, players now get bonus items on every level, but with zero consideration for the veterans who already were at the prior maximum level of 150. This is why I flatout detest Freejam, and will not be playing this game again; aside from the fact that they are absolute screwups and ruined an incredible game, they have no consideration whatsoever for their veteran playerbase- including the ones who spent money on the game. Thankfully, I never did.

the game is objective oriented, so it's not simply a point and shoot with no other option to contribute to your team if your aim is always average compared to the enemy's. if you're a good healer in other games, you can choose to be a laid back support role player in dirty bomb as well and assist your team to victory this way, the demand on good aim alone is offset by so many other ways you can find your way to obstruct your enemies objectives or fast track your team's objective completion.
there is good balance and good bullet damage where it's not a 1-3 hit kill around the corner like csgo for example and that translates into good balance for fps game that you'll only notice after committing hundreds of hours in playtime. after a few hundred hours in csgo, it starts to feel like a showdown of latency more than actual gameplay and unforgiving need of extraordinarily precise aim because high damage bullets magnify the effect of latency advantages and you always feel like you're just not skilled enough of a player to kill first before getting killed but do not blame yourself for lack of competency as how a game's mechanics are designed actually plays a large part to that detrimental feeling you get every time from losing aim battles that require more than ordinary consistency, precision and super fast reflexes. this is greatly mitigated in dirty bomb due to low per bullet damage and if u're skilled u're still going to be the one to bring down the enemy first before he does and you'll experience much lesser of peeking a corner and dying to 1-3 high damage bullet like it is in csgo because you can dodge, run and even skip off a wall to safety as you get more skilled in dirty bomb.
it's completely a skill to win payment system here, you don't have to pay a single cent for character unlocks and loadout cards. playtime alone allows you to unlock everything in the game without losing any technical edge compared to paying players. players that want to unlock characters quicker can choose to pay.
if you been playing enough of fps, you'll feel the balance you've always seeked out of first person shooter games in dirty bomb and it's a whole lot less of downtime watching teammates do jack sh!t after you've gone down to enemies, an ideal scenario for casual gamers!

Not to be confused with one of the Gods of Skyrim, The Talos Principle is a philosophically themed puzzle game and has nothing to do with any of the Elder Scrolls games. Released late last year (2014), The Talos Principle was made by a small European development studio based in Croatia whose only previous notable works are the Serious Sam games. Being a puzzle game, The Talos Principle is a huge departure from the FPS style of the Serious Sam games so I was expecting this title to maybe be a little rough around the edges and maybe expose the inexperience of the development team making a game in a new style, but this was not the case at all. The Talos Principle is air tight, and features some of the best puzzle design and well executed narrative I have ever experienced in a video game.
The game begins as your player character wakes up in a seemingly abandoned garden. Between the lines of computer text scrolling across the screen or the occasional glimpse of your own metallic fingers, you'll quickly realize that your player character is a robot. Your unnamed character soon begins to hear a voice in his head. The voice refers to himself as Elohim (Hebrew for God) and starts referring to you as "my child". But not really in the typical motherly/fatherly parental way; the voice refers to you as "my child" the same way a God would address his creation. The voice then guides you around the garden and asks you to solve various puzzles to obtain "sigils", which will unlock more areas of the garden which will allow you to collect more sigils
The structure of the game is broken down into solving puzzles, obtaining sigils, reading pieces of story text and then repeating the process. This structure and repetitive pacing of The Talos Principle might be the only complaint someone could have against it, unless you don't care for difficult puzzles, which this game definitely has. I've often criticized games for being too repetitive and not offering enough variety of gameplay, but I never really got that feeling from this game. Even though it was a very lengthy (about 40 hours) puzzle game, I never felt like it outstayed its welcome There was enough variety in the puzzle rooms and with the methods used to solve the puzzles that I never got the sense that I was doing the same thing over and over. The Talos Principle felt like a longer version of Braid, but 3D and with different puzzle mechanics. It's what I'd imagine The Witness would play like, if it ever gets released. I really can't stress enough the brilliance of in the design of the puzzle rooms here. The Talos Principle introduces puzzle elements, makes sure you understand how they work, then slowly increases the difficulty and complexity of the puzzles. Some of the later puzzles required me to just stop and stare at the screen and think. I love when games can get me to do that.
Summary
I know we're still very early in 2015 and also this game came out in December 2014, but The Talos Principle will more than likely be my 2015 game of the year. I was totally blown away by the superb puzzle design and the amazing presentation of the story. There's so much about the story I didn't want to reveal here for fear of spoilers, but exploring the island and finally uncovering its secrets felt really rewarding. The Talos Principle is everything I want in a video game. I would highly recommend it to fans of puzzle games or people who enjoy excellent game design

Once upon a time in 2004 a mod was made for the UT2003 engine.  It's name was Red Orchestra (RO) and it was good.  A small but close nit community formed around its ground breaking realism play and iron sight aiming method.  Since then, RO went retail and subsequently released RO2 (aka COD:Eastern Front) but none could hold a flame to the original RO mod.  The community descended into ruins.  For 11 years we wandered the barren wasteland of such publications as Battlefield, Arma, Hero's and Generals, Verdun, Insurgency, and DayZ in search of the 'good ole days' of tactical large scale gameplay.  Until now. The search has ended my friends. Behold our magnum opus: Squad.
The recoil system is the most realistic I have seen. The suppression is just enough to make you cower but not overdone to be annoying.  The beedout and bandage system gives you time to hide and heal but keeps your health low until medics arrive.  The zoom in and hold breath is just right for the distance most engagements happen. The weapon sway is just enough. The graphics are great and not over taxing.  You can hide in the shrubbery.  Snipers do not dominate the game.  The maps are huge and you can flank with out having unnatural boundaries. Squad communication and movement is a must to survive and squad leaders can communicate to each other via push to talk makeing pub games feel like a clan match.  Mobile spawn system keeps a well defined front line of battle without any of the "5 enemies spawning out of a squad-leader's butt behind enemy lines"  bullcrap of the Battlefield series.
Want more? Buy the game with your wampum.

A great puzzle game and a fantastic experience. I am currently in what can be called the endgame, so while I technically haven't finished the game, I have a pretty good understanding of it. Let's start with the technical. The graphics are more than adequate for a title of this price and the optimization is great. Everything you would expect from such a prominent PC developer as Croteam.
Now to the actual gameplay. The puzzles are good. It's not Portal, but it's not far behind. The game starts suffering from too many mechanics near the end, but the tasks are still intuitive. Most puzzles are a matter of concept rather than execution which is exactly what you want to hear about a puzzle game. There are exceptions, but they are few and far between. Overall, it's good even for someone who is not a hardcore puzzle game fan. Another point that should be commended is Croteam's incredible talent when it comes to secrets. Easter eggs and stars (hidden collectibles) are hidden so well that it gave me flashbacks to Serious Sam 1. (In that game you could finish a level in 20 minutes and then see a "Secrets 0/17" on the end level screen)
All of that said, the gameplay is not why I'm recommending this game. The biggest thing by far is the game's philosophical nature.
VERY MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD (SERIOUSLY IT'S THE FIRST 10-15 MINUTES)
Early on you are introduced to two characters, if you can even call them that. One of them will provide an interesting narrative, that will no doubt make you intrigued about the nature of this world and the nature of your own character. The other one is much more interesting. I won't say where you encounter him, but he will constantly meet you through the game and ask you very difficult questions. Your conversations will be centered around deep philosophical problems that have no real answer. He's not a very kind debater and will mock you every time you contradict yourself. I spent a lot of my time arguing with that damn thing and questioning my answers over and over again. The experience really can't be compared to anything else.
SUMMARY:
positives
+ good puzzles
+ well-hidden secrets
+ great narrative
+ good visuals
+ deep philosophical questions that you will be faced with over and over again
+ great soundtrack (that damn tower track, just perfect)
slight negatives
- too many mechanics in the late game
- a few of the puzzles are tedious and will cause you to fail and re-do a bunch of stuff you've done three time already (only a few of these)
- may be too easy for veterans of the genre (this is only a hunch, I'm not one of them)

I went into it expecting a disaster. However, I was pleasantly surprised. Max Payne stands for bullet-time and heavy story. MP3 has both.
Gameplay-wise, it's a standard third person shooter, with the adrenaline-> bullet-time mechanic, and 3 weapons system. You can have two sidearms, and a two-handed weapon. You can obviously dual-wield, but that makes you drop the bigger gun - which you carry in your left hand if you're wielding just one sidearm. Which is a cool, realistic touch, and looks nice. Gameplay is nothing special though, besides what I mentioned, it's run of the mill semi-clunky, but enjoyable, chest-high wall simulator, with two QTE's and some turret sections and shooting galleries (cool scenes, where you slide or fly or fall or whatever and you have to take out as many bad guys as possible in slow-mo). There are collectibles here and there, golden parts for weapons, and clues to the story. The latter are worthwhile to look for. tld;dr - Make no mistake, gameplay-wise, it's still Max Payne
But that I already knew. I was afraid of the setting, sunny Brazil, and the story. Max Payne was all about noire and dark, heavy themes, and mostly took place during rainy nights. Here, I feel like Max Payne 3 is a victim of it's own marketing. While there's plenty of scenes in clubs, with Brazilian party techno, most of the game actually takes place during nights, or dark, rainy days, and two chapters, out of 14, take place in snowy New York. Some take place in dark, closed buildings, much like the construction site from Max Payne 2. The bald Max Payne from the cover makes up for less than a half of the game. Very few chapters actually take place in full sun.
As expect of a Max Payne game, the story is heavy. However, it's pretty good, while not extraordinary. So is the atmosphere, the tone, set by oddly stylized cutscenes and Payne's inner monologues, dark and heavy. MP3 deals with some disturbing♥♥♥♥♥♥we haven't seen in previous games, and Max is visibly sick from years of alcohol and drug abuse, he's still haunted by the demons of the past, and it projects on his current actions and fate in a believable way.
My problems with the game mainly lie in the frequency of cutscenes, which interrupt the action way too often, as well as clunkyness of the controls, however that can be explained by the fact Max is old and fat now, and the guns don't have much feedback in them, not enough meat. These aren't Killing Floor weapons, but nothing ever is.
On a scale from wasted money to freebie, I think my purchase of Max Payne 3 for 2,99€ was a > decent bargain <.
While the game IMHO wouldn't win any year awards, the airport terminal shootout with "Tears" by Health playing in the background has to get a special mention.
PS: I didn't even touch Multiplayer

Possibly the most existential game I've played. Though it is, at it's core, a puzzler. The puzzles are often complex, a few head-scratchers, but sometimes require a more reductionist approach. What may seem complex at first may turn out to be very straightforward. At times it requires you to question the assumptions it has itself given you. Good exercise for the whole brain, as it doesn't train through repetition but demands both creativity and reason, both abstract thought and technical logic. Along with the puzzles a story gradually unfolds. Concepts of self, place and time begin to dawn while another mystery deepens. I like that the story is only hinted at and alluded to, so that you formulate the idea on your own. It makes it that much more meaningful and powerful. It is likely the most existential and eternally relevant topic one could imagine, and the story itself would make a fascinating novel or film. My only complaint is personal, that the game seems to make assumptions concerning beliefs, more specifically, that having them is a universal quality of humans. But this is not at all the case. At times it seemed as though the authors had an agenda to express their own beliefs, but perhaps this was just my suspicion of beliefs in general. The dialogue trees where multiple choice and never once did I actually agree with any of the choices. So it felt like being pigeon-holed and I ended up arguing for a point I didn't actually think was correct. Other than that minor brow-furrowing frustration, I really enjoyed spending time in the beautifully rendered game world. The music was lovely and atmospheric. Extremely smooth play with a good variety of menu options. It's rare that a puzzle game addresses both hemispheres of the brain as well as the subconscious mind. I strongly consider it a work of genius. Oh, and if you decide to play it, I left some messages for you. ;)

You play an artificial being (sort of a robot or android) and are awakened by a mysterious voice calling itself ELOHIM, who gives you the task of solving his riddles. And you do as you’re told. Why? That’s what you have to ask yourself over the course of the game.
The puzzles are very easy in the first two levels, but starting from the third level, they really step up a notch.
You start off by using a very simple tool (the jammer), with which you can shut down electrical devices, later on you can unlock more and more devices to bypass even more enemies or obstacles and sometimes you have to combine some of them in a completely new way or just change your point of view to reach the Tetris style jigsaw piece. In the "limbo" world you are left to roam and explore this strange environment and uncover traces of other subjects that have presumably been here before you.
Although they’re not overwhelmingly good or spectacular, they’re still pretty good and work just fine for this game.
Music is good, fitting the game perfectly. Some nice environmental sounds and mysterious ethereal sounds.
The game is really one of a kind. It made me think, not only about the game, but also about myself, something which hardly any other games I have played have done. There’s a lot of philosophical questions asked and when answering them, you’ll find out some truths about yourself maybe.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game.
The Good:  Visually stunning.  I thought the music fit the theme and found it pleasant.  A classical vibe.  The puzzles are good, with increasing difficulty and need to think out of the box.  The built in hints are quite good  - they don't give away the exact answer but point you at some subtlety that you are overlooking using a cryptic clue.
The Bad:  Solving some puzzles requires multiple steps but unfortunately you can only restore back to the start of the puzzle (voluntarily or involuntarily).  This can require multiple, tedious repetitions of the earlier steps while sorting out the last ones.  The puzzles for the stars sometimes involve obscure or hidden placements with nearly invisible connectors or other features that are next to impossible to spot without help from a guide.
Neutral:  There is a lot of subtle humor in the game if you have some programming background using UNIX or LINUX console interface.  However, only one star puzzle actually depends on knowing a little about code, specifically ASCII character codes.

This is unexeptable ! I had the same issue when I played on non official servers ( because they where closed ) and couldnt continue a game. But a refined version with a heafty price tag of 19.99 euro shouldnt have such a problem.
So in the end of the day the game is awesome and as good as it was the first time you played, but there are big problems with the multiplayer gameplay that are really annoying because not everytime can you play a 2 hour game straight.
For the price of 19.99 I cannot recommened it, I would understand a 10 euro price point but for all of you who want it and feel the same, do note that AoE is the first game to go on sales on steam with really big price drops ( I got it for 3 euro winter sales ) !
