Wolfenstein: New Order is a very weird game to examine from a narrative stand point.
Prior to the game's releases, the dev's emphasized the bizarre campiness, with the nazi moon base, the nazified versions of pop culture classics, and the general speculative nature of the setting.
When I played it, it seemed like this was how it was going. I'm riding in some sort of super B-17/cargo plan hybrid in 1946 fighting off jets, land and fight off robo dogs, and then have to stop a giant mecha. I meet some stock characters, who are likable, and the gameplay is oddly open.
Then we get to the end of this first act and instead I expierenced one of the most gut wrenching scenes in a game that honestly left me feeling awful, and what follows next is a sequence where an almost braindead BJ reflects on his life and helplessly watches the world change around him.
The game does a good job with establishing pathos. Nazis are evil, so here they act evil, but they also do a good job of adding human elements. The main antagonist, aside from Deathshead, is shown having a loving, if rather sleazy, relationship with a younger man but it seems rather earnest. I had this weird feeling about this woman, who basically forced me to pick cards to determine my idealogical background, who is also a normal person with a relationship.
Your staff of allies are also well developed, Max Hass could have, especially, been a character to make my eyes roll but I got a feeling of earnest care for the character for the game. He has no understanding of the world, and the closest thing he has to a father was once a hardcore nazi who backpedeled once he realized what he was doing. The character dynamics are subtle and engaging.
The world itself has a lot of thought put into it. Its certainly not realistic, but it captures the Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥style of a believable fantasy world. There's a sense that this world has aged, even though its new, and that there is a lot of history.
There is also a prison camp scene, and I was worried here. The holocaust is something that has never been touched upon really in gaming, and I was worried that the game's tonal shifts would end up creating a farce but it did a good job. Its a case where I can say it ending with you piloting a nazi mech blasting apart the camp feels appropiate since the entire level is building up to that point. You get the feeling of having to carefully plan and move your way around, and there is this omnipresence of the regime.
And the ending itself is special because it does a good of fleshing out the series' longest lasting Villian, Deathshead. Far from the stoic figure he was in previous games, known for his snark, he is a much more jovial figure. I think the game should have emphasized what the logs only touch upon, that after his near-death in Wolfenstein (2009) he found a new love for life, that he is unhinged in a very different way. He, in own way, views himself as a creator, someone who has used his abilities for the betterment of humanity. And then casts Blaskowitz as the villian in his story, a relic of an old world that can only destroy but cannot create. The line, "When the end comes, we will be judged by what we have made, not what we have destroyed"
Not saying that Deathshead is right, but I had a moment where this over the top character suddenly felt human. He felt like someone with a backstory, a goal, and a motive. And he wasn't wrong, at many times BJ acknowledges that there is a futility to him now and I think the ending of the game is fitting. As much as he wants to just live in peace, he isn't a man who can ever return to that. It gives him a sense of weariness and sadness. The final scene, especially, was poignant since both Deathshead and BJ are ultimately dieing on their own terms, both feeling that their lifes work is done.
The gameplay itself is solid, the guns have both weight to them and are just fun. You can dual wield assault rifles with under-barrel rocket launchers, use a shotgun that fires bouncing slugs, and use knives or sneaky kills. Its nothing super innovative, but its solid.
The levels aren't open world, but they are closer to RTCW's level design where its open maps with multiple passageways. You can try to be sneaky, go loud, or mess around.
I did feel that the laser-cutter was underused. Being able to cut open fences to open alternate routes was okay, and opening vents/crates was fun, but it felt like more elaborate uses for it could be made. There are some chains in the middle part of the game that can be cut, either to drop items on nazi heads or, again, open alternate routes. I think having levels where you could have more elaborate uses, like knocking down towers, cutting the ground underneath nazis, or just doing silly things with it could have helped.
The game has no multiplayer, which in of itself isn't a bad thing, but enemy territories was an amazing expierence and I feel that there sould be an attempt to revive it. With the new tools and setting, the map design could allow for a much more dynamic expierence while remaining true to the objective based gameplay.
Ultimately, if you like wolfenstein games, you'll like this. For standard fans of WWII games, the game is more centered on resistence fighting rather than large set pieces. You always are the underdog, as odd as that may seem considering your arsenal. Alternate History fans will enjoy the detail placed in the setting, they fully realized this verse and used both the classic "what if" like nazi moon bases, but also more subtle references to type of architecture and philosophy the Nazi party wanted society to follow.

Has a significant learning curve if you can get past that and learn how to play properly it is very fun and worth your time. You should probably look up some tutorials online since that is probably the best way to learn as the tutorials provided are not the best.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game.
The Good:  Visually stunning.  I thought the music fit the theme and found it pleasant.  A classical vibe.  The puzzles are good, with increasing difficulty and need to think out of the box.  The built in hints are quite good  - they don't give away the exact answer but point you at some subtlety that you are overlooking using a cryptic clue.
The Bad:  Solving some puzzles requires multiple steps but unfortunately you can only restore back to the start of the puzzle (voluntarily or involuntarily).  This can require multiple, tedious repetitions of the earlier steps while sorting out the last ones.  The puzzles for the stars sometimes involve obscure or hidden placements with nearly invisible connectors or other features that are next to impossible to spot without help from a guide.
Neutral:  There is a lot of subtle humor in the game if you have some programming background using UNIX or LINUX console interface.  However, only one star puzzle actually depends on knowing a little about code, specifically ASCII character codes.

Game Title: Squad - *Review copy received from Fulysics game giveaways.*
Review Date: 12/21/15
My original thought after seeing this was a early access version of arma on a engine that's actually stable.
After having played for about 15 hours the game actually reminds me more of Red Orchestra 2 with a slight influence from Arma added.
I love everything about this game just due to the fact that it's one of the only FPS games that DOES NOT FOCUS on kills or even objectives, honestly.
Currently non-existant. The only story you'll find here are the ones you get to tell from your experiences with your team on the battlefield.
This game focuses entirely on teamwork for the simplest tasks. This was the entire focus of this game and they executed it perfectly. While it's still entirely possible to go lone wolf, it's going to hamper you so much that you really won't be able to make yourself go solo.
Currently, the game features a small arsenal of weapons and explosive devices. Definitely enough to keep you satisfied since the most fun you'll have will come from cooperating with a team instead of getting to use a specific weapon or vehicle to mow people down.
The gun-play feels dead on. Some weapons are a little over zealous with recoil but it honestly just makes you experience a more realistic form of combat. The reality of war is that ammo is expensive and in limited supply when you're in a combat zone, blowing through your ammo by going full-auto is usually never acceptable. More lead doesn't equate to more dead.
Dying in this game can be fairly punishing and it doesn't take alot to kill you compared to most FPS shooters. Your best friend is going to be your medic if you get hurt or go down and you'll want to keep him happy enough to want to keep reviving you. If you play this like COD, you won't last long and every time your medic has to revive you he's obviously risking going down. Which, obviously, means your entire squad could lose the only person(s) able to revive them.
For a early access game, it combines realistic warfare concepts and practices with "fictional-for-fun" perfectly. I love digging tractor tires out of thin air. I've seen people build literal castles out of H-Barriers, Bunkers and Ladders... and it was awesome.
You'll come to realize one of the key aspects of winning a engagement is you and your squads positioning compared to the enemies. Out-flanking is HEAVILY rewarded in this game and if you don't spread out enough to cut off the enemy from flanking you, odds are you'll end up dead.
The graphics overall are really, really good. Not in the sense of crysis or anything like that but that it all fits, works together and offers some really unique maps and combat experiences.
I'd put actual texture quality as being on-par with games like CS:GO, not bad but it has a purpose and it fills it well. Models for players are spot on, some weapons could use minor improvements.
Trees... Trees *LOOK* fine, but currently the entire span of the branches from bottom to top is one entire hitbox area for them. Bullets, grenades and rockets don't go through clear open spots in trees and on some maps there's so many that even on the lowest graphic settings I can only maintain a 25 fps average.
Also, I've only had that issue on one or two maps out of the... eight or nine? That are included in the current EA build. So, "DON'T PANIC" (printed in large, friendly letters).
Flora overall looks great, several times I've actually been saved by doing things that'd normally get you killed in other shooters. Hiding in pink flower crops and popping out to shoot the enemy was pretty amusing.
Grass has that annoying issue like Arma has where it makes prone practically impossible since it can stick through your body/guns... Yeah....
Overall, I'd say the best thing for the graphics is performance and realism improvements. Looks perfectly fine as is.
I couldn't help but laugh every time someone shrieked out for a medic through the in-game VOIP with its built-in "radio-filter", which makes it sound as if its coming through a actual military radio. (Maybe a bit clearer...)
I can't speak for russian made weapons like the AK series, SVD, etc. However, the M4's sound accurate though slightly lowered to make them more communication friendly. Not gonna hear much when you're firing a gun in real life besides the bang after every trigger pull.
That said, there really isn't much else to say about it. If there is ambient sound then I suppose I was too immersed in not getting shot to notice it.
It has room for improvement but what's here already works perfectly as is.
This is going to be entirely dependant on each individuals preference for gaming. If you like a game that's mainly focused on teamwork, coordination, calling out enemy direction and barings constantly... This is perfect for you.
If you're someone that prefers battlefield where it's more focused on team-deathmatch with some side objectives thrown in to win by a technicality, you won't enjoy this game much.
Personally I like both but this is definitely more my style. Arma couldn't offer the level of cooperation that I experience in this game and I'm glad I got to play it and hope to keep playing for a long time.
I've played FPS games since battlefield 1942, not a single one has ever come close to what this game accomplishes. This is the pinnacle of *tactical* first-person shooters.
It has some blatant improvements to make and alot of content to add. I'd love to see more improvements with its build and medical/revive systems specifically. Despite this, the only way this game is going to fail at being a big hit with hardcore military FPS fans is if the developer puts effort into making them hate it.
Here's hoping Arma 4 will have some of the experiences offered by Squad. Of course, I'd just take a simple engine swap thats been desperately needed... Then again, if Squad gets as big as they hope then I won't need another Arma.

After beating the game for the 5th time, this time on the hardest "Über" difficulty I can honestly say without a shadow of a doubt, this is the best game of last year 2014.  Definite Game of the Year of 2014
The story, gameplay, graphics and art are the games strongest standpoints. The game has only a very few minor setbacks, one of which is a poor PC optimization, the game was developed on 3 different systems, on old consoles, new consoles and PC all at the same time, but PC got the worse end of the stick. The game has a vast amount of frame drops when the setting "Screen-Space Reflections" is on. It's an incredible resource hog even if set to medium, the framerate drops from an otherwise stable 60 fps to mid 40 and even mid 30 at times. It is a shame since the game itself looks very good with this graphic option set to the highest, almost every surface and npc has a reflection in a reflectable surface and it really lights up the enviroment. It's a shame machine games decided to go for this incredibly resource hungy type of SSR and didn't go for the SSR that Crysis 3 was using. Other than that, the game has no other minor issues from a technical perspective or otherwise.
Story of the game is so incredibly well written with care and attention to the smallest of details I was really amazed by it. It's a well written, coherent piece of story for a first person shooter. And these types of well written stories don't come often when it's a traditional first person shooter, but machine games managed to nail it down extraordinarily. As I said, the attention to detail was breathtaking, I liked the whole Tarantino-esque cuts and edits with the cutscenes. I have also never played a wolfenstein game with not only such a strong main character but with incredibly well written sidekicks in Caroline and even the muted one called Max Haas, whose whole vocabulary consisted of „Max“ and „Haas“.  Oh and have I told you about the extremely repulsive and charming character all at the same time called Frau Engel? Well she could be the main antagonist of a sequel to new order if machine games decide to do such a thing 
The voice actors did an amazing job aswell, Brian Bloom did an excellent job in voicing B.J. and I also absolutely loved the voice actors of Frau Engel and General Deathshead, they both sounded like true german natives, which is a rarity in modern games, it’s usually an english or american voice actor who is reading the text in german, which doesn’t sound good or authentic at all. So props to machine games for hiring proper german voice actors for the roles of the german speaking characters in the game 
One of  the games stongest standpoints is it’s incredibly smooth gameplay, most of the time you can choose to go stealth or if you are not a fan of that gameplay style you can go all guns blazing, the second choice is most of the time inevitable because of the game design, which is a shame, but this is not a first person stealth game afterall it’s a first person shooter, better said an old school fps. It’s incredibly satisfying moving down the nazis with the heavy machine gun that you dismounet or bringing up two shotguns at the same time and shooting your way through the tight corridors of the eisenwald prison or deathshead compound. The whole gameplay element is very traditional aswell, you don’t need to ADS at all during the whole game which is perfect.  The guns are pretty accurate even at long range and all of them have secondary firing mode. For instance the secondary firing mode for the sniper rifle is a laser gun, how cool is that? 
Another one of the games strongest standpoints are the graphics, or better said the overall art of the game and the world machine games had created. ID tech engine 5 is a game engine that is miles ahead of it’s current competition. The game has so many incredible sceneries and backdrops you just have to stop and enjoy the vistas and views. I was so into the whole art of the game I decided to buy the limited version of the artbook signed by the main art director Axel Torvenius and game designer Tor Frick.
What else can I said about this spectacle of the game, only that I beat it for the first time during one long 14 hour gameplay session, the game is that good, I don’t remember playing a singleplayer game on one gameplay session since I beat half life 2.
Wolfenstein new order is a game without any major flaws, it’s a perfect game for the fan of the old school first person shooter genre with excellent soundtrack, art, gameplay, graphics, music and memorable characters, enviroments and well written storyline.

This one took a lot longer than I expected it to (not because of time spent in game however). Let’s get this rolling.
I – Story [8/10]
Castle Crashers is a 2D, Beat ‘Em Up RPG from The Behemoth. The player can (initially) choose to play as one of four knights. While attending a party at the King’s castle, a dark wizard arrives and steals a mystical gem along with four princesses. The King sends the player on a quest to retrieve the gem, the princesses, and to defeat the dark wizard and his henchmen. The story is simplistic, yes, but it it sets the tone for an amazing journey for the player (and for the player’s companions if the player chooses to bring friends).
II – UI [10/10]
The user interface in CC is great for the genre. Much like the beat’em up games of yore, your health (and mana) bar is located at the top of the screen and you can always see what level it’s at. There’s also a little orb next to it that shows you what item you currently have selected, which is nice. No minimap is necessary here as the levels are very linear and you can only go one way: forward.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
Gameplay in CC is just great and it’s a blast to play with friends. The control scheme is very basic; you can attack, block, jump, make out with princesses, kill your friends so that you can be the one to make out with said princesses, use magic and items, etc. There’s not much to it and that is perfectly fine. I don’t honestly know what else to say on the subject.
IV – Content [10/10]
Castle Crashers has a fairly large amount of content. There are four playable characters initially (this number can go up if you own other games from The Behemoth). From there, you can unlock a ton of extra characters (including two that come from DLC packs.) There is a smattering of weapons from which you can select, all while prancing about in the belly of an antlered toad. Magic is (generally) different for each character and you can pick from a whole herd of animal orbs to accompany you in your quest.
There are a good number of different areas in the game and each has their own enemies and boss battles. It’s a great time and you won’t be getting bored of this one any time soon.
V – Visual [10/10]
The artwork in CC is amazing; I love it. The game may be cartoonish, but it is in no way a child’s game. Enemies who fall to your blade will often lose limbs (or heads) and crumple to the ground in a torrent of blood. Think Mortal Kombat. Okay, not quite that extreme in the gore sector, but still. You get the point.
VI – Audio [10/10]
For better fitting quest music you could not ask. CC has you covered when it comes to triumphant overtures to complement your heroic deeds. Honestly though, even if you don’t end up getting the game, do yourself a favor and pick up a copy of the soundtrack.
VII – Overall [9.7/10]
Overall, Castle Crashers is one of the better games of it’s genre on the market. It may be a few years older, but that doesn’t mean it can’t still compete with the new kids on the block.

Game Title: Squad - *Review copy received from Fulysics game giveaways.*
Review Date: 12/21/15
My original thought after seeing this was a early access version of arma on a engine that's actually stable.
After having played for about 15 hours the game actually reminds me more of Red Orchestra 2 with a slight influence from Arma added.
I love everything about this game just due to the fact that it's one of the only FPS games that DOES NOT FOCUS on kills or even objectives, honestly.
Currently non-existant. The only story you'll find here are the ones you get to tell from your experiences with your team on the battlefield.
This game focuses entirely on teamwork for the simplest tasks. This was the entire focus of this game and they executed it perfectly. While it's still entirely possible to go lone wolf, it's going to hamper you so much that you really won't be able to make yourself go solo.
Currently, the game features a small arsenal of weapons and explosive devices. Definitely enough to keep you satisfied since the most fun you'll have will come from cooperating with a team instead of getting to use a specific weapon or vehicle to mow people down.
The gun-play feels dead on. Some weapons are a little over zealous with recoil but it honestly just makes you experience a more realistic form of combat. The reality of war is that ammo is expensive and in limited supply when you're in a combat zone, blowing through your ammo by going full-auto is usually never acceptable. More lead doesn't equate to more dead.
Dying in this game can be fairly punishing and it doesn't take alot to kill you compared to most FPS shooters. Your best friend is going to be your medic if you get hurt or go down and you'll want to keep him happy enough to want to keep reviving you. If you play this like COD, you won't last long and every time your medic has to revive you he's obviously risking going down. Which, obviously, means your entire squad could lose the only person(s) able to revive them.
For a early access game, it combines realistic warfare concepts and practices with "fictional-for-fun" perfectly. I love digging tractor tires out of thin air. I've seen people build literal castles out of H-Barriers, Bunkers and Ladders... and it was awesome.
You'll come to realize one of the key aspects of winning a engagement is you and your squads positioning compared to the enemies. Out-flanking is HEAVILY rewarded in this game and if you don't spread out enough to cut off the enemy from flanking you, odds are you'll end up dead.
The graphics overall are really, really good. Not in the sense of crysis or anything like that but that it all fits, works together and offers some really unique maps and combat experiences.
I'd put actual texture quality as being on-par with games like CS:GO, not bad but it has a purpose and it fills it well. Models for players are spot on, some weapons could use minor improvements.
Trees... Trees *LOOK* fine, but currently the entire span of the branches from bottom to top is one entire hitbox area for them. Bullets, grenades and rockets don't go through clear open spots in trees and on some maps there's so many that even on the lowest graphic settings I can only maintain a 25 fps average.
Also, I've only had that issue on one or two maps out of the... eight or nine? That are included in the current EA build. So, "DON'T PANIC" (printed in large, friendly letters).
Flora overall looks great, several times I've actually been saved by doing things that'd normally get you killed in other shooters. Hiding in pink flower crops and popping out to shoot the enemy was pretty amusing.
Grass has that annoying issue like Arma has where it makes prone practically impossible since it can stick through your body/guns... Yeah....
Overall, I'd say the best thing for the graphics is performance and realism improvements. Looks perfectly fine as is.
I couldn't help but laugh every time someone shrieked out for a medic through the in-game VOIP with its built-in "radio-filter", which makes it sound as if its coming through a actual military radio. (Maybe a bit clearer...)
I can't speak for russian made weapons like the AK series, SVD, etc. However, the M4's sound accurate though slightly lowered to make them more communication friendly. Not gonna hear much when you're firing a gun in real life besides the bang after every trigger pull.
That said, there really isn't much else to say about it. If there is ambient sound then I suppose I was too immersed in not getting shot to notice it.
It has room for improvement but what's here already works perfectly as is.
This is going to be entirely dependant on each individuals preference for gaming. If you like a game that's mainly focused on teamwork, coordination, calling out enemy direction and barings constantly... This is perfect for you.
If you're someone that prefers battlefield where it's more focused on team-deathmatch with some side objectives thrown in to win by a technicality, you won't enjoy this game much.
Personally I like both but this is definitely more my style. Arma couldn't offer the level of cooperation that I experience in this game and I'm glad I got to play it and hope to keep playing for a long time.
I've played FPS games since battlefield 1942, not a single one has ever come close to what this game accomplishes. This is the pinnacle of *tactical* first-person shooters.
It has some blatant improvements to make and alot of content to add. I'd love to see more improvements with its build and medical/revive systems specifically. Despite this, the only way this game is going to fail at being a big hit with hardcore military FPS fans is if the developer puts effort into making them hate it.
Here's hoping Arma 4 will have some of the experiences offered by Squad. Of course, I'd just take a simple engine swap thats been desperately needed... Then again, if Squad gets as big as they hope then I won't need another Arma.

Long story short: This is the best Beat 'em up I've ever played. Yes, even better than the Ninja Turtles one for SNES.
To start off, I hate Beat 'em ups, because of their simplicity and repetitivness. This game is neither of these things. It has great level design, Upgradable characters and an RPG-like leveling mechanic.
The story is as simple as indie games get, where you go around saving princesess and fighting bosses.
Oh, the boss fights. They're loads of fun and are very varied, and aren't too much of a challenge.
The multiplayer is fun and unlike most multiplayer games(New Super Mario Bros Wii), it's better to cooperate than to screw each other over.
Although controllers are reccomended, they're not neccesary at all, and the PC controls are (by default) comfortable and easy to get used to.
The game doesn't get boring after a LONG while, with most of your efforts post-story going into Maxing out your character stats(and having fun doing it).
The DLC is only $1 a piece, with them adding new characters, weapons and animal orbs.
There's no reason to not own this game if you're a fan of beat 'em ups, and wth the new refund system, trying out this game has never been more worth it.

Well, after Raven's Wolfenscheisse 2009 things simply couldn't get any worse. Task was simple: make an average old-school First Person Shooter game, and fans will say thanks for resurrecting a franchise. And MachineGames did it. They did it well, but unfortunately they couldn't get it any higher.
Good old FPS genre is back. No more magic, no more trading and other RPG parody that Raven tried to bring us in 2009. Classic guns only: pistol/machinegun/shotgun/sniper/grenades + new LaserKraftWerk (LKW) weapon, which after a few upgrades reminds me Railgun from Quake. Yes, there are weapon upgrades, which bring new fire modes and ammo types. There is a Minigun too, but it can't be stored in the player's inventory (both B.J.'s pockets are full with huge automatic shotguns, no place for minigun there), so it can be used until dropped, i.e. in specific areas only.
Wolfenstein: The New Order supports 3 playstyles:
When you are run'n'gunning, you don't care about how smart or dumb (mostly dumb) future peace of meat is. Your only task is to kill them as fast as possible to avoid becoming dead meat yourself.
When using covering technique, enemies seems quite smart, if word "smart" can be used together with AI at all. Nazis are actively using covers, don't lean out of them too often, sometimes changing covers and position, sometimes sticking to the same position, but sometimes run at you all together from different positions. Variety in AI behavior makes the gameplay interesting.
But when you are in sneak mode, AI is dumb as ****. I'm wondering how Nazis could win the war, if their guards are always looking in wrong direction? It's fine, when you sneaked though the vent and got yourself behind the enemy. But if there is no vent, cellar or other way around, then guards always will be looking away from entrance, stairways etc. But that isn't the biggest issue. It seems like Nazis have no perception at all. They are able to see crouched player only if he is directly in front of them. And even in that situation they need to look at you for a few seconds, ask "Was ist das?" and only then, if player is stupid enough to sit still and not hiding around a corner, enemy triggers an alarm. I "like" how Nazis are completely ignoring dead bodies:
That's stupid. Sneak kills are lame and easy, and nothing changes on raising difficulty. I made first playthough on "I am Death incarnate!" and second on "Uber". Uber enemies are harder to kill, they do more damage, but it doesn't really matter, because by default most of them turned their back at you are waiting for a silent knife strike. You can use pistol with silencer instead, but it is harder, because you need to aim to the head. If you missed, then it can take up to 10 bodyshots to kill an armored enemy on hardest difficulty. But in the same time it is enough with one knife thrown to the butt to achieve instant kill.
Corridor graphics are nice. Everything is high detailed and pretty. And it runs well on medium-spec hardware. When going outside... well, those "skyboxes" imitating futuristic Nazi cities could have higher detail.
I'd agree with a "father" of Wolfenstein, Doom and Quake, but not in this case. Starting from very beginning The New Order was promoted with an unique and intriguing story in an alternate history line: Year 1960, Nazis won the World War II. If you check all teasers and trailers, then most content is about story, about the world ruled by Hitler, not about gameplay itself. Story supposed to be the primary aspect in The New Order, but does it?..
I'll spoil a little bit below. But to be honest, there is nothing to spoil here. It is like spoiling a porn movie with saying how it will end :)

Squad is not your typical FPS. This development team started out as a community game creating a mod, simply to make the game that they wanted to play - Project Reality. Using the BF2 engine they accomplished some unbelievable things. BUT times change and that engine got old. So, fast forward to 2015 and here we are, with the Alpha release of Squad.
Already it plays better than most AAA titles. More realistic than BF4, prettier than insurgency, more accessible and less clunky than ArmA, and with more teamwork than all of those combined.
Currently it focuses on infantry combat, and does a pretty damn epic job. Within the next few weeks we will see things change massively with the introduction of vehicles to the mix. Engagement ranges will change, teamwork will improve and coordination will be needed to win. As usual the best place to play is on the
server which has a primer and ruleset established over a decade ago to get the most realistic and fun experience out of this game. They have a history in PR second to none and it looks set to continue into Squad.
Try this out - I can no recommend it enough. If you are sick of generic COD/BF games and want something more, and to really communicate and feel like you achieved something, try out Squad.

I went into Wolfenstein: The New Order with high expectations based on the praise and accolades it had received, prior to my purchase. The game ended up about on-par with those pre-hyped expectations.
What originally left a bad taste in the mouth was the
, which for me is a matter of days - do keep this in mind if either bandwidth or storage is at a premium.
As for the options, I had to fiddle with the settings for a while as my HD 7950 apparently could not handle the textures on high, and resulted in uncomfortable viewing. This was only a minor concern and was fixed quite easily by turning down the texture quality.
Moving on to the game.
I found the gameplay fun in all senses of the word, right from the stupidly large guns to the awkward silence that befel the room upon killing all the dudes in an area. As someone who really comes for the story first, gameplay second, I found  the plot and characterisation to be compelling enough, alongside the beautiful world built through conversations, news articles and even music.
The composers really had the right idea in creating a score from heavy distortion tracks, melodic guitar sections and 'Nazified' 60s pop music. In fact, I enjoyed the OST so much that it now resides in my iTunes library.
The other point is that the game was a perfect length, it did not drag on or outstay its welcome - mostly by moving the plot right along with new scenery rather briskly. There is not a level in the game that I wouldn't deem 'profound' in some way, each being unforgettable in their own way. There was a point where I found myself in a sewer and said to myself "of course, the sewer level" with a pained expression, only to find that its purpose was solely worldbuilding and was not to long either. From start to finish there was a clear objective and all plot detours seemed necessary in its fulfillment.
In conclusion:
I enjoyed it, and if you like a good, fast-paced, action-pack story; I think you will too.

This is one of few non-indie games that I would truly consider to be a work of art. It presents a myriad of puzzles, all with the Portal-like spacial reasoning, but while that is a core aspect of the game, it is not in the core ideas. This game discusses in depth human nature, the future of AI, religion, the future of humanity, how the world deals with disaster, the nature of consciousness, the nature of death, and I'm sure I'm forgetting a few. The complex nature of the writings, video logs, chat logs, and the discussion with MLA contribute to the game in such a way that this work may be considered of actual artistic merit, far more than its pretecessor, Portal.
It is not without its flaws, as is the case in any game, but these flaws are so trivial that they barely detract from the game as a whole. Overall, this game is money well spent. If you are debating whether or not the game is really worth the time and effort, don't. I cherished every moment I played this game from start to finish, and I sincerely hope that many others can do so as well.

This has been one of my favorite new games in recent months. Puzzle games are tricky in terms of difficulty. Too simple and they get boring or tedious, too complex and and they become frustrating to point no one wants to play them. The Talos Principle has found a sweet spot in terms of difficulty. I felt routinely challenged, but never so much that it wasn't fun or interesting. I felt rewarded when solving the puzzles, particularly the difficult ones. While the game offers little in terms of puzzle devices that we haven't seen before (it's the usual fare: boxes, switches, beams of light, and locked doors), each is used in fresh and inventive ways. I have seen some complain that the game was overly long, but I disagree. I felt engaged throughout and was never bored.
That is to say nothing of the plot, another common puzzle game pratfall. [No or VERY minor spoilers] The game portrays the puzzles as a sort of test of AI (that's you). Your ultimate purpose is slowly revealed though a library of text documents unlocked throughout the game. These do a wonderful job of setting up the backstory while leaving enough to the imagination and providing an overall satisfying backdrop for the plot an its conclusion. Through these documents, the developers also take the opportunity to was philosophical about potential issues of AI and consciousness. This may turn a lot of gamers off--if the sheer amount of reading alone didn't--but I think this only enriched the experience. Hell, you can always just breeze through the reading and only do the puzzles. Your loss.
Bottom line: Play this game.

The Talos Principle is an awesome puzzle game with a deep, philosophical story.
Sure, the story is a bit detached from the puzzles as others have said, but it's still really interesting. Also, it's completely optional for those who just like puzzle games, however, I highly recommend pursuing at least a bit of the story, as it really is worth listening to and adds to the game's experience.
I bought this game because I like puzzle games and games with stories (The Swapper, Mind:Path to Thalamus, etc) and thought that this looked interesting. The price tag is definitely worth it, as it's one of the best puzzle games i've ever played. The hard puzzles are hard enough to have you thinking (and you may have to try them a few times or skip and go back to them), but they're really fun and solvable without looking things up. I've had "aha!" moments and moments where I finally figured out the puzzle and facepalmed because the answer was right infront of me the entire time. Maybe my persistence was due to wanting to find out more of the story, as I usually look up the answer to other puzzle games when I get frustrated, but I didn't have to in TTP.
There are a few items that help you solve puzzles:
- buttons on the ground that open a forcefield when something is on them
- boxes (put these on buttons, Other people compare this game to Portal - I don't think they're that much alike besides the boxes/button mechanisms)
- Jammers that jam turrets, fans, enemies, etc
- Fans that blow you/boxes up in the air
- Connectors that let you connect red and blue lightbeams to similarly colored spots
- Memory machine that lets you create a copy of yourself to do actions
And there are a few obstacles to get around in puzzles:
- Orbs that move around and explode when you get near them
- Forcefields that get in the way of you and laserbeams
- Turrets that shoot you when you're in range of them
Puzzles involve using helpful objects to open forcefields, jam turrets/orbs, and focus light beams on specific areas to gather "sigils" - or tetris-like pieces that are used to open doors to other arenas that contain more puzzles.
In summary, TTP is an amazing game that's worth the price, especially if it's on sale. The puzzles can be hard, but extremely fun and unique. The story kept me motivated to solve some of the harder puzzles myself, as I can give up easily sometimes. Would rate 10/10, one of the best puzzle games I've ever played, and I still missed some stuff in my playthrough.

Wow, this game.
If you have any interest in puzzle games in the style of Portal 2, try this one (Portal 1 was more platforming oriented).
The puzzles are sublime, they will make you tear your hair and then doubt your mental health once you finish them. They are all completely obvious yet freaking hard to figure out.
While there is a bit of platforming involved the puzzles are really not about the execution as once you know what to do its generally easy to do it (still you will fail a lot).
The game does a very good job at teaching you the mechanics through 3 difficulty levels of puzzles green, yellow and red. Yet it still leaves some mechanics to be discovered (mainly if you want to get all the elusive hidden stars). Once you get bored with the puzzles there are tons of easter eggs hidden all through the game.
As a puzzle game, this game mainly stands on its mechanics and excellent puzzle design. However the story creates an excellent counterpoint and its presentation will leave you wanting more and more and more and will keep you thinking about what could be possible going on in this strange world.
The game has three distinct endings (plus some variants). You will get 20 hours (at the very least) from this game if you don’t quit halfway through.

This is another amazing installment in the Wolfenstein series.  As a shooter, the gunplay is top-notch.  The weapons look and sound good, handle well, and you can dual-wield 'em (even sniper rifles) if that's your jam.  There are opportunities for stealth too.  The levels are mostly linear, with location and objectives driven by the storyline.  The story, while a bit melodramatic at times, is actually enjoyable.  The supporting cast is entertaining, and most of the voice acting is fine, wacky accents aside. In Max Payne 3 you play a fat, alcoholic, pill addicted, middle aged ex-cop turned security for a rich Brazilian family that is hung up in the past and can't forgive himself. Some how he manages to get shot thousands of times and mows down an army of gang members, psycho paramilitaries, and corrupt cops all in the name of justice. Justice is what keeps him going and despite his faults this one virtue that he holds onto is what keeps him on the morally good side of things. This is one of Rockstars greatest feats in cinematic story telling, you feel as though you are watching a movie but playing the actions scenes. The story plays out like a typical 70's vigilante story in the same vein as Death Wish or even Dirty Harry, It does nothing new or interesting but it still manages to captivate and entertain the same way a big Hollywood blockbuster does. The feel of the game is pretty dirty and gritty for example the settings really help set the tone for the games narrative. The dirty and gritty streets of New Jersey to the disgusting and gross favelas of Brazil really add a nice back drop and setting that compliment the games story and Max Paynes life. Game play wise, it's still the same Max Payne you know and love, bullet time is refined and works really well pitting you in situations that require its use. The game does have a cover mechanic which is nice because in the previous entries to the series you would get decimated by bullets and awkwardly have to hide behind walls. A problem I have is the game seems to try and introduce stealth mechanics, but in the end you end up shooting everyone. It's not that I don't like that they try, but it seems useless and unwarranted if its not going to be actually stealthy. When it comes to graphics Max Payne shines its brightest. The gap between games gives us a new look at our favorite cop with crisp, clean graphics that are realistic and extremely well done. I would recommend anyone who wants a good mindless shooter with a typical story that plays out like a big Hollywood blockbuster to play this game. Not that these qualities are bad, in fact they are actually strengths you just won't too much depth in the games story even though it does say stuff about modern police involvement and structure. Max Payne 3 is one of Rockstars best and another reason why they are giants in the gaming industry, I hope they continue to make Max Payne games in the future.

The Talos Principle is an undertaking every bit as ridiculously ambitious as the project described in its background story. To meet its designers' apparent goals, it not only has to be an intrinsically enjoyable game to play, but also:
Surprisingly, the game succeeds admirably in each of those facets.
The puzzles are ingenious in their design. They start out simple, but the late-game puzzles are among the most diabolically difficult I've ever encountered. What's truly brilliant about them is the way they achieve their difficulty. Any game designer can create incredibly challenging puzzles simply by adding layers and layers of complexity, but The Talos Principle largely refrains from this tactic. It uses a very small set of tools and traps presented in fairly compact levels, and most of them are immune to trial-and-error and simply a matter of epiphany.
The gameplay is well-engineered, and the developers are clearly aware of the fact that puzzle games can be frustrating when given a realistic, three-dimensional, physics-based world and a first-person/OTS perspective. While the world's physics are realistic during all trivial activity, actions directly related to the puzzle have a wonderful snap-to quality. Jumps have perfect, predictable landings, and object placement is 100% accurate. Removing twitch skill and nanometer precision from the equation prevents small inaccuracies from ruining good ideas and keeps the focus on the puzzle. Additionally, it makes it almost impossible to exploit variations in the terrain or any other unintentionally advantageous bounding meshes.
Rather than spoil the story, I'll just say that it's superb. It makes the philosophical and religious analysis in the background immediately relevant, rather than something to be trudged through only by obsessive bibliophile completionists. Several small stories – read, seen, and supposed – unfold and converge expertly alongside the main storyline.
I want to emphasize that it's a story worth enduring to its conclusion. Various portions of it may appear uncomfortably religious or anti-religious, depending on the gamer's perspective on Judeo-Christian beliefs. I thought I knew where the story was going toward the end, and found it aggressively cynical. I recommend that you keep an open mind and withhold judgment until experiencing the finale's insights for yourself.

First of all WOW.
In short, if you're looking for a realistic first person shooter that focuses on squad focused gameplay with a huge enphasis on teamwork, this is the game for you! It's like Arma 3 and Insurgency had a baby but only the good bits went in! Base building, Army sounding radio VOIP system, realistic gun sounds and fire fight sounds this thing is amazing.
YES, it's £29.99. Is it worth it right now? That depends, if you're looking to get your value for money out of stability, a game that has tons of features and a game that genrally just feels polished - No, it's not worth it.
IF, you are looking for great quality gameplay (with alpha related issues) a game that does everything I have stated above and something that is fresh, emmersive and going to progress over time, this is definitely the one for you.
My opinion, WORTH A BUY? YES!
This game is in Alpha but god is it good. I've sank in 10 hours already and I work 50 hours a week, I'm playing this thing every waking second that I can! The sounds in a gun fight and when you are walking around are unparalleled in any other shooter I have ever played! From the snaps of the gun fire passing overhead to the explosions, *KRRRC's" and bleeps on the radio before and after people talk. From the second you enter the game, you are immersed.
The amount of things that are in the game already are amazing! For example, you're using the grenader class and you can see some enemys setting up in the distance and want to show your sniper where they are, you get out your M203 grenade launcher attached to the barrel of your gun, load in some red smoke and fire it 200M across the map to light him up like a red smokey christmas tree for your buddy, ready to blow him away! Or maybe you're in a close quaters fire fight and you don't want to take friendly fire from some troops up on a hill helping you out, load up your launcher with some blue smoke to mark your position!
STORY TIME:
Let me set the scene. Me and my squad of 9 have just pushed our way up through what looks like an opiate field, we've pushed through a few streets and farms and everything seems clear. The squad leader gets word over the radio that Insurgents are fortifying a position North of the objective we need to secure - we head to clear it out.
We push through another poppy field up towards the compound we suspect the enemy to be fortifying, SNAP! Fire Erupts from the compound, tracers are flying everywhere. The squad leader yells at our machine gunner to lay down suppressive fire on a small hole in the wall the fire seems to be coming from, our two grenades start to bombard the compound with grenades from their M203 grenade launchers. The rest of the squad fires at the muzzle flashes they can see coming from the compound, we're all dug in and ready to fight. 30 seconds later the squad leader yells for a cease fire. We've taken them...
40 minutes into the game we've moved up to the final objective, Alpha & Charlie move up to join us in the final assault. We've taken over what looks like a communications area and have began to build it up, we've got sandbags covering us from the sides and on the tops of building and huuuge congrete blocks and barbed wire stopping the enemy getting near us. We begin the HOUR LONG FIRE FIGHT. Grenades, RPG's, Snipers, Machine Gunners, endless smoke grenades and constant resupplies saw us through the long fight with the insurgents.

Bought this game during the midweek madness sale for 7 bucks with all DLC. Gotta say, definitely worth the $.
The singleplayer campaign is about 8-10 hours long depending on if you take the time to go through and find the golden weapons parts. It's also one hell of a ride, with a plot twist that does a good job of hiding itself, but afterwards feels almost obvious. If it were any other game, this might've been a downside, but you get played as the depressed american ex-cop being dragged along for the ride without really knowing why or by whom to the point where it works. Max is also probably one of the most depressing characters I've ever seen, to the point where you half expect him to put a bullet in his skull at the end. (Spoiler Alert: He doesn't.) Again, this would be seen as a downside, but since this is pretty much the basis of the entire game and they pull it off so well, it works. The constant monologuing can become a little much, though it has its moments of charm when you pick up a random pill bottle or secret. All in all, I'd give the singleplayer an 8.5/10.
For a PC port, the controls were actually really solid. I usually play third person games with the 360 controller, but the kb/m controls worked well enough for me to stick with them. I could definitely tell that the game was made with a controller in mind. At the same time though, I didn't feel I was at any disadvantage for not using one. The gunplay is smooth and it's not hard to pick your targets. Bullet time is done well. You have a bar next to your ammo counter that refills as you move and take out enemies. A full bar will give you about 10-15 seconds of bullet time, which is plenty of time to pick off 4-5 guys in a room. If you take too much damage and have pills on you, you enter a bullet time sequence where if you take out the last guy to shoot you, you get a revive. This works most of the time, but often I would find myself holding my gun at an angle that I couldn't shoot the guy until the weapon was eventually at the magic angle to shoot him. Often, this would lead to me dying since I would run out of time to shoot him. I don't know if this is a bug or just an oversight but it happens enough for it to become fairly annoying. Overall though, I would have to give the gameplay an 8/10. The gunplay is great, the controls are tight for a PC port, and the bullet time is fun, but the bullet time revive is fairly glitchy and can lead to some annoyingly slow deaths.
Unfortunately, multiplayer seems to be pretty much dead. I played a few games, all of them being 1 on 1. It's a shame,too. The multiplayer isn't all that bad. The gameplay is fast paced and they even found a way to incorporate bullet time into it.  I half expected it to be dead though. This isn't the game you spend months playing, but rather the game you pick up and play through on a weekend and then bury in your catalog for about 6 months. I'd give the Multiplayer a score, but I don't feel I've been able to experience enough of it to give it one.

The Talos Principle is an undertaking every bit as ridiculously ambitious as the project described in its background story. To meet its designers' apparent goals, it not only has to be an intrinsically enjoyable game to play, but also:
Surprisingly, the game succeeds admirably in each of those facets.
The puzzles are ingenious in their design. They start out simple, but the late-game puzzles are among the most diabolically difficult I've ever encountered. What's truly brilliant about them is the way they achieve their difficulty. Any game designer can create incredibly challenging puzzles simply by adding layers and layers of complexity, but The Talos Principle largely refrains from this tactic. It uses a very small set of tools and traps presented in fairly compact levels, and most of them are immune to trial-and-error and simply a matter of epiphany.
The gameplay is well-engineered, and the developers are clearly aware of the fact that puzzle games can be frustrating when given a realistic, three-dimensional, physics-based world and a first-person/OTS perspective. While the world's physics are realistic during all trivial activity, actions directly related to the puzzle have a wonderful snap-to quality. Jumps have perfect, predictable landings, and object placement is 100% accurate. Removing twitch skill and nanometer precision from the equation prevents small inaccuracies from ruining good ideas and keeps the focus on the puzzle. Additionally, it makes it almost impossible to exploit variations in the terrain or any other unintentionally advantageous bounding meshes.
Rather than spoil the story, I'll just say that it's superb. It makes the philosophical and religious analysis in the background immediately relevant, rather than something to be trudged through only by obsessive bibliophile completionists. Several small stories – read, seen, and supposed – unfold and converge expertly alongside the main storyline.
I want to emphasize that it's a story worth enduring to its conclusion. Various portions of it may appear uncomfortably religious or anti-religious, depending on the gamer's perspective on Judeo-Christian beliefs. I thought I knew where the story was going toward the end, and found it aggressively cynical. I recommend that you keep an open mind and withhold judgment until experiencing the finale's insights for yourself.

Instead of being the though cop with a rough past and a murdered family he became the Cop with a desire to move on from a dark past. The Cop with a past that he had a though time moving on from. When he meets Mona you know that he has a bit of a hard time not being ashamed of himself for leaving his dead wife and girl as a memory.

LASTING IMPRESSIONS
Wolfenstein: The New Order
GENRE
First-Person Shooter/Action
STORY (Spoilers for the first mission!)
Fourteen years. It's been fourteen years since Captain William B. J. Blazkowickz was blasted out of Deathshead's Castle. Fourteen years since shrapnel put him in a vegetative state. Fourteen years he's been sitting in this asylum having his life taken care of for him. Fourteen years since everything went wrong, and only twelve since the Nazis won the war. Blazkowickz isn't going to sit idly by as everything he's worked for crumbles to dust, and when Nazis begin purging the asylum; it seems like just enough to jumpstart his body. It's time to see just how strong the new order is.
GAMEPLAY
The gameplay is very standard for the genre. You have a variety of weapons with which you can wreak havoc throughout the Nazi ranks. All weapons which can be found on enemies can be dual-wielded with the exception of the heavy machine gun. All of the weapons also have unlockable attachments spread throughout the levels such as a silencer for your pistol. Along with many basic weapons there is your main fire arm, the LKW, or Laserkraftwerk. It, like all other weapons, can be upgraded via secret upgrades hidden around all of the games chapters. Finding these are key if you wish to make a deadly weapon out of the LKW. There are four skill trees in the game; Stealth, Tactical, Assault, and Demolition. Each is very self explanatory and will adapt to your play style to provide a better experience. For movement; all the basic abilities are there with a couple additions. If you attempt to crouch while running you will perform a slide. You can shoot while sliding, but you cannot aim down your sights. One thing to keep in mind, and this may be a personal problem, movement seems a bit quicker than most first-person shooters. It isn't that big of a deal, but it is slightly jarring to get used to.
SOUNDTRACK
The soundtrack is mostly ambient, but is definitely a large point of interest. The music is well tailored to fit whatever situation is currently going on. From the haunting chords of a purged asylum to the somber note of human interaction; the music is never out of its element, and that's saying something for a game with such strange and varied scenarios.
VISUALS
This game looks simply stunning; there’s no other way to put it. From any angle this game looks beautiful. The modeling and texture work is fantastic. They put a great emphasis on the eyes of characters. The vibrant blues and greens look quite unnerving at times if I’m being quite honest. Animations are very smooth as well, and the lip-syncing is high-quality work. All around; the visuals provide a truly next-gen feel to the game.
FINAL THOUGHTS
This game has set the standard for the single-player FPS for me. This is one of the few FPS games I've played that has a cohesive story. It's very immersive and quite the ride. The game is a dream to play. All the guns feel amazing to use, and the skills only help to improve the gameplay experience. The sound design may not win any awards, but I for one am a fan. The visuals are FANTASTIC, there's  simply no other way to put it. The dialogue in this game is unbelievable; it has no right to have this good of writing. One thing that I would like to note, and this is HUGE, this game has terrible replay value. The only difference between the two timelines (from what I can tell) is a mechanic, an upgrade, and a character. On that note; Wolfenstein: The New Order has left a lasting impression, and I'm hoping other FPS games begin to follow suit.
Nope, no joke or witty remark this time; just a plain, simple review. Bet you did Nazi that one coming, eh?

At first I did not like the idea of a bald Max Payne who, instead of his good-old black coat, donned a Hawaii shirt and replaced New York with South America. Some of the early screenshots were alarming and I did not want Rockstar Games to have anything to do with Remedy's well-established franchise.
However, this new Max Payne works perfectly! The story is exciting as usual - the dialog is great and as one can guess Max narrates most of the story. The graphics are stunning and even the dodge mechanism has been improved. If we dodge and Max goes into slow-mo we have to be careful with our surroundings - no more hovering Max if an object is hit in the air; Max falls and the slow-mo immediately stops. We have to be more careful and use covers more wisely.
Headshots are now almost mandatory as not long into the game can we first encounter the first vest wearing enemies. The game gradually gets more difficult, in fact, if it is too difficult (if the player dies too often) the AI provides us with extra painkillers to have a successful run after loading the last checkpoint.
The game features a long and excellent campaign with collectibles and those seeking extra challenge can complete the game on higher difficulties which, just like in the predecessor games, get unlocked only after walkthroughs.
I heard the multiplayer option is also very good. I'm not sure if there can be many players online these days but the game's campaign alone worth the purchase.

Oh you can also dual wield every single weapon in the game. There isn’t a huge enemy variety types; there’s just the standard soldiers, flying drones, and a few variations of the heavy; there’s one with a rocket launcher who has a fair amount of health, there’s the one with a shotgun who has a fairly high amount of health, there are the super soldiers who have a high amount of health and there are the large robots who have a very high amount of health. This game also has a much more darker and depressing tone though it isn’t meant to be taken all that seriously, the violence has been ramped up and the game has been made to be a little bit more cinematic then the previous games though you still get a good enough amount of gameplay. There aren’t really any outright problems with the game though I do wish this one section in the game was a longer

It is time. Time for me to sit down and review this game having put in a solid 20+ hours and now have a grasp on what this game is about and what that might mean for you the player/consumer. Take a minute to read through my review and if there are too many words and letters, skip to the end for my final verdict. I use a standard review format on Steam when it comes to categories, so some apply, some do not. This is probably one of the most honest reviews you'll find on here so take that or leave it.
What is Squad? When I first heard about this game I admittedly missed the Kickstarter, missed the big news announcements, missed the gaming convention announcements, I basically goofed and came into this late. I saw the name and the logo on Steam (as an upcoming title) and was immediately unimpressed. "Squad"? That's lame.  Then I watched the trailer. My interest was piqued.
So I did some digging and research. Found out the game is the spiritual successor to the mod, "Project Reality" made by those mod devs. I had played PR when it first came out many many years ago and haven't touched it since. So I had NO idea what they did to it.
I then watched pre-Alpha gameplay and immediately realized this was a game I was looking for. As a former military servicemember (Marine Corps Infantryman), and a tactical realism player this game seemed to fit right into my gaming niche. I found the Kickstarter page which showed vehicles they intended to put in, and other great and amazing features you don't find much in today's shooters.
Fast forward to Steam launch and now I get to experience it. This is a hardcore, unrelenting tactical shooter. It's an in your face, no holds barred look into life on the battlefield. As someone who set foot in Iraq conducting combat operations, this game felt like what real life does (as best as any game can).
You'll find yourself hunkered down behind H-Barriers with snaps of rounds over your head, grenades blowing up nearby, and a constant state of utter confusion as to WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON?! Your radio will be blowing up in your ear as squadmates call out contacts, and you'll be engaged in some brutal firefights. But, not all the time (see below).
Graphics are extremely important to a lot of people in this day in age. Many PC gamers will spend thousands of dollars on ridiculous rigs and expect top notch graphics as a result. So it's worth noting the graphics in this game in my review.
Squad utilizes Unreal Engine 4... which is arguably one of the best engines available to the masses right now on a commercial level. I have a project of my own I am working on with UE4 so while I could be called biased, I did a lot of research. UE4 is strong, powerful, and stable. It's a well built engine that commercially speaking is cheap for the developer, and allows some of the best graphical enhancements available today.
Squad does a really solid job of having graphics that are on par with today's standards, but cuts corners on some things. For example, the player models don't exhibit facial expressions, different facial models to look different than the exact same modeled player. When the player dies they look exactly like the model when they were alive (eyes open, ready to go to work).
The ground textures can be underwhelming at times in some areas, while the overall scope of everything you see on the screen can be absolutely stunning in some maps. It's a toss up but one thing is made clear, the graphics are where they need to be and will only (likely) get better as the game is improved upon, updated, and optimized.
This is why you bought this game or are contemplating it. The combat. This game features a realistic approach to a LARGE SCALE combat zone. Right now only infantry based, you will fight on maps with upwards to 50 vs 50 players through wooded terrain, open deserts, Middle Eastern villages, and more.
Combat in this game is unforgiving. If you slip up, you die. If you run off on your own, you'll probably die. If you move too fast, you'll die. If you move too slow, you'll die. You have absolutely GOT TO work with your teammates in order to succeed. I've seen guys go 70+ kills and less than 10 deaths. I've seen guys go with 10 kills and 70 deaths. Neither player was "better" than the other if they didn't contribute to the MISSION. If they ran off and did their own thing, they were a terrible player regardless of stats.
As I said in my intro, you will find yourself in rabid, bite the neck battles. You may even come down to a hand to hand fight swinging E-tools with your enemy (that happened to me once). But other times you may feel like you're running for 10 minutes only to suddenly die by an invisible enemy (one you never saw coming) and have to respawn again. It's the hard nature of the game and oddly enough just like real life in the sense that you may do a lot of walking and may only see action for a few minutes.
Expect to both love and hate the combat in this game. Expect some amazing experiences that once you put the headset down, you collect yourself and feel good about it... while also getting completely frustrated when your squad didn't work together.
The squad is the backbone of this game. "Upgrades" come in the form of classes for your player. Each one has a player model, and each one has a kit (of gear). Each one unlocks with the more players you have in your squad.
So, starting out with a squad of one... you'll have a Squad Leader. Add two players and you'll gain a medic slot, and a fighter slot (standard infantry rifleman). Add more players and you gain access to RPG kits, Grenadiers (40mm's), and eventually the Marksman (sniper role). Each class is extremely important to the overall success or failure of the team.
I run a PC with the following specs:
AMD FX-8370 (8 core CPU) @ 4.01ghz
G.Skill RAM 16GB @ 1600mhz
Asus GTX 960 2GB
Windows 10
You have to understand one thing right off the bat... this is an Early Access (Alpha) title. If you can understand that and appreciate that, you wont be disappointed. If you expect a bug free game, a game without launcher crashes, CTD's, compatibility problems, etc... you should not pick this game up.
I run an average of about 30fps. Sometimes less (around 20) sometimes more. I have most settings maxed with shadows on Medium. I normally put them on low but this game they appear like disgusting blobs (a fence will look like poka dots on the ground). So medium is my best performance to quality spot for shadows.
I have a few problems with being disconnected from servers (always at the worst time or when I feel like I'm rocking on the server). This is a known issue. But the overall performance of the game is pretty solid for an Alpha (better than most I've played).

Here are a few things that I find interesting about
:
Leveling System - Players have to put in some work to level up, as experience is granted based more-so on enemies routed and hits connected than overall damage done. What I love about this take on level-ups is that it blends well with the player-versus-player elements, and allows the more tenacious ‘crashers’ to gain levels more frequently than those attempting to preserve health; the player-versus-player aspect will be explained in further detail next. As an individual knight gains a level, he has the opportunity to allot a gen number of points into four different traits: Strength, to determine the power of the knight’s attacks; Magic, which improves the knight’s magic attack maneuvers, spell effectiveness, and how much energy a spell utilizes on cast based on the total amount of energy; Defense, which dictates the knight’s health point total; and Speed, which determines how much damage the Bow item deals with each strike and, obviously enough, the individual knight’s movement. Combined with varying statistic-altering weapons, items, and pets, this leveling system permits players to create their own form of strategy.
Player-Versus-Player -
is a cooperative experience, so what could it possibly mean to ‘force’ players to combat against each other? At the end of each stage resulting in the liberation of a princess, only one knight may earn the kiss of valiance from the fair maiden. To effectively decide who is chosen, the players duke it out with all of their acquired abilities and equipment. Unlike most things in this title, a princess’ kiss does not grant any boons, bonuses, or additional equipment; however, it is very satisfying viewing the ‘saltiness’ on friends’ faces when you have stolen the embrace from their colored princess.
Minigames - With various landscapes and degrees of difficulty between the stages, the campaign offers an abundance of cooperative play. But minigames are available to sweeten the deal. I must admit that I have not played too many of them, but the few that I have experienced-like beach volleyball-were so much fun to play with friends and online, win or lose.
Humor - Simply put, from its theme to its plot twists and cutscenes,
is a title that will provoke, at the very least, a snicker. I feel as though I should refrain from revealing too much from this engaging title’s comedy approach as it is very well written. It can also be humorous when played with friends even at points when it is not necessarily meant to be; this is enhanced through splitscreen play.
TL:DR -
is highly enjoyable, especially for fanatics of hack ‘n’ slash and cooperative titles, character leveling and building, and of
previous title,
; speaking of, I also recommend-if you do not already own both games-the purchase of the bundle featuring
and
. I would also recommend the purchase of the Pink Knight and the Blacksmith downloadable content since proceeds are given to various charities. Whether solo or in cooperative play, with
and the downloadable content or not,
is a laughably good time. I had wanted to mention other notable features in this title such as its outstanding level design and themes, gameplay, and specific items but I feel as though I would be continuing on for days if I started. This game is...beautiful.
It tries to be a game not unlike Portal, and a game that answers the question "Are games art?"
It succeeds at both. This game is an experience that is more than worth its price tag, with a story that asks hard questions about AI and humanity; questions that will become extremely prevelant in the years to come.
The gameplay is also great as well. It feels like Portal even though there is no portal gun. Puzzles revolve around a small collection of movable objects and obstacles that are used in almost every combination of ways imaginable.
A few objects are:
-A jammer. This can be used to remove a force field, even if that force field can be deactived through other means. It can also be used to deactive mines, so they don't blow up in your face when you approach.
-A connector. This allows you to connect lasers together. You can connect from/to laser sources, laser receivers, and other connectors, and there's no limit to the number of these things that a single connector can connect to. It's somewhat like the laser redirection cube from Portal, but much more flexible and robust.
-A hexahedron. A fancy name for a cube. Used for standing on or weighing down switches.
There's plenty more, but half the fun is finding new doodads to play with, so I'll stop there.

It is time. Time for me to sit down and review this game having put in a solid 20+ hours and now have a grasp on what this game is about and what that might mean for you the player/consumer. Take a minute to read through my review and if there are too many words and letters, skip to the end for my final verdict. I use a standard review format on Steam when it comes to categories, so some apply, some do not. This is probably one of the most honest reviews you'll find on here so take that or leave it.
What is Squad? When I first heard about this game I admittedly missed the Kickstarter, missed the big news announcements, missed the gaming convention announcements, I basically goofed and came into this late. I saw the name and the logo on Steam (as an upcoming title) and was immediately unimpressed. "Squad"? That's lame.  Then I watched the trailer. My interest was piqued.
So I did some digging and research. Found out the game is the spiritual successor to the mod, "Project Reality" made by those mod devs. I had played PR when it first came out many many years ago and haven't touched it since. So I had NO idea what they did to it.
I then watched pre-Alpha gameplay and immediately realized this was a game I was looking for. As a former military servicemember (Marine Corps Infantryman), and a tactical realism player this game seemed to fit right into my gaming niche. I found the Kickstarter page which showed vehicles they intended to put in, and other great and amazing features you don't find much in today's shooters.
Fast forward to Steam launch and now I get to experience it. This is a hardcore, unrelenting tactical shooter. It's an in your face, no holds barred look into life on the battlefield. As someone who set foot in Iraq conducting combat operations, this game felt like what real life does (as best as any game can).
You'll find yourself hunkered down behind H-Barriers with snaps of rounds over your head, grenades blowing up nearby, and a constant state of utter confusion as to WHAT THE HELL IS GOING ON?! Your radio will be blowing up in your ear as squadmates call out contacts, and you'll be engaged in some brutal firefights. But, not all the time (see below).
Graphics are extremely important to a lot of people in this day in age. Many PC gamers will spend thousands of dollars on ridiculous rigs and expect top notch graphics as a result. So it's worth noting the graphics in this game in my review.
Squad utilizes Unreal Engine 4... which is arguably one of the best engines available to the masses right now on a commercial level. I have a project of my own I am working on with UE4 so while I could be called biased, I did a lot of research. UE4 is strong, powerful, and stable. It's a well built engine that commercially speaking is cheap for the developer, and allows some of the best graphical enhancements available today.
Squad does a really solid job of having graphics that are on par with today's standards, but cuts corners on some things. For example, the player models don't exhibit facial expressions, different facial models to look different than the exact same modeled player. When the player dies they look exactly like the model when they were alive (eyes open, ready to go to work).
The ground textures can be underwhelming at times in some areas, while the overall scope of everything you see on the screen can be absolutely stunning in some maps. It's a toss up but one thing is made clear, the graphics are where they need to be and will only (likely) get better as the game is improved upon, updated, and optimized.
This is why you bought this game or are contemplating it. The combat. This game features a realistic approach to a LARGE SCALE combat zone. Right now only infantry based, you will fight on maps with upwards to 50 vs 50 players through wooded terrain, open deserts, Middle Eastern villages, and more.
Combat in this game is unforgiving. If you slip up, you die. If you run off on your own, you'll probably die. If you move too fast, you'll die. If you move too slow, you'll die. You have absolutely GOT TO work with your teammates in order to succeed. I've seen guys go 70+ kills and less than 10 deaths. I've seen guys go with 10 kills and 70 deaths. Neither player was "better" than the other if they didn't contribute to the MISSION. If they ran off and did their own thing, they were a terrible player regardless of stats.
As I said in my intro, you will find yourself in rabid, bite the neck battles. You may even come down to a hand to hand fight swinging E-tools with your enemy (that happened to me once). But other times you may feel like you're running for 10 minutes only to suddenly die by an invisible enemy (one you never saw coming) and have to respawn again. It's the hard nature of the game and oddly enough just like real life in the sense that you may do a lot of walking and may only see action for a few minutes.
Expect to both love and hate the combat in this game. Expect some amazing experiences that once you put the headset down, you collect yourself and feel good about it... while also getting completely frustrated when your squad didn't work together.
The squad is the backbone of this game. "Upgrades" come in the form of classes for your player. Each one has a player model, and each one has a kit (of gear). Each one unlocks with the more players you have in your squad.
So, starting out with a squad of one... you'll have a Squad Leader. Add two players and you'll gain a medic slot, and a fighter slot (standard infantry rifleman). Add more players and you gain access to RPG kits, Grenadiers (40mm's), and eventually the Marksman (sniper role). Each class is extremely important to the overall success or failure of the team.
I run a PC with the following specs:
AMD FX-8370 (8 core CPU) @ 4.01ghz
G.Skill RAM 16GB @ 1600mhz
Asus GTX 960 2GB
Windows 10
You have to understand one thing right off the bat... this is an Early Access (Alpha) title. If you can understand that and appreciate that, you wont be disappointed. If you expect a bug free game, a game without launcher crashes, CTD's, compatibility problems, etc... you should not pick this game up.
I run an average of about 30fps. Sometimes less (around 20) sometimes more. I have most settings maxed with shadows on Medium. I normally put them on low but this game they appear like disgusting blobs (a fence will look like poka dots on the ground). So medium is my best performance to quality spot for shadows.
I have a few problems with being disconnected from servers (always at the worst time or when I feel like I'm rocking on the server). This is a known issue. But the overall performance of the game is pretty solid for an Alpha (better than most I've played).
