The bottom line is Wolfenstein is fun. The shooting is generally exciting and gets my blood lust pumping. It is a lot of fun to run down the hallways with dual shotties blasting down Nazis. On the down side, the level design isn't very good. There are far too many narrow corridor shoot outs where enemies periodically pop out from behind cover and the AI is generally really weak. It's stuff that was tired a decade ago. The challenge of this game comes from being overwhelmed by numbers. There is a fair amount of ability to get stealth kills by sneaking up behind enemies and knifing them. I can go with the whole alternate universe with crazy new technologies motif, but it seems completely unrealistic that  a guard five feet away wouldn't notice someone being stabbed right out in the open next to him. Also, a lot of locations just seem like the only people there are guards on patrol. There are no scientists at a research facility, for example. The only location that had anything other than troops marching around with their guns out was the actual prison. Obviously a lot of care went into creating a very detailed game world. This game does look really good, but it rings hollow with the dearth of NPC's in the game world. On the other hand, I did appreciate the fact that most of the time you're fighting by yourself. There isn't some annoying friendly NPC that you have to wait for to open doors or finish some other scripted even so you can keep playing. A small but significant touch I really appreciated was that when the level was over it will tell you that if you click on an object the round will end. So you know to go back and stock up on ammo, health, and/or hidden collectables before knowingly moving on. The health system was done well too. There's some recharging health, but only a small percentage will recharge over time. Otherwise, health kits need to be found. There is a lot of game here. It took around 13 hours to finish and the locations were generally well varied. The story was decent. Nothing that hasn't been done before, but  it went well enough to string the levels together. Really, this game isn't that great, but it is fun and it's a sad commentary on the state of single player FPS' these days that this is one of the best that has been made in the last few years.

My last forray into the Wolfenstein franchise was back in 2002 with Return to Castle Wolfenstein. I was 12 at the time, and I didn't play much of it seeing as it scared the absolute crap out of me when the game's paranormal elements came into play. I never took an interest in the Wolfenstein franchise afterwards.
When The New Order came out, I didn't really pay too much attention at first, it seemed to me that it was an IP in decline and probably wouldn't be worth picking up unless it was deeply discounted on a Steam sale. I was so very wrong. I decided to buy it when it was down by 66% to about £11 over the holiday sale after hearing it getting glowing reviews and heaps of praise, but I gladly would have paid the full price for this game.
The game is simply fantastic, and I was amazed at how well it can tell its story and develop its characters while being a very over the top first person shooter. I found myself actually caring about the story and what happened to the characters, it helps that the protagonist is not quite so one dimensional seeming as those in most other shooters. The voice acting is very well done, and the dialogue surprisingly well written. The world feels fleshed out and detailed, which is helped by a plethora of news papers and little bits of letters to cover some history of events between the tutorial / prologue and the main sequence of events in the game some years later.
The levels are nicely designed, with a few little shortcuts here and there and plenty of places to explore for the extras and secret areas which I found myself really wanting to discover. There are versions of songs done in German and details of hows bands like the Beatles changed their names to German and sang in German too. It was nice that your time taken to explore was rewarded with health upgrades and such too. On the subject of collectibles and the like, the Perk system was an interesting addition. By completing various combat based "challenges" you unlock certain upgrades for weapons or for movement etc which added a little progression system to the game. It's by no means necessary, I mean you can likely complete the game easily without unlocking any perks, but they're still handy nonetheless.
The combat is very enjoyable, dual wielding shotguns and assault rifles is something that I realise has been missing from my gaming life. The gunplay has a nice feel, with your weapons feeling like they have some kind of impact, it feels meaty, which is maybe helped by Nazi's heads exploding on rifle headshots. Throwing knives was great, I always seemed to hit them in the crotch though, not that that's a bad thing. Grenades felt a little useless unless you were dealing with the mechanical enemies. I used them only seldomly when fighting regular soldiers. I didn't use the cover system much either, it works well, but I didn't feel I needed it. If you want a challenge I would recommend playing it on a harder difficulty than the recommended one though, I finished the game without struggling much at any point, and most of my 14 deaths were through stupidity than anything else.
On a technical note, the game looks nice enough but it's obvious that it's a console game ported to the PC. It's a good port, but texture qualities in some areas are a bit lacking. It's easy to get over that but some kind of HD texture pack would be a welcome addition. At max settings it runs at 60 fps on my gtx 970 without any dips. There's an FOV slider which is nice to see as well.
Lastly the music was really great, from the metal style of music in the main menu to the acoustic guitar bits at a few of the more emotionally charged bits, it adds to the atmosphere and overall feeling of the game and story.
So yeah, this game was pretty damn good, and I did not expect it to be.

Temporary Review
So far I've only made it to chapter 4, but this is my impression so far.
I have played a good bit of Max Payne 1.
pros-
the bullet time is so much smoother and makes using it convenient
I like that I can easily use bullet time while standing still
so far the story has been good (though Max Payne's incesant moping, angst filled whining gets annoying at times)
AI has proven to be decent; a few time's I have caught them trying to flank me
cons-
the whole game feels more like a cinematic experience than a game really. It's like watching a series of cutscenes and then having a brief period where you get to shoot, only to sit through more cutscenes. They've definitely cut back on the interactivity from the first one. Instead of getting to cross ledges and find levers, you get to watch Max cross ledges and find and pull levers. There were times I completely let go of the controls, because the cinematic scene was running so long. This lead to me suddenly having to fumble for them, when I was either once again thrust into the action, or presented with a bullet time (click once) event.
The checkpoint system in 3 is a godsend, but at the same time, they chose a few terrible spots for respawn. I've found myself respawned right in the middle of a fire fight.
Sprinting doesn't feel like it actually makes you go any faster. In fact, it feels sluggish even.
Gun selection is just awful. I get the feeling it was designed with a controller in mind, not a mouse and keyboard. When in the heat of battle, I can't easily and quickly reach the number keys and expect to hit the right one. Therefore, I use the mouse wheel to scroll through my arsenal. The major glaring problem is that for some undefined reason, you drop whatever enemy gun you've picked up, if you accidentally scroll onto the dual wield option. Yes, you read correctly. You DROP the picked up enemy gun, in favor of dual wielding pistols and uzis. Why they made that an option escapes me. Needless to say this has led to many a frustrating gun battle, when I dropped the very gun I was trying to use, because I accidentally stopped on dual wield.
Conclusion: Fans of Max Payne's story would enjoy this, as it seems like a good continuation.
Anyone just looking for a shooter game, might want to look elsewhere. Unless they don't mind sitting through long cutscenes, or having their action interuppted for a series of cutscenes.
If you are a gamer that likes immersion, this is not the game for you. The back and forth between gameplay and cutscene can be a bit jarring. Not to mention the story's somewhat all over the place narrative. This is not a game where you become the protragonist. Realistically, this really is like reading a book or, more accurately, watching a movie. You get to know characters, you might care about them, but you are distanced because it is not YOU in the situation. Your interaction is limited to words, and what they tell you the about the characters feelings.

On purchasing this game I was somewhat bewildered witht he download size, however the past 13 hours of gameplay required to complete the single player campaign highlighted to me that Machine Games absolutely nailed this game!
I have played previous Wolfenstein games and I'm by no means a fanatic of the series but the latest installment is the most original and involving FPS games I've played in quite some years. The New Order manages to present the player with a delicious blend of fast paced shooter, stealth and a variety of vehicular activites, all of which serve a purpose and do not feel that they are simply there because they need to be.
Further to the game play are the beautiful cinematic sequences that occur as both transitions between levels and features within the level itself, enhancing the compelling storyline and providing the player with emotion towards the characters. The locations in which you fight are alos both varied and detailed providing some level of non linear play.
Regarding characters the allied resisiatnce that you enter throughout the game all have their own personality and there are many axis fighter types ranging from frontline soldiers to mech suits and robots, not to mention some ancient architects thrown in for good measure.
There was some small Vsync issues I couldnt resolve and a small glitch just after surfacing fromt he U-boat in which the player kept veering left with no input but other than that the game played through without hitch. The only area odf the game I would like to change is that it paused when the weapon wheel was on screen.

For me, this game was my childhood, and alongside StarCraft these two are my all-time favourites. Unlike StarCraft, however, I've mostly ignored AoE2's campaign mode but played copious amounts of its multiplayer (only agianst AI). AoE 2 is one of those games where choosing your difficulty really changes the feel of the game. Do you like building your little town and building up one big army of your best? Stick to the original AI. Do you want to feel like death at ending legions is around every corner? Select the new AI and prepare to regeret it.
AoE2 is very much a material-gather game, as a lot of RTSs are, but instead of Minerals and Vespene Gas you'll be hunting down Food, Wood, Gold and Stone as you push through the ages from wooden shacks to stone castles. There's a delicate balance between making enough Villagers for resource income, saving up enough for the next Age, and making sure you can defend your town from attackers. Games typically take me two hours, but I usually take my time and have 5+ AI in teams of two.
What can I possibly say that will make you want to buy this? Well, the art is beautiful and detailed for its time, and the HD updates only improve on this. There are a multitude of tactical options for you to take, be it via Seige, Melee, Ranged or even Sea. Building your little towns and walls is as much fun as the fighting, if not more depending on your play-style. In my option this is the most well-rounded Medieval-based RTS available, with SO many races for you to choose from, each with their own little quirks, art and unique units, I really would recommend it to everyone interested in the genre!
(My gameplay time here doesn't reflect how much I've played the original CD copy)

Shooting Nazis has never felt this good.
+ Some of the best shooting mechanics I've ever experienced. No need for gameplay gimicks to spice things up; it just works.
+ Stealth and cover systems feel natural, as opposed to rigid (Gears of War cover, for instance).
+ The characters are loveable.
+ The art style is fantastic. The Nazis look fearsome and badass.
+ The environments the story takes you to are almost all very unique.
+ Brutal and fantastic soundtrack.
+ Dual-wield every gun you can get your hands on two of.
+ Retro health and med kit mechanics. This can come down to preference, but it is certainly refreshing to see.
+ Best easter egg I've ever seen
+ MAX HASS!
- A few technical issues. Primarily, screen-tearing with screen space reflections enabled.
- Collectibles are hard to ignore if you have compulsive hoarding tendencies in video games (I do). It's neat to find them, but some are hidden in ludicrously difficult locations. It serves as more of a distraction after a while.
- Not the best graphics ever. I'd be thoroughly impressed with them years ago, but they are just satisfactory by today's standards. Some of the textures are awful. Graphics cards anymore are coming with 2GB minimum and 4GB standard memory, so textures should be cranked up, with options for lower quality to appease the console crowd, as well as those with less VRAM.
- Gun sounds seemed pretty quiet throughout. This was primarily evident in the first level, and they balanced out much better in the 1960 levels. They still could have been a bit louder.
- The AI is pretty dumb. They're slow to detect you visually, and they fail to react to their comrades dropping dead from stealth attacks. Oddly, they won't react if you land a silenced headshot on somebody standing ten feet from them, but they will react if that shot misses and hits a nearby object. I rarely noticed their stupidity because I never risked getting close enough to be detected unless I was assured a kill. Once detected, they fight much like you'd expect. It's a firefight, so there isn't much they could do wrong.
- I'm not sure the people who picked the default controls know how keyboards work. On the first level, there is a section that requires you to pull off a sprint-slide maneuver, that is horribly counter-intuitive. But hey, this is the PC, so just remap it.
• At its heart, it is a visceral blend of old-school and modern shooters. As such, it isn't plot driven, like say, BioShock. The plot isn't ground-breaking. It works, it takes you to some really cool places, but at the end of the day, you just care about the characters, and how many Nazis you get to kill.
Good to see this old RTS classic still going strong with a supporting community. Expansion packs are sick.

There are games that come along from time to time that actually impress you.  Wolfenstein: The New Order is just such a game.   I got this game on sale but I would have gladly paid full price for this gem.
As some other reviewers have noted there are some minor flaws about this game.  For instance, the lower resolution environment textures, the quests inside the rebel compound (although I do like the exploration and attention to detail of this place!) and the ladders.  Going down ladders tends to just be flinging yourself to the bottom then spalttering red on the screen.  Why such pinishment for going down attempting to use a ladder from a higher point to get to a lower point?    Seems silly that BJ can be adept enough to duel weild assault rifles and reload them efficiently but cannot seem to grasp a simple concept as going down the ladder in reverse as he went up.
Yet the positive far outweighs these small imperfections.  The large amount of detail, artistic styling and most of all the sound of the weapons makes them all feel satisfying.  I found myself switching between all the weapons more frequently because I actually enjoyed using them.  The weapons also have benefits and drawbacks to them depending on the enemy that you encounter.  Example being that the assault rifles are not as effective at killing heavily armored units as energy based weaponry or explosives.
I also found that character development was done very well.  Finding out certain aspects of the characters backstory throughout the campaign is something that needs to be brought back and Bethesda and Machine Games are setting the bar here for other action games with their story and character development.
The sound design had a great overall feel to it.  Weapon sounds, explosions, background music, ambient sounds, nonplayer characters interacting with each other, etc.  The whole amalgamation of the sound really added to the immersion of the game.  I personally liked BJs intrrapersonal dialogue that is present throughout the game.  Made BJ feel more relatable and further adding to the immersion of the overall experience.
TLDR:  The story, gameplay and overall feeling of Wolfenstein: The New Order are all on point.  A great pickup for fans of the series or FPS enthusiasts alike.  A very satisfying time.  I give it a solid 9/10.

Lets start of with the bad:
--Poor performance--
-Not all players are experiancing this but a large number are. One issue has been tracked down by the devs as an audio issue in the engine that is resulting in users with AMD CPUs having stuttering and FPS hits. The dev team is actively working on this and the following performance issues. (This has now almost been completely fixed)
-Poor preformance is also linked to the way the engine handles their animation system.
-Certian maps are also causing performance issues with certian players.
--Server Issues--
-Connecting to servers is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ When loading into a server your slot is not saved, so it's a race against whoever else is connecting. This can lead to nearly completely loading into the server just to get kicked out due to it being full. (I now experiance this far less)
-For some people when the server restarts, they get disconnected. This would be an issue if you enjoyed playing with previous squaddies/friends and want to get back in the action with them.
--Gameplay/General issues--
-It's not completely clear if your barrel is or isn't making it over cover, leading to constantly shooting into cover rather than over it.
-Tree branches appear to be bullet proof. This makes it difficult to effectively engange indaviduals in a forest setting, and exceptionally difficult to accurately hit enemies with GPs since they like to go off on tiny tree limbs.
-The IU has issues with getting stuck on ones screen. This happens rarely however but the only way to resolve the issues is to disconnect from the server.
-The amount of communication in a squad is directly porportional to the amount of fun had. If you do not have an active squad leader and or do not have any active squad members, you WILL have a bad time.
Now, to the good:
--Teamwork--
Teamwork is essential in squad, its the key factor to winning or losing matches. Interacting with fellow squadmates is essential and enjoyable when one is with an active group of indaviduals.
--Factions--
Currently, there are 4 factions; US, Russia, Insurgents and Militia. All factions are modeled very well and have enough differences that they can be told apart from a distance. Militia are now wearing track suits, making it a bit easier to tell them apart from russian troops.
--Sounds--
-The audio is damn well done, probably better than DICE did in the battlefield games.
-I constantly find myself instinctively yelling over gunfire as it's hard to hear my teammates over all the noise.
-Sounds change depending on the enviroment your in, when inside a building sounds are dampened whereas outside gunfire will echo off the hills.
--Gunplay--
Reloading, aiming and the recoil of most weapons feels pretty solid. The gun models are also of high quality and very well done.
--Maps--
-There are several maps in the Alpha state of the game, all are of a very exceptable size. They vary from straight up wooded areas, to the middle east with mud huts. The terrain mapping and building models are very well done.
-Building System
Fortifying locations to gain the defensive advantage is a very well fleshed out system in squad. Hopefully more constructable objects will be available at a later time.
In conclusion, squad is in Early Access so the game has a long way to go. That being said, if you have a strong rig and a strong desire to play in a team focused semi realistic FPS, then you may want to look into picking this up. For those with AMD CPUs, give it a bit of thought before you buy. For me, using -d3d10 as a launch peramiter makes my game completely playable now.
EDIT: Updated some things to account for the new update, changed the conclusion as the preformance issues have been improved a bit.
EDIT 2: Updated review to reflect 3.9 patch.
EDIT 3: Added more cons and updated stuff about the performance issues.

The Talos Principle is perhaps the best puzzle game ever made, stunning locations make the game look good and the different puzzle elements make the gameplay and puzzle solving fantastic.
You are able to go throughout all of the puzzles in any order you like, they are nice and clearly colour coded (Green, Orange, Red for Easy to Hard respectively) so you can set yourself your own challenges and choose what puzzles you take on.
The Puzzles themselves are great, you get the same "ahh" moment that you would from a Portal game (Which is what I see alot of people comparing this to) and for the 100+ Puzzles they use all of the elements of the ones previous and build from them to create something more challenging.
Ok, Time for the Story, It is very different to Portal, yet, It is similar.
Similarities First: You are in a world, you have some puzzles to solve... And there is someone watching and guiding your every move.
Now where it is different, where it really shines is the way it conveys its story in various ways, through the voice over like in the trailer, recorded messages, and much of it is on-screen by a computer terminal in-game, you read through remnants of different people and their stories, also another way I won't want to spoil.
The story is again, sometimes given via voice over and recorded messages, the voice acting during these sections is top notch, it won't make you laugh like Wheatley voice actor could do in Portal 2, but the way they deliver the lines is excellent for their respective roles, (I was close to crying at one point) <--- That's very hard to do in a game, but if the writing and acting is solid it is achievable.
So for a score, it really can't be described out of 10 really, It shines and sometimes drops the bar a little in some sections, but it's very few and far between.
So... As a score I'd like to say. Portal 1.5 / 10???
Also there are a bunch of fun Easter eggs to find! :D
TL;DR
It's Like Portal, But It isn't, Just Trust Me.

Castle Crashers is a side scrolling Beat 'em up developed by The Behemoth
and released in 2012.
Castle Crashers takes place in a cartoon Middle Ages universe. The knights are sitting around a table eating a feast, but suddenly an evil wizard steals a large gem, and runs off with four princesses! Being a knight, it is your noble duty to save the princesses, the kingdom, and retrieve the stolen gem.
Queue Adventure!
The Castle Crashers recommends you use a controller, when you first launch the game. Anyone who knows me; knows I'm stubborn and refuse to purchase a controller for my computer. So... regarding the controller suggestion: Yes, it would be much easier on your progressing-carpal-tunnel. But, the game is completely doable with just a keyboard.
The controls are pretty basic you have three types of attacks: light attack, heavy attack, and throw item.
You also have a block button that slows you down, but if you time it correctly, it can literally save your character's life.
As you progress through the game your character will gain experience points, money, animal orbs, and new weapons that you can purchase or will randomly drop off enemies. Your unlockables are accessible at the Blacksmith, and there are plenty of things to collect to keep you busy.
There are 12 achievements in Castle Crashers, this is one of those games that is relatively easier to get 100%. However, four of these achievements require playing with at least one other player. One achievement requires being in a four player game.
There are only two achievements worth warning/note: Arena Master (Win 40 Arena Online Matches) and Glork (Win 20 All you can Quaff Online Matches). I won't lie, to earn these achievements, I ran between two computers. My brother was nice enough to be a punching bag, when he was away at work or school.
Alternative strategy: Hit the fourms and see if anyone wants to trade off, you could do something else while you get beat up... …..likeeee Battle block Theater!
Castle Crashers is priced at $14.99, for the amount of time you'll spend playing this game on your own, and with friends, that's a fair price. However if you're the first of your friends to play this game
you should grab the 4-pack so you can play with 3 other friends.
Story: Pretty stereo typical story line, but it's delivered hilariously and without any voiced/text narrative
and with plenty of humor. Gameplay: Suggested controller, but doable with a keyboard alone, I won't pay for carpal tunnel treatment. Shush! Achievements: Fairly obtainable 100% without too much of a time commitment, but you will need another friend or three. Price: Fair, better with a sale, or buying a bundle deal on sale.
All in all, this game appeals to anyone who might have enjoyed playing an arcade styled game, indie platformers, 2D, indie graphics, 4 player games, or just wants to support The Behemoth.

If you like Portal, then getting this game is really a no-brainer (It's completely different in many ways, but Portal is just the only comparable game). If there just wasn't that huge price tag...
Nevertheless, I risked it, and was absolutely impressed!
The massive amount of worlds and riddles of the campaign actually justifies the price of Talos principle (HOWEVER, see my negative points at the end), especially considering the included modding ability, that hopefully will provide some decent community content in the future.
I totally loved the graphics, the music and the mysterious/epic background story. Even though the game is somewhat darker or more mature than portal, it doesn't take itself too seriously and there is a lot of geeky humor involved.
Overall, there hasn't been a game for quite some time, that really got me hooked, where you get this feeling "just one more level", and suddenly its 2AM...
That being said, there are some negative points that were no dealkbreaker to me but might annoy other people:
- To access later bonus rooms, you have to collect stars that are hidden somewhere over the level and much harder to get than the normal sygils. This is totally fine in those cases where you see the star and can think about how to get to it. But in too many cases they are out of sight and involve a tedious search of every square millimeter of the map for hidden rooms/doors that might open under some circumstance. This is clearly a time filler that I would not count to actual game time.
- Balancing of the difficulty seems quite arbitrary, there are many excellent riddles that force you to think out of the box, but even in late levels some riddles are ridiculously easy, while others so frustrating to the point that you eventually start up googling for the solution.
- And this leads to my main problem: Why did they implement a really nice "hint" system, where you receive in somewhat cryptic words a small hint towards the solution, but then only allow you to use this TWO times throughout the whole game? makes it kinda pointless considering that there are hundreds of riddles...  So more than once, my only option was to google the solution, which completely spoiled all the fun of that riddle.
- once you collected a bunch of sygils you have to arrange them in a tetris-style minigame to open a new door. This is the one part of the game I absolutely hate, it becomes boring, annoying, tiresome, repetitive already after the first couple of times. Here, they could have really added some more variety of minigames....
- The background story, although interesting, is mainly delivered through walls of text you could read on computer terminals scattered around the levels... not quite my cup of tea.
Overall, I recommend buying the game if you get a discount.  Yes, mathematically the ratio gametime/pricetag is totally OK, but the devs recycled so much stuff from architecture to textures, to riddles, plus searching for these annoying stars... overall I think the game could have been even a better experience if they sacrificed some game time by removing all the repetitive recycled stuff, but that would mean lowering the price of course....

The story's the best part of this game, but not worth the AAA asking price unless you really like video game narratives.
The puzzles are tedious, uninspired and seemingly endless. The problem isn't that you only have half a dozen tools to work with (prisms, cubes, fans, etc.). And it's not that most of those elements are copied from other puzzle games (Portal, etc.). The problem is that you're rarely asked to use your scant few tools in new or interesting ways. There are almost no Aha! moments in this game—just a long slog of applying principles you learned hours earlier in increasingly complex patterns.
Half an hour into the game, you learn that a prism can redirect a laser beam around a corner to a open door. 20 hours into the game, you're redirecting half a dozen laser beams with half a dozen prisms to open half a dozen doors. It's more confusing, but no more challenging or interesting that it was in the beginning of the game.
There are something like 100 puzzles in the game, and I'd guess about 25 are worthwhile. Many others are unbelievably lazy. Even in the final stages of the game, the solution to some secret bonus puzzles are as simple as using a cube to jump over a wall. The only real difficulty comes from guessing which walls the game designer has arbitrarily flagged as jumpable (95% are impassable.)

An incredible experience for new and veteran players. Massive battles, dogfights, and Mad Max-esque vehicle battles. Strategy plays a large part in this game even though there's so many lone wolves doing their own thing at one given moment. Playing solo is fun, but playing with a squad or an entire platoon is so much better.

Lets start of with the bad:
--Poor performance--
-Not all players are experiancing this but a large number are. One issue has been tracked down by the devs as an audio issue in the engine that is resulting in users with AMD CPUs having stuttering and FPS hits. The dev team is actively working on this and the following performance issues. (This has now almost been completely fixed)
-Poor preformance is also linked to the way the engine handles their animation system.
-Certian maps are also causing performance issues with certian players.
--Server Issues--
-Connecting to servers is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ When loading into a server your slot is not saved, so it's a race against whoever else is connecting. This can lead to nearly completely loading into the server just to get kicked out due to it being full. (I now experiance this far less)
-For some people when the server restarts, they get disconnected. This would be an issue if you enjoyed playing with previous squaddies/friends and want to get back in the action with them.
--Gameplay/General issues--
-It's not completely clear if your barrel is or isn't making it over cover, leading to constantly shooting into cover rather than over it.
-Tree branches appear to be bullet proof. This makes it difficult to effectively engange indaviduals in a forest setting, and exceptionally difficult to accurately hit enemies with GPs since they like to go off on tiny tree limbs.
-The IU has issues with getting stuck on ones screen. This happens rarely however but the only way to resolve the issues is to disconnect from the server.
-The amount of communication in a squad is directly porportional to the amount of fun had. If you do not have an active squad leader and or do not have any active squad members, you WILL have a bad time.
Now, to the good:
--Teamwork--
Teamwork is essential in squad, its the key factor to winning or losing matches. Interacting with fellow squadmates is essential and enjoyable when one is with an active group of indaviduals.
--Factions--
Currently, there are 4 factions; US, Russia, Insurgents and Militia. All factions are modeled very well and have enough differences that they can be told apart from a distance. Militia are now wearing track suits, making it a bit easier to tell them apart from russian troops.
--Sounds--
-The audio is damn well done, probably better than DICE did in the battlefield games.
-I constantly find myself instinctively yelling over gunfire as it's hard to hear my teammates over all the noise.
-Sounds change depending on the enviroment your in, when inside a building sounds are dampened whereas outside gunfire will echo off the hills.
--Gunplay--
Reloading, aiming and the recoil of most weapons feels pretty solid. The gun models are also of high quality and very well done.
--Maps--
-There are several maps in the Alpha state of the game, all are of a very exceptable size. They vary from straight up wooded areas, to the middle east with mud huts. The terrain mapping and building models are very well done.
-Building System
Fortifying locations to gain the defensive advantage is a very well fleshed out system in squad. Hopefully more constructable objects will be available at a later time.
In conclusion, squad is in Early Access so the game has a long way to go. That being said, if you have a strong rig and a strong desire to play in a team focused semi realistic FPS, then you may want to look into picking this up. For those with AMD CPUs, give it a bit of thought before you buy. For me, using -d3d10 as a launch peramiter makes my game completely playable now.

EDIT 3: Added more cons and updated stuff about the performance issues.

Pros:
* Plenty of challenging puzzles with a very nice difficulty curve throughout the game.
* Interesting / thought provoking philosophy integrated into the plot and gameplay.
* Multiple items to use in unique ways to solve puzzles, often with multiple solutions.
* Strong sense of resource management when using limited items to hold open gates, keep enemies stunned, etc.
* Makes very good use of the 3D environment for the laser connectors.
* Good voice acting and sound effects.
* Interesting plot, and unique way of conveying it.
* Map editor / community sharing.
Cons:
* Limited choices for responses in the computer dialogue.
* Some puzzles require extremely counter-intuitive solutions, such as connecting beams all the way across levels, which are connected to an open overworld area, barely visible in the background. Most puzzles are strictly logical, even when very difficult, but some such as this require just desperate attempts at answers that don't present themselves through critical reasoning.
* The temptation of the tower and the computer vs. Elohim gets really overplayed and pretty predictable towards the end. The choices could have been presented more subtly.
* Plenty of cryptic elements. Having beaten the game with both endings, and unlocked most of the secret stars and such as well, I still have no idea what the paint bucket was for.
Overall, definitely a good game. One of the better 3D puzzle games. Difficult, but for the most part in a pretty straightforward way. Not a whole lot of innovation, but solid puzzle design nonetheless. The philosopical texts and messages are surprisingly thought-provoking. Very cool stuff about AI, morality, logic, etc.

For me, this game was my childhood, and alongside StarCraft these two are my all-time favourites. Unlike StarCraft, however, I've mostly ignored AoE2's campaign mode but played copious amounts of its multiplayer (only agianst AI). AoE 2 is one of those games where choosing your difficulty really changes the feel of the game. Do you like building your little town and building up one big army of your best? Stick to the original AI. Do you want to feel like death at ending legions is around every corner? Select the new AI and prepare to regeret it.
AoE2 is very much a material-gather game, as a lot of RTSs are, but instead of Minerals and Vespene Gas you'll be hunting down Food, Wood, Gold and Stone as you push through the ages from wooden shacks to stone castles. There's a delicate balance between making enough Villagers for resource income, saving up enough for the next Age, and making sure you can defend your town from attackers. Games typically take me two hours, but I usually take my time and have 5+ AI in teams of two.
What can I possibly say that will make you want to buy this? Well, the art is beautiful and detailed for its time, and the HD updates only improve on this. There are a multitude of tactical options for you to take, be it via Seige, Melee, Ranged or even Sea. Building your little towns and walls is as much fun as the fighting, if not more depending on your play-style. In my option this is the most well-rounded Medieval-based RTS available, with SO many races for you to choose from, each with their own little quirks, art and unique units, I really would recommend it to everyone interested in the genre!

I received Castle Crashers as a gift from an old friend some years ago, and didn’t get around to finishing it until just yesterday. Its a 90s-style beat-em-up for up to four player coop both local and online, originally featured on Xbox Live Arcade before finding its true home here on PC. While they recommend that you use an Xbox controller, I can safely say that using a keyboard is much more responsive and in the long run will save you some frustration. Combat is fast and frenetic and you can quickly find yourself stunlocked into oblivion, so it is important to learn the game’s exceedingly simple but egregiously spamable combos so that you screw over your enemies harder then they could ever do to you. It’s also one of those games where ordinary packs of enemies are more dangerous then bosses, mostly due to their numbers and worse, a lack of mook chivalry- everything that can attack you at once, WILL attack you at once. I believe I initially left off of the campaign out of frustration over its apparent difficulty, though I now understand that what I thought was legitimate challenge was really just a lot of cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, which I was able to overcome by cheesing the game right back. That said, I enjoyed Castle Crashers’ bizarre art style, colorful palette and responsive controls, as well as its rather large range of characters and weapons. I completed a playthrough as the green knight with a focus on strength and defense, which proved a reltively safe and reliable approach. There is a dizzying lineup of unlockable characters, some of which require at least two playthroughs to acquire. While readily enjoyable alone once one learns how to play, Castle Crashers is an experience best shared with others in coop multiplayer.

I wasn't expecting it from a Wolfenstein game, but this is probably the best FPS of 2014.
The campaign is surprisingly long and has a lot of depth. There's a great variety of locations, and the boss fights are fun instead of frustrating. I loved the perk system and the fact that you got upgrades related to how you play. Also a nice bunch of collectibles that reward exploration were a great touch.
The music was pretty amazing, and the atmosphere it created stuck with me long after I closed the game. And the graphics were mostly great, the caveats being the textures looked a bit low-res at 1440 and there was some pop-in occasionally.
My only big complaints are with the checkpoint system. The checkpoints themselves were sometimes really inconveniently located. They'd be before a big fight, but so far before that I'd have to re-collect a ton of health/armor/ammo if I died. Luckily even on the highest difficulty the game wasn't that hard so it didn't happen often, but when it did it was annoying. The few fights that I got stuck on were almost exclusively because the game has a habit of resetting your inventory across levels, and getting dumped into a situation without cover later in the game can be tough to get out of, especially when working with a limited weapon set. Most of the game was almost a bit too easy though, as ammo was abundant and most enemies were very susceptible to stealth and headshots.
Overally a great experience. If you like FPS's, you'll like this.

One of the best puzzle video games I've ever played. A lot of variety and many "aha!" moments to be had. A few of the puzzles are more busy work than actual brain-teasers but these are few and far in between. For those who have played Portal and are expecting something similar, be warned that this game ranges from pathetically easy to crushingly difficult (much more so than either of the Portal games) in its puzzles, of which there are well over 100. The game's replay value lies mainly in its multiple endings. An absolute must have if you love or even kind of like puzzle games. Even those who are indifferent to puzzle games should try it.
For those who are prone to depression, think twice about playing this game. It's more than capable of striking the fear of god into your heart with existential dread thanks to its philosophical storyline, which can make you wonder about the value of your own life and the lives of those around you.
A $40 price tag may seem heavy for a puzzle game but it's well worth every penny. Best game of 2014 in my opinion.

Team Shooter done right!
There are shooter games by the dozen, and a lot of military team shooters, pseudo-military, ... and I played a lot of different shooters. Still do.
However, to me, three team shooter games stick out as the best of their breed:
1. LMCTF. The best CTF ever, with grappling hooks and custom sounds. 'nuff said. (Q2 days, last millennium)
2. Enemy Territory. A mod on RTCW, great teamplay, lots of fun, creative maps. (also, last millenium)
3. Dirty Bomb. a *fast*, honed team shooter. It's fast and fun. Did I mention fast? and fun? (*this* millenium)
Oh, surprise: #2 and #3 were made by the same team. They were already good when they started.
Enough of the praise. Why is it the best team shooter of this year?
* well balanced base setup - the characters ("mercs") and their abilities, weapons, what you can change and what not
* lots of fine-tuning went into the maps and weapons. There is no perfect place, setup, tactic: it's fluid, changes each match.
* no P2W: what those MacGuffin boxes contain is mostly cosmetics. Still, you want it! And the next, too!
* it's fast, really fast. (did I mention that yet?) No slugging over a map to get a headshot after a minute. Here, you get it right after 2 seconds of sprinting!
* good match duration: depending on game mode, about 30 minutes maximum. Usually won much faster, like 10 minutes. Also, the break between matches is timed perfectly for a pee and grabbing a bite. Or whatever.
* team quickchat is good (not perfect as ET was but still): most useful communications, plus taunts and some funny nonsense. Different by merc and with added variation.
* plus, you have "real" voicechat.
* game modes are standard but well tuned.
* the focus is on *team play* - that is what is rewarded, and needed to win. Not the higher levels win (well, not always) - it's the team which has better teamplay.
To me, it's the best team shooter that you can play today. Fast, (s)team-y fun.

Don't be decieved by the 100+ hours I've spent on this game, that was in better times. The recent updates/bug fixes had the unintended consequence of creating more bugs. The game is now practically unplayable, as if it were possible to make the multiplayer even worse ! 90% of the games you play will lag terribly, and someone will drop out within the first five minutes, to your dismay it will usually be someone on your team, rendering the match distressingly unfair.
The community consists of rank obsessed, loyal, die hard fans that have no regard whatsoever when it comes to fair play and have accepted this♥♥♥♥♥♥and awful broken multiplayer. You can still find unranked, arena type games, such as castle blood, where the objective is to out kill your opponent which levels up your never ending spawn of troops, but these are frustrating due to multiplayer issues.
The biggest trouble is multiplayer, it is totally broken. Some players are courteous enough to rush their enemy when an opponents team mate drops, to end the suffering as quickly as possible, occasionally someone will drop out to even teams, but most laughably carry on as though it's still fair game, despite being 4v3, or 4v2, or worse. You might be lucky and have two lag outs, one on each team making it a fair 3v3 or 2v2. You will roll the dice every time you play, in the worst possible way. I don't blame people for being unsportsman like, it's so hard to actually get a game going, getting through the loading screen, by the end you're just desperate to play something, anything at all, even if you have no chance of winning, or equally, the opposing team has no chance of winning because lag claimed a victim on their side, it's frustating, as the game will almost NEVER play out as intended from the start, you just want that sense of blood and carnage, it's so difficult to reach that point due to the bugs.
People rarely leave out of courtesy to even the teams once a player has dropped or lagged out so the game is instantly over in some cases. If lag claims a victim on the opposing side expect a desperate rush from your opponent in order to rebalance the game, or expect a team mate of yours to capitalise on your opponents misfortune by moving in on the dead players position and building in close proximity to gold, iron etc, often cutting off the trade links for market carts, meaning the opposing team has no chance at all of making a comeback. If the dice roll in your favour,  you may as well go afk, have a shower or make yourself some food instead, that's if you don't lag out yourself, because the game will not be challenging at all, you've basically won, it's 4v3, or 4v2, you are sitting pretty, why not send your villagers to attack the enemy base? May as well try and amuse yourself somehow because it's otherwise no fun at all. This buggy and broken multiplayer has lead to some interesting developments in gaming strategy/style. Some players have adapted to predicted lagouts, by rushing and trying to eliminate a player at the very start, thereby increasing their odds of winning. How sad and pathetic that a game's multiplayer in 2015 is so broken players have to include alternative strategies to accomodate the event within their scope of play. AoE2 was always plagued by terrible multiplayer.
There are so few games in the multiplayer lobby, even at peak times, the chance of you finding one in close proximity is remote which is important because any games you play worldwide will increase the probability of lag and almost certain drop outs. Any communication 'lag' issues with other players is delighfully displayed on the game screen at the start. You will be dissapointed when you join a lobby only to find you lag with another player, the traffic light system green, meaning slim chance of lagg/drop out (but by no means guaranteed), yellow, meaning odds of lag/drop out is over 50%, red meaning don't even bother, it's unlikely you'll get through the loading screen. I mean really these are windows 95/98 issues that never got resolved, it's an absolute disgrace. You will spend more time in loading screens/lobbies trying to play than actually playing.
Having said all that, if you don't mind being unable to play multiplayer, the single player has a lot to offer. Sadly even those that love RTS will, I doubt, wish to spend hours on their own doing the single player campaign or death matches against AI  in this era of gaming. Multiplayer is the only real thing this ancient game has going for it, and that is totally ♥♥♥♥ed. DO NOT BUY THIS GAME, trust me on this, save yourself the frustration, because it never gets any better.

So far, this feels like a cross between Max Payne and Captain America, which is a contender for the most awesome thing humanly possible. However, caveat vendor! There are major performance issues!
I'm usually a really big fan of Bethesda. However, should you purchase this product, you should know that there are serious graphics and gameplay issues /apparently/ tied to driver compatibility. I use an NVidia myself, and to get the game playable, I had to go through the NVidia Control Panel, turn off virtually everything there, and then get past the first mission the hard way. There were frequent lags, video critically lagged behind audio in cutscenes, there was serious texture popping (some of which took maybe a minute to update), and worst of all, there were random moments when the entire game would completely lock up for an arbitrary amount of time. No sound, nothing, and I doubt it had anything at all to do with textures.
I have good reason to believe that this is an implementation issue in the software, as the exact same issue has been reported on machines with much better hardware than my own.
However, once I made the adjustments through the Control Panel (no idea which ones were important) and started on the asylum, everything ran smoothly.
This looks to me like a rushed port to PC. Not everyone has these issues, but they seem to pop up at random. The game is fantastic otherwise; a standard setting 21st century first person shooter.
All the same, I would like to be able to play it with everything turned up, so let's hope for a patch!

I bought this game during the Steam Holiday sale. I bought it literally on just the "Nowhere to run" trailer. Even from that video alone, it's clear that Wolfenstein: The New Order isn't just some thrown together game that you're going to get bored with a forget 5 minutes after you finish. In a word, this game is all about polish. Almost every aspect of the game feels carefully crafted to make a very memorable experience.
First of all, the guns. There's not many of them, but each is fun to use. Also, as you've probably heard, almost every gun can be dual-weld. If you're looking to blaze down a hall dual-weilding auto shotguns, this is the game for you. The gunplay is incredibly satisfying as well.
Second are the characters. In a game that's about mindlessly mowing down Nazis, you wouldn't expect characters that you'll actually care about. But this game has exactly that. There's great dialog and some thought out character development that keeps you invested throughout.
Third is the music. Just the fact that I'm devoting a paragraph to the music alone should tell you how much I loved it. It'll have your head nodding when you're deep in battle, with loud, almost industrial techno. It's soft and thoughtful when the game slows down. It perfectly fits with the theme of battling through a distopia, with lots of high octane action. The soundtrack is on Spotify as well. Definitely check that out.
Lastly, I feel this game needs to be praised most for its pacing. This is an aspect of games I feel like a lot of people don't even discuss. I think this is mostly due to the fact that people expect games and levels within games to be long nowadays. This is presumably due to the notion that if something is long, you're getting more value. However when you play a well paced game like this, you realize this isn't always the case. The game is smart enough to shift between between the action, stealth, time in HQ, and cutscenes at such a fast pace, that it never feels dull for a moment. Because of this, I found myself playing for longer sessions than I normally do. Just when things are about to get dull, a giant Nazi robot will probably attack. Just when you're probably about to get burnt out from too much shooting, the game is probably just about to slow down for dialog. I really wish a lot more games tried harder to achieve good pacing, as it really makes the entire game much more enjoyable. It allows you to experience pieces of the game in enjoyable bursts, rather than dragging on to the point of boredom.
All in all, I can't really see this game disappointing any fan of shooters of action games in general. Unless over the top gore isn't your thing, absolutely play this.

Once I started, I was obsessed with it and hardly played anything else until I completed it.  The ending was not only satisfying, it kind of blew me away.

The game has serious problems with toxic community, in the game and out of it on the forum. We are still not sure how to protect ourselves in it and fully enjoy the game yet.

Its in Early Access and its lacking lots of features, amongst them for example is a working bipod. Also lots of people play the game without a microphone, you will have a hard time playing with these kind of people, so its imperative that you play this game with your friends to fully enjoy it and be effective in combat. That being said, big clans in this community recruit people en masse which means they lack the skill and are incompetent in combat, you might aswell open your own small unit like we did you will be much more effective.
Promised vehicles/kits from Kickstarter might never happen, like Jets and Sniper kits.
Because of all this, I would rate Squad (Early Access) to 6/10 at best. Would not recommend it for anybody yet. I would recommend you to wait until Full Release until more features comes out and maybe then community as a whole will mature aswell. That being said with couple of fixes and new updates rating I would easily rate it 7/10, also Squad offers no game can offer so far except Project Reality. If the goals of 50v50 combined arms warfare are once achieved, Squad might become a dream game.

Castle Crashers seeks to give level-based brawler action with heavy multiplayer emphasis and "comedy". I can't help but cringe as I use that last word. Firstly, the mechanics are pretty solid and overall smooth. There are some exceptions:
-Vertical movement has the typical brawler problem of being 2x slower than horizontal, making it a chore
-Horizontal jumping doesn't keep enough momentum to feel tight
-Hitboxes feel a bit odd before you're used to them
-No actually good combo strings so attacks feel very basic and repetitive throughout the game
Otherwise, the controls and physics seem to pan out well. The graphical style is...2001 Newgrounds flash game. It's really quite bad and its only saving grace is that there are a few vector layers on each sprite for lights and shadow which flash games hadn't evolved yet. They opted for a more cartoonish storybook feel seemingly to fit the..."c-o-m-e-d-y" but it falls flat and feels like an excuse to be lazy.
Much of the humor in the game relies on poop, fart, college frat jokes and having women be creepily fought over for kisses...which they have seemingly no say in. The game includes many references to popular culture, which can rub many people the wrong way.
The game does enough to keep things fresh and alive by having many different knights with different powers, which you don't really get to use unless you put points into that special stat (whoops!). There are many findable secrets that include useful pets and weapons.
If you're looking for a couch co-op game with some secrets and difficulty, but don't care too much if it has flat humor and ugly visuals, give Crashers a try you ♥♥♥♥ing noob.

This game is truly AWESOME. Besides some obvious similarieties with Portal / Portal 2 (some mechanical aspects of puzzle solving), The Talos Principle has much more to offer. It is not about just puzzle solving and collecting sigils. This is not just gathering corrupted fragments of information from somehow corrupted database. The gameplay is non-linear - you feel stuck with one puzzle - go and solve another one! In another worldhub, with different items, or just hang around and enjoy the view.
The best aspect about this game is exploring the mysteries hidden behind collecting sigils.  'what happend to mankind? what is it all about, what is the purpose of solving this puzzles? what am I?'. Conversations with Milton (...a computer program? or not?) I've never quite worked out what to make of Max Payne 3. It's a really curious game. Almost like, I dunno, it's showing off how good R* are at world building first and then there's some Max Payne stuff chucked in there later around that.
The thing is, when it works, it's absolutely riveting and tremendous. Both the game and the story get off to a really slow and shaky start. You spend more time watching Max Payne 3 than you do playing it for way, way too long. Short firefights punctuated by lots of story punctuated by short firefights punctuated by lots of story. It can be really, really frustrating too. But at some point, it kinda settles into a happier (OK, happy is not a word I should really use when it comes to Max Payne) groove.
Then there's the favela which is an incredibly showy-off walking simulator wedged in the middle of an AAA game about shooting people in the head in slow motion whilst muttering about your pills. It's a glimpse into a universe where AAA doesn't rely on shooting people in the face but it's also, again, a guided tour of R*'s DVD collection the way it's pieced together. And that's sort of OK, I guess because it wouldn't -be- R* without that.
And after that, it starts letting you play the game proper. The balance between cut scene and videogame sorts itself out and the little frustrating bits of shooting it let you do before finally transition into longer firefights where it feels absolutely properly tense and urgent.
There's a few missed beats in the story. Sometimes things are a bit too grim and dark and slip into violence for violence's sake to shock you through the face and show you how nasty the people you're up against are but y'know, videogames and the tone is all over the shop. Like someone truly believes it's a sort of Tarantino does film noir but no-one told them that most of the time, Tarantino isn't realllly something to aspire to unless you've got a thing for feet and celebrity.
But then it all comes together in the airport and I'm on the edge of my seat, running through this level, glass shattering everywhere, bullets flying left and right and the game gets the bullet ballet bang on. There's a ACTION BLOCKBUSTER ending to it too and then you're left with that sort of wow, that was actually fantastic sensation for a while until it sinks in that for about 7 hours of the game, you were mainly watching a guided tour of someone's DVD collection and... why couldn't I play more? Why couldn't I step a bit to the left without the game killing me off? But OK, those shader effects are incredible so maybe I can forgive it?
Weird game. I'd absolutely recommend playing it through because if nothing else, only Left4Dead has more muttering about pills in it.

Planetside 2 is... in simple terms, a very solid and entertaining free to play FPS game.
Pros:
+Solid weapon variety, yet, almost all weapons are side-grades or specializations, meaning you're not at any disadvantage just because you're using starting gear.
+Alright faction flavor, unfortunately a bit watered down for reasons I'll get to later.
+Reasonable weapon customization options, typically allowing you to specialize a weapon towards either hipfiring or aiming down the sights, then with some weapons shifting their damage profile towards close range or long range focus.
+Very good design on ground vehicles, other than the ATVs that can mount weapons and cloak they all feel rather fun to fight against or alongside, or to drive and gun yourself. They look nice too.
+The game rewards teamwork strongly and has good mechanics for implementing it, you can even just jump into a random squad by pressing 'insert' at any time if you're playing solo. Solo play is entirely workable in my opinion as well, but requires more map awareness.
+Massive battles, during busy hours there can be multiple 100v100 fights going on around the very large map.
Cons:
-The faction flavor is slightly watered down by the presence of Nanite Systems (adaptation of the abbreviation for "Non Empire Specific or Non Specific" weapons) guns. I would describe these as "Call of Duty guns" to properly capture their role in the game. They're bland, generic, overly easy to use, and sometimes even outright better than their Empire Specific counterparts (mostly unintentionally on the last point). Unfortunately the developers had commissioned the models for these weapons at quite an expense a long time ago, so they're basically stuck implementing and keeping them.
-Reasonably high system requirements. Really this isn't a surprise, this is a wargame with tremendous upper limits of players, vehicles, physically tracked projectiles, and so forth. However, I can run it on mid to high graphics with an i3 processor and a GTX 650 Ti, so it's definitely not "Arbitrarily unoptimized generic FPS game 2015-16"
-The "Air Game"** is entirely isolated and poorly balanced against the rest of the gameplay. Your experience with it if you don't fly yourself will pretty much just be getting insta-gibbed by rocket pods from Empire Specific Fighters when on foot and 1 to 2 shot no matter what vehicle you're in by the Liberator Gunship's Dalton Cannon. the Rocket Pods are an extremely spammable and extremely high capacity explosive weapon with a wide blast radius while the Dalton (main gun) and Tank Buster (nose gun) for the Liberator can kill vehicles before they can even begin to react then the Lib can fly away with impunity. As for your options against air when not in an air vehicle? There's the "Skyguard" for Lightning tanks(which are killed casually by liberators) that can very slowly plink away at an air vehicle's health and maybe kill it if the pilot is asleep and there's two or more Skyguard lightnings around. There's also Bursters for the MAX units, which are armored exoskeletons that cost resources to pull. Same story as the Skyguard. The most effective option is an anti-air rocket launcher for the Heavy Assault, which costs you a fair deal of effectiveness against ground armor in exchange for maybe killing an ESF or Valkyrie(small transports) if there's multiple HA's around or the pilot sits still instead of fleeing, and no chance of killing Liberators or Galaxies(dropships).
**No I don't have any solutions to this, limiting the ammo capacity of certain air vehicle weapons further would probably help, but might be too harsh.
Advice to new players:
1)It's not your gun, it's you. Spending certs(xp) on new guns won't really improve your play early on, as the guns other than the starting ones are often /harder/ to use. Exception: the NC default LMG, the Gauss Saw, is a nightmare for newbies, get the cheap small LMG, it's comparable in DPS and easier to handle.
2)SPEND CERTS ON CLASS FEATURES AND UTILITY ITEMS. I am dead serious about this, your biggest jump in effectiveness will come from building a class specialized to your playstyle from the available traits, utility items, and so forth.
3) Find a gun sight from your current faction you like and stick with it. Ironsights are alright but a gunsight that fits your awareness and preferred combat range will definitely improve your staying power. Generally all sights from 1x to 4x are available across most guns (you have to cert it for each gun though, but they're cheap), then there's a separate set of 6x to 12x for some sniper rifles.
4) Find cover, first, and always. Planetside 2 is a brutally lethal FPS and if you get flanked or caught out while sprinting your odds of survival are very low if you try to stop and fight. Find cover, let your shields recover, and ambush them as they chase you or try to get around the enemy.
The Factions:
The New Conglomerate(NC) are miners, laborers, and other "lower class" employees fighting to free Auraxium (the planet of the game's setting) from the Terran Republic, their gear is modeled after repurposed industrial equipment and 'locally' designed and produced firearms. Big emphasis on shotguns. Their Empire Specific vehicles and weapons tend to be bulky, sturdy, and hard-hitting as a rule.
The Vanu Sovereignty(VS) are the scientists and engineers, nominally those of the original expeditions to Auraxium and their gear reflects it, focusing on energy weapons and hover technology. They practically worship the alien precursor species referred to as Vanu, who they obviously named themselves after. Their vehicles and weapons tend to focus on mobility, quick reloads, and so forth.
The Terran Republic(TR) could be seen as the Big Bad Imperials or the guys just trying to keep everything together, depending on your take on it. They use very classical military doctrine and equipment, their weapons focusing on high fire rate with simple ammunition with an emphasis on miniguns. Their Main Battle Tank has one of the more interesting gimmicks in that it can 'lock down' to increase its fire rate and shell velocity at a cost of mobility.
Old school gamers should never miss that great game.

Civilization can progress as long as previous achievements are not forgotten.
To prevent regression, we need backup. Archives. Libraries.
Archives are not perfect, so we need backups of backups. Many archives, many libraries.
A diary is like a time capsule. It can preserve individual lessons learned. A personal backup, a personal archive.
Quote:
Eternity may only be attained by serving a purpose greater than yourself.
All else is decay.

When I played the Project Reality mod way back when it came out, I preferred BF2 over it, so I never really gave it a chance. I've come to really love realistic shooters like Red Orchestra/Rising Storm, ArmA 2/3, Insurgency, and games that require a lot of team coordination like the recent Rainbow 6: Siege or Dota2.
Squad is a game that has many of those team elements, along with the brutal firefights and cheapness of life that comes with great realistic FPS games.
I didn't really play Project Reality in the day, so I will review Squad without the rose-tinted glasses that many here seem to be circle-jerking about.
It has some problems running well, and anyone who says otherwise is not telling you the whole truth. On the highest settings I consistently got below 60 fps, despite the Auto Setup recommending them as well as a higher resolution than my native one, downscaled. Even after tweaking them, it still dipped below 60 fairly often, and the lowest possible settings gained me a mere 10 fps on average from my tweaked settings, likely indicating it was not a graphical problem on my end.
From an audio standpoint, I believe Insurgency to be one of the finest examples of sound design in an FPS. Currently, I would consider Squad to be of lesser quality (keep in mind this game is still in alpha), and it could stand to gain from the signature crack of a bullet passing by you, and some other minor improvements to add to the experience.
As for the teamwork in the game, it's absolutely required to somewhat participate with your squad. I played a match where the squad leaders didn't communicate with eachother or their squad members, and we got wiped out with a nearly 200 ticket advantage (we lost 300 guys while they only lost 120ish). You see similar stomps in Insurgency or Red Orchestra as well when there is no team coordination and I absolutely love that aspect of Squad, mostly because it goes into more depth. Defending, for example, can be bolstered by building actual defenses and setting up new spawn points, which requires multiple members of a squad to participate.
But that's not to say a lone wolf can't do anything. I find its actually better to have people, especially single persons, to roam around and flank similar to Rainbow 6: Siege. Doing so in coordinated groups usually gets spotted, whereas I often found myself netting multiple kills, and on several occasions wiping out an entire squad, by going it alone. But I still needed my team to bunker down and hold a fort in order for me to do so. Thus Squad straddles the line between participating in the team when it suits you, and doing your own thing when it would benefit you more to lone wolf.
Currently my biggest complaint is that the pacing has always been slow, and it's the same complaint I had with the ArmA series. Even in extremely tense, close range scenarios, Squad progresses at a slow pace. My most adrenaline-filled moments were my flanking maneuvers with and without teammates, in order to quickly get around and attack the enemy. These moments, while certainly not dull, are nowhere near as exciting as say, CS:GO or Insurgency can be. But this doesn't detract from the fun, and for most it will have no impact at all. For me, it merely limits it. A slow drip of an addicting drug rather than a full dose, and who am I to complain about that?
Squad is a great tactical shooter in its own rights. The team aspects to it are phenomenal, unlike any other shooter I've played. It lacks the performance of a game that's seen many years of development, and the polish that such a game would receive, but that is what an alpha is for. Squad has incredible potential, and while I personally would prefer to leave the vehicles out of the game (as they tend to make for slower paced games in general), I await their arrival.
If you like realistic FPSs, Squad is a must-have.

I wasn't sure what to expect when I first started playing Woldenstein: The New Order.  Was it going to be a average shooter with a B-grade personality?  Honestly, I would classify this as a Above-average shooter with some B-movie elements, but there is heart and thought as well.  The shooting is good, and the gameplay is classic FPS.  It is a linear experience, however, the game does allow you to be creative in your Nazi killing.  Personally, I generally liked the Stealthy assassin approach, but the fact that it allows this approach at all is a positive.  What really surprises me is how relfective, and thoughtful the story actually is.  Instead of just concentrating on Nazis on the moon, and other Alt-history fun with technology, you get a feeling of what it would be life under Nazi rule had they won.  Spoiler, it's bad.  It is a dark game, and it says something about sacrifice, the damage done to soldiers because of war, and the horrors that the Nazi are capable.  It was a more emotional game than I expected and that takes a good shooter to a great one.  Do yourself a favor and get this game on a sale, and kill some Nazis....

This is one of the best puzzle games I
played.
The game's puzzles focus on a few mechanics at first. They are more or less easy to solve and
you collect sigils to unlock the next levels. But as you proceed the puzzles get more challenging.
Also you unlock new items to solve some of them. For me they never got boring.
The atmosphere in this game is great. The music calms you down and fits the environments very well.
I bought the soundtrack too. <3
And one of the most interesting things the game has to offer, is the story.
It is told by some terminals you find at the beginnings of the levels or sometimes hidden within them.
They store some texts and also a programm that "speaks" to you.
In this dialogues you are faced by some very interesting thoughts and are asked questions which aren't allways easy to answer.
So if you like philosophic stuff, you shouldn't pass them by.
Though, if you aren't interested in the story... you can just ignore it. You never
to read it.
At last there are also a lot of secrets hidden inside the levels. And stars, which you can collect by solving extra puzzles, which are nearly allways really hard and different to solve than the others.
So based on the stars you collected, or the choice you make when you solved everything, there are also 3 endings!
But don't be afraid. As soon as you colleted the last sigil, all endings are available without playing the whole game again :D
The game is totally worth its price. I played it 37 hours to find and unlock everything, which is way more than some AAA titles offer.
I had much fun and I definitely will play it again. °^°

Where do I even begin? The Talos Principle is phenomenal. It excels at everything it attempts. The visuals, soundtrack (and other audio), voicing, puzzles, pacing, all of it exceeded my expectations.
At its heart, The Talos Principle is a puzzle game. In first (or third) person, you move objects, open paths, and manipulate objects in order to solve the puzzles. But where you are as you do this, why you do it, what you're really doing; the interesting parts of The Talos Principle aren't really the puzzles.
The puzzles are fantastic. The Talos Principle starts you off slowly, allowing you to experiment and learn the mechanics at a simpler pace/level. The different areas of the hub provide varied levels of difficulty which give the game a nice curve.
The score and voicing in The Talos Principle are sublime. The moods set by the soundtrack are fantastic and the voice acting does exactly what it sets out to do. I would be more descriptive, however I wish to avoid any amount of spoilers.
Overall, this is a game that somehow was completely overlooked by most of the media I've followed (and myself, until more recently) yet shines brighter than most AAA games, and really nails its goals. Comparisons between this game and Portal are not entirely wrong, as both have "puzzle rooms" and some similar mechanics (moving boxes around, "puzzle enemies", etc). That said, I feel like this game has left more of an impact/impression on me than Portal 1 or 2 ever did, and that's coming from someone who put hours and hours into Portal 1's trials.
This game is a fantastic puzzler and much deeper than first glances would hint. Get it and enjoy!

TLDR near the bottom of my review!
The Talos Principle, as you can probably tell from all of the other reviews, is a puzzle game that adds philosophy into the mix. The puzzles are very much like Portal and other games like that, but they still provide a decent, and sometimes frustrating, challenge. Not to mention the beautiful graphics. Jamming electric walls, connecting lasers, fans and boxes, this game has it all. The philosophy, however, is where this game really flies.
Every now and then, you'll see some computer terminals scattered around the levels. These terminals contain 3 "documents" each, and these documents contain some ideas and concepts that are very interesting to think about. The documents also give insight into the "story." Sure, it's a lot of reading (Okay, A LOT of reading) but if you read all of the documents you come across, you'll have a much better time with this game. Every so often you'll even get to "talk" to the computer about certain philosophical principles, very much like talking to an actual person. Each dialogue choice you get represents a different way of thinking. Only a few times I was disappointed by the dialogue choices I had. Every time it gives you a decision, I legitimately thought about it, not just a "Eh, let's do this," but a "Okay, let me think about this for a minute," decision. Overall, this game is a must have if you enjoy puzzles or philosophy. Even if you don't, give this game a try. It is definitely worth the time and money.
The only bad part about this game is the hint system. You don't unlock the hints until the later game, and it's about 20 minutes of work for one hint that probably isn't helpful.
TLDR:
Pros: Great puzzles, great graphics, great narrative, debate philosophy with a computer.
Cons: A little too much reading, bad hint system.

America, ♥♥♥♥ YEAH!  That sums this game up.   Utter ridiculous and over the top, sometimes venturing into really dark areas that'll make you go squirm but all in service to the story that Nazi's won WWII and spread their brand of cruelty around the world.
It's clear throughout that Naughty Dog's Uncharted games served as inspiration for developers here.  Gameplay is extremely immersive and some moments like climbing walls while shooting people at windows, or climbing through train wreckage on a bridge will give you a real fear of falling.  Like Uncharted, cut-scenes are rendered in the game engine and are seemless, there's some great acting and facial animation though the German accents at beginning seem a bit....uneven..
Although the game is fairly linear, as expected, areas often have multiple ways to get from A to B as they would in real life.  In fact, the design of buildings, especially interiors, are clearly modeled upon real actual buildings and prisons.  There's a lot of georgeous architecture to explore.
Audio in this title is some of the best I've experienced in a game yet.  The audio engine does a remarkable job giving you an authentic sense of the space you are in and where every sound is coming from, including through walls or many floors away.  You will listen carefully for voices, breathing and footsteps to gauge where enemies are.
Like the Uncharted games and recent Tomb Raider games, this game is like a rollercoaster that occasionally hurls you into some pretty intense action with moments of glorious visuals in between (abandoned hangar, the Nazi Space Museum, etc).  Definitely one worth getting.
