If you're looking for a free game that's actually worth playing (which is really quite challenging) you've found it.
The graphics and sound effects are faultless, which considering some of the big names that run it, is unsurprising.
There are a few issues with gameplay such as the massively imbalanced teams and the flawed 'shuffle teams' vote system (Which requires both the winning and losing teams to vote yes in order for the teams to be shuffled, and why on Earth would the winning team shuffle and jeapordise their easy shot at victory? The developers could solve this issue by making only the losing team allowed to vote for a successful team shuffle)
Other than that, there's a nice selection of characters you can choose to set-up a nice team to match your play style, although some are much more powerful than others and you'll definitely end up using the same characters as everybody else eventually. Some balancing is needed there.
For the first few days I had brilliant fun on Dirty Bomb and would definitely recommend it, though after around 20 hours of gameplay it started to lag. I have high speed gaming internet and I play the game on minimal detail for maximum efficiency and a minor advantage. (The system I run could definitely play on higher details, but I find that maximal framerate is always a bonus when playing fast-paced multiplayer action)
Even after uninstalling and reinstalling the game (in case it was related to the game cache or something) I couldn't solve this issue. My character skips around a metre or two every 3-5 seconds which is probably the servers attempt at correcting my ping (Never over 30ms) but when faced with a team of enemies firing at you, finding yourself unintentionally skipping face-first into a wall is not the best option.
For that reason, the game is no longer playable for me.
It was fun while it lasted.
It may be hard right at the get go, but later it gets really, really fun to play!

A multiplayer game of truly staggering proportions, Planetside 2 thrusts players into a chaotic, three-way battlefield between three factions stranded on an alien, but habitable, planet, Auraxis. The red-clad ranks of the Terran Republic fight to bring order to the chaotic planet by any means necessary, usually with high capacity magazines and blistering rates of fire. The New Conglomerate unites mega-corp funded mercenaries and ragtag armies of workers turned soldiers to liberate Auraxis regardless of cost, present or future. Their armies of blue wage war with powerful, but bulky and slow firing guns from the giants of industry. The Vanu Sovereignty, enamored by the ancient Vanu and their technology, seek to uplift the denizens of Auraxis. Forcibly, with the aid of laser and purple, if need be.
The learning curve is steep, with little to aid newcomers besides a lackluster tutorial and poorly managed starter continent. Many FPS concepts, most notably dying, must be relearned to make the most of Planetside 2's common 48+ vs. 48+ player warzones. Teamwork is essential, as is a balance of support, defense, and offense, for victory.
Progress is awarded with certification points, or 'certs'. These are the in-game currency and can be used to unlock new weapons and gear. However, things aren't cheap on Auraxis and it's worth figuring out your preferred playstyle and certing towards it.
Daybreak/Station cash, which can be purchased with real money, is also available, but is mostly used for buying cosmetics. However it can be used to purchase weaponry as well, should one want to avoid the grind.
Air and land vehicles throw some variety into combat. All in all the game does feel very Battlefront-ish, only way bigger.
It must be said Planetside 2 is not a game for the weak of computer. The sheer scope of battles can make even hardy rigs chug. It is, however, free. So there's no harm in trying. Give it a shot.

I keep coming back to this game and playing it over and over, despite nothing really changing. It's very deep and open-ended, and it has entertained me greatly (including the DLC).
9.5/10
Pros:
-Nonlinear gameplay. Your goal is collect sigils which unlock additional areas, but the basic area is a free roam mode that is similar to something like GTA or even old Rareware games like Banjo-Kazooie and DK64.
-Puzzles are legitimately challenging. You must think outside of the box and the game does not spoon feed the solutions to you.
-Incredibly deep and philosophical ideas. This game just throws them at you and makes you question everything. Most of this is done via your interaction with Milton, from the computer terminals. The choices you make to answer his questions do affect your further conversations throughout the game.
-Multiple endings based on your choices.
-Lots of extra content, secrets, easter eggs, and hints/leads to keep you guessing and searching for more.
-Overarching story is very fun to uncover and seems very relevant to the real world.
Cons:
-The save system is pretty shabby, currently. Maybe it'll get updated in the future, but it is based off of autosaves prompted when you enter/leave certain areas, and you cannot control that. The backup only goes up to 10 or so, and so if you pass 10 checkpoints on your way to check out one thing, you cannot go back. Seems pretty arbitrary.
-Some of the nuances of the puzzle piece interactions can be kind of hard to uncover, such as being able to put a box on a jammed mine or being able to jam fans. This is ultimately good, because it makes the puzzles more challenging, but there were a small handful of instances in which it felt unnecessary.
-There is a recording mechanic that is used to solve puzzles, and there is no option to just "play again" for the recording. This gets really tedious for some of the later puzzles.
-The block puzzles (in which you fit the sigils onto a board) was the only part of the game that I found to not be fun. They are easy enough at the beginning, but the ones towards the latter half of the game are quite difficult and I think that they ruin the mood.
-Graphics are pretty damn good, but some of the textures are really poorly designed when you get up close. They seem even more out of place in comparison to some of the very good textures in the game.
-Audio will consistently lag/stutter when you alt-tab back into the game.
-Price.
Overall: incredible game and incredible experience. Try to get it on sale, though.

America, ♥♥♥♥ YEAH!  That sums this game up.   Utter ridiculous and over the top, sometimes venturing into really dark areas that'll make you go squirm but all in service to the story that Nazi's won WWII and spread their brand of cruelty around the world.
It's clear throughout that Naughty Dog's Uncharted games served as inspiration for developers here.  Gameplay is extremely immersive and some moments like climbing walls while shooting people at windows, or climbing through train wreckage on a bridge will give you a real fear of falling.  Like Uncharted, cut-scenes are rendered in the game engine and are seemless, there's some great acting and facial animation though the German accents at beginning seem a bit....uneven..
Although the game is fairly linear, as expected, areas often have multiple ways to get from A to B as they would in real life.  In fact, the design of buildings, especially interiors, are clearly modeled upon real actual buildings and prisons.  There's a lot of georgeous architecture to explore.
Audio in this title is some of the best I've experienced in a game yet.  The audio engine does a remarkable job giving you an authentic sense of the space you are in and where every sound is coming from, including through walls or many floors away.  You will listen carefully for voices, breathing and footsteps to gauge where enemies are.
Like the Uncharted games and recent Tomb Raider games, this game is like a rollercoaster that occasionally hurls you into some pretty intense action with moments of glorious visuals in between (abandoned hangar, the Nazi Space Museum, etc).  Definitely one worth getting.

The Talos principle is a first person puzzle game with a highly philosophical story behind it. The gameplay involves moving around various objects, redirecting lasers, and using other tools to get the objective. I personally found the story to be one of the most engaging, thought provoking narratives I’ve ever seen in a game. If you express any interest in puzzle games or are looking for a deep engaging story I would advise picking this one up. As for my verdict; this is probably the best game I’ve played in the past few years 10/10.

Planetside 2 is an ambitious Free-2-Play game where you have a Planet (Huge map) with 3 factions fighting for control over its provinces, sounds good but unfortunately its just a really mundane shooter.
First off the community is dying, I remember when I first played it and we must of had at least 200 players all fighting each other over a field and it was ducking epic but now you'll be lucky to get 50 players fighting over a little building/area...Another major problem with the lack of players is that one faction always seems to be dominant, on the character menu it shows you the percentage of players currently playing in each faction and one faction always has about 5-10% more than the other factions making it horribly unfair at times. To make matters worse Planetside 2 is the type of game that
lots of people playing otherwise its just a huge map with nothing in it! The devs, Daybreak Games are the same guys that make H1Z1 so as you can imagine they've gone with the tactic of bleeding the small fanbase dry of money by making almost
a microtransaction but as far as I know they haven't made it Pay-2-Win.
The second and biggest problem is that Planetside 2 is a mundane shooter...Now I am
a fan of Battlefield but it does feel like this game is a bootleg of Battlefield. The weapons in this game all feel the same and sound like pea-shooters, the reloading animations also feel weak. unlock stuff but good luck with that.

I just 100% completed this game last night after 52 hours. That means all secret stars, all three endings and all main game sigils. I LOVED this game. You actually have to think about the deeper philosophy. Well I mean I think you could actually skip talking to MLA at all. That happens sometimes when the computer beeps after you complete a level, but I suppose you could just leave, haha. The story is actually totally optional, which kind of saddens me :( But anyways, you are clearly prompted to read and engage with the story and the characters and depth are all very compelling. MLA will ask you a question and then ask you to think about it and he leaves until next time, which is 1-2 hours of gameplay later. So whereas even deep games aren't really thought about by players or too many people in society, Talos Principle very much spotlights that side of the game, although again, still makes it optional.
There are MANY secrets in the game and easter eggs I have barely tapped into. The puzzles are a bit harder than other games I've played, perhaps on the level of difficulty of Jonathon Blow's Braid. I solved maybe 95% of Talos alone, but looked up hints or direct answers in a few across each part of the game. There is something deeply compelling about this game that drives you to explore and learn more about what ends up being a fantastic story. The first world in fact I restarted the game because I had a hypothesis on how to unlock the first star :P I was wrong, but that's ok. Luckily, the game auto creates about 10 segmented saves so you can quickly jump around play sessions or load the previous game to play the different endings, if you get more than the two main ones ;)
Puzzles are way out of the box. Even the normal puzzles might have you spontaneously guess new mechanics by becoming the scientist we all (hopefully) are or were as kids. The first major star puzzle like this feels a bit cheap when you figure out the solution, BUT that gives you the base knowledge to then expand and solve even more complex and insane puzzles later. Some stars or easter eggs are just insanely deep and took me an hour extra work BEYOND finding all sigils on a level....but they are totally worth it. In one level, you can even get a jetpack to fly around in! Which further might lead to round 2 of that level's secrets :P The complexity of some puzzles also makes me think of Fez, which when I saw the solutions to some of those puzzles, I think my jaw hit the floor and "Turn Down For What" style broke through all previous floors haha. All I'll say is you need general cross skill knowledge in order to make the kinds of connection needed haha. And the extra puzzles are all across the charts. I know Team Meat, from Super Meat Boy, would argue best games teach all mechanics, but I think there is an exception for puzzle games. Sure, it might alienate many mainstream or new gamers, but it adds that much more challenge for those of us up for it.

I just 100% completed this game last night after 52 hours. That means all secret stars, all three endings and all main game sigils. I LOVED this game. You actually have to think about the deeper philosophy. Well I mean I think you could actually skip talking to MLA at all. That happens sometimes when the computer beeps after you complete a level, but I suppose you could just leave, haha. The story is actually totally optional, which kind of saddens me :( But anyways, you are clearly prompted to read and engage with the story and the characters and depth are all very compelling. MLA will ask you a question and then ask you to think about it and he leaves until next time, which is 1-2 hours of gameplay later. So whereas even deep games aren't really thought about by players or too many people in society, Talos Principle very much spotlights that side of the game, although again, still makes it optional.
There are MANY secrets in the game and easter eggs I have barely tapped into. The puzzles are a bit harder than other games I've played, perhaps on the level of difficulty of Jonathon Blow's Braid. I solved maybe 95% of Talos alone, but looked up hints or direct answers in a few across each part of the game. There is something deeply compelling about this game that drives you to explore and learn more about what ends up being a fantastic story. The first world in fact I restarted the game because I had a hypothesis on how to unlock the first star :P I was wrong, but that's ok. Luckily, the game auto creates about 10 segmented saves so you can quickly jump around play sessions or load the previous game to play the different endings, if you get more than the two main ones ;)
Puzzles are way out of the box. Even the normal puzzles might have you spontaneously guess new mechanics by becoming the scientist we all (hopefully) are or were as kids. The first major star puzzle like this feels a bit cheap when you figure out the solution, BUT that gives you the base knowledge to then expand and solve even more complex and insane puzzles later. Some stars or easter eggs are just insanely deep and took me an hour extra work BEYOND finding all sigils on a level....but they are totally worth it. In one level, you can even get a jetpack to fly around in! Which further might lead to round 2 of that level's secrets :P The complexity of some puzzles also makes me think of Fez, which when I saw the solutions to some of those puzzles, I think my jaw hit the floor and "Turn Down For What" style broke through all previous floors haha. All I'll say is you need general cross skill knowledge in order to make the kinds of connection needed haha. And the extra puzzles are all across the charts. I know Team Meat, from Super Meat Boy, would argue best games teach all mechanics, but I think there is an exception for puzzle games. Sure, it might alienate many mainstream or new gamers, but it adds that much more challenge for those of us up for it.

There are no spoilers
in this review, although some easily predictable and present in every modern FPS' plot twists may be hinted. Worry not, you probably already knew that it will happen during the game even before you bought it.
It's not common to start reviewing a shooter by describing it's audio value but since you probably guessed, by the fact that I'm recommending this game, I'm going to start with this game's unquestionably best feature.
Wolfenstein taught me more about rhytm and synergy with audio background than
could begin to dream to do. Countless times I caught myself switching weapons so they would more appropriately fit whatever music was being played.
Fights felt satisfying after they ended, I stood there marvelling the destruction I just laid to Nazi troops and could still hear the music, that accompanied me during the most recent encounter, even though it did fade out already.
It made me feel brave, scared, unsure of the outcome of my actions. The last title that managed to achieve the same effect was
.
Voicework is executed well above today's average, newly introduced characters tend to stick to their native language for prolonged period of times that exceed the usual
scheme.
Topic and structure of conversations try to maintain a respectable level so listening to the dialogues and recordings, that you pick up along the way, is a pleasant experience and not a chore like in other popular titles that concentrate on shooting baddies while having the troublesome obligation to move the story forward in a spoken manner.
I'm not even sure if cutscenes are skippable or not since I have not even once tried to end them prematurely.
Sadly the quality of the story takes a slight dive during endgame. I do understand that helping Nazis to meet their maker using dual-wielded shotguns doesn't prepare great grounds for storytelling but I couldn't shrug the feeling that at some point story writer had a quick glance at Call of Duty's script and questionable decisions followed.
That's a touchy subject. Not because the game is ugly, quite the opposite - I tend to be very touchy when it comes to playing on lowered details because of the restrains of my current system specification. Usually I just don't do it at all but in this case I have made a mistake of giving Wolfenstein a shot for a couple of minutes just to see if I like the game even though the framerate wasn't good enough to call it enjoyable.
Unfortunately it charmed me so much that I decided to sacrifice a bit of image quality just so I could continue my battle against The Reich.
The surprising part was that while it looked slightly worse it didn't take away the pleasant feel of environment, enemies and explosions.
Amount of detail on unit models and levels is remarkable, even with lights and reflections reduced I was able to take pleasure in standing still and observing the complexity of various uniforms and armors.
Animations of both enemies and weapons feel very organic, what you see first behaves exactly the way you expected it to when you get to interact with it.
Enemies are different enough to keep you occupied and interested for the duration of the whole campaign. Consistency of their design and appropriateness in certain environments is also worth mentioning, the way they fit in aids the overall feeling of immersion.
Weapons have weight, at times you can almost feel it. Every gun has a few modes of firing and can be dual-wielded while having each one set to a different mode - think a machinegun in the left hand and a granade launcher in the right one for those
shots.
I'm sure that everyone will find a gun that will best suit their playstyle. My, by far favourite, tool of relieving whole Nazi squads from their duty was
(not the actual name) ripped from a carcass of a mechanical monstrosity just a few seconds ago.
On a related note: gore and violence, always a popular topic in articles, especially for non-gaming oriented audiences.
is violent, but not pointlessly, it excels in showing the practical side of killing with no remorse.
Death animations and close-up takedowns show not only
is happening at the moment but also
. Showing a soldier dying along with all the reasons he wouldn't walk any more or had a huge headache in the event that he somehow didn't die afterwards make an astonishing difference from just displaying a guy getting stabbed while casually patrolling the perimeter.
There's also dismemberment, it is a factor present in most of modern games that feature both humanoids and explosions at the same time, here it is done well enough to make you believe you just blew up a couple of german speaking guys and had
while doing so.
Wolfenstein presents a wide range of difficulties that can be changed at any time so everyone can enjoy it the way they like.
I've completed the whole playthrough on 4th out of 5 difficulty levels and while it felt properly hard and rewarded stealthy approach I see myself having another go on a lower setting to benefit from larger health pool and having the ability enjoy a run'n'gun playstyle that those weapons were clearly designed for.

The Talos Principle is a good game for people who were aching for a real puzzle challenge. With over 120 varied puzzles this game delivers for its hefty price of 45 euros. A little warning though, dedication is required.  Because this game uses only a limited set of elements to create its challenges, puzzles may start to look a lot alike before you're even half way. It  actually caused me to burn out on the game at first.  There were two things that kept me playing.
First, experimenting, exploration and trying to break the physics of the game is greatly rewarded. I have a knack for doing silly stuff in games when i'm burned out on the main and side quests. running, jumping and fooling around. Here I started to mess with the jump platforms. Could I jump over the walls of the puzzle area? Could I take stuff from the area with me? What would could I do with that? Surprisingly this  goofing  payed off. This game rewarded my  'efforts' by reaching extra sigils and easter eggs. It's great fun and adds to being really engaged in the story, because the exploration and easter eggs  give it more depth.
The story, and the way you experience it, was the next thing to keep my attention. I really like games that dare to pose questions to me as a player. Questions like for example: What makes someone human? or what is a soul? or what is  time? It makes the game 'stick' for me, because  thinking about it really really engages me more in the protagonist of the game. Here this works perfectly. You awake as the 'program/soul' of a clueless robot trying to find its way and purpose.  Robots are build for a task, right? But what is that task in this world without humans? What happened here anyway?
The experience of the game adds to the story. The tale of finding your purpose is one of many choices you have to make in 'life' and the feeling that comes with it. A feeling of never knowing you chose right. The Elohim voiceover (brilliantly done), messages and q&a's though the computer terminals and QR-codes were constantly trying to push me around. And when even the puzzles are trying to trick you, you know something is not right. I was always suspicious of who I could trust and what the results would be. Through this concept I really was engaged in the journey of the robot and it's search.
Are you looking for a game that puzzles you in more ways than one? This is it.

Simply put, this game is absolutely incredible. Currently there is nothing else like it out there.
People compare it to portal - in reality it is far superior and much, much deeper.

It is aimed at a mature audience through the driving story, and the concepts and the deep and meaningful points of views you discover on your journey. Futuristic sci-fi themed, the worlds are rich and vibrant, gameplay is smooth, intuitive and the music and voice overs are absolutely perfect. It will require good reasoning to solve all the puzzles, especially on your own.
If you play this game I highly recommend that you solve all the problems yourself, without looking at guides etc. Otherwise you lose most of the emotional rewards of this game (but you will still find it fun).
If you are scared of heights and have a good gaming setup, you are in for a treat! :)
It is fairly long, and depending on how good you are at solving puzzles may take longer.
Money extremely well spent. I hope there is a sequel!
On a final point, if more people played this game, and absorbed the deeper points it puts forward, then this world would be a hell of a lot better off. Unfourtunately, however, most of this world are still in Plato's cave. Let's hope his generation changes that.

TLDR: BUY IT NOW!!!!!
Extended Edition:
I love this game so much that I want to encourage as many people as possible to experience it.
Ill admit, I stated off as a doubter.  Going into this, I worried that it might be just another COD clone with a bare-bones story and under-developed, uninteresting characters, but the thought of killing Nazis on the moon with futuristic weapons was enticing enough for me to buy it - on sale.  Had I known how much I would have loved this game, I would have bought it at full price, these developers have earned my money!
First, let me tell you where the game really hits its stride: The First Chapter!  Most of the games I have played have a little bit of take-up while familiarizing the player with the game's mechanics, then get really fun down the road.  But not with Wolfenstein!!!  This game makes you feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥right out of the gates!  You are thrown straight into combat, even the opening scene feels intense, and it does this without skimping on the details about how to actually play the game.  Hands down, the best "tutorial" of any game I have ever played.  On the back half of the first chapter, there is a point where you are scaling the side of a castle and shooting Nazi's through windows when some music starts playing...  It was a soft bass guitar piece pared with rhythmic snapping reminiscent of of something from West Side Story.  I can only describe the composition as sounding sassy or playful, this juxtaposed against the seriousness of the setting made the game feel like it knew how ridiculous it was, but it also knew how much fun it was and that it was going to give you one hell of a ride.  It was at this point that I completely ditched any worries I had about the game, thinking to myself "♥♥♥♥ it!  This is going to be awesome!"
Wolfenstein is, mechanically speaking, without a doubt the most fun game I have ever played!  I can't point to any specific feature that made the game so much fun, but this was awesome.  The developers have created an action-packed masterpeice; there was never a dull moment and it never felt repetative.  Again, I dont know what they did, but they did it well!
The game has a fairly straight-forward plot with some twists and turns thrown in, but what makes this story special, is that this is one of the exceedingly rare cases where a story is executed so brilliantly as to live up to its fullest potential.  I will openly admit that I can be pretty snobby when it comes to plots, but I honestly cannot thing of a single thing that would improve this story.  The plot also packs quite an emotional punch; something that i was not expecting.
This game also does a great job of developing its characters and it doesn't waste time doing it.  Character dev. starts in the first chapter; conversations between squad mates clue you in to their relationships, and BJ's own thoughts further develop the other characters as well as giving you incite into his own personality. The rest of the characters are diverse and interesting, and getting to know them is a rewarding experience.
In conclusion: This game has everything!  Don't wait, get it now!

Wolfenstein: The New Order provides the perfect mix of action stealth and story. The gameplay is not centered around one form of combat, and allows the player to develop through perks (benefits gained by achieving certain tasks) which play style he or she prefers. Although the game allows the player a majority of the time to choose how to play the game, it does, at times, force the player to use the stealth system orthe fast paced action system. When this does happened it doesn't feel forced, but instead feels more like a fluid transition from one play style to the other.
The characters and cutscenes in Wolfenstein are interesting, exciting and have a certain depth to them that many modern fps games lack. The story has an underlying theme about the treatment of certain peoples during World War II, and although Nazi's never created giant robots they are god damn fun to kill, and each enemy is well-balanced. When playing on the hardest difficulty the levels require a certain sense of creativity to beat which makes the game even more fun.
The scenery in Wolfenstein is only okay, but what makes the graphics interesting and different is the rather subtle filter applied to it.
This is one of the best Fps games I've played and I have to say that it is definitely worth the price.

[Old review]Quick review - best gaming experience I've had in a long time and I remember when Doom was considered amazing.
This is a semi-realistic military sim/FPS, not an arcade shooter.  It requires team play and communications to coordinate with your squad and team.
Teams are balanced extremely well by requiring each squad (max 9 players) to choose from "kits" that are unique to each faction and define which weapons you have access to and how many are in play for each team.  Works really well, and most of the matches I've played have been really close.
To me, it feels a lot like ARMA3.  The biggest issue I had with ARMA3 was how much planning and setup went into playing multiplayer scenarios, and I rarely have time to do that.  This game allows you to jump on a server, coordinate with your mates and play a good, fun and exciting tactical combat game pretty quickly.
Regarding performance, I run a I7-950 @ 4.2ghz, 12gb RAM, GTX770 w/2GB VRAM and the game runs really smooth for me at high/epic settings.  It's early access with frequent updates, so your mileage may vary.
I'm really looking forward to playing this game as it evolves through development!  Keep up the great work devs!

score: 10/10 - masterpiece
similar games: The Swapper, Portal 2
target audience: fans of puzzle games, narrative games
Croteam, the devs of Serious Sam, deliver their masterpiece with "The Talos Principle", a game which does everything right, where you literaly see how much effort they put into this game, how much detail, how much love. Talos Principle is one of those games where you can safely say that it belongs to the best this artform has to offer. It´s a game only an indie developer with a very high budget could make. The Talos Principle is my game of the year 2014.
The base gameplay of Talos is classic puzzling. You have many different puzzle elements and you have many different levels. Like in "The Swapper" you can choose which puzzles you want to solve first, it has a more open level design than games like Portal 2. This means if you are stuck at a puzzle you can just leave it and come back later and because of this the game has a really good flow, because you have always something to do.
Most puzzles are in small areas, so you can quickly understand what you are supposed to do and there wasnt a single puzzle in the game where I had no idea what to do and I never had to look up something on a walkthrough. However there are sometimes really big puzzles where you first think "what the heck am I supposed to do", but these puzzles are designed in a way that at the beginning of the puzzles there is only 1 or 2 things you can do which dont really challenge you, but these things are there so you get used to the enviroment and dont feel completely lost. And these big puzzles are the really difficult ones where you feel really smart after you beat them.
The puzzles themselves are designed extremely well and their difficulty increases slowly but surely.
There are many more things you can do in this game, but those shouldnt affect your decision to purchase this game.
Even if the game doesnt have a huge narrative, constant cutscenes and tons of dialogue, I was always motivated to continue and eager to find out what this game was about. Not only is there a big mystery which you try to solve, in between you are confronted with philosophical questions where you have tons of choices to answer which lead to really interesting dialogues and I was thinking and guessing till the end of this game. It really makes you think, I mean REALLY, especially if you are someone who is interested in these kind of questions. If you are not though, these questions might get a little annoying at the end, but the nice thing is you dont have to do any of this.
This game has multiple endings and its one of the very very few games where having multiple endings makes sense, because they are not simply 3 different paths and you choose one. They are all connected and even if you get one ending, the others still matter in your story. At the end it was satisfying, interesting, thought provoking but also intense, even epic to a degree and it was nice to see how they created a climax for a puzzle game that works not only for its story but also for its gameplay.
There werent many voice actors for this game, but all of them did a great job, but there is also a lot of reading involved in this game which wasnt a problem for me and Im usually someone who skips notes and letters and stuff you find in other games.
"Wow this game is beautiful". thats what I thought many many times while playing this. Every "land" has its own theme which not only looks beatiful, but also fits to the "super"-theme of the game. What I mean is that these themes are not chosen randomly which they appear to be at first. Especially the conflict between the theme of the enviroment and the theme of the puzzle elements. This was something which I didnt like about the game at first, but after you get used to and understand that it makes sense this way I appreciated it.
This game is not only fun to play, fun to listen to and fun to explore but its also simply fun to look at, its gorgeous.
Very beatiful and fitting soundtrack. There is one track for every "land" and the tracks feel like they have been chosen very carefully. You will hear them a lot but they never get annoying, they actually make the puzzles even more fun because you can listen to great music while thinking about the solution to a puzzle or arguing about philosophical questions. Really impressive.
The graphics of this game are also really impressive. There are no loading screens, only when you start the game, you have EXTREMELY huge view distance, performance is extremely good on maximum settings, though my PC might be overkill. Almost every texture is tesselated which looks so good and there is some extremely impressive scenery, like really impressive where you will just say "Wow.".
The only gripe I have are the animations of the character you are controlling, they are a little bit stiff but when you play in first person mode (which I recommend) then you wont notice this anyway.

This is one of my all time favorite games ever.
I wasn't the biggest strategy fan before I played this, this is a crowning example of what the genre can be.
If you have not played it, I highly recommend you do, it is just so good.
I mean seriously when you're playing online with your friends building civilizations up to the peak of technology(as the game allows) and just launching wave after wave of soldiers at your enemies, until they finally give up and sit in the fetal position in the corner crying about how it wasn't fair that you completely decimated them, it's the best feeling, it's the feeling of knowing you are superior to them in every way.
Now there are different ways of playing this game, I generally go for the turtle technique, in that I build up a defensive wall that can be rivaled by no other, which basically means I build walls of guard towers and hide in my keep generating a mass army of paladins, champions, and cannons (I generally play the Franks), usually i survive till very well and then destroy everything when I feel the time is right to unleash hell, of course I mostly play with friends and we almost always play teams cause why not, and they usually just crush opponents while I take my time building up my perfect defenses before joining in on the war at the end.
Generally doing anything costs resources and while we don't usually have difficulty with most resoources certain maps will ♥♥♥♥ you and leave you shorthanded on basic stuff like wood and stone, no scratch that, you will always run out of wood and stone, but that is where the market comes in, and where you will be sure to never run out of gold as long as you have allies, you can buy everything you need which always costs more as you buy so you're guaranteed to get ripped off completely but when you have nearly 100,000 gold who gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥buy as much stone as you want.
Naturally there are other ways to win besides conquest, there is peaceful means such as building a wonder, which is as the name suggests is something like the 7 wonders of the world, and as such is a comparatively giant sized structure like a castle or cathedral or temple or such, that takes like 1000 each of wood stone and gold so it is pretty pricey, but once you near the end of a game you can make like 10 if you wanted to.
There are multiple difficulties, maps, races, and game types which can be randomized based on starting boosts, map size and such, which offer a lot of variation to what you can do. There are also a ton of mods for this game and dlc as well, and based on what I've seen of the most recent dlc it is well worth the cost.
Now you could be wondering what if I've never played an RTS before? What if I only play Turn-based Strategy like civ 5, is this game worth my time?
Honestly, that's entirely up to you, if is looks like you'll have fun, go ahead, like for instance I love this but I honestly didn't really care for the civ games, I like to be able to do whatever I like whenever, I don't like being constrained to doing everything one at a time or however amount i'm alloted per turn, it just feels boring to me and fairly unrealistic, for example I know that while I'm busy establishing my empire, my enemies are doing the same, I know they may attack me at any moment and I should be ready to face them at any time as it can happen any time and I don't have a moment where the game pauses for eveyone else while I spend 40 minutes deciding what to do.
So if you've sat through all my crap and have decided you want to give the game a try, have fun, I always do. If you decided you want to pass that's cool too, no judgement from me, you do you.
If you'd rather not read all this crap and just skipped to the end, Game is fun very fun, still supported after being out over 10 years, and is a blast with friends, play it if you're interested in the RTS genre.
But seriously play it, you really wont be disappointed by it.

Honest and unbiased opinion after 70+ hours (not a pr fanboy... never played it)
Keep in mind this game is designed for realism so it is tailored to that crowd. Also it is still in Alpha.
The Good:
Squad/team mechanics - Ablsolutely love this. Rolls/weapons are limited to what you would actually find in a military unit..basically not everyone in the squad running around with light machine guns and optics (typical of arma groups).
Also the ability for squads to work together and coordinate attacks is just amazeballs.
Base Building (aka minecraft) - The ability to place and build a forward operating base pretty much anywhere on the map  to attack or defend is amazing. You can build items from hesco barriers to tire walls and even bunkers. Some people have gotten extremely creative with this ^^
Maps/Enviroment - Most of the current maps are expansive with a lot of different areas to discover. For those who have served overseas this game does a pretty good job of making you feel like you are actually over there. I know a few people who are Afghan vets that can vouche for the accuracy of content.
The Devs - These guys are awesome. They actually play matches with their fans and listen to what imput they have on the game to make it better.
Ammo - For once I found a game that doesnt automatically refill ammo on used magazines. Say you have two magazines on you. You get into a fight and use 27 out of 30 rounds after which you reload. That second magazine will only have three rounds left when you reload again. Also it does not have a ammo count anywhere on your hud.. make sure you keep track or you will run out when you need it most =)
NO THRID PERSON OR CROSSHAIR!!!! - Great for hardcore gamers!
The Bad:
Sound - While the sound of the weapons are close to accurate, there are currently a lot of glitches or dead spots where you lose all sound for a period of time. Also, there are delays in footsteps from your own character. (example: you are running and it sounds like your footsteps are way off behind you or in some other location. It should sound like you running not someone else)
Level Detail - Keep in mind this is a realism game so in order to facilitate this, they dont have as much detail as you normally would in a AAA title. That being said, the lack of objects or copy paste of certain areas does get kinda old.
Maps - this is suppose to be a realism game but there are no elevation markers of any kind on the map =/
Weapon balistics - little to no bullet drop, recoil is off on several weapons. (basic rifles have more kick than LMG on full auto - mind you this is in any position)
Vehicles - They have been taken out of the current build in order to make sure they are up to par with the rest of the game, however it does tend to make this feel somewhat of a walking simulator at times.
The Price - I do feel it is somewhat high for its current content.
Its Alpha - falling through the map, random kicks from server - lost connection
The Ugly:
IF you run AMD/ATI you will likely not be able to play this game at all or have severe gamebreaking issues if you do.
They know about this and are currently working on the issue - Unknown timeframe.
All in all I would rate this game (as an alpha) a 3.8 out of 5 stars.
That being said. I do recommend it if you like this style of game. Hope to see you on the battlefield soldier ^.~

For a game that lets you slaughter Brazilians by the truckload, I was surprised to see myself not enjoying the peruvian genocide as much as I should have. Not a single ONE of these World Cup rejects screamed "hue hue hue" or asked me to give them money, or threatened to report me. It was like being in a poor charicature of what Brazil would actually be like. Rude, poor people who smell funny were everywhere, true, but not a single Huskar or Bloodseeker in sight. Not only that, but the actual shooting itself just dragged on too long. The game didn't need to last 8 hours. Max Payne 2 lasted only 5 hours, but that was the most enjoyable because the game knew when it had done everything that could be done with itself and packed it in there. How many hundreds of times do I need to pop out of cover and shoot a ♥♥♥♥ing BR in his filthy burrito face until I've proven I can do it a hundred more times? I've passed the test, game. Making me do it more won't make me enjoy it more.
I don't usually say this, but what I enjoyed a lot about this game, and all Max Payne games, is the poetry. Not some pretentious metaphors about butterfly farts in an elevator, I mean the poetry set the mood for the game and painted a picture of the world I was in. Max doesn't have the dark humor he did in his first two games, but Rockstar was intent on keeping with the "brooding ex-cop woe is me I'm so sad all the time QQ" theme and took it as far as they could for better or for worse. Maybe next game they'll finally put Max out of his misery, and for the fifth game we'll get a CUH-RAZY protagonist like an old Dante, he would certainly fit the mood more for all the jumping around I do.

I will recommend this game with a "BUT" involved. This is simply put, your box of legos going to battle with each other with guns on a realistic terrain kind of map with about five different game modes from the start. For some you may find a learning curve in the game, for the more advanced gamer, you will find this a piece a cake other than your building skills and alloted amount of "cpu" to work with at your current level. (working off of a leveling system that dictates as to how many pieces of you can place on your device that you build keeping in mind that each piece will have different "cpu" rating. I enjoy the fact that you can just outright buy your premium membership (lifetime), or you can do a subscription (monthly), or obviously play for free. Playing for free you still gain items, at a slow rate of course, highly nerfed compared to premium users. Whether you are a free user or paid player (monthly or lifetime) ...any of these can purchase "crates" contianing more items to use to build. They are taking part with ABLEGAMERS so if you want to help out disabled kids and what not you can, I know I did. That package comes with 25 crates of goodies, and the rarity of items in the crates are fairly distributed considering what you pay. If you think smart with your build, you can get good use out of your build, but after about 700 cpu and up it starts feeling like you need an edge. Whether that be paying for something or making sacrifices in recyling your building blocks to turn into "dust" that can be used to buy other items in the "forge". Now... enough with my really descriptive review, let me get to the big BUT after at the time of this review I've had 38 hours solid of game play. Great game BUT one major issue game devs, I don't know how, and I don't really want to know how, but there is a major bug in the game that people are exploiting at the moment. Some sort of way of building causes a glitch to where only the gun is visible and the player is not. Also making it to where you can not attack said player so they are invincible. Wolfenstein: The New Order provides the perfect mix of action stealth and story. The gameplay is not centered around one form of combat, and allows the player to develop through perks (benefits gained by achieving certain tasks) which play style he or she prefers. Although the game allows the player a majority of the time to choose how to play the game, it does, at times, force the player to use the stealth system orthe fast paced action system. When this does happened it doesn't feel forced, but instead feels more like a fluid transition from one play style to the other.
The characters and cutscenes in Wolfenstein are interesting, exciting and have a certain depth to them that many modern fps games lack. The story has an underlying theme about the treatment of certain peoples during World War II, and although Nazi's never created giant robots they are god damn fun to kill, and each enemy is well-balanced. When playing on the hardest difficulty the levels require a certain sense of creativity to beat which makes the game even more fun.
The scenery in Wolfenstein is only okay, but what makes the graphics interesting and different is the rather subtle filter applied to it.
This is one of the best Fps games I've played and I have to say that it is definitely worth the price.

Talos is a greatly rewarding experience. It's a puzzle game mixing traditional logic challenges with modern, gorgeous 3D graphics and fantastic instrumental music. The plot doesn't get the centre stage but is interesting and has some non-linear twists that make it a joy to replay the game.
There are three main areas of the game connected with a hub (which is pretty big in itself). Each area has a distinctive theme: ancient Rome, ancient Egypt and medieval-like. The central hub is an ice desert / wasteland / mystery tower combination.
The player is sparingly guided by the voice of the mysterious ELOHIM who seem to have god-like properties. Without giving away the ending and revealing the truth behind the story I can say that the player is given subtle hints about the reality that he or she occupies.
I particularly liked conversations with the DOS-like library assistant. This is a mini-game in itself and a gem to those that enjoy a rich back story and a fair share of reading. This may not be a taste for everyone so don't feel discouraged as you can safely skip most of that if you want to.
The only thing I would like to see improved is to make the difficulty level of some levels more even. Especially in the later parts some very levels were next to rather easy ones (or perhaps I was just lucky?). Given the architecture of the game changing that might be difficult as levels interact with one another in non-obvious ways so I don't expect that to change much.
Pros:
- great game play with rewarding and interesting puzzles
- very good graphics, voice and music
- multiple endings
- lots of puzzles (nearly 140, if I recall correctly)
- game for all ages (no pointless violence)
Cons:
- some uneven puzzles
- some things are very hard to find without help
On the last negative item, I would argue that those hard-to-find elements are entirely optional and are a joy to find if you like that sort of fun.

Personally, Max Payne in his third game is pretty much like me: Everything that happens to him is because he's a drunkard. In this regard, I became quite related to him. The story is somewhat loose at some points, but Max saves the day with his "Charisma" (if he has any, hahaha)
The gameplay is rock-solid, and quite better than other console games (*cough* Last *cough* Of Us) The shooting feels precise using a 360 controller. Also, the bullet time effect after killing a wave of thugs is really dramatic.
On the visuals, I have no regrets, other than having this issue with Direct X 11. The game was running great with DX11, but when I came to my dad's house and used his Panasonic Flat Screen, the game crashed. Switching to DX9 solved the issue. I had no problems on my Samsun Flat TV back at home.
The sound is also quite good. I like the big cast of multi language voices you can find in the whole game.
And as of Reply-Value, the Multiplayer is an addictive TPS. It's kinda slow if you're used to the likes of Call of Duty or Battlefield, but I like it's pace since it let's you think on what to do next, where to run, who to shoot, etc. It also has a high level of customization for your character which ranges from weapons to clothes to ballistic vests. Have to say, People playing here on Steam are far more hardcore than those playing on Playstation 3, thus leading to a better Multiplayer experience in here Steam. Can't tell about those who play the game on 360, but I guess they're somewhat the same level than those on PS3.
On my opinion, this game was quite underrated. As for me, this is my favorite game from last console generation.

Excellent game!!  If you like Portal/Portal2, or Myst, you should enjoy Talos Principle.  As you play through higher levels, the puzzles include additional tools you need to use to solve them (and you have to unlock the tools, occasionally). You are truly interacting with an environment -- you can place objects wherever it is legal to place them.
On the negative side, some of the things you need to complete a puzzle are too well-hidden (at least for me) -- and I seriously doubt that if you didn't spend time crawling over every inch of the play area, walls, etc., that you'd ever find them.  Like a passage hidden in the shadow that you can't see -- you have to walk into it to know it's there.  Or the lever that's so well hidden behind bushes that until you get right on top of it, there's no way to see it.  Stuff like that. To me, it's very frustrating that I have to _find_ the puzzle, before I can _solve_ the puzzle.  And some of the "star" puzzles are so much of a stretch to figure out what the puzzle is, I think it would be impossible without help from the internet.
I haven't been able to determine the purpose of the computer terminals -- if it's just about back story, or if they have something to do with the puzzles.
Best comment I can give:  If these guys publish another game like this one, I'm most probably going to get it.

Well, this was certainly one of only a select AAA titles worth a damn this year (DA:I, Shadows of Mordor and Alien Isolation being the others), even if it did have a few annoying issues.
Story: Honestly, wasn't expecting as much as I got out of the story. It was kinda like the recent Shadow Warrior, in which I went into a shooter expecting all cheese and came out with a surprisingly decent story. The two main characters, Blaskowitz and Anya, are generally likeable. I like that BJ genuinely seems exhausted and worn down by everything that's happened, and his dialogue reflects that. Most the characters of the resistance are at first unlikeable, but then become genuinely sympathetic as you talk to them. I also like how they flesh out the world around you, a world in which everyone genuinely loves the Nazis and paints you as the terrorists. It creates this psuedo- I am Legend (the book) narrative where you're the monsters making everyone scared to leave their homes, but it's cool because they're Nazis. Unfortunately, it also leads to a massive plothole, which is that the game never really explains how killing the main bad guy is going to undo all this. The nazis have conquered every threat in the world and rule over (as the game points out) 75% of the world, and killing one dude isn't going to fix all that. Perhaps the story writers felt the same way, because the game ends without any closure, which annoyed me. I also didn't care for the choice at beginning, which changes a little bit of the story, because it feels like forced replayability, and I don't like that. Still, I did love the story, and only Transistor gave me a better one of those this year.
Gameplay: This was a bit of a sticking point to me. While the day I'm ungrateful at a chance to kill Nazis on the surface of the moon with dual laser machine guns is the day I officialy can't have fun anymore, the gameplay comes across as "Jack of all trades, master of none'. Do you want to run and gun, like Doom or the newer Shadow Warrior? Well, that's not an option, since limited ammo and the lethality of your enemies don't allow that playstyle to be viable. Do you want to use the stealth system to its max? That's not an option either, since you can only (at best) get 2 or 3 guys before everyone notices you. Do you want cover shooting? That's not completely an option either, since nazis spawn in from some weird places (half the time places you already cleared) to flush you out.
Since this is a Wolfenstein game and everyone talked up the shoot 'em up aspect, the moment the game gave me dual assault rifles, I went charging into battle expecting the good 'ol shooter. Instead, I got shredded, leaving me wondering why the game bothered to give me dual guns when I spent most of it leaning out from behind cover and only changing positions when I was getting flanked. A gameplay hint pointed out that I can tailor the guns and such to my playstyle, but there was only one playstyle: walk in, try to stealth kill as many people as possible, then gun a few down as you run for cover and stay there until everyone's dead. I think the issue is that the average footsoldier can slice off too much health and is too accurate, so guns blazing isn't an option. It may sound like I just don't like difficulty, but I've played the Souls series, beat Lunatic+ on Fire Emblem Awakening, and am going new game + on Shovel Knight. Difficulty doesn't bother me, it just feels like the enemies are too difficult for what the game is trying to do. Also, the environment was too dull up until the moon base, so it was occasionally difficult to see the nazis, who blended into the dull environment with equally dull uniforms. I just wish the game would've picked a lane and stuck with it, because it ended with the same exact playstyle through most of the game. The wide open environments were nice, but I couldn't ever make full use of them.  TLDR: it's a restrictive gameplay that clearly wants you to experiment but inherently doesn't allow you to. Still, at the end of the day, I'm shooting nazis with dual-wielded rapid fire lasers on the surface of the moon, what more can I want? I'm planning on restarting on the easiest difficulty, just so I can go Rambo everywhere like I originally wanted.
But seriously, if they're making another one, I hope they decide to let that hotwiring system die a fiery death. I spent most of my time with it hoping the wires rebound close enough that I could use the awkward controls to put them back together before the anemic time allotted reset it.
Technical: I'm running this on a computer from 2010, so I've learned to expect a few problems here and there until I sawp out the graphics card, but there were a few weird issues. First, I had to update the graphics driver, because the lip-synching during gameplay was all off. Once that was done, I came back in and the lip-synching during gameplay was still off. The game would freeze every once in a while, usually after I died, and I'd sit there staring at a black screen for a minute or two before it got back into the game. So there was nothing gamebreaking, but still annoying.
So at the end of the day, though the gameplay wasn't as great as everyone painted it to be, I still had fun, enjoyed the story and hope to see more shooters try to mix things up.

The Talos Principle is a great game in almost every aspect.
+ Stellar music, really fits in with the atmosphere.
+ A decent storyline, but most importantly the way it is presented rocks, (trying to keep it spoiler-free but I can say that it really encourages exploration and fuels your urge to find out more).
+ Intuitive, creative and challenging puzzles. It somehow manages to not feel repetitive or "grindy", even with over a hundred 3D puzzles in the game.
+ SO. MANY. SECRETS. Seriously, it feels like you are breaking the rules of the game, doing parkour and stuff, and then, can you believe it, there is a secret at the end. So well done.
+Visually stunning. Graphics are top-notch in my book and I really like the enviroments. The last world is especially great. Only thing I can complain about is that the lens flare in the desert is sometimes a little too intense. But then again, I suppose it would hurt your eyes to look at the sun in the desert..
+ If you go in blind, which you REALLY SHOULD, some moments are truly impactful. (Once again, keeping it spoiler-free)
+ Controls well with mouse and keyboard. Have not have any issues I can think of. One thing though, it would be great if some features were more clearly explained, like the fact that you can move connectors around while keeping their connected points by using "alternative use".
I do not have any direct complaints, since it feels like the devs really nailed what they were aiming for, but some suggestions.
- More worlds! The game is quite a time-sink if you go for 100% completion without any assistance, but the actual lenght of the thing is not really that long. Would love to see an update or DLC of some kind adding new areas.
- More story options. Not sure how it would work in practice, but having more options regarding your influence in the story would be really nice. (More endings maybe?)
In summary: Buy this as soon as you can, don't watch any videos, don't read any guides, and you will experience one of the best games of 2014.

About 20 hours to complete The Talos Principle. Actually felt a lot longer. Overall, I'd give it a recommendation if you think you could dig a little philosophical history mixed in with your puzzle action.
"About 20 hours" was arrived at after completing all of the official green, yellow, and red sigil puzzles on my own, and then following a guide to pick up the roughly half of the star sigils that I'd missed, as well as following a guide for the giant tower's puzzles. I cleared the "messenger" puzzles on my own, but I still haven't cleared the grey sigil puzzles. By volume, I'd say I solved 70% of the content on my own, followed a guide for 15%, and have another 15% to come back for.
The Talos Principle places you in the role of an artificial intelligence that has been placed in a world filled with puzzles. You're challenged to solve all the puzzles, with the promise of eternal life as a reward for successfully doing so. As you explore, the game exposes you to a variety of western philosophical ideas and ultimately gives you a brief primer on the history and development of western philosophy, more-or-less starting with the titular Talos Principle: that it does not matter what the philosopher believes, they cannot survive without their blood (a materialist argument). Along the way, the game also challenges the player to argue their own philosophical outlook, albeit from a prepared list of common ideas, and sadly even the "expanded" list of options is painfully lacking in nuance. That's the risk of asking someone what they believe.
As for the puzzles, I found them to be pretty enjoyable and well-balanced. The color-coded difficulty rating was pretty spot-on. The tools were varied and techniques for using them were applied very creatively. The puzzles rarely fell prey to irreversible mistakes, as well, which I found most pleasantly surprising; I appreciate how difficult that is to do, and there were very few puzzles I felt I needed to reset due to a mistake. The puzzles also seemed very resilient to cheating and exploitation. That means most of the puzzles have effectively one solution, but the "A ha!" moment from figuring them out is delightful.
In a few exceptional cases I felt like the "puzzle verbs" were unintuitive, and I only discovered them by accident or by following a guide to one of the star sigils. One generally does not think to balance a box on a sphere, for instance. I also developed a specific hate-boner for the hovering mines, but I feel that's a matter of personal preference, as I found them to be extremely nerve-wracking (there's even a mine-based puzzle in the game named "Nerve-Wracking").
In conclusion, this was a much better game than the highly-pretentious name and title art suggested, and now that I've completed the "quick and dirty" ending as well as the "true" ending, I plan to take my time finishing the grey sigil puzzles to get the "bonus on the side" ending.

Max Payne 3 does many things well, but it's severely crippled by several design flaws.
The worst offender: the cover system. It breaks the game entirely. The first two Max Payne games forced you to be constantly on the move to win, always running and gunning in order to move forward. You were rewarded for taking risks. MP3, by constrast, rewards you for crouching and hiding, forcing you to jump from cover to cover with brief snaps of bullet time. This is especially evident on harder difficulties, where you are often instantly killed just for poking your head out. This KILLS the fun that you should be having. Cover systems are all the rage nowadays and they can be done right, but this is just about the worst implementation I've seen.
The comic book style unfolding of the story is also gone, and for the worse. Instead we get blurred-out color-saturated cutscenes. LOTS of cutscenes. Seems like every door between shootouts is another cutscene. They get old fast, and the story and characters are not interesting enough to keep them from dragging.
MP3 can be fun at times, but I would not recommend it to anyone who has played the first two games - you will be disappointed.

From the "I hope you didn't waste 60 bucks on this" department.
I really like Wolfenstein. I played the hell out of RtCW, which had perhaps the greatest multiplayer component ever. Wolfenstein 2009 was so-so, but bearable. But this one is just bad.
Why? Sure it's a beautiful game with some nice combat and good visuals, but it utterly fails in the "tone" department.  The New Order has no idea what kind of game it is.  Is it a balls to the wall action thriller with comedic levels of Serious Sam style violence? Yes.  However, combined with this is a over the top, maudlin sort of story that is supposed to somehow convey to the audience the horrors of war through the medium of said comedic violence. The result is a mish-mash that is almost insulting to the actual victims of Nazi brutality.  You can't go from killing robotic dogs on a Nazi space station, glorying in the absurdity of the whole thing to a contrived concentration camp scene where you kill a mass murderer in the midst of a tearful flashback.  It's like it's a game that's throwing a rubber chicken at you and saying "waka waka" yet expecting you to feel like it's your poor little sister's pet hen that you should've saved from the slaughterhouse.
I feel like The New Order is just adolescent.  Still glorying in violence and guns and bombs, and yet because everyone else expects something adult, it has to throw in some Private Ryan style emotional overlay because without it it wouldn't get into AP english or something.

I went into Wolfenstein: The New Order with low expectations, and for the first 10 minutes or so, it was barely living up to them. The initial sequence didn't exactly sell me on the game, and I figured I was in for a good 6+ hours of thoroughly disinteresting trench warfare against wacky steampunk future Nazis.
Thankfully though, I kept playing through that less than stellar first impression. The New Order turned out to be an unexpectedly excellent title well worth picking up regardless of holiday or summer sale status.
The story is incredibly well written- though a bit heavy handed at times I still really enjoyed it. You have to make some really gut wrenching, gruesome decisions, and there are some scenes that will hit you right in the feels. The romantic aspect of it did seem a bit forced and sudden, but otherwise it was outstanding.
The level design is another part where this game shines- far too often I find myself playing FPS games with what are clearly "filler" levels. Not so here. While everything is pretty much linear, you don't feel like you're dragging yourself through 40 floors of some insufferably dull and long level to meet an arbitrary gameplay timer.
The combat is also pretty well sorted. Stealth is a refreshingly viable tactic- enemies do seem to be a bit on the slow side as far as spotting you goes, but the game flows easily between stealth and action. The officers that sound alarms and call reinforcements give you ample reason to sneak, but can also be dispatched via going in guns blazing. The AI isn't perfect, but enemies react believably to flanking and will try to flush you out of cover.
Also of note is the level to which the game has been polished- perhaps this was not so on release, but I found the entire game to be refreshingly bug free. Save for one awkward world seam in an early level and a single enemy ragdoll that proceeded to flop around and float through the air a bit before settling to the ground, I didn't see much worth writing home about in terms of QA lapses. The graphics and optimization show a similar level of attention to them, and things ran smoothly all throughout, even on max settings.
This isn't to say I don't have any complaints about the game, though. The dual wielding mechanic is profoundly useless in the initial phases of the game, and then becomes almost a necessity because the developers apparently subscribe to the doctrine that you can add challenge to a game by adding absurd amounts of extra health to enemies. It doesn't work, and it's just frustrating to have almost all your health stripped away by an enemy you had to empty two 45 round magazines into their face to kill.
Also, the whole "AHH SNEAKY NAZI!" being captured and stabbed repeatedly quicktime event is overused to a fault. I didn't count, but by the end of the game I'm pretty sure Ol' B.J. had taken at least 10 stab wounds to the lung/heart area and been "captured" 4-5 times. It doesn't really lessen my enjoyment of the game, but after a point it just seems kinda silly.
Overall, I'm going to file Wolfenstein: The New Order under the "pleasant surprises" column, and I'd highly advise that it deserves a second look if you're on the fence about getting it.

Let me start off with the first couple things I look for in a Free-to-play game:
Q: Is it pay to win?
A: Nope, plus everything can be bought with in-game currency.
Q: Crappy anti-cheat?
A: Recently implemented "Easy Anti Cheat", so I'm not sure. I haven't run into many hackers though.

Squad has good potential to become one of the best tactical shooters out there. The gunplay is on point and the teamwork fundamentals are there, but there is still something lacking.
For one, the game is unoptimized in its current state. That's forgivable given its alpha status but optimization should be something that must be fixed. By optimization, I don't mean framerate issues as I've had none. However, the game's graphics seem to be a bit funky; on lowest settings, everything seems to be pixelated past a certain distance which makes seeing enemies from long distances a difficult task. I remember getting shot from a hill but I was unable to spot the people firing due to the pixelization.
The game itself also lacks features in its current state. There are no vehicles which means traversing the map can be tedious and time-consuming. I'm not complaining as I'm all for realism but I wanted to let you know, the consumer, what you're getting with this version of the game.
Teamwork is great. I love hearing my teammates organizing a plan of attack because it really immerses me into the game. Everyone seems to be mature which is good to know. The less-patient players seem to be very few in this game which makes it all the better. Of course, don't expect every squad to be well organized as there are, as in every game, d-bags who try to ruin the game for everyone. If you're matched with people publicly, expect the worst.
Gunplay itself is wonderful. The guns sound amazing; they have the impact and crunch you'd expect from a gun. Bullets drop realistically and taking fire from weapons adds chromatic abrasion to your screen to simulate PTSD. You can switch from automatic to semi-automatic modes on your rifles.
Long story short: if you like infantry-based combat with a heavy emphasis on teamwork, get this game. Be mindful that you may never fire your weapon before dying and that dying costs your team tickets (which, when it gets to 0, causes your team to lose). If you prefer an action-packed shooter, skip this title. Not much action to be had...yet.
Rating for this alpha: 7/10. One of the better alphas out there, but not worth the $50 price tag in my opinion. Wait a year for the game's price to decrease as the dollar-per-hour rate of this game is not worth it just yet.

After playing all 3 games i'm kind of stuck on which one I like, so I figured i'd just do the 3rd one and maybe the others later on.
PROS:
Still feels like Max Payne: Even though Remedy isn't doing this game it still feels like it's actually Max Payne, still that gritty and amazing voice, all of those great lines he does, i'm glad Rockstar could actually capture how he is even though Remedy isn't doing it anymore.
Clues: Around the maps there are clues that can tell the story or show what has happened in certain areas, although some are a little odd, or don't make too much sense, but they are pretty neat to go around and try to find.
Golden Guns: If you roam around the maps and try to find golden parts for certain guns, you can get a golden gun which does more damage, and it can be pretty useful, although some are in some weird spots, or are just obvious and they aren't.
Great story: You will probably need to play the other games to know a little bit about Max's backstory in this game, there are a lot of references going back to older games, and this story is about how Max went from New Jersey into Brazil and him being a bodyguard for a rich family, and of course, knowing Max's luck, it never goes as well as he'd like.
Good sounding weapons: All of the weapons actually do some damage, and sound very gruesome too, even the pistols and really weak damaging guns actually sound like they are doing some damage.
Flashbacks: At certain points Max will have flashbacks to certain areas, these can be from when he was in Jersey to where he first got to Brazil, and seeing what had happened at these certain points to tell you more of the story that's unfolding.
CONS:
Waste of pills: I've realized this, as I was playing if you take pills normally you get half your health back, but if you have pills on you, get shot down into last stand mode, and kill the enemy that killed you, you get 3/4's of your health back, and waste a pill, so why the heII should I bother using the pills regularly and get less health back when I can kill them in last stand mode and get more health back, and then be invulnerable for a few seconds to get up and get into cover? I think they should have done it like this, if you get knocked into last stand mode, you use a pill, kill a guy, and you get half health, if you use a pill normally you get full health or 3/4's of your health back, making it to where it still feels like max payne and not stupid CoD.
Barely used Bullet Dodge: While I was playing I actually hardly used my bullet dodge, cause Max takes for f*%king ever to get back up and I ended up dieing from that, or dieing while in mid air dodging, so I figured "Why use bullet dodge if I can just sit behind cover and blind fire them, they end up dieing anyway..." I ended up clearing out most rooms just sitting against a wall and waiting for them to come over, that's not the Max Payne I know, the Max Payne I know was the one that could dodge and clear out a whole room in a few dodges or so, not sit in the corner and wait for everyone to come over.  Granted, he is getting older, but if I threw a 60 year old guy with some muscle in a room I doubt he'd take 5 seconds to get off the damn floor if he was getting shot at.
Not a huge arsenal of guns: Sadly, you can only carry 3 weapons, god dammit people, Realism gets pretty bloody annoying after a while, You can only hold 2 hand guns or uzis, and 1 two hander, that's it, instead of you know, the huge arsenal you got in the older games, where you would switch around to different guns and constantly find ammo for them, now it's just you pick up a few guns in the level, and every enemy would be using the same thing, so you never really had to worry about running out of ammo for certain guns.
Die a lot easier: You know how in the other games the enemies couldn't shoot for s%#t and you were usually dodging most of their bullets? Well that's the total opposite in this game, now you die a lot easier and every enemy will actually end up hitting you fairly easily, granted some can't shoot for s%$t still so you don't have to really worry most of the time.
On rail shooting: Some ocassions you'll have some on rail shooting sections, like Max will lift himself up on a chain and go in slow mo, and you have to shoot everyone, or ride on a little push cart and shoot everyone across, granted, these are pretty fun, but honestly they are really easy, the enemies don't really shoot you or don't aim at you correctly, it's like they are pointing their own gun at themselves, and plus it takes like 1 shot to kill them all in this mode no matter where you aim, so it makes it really easy.
WHAT I THINK: The game is pretty fun, and I still feel like it's Max Payne, but the problem is, is that the've change so many things around and made things easy and hard in some of the weirdest places in the game, and the difficulty fluctuates like crazy, and when I figured out that hiding behind cover and waiting for them to come to me is easier than finding them, it just becomes a waiting game, and the fact that using pills in last stand is more useful than using them normally means I could just go in rambo style and shoot everyone when I have a lot of pills, get knocked down, kill a guy, get up and shoot them and clear out the room that way.  It gets a 7/10, it's fun yes, but there are just some weird decisions that don't make much sense to me.

Q: Is it pay to win?

From the "I hope you didn't waste 60 bucks on this" department.
I really like Wolfenstein. I played the hell out of RtCW, which had perhaps the greatest multiplayer component ever. Wolfenstein 2009 was so-so, but bearable. But this one is just bad.
Why? Sure it's a beautiful game with some nice combat and good visuals, but it utterly fails in the "tone" department.  The New Order has no idea what kind of game it is.  Is it a balls to the wall action thriller with comedic levels of Serious Sam style violence? Yes.  However, combined with this is a over the top, maudlin sort of story that is supposed to somehow convey to the audience the horrors of war through the medium of said comedic violence. The result is a mish-mash that is almost insulting to the actual victims of Nazi brutality.  You can't go from killing robotic dogs on a Nazi space station, glorying in the absurdity of the whole thing to a contrived concentration camp scene where you kill a mass murderer in the midst of a tearful flashback.  It's like it's a game that's throwing a rubber chicken at you and saying "waka waka" yet expecting you to feel like it's your poor little sister's pet hen that you should've saved from the slaughterhouse.
I feel like The New Order is just adolescent.  Still glorying in violence and guns and bombs, and yet because everyone else expects something adult, it has to throw in some Private Ryan style emotional overlay because without it it wouldn't get into AP english or something.
