It's probably impossible to talk about a first-person sci-fi puzzler with a mysterious overseer without comparing it to Portal, so let's get that out of the way. The Talos Principle's puzzles aren't as fun as Portal's overall; there's more procedural stair-stepping your way through with pretty much the same sets of tools the whole way, to the point that puzzles feel like less of a test of your ingenuity than about your long-term planning and careful attention to detail. Some people will enjoy that, but I suspect more will find it makes later puzzles more of a painful slog than anything. It's especially aggrieving when you discover what looks like a really plausible and utterly out-there solution for a puzzle only to find the truth was much more mundane -- often just a pixel-hunt to find the tiny patch of dirt where one puzzle piece will conveniently interact with everything you need.
You solve puzzles with a pretty humdrum set of tools: buttons that need weighed down, posts to redirect laser beams, short-lived temporal clones of yourself, and so on. If you want to think outside the box (and grab all the pickups necessary for the "best" ending), you can solve optional puzzles to collect hidden stars throughout the game world. These often require working outside the basic puzzle mechanics, climbing map elements, and even connecting pieces positioned in one puzzle to another. The disappointing part about earning gold stars is that you have little incentive to flex your ingenuity on these puzzles unless you can solve *all* of them, or are willing to consult a guide, as one star is just as useless as 29 of them (out of 30).
Where The Talos Principle really shines is in its writing.  Being a lost robot in a Garden of puzzles commanded by the booming disembodied voice of God feels a bit silly, as does arguing basic introductory philosophy concepts with an apparently sentient computer interface. But the more you learn, the more you unravel a really excellent sci-fi story about philosophy, learning, the meaning of being human, and the continuation of purposes greater than ourselves. The story is really what makes The Talos Principle worth playing, and once you consume all the story fluff, it can be hard to want to power through the remaining puzzles to achieve better, more complete endings. When you've read research logs from a massive species-wide scientific project of absolutely cosmic ambition, when you've listened to the stories about how humans face unthinkable catastrophe, and when you've argued with a vaguely Satanic computer about the proof of your own sentience, the order in which you move puzzle pieces to slog through the end of the game gets a lot less compelling.
If you liked Portal for its story, there's plenty to love in The Talos Principle. If you liked it for its puzzles, keep looking.

I went into Wolfenstein: The New Order with low expectations, and for the first 10 minutes or so, it was barely living up to them. The initial sequence didn't exactly sell me on the game, and I figured I was in for a good 6+ hours of thoroughly disinteresting trench warfare against wacky steampunk future Nazis.
Thankfully though, I kept playing through that less than stellar first impression. The New Order turned out to be an unexpectedly excellent title well worth picking up regardless of holiday or summer sale status.
The story is incredibly well written- though a bit heavy handed at times I still really enjoyed it. You have to make some really gut wrenching, gruesome decisions, and there are some scenes that will hit you right in the feels. The romantic aspect of it did seem a bit forced and sudden, but otherwise it was outstanding.
The level design is another part where this game shines- far too often I find myself playing FPS games with what are clearly "filler" levels. Not so here. While everything is pretty much linear, you don't feel like you're dragging yourself through 40 floors of some insufferably dull and long level to meet an arbitrary gameplay timer.
The combat is also pretty well sorted. Stealth is a refreshingly viable tactic- enemies do seem to be a bit on the slow side as far as spotting you goes, but the game flows easily between stealth and action. The officers that sound alarms and call reinforcements give you ample reason to sneak, but can also be dispatched via going in guns blazing. The AI isn't perfect, but enemies react believably to flanking and will try to flush you out of cover.
Also of note is the level to which the game has been polished- perhaps this was not so on release, but I found the entire game to be refreshingly bug free. Save for one awkward world seam in an early level and a single enemy ragdoll that proceeded to flop around and float through the air a bit before settling to the ground, I didn't see much worth writing home about in terms of QA lapses. The graphics and optimization show a similar level of attention to them, and things ran smoothly all throughout, even on max settings.
This isn't to say I don't have any complaints about the game, though. The dual wielding mechanic is profoundly useless in the initial phases of the game, and then becomes almost a necessity because the developers apparently subscribe to the doctrine that you can add challenge to a game by adding absurd amounts of extra health to enemies. It doesn't work, and it's just frustrating to have almost all your health stripped away by an enemy you had to empty two 45 round magazines into their face to kill.
Also, the whole "AHH SNEAKY NAZI!" being captured and stabbed repeatedly quicktime event is overused to a fault. I didn't count, but by the end of the game I'm pretty sure Ol' B.J. had taken at least 10 stab wounds to the lung/heart area and been "captured" 4-5 times. It doesn't really lessen my enjoyment of the game, but after a point it just seems kinda silly.
Overall, I'm going to file Wolfenstein: The New Order under the "pleasant surprises" column, and I'd highly advise that it deserves a second look if you're on the fence about getting it.

It dawned on me that 'Squad' was a special breed of game when my squad made contact with the Taliban in the harsh terrain of Afghanistan. An RPG shell had just impacted the ground in front of me showering my squad in dust and debri. An eerie silence follwed only to be cut by the unmistakable murmurs of 'medic' crackling over my headset. To my right, I saw our medic inch forward not 6ft feet from me, only be ge riddled with bullets from a hidden AK-47 toting insurgent. Of the 9 man team I had been apart of, 4 lay dead and the rest including myself were disorientated and frozen in place as the pitter patter of steps grew louder. Here I was, on the edge of a poppy field, amongst my enemy with my dead squad mates lying beside me. I've never experienced survivor's guilt in a video game but in that moment, I felt it. In the course of 20 minutes, I'd laughed and sworn with my now deceased squadmates and for some reason, perhaps through divine intervention I had been spared. Through all this time it never occurred to me that I could respawn if I were to be killed such was the immersion of the moment. 'Squad' is the greatest modern warfare tactical FPS I've ever played as it breathes life into a genre that was becoming all to stale with nothing but the ARMA series to counter such an accusation. Echo1 signing off.

Max Payne Three is a book wrapped up in a video game. The story is the main point of this game i feel, with a heacy storyline and a dark, depressing character. Max Payne is a 50 something hell bent on forgetting the past in pain killers and booze, which is excellently shown between the "chapters" or levels of the game. The consistant, and leaning toward annoying, voiceovers that Max does of his own life in reflection add a slight depth to the character as everything he says is in hindsight, noting all the mistakes that he made at the moment and foreshadows what happens next. Changing gears the gameplay is a basic covershooter with one intresting concept of the bullet dodge and bullet time. These features are what make the game stand out among its competition. The bullet dodge allows you to slow time and avoid damage all while gunning down your enemies. I think this is a little overpowered but actully can be a plot point. It shows how Max does not value his own life and just tries to do his job.
Overall i feel that this is a 9\10 game. Excellent story with enough variation in the gameplay to make it intresting.

The most treasured RTS, AoE II HD preserves its nostalgic values while adding new civilizations into the fray.
This game doesn't just flat out put civilizations you can play as, but you get to know their history, which is a very nice touch.
Also, any accidental drops in ELO or MMR matchmaking systems are virtually nonexistent, unlike in AoM:EE. When your game crashes, you don't lose any ranking at all.
That being said though, this beautiful, well-crafted game only needs to maximize multiplayer security and robustness to fully ensure that every single minute you spend in multiplayer is just as good as playing the game yourself in singleplayer.
The new multiplayer system in servers have changed. Now there's two types of AoE II games that can be played; Original Game (Age of Kings + The Conquerors) and the Expansions (Original Game + The Forgotten + The African Kingdoms.)
Servers can now choose to either host these two AoE II games. HOWEVER, if you join an Expansions server, you are stuck to a LIMITED pool of civilizations to choose from, unless you own the Forgotten, or the African Kingdoms. I highly recommend that you buy this game in addition with at least one expansion pack in order to prevent restricted options in multiplayer; the selection pool EVEN limits Age of Kings and Age of Conquerors civs.
Overall, it's a great RTS that shows historical values of the civilizations you play, providing the same, satisfying gameplay experience. However, it suffers from crashing in multiplayer games, and the fact that there's a limited pool of civilizations to choose from for people who join Expansions game servers, yet don't own any of the two expansions, hinders multiplayer experience for people who've already bought the original.

Somewhere inside this mess of cutscenes, heavy handed dialogue, tired narrative, and poor decisions is a neat neo-noir game about redemption, death, and trust. There are moments where those concepts shine through the drudgery of the 60 second firefights, 20 second cutscenes cycles - like the introduction mission and the flashback segments. But most of it is dull dull dull. Max whines and grumbles his way through a story both cliched and bizarre. Max fails to protect a woman because...his boss wanted her dead? And Max was hired because he can't protect people? To be the fall guy? Which one?
An paraphrased example of the game:
Cutscene: "I fail. I always fail. Fail fail fail fail."
Gameplay: Then you kill dozens of people in some simple environments.
Cutscene: "Fail fail fail."
I played through the campaign once, dumped some hours into the multiplayer (which is wild, unbalanced, and frustrating), and lamented the loss of both my time and money.
I really liked the idea of a noir story in bright, tropical Brazil. The heavy, somber subject matter contrasted with the jovial, colorful environments and character design. That's not what we got.
I'm not sure what we got but it wasn't very good.

I was unsure about this game at first, I love WW2 games, especially well done shooters. I hesitantly bought this game while it was on sale, hoping that it could live up to the Wolfenstein moniker. I am SO glad I bought this game. While there isn't a whole lot of new and unique things this game adds to the FPS genre, it makes the things established in shooters (cover, dual wielding, alt. fire modes, etc.) really stand out. It's almost refreshing in a way. This game has what I would like to think is probably one of the best prologues that I've ever played, and the alternate Nazi-ruled future where the majority of the game takes place is a really interesting, immersive, and detailed era where I will actually catch myself thinking "Good god, what if this really had happened??". All in all I would give this game a 8.5/10. It is a very solid shooter, it can be a serious game but it never takes itself too seriously, there is always a little comedy to be found. I find myself caring about the characters, and truly hating the villains. And last but not least I have FUN when I play this game, whether it's a casual romp in easy mode, or I feel masochistic and play on some of the harder difficulties. Do yourself a favor and let the inner-patriot in you kill some gott verdammt Nazis.

Boasts 100 players on a match but most servers only have 74 or 50 player matches, but even that many people in a match brings the feel of a large scale battlefield. This is very tactical, team and co op orientated. You are going to die, ALOT, but this game makes you fear getting shot like no other. This game does not favour the lone wolf at all. You'll need to listen and follow your squad leader, like in real life. The best matches are the best coordinated ones, tactically.
Also to add to that fear and immersion are probably the best rifle sounds I've heard in a game to date. I have fired weapons in real life and this is the closest to that sound I have felt, ever. As accurate as you are going to experience bar the real thing, trust me.
This is the best military sim/shooter you'll find alongside Arma imo. It may seem the price is steep for early access, and I had the same reservations, but I really feel it's well worth the money. The most treasured RTS, AoE II HD preserves its nostalgic values while adding new civilizations into the fray.
This game doesn't just flat out put civilizations you can play as, but you get to know their history, which is a very nice touch.
Also, any accidental drops in ELO or MMR matchmaking systems are virtually nonexistent, unlike in AoM:EE. When your game crashes, you don't lose any ranking at all.
That being said though, this beautiful, well-crafted game only needs to maximize multiplayer security and robustness to fully ensure that every single minute you spend in multiplayer is just as good as playing the game yourself in singleplayer.
The new multiplayer system in servers have changed. Now there's two types of AoE II games that can be played; Original Game (Age of Kings + The Conquerors) and the Expansions (Original Game + The Forgotten + The African Kingdoms.)
Servers can now choose to either host these two AoE II games. HOWEVER, if you join an Expansions server, you are stuck to a LIMITED pool of civilizations to choose from, unless you own the Forgotten, or the African Kingdoms. I highly recommend that you buy this game in addition with at least one expansion pack in order to prevent restricted options in multiplayer; the selection pool EVEN limits Age of Kings and Age of Conquerors civs.
Overall, it's a great RTS that shows historical values of the civilizations you play, providing the same, satisfying gameplay experience. However, it suffers from crashing in multiplayer games, and the fact that there's a limited pool of civilizations to choose from for people who join Expansions game servers, yet don't own any of the two expansions, hinders multiplayer experience for people who've already bought the original.

We wipe the squad. Its game over now. Toma18 says [sic] "I love being the one squad that comes out of nowhere and wipes everyone out in seconds". Second.

For starters, it's a puzzle game. You don't see very many of these anymore. Of course there are a bunch of puzzle games in the indie community, but this game was made by Croteam; creators of the Serious Sam franchise.
Each puzzle is sort-of separated in its own little, boxed-in area. You solve the puzzle, collect tetris piece-looking thing, and move on to another puzzle. Once you collect a set of sigils, you use them in a lock. So while the puzzles are separate, they kind of come together in the end.
What's really interesting about this game though is how the story itself is a puzzle as well. In addition to this, the story deals with a lot of philosophical themes and will constantly have you questioning what you do. The game doesn't just tell you the story as you progress through the game. You have to go out of your way to find various things in order to figure it out for yourself. Computer terminals provide documents for you to read, and a snarky AI challenges everything you do.
The game doesn't hold your hand at all. You have to figure out how to use the various devices thrown at you throughout the game. It works wonderfully. Of course, the game can get devilishly difficult at times but level creation in this game is absolutely brilliant, and shows how much hard work was put into this game.
All in all, there's a ton of content in this game, and a lot of different things going on that you don't see in modern gaming. Croteam took a genre that isn't getting much love, and absolutely crafted a masterpiece. I really am enjoying my time with this game.

Our Sgt. has us build defenses and before you know it we have a small but capable FOB from which we provided covering fire and relayed enemy movements to our squads in town.  Our Sgt. got a radio call from 4th squad saying they were pinned down by enemies coming in through the southern entrace of the town.  He made the call to move 2nd squad down into the town west and through the middle to come out on the other side and catch the militia out in the open.  Well the militia saw it coming and in between rounds of AK and RPK fire we were ordered to fall back to the center of town to regroup and resupply.  I look around for my squad and I only see the autorifleman, Dunlap.  Dunlap and I were split from our squad by a sea of angry militiamen.  So we cautiously make our way back through the town.  Covering each other as we cross alleys, streets, fields.  I didn't even know his first name and yet he was my best friend.  Finally catching up to the squad I suddenly hear a loud snap and my vision faded out.  I'd been shot.  Dunlap was calling out to me telling me to hold on but before I knew it he was down too.  We laid there, taking in our last breaths thinking about how we got there.  But it wasn't over yet.  A friendly voice approached.  A fellow rifleman, phozz, had come to our rescue.  After a few moments of silence he said something so profound, so life changing, it shook me to the core..."F*** I don't have a medkit"
-----
For real though, this game is awesome and I can't wait to see where it goes.  There is a learning curve but it's nowhere near as steep as say Arma's or OFP. The distance sounds of gunshots and explosions made me anxious to move up and see what exactly was going on.  The weapon sounds are spot on in this game. I'm a milsim fanatic so I can't recommend this game enough to people who enjoy milsims and tactical shooters alike.  Play it. Love it.  Play it some more.

I recommend this game because it represents a solid effort by a AAA developer, which is a rare thing these days. However, I have many reservations about the game. First, the good: the writing in this game is beautiful, it perfectly represents the "noir" style and Max's depressed sarcasm oozes from every syllable he utters; it's fantastic. The bullet-time is exectued well and the signature dive-bullet-time maneuver is as fun as ever.
Now the negatives: while the writing is beautiful, the plot is near nonsensical. After the the first two missions, I literally have no idea why Max continues to risk his life in taking on suicidal missions for the meager salary he receives as "security" for the Branco family. Ironically, he even questions his motivations himself, lampshading how unrealistic the plot is. Also, while Max's dialogue is an excellent representation of the Noir style the games are famous for, both the setting and realistic characters and plot are not. Max Payne is a game series that in the past has only partially taken itself seriously, and playfully skirted the line between reality and fantasy. This third installment takes itself completely seriously and tries to paint a picture of corruption on a massive scale with a lone depressed gunman who finds himself caught in the middle, but it doesn't work.
Finally, while the bullet-time mechanics are intact from previous games, the intersting and fun gunfights are not. This game very wrongly incorporates a cover mechanic (that is already over-used in every other FPS in the world) with a very poor enemy AI. This mechanic causes every fight to boil down to you and the enemies all taking cover and playing a deadly game of "whack-a-mole" while you and the enemy pop out of cover to fire at each other. Needless to say it is soo booooring! I had to make my own fun by running in gungho and bullet-time diving in the center of mobs to make it more exciting.
Overall, I would say it is a fun experience, but probably not for full price. Wait for a sale. ;D

Wolfenstein series is now over 20 years old and i begun my hobby around the same time. It's interesting to see the progress of two decades, but by the end of The New Order i felt like i just might give up on the whole FPS genre.

Plot is dumb but not in a fun action movie sense. Enemies sure are cartoonishly evil but the rest of the world doesn't seem so bad. Tech has gone forward in great steps resulting in robo-dogs and such which are clearly not to be taken seriously. Then again you see and act horrible violence that leaves people as empty shells (literally) that is perhaps meant to provoke some drama. I wasn't having fun with the story but could not take it seriously either.
Gameplay is divided in two sections: On missions and at base. The base is where you interact with various characters who are visually well desinged and kind of interesting but the objectives you get there are "find a piece of moldy concrete" or "find missing power tool" and such. Even the main character complains about being "just like an errand boy". Still the characters and places are so well made that i liked those parts more than the shooting.
Enemies can take a load of bullets, especially if they're armored, and on the hardest difficulty ammo is scarce. Corpse may only carry 9 bullets so spraying all over is not an option. Of course you don't come to Wolfenstein looking for realism since the name of the series itself has meant Robo-Hitler with two miniguns for over 20 years. Problem is that the movement grinds to a halt when you have to peek from behind a corner slowly firing off hitpoints of something that also only stands still. There are only handful of enemy types. Sure there are diffrent colors and clothes but all carry same assault rifle and behave in the same way. Then there are few types of robots and occasional boss but overall the variation is way too low.
Much advertised feature is that you can dual-wield every weapon and that certainly is the case, but the flip-side is that there are only six or so weapons in the game. Pistol, Assault Rifle, Shotgun, Sniper, Laser weapon/welder and occasional pick-ups like minigun. There are variants of all in different parts of the story set on different years, but i can't tell any meaningful difference between them. Basically what dual-wielding does is make the weapons fire at faster rate at the cost of iron sights. Since there are atleast two weapon options assinged on every weapon key and game brings up what you used last time, you'll more often than not get the wrong thing. For example at the later part of the game there are 4 possibilities of what comes up when you press number "4": Assault Rifle, Assault rifle's underbarrel rocket launcer, two assault rifles or two assault rifles with the primary shooting underbarrel rockets. So too few weapons but still too much to handle.
The laser/weldergun itself is interesting. It allows you to cut a hole in few materials. The desctiption says it will cut "thin metal" but you can only cut chicken-wire, chains and specific crates. You can't, for example, open barrels with it.  It doesn't even leave a mark. Theoretically you can make a hole in a thin metal wall and then shoot through that hole which is really impressive but since you are supposed to go guns blazing there is really no need to do that. The game also has a perk system that is almost unnoticeable. You get automatically a bit better at what you do. For example sneaking a lot gives you quieter footsteps, but during gameplay i didn't notice it at all. Enemies are almost blind anyway.
Wolfenstein is built on ID Tech 5, same engine as Rage. I personally like how many details are in the scene. Where is supposed to be a pipe, Wolfenstein has 5 pipes. A table has not one but 10 books stacked plus a pile of paper. I'd love to see this engine used in a game with more exploration, like Deus EX. Downside is that most of the objects are static so they cannot be moved and that is not good in explosion heavy game. Quality of the textures is sometimes nice and other times Half-life (the first) level and in totally weird places. Wall behind the most important button in the plot might look just awful and other not so important places look good. Wolfenstein runs smoothly even during action scenes but sometimes slows down in meaningless corridors without enemies. Again which is weird. If The New Order shines at one thing it's size: At 44gb The New World was the largest thing i have ever downloaded.
Overall i didn't like The New Order. Everything has been seen too many times and all new things are under-developed. Don't belive the hype. It's often on sale and cheap but so is everything else.

Covering each other as we cross alleys, streets, fields.  I didn't even know his first name and yet he was my best friend.  Finally catching up to the squad I suddenly hear a loud snap and my vision faded out.  I'd been shot.  Dunlap was calling out to me telling me to hold on but before I knew it he was down too.  We laid there, taking in our last breaths thinking about how we got there.  But it wasn't over yet.  A friendly voice approached.  A fellow rifleman, phozz, had come to our rescue.  After a few moments of silence he said something so profound, so life changing, it shook me to the core..."F*** I don't have a medkit"
-----
For real though, this game is awesome and I can't wait to see where it goes.  There is a learning curve but it's nowhere near as steep as say Arma's or OFP.  You can jump right in and the community (so far...don't let me down here guys) has been very helpful and an absolute joy to play with.  The in game VOIP is the best I've ever used in any game period.  It's great to see a competitive shooter that absolutely hinges on team play.  And the sound design my GOD!!! The distance sounds of gunshots and explosions made me anxious to move up and see what exactly was going on.  The weapon sounds are spot on in this game.  My heart was pounding as a sniper was taking shots at us as we took cover in our FOB.  I'm a milsim fanatic so I can't recommend this game enough to people who enjoy milsims and tactical shooters alike.  Play it. Love it.  Play it some more.

All in all this is a solid game, allot to experiment with.
To keep this simple i'll do a short Pro/con list then go into some depth about how the pros balance out some of the cons.
Pros:
- More customization that you can shake a stick at
- Lots of fun learning what works and what doesn't
- Solid Multiplayer
- Getting parts or cubits is fairly simple
- You can sell your designs
Cons:
- New parts are super expensive
- Some parts aren't available to recycle regardless of if you want them
- Sometimes other players or even bots will have weapons that can crush you no problem
- The premium is almost rubbed in your face
- Melee is a bit strange and it needs some work (They should maybe add some limb parts for movable melee parts)
As you can see the cons are short and easily balance our by the pros of the game.  Cubits are hard to come by at first, but as you get the hang of designing ships it gets easier, either through death match rewards or through selling your designs. Designing your bots is super fun and really rewarding (Personally i use a modified version of the base flying bot i call the Dust Runner). You can mix some of the mobility parts to provide back up wheels if your legs get shot out or just some skids to keep flying a bit easier if you crash into something. Balancing weight on your bot is important and makes you feel smart for working out how to do things and weapons can either be mixed to swap out when the time is right or kept the same one for specialisation and extra firing rate while one cannon or laser is recharging. As for melee, as i said, it's kind of weird and i've not seen anyone bother with it, apart from one dude who kept ramming players in his bipedal bot, he died allot.
I definitely recomend this game for a bit of fun or for flat out competitive play, and it's still in early access so there's allot of stuff that could happen in the future. If it's not your thing, it might tickle a friends' fancy and it's definitely worthy of attention.

I was hesitant to buy this game at first, especially with the huge download (around 40 G).
Now that I have it and play it, I'm more impressed that I thought I'd be.  The voice acting and story is interesting, and very well done, imho.  The gameplay is fun, I love playing stealth, and didn't expect it to be as well done as it is.  But sometimes just random blasting and throwing grenades is fun too, and there's plenty of that kind of action as well :P
I run an i7 (4th gen) 3.4 G with 8 G Ram, and an AMD R9 270 2G video card.  I've tried the game full everything, and it runs fine, but the texture pop-in's were a little annoying, though the game FPS was stable, so I brought it down to medium (16 ppf and medium VT cache), and I personally don't see enough of a difference to affect my gameplay, the textures are high compared to other games, even on medium.  I get anywhere from 30 to 60 FPS, but it's stay relatively stable, it doesn't jump too much, so it doesn't bother me.  For me, gaming at 30 FPS is more than enough, so people who won't accept anything below 60 FPS should make sure their rig is better than mine.  Oh, I've also turned on reflections, which apparently affects FPS alot, but it's on for me, and it hasn't affected my gameplay, the FPS is fine.
There is no AA, and at first this bothered me, but after playing a few hours, I hardly notice it.  There's too much action and movement to notice it, imo.  I did try binding keys in console to turn on AA (2 and 4), and it affects gameplay, the whole game slows, instead of running "normal speed".  It makes it easier to shoot :P  but I prefer it running normally (I hardly noticed it at 2 AA, but just enough to prefer no AA at this point).  Also, with AA, there are some glitches here and there, so it's almost better off.  If you can get past the AA, which I normally can't in games, the game is fantastic.  Despite some differences like no AA, etc., the engine is solid, the textures are higher quality than I expected (even at medium), and the FPS is stable on my system.  I don't even notice the lack of AA anymore, which is not common for me.
I can't vouche for other people with lower end systems, or different configs, or people with different preferences (like needing 60 FPS minimum or highest textures, etc), but for me, on my system, I'm impressed with the game, and the quality of gameplay and storyline/voice-acting impressed me enough to forget about the things I usually fret over, like AA.
I'm impressed with this game myself, and give it a 9 / 10, which I didn't expect when I bought it.
Hope sharing my review helps whoever reads it.

Where to begin? It was 9 years in the making, it has a cult following that have been excited for this title since 2003 and it has been developed by a developer with the highest rated games in recent memory.
That aside is the game fun to play? The short answer; Yes! Is it violent and atmospheric? Yes! Is there captain baseball bat boy? Yes!
MP3 has remained very true to Remedy in its style and presentation. This is good, although story related answering machine messages and television programs may have been impressive in 2001 they seem commonplace and at times tedious now. MP3 now benefits from Rockstar's fantastic RAGE physics, these allow for even more believable shootouts and more brutal death animations, often you will see your enemies take buckshot to the face only to recoil and flop to the ground like a crumpled bag of bone and flesh, it is an impressive effect and helps bring Max Payne into the new generation of gamers.
The story of MP3 departs from the gritty streets of New York to enter the crime ridden falvelas of Sao Paulo. The new setting is bright and aesthetically pleasing which contrasts the often brutal portions of the story. There is something increasingly unsettleing about entering further into unfriendly territory as a bullet dodging gunman with a shaved white head. As Max Payne becomes rapped up in the conflict in Brazil, his psychological state becomes intertwined with the events of the game and how he perceives them. This is the height of good story-telling the protagonist becomes apart of the story and is further developed by the events of the previous games making the plot intriguing and immersive as the game play itself.
For those who haven't played MP or MP2 there is a lot to offer. The comprehensive multiplayer allows you to shoot dodge your enemies online and develop your own kits and loadouts as you would in other such competitive shooters. There is also the option to join and compete with a Rockstar "crew" which is the comparable name for a clan. The action is fast paced and rewarding and you will often curse your enemies for being able to plug you with one extra round to finish you off.
Fun and fast paced the competitive multiplayer is not the main focus of MP3 it is evident that the developers at Rockstar took special care to bring the game into the new era of gaming while still maintaining the qualities and expectations of the series' fans. MP3 is dark, gritty and fantastic it is everything we have come to expect from a MP title and it does it with so much style that it is a challenge to put down

Whilst it has two columns of keys you can change, I found that you couldn't put the arrow keys in the second column, but you could put them in the first column by typing over the WASD default keys. Very odd; not good, in fact - but it worked (I don't know if this option was right there from the start or it came later; it's certainly not designed well).
I also found that I couldn't use the number pad keys on the keyboard.
As well as that, you are supposed to be able to heal in-game by using right-click, but that didn't work either (each time I was hit, I would bleed out).
I'm going to recommend this game anyway, because - for most players - it looks like it should be good.
But, for me personally, I feel that it leaves a lot to be desired.

To put it simply: it's a surprisingly fun game. Its plot isn't brilliant, but it's not bogus either. Not revolutionarily new nor mindlessly repetitive, New Order isn't the standard run-and-gun title most people might expect when seeing another iteration of the Wolfenstein franchise. It's worth a run-through. The engine is smooth as butter and gorgeous, the gun mechanics are on par with pretty much any classic FPS excluding Counter-Strike, and the world is relatively believable [with the exception of some mechanical animals].
The creative director of Machine Games said that he thought the positive feedback the game received from critics could be attributed to the plentiful time his company had to polish the game. My only wish is that he had the time to have his team work on a multiplayer, because if the single-player experience is a testament to anything, it's that the "return to your roots" mantra isn't a bad design philosophy. They've done well what they've had to do well and it makes me wonder what they could've done for the PC FPS scene had they tried making something like a competitive multiplayer akin to that of the original Call of Duty. I definitely think they have [or had] something here.
If you want a fun FPS single-player experience, you won't be disappointed. Check it out and let me know what you think!

For Just one voce to do that takes real skill. Very well done.
MP3 tends to become a little difficult (for my skill level). Because of this the constant replaying of levels tends to get a little on the boring side. It looks like Squad might be a good game.
But my experience was negatively impacted by not being able to change the keys on the keyboard to what I wanted.
Most people use the WASD to move, but I use the arrow keys to move - and the game did not allow the arrow keys to be allocated to the movement function.
(Yeah, yeah, someone is going to argue that I should use WASD - well, I don't, I have my reasons, and, besides, if it is what the customer wants and it isn't going to break the game, then it should be in there - all game-functional keys should be able to be allocated to whatever you want. It's 2015, we had the technology to do this years ago, it's a common game option, so it shouldn't be too hard.)
UPDATE: I tried the game again, after an update.
Whilst it has two columns of keys you can change, I found that you couldn't put the arrow keys in the second column, but you could put them in the first column by typing over the WASD default keys. Very odd; not good, in fact - but it worked (I don't know if this option was right there from the start or it came later; it's certainly not designed well).
I also found that I couldn't use the number pad keys on the keyboard.
As well as that, you are supposed to be able to heal in-game by using right-click, but that didn't work either (each time I was hit, I would bleed out).
I'm going to recommend this game anyway, because - for most players - it looks like it should be good.
But, for me personally, I feel that it leaves a lot to be desired.

This game is everything I didn't know I wanted and nothing I expected.  It has its share of the over the top flare of the original Wolfenstein 3D alongside a beautiful story, interesting characters, and a great soundtrack.  The gameplay is simple but nuanced, allowing you multiple approaches to linear FPS gameplay, and enough rewards to make it worthwhile to cover all of your options.  In a world dominated by multiplayer or open world shooters, Wolfenstein is a linear shooter that gets it absolutely right and makes you feel things along the way, a la Spec Ops: The Line.  If you enjoyed that game, you'll definitely enjoy this one.  I can't recommend it highly enough, especially if you can get it on sale.  Warning, replay value is somewhat limited.

Splash Damage has returned, and I have to say, it's way better than brink (too say the least).
Dirty Bomb is a fast FPS game from Splash Damage (SD). Focusing on team composition rather than indervidual skill, the game is a lot of fun to play. The large variety of classes, (commonly referd to as mercs) makes the game very enjoyable as each merc is a different experience. Dirty Bomb is constantly being updated, and although the Devs arent exactly amazing, they do a good job of keeping DB fresh.
The gamemodes: Stopwatch, objective and execution (aswell as ranked) are currently available, although take account of the time of this review as it may have changed by the time you are reading it.
For all the positives I can give this game, it does have significant issues. Firstly, maps. Currently there are only 9 maps in the game, 3 of them exclusive to one gamemode, so a lot of the time it'll seem you are replaying the exact same game. Secondly, balance. Honestly, this game is  '♥♥♥♥ed' in terms of level stackers and team shuffle spam.
Lastly, play the tutorial before going online as it really helps, I cannot stress that enough as this isnt your typical FPS game. Overall, this game is great and I'd highly recommend it to anyone who wants to try a new first person shooter!

This is by and far ONE OF the worst games I've ever played. Specifically, it's one of the worst third-person gimmick-shooters I've ever had the displeasure of purchasing. Good thing I bought it for like... what, five bucks? Complete waste of cash.
Now don't get me wrong, there are some good parts to it. I like the story. Mostly. The characters are somewhat interesting. Somewhat.
That's almost as far as it goes. The graphics are nice too, but a good story and good graphics don't make a third person shooter a GOOD third person shooter.
Let's go into the issue a little deeper shall we?
Gunplay: The gunplay is solid, until you realize that SOMETIMES your bullets decide to come out of the barrel at a wierd angle, and first shot accuracy SOMETIMES does not exist, and persists on not existing until you die. Glitch or not, this should have been fixed long before now.
Reticule: The reticule is far too large for the distances you're playing at. Not a big issue, if not for the following.
AI: The AI is rather smart, which wouldn't be an issue if not for the following. However, the one thing that really bothers me is how insanely accurate even the lowliest gang-banger thug is with his weapon. It's as if he's been training with that weapon his entire life. This is a possibility, but bullets aren't cheap, and most thugs don't sit around training all day.
Camera: This really affects the playability of the game. The camera just... is never where it needs to be, forcing you to adjust it far to frequently from one shoulder to the next to get a SLIGHT bead on an enemy who is shooting you from across the map with a pistol through a chain-link fence, two boards, between a mouse's nad hairs and right into your noggin. Usually, before you even know they're there.
Bullet-Time: I've done a little research, this bullet time is NOTHING compared to what it was in previous games. However, since I haven't PLAYED previous Max Paynes, let's look at it from a new perspective, that of a gamer who didn't have the privilege of playing them. The bullet time is practically useless and never there when you need it. Sure, you can get tons of sweet♥♥♥♥♥head-shot action whenever the script says you need it, but when you REALLY need it, say when there are 10 or so guys staring down at you with near-perfect accuracy and you need to thin their ranks out before they flank and destroy you... nope. Ain't happening. Sorry. Have fun dying.
Scripted Events: There were NUMEROUS times where scripted events drove me up a wall. Specifically, one time when I was playing through one of Max's flash-back moments. In a cemetary, you and Max's pal, some guy I STILL can't remember the name of even though they're the BEST of friends, decides to 'help' by distracting the bad guys for Max. His help consists of running towards them unarmed, then away from them. You have to shoot all the bad guys before they kill your idiot friend. For a while, I couldn't figure out what to do. I'd go into bullet time, shoot six of the seven, and then before whatsisface could get away, an eight guy would randomly pop up and shoot Max's buddy in the back of the head. Needless to say, I tried this about ten times in various different ways to stop this from happening, and stop myself from having to restart. Eventually, I became so frustrated that I QUIT and went looking for answers online.
Turns out his running distraction was near useless anyways. Since the game required you to re-acquire aggro right after he runs off. Otherwise he always gets killed. Yeah. Great distraction.
Unfortunately, there are tons of situations like this.
Gun Switching: This is something that seemed cool until it got me killed 20 times. When you go into a cutscene, (Of which there are about a hundred. I'm not kidding) Max puts his main-hand weapon away in favor of a pistol. Why? Because it looks cool or something. Then it usually thrusts you into a situation where you NEED that 2-hand gun and have to waste time pulling it out. Not usually a big deal.
... Unless it magiks your 2-hand weapon away to wonderland, never to be seen again, leaving you with no bullets in you 1-hand weapons. This happens. More than it should.
Did I mention the ungodly accuracy of the enemies?
Cutscenes: My final argument against this game. There are LITERALLY about a hundred or so. Sometimes, every 20 feet. Literally. I've watched the game more than I've played it. I wouldn't complain about this, if the gameplay itself weren't so awful and the difficulty didn't spike like crazy.
There are many more issues. Level design, linearity, lack of common sense... But those above are the main ones.
35/100. Would NOT recommend.

The Talos Principle is an excellent entry into the first person puzzle solving genera. It is at its essence a game where you solve puzzles by opening doors, jamming radars, and moving droids while using several tools such as tripod prisms, radar jammers, blocks, and more. This central game is fun and the puzzle are well designed. In addition to the puzzle aspect the game also includes a philosophical component with makes it rather unique. While you (a robotic automation) go about solving puzzles you are often encountered by a beeping sounds from computer terminals dispersed around the world. When you approach and read these terminals you engage yourself in a thought exercise of consciousness, free will, life and death. All in all The Talos Principle is a complete package offering puzzles and deep thoughts in a unique and fresh presentation.

An excellent experience, marred by a few small grievances.
Pros:
+ Great weapon variety, enjoyable controls and levels.
+ Combat is visceral, with exploding limbs, heads, etc.
+ Surprisingly good story/characters for an FPS. It's campy and ridiculous at times, grim and disarming at others.
+ Great musical score, sound effects, and voice acting.
Cons:
- 50GB (40ish really) download is insane, and there doesn't seem to be much reason for it.
- Performance is not amazing, framerate was a bit all over the place and had to dial back some settings. The options menu is just bizarre too.
- A few unenjoyable, 'modern game moments' that, while technically not QTE's, may as well have been.
- Kind of weak ending to an otherwise very enjoyable story.
I enjoyed it all the way through, save for those few flaws. Lack of multiplayer may turn some people off, but the fact it's a very focused single-player experience is welcome for a modern FPS. It was challenging, a little frustratingly so at times, but a hardened FPS veteran will probably disagree with that sentiment. Definitely recommended.

Age of Empires 2 is seriously one of the best RTS games out there.
The graphics were created via a method similar to Roller Coaster Tycoon, or more notably Donkey Kong Country (pre-rendered 3D models as sprites). The game is a decade old though, so I'm not going to go on about that anymore.
The gameplay is amazing. I've played many RTS games since I was exposed to this one, and none have matched up. It seems simple, but with all the different civs, bonuses, unique units and techs, this game is very deep and complicated.
If you really want to get good at it, you'll have to learn to micro all your units very well, get very good at managing your resources, and learn a bunch about what counters what.
The online is 50/50, sometimes it works, and sometimes it doesn't, even when everyone has low enough ping. The dreaded desync is always an issue.
There's a few bugs, and the learning campaign teaches you very little, but manages to drag it out quite a bit.
Other than that, I very highly recommend this game.

In a world where most shooter games force you to use just 2 weapons, W:TNO allows you to carry an entire arsenal and switch from a suppressed pistol to dual-wielded assault rifles. Unlike the annual COD release, this really feels like a classic FPS (Doom, Wolfenstein 3D) with modern graphics - your health is finite and doesn't recover on its own, you fight waves of enemies, and the amount of cheese in the plot is just right. Wolfenstein: The New Order's shooting mechanics are sublime. The audio and visual feedback, along with the excellent animations and diverse enemy types all work in concert to provide a joyful shooter romp. And all this is made sweeter by the surprisingly fresh story. Whereas antiheroes and muddled morality systems seem all the rage in today's pop culture, WTNO returns to a simpler time, in which heroes are heroes and villains are horrible, evil♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥whom I wanted nothing more than to see put six feet under the ground. The problem of ludonarrative dissonance (as seen in recent shooters such as Bioshock: Infinite) is not a problem here, because the player experiences firsthand, often in states of powerlessness, the atrocities committed by the bad guys, so often that by the time he or she is locked and loaded with akimbo, fully automatic shotguns, he or she is ready to mete out righteous buckshot justice. More than dull shooting galleries, every fight becomes an act of catharsis. This is why we crave better stories in games - not because of an appeal to some artistic standard set by film and literature, but because of the way it FEELS.
Three-dimmensional characters, wonderfully despicable villains, a romance subplot that, as far as I'm concerned, is touching, and a seemingly meatheaded protagonist who, as you get to know him, turns out to be just a peace-loving country boy fighting for friends, family, and barbeques on sunny, suburban lawns.

I bought this game having never played project reality, but with over 1000 hours in Arma 3 I thought that I would give it a shot since they are quite similar. So yes, I am biased in that regard.
I have played Arma 3 milsim, planetside, and other cooperative war games before, so going into a game and following orders from a random person is not hard for me. Somehow when people buy this game they think that it is going to be a Battlefield like experience, where you spawn in and go fight in a cluster♥♥♥♥ of players. This game however was not at all intented to be played in that manner. The only way you should play this game is through teamwork and cooperation between all squads, which is something I only rarely come across. Also, if you are lucky enough to click the servers tab and actually see servers, most of them with decent ping are either 100% full or completly empty. Most times I manage to join a squad where the squad leader does not have a mic, but on the off chance someone is actually leading a lot of the members are off with other squads and not following orders from the SL. I understand that playing public servers will lead to this problem, but I don't understand how anyone could have fun in this game when they aren't even playing it correctly. If you are someone who wants to go lonewolf then keep playing Call of Duty or whatever ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mainstream FPS is popular nowadays. This game is meant for tactics and teamwork, not Rambo style pushes through enemy lines.
One thing that really bothers me is that every squad has the same composition. There is no room for any changes to the standard fireteam, so each squad functions as their own army without requiring assistance from anyone else. Maybe if there was a weapons squad, AT team, recon unit, etc,,, it would force other squads to fight together to be successful. Also I wish there was a command unit, that allocated resources to FOBs, ordered squads to attack/defend, and overall ensure communication across the entire team.
The overall mechanics are alright, nothing spectacular. The dev team is regularly updating this game and adding new guns, vehicles, etc... There are bugs here and there but they are usually fixed in a timely manner, unless it is the no servers showing up, in that case you need to either reinstall the game or go into the game folder and mess with stuff you shouldn't be messing with. I do really like the FOB system, it adds a lot of cool emplacements and it is quite fun to reincforce a point and prepare for a coming attack; however since most maps are have a single line of progression, it can get pretty boring sitting at a back point waiting for the front one to fail so that you can be attacked.
All in all this game is more arcade FPS than anything, which isn't really my cup of tea. If more people took this game seriously then maybe I would rate it higher but until then I give it a 5/10.

If Wolfenstein: The New Order really brings anything to the table in terms of modern gaming, it is the very cinematic way in which it is presented from beginning to end. It is a solid story with solid acting skill and amazing artistry that immersive and captivating throughout, with an ending that is, dare I say, a bit emotional.
This game is a definate play for the adventerous FPS gamer; it does not disapoint in it's ability to keep on throwing the baddies at you, has a nice line up of weaponry (including the ability to dual weild almost everything), very realistic movement, massive levels, and tons of hidden areas and secrets, as well as a host of unlockable achievments that will make you faster, hold more ammo and a few other things that will make you an Uber Nazi Killing Machine.
But, in spite of this and my recommendation to put the cash down and download this game, especially if you've already played any of the others in the series, I do feel a bit miffed about a certain area of the game that promised something new, but didn't really deliver. Some may consider this a bit of a spoiler (although, I would not). You've been warned:
The first heart pumping chapter of the game ends with you, the player, having to make a choice about which one of your friends, Wyatt or Fergus, is going to die and which is going to live. As I said above, the very cinematic quality of the cut-aways and the good performances of the actors gets you a little attached to these characters already, so it's not really an easy choice, but you have to make it because the game gives you no other choice. So, you make the choice and suddenly you get an achievment called the "Wyatt Timeline" (or "Fergus Timeline").This raised excitement for me, because I imagined that I was basically going to get two games for the price of one; I'll choose Wyatt this time, see how it goes and then choose Fergus to play the other half. To say the least, I got a little ahead of myself. In part, because I've predicted this to happen in gaming for a long time and I thought this was the game that was really going to finally do it. But by the end, it turns out that it only changes a few small elements throughout the game, including some skills you gain and secrets you can access, but it doesn't actually change the game or the storyline itself. It's probably worth playing, and I'll choose that route when I take Wolfenstein: The New Order out for another spin sometime in the future, but my plan to play to the end and then go back and do the second timeline immediately has diminished, so it's on to the next game for now, hoping the creators will take this timeline concept to it's full reality in their next release in this series or any of their other titles to come.
The other disapointing thing about W:NO, and perhaps it's just because I just finished playing Half-Life 2 and Portal for the second time and Portal 2 for the First time, is that the game lacks much in terms of physicality and mutability: There are no objects you can move and drop, plywood propped up against walls does not fall down, you can't pull things off the walls, and there are a ton of valves, switches and levers all within your reach that are completely un-interactive. Again, this may be simply because I've been spoiled by gravity guns, portal guns and companion cubes that I see this stuff and I am now inclined to want to pick it up, throw it or destroy it, because as far as set dressing goes, W:NO succeeds with flying colors; all of this un-interactive stuff, despite not being 'real', brings a rich and life filled depth to the story that really helps to sell where you are, but that illusion dissolves when you find everything painted, welded and hardwired in place.

This is the most brutal, brain-bashingly bloody title I have played in the last three years and I've played plenty of titles that have tried to be just that. Wolfenstein: The New Order, while not technically impressive on the PC with its frame limiter, is a story-driven shooter experience you will not soon forget.
id Software has done an exceptional job making you REALLY hate the antagonist Nazis in the game. Anything bad that happens throughout the story? It is directly the Nazis' fault. And that makes you, Lieutenant Blaskowitz, really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. Add some unique and alive-feeling characters on the good guys' side of things and a guitar solo of the US national anthem and you've got yourself a narrative that explodes with awesomeness.
The gameplay is quick and hands off, just aim at Nazis and start gunning them down. No cover system, no nothing to hold your hands against the teched up, excuse-free Nazis. Melee attacks are quick and satisfying and actually offer and advantage over just running and gunning in stealth situations which were a pleasant surprise when they were presented.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you are looking for an engaging first person story-driven experience with a required element of skill. If you're up to the challenge of ending a genocide and feel like you can pick up the role of the badass Lieutenant Blakowitz, pick up Wolfenstein: The New Order. If not, well then, just let the Nazis take over and see what happens, you sadistic prissy boy.

Ok first things first... if you read no further, take this message with you: BUY THIS GAME, IF NOT JUST FOR THE SOUNDTRACK.
Ok... reading on? I'll elaborate...
This game is an excellent first-person style puzzle game, done in the style of Portal (no, it's not portal, and it doesn't try to be, so don't say it's a clone).
You awaken in a strange garden and hear the voice of one might presume was God telling you what you're doing and what to do. You're immediately thrust into an environment that looks like it came straight ouf of Riven and was mixed with a Pure Moods cd.
The beginning of the game is just learning how to move around and interact with objects, which will ultimately be used to collect Tetris-like pieces called sigils. Sigils play a big part in the game as you play on, where the object is to solve puzzles to unlock further areas to explore. Thrown throughout the game are random tidbits of information stored on computer terminals, complete with a somewhat intelligent computer program that will attempt to test your understanding of the physical world. Also strewn about are lots of QR codes with random blatherings and sparsely helpful information.
As you progress through the game (which can easily span 15+ hours) you will encounter puzzles that don't get terribly challenging, but just enough to test your wit, each getting harder as you go. There's even optional extra puzzles, if you know where to look. As you play on, you will unlock tools that make completing the puzzles a lot more fun. The best part is, there's no one way to solve them (ok some of them there might be, but not always). You can do whatever it takes to bend the rules to meet your goal. There's three different endings each with a message and a cutscene to explain why you are where you are and what's to become of you. Telling any more would just ruin the experience.
The last thing to mention, (also the first), is the music and visuals. This game has some of the best representations of serene landscape I've seen in a while. Coupled with a soundtrack that is on par with Enigma, you'll definitely not regret just firing this up and letting it sit there while you relax.
I had a great time with this game, and even after it's over, it's not over. There's lots of user modded content that will keep you testing your skills against the toughest challenges. I highly recommend this game!

If Wolfenstein: The New Order really brings anything to the table in terms of modern gaming, it is the very cinematic way in which it is presented from beginning to end. It is a solid story with solid acting skill and amazing artistry that immersive and captivating throughout, with an ending that is, dare I say, a bit emotional.
This game is a definate play for the adventerous FPS gamer; it does not disapoint in it's ability to keep on throwing the baddies at you, has a nice line up of weaponry (including the ability to dual weild almost everything), very realistic movement, massive levels, and tons of hidden areas and secrets, as well as a host of unlockable achievments that will make you faster, hold more ammo and a few other things that will make you an Uber Nazi Killing Machine.
But, in spite of this and my recommendation to put the cash down and download this game, especially if you've already played any of the others in the series, I do feel a bit miffed about a certain area of the game that promised something new, but didn't really deliver. Some may consider this a bit of a spoiler (although, I would not). You've been warned:
The first heart pumping chapter of the game ends with you, the player, having to make a choice about which one of your friends, Wyatt or Fergus, is going to die and which is going to live. As I said above, the very cinematic quality of the cut-aways and the good performances of the actors gets you a little attached to these characters already, so it's not really an easy choice, but you have to make it because the game gives you no other choice. So, you make the choice and suddenly you get an achievment called the "Wyatt Timeline" (or "Fergus Timeline").This raised excitement for me, because I imagined that I was basically going to get two games for the price of one; I'll choose Wyatt this time, see how it goes and then choose Fergus to play the other half. To say the least, I got a little ahead of myself. In part, because I've predicted this to happen in gaming for a long time and I thought this was the game that was really going to finally do it. But by the end, it turns out that it only changes a few small elements throughout the game, including some skills you gain and secrets you can access, but it doesn't actually change the game or the storyline itself. It's probably worth playing, and I'll choose that route when I take Wolfenstein: The New Order out for another spin sometime in the future, but my plan to play to the end and then go back and do the second timeline immediately has diminished, so it's on to the next game for now, hoping the creators will take this timeline concept to it's full reality in their next release in this series or any of their other titles to come.
The other disapointing thing about W:NO, and perhaps it's just because I just finished playing Half-Life 2 and Portal for the second time and Portal 2 for the First time, is that the game lacks much in terms of physicality and mutability: There are no objects you can move and drop, plywood propped up against walls does not fall down, you can't pull things off the walls, and there are a ton of valves, switches and levers all within your reach that are completely un-interactive. Again, this may be simply because I've been spoiled by gravity guns, portal guns and companion cubes that I see this stuff and I am now inclined to want to pick it up, throw it or destroy it, because as far as set dressing goes, W:NO succeeds with flying colors; all of this un-interactive stuff, despite not being 'real', brings a rich and life filled depth to the story that really helps to sell where you are, but that illusion dissolves when you find everything painted, welded and hardwired in place.

I bought this game having never played project reality, but with over 1000 hours in Arma 3 I thought that I would give it a shot since they are quite similar. So yes, I am biased in that regard.
I have played Arma 3 milsim, planetside, and other cooperative war games before, so going into a game and following orders from a random person is not hard for me. Somehow when people buy this game they think that it is going to be a Battlefield like experience, where you spawn in and go fight in a cluster♥♥♥♥ of players. This game however was not at all intented to be played in that manner. The only way you should play this game is through teamwork and cooperation between all squads, which is something I only rarely come across. Also, if you are lucky enough to click the servers tab and actually see servers, most of them with decent ping are either 100% full or completly empty. Most times I manage to join a squad where the squad leader does not have a mic, but on the off chance someone is actually leading a lot of the members are off with other squads and not following orders from the SL. I understand that playing public servers will lead to this problem, but I don't understand how anyone could have fun in this game when they aren't even playing it correctly. If you are someone who wants to go lonewolf then keep playing Call of Duty or whatever ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mainstream FPS is popular nowadays. This game is meant for tactics and teamwork, not Rambo style pushes through enemy lines.
One thing that really bothers me is that every squad has the same composition. There is no room for any changes to the standard fireteam, so each squad functions as their own army without requiring assistance from anyone else. Maybe if there was a weapons squad, AT team, recon unit, etc,,, it would force other squads to fight together to be successful. Also I wish there was a command unit, that allocated resources to FOBs, ordered squads to attack/defend, and overall ensure communication across the entire team.
The overall mechanics are alright, nothing spectacular. The dev team is regularly updating this game and adding new guns, vehicles, etc... There are bugs here and there but they are usually fixed in a timely manner, unless it is the no servers showing up, in that case you need to either reinstall the game or go into the game folder and mess with stuff you shouldn't be messing with. I do really like the FOB system, it adds a lot of cool emplacements and it is quite fun to reincforce a point and prepare for a coming attack; however since most maps are have a single line of progression, it can get pretty boring sitting at a back point waiting for the front one to fail so that you can be attacked.
All in all this game is more arcade FPS than anything, which isn't really my cup of tea. If more people took this game seriously then maybe I would rate it higher but until then I give it a 5/10.

This is the most brutal, brain-bashingly bloody title I have played in the last three years and I've played plenty of titles that have tried to be just that. Wolfenstein: The New Order, while not technically impressive on the PC with its frame limiter, is a story-driven shooter experience you will not soon forget.
id Software has done an exceptional job making you REALLY hate the antagonist Nazis in the game. Anything bad that happens throughout the story? It is directly the Nazis' fault. And that makes you, Lieutenant Blaskowitz, really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. Add some unique and alive-feeling characters on the good guys' side of things and a guitar solo of the US national anthem and you've got yourself a narrative that explodes with awesomeness.
The gameplay is quick and hands off, just aim at Nazis and start gunning them down. No cover system, no nothing to hold your hands against the teched up, excuse-free Nazis. Melee attacks are quick and satisfying and actually offer and advantage over just running and gunning in stealth situations which were a pleasant surprise when they were presented.
Overall, I would recommend this game if you are looking for an engaging first person story-driven experience with a required element of skill. If you're up to the challenge of ending a genocide and feel like you can pick up the role of the badass Lieutenant Blakowitz, pick up Wolfenstein: The New Order. If not, well then, just let the Nazis take over and see what happens, you sadistic prissy boy.

I'm a big fan of older id games. Heck, I even enjoyed Doom 3 and Quake 4. But I'm not a fan of Wolfenstein TNO. All its annoyances aggregate into a less than stellar experience.
What's the good? Gunplay is solid. Players can dual wield nearly every weapon. This is handy at higher difficulties since even the weakest enemies take a dozen rounds to drop. Also, guns have alternate fire modes. Although players will have access to all weapons early on, most of the alt modes are not unlocked until later in the game. This breaks up the monotony and balances the game a bit.
The campaign lasts about 15 hours. For a $60 title with no multiplayer, that's the minimum I'd expect. The environments are varied and allow for slight amounts of exploration. So levels feel bigger than what they are. Players can employ different tactics to dispatch enemies. Stealth can be more effective than run and gun at times. And sometimes camping behind a box and popping baddies one by one is most effective. No style dominates the game. At the hardest difficulties, run and gun is least effective. However, after a single playthrough I noticed stealth is broken. Patrols will walk over dead bodies and not sound the alarm. They will only sound the alarm if they see the player or see him kill someone. So there is no need to drop baddies out of sight. Not very challenging.
What's the bad? The game is buggy. During cutscenes, audio and mouth movements don't sync (think Skyrim) breaking the emersion. Turning off Vsync sometimes helps, but then there is horrible screen tearing to deal with. Also, the game randomly freezes briefly at set intervals during the first few missions. The freezing magically stopped after progressing further. Using a controller presents other problems due to inconsistent button behavior. I select alt fire mode, and the map opens. I open the radial and select a weapon, my character briefly freezes while taking damage before the next weapon is available. Under normal circumstances that's annoying. While playing the hardest difficulty it's downright rage inducing.
The graphics are OK but not a great showcase for the id tech 5 engine. Wolfenstein is plagued with inconsistent textures, pop ins, and jagged edges. Lighting effects drastically change by moving an inch. And there are limited advanced graphic options. There is no AA control. The frame rate is locked at 60fps. Currently, SLI and Crossfire performance stinks. Forcing features thru CCC did not help. Another negative: Wolfenstein is a 50gb install. Plus, a huge patch has to be downloaded. Since the graphics and sound are merely OK, the size is just excessive. Here's a bit of irony: TNO looks like it was made using the Unreal Engine with its almost cartoony/almost cel shaded environments and weapons. Artistically, it looks like any recent Unreal-based games. Was this intentional?
I hate TNO's erratic pacing. Between missions, the player hangs out at a base. And the "errands" between missions slow the game to a crawl. Forget about annihilating Nazis around the clock, because the resistance wants you to stop and find mold samples. Kill a few more Nazis and you're stopped again to find a blowtorch. The base and accompanying side missions mimic Dishonored. But this is Wolfenstein....
Lastly, I don't like the story. TNO tries too hard. It felt forced. It felt déjà vu. And the ending was just plain lazy. The aforementioned base exists solely to advance the story, but kills the action as a result. Heck, audio logs appear just for progressing through the game. No need to find em. And TNO holds players' hands thru everything. Someone is always on the radio detailing each step. And when "map updated" appears on screen, "secret" items are revealed on the map with a question mark. Too easy. Too pandering.
Sigh. Overall, TNO feels like a tacky homage. I'm annoyed that one of the final battles was ripped directly from Quake 4. Plus, TNO lacks the brutal combat and creativity of the games that made id synonymous with the fps genre. The new developers tried unsuccessfully to create an emotional backdrop instead of focusing on Wolfenstein's most important trait: Gunplay carnage. I'm all for a good story, but TNO's story was so violent, so gory, and just so over the top that I stopped buying into it. How much damage can the main character withstand? There's a difference between badassdom and just plain ridiculous. By the game's end, I didn't have that, "Oh yeah, come get you some" feeling like I did in Max Payne 3. Instead, I was glad it was over.
Wolfenstein TNO is an OK fps. Unfortunately, TNO assimilates elements from other popular games without creating its own identity. This is not the nonstop ride gamers expect. Even worse, it's a console port that needed months of polish before its PC launch. TNO still has performance issues weeks after launch. Asking 49,99€ for buggy title with no multiplayer is a tall order. Wait for this game to go on sale.

I used to play this game back when it was only on the Sony Online network back in 2012, so I have seen this game change over the years. They have added new continents, new weapons, abilities and a whole new development team. One thing remains constant however, you will die. A lot. Dying and respawning is a intergral part of this game. And you when you first start out you are probably going to spend more time looking at the respawn screen than actually shooting at people. But, little by little, if you stick with it, you will gradually get better. Earn some certs. Get slightly, ever so slightly better guns. Then get sniped by someone a hundred levels above you from three hundred meters away who has a gun they payed real money for.
That being said, if you stick with this game it can be a lot of fun. They have added a lot of new features that make this game a lot easier to get in to. Including a continent for beginners and a leveling system based on achievments to give you the certs needed to not make your character absolutely awful. Of course, once you are through with that you will be transported to the main continents where the aforementioned expert players are.
The combat itself is really fun. Shooting people in this game is so much more rewarding in this game. Mainly because the guns are really hard to use. Bullet drop, tons of recoil and spread. Somewhat low ammunition amounts. But that is what adds to the fun. The vehicles have a bit of learning curve, especially the aircraft.
This game is a free-to-play, so naturally there is a divide between the free and the paid. All of the guns can be purchased with either real money, or certs you get for completing challenges and gaining experience. But I will say this game gives you a lot of content for being free and it rarely beats you over the head with trying to get you to pay for stuff. And honestly, I eventually had to throw the developers a bone and buy a gun just because I felt bad for how many hours I had played and not given them money.
Eventually you will realize that all of you work is for naught. Mainly people in this game just rush into whatever battle they can find and not provide any real strategic advantage. You will see your compatriots begin to farm themselves by rushing into the same choke points and getting slaughtered. You will also need to get used to your "allies" rushing infront of your gun as your fire down a hallway and getting themselves killed. You will also get run over by their vehicles. You will also get blown up by their poorly thrown grenades. You will also hop in a vehicle being piloted by someone else only for them to rush headlong into enemy fire and get you both destroyed. Ah, memories.
Honestly, you should really give it a try, you can use all the classes and all the vehicles from the start, and apparently they are going to be adding some base building content soon. Its probably the best time to get into the game, I mean, it is free after all.

Holy hell is this a good game, where do I even start? Well let's start with the obvious. The gameplay. Holy hell does this game have the tightest gameplay I have ever seen in a shooter. I don't know how to describe it other than just saying it is "perfect". Also there are quite a few things in this that make it stand out from other shooters, like how it doesn't have HP regen and you have to use pain pills to get health back. Also the weapon system allows you to carry 2 side-arms and a long gun. You can also dual-wield both your sidearms but it causes you to drop the long arm because where is he gonna put it? Dual-wielding is pretty simple, you can still aim with right click because the left click shoots both. But the big thing in the Max Payne series is the slow-mo and, much like it's predecessors, it is amazing. Jumping around a corner and headshotting 5 baddies in one quick blast of gunfire feels awesome.
Also the not only is the gameplay good but the story is pretty good too. The actual entire overarching story isn't the most interesting story ever but it is told through the eyes of Max Payne who narrates everything in his awesome gritty style. Another absolutely perfect aspect of this game is the music and sound. For one thing the guns sound right which is good but the music can be really amazing at parts. It just fits in with what is going on so damn well. Other parts has crappy dance club music but that is to be expected when having a shoot-out at a dance club that plays crappy dance club music so it technically fits I guess. Also the graphics look damn good but then again what game made this decade doesn't? All in all I would say that any of these aspects alone would make the game worth it but put it all together and you have something really special.
