This game has now been out for close to 4 years and while breaking off SoE to become a former subsidiary company known as Daybreak, the developers of this game continue to astonish me with just how absurdly stupid they are in their design decisions and overall handling of the game. Let me list some things and explain the how and whats.
------------------------------------------------
1. Any remotely large-scale battles are no longer an actual part of this game. They used to be, but not anymore as 99.9% of all squad/platoon/clan leaders will today without hesitation recall their entire group back to a nearby warpgate if they face even a remotely stagnant/even situation when battling for a point of interest because It is so horrendously more efficient to just zerg-rush locations with vast superior numbers than to actually fight for them. This can mainly be contributed to two things.
A) The disgusting lack of population control that still plagues this series since PS1 as one faction can have 43% of all players while another can only have 19% and the only thing the 19% guys get is a small XP boost. Think you're gonna realistically achieve, capture or defend anything when they have 2.5 times more guys that constantly reinforce ontop of their already superior numbers? Hell no.
B) The game has lost over 60% of It's population over the years due to developer mismanagement and is currently in an all-time low for good reason:
- The worlds are all gigantic and having 1.8k guys across 4 different servers with 3 giant worlds each means that there is literally no chance in hell that "natural" large-scales battles occur anymore.
------------------------------------------------
2. This game STILL manages to run like absolute garbage for many people (even after SoE's publicity stunt that is the OMFG: Operation Make Faster Game which took them 2 years after release to realize that their game runs like a horse-turd that has been left out in the sun) both frame-rate wise and latency and while I don't have any personal problem with this due to my PC being reasonably powerful with a fiber-optic connection (and me favoring low graphics for higher FPS in shooters), the forums are still swamped with people asking for help as to why their up-to-par computer struggles to render 30 frames per second at medium settings and why they died from a guy shooting a corridor where they were 15 seconds ago. Instead of biting down and doing their due diligence adressing this and some of the countless other issues and bugs this game currently suffers from, the developers instead opt in to jamming the in-game shop full with more cráp that to this day still allows a strong argument to be made that the game has pay-2-win elements with some singular guns (pistols included) cost up to 1,000 certification points (weeks of grinding for most people) without attachments and camoflages only being available for real-life money.
------------------------------------------------

So I've put 40 hours into this game, and that's 40 hours I won't be getting back along with the $40 I spent for extra things in game. So without futher delay here are some reasons why you probably should pass on this game in favor of an at home colonoscopy.
First let me start by saying that my 40 hours spent on this was not completely awful.  The game has more than a few good features you won't find anywhere else, and for that reason alone makes this game enticing.  Unfortunately these good features are wore thin very quickly as your forced to drown in the other liquid feces PlanetSide funnels into your mouth.
System requirements:  Now anyone thinking about trying this game out should be very confident in your PC's capability in running it.  They do very little to compact any visual data so if you don't have a strong set up your machine will most likely struggle and die.  My PC ran this game just fine, and my negative opinion doesn't stem from any graphical issues but with that being said this game isn't impressive looking even when you can run it fluidly with max textures. It's like a blind person being able to see for the first time and he's just like.. "Yeah sure, this is okay."
Massive combat:  Massive combat is pretty much this games selling point, the trailers are misleading because you see a few people on screen at once so you think to yourself; "Oy me un me mayts ken go 'round noscoping nubs like in de bleckops!", and you will be horribly mistaken.  The mass combat in this game is unlike anything you will see in other multiplayer MMO's, there are several maps or 'continents' that act as battlegrounds, and each of these maps are generally as large as a map you would see in a modern sandbox RPG.  In these maps are strategic locations you fight over, and in these fights there will be anywhere from 1-100 people running around murdering each other. The game does a decent job making you feel like this is actual combat rather than a preformatted death match.  If you have high levels of anxiety, be prepared to stay crouched behind some boxes crying while hundreds of explosions and gunfire kill all of your friends forming a mass grave around you.
Sounds fun right? No, you're wrong shame on you.  The problems start with friendly fire; oh yes, friendly fire is very active.  Now in most games with friendly fire, there will be that one guy who can't seem to tell friend from foe and will always dump a three round burst into you as you come around the corner.  Annoying, but it's usually only one guy.  But what if I told you that not only were there multiple people like that on your team, they didn't stop shooting until you were dead?  Keep in mind you have shields and a health bar, it takes 2/3rds of a clip to drop people sometimes.  That means these people hold down their mouse button for a solid second and a half thinking they're doing something good.  Of course I could assume there are just that many people who get off on team killing, but somehow I think that's being optimistic.  Aside from that, sometimes friendly fire is just hard to avoid because there's so many people wriggling around on screen.  Everyone uses that zigzag never stop moving technique that's popular with FPS games, but the problem is that you're doing that while 20 people are around you trying to shoot stuff AND everyone else is doing that too.  Which brings me to my next point...
You realize why the mainstream FPS's don't implement mass combat on this scale; aside from the technical issues, it really does affect gameplay negatively.  In a game that promotes squad based tactical actions and gameplay, you instead get 30 individuals playing rambo.  No one communicates in this game, and when they finally do you'll very quickly beg them to stop communicating.  You will realize the futility of it all, and at that point you realize the 'Mass Combat' you were once excited about was a poor gimmick.
Microtransactions~  It's Daybreak, which is normally all that should be said before moving on..  However I feel the need to quickly touch on this subject.  The game is free, mostly.  New weapons can be unlocked with CERTS, a type of currency you gain from leveling up.  You also use these certs to enhance or buy EVERYTHING else from weapon attachments, class upgrades, vehicle upgrades, vehicle weapons, and camo.  You don't get very many certs for leveling up, at BR 15 I think it's possible to earn a total of 3000 certs (I'm probably wrong). Problem is leveling up is fairly difficult in the current state of this game, and requires a very specific and tedious method to grind levels.  Alternatively you can spend real money on Daybreak funbucks (or whatever) which unfortunately I did.  The exchange rate is poor, meaning $40 was enough to buy me one extremely cheap camo and a few guns.  Overall it did very little to improve the experience and once again you feel the futility of it all crashing down on you.
So should you play this?  Well, if you have 12+gigs of hard drive space and have nothing better to do with your empty life than sure give it a try.  Otherwise, don't bother.  It isn't worth further diminishing your faith in humanity.

So I've put 40 hours into this game, and that's 40 hours I won't be getting back along with the $40 I spent for extra things in game. So without futher delay here are some reasons why you probably should pass on this game in favor of an at home colonoscopy.
First let me start by saying that my 40 hours spent on this was not completely awful.  The game has more than a few good features you won't find anywhere else, and for that reason alone makes this game enticing.  Unfortunately these good features are wore thin very quickly as your forced to drown in the other liquid feces PlanetSide funnels into your mouth.
System requirements:  Now anyone thinking about trying this game out should be very confident in your PC's capability in running it.  They do very little to compact any visual data so if you don't have a strong set up your machine will most likely struggle and die.  My PC ran this game just fine, and my negative opinion doesn't stem from any graphical issues but with that being said this game isn't impressive looking even when you can run it fluidly with max textures. It's like a blind person being able to see for the first time and he's just like.. "Yeah sure, this is okay."
Massive combat:  Massive combat is pretty much this games selling point, the trailers are misleading because you see a few people on screen at once so you think to yourself; "Oy me un me mayts ken go 'round noscoping nubs like in de bleckops!", and you will be horribly mistaken.  The mass combat in this game is unlike anything you will see in other multiplayer MMO's, there are several maps or 'continents' that act as battlegrounds, and each of these maps are generally as large as a map you would see in a modern sandbox RPG.  In these maps are strategic locations you fight over, and in these fights there will be anywhere from 1-100 people running around murdering each other. The game does a decent job making you feel like this is actual combat rather than a preformatted death match.  If you have high levels of anxiety, be prepared to stay crouched behind some boxes crying while hundreds of explosions and gunfire kill all of your friends forming a mass grave around you.
Sounds fun right? No, you're wrong shame on you.  The problems start with friendly fire; oh yes, friendly fire is very active.  Now in most games with friendly fire, there will be that one guy who can't seem to tell friend from foe and will always dump a three round burst into you as you come around the corner.  Annoying, but it's usually only one guy.  But what if I told you that not only were there multiple people like that on your team, they didn't stop shooting until you were dead?  Keep in mind you have shields and a health bar, it takes 2/3rds of a clip to drop people sometimes.  That means these people hold down their mouse button for a solid second and a half thinking they're doing something good.  Of course I could assume there are just that many people who get off on team killing, but somehow I think that's being optimistic.  Aside from that, sometimes friendly fire is just hard to avoid because there's so many people wriggling around on screen.  Everyone uses that zigzag never stop moving technique that's popular with FPS games, but the problem is that you're doing that while 20 people are around you trying to shoot stuff AND everyone else is doing that too.  Which brings me to my next point...
You realize why the mainstream FPS's don't implement mass combat on this scale; aside from the technical issues, it really does affect gameplay negatively.  In a game that promotes squad based tactical actions and gameplay, you instead get 30 individuals playing rambo.  No one communicates in this game, and when they finally do you'll very quickly beg them to stop communicating.  You will realize the futility of it all, and at that point you realize the 'Mass Combat' you were once excited about was a poor gimmick.
Microtransactions~  It's Daybreak, which is normally all that should be said before moving on..  However I feel the need to quickly touch on this subject.  The game is free, mostly.  New weapons can be unlocked with CERTS, a type of currency you gain from leveling up.  You also use these certs to enhance or buy EVERYTHING else from weapon attachments, class upgrades, vehicle upgrades, vehicle weapons, and camo.  You don't get very many certs for leveling up, at BR 15 I think it's possible to earn a total of 3000 certs (I'm probably wrong). Problem is leveling up is fairly difficult in the current state of this game, and requires a very specific and tedious method to grind levels.  Alternatively you can spend real money on Daybreak funbucks (or whatever) which unfortunately I did.  The exchange rate is poor, meaning $40 was enough to buy me one extremely cheap camo and a few guns.  Overall it did very little to improve the experience and once again you feel the futility of it all crashing down on you.
So should you play this?  Well, if you have 12+gigs of hard drive space and have nothing better to do with your empty life than sure give it a try.  Otherwise, don't bother.  It isn't worth further diminishing your faith in humanity.

The story is definitely not what you would expect considering the first two games in the series. It had a very Kane-&-Lynch-esque feel to it which is a bit unfortunate. Although it is enjoyable at first it ends up dragging on a bit too long and is a bit of a mess. Definitely the weakest part of the game.
There are multi-player and arcade modes that add replayability to the game, but am unable to comment on the quality of these modes at the writing of this review as I am yet to play them.
Max Payne 3 is definitely worth adding to your collection and give it a play through.

After a long, nine-year-long sleep, Max returns with all the galantry and badassery we´ve come to expect, but this time he does so with some cool new additions which elevate this third entry above its two counterparts.
Some flashback sequences aside, the action has shifted from the cold, dark alleys of New York to the sun-soaked favelas of Brazil, a first in the series, and boy does it suit the franchise well. This setting is Rockstar´s perfect opportunity to boast some incredibly detailed scenarios and astounding lighting effects, not to mention Max´s life-like reactions and breathtaking cinematics.
The story, while engaging from the get-go, does get somewhat muddled by the end, with several different names flying by without giving you a second to give a face to them, but then again, the story has always shared this trait in the previous offerings. What never gets old are Max´s quirky remarks dotted throughout the 12-hour-long campaign, which have become a trademark of the cop´s adventures. The visual design works wonders with the narrative feel, as key words are highlighted when a cutscene hits, giving the title a distinct feel above other, more generic third person shooters.
Of course, what would Max Payne be without bullet time? Dead, that´s what. But fear not, because this aspect which made the first two games so appealing is back, now packed with more over-the-top situations in which to try it out. A cover sistem has been introduced for the first time, and it feels way more natural than just standing behind corners like a big ol´ chump the Max from nine years ago did. Also, this time you actually see your character taking painkillers, instead of just magically regenerating your health for no apparent reason. These cool new features, added to the increase in guns and varied level design, give the title at hand a new dose of realism, to the point you actually feel this guy could totally exist in the real world.
Last, and most probably least, is the multiplayer portion. While it carries over the amazing slo-mo kills and over-the-top action, it can´t help but feel tacked-on, a way to lengthen the game´s overall duration, but definitely not in a good way. It does provide a fun few hours, but that´s probably all you will spend in it.
Overall, Max Payne 3 is an amazing experience, proving Rockstar is not only the master of open-world games, but also really good at trying its hand at relentless, third-person action. It could use a bit of tweaking here and there, and the multiplayer portion could have been better implemented, but that shouldn´t distract you from what this game really is: a fantastic, dazzling, non-stop thriller which will grab hold of you and won´t let go until you see it through.
Pros:
+ Intriguing, if somewhat muddled, story
+ Fantastic audiovisual design
+ Max´s character, a fascinating insight into one of gaming´s most beloved anti-heroes
+ Bullet-time and all the spectacle it provides
+ Social Club integration
+ Voice acting is once again top-notch
Cons:
- Lackluster multiplayer
- Some of Max´s remarks don´t quite impress like they used to back in the day
- A co-op mode would have been gratefully accepted
Final grade: 9.4 (Amazing)

If you have an AMD based computer DO NOT BUY THIS GAME! It is unplayable on the lowest settings. As a PR Veteran I was looking forward to trying out Squad. Alas the game is not optimized for AMD based computers. At this time I do not recommend this game for anyone who has AMD. Intel go right ahead, you're going to have a blast.
Edit: I guess Fanboys are going to Fanboy. Don't get me wrong I think in the long run this game is going to be amazing but UE4 is not great for AMD based computers. The fact that people are downvoting this because it is a negative review of the game shows me the kind of community we are. I thought we were better than this but clearly not. I am raising awareness for AMD users to not buy the game yet. This actually makes them not buy the game yet...which is good. Yes I said it is good that they aren't buying it. Why? Because then they don't leave a negative review as well. One bad review that educates some people is better than twenty negative reviews cause they never saw what I said. So which will it be? One bad review on the front page warning off AMD users for now or it can be twenty bad reviews from AMD users. Once AMD issues are solved I heavily recommend the game to AMD users, until then though I only recommend it to Intel Users. That is why I'm leaving a negative review. As I have said already once UE4 is friendly to AMD users I will recommend this game to everyone and it will be a thumbs up from me. AMD users currently should buy at their own risk. I will keep this review updated. In the meantime I hope people find this helpful rather than just downvoting it since its negative. This review in my opinion will help the game in the long run. One negative review that will be changed to a positive in time or twenty+ that will always be left as negatives. It is the communities choice.
Edit 2: I want to stress that the lack of support for AMD based computers is not Offworld Industries fault. This is an inherent problem with UE4. The Devs cannot do anything about this problem. Some people have managed to have great success with AMD in this game and others like myself cannot play. Some people cannot even get into a match. This is a good game, I'm sure I'll enjoy it in the future. But I cannot leave a positive review of a game that doesn't even work on my system currently. It would be a huge disservice to many people if I did saying "10/10 would tacticool again" and I am leaving this feedback for them so they make a practical decision on what they spend their money on. I look forward to watching this game develop. I'll keep the review updated as it progresses. This is currently the only review I have ever written about a game which should show I clearly care enough about this game to review it. I want this game to succeed, but not at the expense of people who can't even play it.

I knew, 30 seconds into the public test that I would love The Talos Principle, and the full game did not disappoint. My favorite aspects of the game include:
The music
The voice acting (even though there are only 2 voices)
The environments/lighting/atmosphere
Each of the endings
Yeah, a couple of the endings are lack-luster, but within the context of the game, each ending has a purpose. The game as a whole would be incomplete without any one of them. For me, it was a thrill to go back and play them all, when each one gave a bit more information about the world.
Just enough information to speculate and give ideas, but little enough that the lore ends up arguably being whatever you see in it.
The puzzles, being the main gameplay mechanic, are not too difficult. The few that had me stumped were solved by leaving the area, doing other challenges, and coming back to them with fresh eyes. The more intense Star puzzles, though, kicked my♥♥♥♥♥in a very welcome manner. The game is also replayable at least twice, if you become invested in the philosophy and backstory of the game.
I would recommend The Talos Principle to anyone who loves puzzles, and also to all of humanity.

Whats so addicting about this game? ... The gameplay, period... There are daily missions to do and even though most characters are locked I have 3 so far and about to get 2 more, I don't think I've put much effort, in fact its the missions that kept me going where in other F2P FPS games they usually lack any meaty reward ; or the drive of the mission gets burnt out very quickly!
The missions are good but dont expect a huge treasure chest.. They usually give in-game currency at a decent boost allowing even an average player close to at least 1k a game at some points, bonus for fist wins give you up to 1k, theres alot of points to be earned which reminds me of battlefield / team fortress where if you wanted to level up then choosing a support class like for medic or any ammo providing class is a first choice, meaning you will get ammo, and meds.
The system is similar to Overwatch when select a character or "merc" which is usually the default "card" loadout, each merc has multiple loadouts that can be purchased or earned in various ways.. Although not completely original.. It reminds me of an Overwatch / Battlefield w very squad and team oriented combat abilities.. Some classes are generally going to suffer a kill death ratio loss simply because they are underpowered.. However having those classes like mentioned before give the player an opportunity to milk the crap out of that xp and these players are praised as gods sometimes because they can turn over a battle in minutes!
The actual gameplay is very fast-paced, but expect bullet sponging and some point.. It's annoying but only to a point.. I do feel that some classes should be rebalanced, but lets face it thats EVERY game.
Movement is actually key and suprisingly it is very encouraged.. Every game mode is based on some objective in some way so theres always things to do and positions on the map changing for flanks. This makes the maps alot less boring which is a tip of a hat to Team Fortress in my opinion.. You play the same damn map 20 times but it feels so different because of the players use of each class.. Then stack on the loadout "cards" which swap weapons and give the mercs specific abilites that enhance certain playstyle quality this makes for a nice melting pot.
I think they should offer more control over graphical settings in there engine, what is offered is very impressive but that option of on or off is , in my opinion, not enough control
Please add more varitey of maps, this is what I am waiting for
The selection of weapons is hearty but not that expansive, some weapons are generally common but I don't see an issue of the "one" over used weapon.. not yet at least
Rebalance of weapons, just make a tweak to the hitboxs, its NOT THAT BAD.. just sometimes it feels like it should take maybe one and a half more shots? Does anyone experience this? Still only an opinion..

When I first got the game, I loved it to pieces, couldn't stop playing it, but then they basically demolished the tech tree, which made it quite boring. I took a bit of a break to let them sort the game out, and hoped I would come back to a game I could love again, but no such luck. I've watched this game slowly regress into a grind-until-your-fingers-hurt kind of game. It used to be that higher ranked players would get better rewards, and that skill was actually rewarded, now it's possible for a brand new player to get top tier (sorry, "legendary") gear, as long as they top the learderboard.
I'm not saying the old version of the game was perfect; some aspects of the game have improved with updates, but it's almost impossible to find a game without some annoying bot which is almost impossible to kill. In most games, that's a perfectly acceptable event; somebody has more skill at the game than you - but with the integration of the Factory, hundreds of players can have the exact same bot, and all they need is some in-game currency, which is handed out to anybody and everybody.
I'm recommending this game because, as a general idea, it's a great game, but I'd still like to see some tweaks.
side note: I do understand that no game is perfect; but I feel that despite its progress, this game has taken a bit of a step backwards in the overall scheme

The third problem is a combination of the first two, where you will go into a cutscene and come out of it with enemies standing right in front of your crosshairs and instead of having your shotgun or rifle selected, you instead have out your single pistol and if you go to switch to your rifle after taking cover, the game will drop it on the ground. There are a huge amount of comments regarding the cost and some negative reviews based on this fact. Personally - as an Arma player and big fan of realism games - SQUAD looks  like it has the potential to be amazing.
Yes I was initially surprised at the 30 quid price tag for an early access, but given people paying EA/DICE hundreds to get all of the recent Battlefront content, I seriously know which game I'll get more value from (squad).
This game IS fantastic. It has the suspense and adrenaline fueled madness that one might expect from a shooter adopting a realism stance that's only comparison I can think of would be Arma or Insurgency. It's fantastic when you get a squad that works together and deploys effective tactics to flank your enemy or identify hot spots. You really do get immersed and lost in the fight.
Key word here guys is TEAMWORK. Don't get this game if you want to run around shooting down the entire enemy team single handed. The heartbeat of this game is teamwork, and done effectively it can be immensely rewarding and fun. The first time I heard the radio bleep effect on the squad VOIP I had the biggest smile on my face. It truly feels great.
We all hope — given the large amount of games never leaving alpha — that Squad will deliver on it's promising start. But I fully endorse the price tag at this stage. I've bought dozens of triple A titles and regretted the money I lost on games that don't deliver, but squad is shaping up to be a game I can loose myself in. Yes there is a tone of work to do, it is after all in alpha. But I feel my 30 quid is well spent and already find myself being heavily addicted to this game and even right now I want to jump in, find me a squad and join the fight.
It simply comes down to this. If 30 quid is a lot of money to you, and to most of us it is - and you feel *unsure* on SQUAD, then hold off. But I guarantee, providing you're not looking for a COD/Battlefield experience, then you'll love this.

First off - I love this game, it is the spiritual successor of the (now) free "game"(/mod) Project Reality (
).
The focus of this game is teamwork, coordination, and realistic combat (as far as you can go without losing the fun in a "game"). Some people title it a MilSim, when it really isn't and it is not trying to. Instead, it finds a good balance between MilSim and FPS.
Actually, why am I so convinced that the game will be great when it leaves Early Access? Well, firstly, because many of the developers are (former or current) developers of Project Reality, which I spoke about, above. And they worked on that Battlefield 2 mod for over 10 years now, taking so much out of that over 10 year old engine that you wouldn't believe. They made a game targeted for 2x2 km battles and turned it into a full-scaled huge military game with so many assets and aspects, that it turned into a niche in itself.
But - With a NEW engine and therefor: new possibilites, new aspects, new features, less bugs (because finally, this concept on a new engine without over 10 year old restrictions). And I have so much hope and love for this game, because this niche is something very special to me.

Performance is a very wide factor because everyone experiences different things.
- AMD CPU users seem to suffer under various unoptimizations under the current Unreal-Engine-4 build (obviously developed by Epic, and not Off World Industries who made Squad).
The game relying on this engine means it suffers the same issues but then again has a very dedicated development team which is focused on the engine alone and will fix these issues sooner or later (they'd be working on it by a few days by now as I read).
- AMD GPU users (like me) have issues with certain driver-versions. I had huge problems with the 15.x drivers no matter if I ran under Crimson or CatalysControlCenter Software. Downgrading to 14.x and applying various INI-file twaks I found on the official forums (
), made my game hop to 60 FPS on my pretty old AMD HD 7970 @ 3GB VRAM.
Right now, everything is working as it should and I'm super happy about this.
Obviously, this whole topic is something still being worked on heavily and also
The gameplay is already very similar to Project Reality INF-only layouts, you basically rely on your team communication, on your Squad Leader and on your teammates (damn, what would you do without medics in this game?). Lonewolfing without being in a Squad is a No-No, just like RPG-spamming (will be gone once the supply system which'll be bound to vehicles is finished) and not talking while being an SL (you can very well not talk as a squad member, but please don't do squad lead in that case).

The Talos Principle mixes a first-person puzzle (think Portal) with an absolutely unhealthy amount of philosophy.
The puzzle mechanics seem limited, but the designers did an amazing job of creating incredibly complex puzzles out of a few simple pieces. And with each puzzle you solve, the game seems to show you five more that you need to complete. Plenty of content!
Throughout most of the game, you'll be asked questions. Deep ones. Questions that will challenge your views on morality, reason, logic, and even your definition of reality. This, combined with the puzzles, left me with quite a few enjoyable headaches.
On top of that, there's a plotline that will tease you repeatedly, and leave you asking questions that no other game has before.
If you manage to take a breather, you'll find yourself in a world with breathtaking scenery and a soundtrack that gives you goosebumps.
I can't see myself playing through it twice, but I'm oh-so-very-glad that I did it once.

The Talos Principle may be one of the single greatest games I have ever played. I cannot recommend it enough. It cost me 40 dollars, but I would have definitely spent 60 for such a wonderful game.
Gameplay:
Outstanding. The puzzles are extremely fun, and the later ones are challenging enough to push your puzzle solving skills to the limit, but not so ridiculous as to needlessly frustrate you. At first I wasn't impressed. It just felt like Portal, but with Jammers and Lasers. But as I unlocked more puzzles and the tools needed to solve them, I started to change my mind. The puzzles are very well thought out, and you have to really think outside the box for the difficult ones.
Graphics:
It's nothing that's going to push your hardware to the limits, but it's a breathtakingly beautiful game. There's not too much to say here. It's simply a good looking game.
Plot [SPOILERS!]:
From the moment I started the game, I knew I wanted to find out what was really going on. Elohim seemed off to me, and the glitches everywhere that make it obvious you are in a virtual reality made me adamant about findind answers. As you advance through the game, you receive more and more clues about what really happened. There were many points in the game that I was overwhelmed when hearing about what happened, that it made me cry. Literal, actual tears. Before I go on, I know there are multiple ways to "complete" the game, but I consider the Ascension Ending to be the true ending. At first, I didn't really like the ending. It didn't satisfy me. But then I thought about it, and that's because it was (seriously SPOILERS) it wasn't really a happy ending. And I realized that wasn't fair of me to not like the ending just because it's sort of sad. The point was for it to be sad. And the more I thought about it, the more I started to get emotional, and I started to cry more. The Talos Principle is a game whose plot moved me to tears on multiple occassions. Granted, I'm a little sensitive, but that should tell you the plot is definitely of good quality.
I STRONGLY recommend this game, especially to those who love puzzle games. The gameplay alone is worth it. I'd say the even the plot alone is worth it.
If I had to give the game a score, it would be something like:
Gameplay: 9.5
Graphics: 9
Plot: 9
Overall: 9
It's free and better than most AAA titles, why haven't you got it yet?

Max Payne 3 is a fitting continuation of the Max Payne series. The gameplay feels modern with realistic and detailed animations for any action. Yet it retains the enjoyable gameplay of flying through the air in slow-mo whilst popping heads and landing in real time with the area clear. This is the bullet time gameplay Remedy pioneered with the original Max Payne in the wake of The Matrix and has inspired a host of titles since.
Gameplay
Rockstar has kept the formula left by Remedy in addition to new features such as last stand where at least one bottle of painkillers will give the player a chance to take vengeance by slowing down time and focusing on your killer. This feature acts as a safety net but when your attacker is obscured or your clip is empty, it’s a painfully slow, unskippable animation of Max clumsily dying. DEAD is likely a word you’ll see many times especially playing on hard. Luckily, after a couple of retries, you’ll start respawning with extra painkillers, extra ammo and return to full health. It’s hard to blame the game however, more often you’ll blame your own hastiness, inaccuracy or the lack of using cover, another new feature.
The Rockstar guys have been implementing cover mechanics, made famous by the Gears series, in their games since GTA IV and it’s not much different here, except Max’s love of standing up from prone into the line of fire instead of snapping from prone directly into cover. Blind fire from cover became an increasingly useful tactic to pick off rapidly approaching enemies, who in general were quick to flank or use cover as well. Though, when your reticule is placed over the enemies last known location, it can be annoying when they don’t move out from cover until your reticule is moved slightly elsewhere. This breaks the realism and adds some cheapness to the design.
There is often extra slow-mo, John Woo-esque, set pieces that keep the game fresh and add new scenarios, but the gameplay is solid throughout. This was a huge relief coming into the game as a massive fan of the original Max Payne games.
Story
In keeping with tradition, the storyline is nonlinear and narrated by Max Payne but does not feature the iconic graphic novel, still panels from the previous games. Instead there are constant distortion effects during cutscenes, including scanlines, highlighted words, 24-style screen segmentation and disorientating colour bleeds. This was to highlight Max’s depravity in drink and drugs but it ends up being distracting. I’d take graphic novel panels over these cutscenes any day. The dialogue is good and Max is an engaging character but its dark story and unlikable characters, except Max, do make the story drag on longer than it should.
My biggest problem with the story is the disconnect from the first two games. Mona Sax survived in my game. Their romance kept them alive. Yet she is only mentioned as a passing fling, which ruined the connection I had with Max and Mona in ‘The Fall’. In the Remedy games, Max always attempted to apply meaning to everything to justify his actions. It was endearing to see a character so dark just searching for peace and normality. Yet Max Payne 3 puts all his torment down to drink and drugs. A character trait rarely mentioned previously and more often his grief and lust for Mona drove his decisions. His dead wife is still the crux in which Max is searching for redemption yet his last words in ‘The Fall’ were ‘I had a dream of my wife. She was dead. But it was ok.’
Details like this all start to make it feel the change of developer has affected the series’ tone. Not having Sam Lake as lead writer has definitely shifted Max’s dialogue from poetic, dark humour to just plain dark. The names of the difficulty levels have also changed from Detective|Hard-boiled|Dead on Arrival to Easy|Normal|Hard. Admittedly, this is a minor issue, but if it means the same it should just be called the same to keep continuity. Rockstar should’ve paid more attention to the series traits, big or small, that made Max Payne such an appealing IP in the first place.
Technical
Everything thing from the animations, the guns, the bullets, the sounds, the music, the destructible environments, the detail, the facial animations, the lighting, the framerate, the voice acting, the 3D and the level designs are all superb. There’s not much more to say when a game has a Rockstar seal of quality.
Verdict
Shooting people with hand cannons has never been more satisfying than in Max Payne 3. I just wish Rockstar treated the canon the same way. Special mention to James McCaffrey for his amazing, continuous portrayal of Max and for his likeness.

This could've been a good game if only for a couple of big things.
1) Graphics
It's pretty much RAGE with updated graphics honestly. What I was most surprised about was the performance hit my system was taking when I turned every thing up. Turns out for the PPF and Shadow Resolution setting you must set them on 16 and 2048 regardless of your system specs because this port isn't optomized for PC. Other things that bother me with this game being a port is that the performance for this game feels subpar even after setting in the fix, VSYNC is completely broken the only thing turning it on does is create texture load ins. (remember that in RAGE? Oh yea they never did fix that) There is no AA for this game, funny how this is a PC game too.
I got my game running smoothly at 1080p 60FPS (for the most part some parts just tank to 40ish when it opens up like the Miner area) using everything turned up except those two number ones. And it played pretty smoothly for some odd reason however almost every cutscene had random hiccups and stutters all of a sudden where it would freeze for a split second and audio would cut out. Not that big of a deal but pretty dumb, I know it was with this game and not my system either.
2) Pacing
This is probably my biggest annoyance. I played the game on hard cuz I watched Frankie start this game on Normal and it was just too easy, I've also heard this game is too easy to be a Wolfenstein game, they're right it is. Playing it on normal will bore most players out of their mind, because a lot of this game is simply cutscenes. And I have a feeling this game would be even easier in some parts. And this is why I feel like developers don't actually playtest their game outside of "developer mode" and look for the experience a player gets. Either that or the playtesters they have are simply too good or too bad at games.
On hard mode, regular soldiers are still easy as pie, however certain enemies become stupid hard. For instance at the prison level the big soldiers with shotguns have perfect aim with a shotgun from miles away, something that's not possible to even do with the gun. At far away they do 20ish damage per shot (keep in mind you have between a 100-140 health around here), up close they will do 70 - 100 damage. Of course that wouldn't be a problem just stay the hell away right? And here's the other problem lack of ammo. I think of myself as someone who can aim not AMAZING but well enough where I'm definitely above average. Of coruse for some reason in the most challenging or frustrating areas I found for this game I found a consistent lack of ammo. With many times I had to simply give up because I ran out of ammo for a specific gun, this in turn would cause me to use a pistol or shotgun or different type of killing methods (by force) on other enemies so that for the specific gun I do need for the much harder enemy I will have the necessary amount of ammo to take them down.
Sounds simple enough, now about those checkpoints....see sometimes the checkpoints are cleverly placed in correct places. And sometimes you're going to rip your hair out in frustration of having to do the same scene for the 3rd or 4th time. I know it doesn't sound like a big deal having to do something 3 or 4 times in a video game shouldn't be too bad. However when the scene between checkpoints is about a half hour long that in turn takes about 2 hours of time just doing the same thing over and over again often times having to die because you ran out of ammo again. Is this suppose to be a survival horror game? Or an arcade shooter? Or is this a stealth game? I feel like this game can't make up it's mind and forces all three modes on you in the end doing none of them really correct. The healing mechanic is okay and makes sense, except that it encourages sitting in behind cover for 30 mins at a time and shooting, kind of like every other game out there.
The last gripe I have about the pacing of this game has to be the way enemies are introduced into the world at certain points. See enemies don't come out of doors or areas or anything...they are literally spawned in. They won't spawn them in front of your eyes they will move the spawn locations if you are in the spawn location, but what this means is that the enemies can literally appear from nowhere on your sides or behind you without any indication of them getting there, and considering that you die in literally 2-3 seconds of shooting in this game and that checkpoints can take you back a half hour into the game you can imagine how frustrating this can get.
3) Controls
This game was optomized for the Xbox Controller plain and simple but even on the 360 controller it's bad. Throwing a knife and melee are merely tapping the Right Stick or Holding the right stick. Hope your controller is clean. It's a lot easier to mess up then you think. Movement feels clunky to me, holding the Lb button switches weapon but tapping it throws a grenade, you can only imagine the fun you'll have with that. Switching weapons using the Lb button is so clunky and slow I feel like half of my deaths were due simply to that, a lot of times you select a weapon and it simply won't switch for you instead making you wait a second or two for no reason. Other times it will be done instantly. Lastly many times there are invisible barrier that block bullets whether they be around walls or between fences, Ive literally emptied clips between fences and missed every bullet, testing it of course I just can't believe some of the things left in this game. Some walls protrude around corners more than the actual corner, I've tested this, which means it will either block bullets from the invisible corner or the bounce grenades back at your face. Have fun with that. These issues with textures not matching to walls was found in RAGE as well, and has simply carried over.
4) Story
A joke, literally. Have fun with it though and try not to take it too seriously because if you do you'll be facepalming half the time. It makes no sense, is literally impossible and in the end goes against everything it's suppose to be standing for. Isn't it ironic how this "anti-racist" game is in itself a racist game? Every main character in this game has Aryan features, even the Jews don't look like Jews in this game. It's like they're afraid to show anyone NOT ARYAN. LMAO. The Nazis themselves however don't even look "Aryan" they actually look non-Aryan LMAO! The majority of Nazi commanders for instance are super pale nerd looking types, none of them are actual stereotypical Aryans. You are the stereotypical Aryan however, you and your random lady nurse who's a ♥♥♥♥♥ it seems as she enjoys implied♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥a vegetable. Also since 80% of the world are brown eyed, you only find a handful of people with brown eyes around, there no brown eyed people among the resistance, I guess the only ones who are vehemently against the Nazis are Aryans who would fit in perfectly.
The history behind the Nazis winning is laughable, the Nazis are the most evil thing in the world apparently. They betray Italy...for no reason. They betray Japan and control them and China...because they're superior. They of course refuse to mention the Nazi-Arab alliance because that would imply the Nazis were accepting of brownish skin people, and completely go against whatever this game is trying to say about Nazis. It's just easier not to mention Arabs in almost every Western game unless you're shooting them I suppose.
Of course the Nazi's defeating the US was another story, they have to specifically mention how the rebels put up such a good fight to the Nazis and made them desperate, this game reeks of vehement patriotism to the point of no belivability. It just feels like a game written by Westerns, I wanted a game where the universe truly felt like the Nazis controlled the world, this is not it. Not it at all, it's literally the opposite,

Return to Castle Wolfenstein was the game that got me excited to dive back into the series, This time the Occult was brought in to add more of a narrative and lets not forget the melding of man and machine. This game is everything I wished Portal was.  The graphics and flavor are phenomenal, it has a unique and stimulating "storyline" (whatever it is you would call it), and many of the puzzles are utterly clever. I rarely leave reviews for things but I'm leaving a review for this because I think this game is truly a masterpiece.  I don't know if I'd change a thing about it!
I should mention that I'm really good at these games.  In fact, I even impressed myself with the speed at which I solved some of the harder puzzles (sometimes disappointing since the act of failing is part of the fun!).  Yet, it still took me an extremely enjoyable 30 hours to beat the 100+ puzzles, which puts it at about $1.33/hour for entertainment.  That's a no-brainer in terms of entertainment value.  (EDIT:  I haven't yet collected all the star sigils and solved the extra puzzles... that'll probably get me well below $1/hr :))
One important note:  The puzzles start out pretty easy. This wasn't ideal for me, but it's probably perfect progression for "standard" players to learn the mechanics and interactions before getting fancy.    If you find yourself under-stimulated at first, stick with it.  I promise you there's plenty of good stuff to come!

This game is a disappointing entry into the Wolfestein series, and while it looks very nice and has a cool setting, it just falls flat in so many ways.
The combat doesn't really feel like its quite as polished as it should be. It's one of those shooters where your gun takes up the whole lower portion of your screen while aiming and you always try to hit the enemies head, so you pretty much can't see your enemies when you aim down sights. Enemies are perfectly accurate when firing through fire and smoke that you can't see through at all, making some parts of the game incredibly frustrating if you have a bunch of enemies sitting upwind of a burning car in the black smoke where you can't see them but they are pouring buckets of bullets into your head. The dual wield mechanic is cool, but there is rarely ever enough ammo for it. There are also way too many enemies that are just a huge bullet sponge and have no meaningful weak spots or special mechanics that let you fight them in any other way than to just isolate them and burn them down with a powerful weapon.
The game is also extremely short and disjointed. Overall it takes just around 10-12 hours to beat, which is OK if you buy it on sale, but for 60 bucks it's a bit short. I guess you could get twice that out of it if you went back for every single trophy. You can literally go from being in Berlin to being on the moon in a single button push in this game, because it tells the story at such a breakneck pace. The game is very unforgiving about letting you backtrack for trophies or side missions. you often have to guess whether jumping down some hole will lead you to a treasure and then bring you back to the main path, or is the way forward in the level and if you go down it you will miss out on everything else.
The plot in this game is also just absurd. (Spoilers beyond this point) The plotholes are so huge, this game would attempt to fly a helicopter through them. Yea, the resistance has a helicopter base inside the sewers in the middle of Berlin, and the Nazis don't notice this until it becomes convenient to have some people killed or captured to up the stakes for the final act. Never mind the fact that you captured a nuclear submarine-battleship-aircraft-carrier from the Nazis two missions before, everyone still hangs out in the sewers because that's so much safer. At one point you put on a nazi uniform, board a spaceship to the moon, go through moon security, and then take your uniform off and proceed to shoot up the entire moonbase, because disguises only work in cutscenes. The entire game is full of parts like this where the story advances you to another action sequence while basically handwaving that the world is supposed to be under Nazi control and you're their most wanted.
My biggest beef with this game is how weirdly racist it is though. The game starts off with a mystery: Where did the Nazis get such superior technology? Aliens? Time Travel? Unethical Research? Dark Magic? Nope. Actually in this universe Jews are 500 years more advanced than everyone else, and the Nazis killed them and stole their stuff. I'm not even making this up, somehow in a game that should be all about how the notion of racial superiority is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t the central plot point becomes that Jews are smarter than everyone else. They also give you a mentally handicapped companion who happens to be a giant with the strength of ten men. Whoever wrote this seems to think that the Nazis are shown to be wrong wrong if someone else is superior and because they overlooked the usefulness of a mentally handicapped person. What they should try to tell us that nobody is superior, and that people have value even if they don't have hidden super strength. So in the dumbest possible way someone managed to make a whole game about killing Nazis and still ends up spreading their values around.

Remember that sense of wonder and amazement you felt the very first time you played Portal? Take that feeling and expand upon it like you've never imagined before. Talos Principle is a stellar puzzle game, but an even better philosophical adventure that makes you question almost everything you ever believed you knew about what it means to be a person.
The story follows the general theme of the garden of eden as you work your way through puzzles for the sake of your creator, trying to uphold (or not) your one covenant with Him, all while having your inner most held beliefs picked apart by a mysterious and dangerously intelligent being. I would love to say more, but anything else would be spoilers. What I can say is the way it is presented, and the finer details of the backstory in the game terrified and saddened me in a more genuine and primal way than I had ever felt before from a game.
The game has multiple endings and more secrets than I could ever hope to find and the puzzles range from easy to mind breakingly hard, but interestingly never once have they felt impossible. Sure, you might want to step away from one puzzle you're stuck on to work on another, but once you've come back, the answer almost always seems to materialize right as you need it. There is a very smartly done in-game hint system, though you get very limited uses of it, so really hang on to them until you absolutely cannot figure out what to do next. Even then, the hints may seem simplistic in a 'well I already knew that' sort of way, but often if you think on how the hint is worded, often the hint goes deeper than it may suggest on the surface. The other half of the game is the philosophical adventure, often carried out through something akin to a text adventure "tell tale games" style dialog tree. This part of the game is brilliant in how deep it forces you to look into yourself...or not. It all really depends on your own choices. I cannot stress this enough: Ive never been more convinced I was talking to a real thinking entity in a game before.
All in all, Talos Principle is a smart game that knows its smart, but isnt pretentious about it and respects your own intelligence. I would highly suggest this game to anyone. You'll come out a changed human.

To get this immediately out of the way: I like this game, I really do.
However, I'm not good at explaining what is good about things, so I apologize in advance if this review comes off as mostly just complaining. Okay, so...
The Talos Principle is, for all intents and purposes, a Portal-like puzzle game, and it certainly plays the part in terms of gameplay. The controls are intuitive and getting your way around the puzzles is pretty intuitive as well... for the most part. The puzzles are bound to keep you occupied for long hours, and many of them will provide a sense of accomplishment if you manage to complete them on your own. The game's graphics are absolutely stunning - the textures almost never get blurry or pixelated even from up close, which is something I've never seen before in a video game. As for the story... I will get to that in a moment.
Now, I must point out of a few problems. First off, there are two major flaws in the puzzle design.
The first flaw is that on numerous occasions, the game fails to explain certain mechanics to you and inform you that you are capable of doing this or that. This results in you wandering aimlessly around the level until you either stumble upon the solution via sheer dumb luck, or look it up on YouTube in defeat, only to exclaim "HOW WAS I SUPPOSED TO KNOW THAT?!?" when you see where the problem was.
The second flaw is that there is a number of situations where the level layout and/or the placement of vital objects is so unintuitive that you can end up trying to figure out the solution to no avail, and when you inevitably look it up on YouTube, you will realize that the entire problem was that you missed an object hidden behind a wall, and including this object into the equation makes the solution instantly clear.
Another problem I have with the game is the very beginning, right after you jump off the pedestal: it's simply way too threatening and unwelcoming, at least compared to how the Public Test (i.e. the demo) starts out. In the Public Test, the are no enemies at all and the overall atmosphere is much more peaceful and laid-back, allowing you to calmly approach the problems set before you and familiarise yourself with the puzzle elements in a perfectly safe environment (well, except for walking into the water). The actual game, on the other hand, immediately throws at you the floating bombs AND the turrets, creating a much more hostile atmosphere that might scare away some of the newcomers. My recommendation is, if you are planning to get the game, then BEFORE you do it, absolutely make sure to play the Public Test first. It will give you a much better training environment and prepare you for the challenges from the actual game.
Now, regarding the story. The game is pretty much built around the basic question: "What makes you a person?", and everything related to it, in particular the question of whether a robot can be a person. I must say, I admire the developers for trying to go with such a serious subject matter for the narrative, and it definitely makes you think. However, while all the philosophical divagations seemed mildly interesting at first, they slowly started getting on my nerves as the time went on, to the point where about halfway through the game I was so fed up with it all that I decided to put the game aside for about a month.
The fact that you aren't going to get the full picture and what this is all building up to before the very end of the game only makes matters worse, as I started thinking that the puzzles and the narrative are completely detached from one another, and the game would do perfectly fine without the latter. It turns out that the narrative really IS vital to the experience, but you won't know that before you get to the aforementioned very end. My recommendation is, have faith in the developers, but don't bother yourself with the random texts on the computers or with the floating radio recordings, unless you really want to. They will just make you feel as if the developers were trying to shove all that philosophy down your throat.
In the end, The Talos Principle is a pretty surprising game in various aspects (positively, that is) and definitely worth checking out. I just wish it had more of the Valve polish when it comes to puzzle design, as well as some other things. I'd say it's somewhere around 8/10.

Wolfenstein: The New Order quickly became my favorite game of 2014. The game is able to perfectly encapsulate and streamline everything that was fun about the previous games in the series.
The gameplay is perhaps the strongest element as it is extremely well designed and goes back to an older style of action/FPS where any level can have multiple paths and approaches; essentially creating small linear playgrounds. The game achieves an amazing aesthetic as both the audio and the visual design work perfectly to complement and convey the narrative and setting. I found that the games amazing visual design with a massive amount of care, detail and thought allowed for such a rich and interesting atmosphere to be created within the game. Events in the story are often able to tug at my emotions, either making me sad or making me incredibly pumped. It should also be mentioned that the graphics are amazing and 100% on par with todays modern standards.
This is a game that will both appeal to every last bit of nostalgia in you while also keeping you guessing every step of the way with an interesting premise. In my opinion it is a 10/10 and undoubtably worthy of being in ones game library.

This game is filled with so much nostalgia, I can hardly contain myself. If you enjoyed playing Age of Empires II in the late 90's and early thousands, this is a wonderful reboot. The developers have done an excellent job of updating systems, so that newer computers can run the game without a problem.
However, even though it was rather unpopular with most people, the game is dated, compared to Age of Empires III. Even though there are little bonuses and special techs available to each civilization, many of the civilizations feel the same. Giving trebuchets to Aztecs and Franks alike makes very little sense, when the developers could revamp all of the Central and South American cultures to have Arrow Knights and Skull Knights from AOE III perform the main functions of trebuchets, scorpions and mangonels/onagers.
In order for the game to feel updated and fresh, perhaps the developers should consider adding some extra, unique unit upgrades, which they played with in some of the newer civilizations, like the Indians, who have Imperial Camel upgrades. To help fix the blandness of many of the civilizations, the Britons could upgrade Scout Cavalry to Hobilars, which are somewhat stronger than Light Cavalry, but not nearly the same as Hussars. The Teutons could upgrade Champions to Doppelsöldners or Landsknecht Mercenaries. This would add new components to the game, and make it feel special once more.
With all of that in mind, if you love RTS, and you enjoy gaming classics, this is for you. However, if you don't want the new civilizations, nor do you care about gaming online, everything feels mostly the same as the original gaming discs.
I foresee a lot of improvements as the game develops, and the new content does add a lot to the game.

FUN MIXED WITH DISSAPOINTMENT
--------------------------------------
While being very much fun at times, this game overall fails to meet the high expectations set by the overwhelmingly positive reviews out there. Technical issues, utterly boring stealth sections, poor decisions regarding gameplay and setting and bland story are all factors that spoil the nazi-killing fun. While being refreshing for the FPS genre, Wolfenstein: The New Order is a missed chance to bring the old-skool formula back to its glorydays.
1. Technical issues
The choice for the Id engine is an odd decision. While it admittingly delivers some damn nice background images and gives the game an artsy feel, it has some serious downsides. One is the gi-normous file size, with a whopping 44GB. Another is the texture pop-in, that seems to be typical for some implementations of this engine. Every time you make a turn, the texturing to the side of your FOV lags slightly. Especially in tight places with a lot of objects, this can really be annoying. While not hampering gameplay, it makes the game look kind of cheap. Another problem that spawns from this are the long loading times. Okay, back in the days we spend long times looking at loading screens. In this day and age, it kind of feels awkward. Oh, and the textures... Up close, they are simply a disaster. Black objects are smeared with the green ugliness typical for low-res texturing, and overall the objects look damn terrible.
2. Setting and storytelling
First of, let me explain that I simply love the alternate history-theme. Nazis having won the war and ruling the planet, is damn terifying, and is very well played out in this game. Bits of newspaper articles lying around give a nice insight in how our favourite baddies did the trick, and the Germanic interpretations of popular 60's rock songs were down right hilarious (Die Käfer playing 'blaue U-boot'? I tip my hat to that one!).
But still, it doesn't feel right. The atmosphere is waaaaaaay too serious. The game keeps setting the focus on the hardships and the terror of the war, the powerlessness of the conquered, and so on. This would be a great angle for a realistic WWII shooter, but here it is so out of place!  I mean, WTF? A dude dual-wielding auto-shotguns against giant nazi mechs, Panzerhunde, and even frickin' SPACE NAZIS! How can you possibly ask anyone to take this seriously? I get it, the makers tried to give the story and the characters some depth, and they succeed. A little bit. There's a love interest, and B. J. Blascowizc has these internal monologues giving some insight in his feelings, and he has these huge blue puppy-eyes in the cutscenes. But screw that. You can't present him as an unstoppable, primitive nazi-killing machine, and still trying to make him a real person. You just can't reconcile these things, and it's plain obvious throughout the entire game. What this game could seriously have used is some more tongue-in-cheek humor, more Tarantino-like moments (the scene in the train is an instant classic, though!), more bravado, more over-the-top character presentation. It just feels like the makers couln't reach a decision on what it actually was that they were trying to be: a B-movie style game, or an A-movie story. They tried to be both, but that simply doesn't work. The right choice would've been to be a kick♥♥♥♥♥B-movie.
Related to this, I can tell you that the story is laughably poor after the first few hours. Some awesome antagonists are presented, but then disappear for nearly the entirety of the game! This takes away any drive to go out and kill these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. As for the rest, the story is incredibly straightforward, and features some initially interesting characters. Lack of real interaction with them, or overall lack in storytelling, renders you not giving a flying s*** about them in the end. And that end is incredibly derpy. Something with atomic bomb and stuff. Whatever.
Finally, there's the setting in which the gameplay takes place. While level-design is quite good, it just lacks the right atmosphere in my opinion. The levels are often way to lighted, too familiar looking. It lacks some real evilness. Entire cities made of concrete? A Gibraltar bridge? An exposition? Meh. Not really frightening. I had hoped for more creepy settings, like in the previous titles in this franchise. Even the bloody concentration camp bades in beautiful summer light, which makes it look more like a holiday camp. Come on, the reality of these things was dreadful and horrific. At least try to portrey this dread and horror in the atmosphere and setting!
3. Gameplay
Shooting Nazis in the face! Blowing their limbs clean off! What could possibly be more awesome then that? So how can gameplay even be an issue, you might ask? Let me explain.
First of all, there is just not enough of it. There are long cutscenes with bad story, breaking down the pace. In actual gameplay, there are inexplicably long intervals of exactly jack s*** happening. Exploring sewers full of nothing? Empty corridors? A moon walk in near-zero G WITHOUT Nazis to shoot? What the hell? Not my bloody idea of fun. This title is portrayed as a game that is purely about killing nazis, but it fails to deliver on exactly this aspect!
The sections in which you do get to f*** s*** up are nice, though. Gunplay feels solid, and it's awesome to completely wreck a place. But you spend the entirety of the games shooting the same exotic toys, like: a pistol! An assault rifle! A sniper rifle! A shotgun! Woopty-f***ing-doo. Boring. Ammo is scarce and enemies drop almost nothing of it. Boring. The game actively pushes you to use cover and lean to shoot. Boring. I think we all expected doing stand-up gunfights with long triggertimes, not cover-to-cover fighting, picking your shoots carefully? A shame that MachineGames decided to use the modern appraoch to the FPS genre, instead of using the perks of the old-school titles. Nope, the old-school aspect seems to be largely restricted to health-kits, armor pickups, and boss-fights. A pitty.
The biggest anoyance for last. The stealth mechanics.
Okay, great to give your players a bit of freedom in playstyle, but this? The game requires you to a) be stealthy or b) face impossible odds with hardly any ammo to come out alive. So there goes your freedom. Or it just forces this style on you. I like stealth-gameplay a lot, but here it is tottaly out of place, and terribly implemented. Stealth means just following the obvious paths through -guess what!- airvents. However, you can simply walk over to your enemy crouched. He will never hear you, he is always placed neatly with his back to you, and is incredibly stupid. "Hmmm, somebody lurking over there? Let's totally not check that out". "Hmmm, I think there's a guy over there pointing a gun right at my face, but he's crouched, so I can't see him!". Yes, the crouch button is simply a "now you see me, now you don't" button. Sticking to the shadows? No need. Walking slowly? No need. No need whatsoever to have any skill at this. And the amount of these stealth-sections are enormous. So we have and "stealth" sections, and long cutscenes, and parts with nothin happening? Turns three quarters of this game into a massive snoozefest, for no reason whatsoever.
4. conclusion
Yes, shooting nazis robots and evil technology IS fun. But this fun is limitted dramatically by the heavy amount of flaws that this game has. I am glad that people are willing to return the old-school genre to its former glory, but never mind what all the reviewers out there said, this Wolfenstein installment fails to do so properly. It is my sincerest hope, however, that the MachineGames will have a second try, because this franchise deserves its place in gaming history AND future! But the current effort is simply lacking.
If you want a good modern old-school game, buy Shadow Warrior.

To get this immediately out of the way: I like this game, I really do.
However, I'm not good at explaining what is good about things, so I apologize in advance if this review comes off as mostly just complaining. Okay, so...
The Talos Principle is, for all intents and purposes, a Portal-like puzzle game, and it certainly plays the part in terms of gameplay. The controls are intuitive and getting your way around the puzzles is pretty intuitive as well... for the most part. The puzzles are bound to keep you occupied for long hours, and many of them will provide a sense of accomplishment if you manage to complete them on your own. The game's graphics are absolutely stunning - the textures almost never get blurry or pixelated even from up close, which is something I've never seen before in a video game. As for the story... I will get to that in a moment.
Now, I must point out of a few problems. First off, there are two major flaws in the puzzle design.
The first flaw is that on numerous occasions, the game fails to explain certain mechanics to you and inform you that you are capable of doing this or that. This results in you wandering aimlessly around the level until you either stumble upon the solution via sheer dumb luck, or look it up on YouTube in defeat, only to exclaim "HOW WAS I SUPPOSED TO KNOW THAT?!?" when you see where the problem was.
The second flaw is that there is a number of situations where the level layout and/or the placement of vital objects is so unintuitive that you can end up trying to figure out the solution to no avail, and when you inevitably look it up on YouTube, you will realize that the entire problem was that you missed an object hidden behind a wall, and including this object into the equation makes the solution instantly clear.
Another problem I have with the game is the very beginning, right after you jump off the pedestal: it's simply way too threatening and unwelcoming, at least compared to how the Public Test (i.e. the demo) starts out. In the Public Test, the are no enemies at all and the overall atmosphere is much more peaceful and laid-back, allowing you to calmly approach the problems set before you and familiarise yourself with the puzzle elements in a perfectly safe environment (well, except for walking into the water). The actual game, on the other hand, immediately throws at you the floating bombs AND the turrets, creating a much more hostile atmosphere that might scare away some of the newcomers. My recommendation is, if you are planning to get the game, then BEFORE you do it, absolutely make sure to play the Public Test first. It will give you a much better training environment and prepare you for the challenges from the actual game.
Now, regarding the story. The game is pretty much built around the basic question: "What makes you a person?", and everything related to it, in particular the question of whether a robot can be a person. I must say, I admire the developers for trying to go with such a serious subject matter for the narrative, and it definitely makes you think. However, while all the philosophical divagations seemed mildly interesting at first, they slowly started getting on my nerves as the time went on, to the point where about halfway through the game I was so fed up with it all that I decided to put the game aside for about a month.
The fact that you aren't going to get the full picture and what this is all building up to before the very end of the game only makes matters worse, as I started thinking that the puzzles and the narrative are completely detached from one another, and the game would do perfectly fine without the latter. It turns out that the narrative really IS vital to the experience, but you won't know that before you get to the aforementioned very end. My recommendation is, have faith in the developers, but don't bother yourself with the random texts on the computers or with the floating radio recordings, unless you really want to. They will just make you feel as if the developers were trying to shove all that philosophy down your throat.
In the end, The Talos Principle is a pretty surprising game in various aspects (positively, that is) and definitely worth checking out. I just wish it had more of the Valve polish when it comes to puzzle design, as well as some other things. I'd say it's somewhere around 8/10.

If your goal is to blast through this game, then it might not be for you. The Talos Principle is best appreciated by taking your time, exploring each small world and taking the complexity of the puzzles. Others have said that the connection between the puzzles and the philosophy in this game is lacking. That may be the case, but as far as integrating philosophy into a video game, this is one of the better attempts. Although there is no driving narrative, there is a set of questions that arise throughout the game about who you are, who is Elohim, and why you are doing what you are doing. You gradually piece things together by reading files on computer monitors, which often integrate well chosen passages and insights from mostly ancient philosophical sources.
The puzzles start off simple and then get much more difficult. Even the more difficult puzzles, however, can be beaten with enough persistence. Therefore it maintains a good balance that puzzle games require: a challenge without losing its player's interest. If like me you have been looking for a game that calls for you to slow down, think, and appreciate the complexity of a created world, then pick up the Talos Principle.

This game might be early access, but it is the BEST tactical shooter I've ever played.
Take all of the best aspects and pacing from games like Insurgency and Battlefield and combine them with a sense of scale like the ARMA series - that is Squad. Hardcore and unforgiving firefights, with team ability to build forward rally points and bases -- reinforce existing compounds with sandbags and ammo caches. Medics that can pick up and heal downed and wounded players -- support units bring machinegun suppression and grenade and rocket launchers to dominate dug in enemies.
I wasn't expecting this game to be this good, especially not in such an early stage of development. With only room to grow and improve, and an active player base - Squad is the game to keep an eye on.

Philosophical Puzzler
tl:dr version:
Pros:
+ Lots of puzzles
+ Pretty landscapes
+ Some devilishly tricky and hidden puzzles
+ Interesting philosophical undertones
+ Multiple endings
Cons:
- No new puzzle mechanics, all recycled from previous puzzle games
- Philosophical undertones are fairly disjointed
The Talos Principle is a first person (you can switch to third person) puzzle game with a philosophical undertone loosely told throughout the game.  The comparison everyone makes is to Portal, and that is a fair comparison and probably the closest comparison to a well known game that could be made.  While the game lacks any new groundbreaking mechanic, like Portal had, and it uses mechanics recycled from other puzzle games, it combines these mechanics well to form some really tricky puzzles that sometimes challenge you to think outside the obvious mechanics.  Especially the star puzzles, those often make you think outside the box, or even outside the puzzle.  There were some puzzled I smashed my head against for well over an hour and my brain couldn't make the leap and get out of the rut, but once I did and had that breakthrough, it was extremely satisfying to see the solution form in my hear.  That aha moment is a great feeling.
The philosophical part of the game is presented through text documents and audio logs found throughout.  It's pretty disjointed and up to you to form your own conclusions about what happened before and what is happening now.  While I appreciate the game allowing me to piece things together myself, I feel the philosophy could have been tied together better, both to other parts of the philosophy and to the puzzle elements.  As it stands, the puzzles and the philosophy are pretty much 2 separate entities that happen to exist in the same game.
Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game, even if I got stuck and frustrated many times on some of the trickier puzzles.  The feeling of joy of overcoming those puzzles made it worth the frustration, though.  If you enjoy puzzle games, I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to you.  It;s the best puzzle game of 2014, in my opinion.

*Sigh*  I wish I didn't have to do this.   They have made so many improvements since I first begun, a lot of which I actually recommended precisely, (SMG's having travel was awesome).
It really is a lot of fun to play. I like most of the 'gameplay' changes they have done, I think they've been pretty great. Battle is my favorite mode.   And I have found myself putting small amounts of money into it on occasion to get premium.
But there are some things which absolutely ruined the entire concept for me.. and honestly they can be fixed fairly simply.
#1)  Currency. At the moment called 'Robits' I think. You used to be able to receive a fair amount of it from completing a match. With this money you could go ahead and purchase anything you want to.  Every match felt very rewarding and you got what felt like a fair compensation for your efforts and participation.  This has been changed.  Now you receive, first of all, the worth is far less.. but you receive a completely random slew of parts.  The only way to even make this currency is to jot down or remember what parts you got in particular, and go to the store and then exchange them for robits.  Time-consuming and inconvenient.  The *only* benefit to the current system is that you have the chance to receive rare, exotic 'bling' items that you couldn't before.   But the fact that you are given paltry, sorry little rewards for a match now is extremely disappointing. The fact that you have zero choice over what parts you get initially is very disappointing.  The fact that exchanging the parts for money literally requires remembering which random pieces you got or writing it down, is thoroughly disappointing.
#2) Daily win Bonus:  WHY did they take this out?  I loved these.. these are why I played the game.. I play many games and don't always have time for Robocraft. But getting a win in with each robot, each day, and being rewarded for that, felt great!  Felt very nice to accomplish. Please bring that back. Now you only get a paltry bronze loot crate for a log-in per-day.  Blegh.  So it encourages people to log in, not to play.
